# ALCHEMY

# BY ANDREAS LIBAVIUS,

# REVISED,

# AMENDED, AND

# ENLARGED, AS WELL AS

# WITH DOCTRINES <note>original: "dogmatibus"; referring to the established principles, teachings, or theoretical frameworks of the chemical art</note> &...

---

## Andreas Libavius, Giovanni Battista Coccini

<note>Andreas Libavius (c. 1550–1616) was a German physician and teacher who is often credited with writing the first systematic textbook of chemistry. While he believed in the possibility of transmuting metals, his work focused heavily on clear instructions and the preparation of medicines. Giovanni Battista Coccini is included here as a bibliographic reference in the modern archival record.</note>

<summary>This is the title page for Andreas Libavius's "Alchymia," a foundational text that transitioned alchemy into a structured academic discipline. This specific edition is noted as being "revised and enlarged," reflecting the rapid growth of chemical knowledge in the early 17th century.</summary>

<keywords>Andreas Libavius, alchemy, history of chemistry, scientific textbooks, 17th-century science, chemical doctrines</keywords>

# OF THE STONE

| *Body:* | *Soul:* | *Spirit:* |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **IN** the first operation, copper <note>original: "æs"; also refers to bronze or the base metal</note> or **Venus** <note>In alchemy, Venus is the symbol and name for copper</note> emerges from the sea; which is also called Earth. Truly, that sea is the mercurial liquor, which is the spirit of mercury <note>mercurial spirit refers to the volatile essence of quicksilver</note> highly purified through a sevenfold sublimation from vitriol and salt, as well as by other means, and freed from terrestrial and watery excess; it is the only thing that can dissolve gold mixed into it. It must, however, be reduced through a most ingenious sublimation by means of tartar <note>original: "tartarum"; potassium bitartrate used as a flux or purifying agent</note>, so that absolutely nothing of the salt or any mineral remains with it, but that it exists as the purest Mercury: in which there is proportional sulfur: and which some use alone from the beginning, while others add prepared gold or silver, so that in this way the **old man** <note>original: "senex"; an alchemical allegory for the heavy, solid matter or the "king" (gold) being dissolved in a bath</note> may sit in the bath. It is the Element of Earth. | **VIRGIN’S MILK** <note>original: "LAC Virginis"; a name for various white chemical secretions or solvents, often a lead acetate solution or mercury sublimate</note>; living water, which is again instilled drop by drop into the separated body, and is coagulated with it by diligent fire. It is the dew distilling from heaven upon the dead body. It is the **Azoth** <note>The universal solvent or the essential mercurial spirit</note> washing the black **Laton** <note>original: "Latonem nigrum"; the impure metal or "lead" stage of the work before it is whitened</note>. It is the Element of Water. Note that this water is sometimes composed from the start from the Mercury of the reduced body and raw mineral, but purified. | **P**urified quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum viuum"</note> by which the first coagulated matter is dissolved in the second operation: And then the true **raven’s head** <note>original: "caput corui"; the *nigredo* or black stage signifying putrefaction and the beginning of transformation</note> emerges through solution or putrefaction. But by coagulation, it becomes white quicklime <note>original: "calx viua alba"</note> and the elixir, which is also called oil, arsenic, and likewise air, etc. The **Fire** is the red lime after fermentation in the third operation: in which there is also a repetition and succession—indeed a transmutation—of all the Elements in order. |

<term>On the Stone of the Philosophers</term> (The legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and acting as a universal medicine), <term>Alchemy</term> (The ancient art of transformation), <term>Great Work</term> (The total process of creating the Stone), <term>Phoenix</term> (A bird symbolizing the final stage of rebirth and the "Red" Stone), <term>Nigredo</term> (The "Blackness" or first stage of decay), <term>Albedo</term> (The "Whiteness" or stage of purification), <term>Rubedo</term> (The "Redness" or final stage of completion), <term>Sun and Moon</term> (Symbols for the male/Sulfur and female/Mercury principles), <term>Alchemical Marriage</term> (The union of these opposing principles to create the Stone).

<note>The following describes a complex alchemical illustration: A large central sphere represents the world of the "Great Work." It is supported by figures and contains symbols of the three major stages: a crow for the "Blackening" (Nigredo), a white bird for the "Whitening" (Albedo), and a phoenix for the final "Reddening" (Rubedo). Above, a King and Queen represent the union of Solar and Lunar qualities, while a multi-headed dragon at the base represents the raw, chaotic matter that must be conquered and transformed.</note>

It emphasizes that the creation of the Philosophers' Stone requires both human "labor and industry" and the "blessing of God."</summary>

# EXPLANATION
## OF THE FIGURE.

**Henricus Kuhdorferus provided the complete picture in the Year of our Savior's birth 1421, and added it to an ancient manuscript written in the year 1028.** <note>Henricus Kuhdorfer is a legendary figure often associated with early alchemical manuscripts. The date 1028 is likely an attempt by the author to claim ancient authority for the work.</note> However, since the art of painting is not our specialty, we have at least provided the ground plan <note>original: "ichnographiam"; a schematic or layout of the image</note>, so that anyone may decorate it as they see fit. The empty spaces are to be filled with these things:

**A.** A fire of small flames is placed beneath the glass, made from coals.

**B.** This region is occupied by a winged dragon with a long tail, crowned like the Basilisks they imagine. It lies on its back with its feet turned upward, and bites its turned-back tail with its mouth, so that it is the one they say devours its own tail <note>The Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of the cyclical nature of the alchemical process—dissolving and solidifying.</note>. It is horrible in appearance, green in color, with a gray or ash-colored tail.

**C.** An eagle must be painted here with yellow feet and beak, wings spread, and varied feathers in the wings, body, and tail, such that some are white, others black, green, yellow, or crimson, as if it signaled a Peacock’s tail or a Rainbow. <note>The "Peacock's Tail" refers to a specific stage in alchemy where many colors appear in the flask before the final goal is reached.</note>

**D.** A black crow should be painted in the field.

**E.** A red rose in a silver field.

**F.** A white rose in a red field.

**G.** A maiden’s head in silver in place of the Moon.

**H.** A lion’s head in gold for the Sun.

**I.** One red rose in a silver field.

**K.** A saffron-yellow candle along the length of the tract.

**L.** Three golden stars in a silver field.

**M.** Six blue stars in a golden field.

**N.** A white or silver candle (at other times also saffron-colored).

**O.** Three white roses in a red field.

**P.** A King carrying red or blood-colored lilies in his hand.

**Q.** The wife or mother of the king carrying white or silver lilies.

**R.** A silver candle.

**S.** A red candle.

**T.** A plate of a Golden Crown.

**V.** Candles in a globe. <note>original: "pomo"; literally an apple or fruit, but in alchemical diagrams, it often refers to an orb or a decorative sphere.</note>

**X.** Golden and silver lilies.

What each of these signifies is not easy to say, as the applications are diverse, and there is even diversity in the work itself. By the fire placed beneath the glass, you may understand elemental fire; by the yellow, red, and white candles within the glass, the hidden fire of the Sun and Moon. By the candles in the crown, another fire, which they call "of three threads," or even the heat of the Sun. The Dragon is the <term>Philosophical Mercury</term> (The specialized, "living" form of mercury used by alchemists), which elsewhere signifies volatility and dissolution; by the eating of its tail, it signifies coagulation and fixity. The black crow denotes the blackness of <term>putrefaction</term> (The stage of breaking down and rotting matter to purify its essence); the varied eagle denotes the various colors appearing in <term>fermentation</term> (The stage where the Stone's power is increased). The different roses in different fields indicate the different nature of the two luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon, or Gold and Silver.</note>. For the red stone is made from both red and white, as is the white stone. So it is with the King and Queen, the Lion and the Maiden, which also signify male and female matter. The six blue stars are believed to designate as many parts of Mercury; the three red or golden ones designate as many portions of the body to be dissolved; at other times nine Eagles and parts of the liquid. For since there are twelve in all, three are understood by the three roses which are joined at the beginning to the one red rose.

*   **V**, **X**, **Y**, **Z** (At the top of the vessel's rim)
*   **I**, **K**, **L**, **R**, **S**, **M**, **N**, **O**, **T** (Along the upper interior arc)
*   **P**, **Q** (Designating the King and Queen figures) <note>In alchemy, the King and Queen represent the two primary principles—often Sulfur and Mercury, or Spirit and Soul—whose union or "marriage" is required to create the Stone.</note>
*   **G**, **H** (Within circular medallions on the left and right)
*   **F**, **E** (At the mid-lower sides)

# EXPLANATION OF THE MARKED
## PLACES.

A. A prop or foundation like the earth.

B. Two giants or Atlantes who, sitting on the foundation to the right and left, support the globe on their shoulders and brace it with their hands. <note>In alchemical art, Atlantes often symbolize the physical strength or the stable "fixed" forces required to contain the volatile chemical reactions within the vessel.</note>

C. A four-headed dragon, which breathes upward toward the globe from its four throats the 4 degrees of fire: from the 1st mouth issues something like air; from the 2nd, thin smoke; from the 3rd, smoke with fire; from the 4th, pure fire. <note>The four degrees of fire refer to the traditional alchemical heating stages, ranging from a gentle "lukewarm" heat to a fierce, direct flame.</note>

D. Mercury with a silver chain, to which two beasts lying at the sides are bound.

E. **Green Lion.** <note>original: "Leo viridis." The Green Lion is a famous alchemical metaphor, usually representing a powerful mineral acid or a raw, "unripe" form of mercury capable of dissolving gold.</note>

F. A crowned dragon with one head: And these two beasts signify the same thing, namely the mercurial liquor, which is the first matter <term>Materia Prima: the primitive, unformed base substance required to begin the alchemical process</term> of the stone.

G. A three-headed silver eagle, which, with lowered heads, indeed seems to wither in two; from the third it pours out white water or mercurial liquor into the place of the sea, which is marked H.

I. An image of the wind emitting spirit downward into the sea below.

K. An image of the Red Lion from whose chest red blood flows into the sea below etc. which is to be colored as if mixed from silver and gold, or white and red. The image is adapted to the body, soul, and spirit according to those who also require three at the beginning: or to the blood of the Leo [the Red Lion] and the gluten of the eagle. For those who take three have a double mercury. Those who take two have only one, which is reduced from crystal or the immature metal of the Philosophers. <note>The "Red Lion" typically represents the final, "ripe" stage of the matter, often associated with sulfur or gold.</note>

L. A stretch of black water, as in chaos; and it marks the putrefaction <term>Putrefactio: the stage of decay or "blackening" (Nigredo) where the old form of the matter is destroyed to allow for a new birth</term> from which emerges a certain mountain, black at the base and white at the peak, so that from the peak a silver spring flows down. For it is the figure of the first solution and coagulation: And again of the second solution.

M. This mountain.

N. N. Black heads of ravens looking out from the sea. <note>The raven is a standard symbol for the Nigredo or "blackening" stage, signifying death and the separation of the soul from the body.</note>

O. Silver rain falling from the clouds onto the mountain peak; by which both the nutrition and washing of Latona <note>original: "Latonis." Latona, or Leto, refers to the darkened, "impure" matter that must be washed white.</note> by Azorh <note>Azorh, or Azoth, is a name for the "universal solvent" or the essential mercurial spirit.</note> is designated, as well as the second solution by which the element of air is drawn out of the earth and water (Earth is represented by the mountain: water is that first liquor of the sea.)

P. The form of clouds, from which comes dew or rain and the nourishing liquor.

Q. A likeness of the heavens in which lies a dragon on its back devouring its tail, and it is the image of the second coagulation. <note>The dragon biting its own tail is the Ouroboros, representing the circular nature of the alchemical process and the unity of the beginning and the end.</note>

R. R. An Ethiopian man and woman supporting the two upper lateral globes. They sit upon the larger globe; and in passing <note>likely a typo: the original "ebiter" should be "obiter" (in passing/incidentally)</note> they mark the blackness of the second work in the second putrefaction.

S. Here is designated the pure silver sea, which signifies the mercurial liquor, by which means the tinctures are joined.

T. Paint here a swan swimming in the sea and vomiting a milky liquor from its mouth. This swan is the White Elixir, white lime, the arsenic of the Philosophers, common to both ferments. It ought to support the upper globe with its back and wings.

V. **Eclipse of the Sun.**

X. X. The Sun immersing itself in the sea—that is, in the mercurial water into which the Elixir must also have passed. From this comes the true Eclipse of the Sun, on whose sides a rainbow <note>original: "Iris"</note> must be painted on both sides, to designate the Peacock’s Tail <term>Cauda Pavonis: a stage where the matter in the vessel displays a multitude of iridescent colors, like a peacock's feathers, signaling the transition from blackness to whiteness</term>, which then appears in the coagulation.

Y. Y. Y. Eclipse of the Moon likewise having a rainbow at the sides, and near the bottom part the sea into which the Moon is submerged; it is the figure of the white fermentation, and both seas should be somewhat dark.

Z. The Moon gliding into the sea.

a. A silver queen adorned with a crown, stroking a white or silver eagle standing by.

b. A purple-clad king with a golden crown having a golden Lion standing by. In one hand the Queen carries white lilies, the King red. <note>This "Chymical Wedding" of the King and Queen represents the union of opposites (Sulfur and Mercury, or Masculine and Feminine) to produce the Stone.</note>

c. A Phoenix standing on a globe and burning itself; from the ashes fly forth many silver and gold birds. For it is a figure <note>the original Latin text "figuam" is a scribal error for "figuram"</note> of augmentation and multiplication. <note>The Phoenix represents the final stage of the work, where the Stone is multiplied in power and quantity through fire.</note>

It maps out the transformation of matter from its "black" state of putrefaction to its "white" and "red" states of perfection.</summary>

<note>The following is a key to an alchemical emblem depicted above it.</note>

A. **The double Lion** of one head, by which is signified the <term>first matter: the raw, unrefined starting material of the alchemical process</term> of the Stone from a double lion-like mercury; that head vomits green water, which is the "mercury of the philosophers" <note>original: "mercurius philosophorum"</note> born from two sources. It is called elsewhere the **Green Lion**. <note>The Green Lion often represents a strong mineral acid (like vitriol) or the raw energy of nature that "devours" metals to purify them.</note>

B. **Lions** on both sides, five in number as if on the steps of Solomon <note>Refers to the six steps of the Throne of Solomon described in the Bible, here used to represent stages of purification</note>, to represent the five metals of one lion-like root and of cooked mercury; these can pass over into the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note>: the lions on the right side strive toward the Sun; those on the left toward the Moon, and this is observed in the work through the success and transformation of their powers. Not without mystery does the highest Lion look back at the lower ones, etc.

C. The effigy of the **Sun**. <note>Symbolizing Gold or the masculine principle, Sulfur.</note>

D. The image of the **Moon**. <note>Symbolizing Silver or the feminine principle, Mercury.</note>

E. The **Bath** in which the King sits with the Queen. It is also the figure of the marriage bed for generating like from like: likewise, it is the garden in which the tree grows with the apples of the Hesperides. <note>In mythology, these were golden apples; in alchemy, they represent the successful creation of gold.</note>

F. The **King** with a crown and lily-tipped sceptre, as if addressing the Queen. <note>This "Royal Wedding" or Conjunction represents the union of opposites required to create the Stone.</note>

G. In the middle, the tree produces golden apples, while golden stars surround the crowns, to designate multiplication and increase, or even the fruit of <term>projection: the final act of alchemy where a small amount of the Stone is thrown upon base metal to transform it into gold</term>.

->On the Philosopher’s Stone.<-

# A COMMENTARY ON THE PHILOSOPHER’S
## STONE.

**I** have no fear—now that so many others have released works concerning the Philosopher’s Stone into the public eye, filling the world and the minds of those eager to learn with books rather than with the reality of the matter—that I too should appear in the light. For I know how obscure the commentaries of others are on this subject; they themselves know how much they have written that deviates from their own true meaning, dragging the reader far away into something else entirely. I shall publish my own feelings—things which I have partly seen, and partly tracked down and investigated from the writings of the philosophers and with nature as my guide—without contempt or envy toward anyone, and without the use of verbal riddles <note>original: "ænigmata"</note>. Nor am I unaware of how many difficulties I expose myself to, or how many weapons I face from those who bite and criticize, or from those who oppose my opinion. But I do not care for their bites, nor do I force anyone to agree with me. My mind is set either on openly attaining what truth has led me to teach, or on providing others with the handle to explain it. If anyone rages against me with words alone, without demonstrating the matter itself more clearly, he shall be doing nothing different from the <term>sophists: those who use clever but false arguments</term>, and he will not be worthy of exchanging a single word.

<margin>No protection or support is granted to the Paracelsians in this writing.</margin>
Furthermore, I protest before everyone that I in no way wish to entice men with flatteries, nor knowingly plunge them into the loss of their goods, much less deceive them of my own accord. Just as I believe I have philosophized generously regarding other matters without the vice of <term>rashness</term> <note>original: "ἀπονοίας" (aponoias)</note>, I intend to do the same regarding this not-unpleasant part of philosophy. Nor is there any reason for the Paracelsian counterfeiters to seek any patronage for themselves in my philosophical views. I would not even turn my hand for their sake, as they are unworthy of any noble conversation in letters. If anyone allows himself to be deceived by them on this account, let him be at risk by his own fault. Let no one think that I have drawn my knowledge of this matter from the foul pools of Paracelsus, even though it is sometimes necessary to use the same words found in his works, which were taken from the monuments of the ancients. It must be known that we too have made progress, drawn from the doctrine of the most ancient philosophers and the most evident experiments of our own time, insofar as God, the fountain and giver of all good things, has supplied each person. Nor should anyone think that those of us already publicly known for the art of Galen <note>Galen was the ancient Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium; the author identifies as a traditional "Galenist."</note> are so lazy as to not investigate what is true in this science. Indeed, this science is not for every talent, whether you look at the knowledge or the practice; it requires altogether a practiced industry, such as you will find today in none of the Paracelsians. Nevertheless, God has not been so unkind to us that He has closed off the riches and treasures of His goodness to everyone. I know many distinguished and hardworking men in the Galenic profession <margin>The Paracelsians are stupid braggarts.</margin> who are not ignorant of this craft, but have explored all its most hidden corners. These men, if I should fail in anything, will—without consulting the Paracelsians—supply what is missing, not only with words but with labor, in their own time when it seems right. But there is no need for words where the results themselves are expected.

<margin>The care of the ancients in the investigation of minerals.</margin>
Since the philosophers were skillfully engaged in the contemplation of natural things, and most especially minerals, they successfully investigated, among other things, whether they could either imitate by art what nature produces, or at least produce it more successfully and quickly—just as experience itself declares can be done in the care of animals and plants. They were charmed most of all by the dignity and price of metals and gems, which are a very useful support for sustaining life in sickness and other necessities, and also by their presence in nature; thus they began to work most intensely upon them. Certainly, those who read Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>, Geber <note>An 8th-century chemist often called the father of early chemistry.</note>, and others, discover that they were occupied most especially in explaining the nature of minerals, and among these, metals. Surely no one could be persuaded that this was done for the sake of naked knowledge alone. <margin>Art can help nature and correct its errors to some extent. The nature of metals. Imperfect metals. Examples of transmutations.</margin> They strove to arrange matter more successfully, to correct the "abortions" and errors of nature, and to procure the best end in that genus. For it was long ago confirmed by the decrees of the philosophers that this is intended by nature, just as the use of things has taught: that acting and suffering causes can be directed by art, so that what would otherwise have degenerated might come forth sound and blameless. Now, metals are ambiguous toward one another. One is born not only in the matrix of another, but also in its very embrace, so that it appears that the ignoble metals are nothing but something raw and undigested, which due to some indisposition could not be sufficiently worked out, even though otherwise the material principle according to its kind was the same. It is known even to the common people that iron, steel, and copper can be changed among themselves with a few additions and easy labor. Artisans have proven the same with white, black, and ashen lead, as well as with antimony <note>original: "stibium"</note>. From lead comes litharge <note>Lead monoxide, a secondary mineral.</note>; from this same litharge, lead returns. And metals pass into stones, glasses, and liquids, from which they are sometimes reduced. Learned men have conceded that the best silver is gold that is only slightly lacking in color and constancy. The greater part of nations is persuaded that gold is, as it were, the compendium and sum of all things. Therefore, it was asked whether the higher could not be made from the lower, and by what things subtracted, added, or otherwise changed.

<margin>Vices of metals</margin>
It has been discovered that certain vices adhere deeply in the root and are born with the matter, which degenerated as soon as it was first produced from its "seed-bed" <note>original: "seminario"</note>. Some vices were added during generation, but in such a way that they sat deeper and cannot easily be removed while preserving the substance; others, however, sit more lightly and are sometimes separated by nature of its own accord.

<margin>The power of the seeds of metals</margin>
This also has been observed: that metals do not consist immediately of the elements, but have their own <term>crasis: the specific temperament or mixture of qualities</term>, which multiplies itself with an analogous motion by seeds. Therefore, in those things where the seed-like power of metals is not present, it is permitted only to God—who is both the author and preserver of that power—to make metal, as if from wood, salt, water, etc. Nor is it granted to any man to compose the elements in any way he likes and induce a "crasis" that belongs to metals. Therefore, the seed of metals had to be hunted, and it had to be prepared and cherished in such a way that nature might make from it that which is best. Metals are indeed dissolved into elements; but they are not composed from them anew, just as you could not make a human body from a dissolved human or plant body by attempting a new composition. For the "crasis," restorable by God alone, has perished. Secondly, they are also dissolved into mercury <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note> and sulfur, and that also...

<summary>The author defends the study of alchemy as a legitimate branch of natural philosophy and Galenic medicine, arguing that "art" can perfect the "errors" of nature in metals. He sharply criticizes Paracelsians as "braggarts" while asserting that metals grow from specific "seeds" or constitutions that must be understood to achieve transmutation.</summary>

<page-num>58</page-num>
<header>Alchemical Commentary, Part II, Book IV.</header>

<margin>
The method of the coming together of metals.
Metallic matter.
</margin>
...and so on, but even from these things by themselves, you can bring back a metal no less than you can bring lead from lead-glass, or wood from the ashes, salt, and water of wood. The philosophers therefore indicated that those principles are to be sought from nature in their natural union, and corrected by art, and thoroughly perfected by applying what is necessary. This seemed easy if mercury, received from nature, were purified in the best possible ways, and brought to its maturity by the application of heat and analogous vessels. For from whatever juice metals consist—whether it first came together in the form of a vapor <note>original: "halitus"</note>, as Aristotle holds, or received a seminal power when it first existed—that juice is called mercury. But since the "spurious" can hardly, if at all, be distinguished from the "legitimate"—namely, the fertile mercury, which already has the seed and potential of metal, from the sterile—and then even if it is certain that it has received the metallic disposition and power, the outcome remains uncertain whether it will turn out to be the best metal or a monstrosity. Indeed, too much time and expense would be required.

<margin>
The seed of metals.
</margin>
They found another, less difficult and expensive way by which they might reach the same goal. Just as in plants and animals each thing propagates itself by the benefit of a seed generated within it, in which both the virtue and potential of the whole is enclosed—so that the seed is <term>δυνάμει: potentially</term> that which the thing whose seed it is, is in act—and afterward, by the application of heat, digestion, and proper nutrition, it even turns out similar to the original in substance; they judged that it would be the same in the genus of metals, following the same analogy. 

<margin>
Metallic seed cannot be collected from a sparse matrix on its own.
</margin>
Therefore, they turned their greatest efforts to investigating the seed. Two methods occurred. One, that it be snatched from the womb of the earth; the other, that it be taken from the tree (so to speak) in which it is born. Paracelsus indeed, in his foolishness, thought it could be found formally <note>meaning as a distinct, visible substance</note>; but of it being found and shown to the senses, we first desire an example. Miners sometimes recognize traces of it in immature veins; but since it is volatile and dispersed, they do not dare to extract it. It is easy to understand by the aid of reason that in immature veins of bismuth, there is both this seed and silver; and one must wait for maturation—which has indeed followed, as the histories of miners testify—and so it is in other cases. But to separate the seed by art for one’s purpose is a work of great labor. They approached the tree itself, and sought the desired thing from metal perfected in its own nature. Just as in men, cattle, and plants, likewise perfected in their substance, you find indeed a seminal humor, but not always a seed successful for procreation; so it is in metals. Yet the matter is more direct here, because what is found in cattle as separate entities—namely the male and female—is here in one. Nor should nature be thought defective in this part, as if she granted seed to one and denied its <term>dynamin: power or potential</term> to another. 

<margin>
Our Sulfur and Mercury are perpetually only in metals: whatever the sophist may prattle.
</margin>
Where silver or gold was present, absolute in all its parts, they found it more closely. Where it was weak and, as it were, diseased, the disease had to be removed first by art, and the integrity of nature's power excited toward the seed. This is that thing which they call the "stone," which they call the Elixir, the soul and seed of gold, the tincture, and other names; which, when projected into its own matter, disposes it toward the best. It does not only dispose it, but immediately—since it has the closest aptitude—it changes the matter to become such as the body from which it was extracted. This is what they call "tinging" <note>The alchemical process of "coloring" or transforming a base metal into a noble one</note>. Here there is a difference between minerals and living things. 

<margin>
The Philosopher's Stone.
Tinging.
</margin>
For mineral tinctures, when they are strong and firm in well-disposed matter, act immediately, just as fire immediately turns naphtha into a spirit like itself. In living things, a series of intervals is required. However, in nature metals are not made suddenly, nor is the stone itself 

<margin>
The Stone in nature.
</margin>
prepared in a moment. Thus, here they agree again. Furthermore, when I said that whole and perfect seed is in the nature of the perfected metal, it does not differ from what they say: that the philosopher’s stone is found created by nature, and needs nothing except that the superfluous parts be removed. For art cannot give essential power, but is forced to receive it from nature; as it is there, so it will be in the artifice. In this art, where perfect and absolute virtue is sought, it is necessary that the seed cannot be sought from anything imperfect, nor from a void in the metallic mass. 

<margin>
The Stone from metals.
</margin>
Truly, however, that which is so perfected by nature is nonetheless imperfect for the end of the art. For it has some indispositions which prevent gold from being able to seed itself and generate its like in suitable matter. These are what is rightly called "superfluous," and it is not just a certain quality, but a corporeal grossness, from which the soul of gold is drawn out by art; this is taken, and the other neglected. Furthermore, it is asserted that both powers, the masculine and feminine, are contained in one, just as in 

<margin>
Others take the Sun for the male, as also sulfur; and mercury for the female.
</margin>
plants. But nonetheless, the philosophers afterward took two bodies—gold as the male, and silver in place of the female—more successfully mixing the common matter for each ferment, and tempering the fiery nature of the masculine body. From this, a disagreement arose in the writings of authors. Some mention only one perfected thing, as some contend for gold alone, or 

<margin>
Where the seed may be drawn out.
</margin>
silver alone. Others require two, namely those who make a common matter for the "white" and the "red" <note>referring to the White Work (silver) and Red Work (gold)</note>, and afterward animate certain parts separately with their own ferment. Moreover, that very seed can neither be drawn out from the perfected metal without a "familiar liquor" by which the joints of the perfected things are opened and destroyed, nor perfected without the "primordial menstruum" <note>The primary alchemical solvent</note>, which possesses the nature and power of the first metallic matter. And yet 

<margin>
The Mercury of the Philosophers.
Symbols of mercury.
</margin>
only one menstrual and feminine nature is required. They therefore made him whom they call the "Mercury of the Philosophers," in whom is the nature of both perfected things, and additionally the primordial menstrual matter fertilized with feminine virtue. From this, so many riddles have arisen: namely, that all things came from water, and all things must be reduced to water; all from one, all into one; and that it is one thing, in which however two, three, and four are enclosed; and that one circle is made, which must be reduced to a square, a triangle, and finally again into a double circle 

<margin>
What the Philosopher's Stone is.
</margin>
where raw and corporeal mercury concur, and almost innumerable similar things. This mercury is the principle of the work, and the true matter, as I have clearly declared elsewhere. It is clear, therefore, that the Philosopher’s Stone is nothing other than the seminal essence of the perfected metals, used to perfectly transmute others into their nature; and that it is prepared from perfected things and given transmuting efficacy by art to the likeness of those bodies from which it comes. This cannot happen except in things similar in genus—namely, in metals reduced to their first matter, or provided with its nearer potential.

<margin>
Why it is called a "Stone."
</margin>
As to why it is called a "stone," and not rather by its own name by which it might be more easily known, a certain person says it is done for this reason: because it is a brittle thing, which like stones can be ground; but he is not mistaken who judges it was so named for the sake of concealment. For they were accustomed to use any names, even from the slightest similarity...

<header>On the Philosopher's Stone.</header>

# On the Philosopher's Stone.

<margin>Red and brilliant Panosius: or even the mercury that hides the seed of gold in stony veins, which must be dug out from there like the "fifth nature" of the stone. But it matters little whether the true cause is known or hidden, provided we know the thing itself. Nor indeed is that name only given to this seminal principle. Sometimes they call gold and silver itself by this name; sometimes mercury and other things; and there are various stones of the philosophers scattered about. There is a mineral stone, a vegetable one, and an animal one; some distinguish between these, while others say they are three aspects and three names for one single thing.</margin>

<margin>The copper of the philosophers, while it is first cooked, becomes water; the more it is thickened, the more it becomes water; the more it is saturated, the more it stands above every metal, from which the name of the Philosopher's Stone is derived.</margin>

The author of the *Greater Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> reports it thus: *There are three stones, and three salts, from which the entire mastery consists: the mineral, the plant, and the animal. And there are three waters, namely: solar, lunar, and mercurial. Mercury is the mineral; the moon [silver] is the plant, because it receives two colors into itself, whiteness and redness; the sun [gold] is the animal, because it receives three, namely: constriction, whiteness, and redness, and it is called the "great animal," etc.* And a little later: *There are three stones of the philosophers: mineral, vegetable, and animal; triple in name, but one in being.* For this author, these names represent different parts and aspects of a diverse composition within a single thing. Others look to three distinct operations in making the Elixir, so that the first is "mineral," where there is simple solution and coagulation here as if in a mine; the second is "vegetable," by which the power is now doubled and exalted in imitation of a growing plant; the third is "animal," because the dead body then receives a soul through the ferment.

<margin>Geber's triple medicine.</margin>

Geber <note>An 8th-century Arabic alchemist, often called the "Father of Chemistry"</note> seems to designate nothing else by his "triple medicine," of which the first only alters imperfect things without sufficient completion; the second induces at least some mark of perfection; the third renders that upon which it is cast absolute in all measures. And although he hides the matter with sophistry <note>Intentional puzzles or misleading language used by alchemists to hide secrets</note> and brings forward contradictory examples, nevertheless we are convinced that these are only intended as specific instances, so that from the sophistry a declaration for the true work might be brought forth. For otherwise it is true—according to consistent authors—that the stone perfected by the first operation, because it is still volatile, provides only an alteration in color, but not consistently; the second operation indeed tints even further, but not essentially; the third absolves and completes all desires, if legitimate multiplication and preparation for the <term>projection: the final act of throwing the alchemical catalyst onto base metal to transform it</term> are added. The author himself, in his explanation of the third medicine, says: *it does not differ at all in essence from the medicine of the second order, except through the most subtle degrees of preparation, in its concoction, and a longer persistence of labor.*

<margin>False stones.</margin>

But we do not wish to quarrel with anyone over these matters, since they are of ambiguous interpretation. Those who have thoroughly misunderstood the Chemistry of the ancients, hearing of the stone, salt, liquor, etc., being distinguished by that triplicity, thought that one stone was made from minerals, another from vegetables, and a third from things that were animals. Thus they have wasted away among mineral spirits, parts of plants, and the excrement of animals. Some have distinguished the three chemical principles—salt, sulfur, and mercury—in this way; others have called distilled oils, salts, and liquors by these same names. Whence there is one who writes: *We do not call the concocted oils, such as oil of antimony, oil of sulfur, or coagulated and consumed mercuries, the Philosopher's Stone.* There are some who decorate "potable gold," the "tincture of antimony," and the "spirit of vitriol" with these names. Perhaps those who call any essences made from minerals "mineral stones," from vegetables "vegetable," and from animals "animal," should be considered simple rather than foolish.

<margin>The ignited stones of Paracelsus.</margin>

But here too we shall not be combative. Paracelsus <note>A revolutionary 16th-century Swiss-German physician and alchemist</note> has one stone which he calls that of the ancients, which tints metals; and another by which he heals a poorly disposed body in a manner similar to metals, whose power is not specific or essential, but acquired from preparation. Those who follow him believe this is made from the "element of Mercury" <insert>most people take this to be sublimated mercury, which they also call the 'mine of mercury.' There is something in this, but the labor is greatest. There is another thing in which it is found</insert> more closely, although no one can affirm anything for certain, and the knowledge may be buried with its master, if there ever was any. Those who acknowledge only the stone that transmutes metals do not agree among themselves, one proclaiming this and another that. Even the craftsmen profess a "particular work" and a "universal" one; one "lesser" and another "greater." There is also a "middle" work, of which Geber spoke, who distinguished his triple medicine in this way and called the third the "order of the greater work," of which Thomas <note>Likely referring to Thomas Aquinas, to whom alchemical works were falsely attributed</note> also makes mention. Pico <note>Pico della Mirandola, a famous Renaissance philosopher</note> reports that a certain man boasted that he held more than twenty ways of making gold.

<margin>Certain particular tinctures: I. An image of the true stone.</margin>

There is also a frequent sophistical <note>Imitative or "cheat" method</note> method among the followers of Paracelsus, from which various stones arise, some of which I will review. Let oil of antimony, oil of sulfur, and prepared oil of vitriol, and finally cinnabar, be mixed together in proportion; and in a large retort (as they call it) roasted with an equal quantity of strong <term>aqua regia: "royal water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</term>, let them be digested in ashes at the first degree of fire for a month. Let the <term>phlegm: the watery, tasteless distillate</term> be drawn off and returned again to the matter at the bottom, which should be repeated until the white moisture no longer appears. Then, with the glass closed, let the matter be digested in a sand bath, and in the space of thirty days it will coagulate. Resolve the coagulated mass in a cool, damp place. Coagulate the solution again in hot sand, and it will become a stone, which you should dissolve and coagulate a third time in the same way; it will turn out like a dense carbuncle <note>A deep red gemstone</note>, though with less transparency, as if with a certain darkness. This is the "philosopher's stone," to be multiplied with a thousand parts of Hungarian gold, and one part will tint eighty parts. However, silver must first be tinted from mercury, and afterward changed into gold. Behold, one "philosopher's stone," which you will nevertheless never free from the suspicion of being a sophism.

<margin>II. Another shadowy stone.</margin>

Others command that the Sun [gold] <insert>you can understand the Sun and Moon of the philosophers, which are stones made through sublimation from the principles and elaborated with much study so that the Sun is like a ruby or carbuncle, and the Moon like a diamond or the clearest crystal. These, when reduced into the "first matter," show that mercury which is sought from the beginning,</insert> or the Moon [silver] be resolved into mercury, which they divide into three parts; and one being saved, they add to the other two a seventh part of the body from which it was made, which they call "ferment." They do not add it all at once, but in parts. This is gold or silver reduced into the thinnest leaves or a powder.

<margin>Here the Sun is said to change into a "whitening eagle" and lose its redness; likewise the earth is turned into water. Now the water is said to vanish into fire. Mercury is born to be fixed by the "scent of the body."</margin>

The mercury is enclosed in a small gourd-shaped flask which, after the ferment has been put in and well mixed, is closed most exactly so that nothing can breathe out. It is thus placed in hot ashes for a month until the body is dissolved in its own water or mercury; once this is done, more is added into the resealed glass, and this is done a third time until the whole body is consumed and received by the mercury. For it joins with it most willingly and is even "fixed" by it. Thus "the Dragon has devoured its own tail," as they say, although the meaning of this is rather the opposite. When the ferment is finished, the mass is transferred to a "viola" or a "matrix" (which is a type of cylindrical glass closed on both ends, leaving only a small hole), which is filled only to a fourth part and shut as tightly as possible. It is placed in a warm sifting-sand bath for several hours (perhaps 12) so that the mercury can ascend and be sublimated. When it climbs, the glass must be turned so that it returns again to the bottom and is raised up once more; this is repeated until it is "fixed" by its own body. They say a small fixed pulse always remains at the bottom.

<summary>This page explores the various definitions and classifications of the Philosopher's Stone, distinguishing between true alchemical processes and "sophistical" imitations. It details the "triple medicine" of Geber and provides specific recipes for creating "particular" stones using oils and sublimation.</summary>
<keywords>Philosopher's Stone, Geber, Paracelsus, Rosarium Philosophorum, Alchemy, Transmutation, Triple Medicine, Aqua Regia, Sublimation, Ferment, Mercury, Gold, Silver</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the Philosopher’s Stone from page 59, moving from general definitions to specific recipes and the chemical operations required to fix the "mercury of the bodies" into a transmuting tincture.</meta>

...to restore: so that in this way it is gradually fixed and "dies," being converted into a black powder. This is worked with a stronger fire until the proper colors appear; finally, a white <term>calx</term> <note>A powder produced by heating a metal or mineral to high temperatures</note> is left from the Moon <note>silver</note>, and from the Sun <note>gold</note>, a purple calx like clotted blood. They mix this powder with the reserved third part of mercury, and thus increase it by fixing it in the same way. They multiply the increased substance by adding a fourth part of common quicksilver prepared through <term>oxalme</term> <note>likely a mixture of salt and vinegar or an acidic salt solution used for purification</note>. They fix this again under a different regime; once fixed, they add another fourth part, and so on infinitely. However, no more than a fourth part should be added, for it cools the mixture too much. If you project one part of this increased powder from the Sun over fifty parts of molten silver, it turns into gold; and if one part of the lunar powder is projected over fifty parts of melted copper and lead, it will become silver. If it were multiplied not with common mercury, but with the "mercury of the bodies" <note>mercury extracted directly from metals rather than mined</note>, it would <term>tinge</term> <note>transform the color and nature of a base metal</note> ten times more. Some increase it ten times with the corporeal mercury and then with the common. This process is confirmed by a certain saying: <note>original: "Nisi terra vertatur in aquam, aqua in ignem, spiritus & corpus non coniunguntur."</note> *Unless the earth is turned into water, and the water into fire, the spirit and the body are not joined.* Also: <note>original: "Quanquam sol est rubeus totus; tamen in eo latet albedo mercurii abscondita; & in mercurio occultata est rubedo solis, nec apparet, nisi artifex sapiens eam producat."</note> *Although the sun is entirely red, yet within it lies hidden the whiteness of mercury; and in mercury, the redness of the sun is concealed, and it does not appear unless a wise craftsman brings it forth.*

<margin>III. A partial tincture.</margin>
Others resolve gold into a tincture and a white mercurial body, which they call that "dead earth"—dead indeed, but noble, for from it that most precious salt and mercury of the philosophers is made. This matter is unknown to most and sought by few in such lowly ashes. They call the tincture the soul and <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" represents the active, masculine, or coloring principle within a substance</note> of gold. A portion of this, as much as is drawn from half an ounce, can in turn change half an ounce of silver into gold, besides the white body, in which there is no small profit. If this is projected over <insert>Hungarian gold</insert> <note>Highly prized for its purity in the early modern period</note> that has been perfectly purified, and this again over another, up to the fifth "exaltation": they judge that the Philosopher’s Stone has been completed. With half of this, they transform silver; the other half they increase infinitely. For they have persuaded themselves that the more often it is mixed with gold, the more subtle the elixir becomes. But if there is any truth beneath these claims, the preparation of the tincture and the body of gold will not be so simple.

<margin>IV. Tincture.</margin>
Some reduce gold into a mercury, which they precipitate; and they cast it into precipitated quicksilver from the mine through mutual soakings and coagulations, the other having been reduced to water, or through sublimations. That which is fixed, they reduce in part. The other part they convert for augmentation.

<margin>V.</margin>
Others make crystals from gold, and from these, quicksilver, which they afterwards treat as has been said.

<margin>VI.</margin>
There are those who join the calxes of "perfect bodies" <note>gold and silver</note> with mercury that has been sublimated four times from sal ammoniac and <term>vitriol</term> <note>A sulfate mineral or sulfuric acid</note>, and thus they fix the volatile part together. They reduce part of the fixed substance and consume part in the augmentation.

<margin>VII.</margin>
Others distill urine; others <term>aqua regia</term> <note>A highly corrosive mixture of acids capable of dissolving gold</note>, in which they dissolve the calxes of metals, and cook them again, and turn them back into water and reduce them, until they believe the "fixed elixir" has been produced. When this is projected over mercury, they falsely claim it turns it into metal.

<margin>VIII.</margin>
Others fix cinnabar with the cement of perfect bodies. But if I wished to recount the "stones" of everyone, I would waste both my oil and my labor. None of these things agree with the precepts of the philosophers, for whom there is only one—and that one universal—stone in the experience of the world, not many, however many may be spoken of.

<margin>The matter of the stone.</margin>
From what matter it is made has already been said. Only the "composite water of the philosophers" is required; regarding its composition, all the [Alchemical] Fathers amicably agree, and nothing foreign is found in it. Nature provides it all; Art purifies and composes it, as we wrote regarding the mercury of the philosophers.

<margin>A note on solution.</margin>
Regarding this, you will note that I have learned by experience that the more often and more diligently the bodies are thinned by preparation, the more quickly and reliably they are dissolved. However, there is a certain limit to this thinning. For those things which become entirely "spiritual" <note>vaporous or volatile</note> do not remain in the work but mock the hope of the craftsman. Therefore, it has been judged that repeating the preparation seven times is sufficient, so that in three things, three "sevens" <note>cycles of seven</note> are completed. Each time, the "secret of tartar" <note>likely a purified alkaline salt or spirit derived from wine lees</note> must be used to wash away impurities. This is a corrected spirit, although they also use other salts. In this way, what the craftsmen write is true: that no other <margin>How other mineral metals are added to the stone.</margin> mineral enters the essence of the stone, nor anything from base metals—except for those used in the preparation, and these in the transmutation. [Note that some craftsmen put no metal in at the start, but only a double mercury; some also add the mercury of the Sun or Moon from perfect metals; others require a metallic mercury, but its metal is equivocal.] Yet they remain equally on both sides, as these are transformed and those are separated afterward. Thus, I have followed the progress of the tincture in preparing gold, but in silver, I followed solution through <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Nitric acid</note>; and thus aqua regia and aqua fortis are sometimes not undeservedly called the "keys of the rosary." But as has been said, care must be taken that nothing of them remains, and rather that the aqua regia be made from saltpeter, salt of urine, and [sal] ammoniac. For if vitriol is added, its power cannot be washed away; however, this does not seem to me to be very suitable, since it has been discovered that even in perfect bodies, the vitriolic nature (which is drawn from them) does not hinder anything—but here, something "more than perfect" is sought.

<margin>Chemical operations necessary for the stone.</margin>
The operations by which the art is perfected are many or few, depending on various perspectives and divisions. All are sometimes included under **solution** and **coagulation**, as these are the primary ones. Sometimes these are named along with many others, such as washing, fixing, reduction, sublimation, calcination, etc. But in truth, in the preparation, **distillation** and **separation** along with **amalgamation** are of the greatest importance; although while we separate, we also dissolve, reverberate, calcinate, refine, etc. In the progress and management of the work itself, we dissolve through **putrefaction** (in which a certain sublimation and calcination also appear); we separate the dissolved matter into elements, later join them, "imbibe" or nourish them, wash them, and thus finally obtain **coagulation**. Once this is done, the "body" is resuscitated and animated, where **fermentation** and the remaining operations recur again. The end is the appearance of the colors along with **fixation**, which is followed by the **multiplication** of the substance for tinging, and finally **projection**, the end of which is **transmutation**. Such is the nature of all operations.

<margin>Instruments of the works.</margin>
The instrumental causes of such labor are manifold, among which the most important are the arrangement of the vessels and the fire, managed with industry. After the preparation, there is no need for any furnace other than the **athannor** <note>A self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a steady, constant heat over long periods</note>, in which the whole mastery is completed. However, when one must reverberate with the fourth degree of fire, it is,

## On the Philosopher's Stone.

<margin>The Violet or Geranium.</margin>
It is true that a furnace is also used, although that degree of heat is not required at the birth of the stone. Hence it is said that the work is done in one furnace; but it is also completed in a single glass, which is a small <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation</note>, though more suitable is the one they call a **violet**, which has two openings, neither of which should be overlooked. The first is used before the Hermetic union; the second requires the glass to be sealed solid everywhere. <margin>Double fire.</margin> The fire is twofold. The whole is dry and spiritual: for a flame must not be admitted to the glass until the stone is already perfected; but there is another fire which is internal and innate. <insert>[This is in the solar mercury which is made through reduction into the first matter and is called sulfur, the male, etc.]</insert> The degree of this fire cannot be perceived by the senses, yet in its effect it surpasses the common elemental fire of the public, since the latter cannot achieve what the former does in destroying bodies through solution. There is another external fire, which they call mundane and elemental, and which some do not use at the beginning while the <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage of decomposition where the matter turns black</note> is active. Furthermore, many people teach many things concerning vessels and fire; but regarding the method of fire, I have seen nothing clearer than these: read the *Testament* of Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century alchemist</note>, Job of Padua, the *Practice* of Boniface, etc., which exist in a certain German book titled *Pandora*, although even here the whole art is described in such a way that darkness is mixed into the light itself. I have seen the things themselves described by no one more clearly than by Arnold, and recently also by Penotus in his *Philosophical Axioms*. From that work, I shall translate into English <note>original: "in Latium" (into Latin)</note> what I judge necessary, and add it to the end of this treatise. <margin>Time of completion.</margin> The time in which the whole is finished is not certainly defined by everyone. Some have reduced it to ten months, or nine, in which a conception is perfected in the womb, although this too is variable. Others have set it at three years, others even less. But many causes of inequality arise. For not only do the methods of working differ—as we sometimes achieve the same result through various means, either by a shortcut or through long-winded ways, according to the craftsman's skill—but also the movement of the matter, the diligence of the apparatus, and other similar things. Therefore, without an exact description of time, they command the craftsman to act until perfection, and they determine each individual action by its own signs, so that he may know what must be established and when.

<margin>The spirit of the craftsman.</margin>
But I come to the operations themselves, which the masters command a man to approach initially as a pious person, frequent in prayer, who undertakes and completes such a great art not for the sake of profit and worldly pleasures, but for the study of the wonders of God in nature, from which the glory of the Creator arises; and thereafter for the purpose of helping the health and needs of his poor neighbor. For where there is labor without prayer, and an evil purpose, let no one even dream of success. Furthermore, he must be instructed in natural science, and especially in the knowledge of his subject; he should be free from rashness and stupidity, one who understands the signs of the matter, and if anything goes astray, can easily correct it. He must watch over the work and be entirely accomplished in this kind of science, able to bear the delay of the work with a patient mind. In such matters, the Paracelsians <note>Followers of Paracelsus who often mixed alchemy with mysticism and medicine</note> seem to me to sin greatly, seeking I know not what spirits to be present as instructors and directors of the works; they inscribe crosses and other characters on the vessels; they observe the constellations of the stars most curiously; and meanwhile, being rash, stupid, and inexperienced, they achieve as much as those who do nothing at all. Therefore, they are to be laughed at with their religion and their most superstitious bubbles of words. It is holy and auspicious enough that which is undertaken with pious prayers, according to nature and the ordinary sciences, by one who is destined for that duty by his profession and who looks toward a good and high end.
<margin>The delusions of the Paracelsians.</margin>

<margin>Choice of matter.</margin>
Let there be ready, therefore, the best gold, such as Indian, Arabic, or Hungarian; and silver sought from the most fertile and well-disposed mines. For there are some things which provide gold or silver, but it is weak and unfruitful in its "spermatic" virtue. Some extract it from coins; but not only is the mixture of these disapproved of, but also the stain which they have contracted therefrom, unless it is very small or can be washed away again by a skilled craftsman. But from wherever it is taken, whether gold or silver, it must be purified to the highest degree: the former through the fusion of <term>antimony</term> repeated seven times, always adding what they call roasting and then washing or wiping away with spirit of <term>tartar</term>, from which it becomes very noble; the latter through cupellation and washing. If you industriously <term>calcine</term> <note>reduce to powder by heat</note> them through waters, both bodies will be even more obedient to solution. Otherwise, they are merely hammered out into the thinnest foils, which—so that they are greedily received by the mercury—they do not wash, or they scrape and <term>reverberate</term> <note>heat in a furnace where the flame is deflected onto the matter</note> those that have been taken. Some take the thinnest leaves; others, powders. <insert>[Note: this is said of natural gold and silver, although they are not always used at the beginning but first in fermentation. Thus the conjunction is not at the beginning, even when they are used.]</insert> Let the weight of each be equal, namely half an ounce, or as much as your fortune allows. If you wish to experiment in the Sun <note>gold</note> alone: an ounce is prescribed. Some command a double quantity; but then vessels that are too large are required, and the fire cannot be so industriously ruled; nor is a great quantity necessary, since increase and multiplication sufficiently compensate for it. Remember, however, that no other metal or other thing is required here except **electrum**, which is called "part with part." As the body you sow, so shall you reap. Like begets like: and Gold is the soul and the male; silver is the body and the female, although they are not usually called by those names at that time. From these must be made the "first matter," that is, the mercurial liquor. For the seed in bodies is a potentiality. In the primeval liquor it is made active, which generation also indicates. Now, there are many ways by which we can achieve any kind of solution, but only one has pleased <margin>Others have taught that raw mineral mercury, and not corporeal, should be taken; they even defend Penotus on this. But in the royal [process]... why is it raw...</margin> the masters; all the rest destroy the seminal power. It is, however, through raw mercury, which already represents the seminal <term>menstruum</term> <note>a solvent</note> in action, and can likewise bring the hidden virtue in bodies into action. Let this also be purified seven times and made completely "astral," so that it is freed from all leprosy and foreign blackness, and even from the sulfurous stain and unfit moisture, so that it can penetrate into the innermost parts of the bodies and, the enclosures being loosened, take up what is familiar to its own nature. The quantity of this should not be small. For it is required not only for the double solutions and coagulations, but also for fermentation and multiplication, although others allow here also quicksilver refined by <term>oxalme</term> <note>a mixture of salt and vinegar</note>. <insert>[that which he does thereafter will have a use: but it is not the mercury of the philosophers.]</insert> Its proportion should be twelvefold to the quantity of the bodies, and that also in the augmentations, by which it grows not a little. Therefore you will consider how much was necessary. Let this also be extracted from the best mines, where the learned liquor and...

<margin>
On common,
unrefined,
and minimally
processed
materials, and a 
certain
immature metal
which some
call lead or
brass, obtained
nearby.
</margin>
... they are not found, nor is it corrupted by lead, whether in the ore or outside of it. Therefore, some seek out a rich vein of it and, without using fire, draw it out through vinegar and other methods. Although this diligence might seem superstitious, fire must eventually be used for its purification and alteration. Others seek it from gold mines or silver excavations, looking for those of closer origin, such as the Spanish, Carinthian, or Joachimsthaler <note>Joachimsthal was a famous mining town in Bohemia, known for its silver.</note> varieties. From these, let a **mislagma** <note>original: "mislagma"; a technical term for an alchemical mixture or paste</note> be made, as is customary among goldsmiths, but with greater care and in the cleanest of vessels. If you have prepared everything correctly, you will see how greedily the "body" is devoured by the "spirit," and immediately at the beginning, the signs of the future work will appear; first a blackness, then various colors will emerge. For an amalgam is made—here, consider what I mean and what kind of union occurs under heat. It is a marvel that it turns black so quickly, even though the bodies were so purified that no dregs remained. He is deceived who thinks that this blackness, in this art, is merely a type of dross. This is the "marriage in the bath" <note>An alchemical metaphor for the chemical combination of substances in a liquid medium.</note> about which the philosophers discuss so extensively: *Introduce the yellow man with his white wife into the bath after their marriage.* And as Arnold <note>Refers to Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century alchemist.</note> says: *Keep the water distilled seven times aside.* This water is the "mercury of the philosophers" which acts as the solvent for the marriage, and so on. Thus it is called the volatile spirit, which, having worked its way into the innermost natures of the bodies, makes volatile things out of the fixed ones, and in turn acquires a tendency toward stability with them. This is the "raw chamber" into which the spouses are to be introduced. But it is not for us to find the words of the artist; he who knows these things and afterward diligently studies their books will understand that these things agree with them. For let no one think I have neglected the monuments of the philosophers, but rather that I have referred all their words to these practices, weighed them, and in turn judged these practices by those words and the nature of the matter.

<margin>
Procuring
the solution
and 
putrefaction.
</margin>
This amalgam must now be "digested" <note>Slowly heated to encourage a chemical change.</note> so that from all these parts that one "water" is plainly made—the "philosophical thing," or a circle containing within itself a triangle and a square, or like a pentagon composed of a square and a triangle <note>This geometric description refers to the "Squaring of the Circle," a symbol for the creation of the Philosopher's Stone from the four elements.</note>. This is accomplished by the power of the mercury, which should not remain idle in a suitable material. For although it appears cold on the outside, they possess an internal fire, which is called into action by mutual interaction and suffering—an insensible fire, just as heat is sensibly produced in sharp waters <note>Acids</note> and metals. For this reason, it is also called the "sharpest vinegar," "salt," "vitriol," "alum," and any other corrosive names from which it takes its title due to a similar power. There is no other reason why it is named the "fire of Gehenna" <note>The fires of Hell; used here to describe a fire that burns without a visible flame.</note>, etc.

<margin>Understand these things literally.</margin>
Therefore, it is enclosed in a small <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped flask</note> or a **violet** <note>A specific type of alchemical vessel mentioned on the previous page.</note>, but neither larger nor smaller than is right, so that the action can be completed in the proper manner. They think it is sufficient if one-third of the vessel is empty. It should be noted that there ought to be several such glasses of varying capacity. For in the beginning the quantity is small, but later it grows. And yet, if you consider the nature of the matter, it can be completed in a single form of glass. The author of the *Pandora* <note>A famous alchemical compendium.</note> uses crescent-shaped and egg-shaped instruments. Others prefer the form of the **Aludel** <note>A series of pear-shaped pots used in sublimation.</note>, arranged so that the neck, narrowed and cut away, can be inserted into another glass serving as a lid, like two segments of a globe enclosing each other. This glass seems more convenient to me for frequent openings. In this way, care can be taken so that nothing falls from the seal. For it is closed in the middle of the neck, with paste smeared around the outside. But whatever vessel you use, it must be carefully blocked and placed in pure, washed ashes, contained in an oval dish or a globe like the one described by the author of the *Pandora*. Others wrap it in cotton and enclose it in a "philosophical egg" made of oak wood, crafted on a lathe and able to be opened. But the "violet" or "geranium" vessel does not fit here. Thus, those who use this method have an oblong box made for themselves, also of oak and able to be folded, and they place their vessel in it. Thus they lay the "King" to rest with his "wife" in a private chamber or place where no force can harm him.

<margin>
In putrefaction,
gentle warmth
is to be 
applied.
</margin>
And some forbid all force of external fire, even the heat of the Sun; some apply a very weak warmth. I, when I put the matter to the test, discovered that external warmth is managed more correctly. For just as in <term>aqua forti</term> <note>Nitric acid</note> poured over metals, interaction occurs even in cold air, yet it comes into action faster with the heat of a hand or coals. This is also known in the rest of nature, especially in the decomposition <note>putrefaction</note> and the generation of an embryo, to which this work is compared. So it is in the solution: you must labor as one does in the dissolving of bodies. Therefore, it is necessary to continue a slow fire over it. Likewise: *It is necessary that the dissolved material rot in heat and moisture*, etc. However, once the beginning of the mutual digestion has occurred, the matter proceeds even without external heat, unless the air is plainly freezing. For then silver-like stones or rays appear in the glass, which certainly hinder the internal fire, since such "congealing" is contrary to "solution."

<margin>Renewal of the solvent.</margin>
But truly, just as the power of other naturally acting agents is not infinite but eventually grows dull against stubborn matter, so it is with mercury. Just as when metals are dissolved in nitric acid, the acid must be renewed and changed—and as in extracting tinctures the <term>menstruum</term> <note>A solvent, often compared to biological fluids in alchemy.</note> is exchanged for a new one—so here, when the "stomach of the ostrich" and the **Azoth** <note>Technical terms for the universal solvent or mercurial spirit.</note> have been weakened and their "teeth" dulled, a new one must be substituted.

<margin>
The Green Lion.
The Green
Duenech, etc.
Twelvefold
mercury.
</margin>
For it is not possible for the entire quantity to be dissolved by a single batch of solvent. I am not unaware that some name the entire quantity, which is twelvefold, all at once, and want the glass not to be opened nor anything further added once the union is made until the completion. But it is clear that they either deceive or have been deceived by the phrasing of the authors. Since legitimate interaction and passion must occur between determined parts, "putrefaction" would not occur in such a large amount of water, just as it does not in the sea; and the "seminal power" would be suffocated by the abundance of the solvent, not drawn out. Moreover, the parts nearby would act just as much while the others remained idle, and thus the solution would be imperfect. Indeed, the authors, by naming twelve parts, indicated how much mercury was required for one completion; they did not say it should be put in all at once.

<margin>Unlocking.</margin>
The same is true of the "reseration" <note>The opening or unlocking of the vessel.</note>. Re-closings are not forbidden during the solution stage, which is clear also because they must be allowed during the "nutrition" stage; but when the stone is ready to be "fixed," then they do not open it before the final perfection. Therefore, let the total mercury at the beginning be distributed into three parts, any one of which is matched to its body, even in a twelvefold increase. And each of these in turn should be divided into three parts which are put in first, and nine which are added later at distinct intervals. When, therefore, through a period of eight days, or at whatever time its sign appears, and you know the power of the first water is dulled, and it has stunk in its decomposition...

It argues for the gradual addition of mercurial solvent rather than adding it all at once, comparing the process to biological generation.</summary>
