<page-num>63</page-num>
<header>On the Philosopher’s Stone.</header>
<sig>FF 2</sig>

## On the Philosopher’s Stone.

<margin>A black film.</margin>
You will contemplate the work and watch whether any black film emerges, which is like a spider's web. This is the sign of beginning putrefaction, and Saturn is then said to preside over the work on account of the black color and the coldness. If it appears, it is separated. However, it was not seen by me so immediately. Others designate the "philosophical month" as lasting 40 days. Therefore, one usually proceeds without separation, and new water is added first; the quantity of this should be half the quantity of both bodies together, or equal to one of them. Thus, it is sharpened anew, and again it tests its strength upon the body. Some separate the entirety of the first water by squeezing it through leather <note>original: "per corium exprimendo"; a common method for filtering mercury or metallic mixtures</note>. But to me, this seems inconvenient; a mere sharpening of the strength is sufficient. Nor can the fixed part easily emerge and be sublimated if the water does not overflow—much less can the raven be successfully beheaded <note>original: "decollari coruus"; an alchemical metaphor for removing the blackness or "head" of the matter</note> and its skin stripped away. For this reason, the glass is opened circumspectly, and once the mercury has been injected, it is put back in its original place and closed until five days have passed. For in that interval, unless some error has been made, a small portion is again dissolved and sublimated. If not yet, one must wait until it happens. Nevertheless, I achieved it after five days, until there was a sufficient abundance of water and the blackest skin appeared, with the thickest darkness throughout the whole glass, as if the raven's head <note>original: "caput corui"; a famous symbol for the "Nigredo" or black stage of alchemy</note> arose from the earth; putrefaction would then be finished, and the infant born. Then I gradually drew off the skin and put it aside; if the work does not succeed, start again.

<margin>The blackest and most subtle soot. Black earth, unless it retains something mercurial, does not receive nourishment.</margin>
Pay close attention to this color. For it ought to be black like soot. Hence it is called "blacker than black." If you touch it with your fingers, it clings so subtly that it cannot be removed except by washing. If you sprinkle it into water, it sinks, where previously, when mixed with it, it turned the water completely black. It can indeed be washed away with water so that it separates entirely from its body, but this is not at all advised. For, to stay silent on other inconveniences, it cannot be nourished afterward. It flees its own water as if it had never been joined to it by any kinship. Therefore, the blackness with its film must be removed by a feather. The natural time for this is when it appears sufficiently black and dark. But since this hardly happens before the fortieth day (which is the philosophical month), and sometimes the beginning only emerges at that very time, craftsmen define this day for waiting for the separation, meanwhile increasing the solvent <term>menstruum: a liquid used to dissolve or extract substances, named for the monthly cycles of nature</term> every five days as was said. Then, therefore, their axioms take place: concerning the newborn infant, the beginning of the true tincture, the true seed, the raven's head, the ash not to be despised <note>original: "de cinere non vilipendendo"; a reference to the belief that the seemingly worthless residue contains the secret of the work</note>, the black earth which at the beginning stands above the water, and many other things. Then also, by the best right, that liquor is called "virgin’s milk," <note>original: "lac virginis"; a term for the white mercurial liquid used as a solvent</note> "doubled mercury" consisting of the mercury of the bodies and the crude mercury, and so on. Then the elements have separated, and the putrefaction is complete; the hot and dry—or the fiery—has emerged from the hidden into the manifest, and with it also the ethereal. The cold and moist water, along with a portion of air, is that mercury. <margin>Separation of the elements.</margin> The inert earth and the thick body remain at the bottom like a dead head <note>original: "caput mortuum"; the useless residue left after distillation or sublimation</note>. [Not everyone has everything chewed up and thrust into their mouths. You will therefore seek out the meaning from the rest.] Although later that blackness is also called "earth," etc.—all of which I have seen to agree so well with the nature of things and by the evidence of my eyes, and I have touched that impalpable powder with my hands, so that no one should think the philosophers have deceived us. After the fortieth day, therefore, or whenever the completed blackness is manifested (which the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> warns is unequal, in the name of Bassantius, who says one work is finished more quickly and another more slowly due to the diversity of cooking; I add also the disposition of the material), you can segregate it; piece by piece every five or ten days, according as it emerges in a mass or more rarely. Some wait until the end. But this seems inconvenient to me because, when it is finished more slowly than expected, we cannot detect the certain completion. But if it is drawn off bit by bit, you will easily see whether anything remains or nothing. The whole cannot be dissolved. For the whole is not seed and soul, unless perhaps you have fallen upon the marrow of gold, or by art have changed the whole into the "fifth being" <note>original: "quintum esse"; the quintessence</note> through the quintessence. It is enough if the most subtle aerial part is segregated with the fiery part. For these alone are sought under the name of sulfur and the soul of gold. Thus from one, two were made, and four, and the circle was changed into a square, in which nevertheless a trinity appears, so that it is rightly said to lead from unity through duality into trinity and the quaternary. There are two sublimated things: namely, the blackness and the water remaining with the body enclosed within it. There are three: the sublimated spirit, the mediating water, and the body fixed at the bottom—or the infant, the parents, and the solvent. There are four according to the number of elementary qualities, and the elements themselves are analogically accommodated thus. When all things are rightly performed, the birth will be completed in a quarter of a year, or ninety days. If an error has been made anywhere, or the work delayed, it will be later, and often by double or triple the time; so much does a disturbance or error hinder the work, which cannot even be fully corrected if the craftsman is not industrious.

<margin>Nutrition and washing.</margin>
The produced seed must be guarded zealously, lest its power be dissipated. Therefore, however much there is, it is immediately placed for nutrition in a peculiar vessel <note>original: "getanio"; likely a specific type of small flask or cup</note>, but a small one according to the quantity of the material. And gradually it is fed with its own blood and flesh, or virgin’s milk, until the remaining quantity has also been added. Some, however, wait until the whole collection is gathered by coagulation. But as I said, the delay is merely so that the virtue does not fade away, and the coagulation does not fail afterward. [Note this also at the beginning. For as soon as the first matter is elicited from its body, it must be placed for putrefaction; otherwise, it loses its power.] In which opinion Bernhard <note>Bernhard Trevisan, a famous 15th-century alchemist</note> also warns that as soon as the stone is born, it must be fixed.

<margin>The furnace.</margin>
Hitherto there was no need for a furnace. For the matter could be carried out in any temperate room. But now an Athanor <term>athanor: a furnace designed to maintain a uniform heat over a long period</term> is required, which should be constructed with geometric proportion according to the quantity of the material, and so that the external fire can be applied through various degrees. And there is so much in this that even Thomas Aquinas <note>While Aquinas is a famous theologian, several alchemical treatises were falsely attributed to him in the medieval and Renaissance periods.</note> asserted that the entire mastery lies solely in the governance of the fire, through great industry. For the power of a well-governed fire works the stone with modest labor and little expense. One must consider, however, what the tender and very volatile material can bear. A greater heat burns it up and raises it; it does not conjoin. A lesser heat allows the death to waste away and does not unite. Hence, at the beginning of the first degree, it should not transcend the middle. In the process, however, when the quantity has grown and a part is now fixed, an even more intense degree must be used. If you fail, you destroy the work and lose the expense and labor applied. This precept cannot be explained in any other way. <margin>Coals.</margin> Use, therefore, your own intellect and skill. Some establish oak coals as the fuel of the fire; others use juniper coals buried in ashes; some use wicks [Phædro <note>Likely Georgius Phædro, a Paracelsian physician and alchemist.</note> and others use something similar: lamps. And these can provide a certain highly hidden fire: Phædro at the beginning used dung, later ashes, as did Lull <note>Raymond Lull, a major figure in medieval alchemy.</note>.]

It provides instructions on the timing of this stage, the separation of the elements, and the transition to using a regulated furnace (Athanor) for the subsequent stages of the Great Work.</summary>

# Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book IV.

By the number of threads; some say one thing, others another. I have made trial with living coals, which provide a heat that is not violent but nonetheless stable. While up until this point you were permitted to sleep soundly on either ear <note>A Latin idiom meaning to be completely free from worry.</note> and never even wander through the fields and gardens, the work now requires a vigilant and industrious person—unless you possess such skill that you can administer the fire of sloth <note>original: "ignem acediæ"; referring to a low, slow heat that must be carefully maintained so as not to go out or become stagnant.</note> at the same constant degree of heat as the material requires. I commend this to your industry and experience. The one thing to be strived for is that, just as moisture and coldness (the element of water) previously dominated, now heat should prevail, according to the proportion of the material. You should also know that this conjunction is necessary, and that which was previously volatile must now become fixed—which is the reverse of what happened before. 

<margin>Make the volatile fixed.</margin>

For although Philip Ulstad <note>Philip Ulstad (active 1500-1543), a physician and alchemist known for his work on distillation, *Coelum Philosophorum*.</note> used this sulfur by itself for medicine, it nonetheless offers no use in transmutation, nor is it even praiseworthy in treating diseases unless it is further exalted. In this sentiment, we read in the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note>: *“All things come from water. This water is divided into a dryness which they call earth, and an unconverted water, which is preserved for irrigating and moistening the earth; for dry earth does not produce much fruit unless it is frequently moistened from above by its own rainwater. And others say it is necessary that the dragon devour its own tail, and that the infant be nourished, who otherwise could not preserve its life for long, nor provide a return for the labor in such a small quantity.”* <note>original: "Omnia ex aqua... draco deuoret suam caudam..."</note>

Indeed, for certain reasons, I did not proceed to the subsequent steps in my first experiment. Therefore, I will not write now of what I myself have seen and discovered, but I will communicate to you what I judge can be done based on nature and the commentaries of the masters. Do not think that I will put forward trivial or vain things. For although I did not proceed to the "refined work" <note>original: "lautificium"; likely referring to the final, glorious completion of the Stone.</note>—which I do not affect—I have nonetheless witnessed the power of nature through certain experiment. From this, as if from explored ground, I can establish that the philosophers wrote nothing false, even in the steps that follow. The reasons that befell me did not befall you, so you may proceed; but I warn you to be circumspect. For that coagulation unto constancy is not a task for an ordinary mind, yet most certain experience teaches that it is not impossible and must be done by the power of all bodies. You have heard that the elements were separated. But reason and the artisan's logic persuade us that they must be joined again essentially, so that a body nobler than nature gave might exist from them. Nor is that labor reckless. If they acquired nothing by separating them, what was the point of sweating over this?

<margin>The purification of the elements.</margin>

Therefore, each individual part must be exalted separately and stripped of superfluities, so that when they later meet in union, they may conspire with the most powerful forces into a new body. Take away, therefore, from the mercury what is unsuitable, and handle the infant born from sulfur as tenderly as possible, so that it does not lose its strength. Enclose this separated weight <note>The OCR "griuem" is likely "grumum" (clot/mass) or "gremium" (bosom/interior), referring to the concentrated matter.</note> in a suitable vessel <note>original: "geranio"; likely a transcription error for "organo" (instrument) or "vaso" (vessel).</note>. Place it in moderate heat in a triple vessel of ash. Allow it to rest there for eight days, or until you see it, as if thirsty, seeking its own milk. Know, however, that it is impossible but that some mercury remains with it during the proper segregation. But see that it does not exceed the proportion. For it would coagulate more slowly than is right; indeed, a dry nature could not attack this abundance. Thus, your coagulation would be in vain. For the sake of this conjunction of mercury, 

<margin>If he errs here, do not blame me; I wrote clearly enough.</margin>

it can even be without food for quite a long time. But when nourishment is required, open the glass and either from the material itself—well mixed—sprinkle the mercurial moisture in very thin droplets upon the dry body, or moisten it with subtle skill, as much as the matter itself seems to require. For a certain weight is not given here, but is left to the judgment of the artisan, with this rule established: *“See that the moisture does not equal or exceed the dryness, and that the subtle nourishment is not smoked away from the body by the force of the heat.”* <note>original: "Vt deat ne humiditas æquet..."</note> For a union is required, as well as permanence and penetration through the innermost parts. Thus, even after the instillation of the "virgin's milk" <note>A common alchemical term for the mercurial water or solvent used to nourish the "infant" Stone.</note>, they leave the whole in cold ashes so that the moisture may be thoroughly imbibed; and I testify that this does not happen if this powder is placed there alone, or not properly allowed to penetrate the surface. This matter is full of tedium and nausea and is quite prone to error. When the food has been taken in this way, it must also be digested. Therefore, it is returned to its heat for eight days, or as long as is sufficient for the digestion and coagulation of the instilled moisture; plainly in the same way that either sarcocolla <note>A Persian resin used for healing wounds, here used as an analogy for the alchemical binding process.</note> is commanded to be nourished with human milk, or as other chemists attempt the union of separated parts through "inceration" <note>The process of softening a substance to a waxy consistency.</note> or "imbibition." Just as that dryness is then more corporeal and does not flow, even though it appears like an ointment (whence it is also called an oil), so too the instilled mercury must turn out doubled. And I have observed that when it glows, it takes on their appearance and is thoroughly blackened. Others think the mercury is consumed in this way, just as iron is by salt or rust—a phrasing not consistent with the art. It imbibes and fixes it into itself. But if it is too copious, it seeks the bottom, with the blackness floating on top as before, and it does not lose its nature—which, however, was what was sought. When the time for that coagulation passes and it is finished, supply more nourishment, and proceed thus until that black dryness has imbibed all its juice and transmuted it into a constant body. This should be completed in 90 days, so that the time of coagulation corresponds to the time of dissolution—unless some error is found, or it is found remotely, so that it may be finished sooner. Remember that in dissolution, not too much mercury should be used, although perhaps we could stop in the middle of coagulation, were it not that the dispersed virtue must be recalled into one. This, however, must be observed: as the boy now grows (that is, as the dry material increases by the addition of food), in the later nourishings even more "milk" must be sprinkled on, according to the proportion. This is different from the dissolution, where an equal amount was poured in at intervals. Do not hurry. Rejoice if you achieve coagulation, whether it happens in the defined space of three months or longer. That slow hope is compensated by a more bountiful fruit. If you know how to give the fire skillfully, you will profit much. The philosophers advise, and reason persuades, that these things must be carried out according to the rules of the art. Thus it is written in the *Assembly* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: *“I advise that the quicksilver which is made from many things be congealed so that two become three, and four one, and two one; which is the four elements being separated, and reducing the visible parts to unity. Also: Do not pour the water all at once lest the fire be submerged, but pour it in little by little. Cook gently for a long time, etc.”* <note>original: "Moneo vt argentu[m] viuum..."</note>

In the same book are also these words: *“Beware that the secret does not smoke away. When the whole is dry, moisten it again with vinegar.”* <note>Alchemical "vinegar" usually refers to a sharp solvent, not household vinegar.</note> *“And the woman is given who slays her husbands,”* which is nothing other than the mercury being instilled and imbibed by the dry powder in the meantime, or congealing, which happens in distinct turns, as much as it can take in.

In the *Greater Rosary*, which stands under the name of Arnold of Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>, the same matter is discussed clearly in this manner:

<margin>The hinge of the business turns on this; and thus it is the cause of many errors.</margin>

*“Take that water, and pour a certain quantity onto the white earth (note how the names of the same thing vary). Grind it very lightly until the earth has imbibed a fiftieth part of its water. For the earth must first be nourished with a little water. Then the quantity must be increased little by little. Frequently grind the earth and imbibe it by cooking for eight days, and by lightly calcining it. If you wish to mix the whole at once, you are deceived. Imbibe only as much as is missing. Pour the water according to the weight, neither exceeding nor falling short. Always after calcination, or when the water is imbibed, you must let the material settle in dung for seven days.”* And

It cites numerous medieval and Renaissance authorities to validate the specific weights and temperatures required to achieve the "white" stage of the Philosophers' Stone.</meta>

<page-num>65</page-num>
<header>On the Philosophers’ Stone.</header>
<sig>FF 1</sig>

# On the Philosophers’ Stone.

...then proceed by letting it drink <note>The process of "imbibition," where a solid (the "earth") slowly absorbs a liquid (the "mercury") until it is saturated.</note>. See also the rest of chapter 15, from which those words are excerpted; and note that both the weight and the days are named quite clearly, which you will rarely find among other authors. This sentiment is repeated in the *Rosary of the Philosophers* under the name of Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist. The *Rosarium Philosophorum* is a seminal alchemical anthology.</note>, which *Rosary* they think was collected by Bernard of Trevisan, whose words are these: *“Beware that you do not let the earth drink except little by little, and gradually with long grinding <note>original: "tritione"</note>: add to this: after the drying of the earth. Furthermore, the weight is to be noted everywhere in this, lest excessive dryness or superfluous moisture corrupt the things to be administered. Pour on as much as the dissolution added, and in the drinking, dissolve as much as was lacking. The end is whiteness: there it will have exhausted a fiftieth part of itself. Sublime with the strongest fire you can, until it ascends upward in the manner of a most white powder, etc.”* To these words, certain more correct instructions have been added, though you will easily notice the purpose for which they were placed there. Indeed, the rest of the masters teach the same. One should not worry about those sprinklings of mystery and hiding places where the exact truth of the matter is evident.

<margin>Sublimation.</margin>
Note, however, that when he says, *“until you ascend, etc.”* he means that sublimation <term>Sublimation: in alchemy, this often refers to the "exaltation" or purification of a substance, raising it from a "low" state to a "noble" one, rather than just the physical change from solid to gas.</term> by which spaces are not changed, but degrees of nobility. And the whiteness lurking in the blackness goes out from the innermost center to the surface, which is to "ascend." Likewise, what he adds about the fiftieth part being consumed, which the whiteness then receives, must be understood as the total quantity of "virgin’s milk" <term>Virgin’s Milk (lac virginis): a symbolic name for the mercurial water or solvent used to "nourish" the stone.</term> instilled by fiftieths. When, indeed, all has entered and been received, then at last we use a greater fire, and we burn it thoroughly so that it becomes white; without this being present, a greater fire is not required in this part. Some, when it has become white, call it "virgin’s milk" and "arsenic"; and the operation which strives toward this is that "washing" described by Arnold.

<margin>The Latten is the nourished seed of the stone, still black.</margin>
For when he speaks of "washing the Latten" <term>Latten (Laton): a term for the impure "bronze" or base state of the matter before it is purified into silver.</term>, it is nothing other than when that seminal body has been nourished, to lead out the hidden whiteness from the open blackness by a degree of fire, just as if you had purged it by washing with elemental water. Nor is that power of whitening only in the fire, but also in the virgin’s milk. Thus it is said in the *Rosary*: *“Azoth and fire wash the Latten and take away the darkness from it.”* <note>Azoth is the essential transformative agent in alchemy, often identified with mercury.</note> This same whitening through grinding <note>original: "vitionem," likely a typo for "tritionem" (grinding/rubbing).</note> is also called sublimation, the preparation of which is always made with the mercurial water already well known. Nor should it be believed that this whiteness is that which is desired in the perfect Stone; rather, it is compared to the brightness of white lead or tin.

<margin>The Whiteness of the Latten.</margin>
Therefore, this dominion is also ascribed to Jupiter: whose whiteness is not fixed and still retains something of a livid hue. For this reason, the whitening heat must not be excessive, otherwise it escapes. And thus far the first part of the art is completed, and a "medicine of the first order" <term>Medicine of the First Order: A preliminary stage of the Stone that can transform metals but is not yet stable or "fixed."</term> is made according to Geber <note>Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan), the foundational figure of Arabic and Western alchemy.</note>. They say one part of it tinges ten parts into Silver <note>original: "Lunam" (the Moon/Silver).</note>, but not consistently, and with scarcely one degree of quality. Ademarus, explaining Geber, denies that it enters [the metal], because it would rather turn into glass. Nor would it be advisable to lose anything, since this is a counterfeit of true perfection, and those who stop here, where they ought to begin, do poorly. Paracelsus says somewhere that this order of operations is mystical: to calcine, to sublime, to dissolve, to putrefy, to distill, to coagulate, and to tinge. Without a doubt, he drew that from the documents of the teachers. For these operations have thus far been fulfilled in one way, as has been shown.

<margin>Distillation.</margin>
They call it "distillation" when the mercurial water is sent down into the glass over the earth, and is fixed.

<margin>The second operation.</margin>
The second operation is nothing other than a repetition of the above process, by which greater dignity is acquired, and it becomes a "medicine of the second order" for silver. Here, in place of the natural bodies, is the preceding stone whitened by the mineral; for the menstruum <note>A solvent; the liquid part of the work.</note>, mercury is again used, prepared in the same way as the first, or the second part of the first division, but in a greater quantity since the body has now increased and been made larger. Some say that common quicksilver prepared through *oxalmen* <note>A mixture of vinegar and salt used for cleaning metals.</note> can also be used in the same way. But the former way is more advisable. This is described by the artists in almost the same words as the first. For thus it is in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>:

<margin>Note of the three, etc. water through and vinegar.</margin>
*“It is necessary to take one part from our bronze <note>original: "are noſtro"</note> and three parts of permanent water; let them be mixed in a vessel <note>original: "ficto," likely a ceramic pot</note> and cooked into a thick stone, which is cooked and allowed to drink, so that it becomes earth.”* After the three parts have been mixed with the stone through an amalgam or grinding, let both be enclosed in a new flask <note>original: "geranio," referring to an alchemical vessel</note>, and set aside in ashes, whether warm or cold, as before. Likewise, let nine parts be submitted at their own intervals, and once the body is resolved, another blackness emerges; if this lingers, it is a sign that dryness is prevailing. Therefore, more moisture must be added, just as the author says in the *Rosary*: *“If the whole has not been sublimed, let a quantity be added again to that unfixed part, until total elevation by the fire of putrefaction, or by our mercury.”*

<margin>Total solution.</margin>
Where it should be noted what he pronounces concerning "total sublimation." For in the first operation, something dreggy and unfit for dissolving was left behind, known as the "dead head" <term>Dead head (caput mortuum): the useless residue left after distillation or sublimation.</term>. But here, nothing ought to remain.

<margin>Sophistical emulation.</margin>
Therefore, those who have imitated these precepts by "sophistry" <note>Sophistry here refers to "false" alchemy—chemists who followed the literal words but missed the true chemical or spiritual meaning.</note> strive to elevate all of their sublimed Mercury so that no dead head is left; once this is done, they finally add the fixed body and the ferment, with which they might again fix that which they made volatile. [There is some sense to this sophistry. Think on it, then, because we are forbidden to make it public. However, it is explained elsewhere.] This is also completed in ninety days, in the middle of which the "Raven’s Head" <note>A symbol of the *nigredo* or black stage of the work.</note> is born, and then when it is seen, the "decapitation" also proceeds as before. The Mercury which is left from the separation has a consistency like oil.

<margin>Oil of the philosophers. The Dragon.</margin>
Therefore, it is then called the "Oil of the Philosophers." The blackness itself is called the "Dragon," and it is to be nourished in the same way as the infant of the first operation, just as the words of the artists have it: *“The Dragon is born, and it feeds on its own body, and it kills itself, and it is submerged in it, or finally hidden, when the whiteness comes upon it.”* Although it is commanded by the artists that the quantity should be exactly twelve-fold in this work as well, one must nevertheless pay attention to what the nature of the stone can bear, lest excessive moisture hinder the coagulation. Once all the food is consumed, it is transmuted into a higher whiteness by a sharper fire, and it becomes the "Elixir of the Philosophers."

<margin>Elixir, by which name the fixed stone is also called.</margin>
Furthermore, a more abundant heat is used in this second coagulation than in the first, but nonetheless according to proportion, so that the substances do not flee away. Thus stands the second work and the medicine of the second order for silver, which they say can tinge, but more deeply and copiously than the former, though even this does not please [the true master].

It could also be exalted a third time in the same way, but lest the hope of the artist be drawn out longer than is right, or the material become too subtle, and so that it can be perfectly fixed more quickly: one passes to fermentation. Where you will note that this stone is not yet perfect, because it is still subject to the powers of mercury and can be dissolved, which is contrary to the dominating nature of the perfect stone—which is such that it is no longer dissolved by quicksilver except by a singular artifice (of which below), but rather the stone itself converts and changes the mercury. Next, this elixir will waver toward gold, and silv— <meta>catchword: argen- (argentum/silver)</meta>

<summary>This page describes the transition from the first "washing" of the alchemical matter to the second operation, where the substance is nourished with "mercurial milk" to reach a higher state of whiteness. It details the symbolic birth and death of the "Dragon" (the raw matter) and warns against the errors of "sophistical" alchemists who fail to achieve a total sublimation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the alchemical "work," moving from the creation of the base material to the crucial stage of "fermentation." It explores how the Elixir is multiplied and the specific roles of "Red" and "White" ferments, while critiquing the methods of famous alchemists like Paracelsus and Thomas Aquinas.</meta>

<page-num>66</page-num>
<header>Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book IV.</header>

...silver. Therefore, there is a kind of common material for both ferments, and that which is "stained" <note>In alchemy, "staining" or "tinging" refers to the process of changing the color and nature of a base metal into a noble one.</note>, or to which it is committed, takes from it a soul and its entire nature. It is not only fully fixed <note>To "fix" a substance means to make it resistant to heat, preventing it from evaporating or sublimating.</note>, but it also acquires the fixing and transmuting power of the other disposed things into its own nature.

<margin>The administration of fermentation.</margin>
In the beginning, this Elixir is divided into two portions, one of which is destined for the **white ferment**, the other for the **red**, although this depends on the judgment of the artist. The white tincture can also be perfected by fire alone so that it becomes red, and thus that division might rather apply to the white tincture. But then the artist hurries, and the red tincture is prepared more closely by adding the red ferment bit by bit. Regarding the material of the **White Elixir**, it is likewise taught that either the whole of it can be perfected, or a certain part of it; and this equally applies to the other part. This is done so that the resources are not exhausted all at once, and so that everyone can complete as much as they have in their fortune. But the better reason is so that there is an opportunity for **augmentation unto infinity**. For while one part is finished through the ferment, the other part can meanwhile be increased through common mercury <note>original: "mercurium communem"</note> according to the process described above, so that there is always a supply of the material of the Stone, and there is no need to start over from the beginning. I think this is the reason why certain philosophers have "mutilated" the work <note>hiding or omitting steps</note>, because they consider that Elixir only as the material of the Stone; once acquired, we finally arrive at the treasury of nature. It ought to be sought from the inner chambers of nature, made by nature herself, but since so many difficulties stand in the way—making it most difficult to recognize and find—it is more quickly prepared by art than searched for within the enclosures of nature.

<margin>Thomas <note>Likely referring to the alchemical texts attributed to Thomas Aquinas.</note> dared to do this, as he orders one to ferment first, and later adds two operations.</margin>
However, that advice of "mutilation" is not approved by everyone. For it was marked with the crime of perversity and envy, as is reported in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]," one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts.</note>, saying it is a wonder why the envious put the end before the beginning in their treatises, when the master treats first of the "water" and afterward of the "ferment." **Paracelsus** <note>The famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist (1493–1541).</note> could also be accused of this perversity when he orders one to take the <term>rose-colored blood of the red lion</term> <note>A symbolic term for the secret "soul" or tincture of gold.</note> and the <term>glue of the white eagle</term> <note>A symbolic term for sal ammoniac or a specific mercurial substance.</note>, etc. But let those things be dismissed.

That part which we wish to ferment must be united with an equal amount of ferment: white to white, red to red. But here authors vary in part, and in part are quite obscure. The author of the *Thesis at the Entrance of the Assembly* <note>original: "thesum in vestibulo turbæ"</note> judges that fifteen grains of ferment suffice and are suitable for the fermentation of the "Greater Work." Others require an equal quantity of silver, seven times purified, for the white stage. **Thomas** orders one to take only a seventh part. In the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical anthology.</note>, a fourth part is named, but something else is understood. If there is any clarification to be found from the rest of nature, the truth leans toward the first opinion. For such is the power of the ferment that it can animate a hundredfold, indeed even a thousandfold mass, and finally turn the whole into ferment, since its nature is subtle, penetrating, spiritual, and effective. Nor does the addition of a whole "body" <note>unprocessed metal</note> please me. For the Stone must be entirely spiritual. Therefore, both from the bodies and the mercury, the "earthly dregs" <note>impurities</note>—admitted at the first birth of the material—are removed here during preparation and there during dissolution. But there is a reconciliation in this: that through the **Quintessence** <note>The "fifth essence," the purest and most potent form of a substance.</note> even the whole body is turned into a "fifth nature." Since the ratio here is different than in the beginning, the integrity of the body is no obstacle, provided it is perfectly purified. However, since it is nonetheless more sluggish by reason of its astral essence and tincture, it is no wonder if the author of the *Thesis* takes grains, while others take an equal quantity of the prepared body.

<margin>The red ferment.</margin>
Furthermore, in gold, the ferment is the **tincture**, or gold brought to the nobility of a tincture by frequent <term>cementation</term> <note>A process of refining gold by heating it with various minerals.</note>, so that it is no longer recognized as gold; it is clear that it has the power of a tincture from the fact that it changes the "body of the Moon" <note>Silver</note> as much as the tincture itself does. Therefore, it is not ineptly called the "blood of the red lion," which is to be joined with the "glue of the white eagle" and coagulated according to the process of the ancients, so that it becomes the **"tincture of the physicists,"** as found in the book on tinctures by Paracelsus.

<margin>Concerning the tincture of Paracelsus; from which some derive this way.</margin>
While I note these things (to digress briefly from my purpose), there comes to mind what the same author produced in that same book regarding the correction of the method of the ancients. He denies that the ancients fully perfected the tincture; we are led by their discoveries only to the beginning. But what he denies, he soon takes back when he says they led the "mastery of the tincture" to some perfection, and finally, through the process, brought it about that it took on a **Salamandric nature** <note>A nature that can live and thrive in fire without being consumed.</note>, as he says in chapter 5, and he commends that way as one to be followed. Although he involves himself in a stable assertion and deceives his listeners according to his custom, he nonetheless seems to me to want to correct the work only in the beginning: as if those philosophers used a way that was too long for the first operations. If **Astronomy** had been in harmony with **Alchemy**, he says, they would have reached the treasury of the "Red Lion" by a shortcut. It is as if he were saying the abbreviation of the work lies in this: that not "bodies" <note>metals</note> should be taken, but their **"stars"** <note>The essential, celestial power within the metal.</note>, or their tinctures and essences prepared by a short artifice. Once these are joined in the conjunction of the Sun and the "Celestial Mercury," with the Sun dominating, coagulation and exaltation must be procured, so that a true **Elixir** emerges, according to the ancient process in the final part. He calls those alchemical stars of his the "blood of the red lion," which lion he had said in the beginning was the material of the tincture, which through the art of **Vulcan** <note>Alchemical fire.</note> can emerge from three into one essence, and which, with the help of nature and the artist, can transform itself into a "whitening eagle," so that from one thing, two are made, the brightness of the sun not remaining after it has come into the hands of the artist:

<margin>This is perhaps what it means to transform oneself into the whitening eagle.</margin>
let this first be the "star"; the second is the **"glue of the white eagle,"** which although it is sometimes the same as sal ammoniac, here it clearly signifies **Mercury**, just as he gives it the name "eagle" throughout his *Greater Surgery*. He means, I think, that the tincture of gold is to be joined to mercury reduced to its essence (which I see some attempt in the sublimate and the <term>calx</term> <note>A powder produced by roasting or burning a metal.</note> of gold, or a liquor of both dissolved; he himself somewhere says to take hydrargyrum <note>quicksilver/mercury</note> from a sublunary body until it is turned into the nature of mercury, and the whole "waxed" <note>softened to a wax-like consistency</note> mass afterward spontaneously resolves into a mercurial water, which he coagulates, and he deems it worthy of the name **"mercury of the philosophers"**). Both being reduced into one liquid form must be thickened according to the manner of the ancients, in which, if any shortcut exists, the final operation in fermentation must necessarily be understood, as I shall soon explain more fully.

<margin>The process of the ancients according to the opinion of Paracelsus.</margin>
But which process of the ancients does he indicate? The ancients, he says, putrefied the **Spagyric Lily** <note>The "lily" is a symbolic name for the pure alchemical matter.</note>—or that material of the tincture which he called the "Red Lion"—for a **philosophical month** <note>Typically forty days.</note>. I do not disagree. They separated the humid spirits through distillation until the spirits were elevated: which is that very thing I explained above concerning the dissolution and coagulation, which dryness raises out of the humids, and which they name both "distillation" and "sublimation," and it is the first operation in the artifice. He continues: soak the humid spirit again—

<summary>This page discusses the crucial stage of alchemical fermentation, detailing how to multiply the Elixir into "White" and "Red" forms. It critiques Paracelsus and other authorities on the proper ratios of ferment to material and the symbolic union of the "Red Lion" (gold) and the "White Eagle" (mercury).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical critique of alchemical processes, specifically focusing on the transition from traditional methods (Geber, Arnold of Villanova) to the controversial "shorter path" proposed by Paracelsus. It details the preparation of the "Lily" and the final stages of the Great Work.</meta>

<page-num>67</page-num>
<header>On the Philosopher’s Stone.</header>

# On the Philosopher’s Stone.

They imbibed the <term>dead head<note>original: *capite mortuo*. This refers to the useless residue or dregs left after distillation or sublimation.</note></term> and sublimated it until all the dry parts were raised up. He describes the meaning of these words to us according to the operation by which the matter is perfected and even further increased, so that the dry spirits are entirely raised and exalted above the "dead head," perhaps into an elixir. However, he calls the "dead head" the essence remaining after coagulation, and by "humid spirits" he does not mean those previously coagulated, but new mercury. He adds: *they joined the purified humidity and the dry spirits through the pelican a third or fourth time, until the whole dried lily remained at the bottom.* This is a long path. It is certainly not false that in the past, a solution with coagulation was attempted a third and fourth time in its own vessel—which he calls a <term>pelican<note>A "pelican" is a specialized alchemical flask with two side-arms that feed vapors back into the body, used for "circulatory" distillation.</note></term> because of its power to exalt the substance—but this third and fourth repetition had long ago been cut short by Geber, Arnold, and the others.

<margin>Those who immediately add gold and mercury at the start, and join three mercuries together, seem to have done poorly in completing the stone.</margin>
Something new and even greater seems to be promised, by which even the first and second operations might be transformed for the better. Whether this can be done through the reduction of the bodies and the spirit to an <term>astral essence<note>A Paracelsian concept suggesting a celestial or "star-like" purity within matter.</note></term> in the manner I touched upon before is a great question; yet in such obscurity, you will find few, or rather no judges, nor has anyone since Paracelsus shown a shorter way without deception. But we must attend to the rest. He says that in the first century, the <term>Spagyrics<note>Alchemists who follow the Paracelsian method of "separating and recombining" substances.</note></term> made two things from one simple thing. However, when that discovery had been lost for half a century, those who came after took hold of two names for that simple thing, which they called by one word, the **Lily**, as the subject of the tincture. If these things are true, they do not indicate a correction, but a departure from the method and matter of the ancients through ignorance. Truly, by that name, he criticizes the philosophers who succeeded the ancients, while in the meantime the complete craft was broken or not continued—the final part of which follows in the fifth chapter. And it is strange that two names for a simple thing should merge into one, and from that the **Lily** was born, whose matter and subject must necessarily have been either the same as or different from the subject of the ancients. Let all look into this, both the ancients and the moderns. Therefore, these were not empty names. Indeed, I remember such a thing being suggested to me by a certain craftsman of no small erudition and experience, who maintained that the matter of Hermes and Geber was far different. But he has not yet persuaded me.

<margin>One takes away from the other. Both are mercurial, of the same nature and origin.</margin>
Moreover, those two things which were made from one, I also explained above in the separation of the elements. For they are nothing other than that "glue of the body," or double mercury, and the soul or sulfur extracted from it; if these two are joined in turn, they can not undeservedly be called the matter of the tincture, though somewhat closer to it. But in this, I see nothing different from the ancients. Now (he says further) *the imitators of nature putrefied this matter in the earth like a woman for her time, since before this "breaking," nothing comes of it, nor can any secret emerge.* By "breaking in the earth," he means putrefying in the "raw mercury born in the earth"—this is what he wants for the matter from the more recent authors, whose way he approves. He thus denies being the corrector and inventor of this himself, and approves the zeal of the later philosophers at least in this solution, which the facts themselves say should be credited to the ancients. If it must be "broken" [<insert>This "breaking" is mystical, occurring either at the start of the work or during fermentation; however, it is different in each place.</insert>], then before it was broken, it was whole, and was coagulated and fixed by nature. What else is this than a body perfected by nature? It is then "philosophically broken" when it is thoroughly brought back by its own match and familiar water, and is dissolved into two or four parts. No other "breaking" can take place here. Truly, it is certain that the same was known to the ancients. Therefore, there is nothing new here yet. Next (he adds) *they gently abstracted the humid spirits from the matter,* (which means they coagulated them, so that humidity was no longer manifest) *until finally, by a greater force of fire, even the dry spirits were sublimated.* Here the same thing is pronounced again that was said a little before concerning the ancients: and two degrees of fire are described in the coagulation, one very light in the beginning, the other more intense at the end, by which the whiteness is also procured. Finally *the dry spirits (he says) they incorporated, and brought the masterwork of the tincture to some perfection.* That incorporation is nothing other than either the elaboration of the repeated work—so that the earlier dry parts and the later ones are reduced into one body—or fermentation: and both are in the process of the ancients. If now, according to this, the **blood of the red lion** and the **glue of the white eagle** are to be joined and coagulated: what do you judge to have been "corrected"? By all means, take the <term>calx<note>A powder produced by heating a metal or mineral.</note></term> or tincture of the bodies, and the essence of mercury, dissolve, and coagulate and perfect it according to the ancients; Paracelsus knew nothing beyond them, unless he thought that by a single operation both the preparation of the matter and the fermentation happened at the same time, if the tinctures or essential secrets were taken and completed according to only the last part of the ancient craft. However, he describes it thus, and continues from the above where he mentioned the Pelican, namely that for a third and fourth time *the dry spirits were conquered in the Pelican, and thus the Lily was dried out by the help of the Pelican, and fixed by a due increase of fire for so long until, after the changing of all the colors, it became blood-red from blackness, and put on a Salamandrine nature,* <note>A substance of "Salamandrine nature" is one that can survive and even be perfected by the highest heat of the fire, much like the mythical lizard thought to live in flames.</note> which process is true, and also to be held for the future. Thus, after we have learned from the Alchemists to observe the degrees of fire, to vary the vessels, and also (as in the beginning of the book) to digest, distill, sublimate, reverberate, extract, dissolve, coagulate, ferment, and fix: as soon as that **Lily** has been heated in the <term>philosophical egg<note>An oval-shaped glass vessel used for the slow heating of alchemical ingredients.</note></term>, let us cause it to become, by a marvelous appearance of color, blacker than a crow, and then in its own time whiter than a swan, and finally from yellowness into an Indian red (otherwise known as a carbuncle or ruby). These are those teachings of Paracelsus by which he attempted to correct the ancients. But again he contradicts himself: while at first he said we arrived at the principle of the tincture by their guidance, now he says they themselves perfected it all the way to the Salamandrine nature, and then he wants us to imitate their final process. Furthermore, it is now clear enough that he shortens the ancient craft so much that he retains at least one operation, namely that which is described in fermentation.

<margin>Paracelsus seems to have reduced everything to only one fermentation.</margin>
Let us therefore now follow this; and since the ancients prepared their matter with long labor and collected the "seed" from the bodies through raw mercury (as the author of the *Rosarium* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> openly attests that it cannot be done otherwise), let us nevertheless believe that a new way through the "stars" became known to Paracelsus—namely, the blood of the red lion and the glue of the white eagle.

Whoever you are, therefore, who wishes to make the stone from the doctrine of Paracelsus (of which, however, he is not the inventor, but only the shortener, if he writes the truth), take the **tincture of the sun** <note>Gold.</note> and join it with the purest part of mercury elicited and prepared by the astral art of the chemists, namely three parts to one simple part, for clearly the process of the ancients must be observed. Thus an amalgam will be made, and that tincture will sustain the role of the seed and the ferment together, and will have the power of both. Place both, thus joined in the form of an amalgam, in the <term>geranium<note>Unclear technical term, likely a specific type of vessel or furnace setting.</note></term>...

<margin>The process of the Paracelsian stone: but the beginning is revealed.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of alchemical procedures, specifically contrasting the traditional methods of the "ancients" like Arnold of Villanova with the shorter, "astral" methods of Paracelsus. It details the transition from the black stage (nigredo) to the white (albedo) and red (rubedo) stages of the Great Work.</meta>

<page-num>68</page-num>
<header>Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book IV.</header>

<margin>
Heated together in his "Physic" <note>original: *Physico*. Likely referring to a "natural" vessel or a specific type of alchemical furnace described by Paracelsus.</note>.
</margin>
...at the faint heat of the ashes, and let it putrefy; however, at regular intervals, you must still add nine parts of <term>gluten<note>original: *glutine*. In alchemy, this refers to a binding "glue" or a sticky, cohesive substance that unites the different parts of the matter.</note></term>, unless perhaps Paracelsus departed from the rule here as well. Because this "gluten" is something astral, he poured it all in at once so that he would not need to open the glass multiple times. When the substances have remained thus coupled in putrefaction for their allotted month—which must necessarily be shorter than the "month" described by the ancients, for astral things act more swiftly—the blackness will appear; or, as he says, it will turn out blacker than a raven with a wonderful appearance of colors.

<margin>
Gluten consists of white and red things, and it is impossible for the body of Gold to be dissolved otherwise in this art.
</margin>
Know that in this blackness, whiteness is hidden. Therefore, separate the elements now, and bury the "black earth" in another glass; unless here again he disagrees with the ancients and commits that separation to nature alone without manual operation. He allows them to act upon one another so that dryness now overcomes moisture, and gradually <term>fixes<note>Fixation is the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note></term> something of it. He does this despite the fear of the ancients, who believed that an infant is more likely to be suffocated by too much food than nourished by it; because Paracelsian things are "astral," no such thing can happen to them. Nourish the buried matter gradually, or, if another way pleases you, let the <term>dragon devour its own tail<note>A reference to the Ouroboros, symbolizing the circular process where a substance acts upon itself to achieve purity.</note></term> and kill itself for a while without increasing the heat, until the moisture is changed into dryness and the blackness into whiteness. This whiteness must be further cherished with a larger fire—namely of the second degree—so that it is gradually fixed and becomes accustomed to the fire. Thus it will turn out silvery and whiter than a swan, but in such a way that meanwhile the "peacock's tail" is also seen, namely an iris with a wonderful variety of colors. If you were to take the matter out now, you would have white roses, or the "stone for the white." After the whiteness, by increasing the fire to the beginning of the third degree, a yellowness will emerge, which will gradually be followed by a redness, ending in a purple of a bright ruby. The fire at the third degree and higher will fully fix this, and through proper <term>circulation<note>Refining a liquid by continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel.</note></term>, you will adorn it with the highest transmutatory power.

<margin>
See that you understand these things.
</margin>
In the book *On Long Life*, this practice appears: *Reduce the mercury through elevation until it goes into a fixed crystal. Then digest it through resolution and coagulation, and join it with gold so that it becomes its own ferment. Then act according to the prescription of Hermes until the end of the stone.* Such is the Paracelsian way.

It should also be known that the ancients, such as Arnold, mentioned the <term>calx<note>The powdery residue left after a metal is heated or "burned" in air.</note></term> of bodies, or the tincture, and sometimes did not join both bodies; but they also suggest in their experiments that this path is not sufficiently safe or secure. Among those same authors, you may find that the stone produced after the first operation can perform <term>tincturing<note>The act of transforming a base metal into gold or silver.</note></term>; and it is not absurd, if you do not proceed to the second operation, to instead move immediately to the fixation which Paracelsus teaches by a clever management of the fire.

<margin>
Paracelsus favors a "viler" [shorter] stone than the ancients, based on the evidence of the matter.
</margin>
But it is to be feared—as the ancients experienced—that at first, it might not only fail to tincture well, but also be impossible to multiply. Furthermore, the solar power may fade away unless a smaller amount of "water" is used. Therefore, <term>fermentation<note>In alchemy, adding a small amount of gold or silver to "ripen" or "direct" the elixir.</note></term> was invented later for no other reason than this: because the stone generated at the beginning and increased by the second operation was weakened by an excessive mercury-like quantity. Thus its power was destroyed and could not raise itself up again unless an effective ferment was added once more, like a soul. But Paracelsus, despising the fear of the ancients, takes up that which they had not indeed rejected, but had preferred to spend more time on something certain and more fruitful, rather than consuming even a short time on something uncertain, deceptive, and not so fertile. Certainly, if he had followed the process of the ancients, he would not have died in poverty.

Now, it is read that someone made gold and silver, but he saw little of it, and he saw the end of his stone (if indeed he made it himself and did not receive it from elsewhere, as well as the method of making it)—an end which the ancients keep far away from those who act correctly. It is therefore more advisable for this reason to follow them.

<margin>
The "Lesser Work" of Thomas.
</margin>
This also comes to mind: what Thomas Aquinas wrote to Brother Reginald, where he orders him to abstain from the "Greater Work" because of the excessive time and long-term care it requires. But nonetheless, he promises him "mountains of gold" from another work which he prescribes to him. By what other name would you call this except the "Lesser Work"? It seems, therefore, that Paracelsus seized upon this and claimed the invention for himself; it is well known that he suffered from this disease of vanity. Nevertheless, in the discipline of Reginald, there are also three operations, for which Thomas gives the reason: the more the medicine is <term>digested<note>Subjected to gentle, consistent heat.</note></term>, the more subtle, penetrating, and tincturing it becomes. Unless he described both the greater and lesser works at once, but indicated by word of mouth how one might reach the end—though not so profitably—through a single operation. I suspect this is true, as Philosophers tend to be quite crafty in this business. Above, we reviewed several "lesser works." It is possible that by a similarity of words, something is denoted that can be perfected in a few days. But I will say more about Thomas in the explanatory model. Now I shall return to the subject.

It was said above that the ferment is twofold: gold for the red tincture, and silver for the white. There is disagreement among craftsmen about its quantity as well as its quality, since some take only these bodies in a highly purified state, while others take their essences or tinctures. From this, however, we have sought a reconciliation: namely, that those who prescribe a smaller weight should be understood as referring to extracted essences, and the others to whole purified bodies. Let us practice what is easier: take an equal weight of the purest silver for the part of the Elixir which we wish to turn into the white tincture, and an equal weight of pure gold for the other part of the red tincture. The method of joining them is either to melt and fuse the ferment at the fire and afterward mix in the Elixir, stirring it well with a small rod in the crucible until they are united in every tiny part; and once united, let them be thoroughly roasted. Or, by making a common <term>amalgam<note>A blend of a metal with mercury.</note></term>—of gold with fire, of silver without fire—and then mixing them exactly. But there is this difference: here the "philosophical water" is added immediately, whereas there it is not; but after the mixing, the amalgam must first be made. In both cases, let there be one part of the fixed and three parts of the non-fixed, so that the sum of the volatile exceeds the sum of the fixed, just as in the preceding operations. For then both this and the rest correspond to the first practice, just as it is written in the *Rosary*: *Cook them together with a very slow fire and coagulate that ferment so that it becomes like an imperfect body, with the opening of the vessel closed: let it be done in all things in the same way and order as was said.*

<margin>
Three things are here: the ferment, the Elixir, and the water which is the medium for joining the tincture.
</margin>
However, there is a certain "scruple" [doubt] in that book. For it dissolves the ferment not in three parts, but in an equal part of its "mercury water." But this is a certain perversity, introduced by the desire to hide the truth. While he says that it must be done in all things as before, nothing in the practice is to be changed. Therefore, the triple proportion must be retained, otherwise the blackness would not appear, nor would the moisture conquer, since the Elixir is now far stronger than in the previous stages. But when he says: *Dissolve the ferment in an equal part of its mercury water,* he is designating the quantity of the ferment and the fermented thing. He orders that the elixir—which he calls "its mercury water," that is, the water extracted from the same body from which the ferment is taken, and already coagulated into an elixir—be of equal weight...

It also touches upon Thomas Aquinas's "Lesser Work" as a possible source for Paracelsus's techniques.</summary>

<page-num>69</page-num>
# On the Philosophers' Stone

<margin>
Geber asserts this. <note>original: *Hoc asserit Geberus*. Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) was the legendary 8th-century father of alchemy whose works were central to European practice.</note>
</margin>
<margin>
The Peacock’s Tail. <note>original: *Cauda pauonis*. A stage in the alchemical process where the matter in the vessel displays a shimmering array of iridescent colors.</note>
</margin>
<margin>
The white tincture can turn red.
</margin>
<margin>
Gold is made from silver.
</margin>
...to be with the ferment. Otherwise, he commands that one part of the ferment be taken and three parts of the **imperfect body**. This should be understood, according to the custom of such Philosophers, as the combination of the entire fermented body (for here the whole is called the "ferment") with the **mercurial water**, which he calls the "imperfect body" out of a desire for secrecy. Therefore, if the first practice is to be maintained, you should place it for putrefying and dissolving; once dissolved, you will separate it and join it again through nutrition as described above. No **residue** <note>original: *caput mortuum*, literally "dead head." The dross or useless solids left after distillation.</note> appears, because by the power of the essence, the whole is turned into a spiritual body. Here also the time is shorter by half, because of the strength of the **newborn child** <note>A metaphor for the evolving Philosophers' Stone.</note> and the tendency of the mercury toward coagulation, as well as the friendly union of the spiritual parts. For here the soluble body is more spiritual, and thus it is resolved more quickly. In the coagulation, before the whiteness appears, you will see wonderful colors of every kind, which they have called by metaphorical names such as the Iris, the **Peacock’s Tail**, and others; and this happens in the white stage as well as the red. For up to this point, they share the same path. 

When the whiteness has appeared, let the fire be vigorously increased, yet remaining within the nature of silver. For the matter is now **of the moon** <note>original: *lunatis*. Alchemists used "Luna" to refer to silver.</note>, silvery, marble-like, fixed, and does not easily suffer damage from the fire. And then, as Geber says, there is no longer a need for opening or changing the vessel. For here it is true what they write: that the work is **PERFECTED** in one vessel. You must know, however, that this white tincture can also be turned into a red one by a more abundant fire, just as I said above; and the author of the *Rosary* <note>Referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> confirms this from Arnold [of Villanova], saying: *Through decoction alone, whiteness can come to redness; by thus continuing the fire, our white matter, if diligently cooked, is most excellently reddened. Let it be cooked with a dry fire and dry calcination until it is as red as cinnabar, to which you should henceforth add no water nor any other thing until the red is cooked to completion.* He says this clearly enough. From this arose the axiom that "all gold was previously silver," and that the best silver is, in its near potentiality, gold—as Cardano also wrote. You see, then, that your hope is indeed prolonged, but the expenses are diminished. Therefore, if you prefer the latter to the former, you can use only the white ferment; and when the perfect whiteness appears, you may multiply one part and perfect the other part into the red. 

But there is a secondary reason why they nonetheless give instructions concerning the red tincture. I suspect that while it can be done this way, the tincture is not as effective as if it were animated by a red ferment. It is not obscure that Paracelsus seized upon this as an opportunity for his "abbreviation" <note>Paracelsus was famous for claiming he could perform alchemical works faster than the "ancients."</note>; but while he followed one thing, he neglected another, and in his vain zeal, he called himself the "corrector of the ancients." Remember that in the fermentation and preparation of the red tincture, the heat is always increased, because the body is most perfect and must be cooked to the highest nobility. The rest is consistent. For here too occurs the sending of equal parts of the ferment and the **elixir** by flux, in a stronger fire for several days; afterward, the mixture is drenched with mercury and dissolved, as it is said: *Take a part from the second composition, and a part from the ferment of gold, and place upon them the clean water of sulfur (mercury), etc.* Here too appears the blackness, the peacock’s tail, the silvery whiteness, fluidity, and finally the highest redness of a toasted ruby. One must, however, pay attention to the degree of **fixation**, lest you leave the elixir imperfect. Thus, if a part of it, placed on a glowing metal plate, gives off smoke, it is not yet fixed enough; but if it flows like wax without smoke and penetrates the metal, it is sufficient. If not, it must be returned to the fire until it has acquired its constancy.

---

<margin>
Why multiplication is kept silent.
</margin>
<margin>
German chatterers publicly professing to be secret Philosophers. <note>original: *Germanici graculi*. A "graculus" is a jackdaw, a bird known for noisy chattering; the author is mocking those who talk too much about alchemy without understanding it.</note>
</margin>
<margin>
Projection. <note>The final act of alchemical transmutation, "projecting" a small amount of the Stone onto base metal to turn it into gold or silver.</note>
</margin>
<margin>
The form of transmutation.
</margin>
It follows now to speak of **multiplication** and the art of **projection**. For as Geber says, unless this is understood, the elixir does not enter or tinge the metal because of its subtlety; some medium is required so that the ignoble and the most noble can be joined, just as the soul adheres to the body by the mediation of the spirit, heat, and moisture. And multiplication and augmentation unto infinity is the only thing that can fulfill a bold hope and attain that dignity of the Stone leading to immense treasures. But my purpose was only to assist medicine, and nonetheless to praise the power of GOD in nature by some specimen. I judge it sufficient, therefore, if you can tinge even a little, and yet more greatly assist the health of your neighbor in sickness—to say nothing of that inexhaustible thirst for knowing the ancients. 

Thomas [Aquinas] <note>Many alchemical works were falsely attributed to the theologian Thomas Aquinas in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> judged it a most grievous sin to reveal the secret of multiplication and augmentation unto infinity (for these are two operations) to secular men. And certainly, it is to be feared lest those German chatterers seize these things and, once translated into the vernacular language, they be prostituted even to rascals. Therefore, it is better to keep this part in secret. I add this for the sake of good men: that in the works of Geber, Bernard [Trevisan], Thomas, and others, the precepts of this matter are clear enough, but they are not understood by anyone who does not know the entire practice to a hair's breadth. I append the words: *The multiplication of the elixir happens in two ways: one by the reiteration of solution and coagulation in the stone; the other by the projection of the first stone upon a white or red body in such a quantity that the same body is also turned into medicine. And then these shall be put together to dissolve in their own water and menstruum, and thus the first elixir is the ferment of such a tincture, etc.* 

If you are well-versed in the authors and the practice described above, you will understand the matter. But do not let yourself be called away by abstruse thoughts, as if something mystical were being said. Many are hindered by such a fantasy, so that they do not understand even the plainest things; and though a thing is called by its own name, they still do not believe it to be so, having so fascinated themselves with those hidden mysteries. 

Regarding **projection**, if its medium has been prepared through multiplication, the matter is easy, and has been sufficiently explained by us in the *Chemical Precepts*. If the elixir has the form of an oil or water, metal plates are extinguished in it, or it is dripped onto glowing metals. But if it is a powder, the metals must be reduced to their **prime matter** <note>original: *primam materiam*. Often referring to reducing metals to a liquid mercury-like state.</note> through mercury. Sometimes, however, it is also sown onto the glowing plates of purified metals. Pico [della Mirandola] testifies that he saw entire things changed; let his credit remain with him. For the tingeing of mercury, an example exists in the letter of a certain servant of Paracelsus, which Neander published. But Thomas had long ago described the practice to Reginald in these words: *Take a goldsmith’s tile (a triangular earthenware crucible) and coat the inner part with a little tallow. Put in as much mercury as corresponds to the proportion of the medicine and place it over a very gentle fire. When the mercury begins to smoke, throw in the medicine enclosed in wax or paper (as assayers do), and place a firm, broad ignited coal over the hole of the crucible already prepared, and apply a strong fire. When the whole has been melted, pour it into an ingot mold coated with tallow (the oblong iron vessel of assayers and minters), and you will have the purest gold or silver according to the nature of the ferment applied. If, however, you wish to multiply your medicine, do this in horse dung just as I have taught you by word of mouth, etc.* Thus says Thomas.
