<meta>This page continues the discussion of the final stages of the Great Work—multiplication and projection—and begins a commentary on the foundational text of alchemy, the Emerald Tablet.</meta>

<header>Alchemical Commentary Part II, Book IV.</header>

Geber says that some things tinge sevenfold, some tenfold, some a hundred parts, others a thousand, others even infinitely; and Bernhard expressed an incredible sum, just as others are quite generous in this matter. It was said above that after the first operation, one part tinges ten, or seven as Geber says; after the second, even more, and some claim fifty, or seven times seven. After fermentation, multiplication happens by hundreds; then by thousands in **projection** <note>The act of casting the Stone onto base metals to transform them into gold.</note>. Truly, it reaches infinity by reason of augmentation. For there is no infinite power in a finite thing. Therefore, it is not to be understood as if one part could tinge infinite parts. The ancients were not so delirious. And thus, whatever number you put forward, you can justify it. But enough on these things for now.

<margin>Power in medicine.</margin>
In medicine, for preserving health and removing diseases, no fewer miracles are ascribed to it. It is said that this **tincture** <note>The Stone in liquid or powder form used as a universal medicine or elixir of life.</note> renews the whole body, strengthens all the spirits, invigorates the nature of all limbs, and so on for all the rest; so that it serves not only for healthy living but also for achieving a long life like that of the first fathers <note>The biblical patriarchs, like Adam or Methuselah, who lived for centuries.</note>. Yet, in this dross of a world, no one should hope for such a thing for themselves, nor do we read of any artist who procured it for himself. Therefore, many of these claims must be considered hyperbolic. Perhaps medicine would be content if it purified the blood, brightened and strengthened the spirits, expelled poisons, removed fevers, and cured apoplexy, gout, paralysis, epilepsy, and other great evils more successfully than common medicines. Thus, by God's favor, it would grant a sufficiently comfortable health to good and worthy men for carrying out the duties of this life, which at last a peaceful old age and a pious death would succeed. No one would want to be a **Methuselah** <note>The longest-lived person in the Bible, said to have reached 969 years.</note> unless he were a tyrant. The things that the Paracelsians and that wicked impostor Arnaldus <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist often criticized by later writers for being too obscure or fraudulent.</note> declaim are far too futile. Thus I think I have completed this task, as much as I have discovered myself, learned from the ancients, been able to attain by reason, and judged lawful to reveal. If readers think I have used more words than they would like, let them consider that it was done not without purpose: that the abundance of words might suspend and delay crude minds <note>A common alchemical trope: writing verbosely to hide secrets from the "unworthy" or "vulgar" reader.</note>. Now I will add some dogmas of the ancients and moderns, by which the described Theory and Practice are confirmed.

---

->THE EMERALD TABLET<-
->OF HERMES.<-

**I**t is true, without falsehood, certain and most true. That which is below is like that which is above. And that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of the **one thing**. And as all things were from one, by the meditation of one: so all things were born from this one thing by adaptation. Its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon. The wind carried it in its belly. Its nurse is the earth. The father of all **perfection** <note>original: *thelesmi*. A term of uncertain origin, likely from the Greek *telesmos*, meaning "completion" or "consecration."</note> of the whole world is here. Its power is complete if it be turned into earth. You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently, with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth to heaven, and again descends to the earth; and receives the power of the things above and below. Thus you have the glory of the whole world. Therefore all obscurity shall flee from you. This is the strong fortitude of all fortitude: because it shall overcome every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing. Thus the world was created. From this shall be wonderful adaptations, the mode of which is here. Therefore I am called **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>The "Thrice-Great Hermes," the legendary founder of alchemy, associated with the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth.</note>, having three parts of the philosophy of the whole world. What I have said concerning the operation of the Sun is complete.

---

->COMMENTARY.<-

<margin>Ramus <note>Likely Petrus Ramus or a similar commentator.</note> also explained this in his chemical letters according to Hortulanus, Lull, Arnaldus, and the experience of the thing seen with his own eyes. See below concerning the followers of Lull.</margin>
Bernhard Hortulanus <note>A 14th-century commentator on the Emerald Tablet.</note> and others produced this tablet and illustrated it with their commentaries, as did Paracelsus in his writings on the *Apocalypse of Hermes*, which however has not reached me. There are those who bring forward some other version, perhaps fashioned for their own private dreams. But this version quite suitably designates the art described so far, although with a sharp brevity joined with obscurity. It notes the matter and the subject of the work through its essential parts, and simultaneously the procreating causes, using the philosophers' accustomed likeness of father and mother; namely, that a father and mother must concur to give birth to one miraculous thing, through marriage, in a certain spiritual bedchamber. That is: **gold, silver, and mercury** are hammered home by all Philosophers even to the point of nausea, and it is understood from the end as well, since the offspring is always like the parents; and in the **spermatic body** <note>The "seed" or life-force of metals.</note> lies hidden the potential of the act of generating: nor can gold and silver be made by any art, unless the seminal power conceived from them is introduced. Therefore, those are not to be listened to who dream for themselves of I-know-not-what, to be found in Utopia rather than in the nature of things, and who by this very fact manifestly expose their trifles to the light; because they can produce nothing from that principle they dreamed up, other than sophisms that should be publicly punished. Nor is **Venus** <note>Alchemical symbol for copper, but here used to represent the spiritual attraction or "spirit."</note> anything other than the spirit which we call Mercury, which is made clear by Democritus and all others: that nothing foreign ought to enter; but only that which is kin to metals in the genus of its material essence; from which they are made, and into which they can again be reduced, and it is called "water that does not wet," "permanent water," and by other names. When he says its nurse is the earth, it is understood as the earthy body, which, remaining at the bottom of the glass, is not entirely dissolved. [Know that these mysteries do not have only one meaning: therefore artists vary in their explanation.] For in that body lay hidden the soul or that seminal principle; and it was brought up as if by nursing. It is snatched away, however, and produced from the earth through philosophical **exaltation** and the separation of the elements. It cannot be understood as the matter of imbibition, or the **dragon's tail**, or the **virgin's milk** <note>Various alchemical terms for preparatory liquids or stages of the matter.</note> by which the newborn infant is nourished. For although mercury was previously called earth, after the **sulphur** has arisen, it no longer maintains that office and name, unless one wishes Hermes to have obscured it by such a **catachresis** <note>A rhetorical term for the strained or ironic misuse of a word.</note>. But there is also another "earth" when he says: *Its power is complete, if it be turned into earth:* which is that Solar and Lunar body, reduced through putrefaction into earth and ashes, which we call **black sulphur**, for which the word "earth" is also used by other artists. But as enigmas and mysteries have many interpretations, so does this. Thus others distinguish the meaning in this way: *If it be turned into earth, you shall separate the earth from the fire,* [a coagulation such that it is not fiery but earthy. In the beginning of the first operation, it is water. From this becomes...

<summary>The author discusses the multiplication of the Stone and its medicinal uses before presenting and commenting on the "Emerald Tablet," the central text of alchemical philosophy attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of the Emerald Tablet, focusing on the elemental transitions and the movement between the earthly and celestial realms, before transitioning into the alchemical principles of Geber.</meta>

<header>On the Philosophers' Stone.</header>

*...earth: then air: finally fire. See therefore that you do not anticipate.* <note>original: "terra: inde aër: Ultimo ignis. Vide ergo ne anticipes."</note>] etc.; it is as if he says: if the power of that wind or **mercury** <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the fluid, volatile principle of matter.</note> has attacked the earth and dissolved the body—which is to say, it has turned its strength toward restoring gold and silver—then the earth must be separated from the fire. This means leaving the earth at the bottom, while the fiery parts, which are that elevated blackness, are set apart by the <term>severing of the crow's head</term> <note>The "severing of the crow's head" (decollatio corvi) refers to the end of the *nigredo* or blackening stage, where the impurities are removed.</note>, or the division of the elements. This opinion seems to agree with practice, even more clearly. And then this also appears when he says, *its nurse is the earth*, meaning that this wind ought to be nourished by the earth, not drawn out from drinks; this is what Thomas <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Thomas Aquinas, a name attached to several alchemical treatises.</note> asserts, and in the *Manual* it is called the <term>Ostrich’s stomach</term> <note>A technical term for an alchemical furnace or vessel capable of "digesting" or breaking down metallic substances.</note> growing in the earth. Thus, the subtle is the aerial and fiery part; it is that which remains coagulated at the bottom. And yet it differs from the other not in substance, but in quality. He further adds *that this miraculous thing ascended from the earth to heaven*, which is nothing other than it being led out of the body and **sublimated** <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects again as a solid; symbolically, it represents spiritualization.</note> through the surface upon which it floats. For to the Philosophers, "Heaven" is the upper concavity of the glass vessel. But *it descends again into the earth*, which happens in **coagulation**; where that which previously floated now settles at the bottom; what previously flew is now fixed. And thus it acquires the nature of both volatile and fixed things, which accords with this axiom: *that which is above is like that which is below*, etc., according to the distinction of act and potentiality. For in this art, one must make the fixed volatile, and from the volatile, in turn, make the fixed, just as practice shows.

Furthermore, you shall establish this: when you consider that in the stone of the first operation, there is not only that "celestial sulfur" present, but also <term>virgin's milk</term> <note>A common alchemical term for a white mercurial solvent or the purified matter at a specific stage.</note>. The former is constant by itself, while the latter is inconstant; yet in union, both natures merge, and finally, fixedness alone dominates in the ultimate perfection. It overcomes every subtle thing with that fortitude—or rather, the strongest stone—and penetrates every solid thing. This should be understood regarding things analogous in nature; that is, any mercury and coagulated metals. For like acts upon like in a determined way.

The world, he says, was created just as he fashions his stone: which he explains regarding the watery and dark face of the world, in which the earth lay hidden before light and separation. And certainly, when the **blackness** <note>The *nigredo* stage of decomposition and purification.</note> has arisen, no other face is discerned. The matter indeed moves and fluctuates in the glass; but nothing except black is seen.

Thus it is manifest that the practice shown above agrees with the Hermetic discipline. However, it seems he wishes for Paracelsus's shortcut, as he mentions neither the repetition of the work nor fermentation. Indeed, at the end, he mentions only the operation of the Sun <note>The "Sun" (Sol) is the alchemical symbol for gold or the perfected masculine principle.</note>. Therefore, it can be believed that he fashioned his work solely from the Sun, which is the most powerful operating cause. But these things were also discussed in the declaration of the practice.

# THE DOCUMENTS OF THIS ART
## ACCORDING TO GEBER.

<margin>
We disclose the arts investigated by us alone for ourselves alone, and not for others, yet they are most true and entirely complete.
</margin>
Here the author attributes to himself the discovery of various medicines, and especially that which is most perfect, which alone can take the place of ten tinctures. *We have found one medicine,* he says, *through long inquiry, the greatest labor, and certain experience, by which the hard becomes soft, the soft is hardened, the fugitive is fixed, and the foul is illuminated with a marvelous splendor.* However, how that medicine is to be prepared, he denies having declared in one single place, but has scattered it through various books, one of which explains the other. Nevertheless, he especially commends to us the "Sum of Perfection," although he also proclaims the discovery of truth, which he claims has nothing of the Sophists <note>In alchemy, a "sophist" was a term for a fraud or someone who used deceptive, non-alchemical methods.</note> in it. We shall collect what seems most clear.

<margin>
We do not hand down our science in a continuous discourse, but dispersedly in various chapters. The properties of medicine about which Rogelius spoke.
</margin>
He describes seven properties of the universal medicine in the book on the *Discovery of Truth* or *Perfection*: which are: 1. **Oiliness**, which in **projection** <note>The final stage where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transform them.</note> provides the melting and opening of the matter. 2. **Subtlety** of the matter, which provides entry, immediately necessary after melting. 3. **Affinity**, which ought to exist between the elixir itself and the thing to be transmuted, which is necessary for coherence. 4. **Radical humidity**, which congeals and solidifies the restrained similar parts. 5. **Clarity** of purity. 6. **Fixing earth**. 7. **Tincture** <note>The coloring or transforming power.</note>.

You will likewise find these seven properties in the described elixir. And each one also proves that it can be made from no other thing except mercury, coagulated and dissolved. For he wishes it to be entirely mercurial, just as these axioms hold: *Mercury coagulated by a medicine which adheres to it most deeply, and is mixed with it through its smallest parts before its flight; which medicine must be of a more liquid melting than the bodies themselves, a most subtle and pure substance, adhering to it by its nature, and likewise very easy to melt.* Now, nothing is more familiar to mercury than mercury itself; next gold, and thirdly silver. It follows from this that it must be made from mercury. And so he says: *From mercury we can draw out the medicine and perfect it.* Likewise: *Mercury does not allow itself to be divided into the parts of its composition, but either remains whole or flees whole; and in it is the cause of perfection.* In no other thing is this perfection found. For it overcomes fire, and is not overcome by it, but rests in it in a friendly way. If you cannot accept this regarding perfected gold—(distinctly, however, since there is one gold of the art and another of nature, both indeed agreeing, but in their proper place and preparation)—you will find it in no other thing in all of nature. Elsewhere he also adds: *Those bodies which contain more mercury are more perfect. In all your compositions, strive so that mercury overcomes.* And if you can achieve perfection through mercury alone, you will be a seeker of the most precious perfection. Likewise: *The medicine is drawn from those things which are most closely joined to the bodies. But there is no other thing as suitable as mercury. Therefore, this is the true medicine.* And: *The medicine is taken from mercury while it remains in its nature, but receiving fixation, which is done through sublimation.* Furthermore: *When quicksilver, prepared into a medicine by our art, is cleansed and reduced into a most pure and shining substance: if it is projected upon imperfect things, it illuminates them and perfects them by its fixation.* And it ought to bring five prerogatives especially: namely, purity, color, fusion, permanency, and weight, as he says elsewhere. It is clear from these things that Geber takes his tincture from mercury sublimated by the art, that is, exalted and fixed. Now, however, it cannot be truly and perfectly done except through perfected and fixed bodies. And indeed, he himself confessed that it cannot be fashioned from the bare, fleeting, and crude substance, when he said, *it is indeed from mercury, but not perfected, as it is from the bodies.*

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of alchemical principles, moving from the general elemental theory of the Emerald Tablet to the specific practical instructions of the medieval authority Geber regarding the extraction of the "Medicine" from metals.</meta>

<header>Alchemical Commentary. Part II. Book IV.</header>

Likewise: The **Medicine** <note>The "Medicine" refers to the Elixir or Philosophers' Stone, which heals "sick" (imperfect) metals by turning them into gold or silver.</note> is drawn out from the metallic bodies themselves, prepared with their own sulfur and arsenic; similarly, it is prepared from sulfur and arsenic alone (which are symbolic names used in the craft of the stone for the elixir, etc.), and likewise from the bodies alone. However, it is drawn more easily and appropriately from quicksilver [mercury] alone, though not more perfectly. He judges therefore, as the present practice holds, that it must be led out from the bodies. But since the extraction must be done through some solvent, or by heat alone, or by grinding and pressing, or other means, the question is: what must be done here? Geber answers that the ease of extraction lies in mercury, hinting that the **Mercury of the Philosophers** <note>A refined, "living" form of mercury, distinct from the common liquid metal.</note> must be made by means of actual mercury. Note here that common mercury cannot be used, but another prepared by art, in which alone bodies liquefy. This consists of soul, body, and spirit, and is prepared with great effort—not without quicksilver, yet it is not quicksilver. For like easily takes to like, the subtle is joined to the subtle; and again, a kindred thing fixes a kindred thing, since it was first fixed itself. By "bodies," the perfect metals [gold and silver] are understood. And so, in his discourse on the discovery of truth, he describes their properties:

First, they must possess within themselves a most subtle and incombustible earth, fit for <term>fixing</term> <note>Fixation is the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note> and entirely fixed with its own radical moisture.

Second, they must have an airy and fiery humidity uniformly joined to that earth, such that if one is volatile, so is the other; and that this humidity is above all other humidities, awaiting the heat of the fire until the complete term of its sufficient thickening, as much as its completion requires, and that it remains inseparably attached to the earth's humidity without evaporating.

Third, the natural disposition of the moisture must be such that, by the benefit of its oiliness, it tempers the earth attached to it into a greasy, homogeneous mixture through the conversion of each into the other across all their properties. This union and inseparable bond must be so equal that, after the final stage of preparation, it provides a good <term>fusion</term> <note>The ability of the material to melt and flow like wax or metal.</note>.

Fourth, this oiliness must be of such purity of essence, and so artificially cleansed from every combustible thing, that it does not burn the things with which it is intimately joined, but rather protects them from combustion.

Fifth, it must have within itself a clear and splendid <term>tincture</term> <note>The coloring principle that allows the Stone to change the color of base metals to silver (white) or gold (red).</note>, either white or red, clean, incombustible, and fixed.

Sixth, the whole compound, once <term>waxed</term> <note>Inceration: the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it has the consistency of soft wax.</note> with its final completion, must be of such subtlety and thinness of matter that, after the final term of its boiling, it remains in a state of very thin fusion during <term>projection</term> <note>Projection: the final act of throwing the Stone onto base metal to transform it.</note>.

These properties can belong to nothing in the entire assembly of metals except the perfect metals. If you weigh these sayings carefully, you will find that something has also been added regarding the method of preparation and the nature of the tincture composed from it, which, just as it agrees in nature with its beginnings, so it agrees in its effect in dyeing the bodies.

<margin>Mercury from Mercury.</margin>
To these words you can add this: since the medicine must tinge—namely, making things white or yellow—he admits this cannot be accomplished without a mixture of a tinging thing that is of that nature. This substance of mercury, he says, is drawn out from the bodies and from quicksilver according to nature, since they are found to be of one nature. In another place, he even teaches with such subtle phrasing: *Study to resolve the Sun [Gold] or the Moon [Silver] into its own dry water, which the common people call mercury: and do this so that a twelve-fold portion (of prepared mercury) contains one part [of the metal].* It seems Geber immediately places the perfect Solar or Lunar body in a double-twelve-fold amount of Mercury at the start, which is reasonable. Others wait for the <term>ferment</term> <note>A small amount of gold or silver added to the "Medicine" to act as a yeast or seed, directing the transformation toward that specific metal.</note> of the perfect body. For if you govern it well with a slow fire, you will find that within forty days that body is converted into pure water. The sign of dissolution is **BLACKNESS** appearing on top. But if you strive to complete both works, the white and the red, dissolve each ferment by the method already described and save it. Our quicksilver is extracted from quicksilver, which we want for a ferment, etc.—which doctrine is the same as ours. It is therefore certain, according to Geber’s opinion, that the matter of the stone is that very thing which he named in the work.

Since there are two perfect medicines, one for the white and the other for the red, both are nevertheless from one principle and nature, nor do they differ except by the addition of color, or as others say, the ferment. Geber speaks thus: *The Solar and Lunar medicines are of one essence and manner of acting (the matter is the same and the method of preparation is the same); there is only the addition of the yellowing color, which is perfected by the purest substance of fixed sulfur, so that if we wish to make gold, the medicine contains this color; if silver, it does not.* This can be explained in two ways, as in practice: most especially, however, regarding the white elixir being perfected into the red only by a longer stay in the fire. For he says: *It does not differ at all in essence from the medicine of the second order, except by the subtlest degrees of preparation in its making, and by a longer persistence of labor.* Likewise: *The Solar medicine needs one degree in the complete preparation of its pigments, the Lunar another; namely, the former needs the administration of the tinging sulfur, while the latter does not.* These things seem to me to be said regarding the exaltation of quality. For otherwise, even the white Elixir needs a white ferment. However, I will not fight over an ambiguous phrase. Other precepts of general preparation follow in another chapter. *It does not change,* he says, *unless its nature is altered: nor is it mixed thoroughly in its depths unless it is first separated forever through the refining preparation described under sublimation. Its impression does not remain unless it is fixed. It does not shine unless the most brilliant substance is drawn out from it by fire in its own way. It does not provide perfect fusion unless it can harden the soft and soften the hard: which happens if it is fixed by the trial of fire's governance, and the moisture is deleted to the extent that the hard or soft requires. If he wants the soft to be hardened, let him use a vehement fire; if the opposite, a gentle one, for that preserves moisture. The cause of great weight is the subtlety of the substance of the bodies and the uniformity in their essence.* It must therefore densify the parts. Subtlety must be sought both in the preparation of the bodies to be changed and in the perfecting medicine, etc.

<margin>On preparing mercury through sublimation.</margin>
<margin>The division of prepared mercury into two parts: a present question of the craft.</margin>
<margin>And place it in a corner [aside].</margin>
<margin>Note that the fixed and non-fixed are of the same nature and root: which, while it is dissolved again as if by fission, differs like the raw, etc.</margin>
What the specific practice of the perfect white medicine is may be learned from these words, though they require a <term>Delian swimmer</term> <note>A classical proverb meaning a very skillful person; referring to the difficulty of Geber's "sea" of text.</note>. *Take that well-known stone,* he says, *and by the method of separation, divide its purest part, and set it aside* (which is: from the mercury, draw out the subtlest substance separated from the coarse by sublimation). *Then, of that which is the purest part, fix some, and leave some. When it has been fixed, dissolve from it whatever was soluble; what was not soluble, send to <term>calcination</term> <note>Calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "ash."</note>; and from here, repeat the solution over the same, until again that which is soluble in it is entirely dissolved* (which are to be understood as the coagulation of its mercurial part, whereby while it is dissolved, the body is simultaneously fixed; and the resolution of the body. For the whole is not dissolved in one turn, but the mercury is changed part by part, which he calls calcination and repeated solution, meaning no other solution than that which is done by mercury). *Let this order be kept twice, until a greater quantity is dissolved.* (For in the beginning, the whole cannot be dissolved, as we indicated above.) *Afterward, mix all the things that emerged from the solution and <term>coagulate</term> them.*

<meta>This page continues the practical instructions for the alchemical work, specifically detailing the creation of the "White Stone" (for silver) and the "Solar Medicine" (for gold) according to the medieval authority Geber, with interpretive glosses likely added by a later commentator referencing Paracelsus.</meta>

<page-num>73</page-num>
<header>On the Philosophers' Stone.</header>

# On the Philosophers' Stone.

vessels: <gloss>that is, the "raven’s head" <note>original: *caput corvi*; the black stage of the alchemical process signifying the death/decomposition of the matter</note> must be collected and placed in a glass vial <note>original: *geranio*</note> through frequent separations, and sprinkled with its own "milk" <note>a mercurial liquid used to nourish the "seed" of the stone</note> to be coagulated.</gloss>

Then by roasting lightly, preserve the coagulated matter in a tempered fire, until a greater fire can be administered to it as required. <gloss>Since the coagulated matter is still quite tender, it must be accustomed to the fire little by little, until a suitable fixity <note>original: *fixitas*; the ability of a substance to remain stable and not evaporate when heated</note> is generated within it, just as was said at the end of the first work.</gloss>

From there, proceed according to the first order of solution, until everything that is soluble within it is dissolved again. Coagulate it once more, and keep it in a tempered fire, until a greater force of fire can again be applied for its perfection. <gloss>This is the process of the second operation, which corresponds to the first in every way, except that here the whole is dissolved, and the substance becomes greater in power and mass.</gloss>

Repeat all of these steps four times. <gloss>This is that multifaceted and long path which Paracelsus seems to take, but Geber himself later shortens it by the addition of a "ferment" <note>original: *fermenti*; a substance, usually pure gold or silver, added to the medicine to "tilt" it toward that specific metal</note>.</gloss>

And finally, calcine <note>original: *calcina*; to reduce a substance to a powder by high heat</note> it in its own manner, and thus by sufficiently administering it, you have revived the most precious earth. <gloss>This is the completion of the white elixir, which is brought to a silvery whiteness by the fire of a reverberatory furnace; this is what he calls "calcinating."</gloss>

Now take a certain quantity of the upper part which you had not fixed. <gloss>Now he approaches the "multiplication" and the preparation for "projection" <note>the act of throwing the finished medicine onto base metal to transform it</note>, which is done by means of the same mercury.</gloss> Join it with the subtle part of this earth in the manner of a union by the smallest parts, which is done through sublimation <note>original: *sublimationem*; here meaning a "physical" or natural raising of the substance’s essence</note> (but understand this as a natural sublimation based on the analogy of the things above) until the fixed and the non-fixed are raised up entirely. <gloss>Let both become of the same nature—that is, a part of the virtue of the Elixir.</gloss>

But if it is not raised up entirely, add to it again a quantity of the non-fixed part, until it suffices for its elevation. <gloss>For in order for both to share the same nature, the whole must also be made volatile; this does not happen if you have poured on too little moisture.</gloss>

<margin>Note the ambiguity of sublimation.</margin>
Therefore, when it has been raised, let its sublimation be repeated. <gloss>Or rather its coagulation, and yet the "sublimation of power" also fixes the matter.</gloss> Continue until the whole is fixed by this administration.

When the whole has been fixed, repeat the process with a (hundredfold) quantity of the non-fixed part; after the quantity is "drunk up" <gloss>meaning once it is dissolved and then coagulated again. For this work must be repeated quite often, and likewise the medicine is produced</gloss> through the technique known to you, until the whole is raised up again.

When this is done, let it be fixed again, until it achieves an easy fusion along with its glowing. <gloss>Which means that the medicine must be tested by the transformation of a metallic plate or mercury; if the test results in silver, it is correct. If not, it must be fixed more fully.</gloss>

This is the medicine which transforms every imperfect body, and every kind of quicksilver, into the most perfect silver.

Hitherto Geber has taught how to make the White Stone in the same manner as was said above, except that he spoke more obscurely, prescribed more operations, and remained silent regarding the true names of things, concealing weights and times—which, however, you will easily recognize from the things said previously. He treated the preparations of the bodies and the mercury, the vessels, and the manner of heat in a scattered fashion. Likewise, he mentions certain colors, namely blackness, whiteness, redness (or yellowness), and brilliance. But let us also look at the precepts concerning the **Solar Medicine**. <note>The "Solar Medicine" is the Red Elixir used to create gold.</note>

<margin>Fermentation.</margin>
*“In order that the solar medicine may be prepared,” he says, “an addition of non-burning sulfur <note>original: *sulphuris non adurentis*; a metaphorical term for the "ferment" or the essential color extracted from the matter by long-lasting fire</note> is made to the previous work: through fixation and calcination, so that you attend to the perfect administration skillfully, and to the multifaceted manner of solution with much repetition, until it becomes pure—provided that this perfect administration, which is carried out through sublimation, precedes it. The manner of this addition is that the sublimation of the non-fixed part of the stone and the technique of joining be repeated, until it is raised up with it, and fixed again, as will be done.” <gloss>Add the ferment to the white Elixir: Dissolve it by means of Mercury so that the whole is sublimated, then coagulate and fix it in turn.</gloss>*

*“And the more often the order of the abundance of this completion is repeated, the more the abundance of this medicine is multiplied. <gloss>These things pertain to "augmentation" <note>increasing the power or volume of the stone</note>. For if you ferment it more often—which does not happen immediately in every repeated operation, but according to Geber in the fifth, or in others in the third [or even if you dissolve and coagulate it more often]—the medicine grows more abundantly in weight and power</gloss> and its goodness is increased more, and the increase of its perfection is greatly multiplied.”*

*“The intention of the completion is that through the manner of sublimation, the stone and its addition <gloss>the mercury and the ferment of gold must be exalted to the highest purity</gloss> may be most perfectly cleansed.”*

*“And after the sublimation, using the methods of the arts, that which is volatile in it should be fixed <gloss>through solution, putrefaction, and grinding. [Grinding signifies solution in mercury; sometimes also the reduction of the Philosophical Sun and Moon to their first matter]</gloss>, which all coincide as one and the same: sublimation, separation, washing, imbibing, and fixation—which are those arts by which it is worked until it is fixed. Let the fixed become volatile again, and the volatile fixed again. <gloss>Which is the repetition of the work with new mercury during multiplication.</gloss> In this order is completed the most precious secret, which is above every secret of the sciences of this world, and an incomparable treasure. If you exercise yourself in it with endurance of labor, greatest constancy, and the duration of immense meditation <gloss>from which I think you will now be relieved by this treatise</gloss>, you will find it; without this, you will not. It can happen to this medicine in the preparation of the stone, through repeated good administration with industrious caution, that it transforms quicksilver infinitely into true gold-making and silver-making substance, and this depends on nothing but its multiplication. <gloss>The same medicine can be prepared for "gold" <note>Sun</note> and "silver" <note>Moon</note>, such that it tinges mercury infinitely. But then it is necessary that the medicine itself be increased in proportion. Therefore, let these things be understood regarding multiplication and augmentation, which are nothing other than repetitions of the work, always with new "menstruum" <note>solvent</note>, and it is done in a shorter time, etc.</gloss>”*

*“Praise be to Blessed God, by whose help and by applying labor I have touched,” says Geber, “and with my eyes have seen the completion of that mastery.”*

<margin>Projection.</margin>
Since there is likewise some difficulty in <term>projection</term><note>The final stage of the Great Work, where a small amount of the "Stone" is thrown onto molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note> onto certain bodies, the same Geber provides several methods: namely, that both the medicine and the metal should be dissolved, either by an aqueous solution or by melting (fusion). Alternatively, one may be mixed with "spirits" (mercury), which are then frequently sublimated from it. This is the method commanded by Paracelsus, who repeatedly <term>sublimates</term><note>A process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification.</note> mercury from metals until they become so fluid that they melt over a candle flame and are turned into what he calls the "mercury of the philosophers." This is truly the material to be <term>tinged</term><note>Colored or transformed; in alchemy, "tinging" refers to the qualitative change of a base metal into a noble one.</note> in the lesser metals, for in this way they achieve an entry through their smallest parts. But the tincture itself must be prepared with its own "body" so that it may hold together. He continues: to grant entry to things that do not naturally mix, let the body we wish to tinge be dissolved, and let the tinging agent be dissolved as well. However, let there be a solution not of all parts, but only of certain ones. Then let that body, and no other, be <term>imbibed</term><note>A process of soaking a solid in a liquid so it absorbs it, like a sponge.</note> by alternating turns.

To judge whether you have truly produced gold <note>original: *solem*; literally "the Sun"</note> and silver <note>original: *lunam*; literally "the Moon"</note>, Geber adds tests of perfection. Among these are the common ones: color, weight, and malleability (extension). The more professional tests include <term>cupellation</term><note>original: *cineritium*; a method of refining precious metals by heating them in a "cupel" made of bone ash.</note>, <term>cementation</term><note>original: *cæmentum*; a dry refining process using salts to remove impurities from gold.</note>, ignition, fusion, fumigation, the mixing of sulfur, extinction, <term>calcination</term><note>Reducing a metal to a powder through heat.</note> and reduction, and the reception of quicksilver. To these, more recent authors add solution through <term>aqua fortis</term><note>Nitric acid, used to separate silver from gold.</note>, the touchstone <note>original: *lapis lydius*</note> with coloring, <term>quartation</term><note>A process of refining gold by alloying it with three parts silver and then separating them with acid.</note>, and so on.

<margin>Summary of Geber.</margin>
The sum of the whole Geberian art is this: Let the Stone be taken, which is known in the various chapters. Let the work of sublimation of the first degree be performed upon it with constant diligence. For thus it is cleansed of corrupting impurity. The sublimation is then perfect if it reaches such a level of fineness that it becomes most pure and ultimately volatile <gloss>this is the preparation of mercury</gloss>. Let it be fixed by the methods of <term>fixation</term><note>The process of making a volatile substance stable in fire.</note> until it remains still in a harsh fire. Here lies the goal of the second degree of preparation. <gloss>This does not happen except through perfected, fixed bodies. Thus, composition, solution, and coagulation are noted here. Take note that Geber refers everything to mercury, as if the entire hinge of the work turned on this and not on the "bodies" (metals); the bodies merely provide the fixation and the tincture, whereas others place the principal role in the bodies and make mercury partly an instrument and partly a co-essential partner.</gloss> The Stone shall also be treated in a third degree, which consists of the final completion of the preparation: namely, that he may conveniently make the now-fixed Stone volatile through sublimation, and the volatile Stone fixed; the fixed dissolved, and the dissolved again volatile, and the volatile again fixed, until it flows and transforms in a certain solar <note>gold-making</note> and lunar <note>silver-making</note> completion. <gloss>Repeated operations are noted—second, third, and fourth—by which it is perfected in both mass and power so that it may be able to tinge.</gloss> Thus ends Geber.

## FROM ARNOLD OF VILLANOVA.

Regarding this author, we also read in public writings that he produced gold through this art which passed every test. Since he encompassed that art in his writings, it will be worthwhile to confirm the practice described above with his testimony, as he was a craftsman who proved by effect and reality what he wrote. I will select only the more notable sentences from his *Rosary* and his *Flower of Flowers*, through which the rest will easily become known even to any reader.

<margin>Praise of Mercury.</margin>
Just as we heard Geber ascribing the greatest importance to mercury in the entire craft of the Stone, so we see Arnold doing the same. For he reports of it: "It alone, since it is metallic, contains within itself everything we need for our mastery. All other things turn to ash. Quicksilver contains within itself its own good and fixed sulfur, by which it coagulates into gold and silver according to the different modes of preparation." From this, the material of the craft is clear: it is not the mercury of the common people, but that of the philosophers, which has its own natures within it—both volatile and fixed, both mercurial and fixed-sulfurous. From this is made a medicine of a substance more subtle and of a more liquid fusion than the metals themselves, and of a greater fixation and retention than mercury in its own natural state. This medicine, therefore, receives its temperament from the perfected fixed bodies and from mercury, from which it must be fashioned. For thus he writes of the material:

<margin>White and red sulfur from silver and gold through mercury. Take care that you understand the names "gold" and "silver" correctly, for there is a different understanding for the second part of the art.</margin>
> **White and red** sulfur are obtained from one material through different cooking, nor is it found except in two bodies, **GOLD AND SILVER**, which are to be subtly prepared so that sulfur and mercury may be obtained from that material from which gold and silver were produced underground. Gold is the tincture of redness, and silver the tincture of whiteness. Likewise: The Stone is drawn out from bodies and mercury according to nature. Without the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note>, no tinging quicksilver is generated. Without gold and silver, you cannot tinge. For gold has the golden color, and silver the silvery color. And: "Whatever a man sows, that he shall reap." It is extracted from gold and silver, in which the substance of sulfur is most pure. Its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon. I advise you not to work except with mercury and Gold for gold, and with mercury and Silver for silver. For in these **ALONE** does the benefit consist. Let the purest substance of mercury be drawn from those bodies, for the <term>Elixir</term><note>The medicine or Stone used for transformation.</note> consists in them alone. It is necessary that you labor in the solution, sublimation, and refinement of Gold and Silver; for these two bodies are sufficient. Thus the material is expressed clearly enough by Arnold in his *Rosary*.

<margin>The Stone from two bodies, but not the common ones.</margin>
Whether, since there are two tinctures, one should be taken from only one body, he indicates with these words: "It is necessary that the Stone be able to be drawn from the nature of two bodies before it becomes the Elixir." Likewise: "In the beginning of the operation, the work of the Sun and Moon agree in everything; they differ in the mode of fermentation. And the medicine is one in essence and in its mode of acting; and its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon, whose marriage must be performed." Therefore, when he later forbids several times that we mix the two works, it must be understood regarding the <term>ferment</term><note>A piece of pure gold or silver added to the medicine to "direct" it toward becoming that specific metal.</note>, where the white elixir (the part destined for silver) receives the ferment of silver, and the red elixir that of gold.

<margin>Mercury is the medium of extraction.</margin>
It is therefore sufficiently evident that this Mercury and sulfur—or rather, the fixed sulfur it contains, which must become the tincture—must be born from gold and silver. <note>Note the discrepancy: "from gold and silver" versus "from gold or silver." Both are true in their own sense.</note> But since this cannot happen without a medium, he explains this too when he says: "Mercury is mixed with gold and silver and is fixed through them with great ingenuity; and mercury receives what belongs to its nature and rejects what is foreign." Likewise: "It can be drawn from bodies with their sulfur or arsenic <note>as cited from Geber</note>, but it is found more easily and perfectly from quicksilver alone." In it is the ease of extracting that subtle substance, since it already possesses the substance in action. And: "The dry and coarse Stone is dissolved into quicksilver, so that it may be reduced to its first nature." This is done **ONLY** through quicksilver <gloss>understand here the twofold mercury of the art, not common quicksilver</gloss>, because this alone can reduce Gold and Silver to their nature or <term>prime matter</term><note>The original, formless state of all metals.</note>. And: "Water distilled seven times, keep a portion of it; for that is the dissolving mercury of the philosophers, making the Marriage, and the water of life that washes the black earth." From which it is clear that...

->On the Philosopher's Stone.<-
<note>Latin: De Lapide Philosophorum.</note>

# On the Philosopher's Stone.

That perfect <term>quicksilver</term><note>Also known as mercury. In alchemy, "quicksilver" often refers to the essential "spirit" or "soul" of a metal rather than just the common liquid element.</note>, existing potentially within perfect bodies, must be called forth by another quicksilver that is already in an active state. There are no more than two: one belonging to the bodies, and the other crude. The former exists as a potential, the latter as an act. It is therefore necessary that the former be elicited by the latter.

<margin>Nature and art conspire in the work. Books can teach the art.</margin>
Thus, three things in total concur for the material of the stone: gold, silver, and mercury. From these it is made, as the same author says, *by Nature and by art*, because nature desires to be perfected, having within itself the cause of its own increase. Yet it is necessary that it receives its motion from art, so that the <term>Elixir</term><note>The final, perfected substance capable of transmuting base metals or granting long life.</note> may be complete. There is also a requirement for the skillful management of hands and the support of resources, just as he says: Three things are required in the mastery—Genius, manual labor, and free choice, which demands wisdom, riches, and books. (Do not altogether despair that the art can be learned from books with God’s favor, of which he also said at the beginning, "a book opens a book," etc.)

<margin>Preparation of the matter.</margin>
Once these foundations in the material and the driving cause are established, he also explains how the individual parts ought to be prepared, albeit somewhat obscurely. He commands that water be distilled seven times, though he seems to mean that water which is found in the <term>separation of elements</term><note>A process of breaking down a substance into its fundamental qualities—fire, air, water, and earth—to purify it.</note>; such are the hiding places of the philosophers. They rarely explain external things in their proper places, and they are particularly evasive regarding that separation of elements and the preparation. <margin>Mercury is prepared through distillation by <term>sublimation</term>, and it becomes the gold or silver of the philosophers. These, when reduced to the first matter, receive the power of reducing metals.</margin> The end goal of this distillation, however, is that its earthy dross be removed, superfluities taken away, and absences supplied, so that the spirit becomes entirely lucid, subtle, penetrating, and free from all impurity. He commands this to be performed with glass and salt: in the same way that Geber also wished it to be most correctly <term>sublimated</term><note>Sublimation involves heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again, used here as a purification technique.</note> from the lime of eggs or marble, and purged with salt. For there are two purifications of it: one through distillation or sublimation (for they are the same thing, nor should one understand the common sublimation from vitriol and salt. For although it can be done in that manner, it is far more laborious and ingenious, and common <term>sublimated mercury</term> remaining in its own nature can have no place in the art); the other is through washing with refined salt water. The former has its place in <term>dissolution</term>, the latter in multiplication, increase, and projection, etc.

<margin>Preparation of the bodies.</margin>
Regarding the bodies themselves <note>The "bodies" usually refer to the solid metals, gold and silver.</note>, he suggests they can either be <term>calcined</term><note>Burned to a fine powder or ash through intense heat.</note> or taken whole. If they are calcined, he says they dissolve more easily, but are handled with less security.

<margin>Weight.</margin>
The weight at which they are to be joined is clear from these words: *Into the purged mercury, place the clean bodies, weighed in an equal balance: strive so that you always have more of the mercury, etc.*

<margin>Extraction.</margin>
The following teaches that once joined, they should not remain in their own nature, but be turned into the "first matter": *Labor,* he says, *in the dissolution of the stone, so that you segregate the purer parts from the bodies, and having cast away the heavier parts, complete the work with the lighter ones.* Likewise: *The first work of the philosophers is to dissolve the stone (for so they customarily call its material) into its own mercury, so that it may be reduced into the first matter, that is, quicksilver. Labor first in the dissolution and sublimation of the two <term>luminaries</term><note>The Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver).</note>, so that from them mercury may be made, which is to make bodies incorporeal.* <margin>From this you will easily gather which are those bodies of the art from which the mercury is to be made.</margin> But it is superfluous to transcribe everything.

<margin>Practice.</margin>
I come now to the practice. He teaches it thus: *Purge the mercury and the bodies; mix, grind by turns, and <term>imbibe</term><note>To soak or saturate a solid substance with a liquid until it is absorbed.</note> in a bath.* (You will easily understand that the grinding must be done through the mercury, which is the dissolution, applying the warmth of the bath). *Distill through a filter (which is metaphorical, or a figure of speech for "separate"); collect the blackness floating on top separately (he calls that the <term>Crow’s Head</term><note>Latin: Caput Corvi. A famous alchemical stage—nigredo—signifying the death or decomposition of the old forms before rebirth.</note>. Heat acting on moisture, he says, causes blackness).* <margin>The black oil is to be collected.</margin> For that is the oil, and the true sign of dissolution; when it is dissolved, it reaches the limit of sublimity, where it is separated from the lower things, etc. Guard it cautiously, lest it fly away in smoke. He also explains this in these words: *Place the whole dissolved stone on the surface in temperate heat, so that it may <term>putrefy</term><note>A process of decomposition through gentle heat, essential for the transformation of the matter.</note> and be digested for a <term>philosophical month</term><note>Typically 40 days, though alchemical "months" can vary in length.</note>, so that all things return to the first matter and become quicksilver. Into this material, the form is introduced; it is BLACK in color, subtle and discontinuous to the touch, and this is the sign of perfect dissolution.* <margin>The Crow’s Head is a black substance, a discontinuous matter generated in the philosophers' mercury by heat from moisture, etc.</margin> For heat acting on the moist first generates blackness, which is the Crow's Head, and the beginning of our work, by which the stone is dissolved into mercury, or mercurial water. Once this dissolution is performed, he commands it to be divided into elements, where air is called mercury, and the blackness is called <term>Laton</term><note>A term for the base, unpurified "bronze" or "black" state of the material.</note>, or black earth, which must be washed so that it afterwards becomes white. (Thus he also sometimes says the earth is white; do not care about the earth from which the substance is made, provided it has been—that is, it has turned out to be—a white and fixed substance). Likewise, the water is Mercury, or <term>Virgin’s Milk</term>, with which the blackness is washed away. He even ascribes fire to the Mercury, but all things are done rightly. Fire and air are together in the blackness; earth and water are in the mercury; and first indeed the mercury appears, and after coagulation, the earth, etc. <margin>Elements. Earth. Water.</margin>

<margin>Nourishment.</margin>
Once the division is made, the medicine is roasted over a fire for a longer time (for this heat is greater than in the beginning, where others commit the work only to a certain internal heat). And let it be nourished like a child at the breast. The practice of nourishment is described here: *Pour a certain quantity of water upon the white earth (which is to become such, though now it is black). Grind well and gently, until the earth has drunk up its fiftieth part of the water.* <margin>Concerning the weight in this nourishment, and in all others: see the general precept in chapter 22, book 1, of the *Rosary* of Arnold [of Villanova]. The weight of nourishment.</margin> (That "grinding" is a sprinkling, by which the water, working its way in, as it were dissolves and breaks down the earth). For the earth to be nourished is at first given a little water. Then its quantity is to be increased little by little, following the example of a newborn. Therefore, grind the earth often, and imbibe it for eight days by cooking and gently <term>calcining</term> (do not understand this as external calcination, but he calls the cooking in the fire during the movement of calcination by this name). If you wish to mix the whole thing at once, you are mistaken. Do not remove your hand from grinding, soaking, roasting, and coagulating, until the water is entirely dried up and drunk by the white earth. The weight of the individual nourishings, or how much you should cast in at once: Imbibe only as much as is missing. Pour on water that is neither exceeding nor lacking in weight. (You will easily understand that the matter is committed to your own prudence). After calcination, you must always putrefy the matter in <term>dung</term><note>A traditional alchemical heat source, providing a gentle, steady warmth like that of a compost pile.</note> for seven (or eight) days, and then proceed by soaking. If the earth is not white, grind it with water and calcine. For <term>Azoth</term><note>A term for the essential transformative agent or universal solvent, often identified with mercury.</note> and fire (the water or Virgin’s Milk and the external heat) wash the Laton—that is, the foul impurity. These words also pertain to the same: *When the earth has drunk up the fiftieth part of its water (that is, all fifty parts), sublimate it with a strong fire (it will burn so that it is sublimated in quality, not substance) until it ascends in the form of a very white powder (he speaks thus by analogy to other sublimations in order to hide himself. Thus when he says: the dregs that remain after sublimation are to be cast aside, it is the same as if he had said, if it cannot be fully whitened, this should not be a concern. For in this whiteness something obscure remains. Whence it is also compared to tin.)*

It emphasizes the synergy between nature and the alchemist's art, using metaphors like "Virgin's Milk" and "nourishing a child" to describe the refining process.</summary>

# Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book IV.

<margin>NB. Third operation.</margin>
Thus the first operation is finished. The second and third follow, described in chapter 17 of the second book of the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarii*. Refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational alchemical text.</note> as follows: *Take this coagulated stone and grind it again with red water (mercury) and coagulate it into a stone as before. And repeat this a third time, coagulating with a strong fire (for here the stone is more stable, and is of a near-silver whiteness, though not the highest; that is introduced with greater heat). What rises in the form of a powder is the whitest sulfur (that is, the highest whiteness is manifest); what remains at the bottom (do not understand this as physical distance, but as potential, or what is hidden—for beneath the whiteness, redness lies hidden in potential, because it can be changed into redness by fire) is the best red sulfur.* This <term>tinctures</term><note>To "tincture" means to fundamentally change the color and nature of a metal.</note> mercury into white gold. There is no need for you to extract the redness, but cook the stone until it turns red.
<margin>How redness is drawn out from whiteness.</margin>

<margin>Fermentation.</margin>
<margin>On the weight of the ferment, chapter 24 says it must be equal to the increase or <term>elixir</term>. See the rest there.</margin>
<margin>The necessity of ferment.</margin>
<margin>Elixir: fermented mercury.</margin>
<margin>Note that the processes of dissolution and coagulation in fermentation are kept secret.</margin>
Fermentation follows, which is covered in chapter 18 of the second book of Arnold’s *Rosary*. From it come these precepts: *The bodies to be joined to mercury must first be <term>calcined</term><note>Reduced to a fine powder by the action of heat.</note> (For such is the ferment. In earlier passages, he preferred them whole) so that the mercury may be joined to them and penetrate them. The lime <note>The powdered material resulting from calcination.</note> is to be ground with mercury so that the two become one. This body must be imbibed by the mercury and sublimated. (The body of the stone, which is called "dead" in respect to this animation) therefore bodies are sublimated so that they become spirits and the gold, silver, and mercury may be joined. These (two ferments) are not to be mixed. For the color of the Sun <note>Gold</note> does not suit the Moon <note>Silver</note>, nor that of the Moon the Sun. Therefore, join red mercury with the white. Without ferment, you can produce neither Sun nor Moon. Therefore, the whitened mercury (that white stone already made by the previous works) must be fixed so it does not evaporate (flee from the fire). Thus, something must be added that remains in the essence and quality of nature: as if you add that body with which it was first prepared—that is, gold or silver. (The ferment must be taken from the same bodies from which the stone was extracted). Therefore, add these to it so they may give birth to a thing like themselves, and from the conjunction, an elixir is made. If you wish to ferment, mix the body with sulfur (blend the body of gold or silver with the previous stone or elixir not yet fixed) so that all becomes ferment. Let the ferment for the red be red—of the Sun for the Sun—and white for white—Moon for the Moon. There are no more ferments, nor can the elixir be fixed except by the fixed, which things are clear enough.*

Having said these things, he adds multiplication, in which he says, *that the sum of the fixed must exceed the sum of the volatile (not in quantity but in power) so that the mixture of both is turned into a volatile spirit. The method: a little of the purified sulfur is to be projected onto much of the body, and the sulfur turns the body into a powder of its own color. This color of the body is projected upon the spirits of the Sun and Moon (this is the transmutation of <term>quicksilver</term> into gold or silver).*

Sulfur cannot enter without the medium of water, which intercedes between the sulfurs and the ferments in every disposition. Therefore, the earth must be taken first, which is close to the ferment; secondly water, which approaches the earth; thirdly air, which comes near the water; fourthly fire for the red elixir. For the white is contained in air, water, and earth. Once joined, dissolve them in a well-closed vessel, wash, and dry. For water is the medium joining the tinctures, etc.* (He notes the common process of fermenting, multiplying, and providing entry; everywhere water or mercury must be used, etc. *If you wish to make a projection upon the elixir: make a lime from the matter of the body upon which you wish to project, and mix it with the ferment. If it is of the Sun, take the Sun; if of the Moon, the Moon. For the marriage is nothing other than the conjunction of the ferment with the body to be transmuted, etc.* He speaks of the projection for tinting and making entry, which does not happen unless the medicine is first fermented and mixed with the lime of the same, etc.)
<margin>Marriage.</margin>

<margin>On the colors.</margin>
<margin>They desire the burning of putrefaction and restore the color.</margin>
Certain precautions in the whole process: *In the conjunction of the stone, note three colors: black, white, and red. See that the work does not turn red before blackness. If this has happened, it is an error (this can be allowed in fermentation, but not at the beginning); by cooking everything in white water so that it turns black again (the water must be increased, for you added too little). Do the same if it turns red before whiteness. If the medicine will not mix, dissolve that which it enters, and that which it does not want to enter. Mix both solutions, and then project the medicine. (That is, in the projection upon the body, the medicine is not always mixed, due to its subtlety and the unsuitability of the body to be transmuted. You must therefore choose something into which you know the stone enters well, and dissolve this with quicksilver; dissolve the other unsuitable body with the same. Mix these two, and then the stone will be received.)*

*If the metal to be changed is not tinted, the medicine is [weak], so add more tincture. If too much, as usually happens in the solar tincture but not the lunar, use less tincture and more metal. If the tincture does not remain in the assays, it is not fixed enough, nor sufficiently imbibed. Therefore, put it in a crucible and sprinkle the "air" or "oil" (that is, purified mercury—the "oil" or "air" is elsewhere the mercury of the second operation, it is also made from arsenic, that is, the elixir, whence it is called "oil of arsenic") until it melts like wax, and that over a fire, etc. (He means it must be perfected through the repetition of dissolution and coagulation. So also in chapter 26: if it smokes, he repeats the imbibitions until it is perfect; namely, sublimate that which is fleeting and mix it with what is not fleeting, and sublimate again until nothing more rises. Then test it on a plate. Those sublimations are not common like in <term>sublimated mercury</term> which they want to fix in a similar way, but physical dissolutions. For the stone must be perfected to the point that it is no longer dissolved by the "water of mercury" except by hidden art, since it ought to tint most strongly, so that it is stable on a red-hot plate.)*

<margin>Parts: 1,000,000.</margin>
On multiplication he also has this: *Project one part of the Medicine upon a thousand of mercury purified by vinegar and salt, and it is perfected into gold or silver. (Likewise, a tincture is made) which thousand parts tint imperfect bodies by the same power, if you project one upon a thousand, etc. See regarding the increase, chapter 28.*

<margin>From the book called the Flower of Flowers.</margin>
The same Arnold, in the book entitled *The Flower of Flowers* <note>original: *Flos Florum*.</note>, teaches nothing else, as these few things can testify. *If we wish to arrive at the perfect mastery (he says), we must first have the Philosopher's Stone (its material) pure and clean as it is in its mine, and sublimate it, so that we may draw from it what is pure and clear. Afterward, we must make it descend, then distill, calcine, dissolve, coagulate, fix, and wax it. This is the whole practice and the reduction to the first matter.*
<margin>Dissolution.</margin>
*Dissolve the white stone (silver) with <term>blessed water</term><note>Usually refers to purified mercury or a specific alchemical solvent.</note> (cleansed mercury) bit by bit—not all at once—until the proper amount of solution is reached. Cook over a slow fire in glass until blackness appears on the surface. Draw this off subtly as often as it appears; repeat with three cookings, until the water remains clear. Now you have the earth and the water. Take that earth and the collected blackness, and having placed them in glass, pour on the aforesaid water until it swims over it. Cook over a slow fire for four days. (Note the deception. It should not swim over; nor are four days enough, except just to mix them). Then add water again and cook successively until it is white, shining, and clear. This is what the Philosophers have sought.*
<margin>Coagulation.</margin>
(Thus far the first operation.) *This earth (it is so named, as in the first coagulation of the *Rosary*, from which the white stone emerged) putrefies with water and is cleansed; once cleansed, the mastery is directed (This is the second operation, for with mercury*

<header>On the Philosopher’s Stone.</header>

*The stone must be putrefied <note>original: *putrefieri*. In alchemy, putrefaction is a stage of decomposition or "death" of the matter before it can be reborn.</note> again and coagulated as before.* The earth is cleansed and whitened by means of water. Water, with the intervention of heat, coagulates and thickens with the earth. Once thickened in this way (near the end, however, all the water is already absorbed), it is cooked with a strong fire in a glass gourd <note>original: *cucurbita vitrea*. A gourd-shaped flask used in distillation.</note>, etc. Then the ferment is taken. (Fermentation: And note here an abbreviation of the work. For otherwise, the same would have to be repeated a third and fourth time.) *Use a fourth part of gold or silver, or for one pound of the bodies, use three ounces of ferment.* (Equality is found in the whole substances; if the lime <note>original: *calx*. A powder produced by heating a metal.</note> or tincture is taken, there is inequality.) *The ferment is also made dissolved, and made like earth, just like an imperfect body: join it, prepared in the same way and order.* (There is no other way of acting here than in the preceding operations.) *Moisten it with the aforementioned water (new mercury), and cook it for three days or more. Then moisten it again with the aforementioned water and cook as before, and repeat this until the two are reduced into one body, which, once joined, if the color will no longer change: (let the whole be black. Then separate and coagulate, etc. Then pour over them (the born blackness) the aforementioned water (the virgin's milk from which the blackness has been separated) part by part, little by little, until it drinks as much of it as it can, always giving it new water (this is the nourishment and coagulation of the infant).* In this way, spirits are mixed with bodies and united to them: and the seed is joined with mundane bodies, which could not happen before because of their impurity and thickness. But now it is joined to them, and grows in them, and increases its own number, and is multiplied infinitely, provided you have performed the true artifice. (He says much in few words: especially regarding the utility of fermentation, which is the cause of the <term>tincture</term><note>A substance capable of deeply penetrating and changing the nature of other materials.</note> so that it can be joined with metallic bodies, multiplied and increased, etc.)

<margin>Permanent water is not without its body.</margin>
*The foundation of the art is the reduction of the body into mercury, which is the philosophers' dissolution. That which is dissolved is permanent water, which cannot be permanent without its own body to which it is joined and united, etc.* Here he has explained most clearly the entire artifice in its natural order, without deceptions. Furthermore, he also declares certain obscure phrases and the names used by practitioners. Concerning colors, he also adds these: Black appears in the mortification, while the body is turned into earth. Many colors precede the whitening: (namely in the fermentation) the end is whiteness (in the red work, it is redness.) *Colors appear in the conjunction of the prepared and fermented bodies: (which is a universal rule throughout all operations.)* So much from Arnold.

## THE OPINION OF RAYMOND LULL.

Dissolve the fixed (gold or silver) with the non-fixed, or the non-fixed mother. (Mercury. The philosophical mercurial water, not the common kind which he calls Mars in the generation of metals, with sulfur performing the office of the father.) *This does not happen unless they are joined in a vessel that is not wide, lest one flee or depart from the other, and unless they are tormented by fire.* (In previous writings, he said the shape of the vessel or the form of the glass should imitate the form of the heavens, by which words he notes a great deal. And what he says here about being "tormented," he previously expressed through the light cooking of a slow fire: by which the body is overwhelmed, refined, and rendered impalpable, which agrees with the "born blackness.") *And then the one works upon the other, and they become one thing, just as they were before* (they pass into mercury or water, which is the <term>first matter</term><note>The primordial, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made.</note> of bodies) *thus they fight with enemies (they resist dry fire through an impregnable moisture) and the thick part ascends to the upper parts (when the body is dissolved in physical putrefaction, it emerges to the surface in the form of a black skin and powder).* Guard yourself well, lest it perish. *Thus the highest fixed part becomes volatile.* This thing is called dissolution, and the heat immediately works blackness. This is the impregnation, and the internal dissolution, and the key to the whole art.

<margin>Interpretation of dung <note>Often referring to the gentle, moist heat of a horse-dung bath.</note>.</margin>
<margin>The Emerald of Hermes <note>Refers to the *Tabula Smaragdina*, the foundational text of Hermeticism.</note>.</margin>
*It can neither beget nor be corrupted unless it has fulfillment* (He denies that what is dissolved in this way is sufficient, but that perfection is required) *thus the white grain is dead, and it brings forth a hundredfold fruit. It ascends from the earth into heaven, and descends from heaven to the earth. That which is corporeal, by thus sublimating the spiritual, becomes spiritual-corporeal by descending (which words designate dissolution and coagulation, the former of which causes the dissolved body to ascend: by the latter, the water or "virgin's milk" poured back upon the dry powder is coagulated into the white earth, which they call "foliated").* And it gains the power of the higher and lower things, *that is, when the dissolution occurs, and the strong burning is moved in the vessel like boiling water, and the body ascends. And this is distillation and sublimation, through which the wise men will it to be cooked for a long time and fixed in the fire. This is calcination and coagulation.*

*And thus the white is begotten in the dry, and in the white, the yellow; in the yellow, the red.* (In like manner, through dissolution and coagulation, as was said in the preceding operation, he signifies that the white <term>elixir</term> is made in a dry fire. Furthermore, in the same way, he also signifies that the red elixir follows from the white by means of the yellow, with a more abundant fire.) *Between the black and the white (completed and fermented), all colors appear, (the peacock's tail)* <note>original: *cauda pavonis*. A colorful stage in the alchemical process symbolizing the transition to the white work.</note> *which are nevertheless ignored, since they are unstable until the true whiteness comes forth, which is the true white elixir, united from transparent things* (pure and bright. For they are not transparent like glass) *not otherwise transparent than a pure heavenly mirror (which is not transparent), it arrives there gently, by the operation of men.* (The artifice leads nature ingeniously and gradually, without force or haste, to the perfection of the stone.)

<margin>Time.</margin>
*The work is perfected in three forty-day periods.* (The treatment is more clear if the whole work is divided into three parts. For by the "forty-day periods," just as many operations are to be understood, whether they are finished in forty days or not.) *In the first forty days the man commands, whose sperm is united to the woman without separation. In the other forty days it is formed and receives a soul and spirit and tincture, and is quickened (These agree with fermentation, therefore there the two preceding operations are joined.) In the third forty-day period the pure fruit is born; let it be fluid, meltable, nor let it fear the fire, in which it rests as a friend. (These concern multiplication and increase, as well as full resolution, if by chance anything fleeting were still joined to it.)*

<margin>Use in medicine.</margin>
<margin>Malleable glass.</margin>
<margin>Gems.</margin>
*It is effective for all diseases, except for the decreed end of death. With this tincturing spirit, we make glass that is workable with a hammer and unbreakable. From crystal, we make carbuncles <note>Red gemstones, often garnets or rubies.</note> according as the planets are mixed with them.* (The use of the tincture is primarily in healing the sick, in perfecting metals and mercury: in softening glass, in manufacturing gems, and in immediately thickening things into salt without fire, etc.)

<margin>The white stone.</margin>
<margin>Testing the medicine.</margin>
<margin>Virgin's milk washed six times.</margin>
*If you wish to work toward silver, you do not need to proceed as far as redness. But when the true whiteness has emerged (after the fermentation of the elixir with the white body), stop, and make a trial of the medicine, to see if it has easy fusion in both hard and soft materials. If not, add a part of virgin's milk, that is, mercury distilled seven times: and it is dissolved, distilled, sublimated, coagulated: and it flows easily like wax without smoke. And with this medicine, by reiterating the works, it can be led to such excellence that it transmutes...*

mercury infinitely into Silver <note>original: *Lunam* (the Moon). In alchemy, the Moon always represents Silver.</note>: And so with other imperfect things. (He notes two things: the rectification of the medicine while it is still smoking, which is done by a new operation of dissolving and coagulating; and the augmentation, by which, through repeated operations, it increases immensely.) *If you wish to work toward the Gold <note>original: *solem* (the Sun). In alchemy, the Sun always represents Gold.</note>: cook the medicine longer in the fire until it turns red. For redness is perfect digestion. And there is one Elixir prepared for both the white and the red at the same time.* (He does not think a red ferment is necessary, because the fermented white medicine can be exalted by longer cooking until it turns red.
