Thus far Lull <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval logic and alchemy.</note>, who is quite obscure; yet he does not disagree with those mentioned above. Some admire him greatly. Others deny that he knew the stone. But the proofs are ready at hand.

### THOMAS AQUINAS <note>While many alchemical works were attributed to the great theologian Thomas Aquinas, modern scholars generally consider them "pseudo-Aquinas" texts written by others using his name for authority.</note>

<margin>The Matter.</margin>
*He designates the matter first, saying:* Work with mineral mercury, which comes straight from the vein and has never been used in any other work. (The "vein" of this is gold and silver, from which it is extracted as if from a mine, nor has it ever been used elsewhere in that [its own nature]. It is the perfecter of our work, the savior from burning, and the result of fusion. When it is fixed, it is the tincture of whiteness or redness, etc., and it does not return from its commitment: it is friendly to metals, and a medium for joining tinctures, because it is mixed into them, entering deep, penetrating, and adhering.) (The matter of the stone is mercury extracted from the perfect [metals], which, when it is fixed, becomes the tincture whose properties those are, etc.)

<margin>Philosophical mercury to be fermented.</margin>
*And although our work is perfected from our mercury alone, it nonetheless requires a red or white ferment. It is therefore mixed more easily with gold and silver, and becomes one with them, since these two participate more in its nature, and are thus more perfect.* (This anticipation speaks not only of the animation through the ferment, but also of the composition of that mercury; for the following things testify to this.)

<margin>Gold and Silver for the red and the white.</margin>
*Gold and Silver, containing more of mercury, are mixed for the red and the white.* (Note that they must be mixed with mercury for both. Therefore, the speech of the wise <note>original: *sophotorum*</note> concerns the elixir and the making of mercury. Otherwise, for the red only Gold is mixed, and for the white only Silver, and these are mixed not with mercury, but principally with the elixir.)
<margin>Gold and silver are friends to mercury.</margin>
*It is mercury alone that perfects the work, nor should anything foreign be added to them. Gold and silver are not foreign to it. For at the beginning of the work, they are reduced back into their first nature, that is, mercury.* (He gives the reason why it is mercury alone, and yet bodies are mixed with it: because they are reduced into quicksilver, or that mercury is elicited from them. It could be said they are not foreign because they are nothing other than coagulated mercury, which must be dissolved by the crude, currently fluid state.)

<margin>The importance of fire.</margin>
*Our entire mastery lies solely in the governance of the fire. Through great industry, the power of a well-directed fire works the stone with modest labor and little expense.* (The acting cause is external: heat and ingenuity.) When our stone (understand perfect bodies, not common gold and silver) is once dissolved into its first nature, that is water, virgin's milk <note>original: *lac virginis*. A common alchemical term for a white liquid or solvent.</note>, or the dragon's tail <note>original: *cauda draconis*. Often refers to the dregs or the final stage of a process.</note>: it calcines, sublimes, distills, reduces, washes, and congeals itself. And by the proportional power of the fire, it perfects itself in one vessel, without any other manual operation. (The other principal cause is the appetite implanted in the matter, or its power and disposition toward the perfect stone. Thus, when those powers are called into action by external heat, these things follow spontaneously in their vessel.)

<margin>Selection of mercury.</margin>
*The selection of mercury: Take 2 pounds of mineral mercury, which has not been in any previous work, and pass it through a thick linen cloth three times. Then through a hare's skin, and after this again through a dense cloth. If anything remains in the skin from its thickness, being filthy or fatty, it is not suitable for our work. If nothing appears, it is fit. With this, and with nothing else added (that is of a foreign nature), both works can be perfected.* (I take this to mean the crude state by which bodies are dissolved. Such mercury, so pure, is not found, or at least hardly ever, in nature. For it is polluted in the mines, and by sulfurous vapors, and is corrupted by others. Therefore, it must be prepared by art, through distillations, washings, etc.)

<margin>Practice.</margin>
*Practice:* (which is, however, very intricate and mixed. For in the very first operation, he deceives by mentioning the ferment, and either puts the third step before the first, or divides the first, and calls something "ferment" not because it already is, but because it is sought from the same matter. I will set down his description and warn where he wanders off.) *Take two ounces of common purified gold, that is, heated in the fire* (because it is the ferment of redness) (elsewhere, more than an ounce should not be taken in the first operation. Thus, it must be thought that the discussion here is about fermentation: where the elixir is taken at will, and an equal ferment is added to it, as if here there were one ounce of elixir and one of ferment. When he calls it "common gold," do not understand it as the vulgar kind, but the common elixir made from gold and silver, which is the common matter of the red and white ferment. And therefore he also says *heated in the fire*, that is, what has already been coagulated twice by the power of fire in the first and second operation.) *Cut it into small pieces with tongs. Add fourteen ounces of mercury.* (In fermentation you can indeed take less mercury, but nevertheless, if you have not taken enough, it will not putrefy. Thus, necessity will compel you to add more.) *Make the mercury smoke in a tile, and dissolve the*
<margin>Washing away the blackness.</margin>
*gold in it. Stir it with a wooden stick until the gold is well dissolved and mixed. Pour the whole into clear water in a glass dish. Wash it frequently by rubbing and changing the water for so long until all the blackness <note>original: *nigredo*. The "black stage," often the first major sign of success in the alchemical work.</note> leaves the water.* (The beginning is about fermentation. The progress of the amalgamation fits the start of the work. Thus he has hidden himself here. You, therefore, should understand that one ounce of gold and one ounce of silver are to be mixed separately with a certain quantity of purified quicksilver by the method of amalgamation described. [Note that little credit is given to Thomas in this art, as he seems to echo the words of others and mix specific things with the universal. It is said he learned something from Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century polymath and teacher of Thomas Aquinas, also heavily associated with alchemy.</note>, but it is even doubted whether he rightly knew the art.] *If you wish to pay attention, "the voice of the turtle-dove is heard in our land."* <note>original: *vox turturis audita est in terra nostra*. A quote from the Song of Solomon (2:12), used here as an alchemical code for the "springtime" or successful start of the chemical reaction.</note> (An admonition to pay attention as if something of a mystery lies hidden in those words, namely both the beginning of the work and the fermentation, as I said.) *Once the blackness is removed, pass the amalgam through a tied leather, and squeeze everything out except 2 ounces. And 14 ounces will remain from the leather. These are the things suitable for our operation. Note that there should be no more nor fewer than two ounces in the leather from the whole matter. If there is more, take it away; if less, add some. Reserve those two squeezed-out ounces, which are called "virgin's milk," for the second operation.* (When the amalgam is made and more mercury is added for the sake of the mixture, it is afterward separated again, down to three parts which...)

<header>Concerning the Philosopher's Stone.</header>

## Concerning the Philosopher’s Stone.

The matter ought to be surpassed by moisture. Here, Thomas <note>Pseudo-Thomas Aquinas</note> commands to squeeze the whole thing out, yet nonetheless, a certain quantity must be added afterward. He switches the names around when he gives the title of <term>virgin’s milk (lac virginis)</term> <note>original: *lactis virginei*. A poetic term for the white mercurial liquid used to nourish the alchemical "offspring."</note> to two ounces, which actually belongs to the <term>menstruum</term> <note>A solvent or "blood" of the matter.</note> after the blackness has been removed—or at least to the mercury that is destined to become the virgin’s milk. This is one interpretation. There can also be a more occult or metaphorical one: namely, that the "filtration" refers to the separation of the blackness and the virgin’s milk; to ensure no undissolved bodily matter remains in it, they squeeze it through leather, etc. But it is difficult to fully unravel every riddle and perfectly match it to the author’s original meaning.)

Let the matter from the leather be placed into a glass vessel, and this into the small furnace. Once the lamp is lit, let a continuous flame strike the vessel and the matter enclosed within it in a direct path, but do not let the flame itself touch the pot; let all parts of the furnace be similarly well-sealed with clay. (*These instructions are common to every operation, provided you observe the differences in heat—which in the <term>solution</term> stage is almost non-existent outside the vessel, but in <term>coagulation</term> is slow and steady, etc. However, Thomas should have spoken of the solution first. But omitting that, he treats coagulation, and does so while keeping silent about "nutrition," which is nevertheless required both in the first operation and in fermentation. By the flame "striking the pot" without physically touching it, he is describing a vaporous fire, and implies that the glass sits within an oval pot, or <term>philosophical egg</term>, buried in ashes.*)

If after a month or two you wish to look for the "flowers of wine" <note>A metaphor for the initial signs of chemical change or fermentation.</note> and the primary colors—namely black, white, yellow, and red—then, without any work of your hands, through the governance of fire alone, "the hidden shall be made manifest, and the manifest shall become hidden." <note>A common alchemical maxim: making the internal soul of the metal visible while its external body disappears.</note> (*He had begun with fermentation. The same point is touched on here. In the first operation, the blackness should appear after a month, but the whiteness not at all, and much less the redness. Therefore, all of this is true regarding "fermentation," where solution and coagulation are completed in 2 months or 90 days. The true blackness and whiteness appear in the "white work" along with the <term>peacock's tail</term> <note>original: *cauda pavonis*. An array of shifting iridescent colors signifying a stage of the process.</note>; in the "red work," of which he speaks here, the blackness, whiteness, and redness proceed in their own order, having previously been hidden.*)

<margin>Powder, dead earth. Magnesia.</margin>
Thus our matter leads itself to the perfect <term>elixir</term>, turning itself into a very subtle powder, which is called *Powder, dead earth, or the dead man in the tomb, or thirsty magnesia, because the spirit is hidden within it as if in a tomb, and the soul has, as it were, withdrawn.* (*He is hinting at the blackness of the first operation rather than the red ferment. They usually call it by these names based on similarity. For it is an impalpable black powder, blacker than <term>magnesia</term> <note>In this context, not magnesium, but a dark mineral like manganese or stibnite used as a "mother" for the stone.</note> or antimony, plainly dry and dark, etc.*)

<margin>26th week.</margin>
Then, from the beginning up to twenty-six weeks, that which was thick is made thin; the light becomes heavy; and the harsh becomes sweet as honey and the bitter is changed, the conversion of natures being secretly completed by the power of the fire. (*These things are only true of the "first operation," which is completed in four months, or twice 90 days. In the first ninety days, the body is dissolved and blackened; in the second, it is coagulated by the power of the fire, through which the "born earth" and the "virgin’s milk" also undergo these mutations.*)

When you see your powders dried, if you desire a test and a return on your expenses, they will "tinge" <note>To transform a base metal into gold or silver through a "tincture."</note>. One part alone tinges seven parts of well-purified mercury. (*This clearly refers to the completion of the first work. At that point, the white stone already produced is too weak to tinge many things; indeed, it is quite fleeting, which is not the case after fermentation.*)

<margin>White fermentation.</margin>
Concerning the White. Mix the ferment of the Moon <note>Silver.</note> with seven parts of mercury, in the same way as you did for the red. For the matter is the same, but the ferment is different. *Silver leaf is more useful here than a solid mass, because it has a certain mixture of mercury within it; and the amalgam should be made with cold mercury, not hot.* (*He speaks openly of fermentation here, and it is proof that he has inverted the work, putting the end in place of the beginning. For when he says the matter of both ferments is the same—which is nothing other than the "common elixir" which he should have explained first—he reveals his cunning. The reason why silver leaves are more useful here than masses is trivial. Dross should be left nowhere; nothing impure should be admitted anywhere.*)

<margin>Quintessence of gold.</margin>
The <term>quintessence</term> is extracted from the Sun <note>Gold.</note> in a <term>pelican</term> <note>A specialized alchemical flask with two side-tubes that circulate the liquid back into the body, named for its resemblance to the bird.</note>, by the subtle ingenuity of fire. *Mineral gold and silver have so much impurity mixed within them that their purification to suit our purpose would be no "child's play," etc.* (*He does not deny that gold and silver are the matter of the work, provided mercury is added, as he affirmed a little earlier regarding the Sun. But if one did not wish to extract it by the mercurial art, they would experience difficulty. You can also understand this as referring to unprepared materials. For that saying is true regarding prepared ones. To distill mercury seven times, to melt it seven times through antimony, to blast it, to wash it, to make tartaric spirits, etc., is not for "children and women"; but only after the "conjunction," when the craftsman has judged the joints, should he sit by and guard the lamp, etc.*)

<margin>Operation II.</margin>
The second operation. Take the body of our first work with the virgin’s milk (*with which it was united into a white stone through coagulation*); add seven parts of new mercury, according to the weight of the stone itself, and let the mercury be purified. Squeeze it through leather, and save the seven parts that passed through. Wash it, and place it in the glass in the furnace, as you did in the first work: governing the whole thing for such a time or thereabouts, until you see the powders made again (*the medicine coagulated a second time into a white stone*); take it out, and if you wish, tinge. These powders are much more subtle than the first, because they are more digested, and one part tinges seven times seven <note>49 parts</note> into elixir.

<margin>They tinge 49 parts. Operation III.</margin>
The third operation. This is the same as the first and second. The powders born from it tinge 343 parts—namely seven times [the previous amount]—surpassing the former ones by one part. The more the medicine is digested, the more effective, subtle, and tinging it is rendered.

(*He has depicted the same process of amalgamating the stone with sevenfold mercury, squeezing it through leather, and "fixing" it. But remember, this third operation is sometimes set down by Geber, while others omit it due to the length of the work, substituting fermentation instead. At the end, he forbids being occupied in the "greater work," because one should pant for duty rather than profit. However, that differs from the "small work" only by repetition, multiplication, and augmentation to infinity, for a perpetual time. Therefore, there would be nothing else to do but sit by the fires and remain in the workshop for one's whole life. It is better to have brought the stone to a certain completion once, so that a fruit not to be regretted may be carried away. Further augmentation should either be omitted or left to others.*)

It emphasizes the metaphorical "death" of the matter and the practical necessity of indirect heat in the furnace.</summary>

# Alchemical Commentary. Part II. Book IV.

However, this matter would be more fruitful than any other artifice, and anyone could easily find those who would carry out a perpetual labor with a great number of hired servants, if it were intended for a dull mind <note>original: *crassae minerue*. An idiom meaning someone lacking refinement or deep understanding.</note>. In a manuscript book, a certain practice is described involving sulfur resolved into its elements; the author or translator of this work asserts that it is the stone for the white and the red, which **Thomas Aquinas** <note>Referring to Pseudo-Thomas Aquinas, the medieval philosopher to whom many alchemical works were falsely attributed.</note> explained in the book *On Essences*, in the chapter on the *artificial being of metals*. He claims this is the best art in the entire category of secrets, which all craftsmen have studied and hidden behind foreign words. 

This process first dissolves sulfur into its elements by preparing it with linseed oil and dissolving it with brick oil <note>original: *oleo lateritio*. A common alchemical solvent made by distilling bricks soaked in oil.</note>. It rectifies the elements, as we said above regarding the elements. It imbues or "nourishes" the white earth with an equal part of the water element, until it flows like wax on a red-hot plate, and then it silvers it. Afterward, it makes the same earth drink the air element, distilled seven times, for the same purpose. With one part of this, he fixes five portions of raw mercury, and repeats the same in another vessel with new earth, a second and third time. Thus, he says, the white <term>elixir</term> is made. He melts a half-ounce of this with a thousand-fold amount of whitened and prepared **Mars** <note>Iron</note>; from this, in turn, he projects one part onto ten portions of **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, from which silver is made. Likewise, he cooks a half-ounce of the same elixir with a weight of mercury into silver. 

To create gold, however, he nourishes and imbues the fire element with water seven times: and again seven times with rectified "airy oil," until it flows like wax on a silver plate, asserting it has the color of gold. He cooks one part of this also with five parts of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, as before, and repeats it a second time with an equal portion to make the red elixir. He melts this with a thousand-fold amount of silver (made from earth and mercury just before), yet adding a half-ounce of prepared **Mars** to every pound. From this, he says, **Sol** <note>Gold</note> is made. 

But that author is mistaken, whoever he may be, unless he is acting more like a **Sphinx** <note>i.e., speaking in impenetrable riddles</note>; and if he writes anything true at all, he merely produces a mastery of an apparent mixture. **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus</note> wrote of such things that they do not survive the "seventh fire" <note>A test of extreme heat to prove the purity of gold.</note>. The Philosophers make their Stone from their own Mercury, and they extract it from gold and silver; they do not work without metals. For them, there is a "ferment" of gold or silver; there is a **permanent water** <note>original: *aqua permanens*. A central alchemical concept referring to a universal solvent that does not wet the hands.</note>, etc. They do not admit the common sulfur of the masses, nor any such distillations or separations, as has been sufficiently stated thus far. So much for Thomas.

->## From Bernard, Count of Trevisan.<-

<margin>15 craftsmen with Bernard.</margin>
<margin>Powerless minds expect great wealth from Chemists.</margin>
<margin>The truth of the Art.</margin>
**H**ere he indicates that he perfected the Stone in the seventy-third year of his age, after many labors exhausted in vain, and after all other things were tried rashly and immense expenses were squandered. Finally, he attained the truth, and had in his company fifteen other craftsmen, likewise skilled in the same art. He even recovered all the things previously spent without fruit, etc. 

But it is a wonder that so many craftsmen did not make mountains of gold and silver, if indeed what the Philosophers write about **multiplication** <note>The process of increasing the quantity and potency of the Alchemical Stone.</note> and increase is true. Yet **Bernard** indicates that these riches are not sought by true craftsmen—though some greedy men, insatiable in their lust for wealth, judge them by their own depraved character—but rather, having sworn a vow of silence regarding the art, the Philosophers rejoice in both the knowledge of the mastery itself and the fruit that befits a Philosopher. Therefore, Bernard is not to be despised, as someone recently did, who knows not what crimes, or extravagances, or exiles he charged him with. Nor is the art to be condemned just because craftsmen do not satisfy the corrupt appetite of the greedy. There are so many weighty authors of its truth that even **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola, the "father of mineralogy," who was often skeptical of alchemy.</note>, who is otherwise somewhat unfair to Chemists, does not dare to repudiate it as false. Even today, there exist eye-witnesses and faithful witnesses to the fates, who have seen chemical gold and silver; and I have elsewhere proven that nature itself is not opposed to it, etc. But to explain Bernard’s opinion, I will now use only two writings: namely, the *Epistle to Thomas of Bologna*, and *Hermetic Philosophy*—although the *Rosary of the Philosophers* is also attributed to him, which confirms what is written in those works and explains it even more clearly.

<margin>The matter of the stone.</margin>
<margin>1,200,000.</margin>
He summarizes the whole work in a few words: *Our work is made from **one root**, and is taken from two mercurial substances that are plainly raw and purely clean, extracted and composed from minerals, resumed by fire as the matter requires, and cooked continuously until the two become one. In this one, after they have been joined, the body is converted into spirit, and the spirit into body. Then this fire must be increased until the fixed part contains the volatile part within its own color and nature. Know, for certain, that when it is properly joined, it transcends all things and brings them into its own virtue. Afterward, it tinges one million two hundred thousand parts <note>original: *millies mille, & ducenties mille*. 1,200,000.</note>, of which you should be entirely persuaded.* It also multiplies itself in mass and virtue, as **Pythagoras**, **Isindricus**, and the *Codex of Truth* openly and clearly indicate. These are the Count’s words in summary.

<margin>Doubled mercury. Bodies.</margin>
<margin>Fire.</margin>
These things are declared most openly throughout his writings, so that it is evident to all that he had no other art besides the one I described above. The **one root** is metallic Mercury, which they call the **first matter**, which in the art is "doubled," as Bernard himself says: namely, raw and coagulated; or corporeal (extracted from bodies) and mineral. 

As for what those "bodies" are, he has taught elsewhere: namely, none other than the perfect ones, **gold and silver**. In the beginning, they are often different than they are during fermentation. Nothing, however, prevents them from being placed there even at the start, provided it is not without the "double mercury," and that they are handled separately, not together. For extraction and boiling, he employs fire—both internal and external—concerning which he says it must be adapted to the proportion of the matter. That is, it must never fail until the end of the constant union of the two mercuries, in which the goal was to make the perfect bodies spiritual, and conversely, to reduce the mercurial spirit into a body. Thus, the whole generated from them would have the nature of both bodies and spirits, which is also found in the elixir. 

This is accomplished by two operations: by **dissolving and coagulating**. After these, the internal fire is to be increased through the **fixed ferment**, so that the volatility of the elixir is brought to constancy, and the tincture and nature of the ferment are bred into it. In this very stage, an intimate mixing and union must occur, lest one desert the other, but that a homogeneous nature and force be created everywhere. And thus the Stone is made fixed through fermentation, for gold or silver, whichever is preferred. Once this is done, it has simultaneously acquired a transmuting power, by which it can turn and transmute all imperfect and related mercurial bodies into its own nature—so that from a golden elixir, gold is made, and from a silver one, silver—to such a degree that one part tinges very many parts: just as if it were first multiplied by mercury, from one part...

<summary>This page critiques Pseudo-Thomas Aquinas's sulfur-based alchemy as a "mastery of apparent mixture" before introducing Bernard of Trevisan, who emphasizes that the Stone is made from "one root" (mercury) and perfect metals (gold and silver).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Philosopher's Stone, moving from the specific recipes attributed to Pseudo-Thomas Aquinas to the broader philosophical and allegorical teachings of Bernard of Trevisan, specifically regarding the "multiplication" of the Stone's power and the allegory of the King's Fountain.</meta>

# On the Philosopher's Stone.

...they become a hundred: one of these produces a thousand, and of these, one tints <note>original: *tingit*. In alchemy, "tinting" or "tincturing" refers to the Stone's ability to transform the color and nature of a base metal into gold or silver.</note> a thousand, which is a number of a thousand times a thousand, etc.

<margin>Multiplication.</margin>
With these there is also the multiplication of quantity. For the stone, dissolved and coagulated by new mercury, always increases. This is the genuine meaning of the sayings of **Bernard** <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist known for his search for the Stone and his allegorical writings.</note>. But let us also survey the axiomatic instructions more worthy of note.

<margin>Which crude mercury is used.</margin>
<margin>The opinion reduced to a few words.</margin>
<margin>Mercurial water.</margin>
Concerning the matter of the stone, he discusses many things in his address to **Thomas** <note>Likely referring to the *Letter to Thomas Aquinas* attributed to Bernard.</note>, in which he teaches that perfect bodies—namely, gold and silver—must be cooked in mercury and dissolved. He specifies using crude mercury from the mine, though prepared through distillation and other purifications, so that it does not lose its humidity or become altered by salts and vitriol <note>A term for sulfate minerals, often used as corrosive agents in early chemistry.</note> (as happens in "vulgar" or common sublimation, which contributes nothing to this craft), but rather retains it. For he says: *These species (gold and silver) are to be cooked in mercury, and it is their water; there, by altering them, it interchangeably receives their changes.* And: *If gold is cooked in quicksilver (that is, dissolved properly and by the natural way of the art), that quicksilver will acquire the natural properties of that gold.* And: *He does not find the truth who follows any teaching that alters mercury—which is the seed <note>original: *sperma*.</note>—before the conjunction of the metallic species with it.* Mercurial water is not clear and transparent, but is mercury itself. For no water, by natural reduction, dissolves a metallic species except that which remains with them in matter and form, and which the dissolved metals themselves can again congeal. The Sun and Moon <note>Alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver.</note>, when dissolved in mercury, are held hidden. For their nature is hidden in the mercury until they are re-thickened. In Hermetic Philosophy, he names the first matter as "mercury" and "sulfur," from which the stone is made; but he doubles the mercury and indicates that nonetheless three things come together when he says: *Join the red man to the white wife in a crude chamber.* Therefore, although he often speaks as if only one perfect body should be dissolved in mercury, two must be understood to work together so that a common <term>elixir</term> <note>A medicinal or chemical substance capable of changing metals or prolonging life.</note> may be made from them. 

->(The power of three, two liquids, one essence)<-

<margin>In mercury, etc., the natural conjunction of the male and female seeds occurs, as in the sea, etc.</margin>
<margin>The double heat of the fire.</margin>
To what end this matter must be brought, he advises with these words, saying *that by the art it must be made more than perfect, so that it may be able to perfect others.* The method of this is called "cooking" or "solution," etc., in which a double fire is used. For he says: *For our craft we have a double heat, which is why it perfects so quickly, namely sulfur (gold, or what is in gold) and fire.* For nature must be assisted by fire, and there is no other help besides this. If the fire is stronger than is right, it hinders the movement and mutual action; if it is weaker, one thing is not changed into the other. Let the fire be vaporous, moderate, continuous, not excessive, subtle—now bright, now pressed down, enclosed, and incombustible.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
<margin>Blackness.</margin>
<margin>Weight.</margin>
He also indicates the process: namely, that it must first be dissolved, though not precipitantly, lest it happen before its time; and that first the <term>blackness</term> <note>original: *nigredo*. The first stage of the alchemical Great Work, symbolizing putrefaction and the stripping away of old forms.</note> must be produced. Unless this happens, the whiteness and redness do not follow. The cooking of the mercury must be carried out in a triple vessel; the weight must be sought out by subtle <term>stoichiometry</term> <note>original: *stochaimo*. Referring here to the balanced proportions of the four elements (fire, air, water, earth).</note>, and as much moisture must be given as can be digested by the heat, as I advised regarding coagulation; and let it not be excessive. For much resists much, while a few things are more quickly overcome. Gold is dissolved in mercury since it is nothing other than mature quicksilver, which may assist the immature quicksilver through the cooking of the art and the perfecting of nature. But let the books themselves be read. It will appear to no sane person that all these things agree with what was said above.

<margin>The enigmatic practice of Bernard.</margin>
<margin>The Fountain.</margin>
<margin>Note, only the king is named because the fermentation process is considered: or the simple work for exaltation. 10 months.</margin>
If anyone desires a taste of the enigmatic practice, he may be guided thus. Bernard proposes a certain <term>fountain</term> <note>original: *fontina*. A diminutive meaning "little fountain," a central allegory in Bernard's work *The Parable of the Fountain*.</note>, which he describes as follows: *The fountain is of wonderful virtue, more than any other in the whole world (for no corporeal creature is similar to philosophical mercury: in no mineral or vegetable is nature so wonderful). It is prepared only for the King of that province, whom it knows well, and he knows it in turn; it attracts him, and he is in it for 282 days, and it renews the King so that he exists as invincible, and thus he perishes.*

(This mercury is prepared by craftsmen primarily for dissolving and exalting gold into the stone, though sometimes also for silver. However, there is such familiarity between gold and quicksilver that they unite and rest together in a friendly way, seeing as gold is mature and coagulated quicksilver. Therefore, just as water takes in ice, dissolves it, and unites it to itself inseparably, so also mercury prepared philosophically—and if it be a mineral mercury, or if it be the gold of the art, the kinship is even closer—unites with gold if the process of the art is followed. Those "days" reach almost ten months, the time in which they wish the stone to be perfected, although Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, another seminal alchemical author.</note> describes no certain time. This is indicated here by the "renewal of the King," by which he emerges with such virtue that he cannot be conquered. When he says "for the King of that region," let the metallic genus be understood. He "perishes" in the fountain because he is destroyed and passes away into the stone, etc.)

<margin>The protection of the fountain.</margin>
The King commanded this fountain to be enclosed, first by a round white stone, and the fountain itself approaches the clarity of silver of a celestial color. Then he erected an oak tree, split through the middle, so that the rays of the Sun might be kept away. Furthermore, you see it well-protected on all sides by strong walls of beautiful, transparent stone, and the oak split in the middle: this is done because the nature of the fountain is so wonderful that it would penetrate everything if it were provoked to anger, and if it were ignited, we would all perish.

<margin>Fire is not used in the solution: nor cold: therefore vapor.</margin>
(That mercury is enclosed in a round glass, which they call a "violet" or "geranium," and this in turn is placed in an oblong oak box that opens in the middle. The color of the mercury is like bluish-silver. The oak box is added so that neither elementary heat nor the heat of the Sun can reach it. For as long as it is in the box, there is no need for external fire, but the internal fire acts. Afterward, the box is of no use. Fire should not be applied at the beginning, because the matter would be destroyed, and the <term>putrefaction</term> would be rendered void, or the solution would not succeed, and thus all things would perish—that is, the oil and the works.)

I saw the King entering the fountain, but not exiting in the same way. As soon as he entered and the guardian shut him in, he could no longer be seen until after a hundred and thirty days; then he began to appear and to grow bright. The janitor who performs this care continuously heats the bath for him to preserve the heat, which is driven secretly into the clear water, and he carries this out without ceasing, day and night.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the alchemical teachings of Bernard of Trevisan, specifically transitioning into the famous allegory of the "King's Fountain." ### Alchemical Commentary Part II. Book IV.

<margin>
Note that there is a different meaning if only two mercuries are placed at the beginning. The reasoning is different in fermentation.
</margin>

(Gold absorbed by mercury is no longer seen in its own color and whole nature. Yet it gives signs of its presence after several months through a lemon-yellow or reddish color. This bath must be cherished with external heat so that the internal sulfur of the gold may come into action and work upon the water.)

<margin>
Colors in fermentation.
</margin>

*The King at first has a golden garment, then a breastplate of black silk; his undergarment is snowy white, and his flesh is blood-red.* (The order of the appearing colors. Gold at the start is of its own color. Therefore, its blood-red tincture should not be taken, nor its whiteness, but the gold itself, pure and perfect in its own color. When it is dissolved in quicksilver, blackness or the "crow’s head" <note>original: *caput corvi*. An alchemical term for the "nigredo" or black stage, signifying the death and decomposition of the base matter.</note> emerges. When the coagulation is finished, whiteness appears; however, in silver-like fermentation only, with more abundant fire, a blood-red color also emerges, and then the stone is complete.)

<margin>
The keeper of the bath.
</margin>

*When the King proposes to approach the little fountain, he dismisses all foreign attendants, and no one enters but himself; nor is anyone permitted to approach except for the one who has care of him, who can be the simplest person, since he contributes nothing else but the heating of the bath, yet he does not approach or enter.* (These things are said concerning the "simple work" or the golden ferment. Nothing foreign is mixed into the work. Sun and Moon <note>Alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver.</note> are not foreign, says Thomas, since they are coagulated quicksilver, agreeing with the crude sort, from which the mixed "mercury of the philosophers" is extracted and called "quicksilver from quicksilver." Regarding the guardian or minister, the matter is clear; however, those things must also be considered which Bernard ingeniously noted regarding the administration of the degree of heat. It is necessary, therefore, for that heater to be governed by the skill of the artist.)

<margin>
The intimacy of gold and mercury.
</margin>

*The little fountain and the King love each other wonderfully. She attracts him, not he her. For she is like a mother to him.* (It is known that gold is most greedily absorbed by quicksilver, and it must be joined to it through an amalgam as well. When he says the King does not attract the fountain, it can be understood as the penetrating power of mercury, which works its way into the gold, and not the gold into it. The matter is explained by the argument of similarity with a mother, who often loves her child without reciprocal love. She is the mother because the "first matter" of gold was mercury; as he says: at other times she also bears the name of a woman.)

<margin>
Metals to be transmuted.
</margin>

*There are only six persons in his retinue, awaiting his death. If he should die once, they would obtain the kingdom as much as he, and by equal right they would be kings; therefore they serve him. For they await him, to whom they owe all their goods.*

<margin>
A description of gold.
</margin>

(In the category of metals, seven species are counted, if quicksilver is included—though it is not a metal. Besides gold, six remain; of these it is said that they owe every good to gold. For Nature, striving toward the best, makes those others along the way; then, through the elixir and tincture of gold, into which it has passed after its slaughter or destruction <note>In alchemy, the "destruction" of gold refers to its dissolution into a liquid state so it can be reborn as the Stone.</note>, they are likewise tinted into gold equally noble. Thus they occupy his kingdom.)

*The little fountain is older and more mature than all those under him. He is indeed worn out by old age, yet none of his subjects can endure as much cold and heat as he; nor so many rains, winds, and other things or labors. Once he has been renewed in this fountain, none of his companions can kill him. All were made from the fountain in the beginning and have their goods from there, just as he does. Therefore, because of the love with which the fountain is moved toward him, as his first mother, she attracts and kills him. The same one later rises again through her, and for the substance of the kingdom which is in very minute particles, each of the companions receives his portion and becomes as rich as he; and they are all equally wealthy.* (Gold is said to be older than quicksilver, if you understand it as the "philosophical mercury," which is drawn from gold. It is obvious that the tincture excels all other metals in strength, and it is common knowledge that none lasts as long in fire, in *aqua forti* <note>Nitric acid.</note>, and mercurial water, in the vapors of sharp things, and in other trials, as perfect gold does. 

From mercury—though one is the philosophical mercury and another is common quicksilver—as from the first matter, all metals are born. Whatever good they have received, they have from it, and for the same reason they can also acquire the final perfection, but nonetheless through the King, or by his benefit. Therefore, it is necessary for it to be dissolved by quicksilver, exalted and thinned, so that by a small portion it can tint <note>Transform the nature and color of.</note> much of another metal; and because they all have a kinship among themselves because of mercury, they can all equally be turned into gold.)

*The King alone enters the fountain, nor can any of the foreign attendants or companions enter; although they love her, they cannot enter, since they have not yet earned it.* (The same thing was also said before: that gold and mercury alone constitute the art. Although the remaining metals are also friends to quicksilver, they are excluded because they are imperfect and impure.)

<margin>
The succession of colors.
</margin>

*When the King first entered, he handed over his discarded golden tunic to his first attendant, Saturn <note>The alchemical name for Lead.</note>, who guards it for 40 or 42 days, if it is eventually owed to him. Then the King takes off his black silk breastplate, handing it to another attendant, Jupiter <note>The alchemical name for Tin.</note>, to be guarded for 20 days. Jupiter grants it, by the King’s command, to the beautifully sparkling and glowing Moon <note>Silver.</note>, who keeps it for twenty days. Thus the King is in his honored, pure white undergarment, and he places it upon Mars <note>Iron.</note> to be kept for forty or forty-two days. From Mars, the Sun <note>Gold.</note> receives it, God willing, yet not sufficiently clear and shining. When he has guarded it for forty days, he becomes exceedingly beautiful, tinted with an excellent blood-red, and he keeps that seized cloak.* (The process of the operations is described through the signs of the colors. The golden color of the Sun vanishes and lies hidden under the lividity of Saturn, whose blackness emerges on the fortieth day. Thus the golden splendor lay hidden in the cold for so long. Afterward, it changes into blackness, after which Jupiter is said to dominate. The blackness indeed lasts quite a long time, yet eventually it changes into whiteness, which at first is tin-like, after the first operation is finished. In the ferment likewise there is a change from blackness to whiteness, but silver-like. However, regarding what he says about that hand-off being done by the King’s command: it must be understood as the power of gold, under that dominating color, turning toward this end—that it may reach the red—by its own nature; and it is then called "white gold" in the golden ferment. Therefore he says the King is then in his honorable white cloak, because of the nobility by which it could become the most precious silver if we wished to tint. Yellowing like copper succeeds the whiteness, and finally the blood-red color of the tincture. This succession of colors is said to happen for this reason: because nature does not come to the final metal except through intermediates, as if it first makes lead from quicksilver, which is lightly congealed quicksilver, then tin, then silver, copper, and gold; but nonetheless there is disagreement on these matters, as is said elsewhere.)

<margin>
The benefits of transformation.
</margin>

*Then the fountain opens itself, and when she has given them the undergarment, the gown, and the breastplate, she offers them at once blood-red and highly colored flesh to eat, and then their greed is satisfied. When they have received the white undergarment, four of them, if they wish, can attain great dignity and honor, but they hold no more than half the kingdom. Therefore, for such a small gain...*

<summary>This page details the alchemical allegory of the "King's Fountain," explaining the dissolution of gold into mercury and the subsequent stages of color (black, white, red) represented by planetary attendants. It emphasizes the "kinship" of all metals through their shared mercurial origin, which allows for their eventual transmutation into gold.</summary>

-> # On the Philosopher's Stone <-

...they wait rather for the end, so that they may possess the crown of their King by full right. (This indicates that in the completed transmutation of the Stone, the substance and dignity of gold are bestowed upon the imperfect metals at the same time. If anyone wishes to tint <note>The process of "tinging" or dyeing a metal to change its nature.</note> before the completion, it can be done when the silver color and perfection have been introduced—just as when the white or red ferment has been given and the solution is made, and the coagulation reaches a silver whiteness, they can be tinted into silver. But the author says this is not advisable; one should rather wait until the perfect redness emerges through the power of fire. Once this is done, they reach the full status of gold.)

No physician or any other thing is present except for the keeper, who does nothing else but heat and regulate the fire perpetually. However, he has more labor at the end than at the beginning, for then the fountain is set ablaze. (Many people carry around various medicines and fake recipes. The author rejects these as useless and admits nothing except gold and mercury <term>hydrargyrum: liquid silver or quicksilver</term>, from which the primary matter of the Stone is made. The caretaker of the fire works harder at the end of each coagulation than at the start, because the Stone, having been gradually exposed to a slow fire, has gradually learned to endure it. The constant whiteness and redness are not produced except by a strong fire, which—after the ferment is united—can no longer harm the Stone even if it is at the highest degree, unless it is not yet perfect enough and still smokes upon a glowing metal plate.)

The whole world has it before its eyes, and yet does not recognize it. (Examples of Nature are encountered everywhere, yet men are not wise enough to think that just as it happens in other things, so here the metallic grain must be destroyed so that, through heat and seminal power with the application of suitable nourishment, it may grow. Certainly, a thing does not come from just anything, nor is it nourished by just anything, nor does it happen by just any fire or in any place. Vegetables require things suitable to their nature, as do animals. Therefore, minerals—which stand between the crudely mixed and the vegetable—also have the rudiment of a vegetative power. From man comes man, by human seed and blood. From gold comes gold, by golden seed and nourishment, etc. But there are also certain things in the Work which, even if they were shown to everyone, would still not be recognized—such as the blackness. Thus, everyone sees gold, but they do not recognize its multiplying and transmuting power.)

<margin>Those six can also be understood as the disposition and qualities in the process of the Work.</margin>

If they wish, those six can purge the King again, shut for three days in the fountain, so that on the first day, with the heat persisting, the golden breastplate is changed to black; on the second, a white undergarment appears; on the third, blood-red flesh. When this is done, God multiplies him a thousand times a thousand, and ten times more. (The red tincture, by which those six metals are turned into gold, can be multiplied with new mercury, so that one portion results in an increase as many times as he says—that is, unto infinity. The augmentation is completed in three days if the Stone has been brought to such fineness; otherwise, in the mind's eye, it takes three months, etc. That augmentation differs in no way from the preceding operations regarding the process and the signs. For here, too, it turns black in solution, turns white in coagulation, and finally turns red.)

Secretly I came to the fountain, and I unlocked everything with the keys provided, inspecting the book which I had carried back as a victor. But while I was admiring its remarkable splendor, I became drowsy and it fell into the fountain, which made me indignant. I gazed and searched with my eyes, but my sight grew dim, and nothing met my gaze. I began to drain the prescribed fountain, and I proceeded in that work so strenuously that nothing remained except a twelfth part of it with a tenth. I insisted on draining it all. But it clung together too tenaciously. While I was in that labor, there were those who wished to meet with me. Therefore, I was pulled away from the work and I departed, after first carefully closing everything so that no one would discover I had been there and had drained the fountain, and so he might not steal the little book from me. But when the heat of the bath, intended for washing the King, rose up into the work and was set on fire because of a certain mistake, I was in prison for forty days. At the end of these, I returned to contemplate the fountain: and behold, black and dark clouds appeared, which lasted for a long time. But to explain myself in a few words, at the end I finally saw everything that I had anxiously desired in my prayers, nor did I endure so much labor thereafter.

<margin>The Draining <note>original: *Exantlatio*. Refers to the exhausting labor of drawing out or draining.</note></margin>

(Everything he said above applies to the first conjunction of the gold of the philosophers and mercury—which are two mercuries: one of a golden and sulfurous nature, the other of a silvery, feminine nature, etc. What is now set down pertains to the true fermentation, though the word "fermentation" is also used for the earlier stages. He says, therefore, that he had the golden book—that is, the purest gold—so that it was of a marvelous splendor. He entrusted this quite fearfully to the mercury, as if he thought it lost. For immediately it lost its natural color and joined with the mercury, so that it was no longer visible to the eyes. Once the amalgam <note>original: *amalgamate*. A blend of mercury with another metal.</note> was made, he left a twelfth part with a tenth—indeed even an eleventh—with the gold; that is, three parts out of twelve. For the remaining nine are submitted in their own time (as I now declare). In the intervals, with the vessel closed, he was able to attend to other things and spend time with friends, so as not to be always stuck to the work. After forty days had passed, during which the fountain was left alone, the crow's head <note>original: *caput corui*. The black stage of alchemy.</note> appeared, and it lasted a long time. For it remains not only until the complete solution, but also in the coagulation for ninety days at the start, until the whiteness is drawn out by the power of fire. And this takes place in both the first and second operations. In the remaining stages, blackness also appears, but it does not last as long. Finally, the mind is filled with its desire. Regarding that "draining," it can also be understood another way, namely concerning the solution of gold at the beginning. For however eagerly we <unclear>demand</unclear> it and wish to extract it all, we cannot do so because of the tight and stubborn union, except in the ferment, where the mercury is sharpened by the elixir. But what the "twelfth part with the tenth" means then, unless the former is taken as silver and the latter as gold, I confess I do not follow. This is still according to the opinion of Bernard.)

### ALANUS <note>Likely referring to Alan of Lille, a 12th-century scholar to whom alchemical works were often attributed.</note>

<margin>Solution.</margin>
<margin>Blackness.</margin>

Take the best mercury, which has been sublimated seven times. Rectify <note>Purify a liquid by repeated distillation.</note> it by adding one part quicklime <note>original: *calcis vivæ*</note> and half a part crude tartar. Thus it is properly cleansed. Or, clean it as best you can (others wash it with wine and salt until it no longer turns black; then they distill it, and thus the thickness is removed, leaving the subtilty behind). Mix three parts of this with one part of gold or silver drawn into thin leaves <note>original: *bracteas*</note>, so that it results in an amalgam. This done, add to it nine parts of cleansed mercury and shut it in a knotted vessel; place it in cooked ashes <note>A sand or ash bath for even heating.</note> so that they slightly exceed the glass. Apply a slow, continuous heat. Thus the "old man" sits in the bath. Leave it there in the closed vessel until the visible mercury is hidden and the hidden body is made manifest. The philosophers call this solution and sublimation, and by other names, though it is one labor, one regimen, one vessel, and one furnace. If it stays in moderate heat for forty days, a blackness appears at the top like black pitch. That is the crow’s head <note>original: *caput corui*</note> of the philosophers and the mercury of the wise.

<header>Alchemical Commentary, Part II, Book IV.</header>

<margin>Extraction of the soul.</margin>
The soul of the body of gold or silver is extracted by means of mercury. The spirit of mercury is animated; the soul is joined to the spirit uniformly, etc.

<margin>Preparation of the philosophers' mercury.</margin>
<margin>Within 40 days.</margin>
One part of gold or silver leaf (the thinner it is, the more quickly the mercury is made) and twelve parts of the best purified mercury are mixed together. They are placed in a small furnace in dry ashes and cooked with a moderate fire. When they have remained in the "fire of wisdom" <note>A steady, controlled heat used by alchemists.</note> for a "philosopher's month" <note>Often a period of 40 days rather than a calendar month.</note>, a horrendous blackness emerges, and one color drives out another until finally one exists alone; this is the **mercury of the philosophers**. Such an extraction of the soul by the spirit of mercury does not happen all at once, but in several stages; it always comes out little by little until the work is completed. There is one way: grinding and cooking. Mercury grinds, fire cooks. The vessel

<margin>It comes out a little at a time.</margin>
<margin>What the blackness is.</margin>
<margin>The 4 Elements.</margin>
should always be closed, the fire continuous. The blackness which appears on the fortieth day is nothing other than the dissolved body. For spiritual things are raised up. If the water has reduced the body to an impalpable essence and dissolved it into blackness, the solution is fulfilled, and the tincture is in the blackness; and the four elements have come forth, so that you have air with water, and fire with earth. That which is dissolved is raised up with the mercury, although the greater part is always below. See the rest as well, for <term>Alanus</term> <note>Likely referring to Alan of Lille, a 12th-century scholar to whom alchemical works were often attributed.</note> is quite open in his writing.

## A CERTAIN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
<margin>Blackness and sulfur.</margin>
Take equal parts of silver and gold: twelve parts of Mercury. Putrefy and dissolve them with a gentle fire, and do this until a redness appears, which is called <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of metals.</note>. If the whole is dissolved so that nothing remains intact at the bottom, it is finished. (He orders it to be squeezed through leather, as Thomas does. If the whole thing passes through, then the whole is dissolved.) Place this <term>crow’s head</term> <note>original: "caput corvi"; a symbol for the "nigredo" or black stage of the alchemical process.</note> in a vial in water (in a shell) and separate the mercurial water from the body by distilling, and segregate the four elements (this is done by a feather, not by fire).

<margin>Coagulation.</margin>
<margin>Sulfur of metals.</margin>
Join the aforementioned water with the black earth as many times as necessary until the earth has soaked up all its water and turned white. Once this is done, <term>sublime</term> it <note>A process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then becomes solid again, used for purification.</note> (urge it with a sublimating fire so it is exalted in quality), and you have the sulfur of metals. When it has perfectly whitened (which happens after the ferment), it is the **elixir for the white** <note>The stage capable of transmuting metals into silver.</note>. Increase the fire so that it turns yellow and then red, and you have the **elixir for the red** <note>The final stage capable of transmuting metals into gold.</note>. It is necessary that you first feed this stone its natural food. Then proceed to the tinging of metals. (The

<margin>Preparation for the entrance.</margin>
<margin>Time.</margin>
preparation for the "entrance," which occurs if you add the <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery residue left after a metal is burned or oxidized.</note> of its own body of gold or silver, depending on which type of tincture is being made.)
The time for completion is 12 months. In 30 days, the earth is born from <term>Saturn</term> <note>Lead.</note>. In 100 days, the living mercury grows into water. After 60 days, air grows from the sulfur. During the remaining days, the soul descends upon the earth and receives the power of things above and below. Then an image of many wings will emerge; it will conquer and will not be conquered by any fire.

## THE BOOK OF PANDORA.

<margin>Preparation of mercury.</margin>
<margin>Mercury of the philosophers.</note>
Wash the mercury with male urine, adding a little salt, and do this until it is strained out pure. Pass the mercury through leather and sublime it without any additives, so that it becomes like a crystalline mirror. Use this in dissolving gold or silver. It is called the "spirit" which turns gold and silver into a mercury like itself, which is called the **mercury of metals** or the **mercury of the philosophers**. Mix 9 parts of this with one part of gold or silver leaf or calx into an <term>amalgam</term>. Let them putrefy into blackness, by which they may be separated, etc.

<margin>Degrees of fire.</margin>
The degrees of fire are managed by oak charcoals in an earthenware pan with holes poked in it unevenly, according to the measure of the degrees. The hole for the 1st degree is made in the middle, with eight others surrounding it. It should hold 12 ounces of charcoal. For the 2nd degree, the holes should be wider and the coals doubled. For the 3rd degree, the holes are widened again and triple the charcoal is put in. The 4th degree is a bare flame fire. The material is enclosed in a "geranium" <note>A specific type of alchemical vessel or enclosure.</note>, which is placed in an oval earthenware bowl containing washed ashes, etc.

## FROM GEORGE RIPLEY, EDITED BY PENOTUS.
<note>George Ripley was a famous 15th-century English alchemist; Bernard Gilles Penot was a 16th-century French alchemist and physician.</note>

Pay diligent attention to the "breadth" of our stone, and begin in the West, where the **red male** and the **white wife** shall become one, betrothed by the spirit of life, so that they may live in love and peace. (He has three things here: gold, silver, and mercury, although most name only two.) Let the earth and water be equally proportioned, and one part earth for three parts spirit; this is also a good proportion, which is 12 parts spirit for 4 parts of earth or body. You ought to take three parts of the female and one of the male (others explain more clearly: here, the "male" refers to both bodies, and the "female" refers to the mercury). The less spirit you use in this "marriage," the more quickly you will finish your calcination, etc.

After the selection comes the **solution**, about which he says: That is the "killing" of the bodies for a long time in a bath or in dung, until 90 nights have passed in moist heat. Soon the blackness will be your indicator, etc. From this comes the **coagulation**, about which he says: The substance is nourished by its own <term>menstruum</term> <note>A solvent, though here used metaphorically as a nourishing fluid.</note>, and when the matter has become white, the spirit will be frozen with the bodies. Then follows the **repetition of the work**, about which he says: When you have made seven "imbibitions" <note>The process of repeatedly soaking a solid in a liquid and drying it.</note>, then you must turn the wheel, etc. Likewise: You shall turn the wheel three times, etc. After that is the **fermentation**, about which he speaks on page 84.

Before the perfect white stage—once the bodies are dissolved, divided, putrefied, and calcined—colors of inexplicable beauty will appear. After that white, a lemon-yellow and a false yellow will appear, and then the unchangeable red blood will appear.
Our **red male** does not tinge, nor does his wife, unless they are "tinged" (fermented). Fermentation is followed by **exaltation** for the purpose of "projection" <note>The final act of throwing the Stone onto a base metal to transmute it.</note>, about which he speaks on page 89; likewise **multiplication**, on page 86.

See the rest as well, and diligently compare what has been said. You will find the art whole and complete, provided you observe our order and apply the allegories. Add also those things which Penotus added concerning the "birth of metals," in which the preparation of the philosophical mercury is described. There is no true Philosopher who does not put forward those things which have been explained so far, even though the phrasing may seem strange and there may occasionally seem to be disagreement.

<sig>HH</sig>

### 1. Ezra 8.

<margin>Aristotle in *On Marvelous Things*:</margin>
**A**mong the items brought back from Babylon, there were two vessels of the finest shining bronze <note>original: *æris fulgentis*; Ezra 8:27 describes these as being as precious as gold.</note>, as beautiful as gold. 
Among the Indians, they say a bronze is found that is so bright, pure, and free from rust that it cannot be distinguished from gold by its color; however, among the cups of King Darius, several jars were found which could be recognized as being made of bronze rather than gold by no other means than their smell.

Indeed, Pliny says in *Book 34, Chapter 2* that once <term>orichalcum</term> <note>A golden-colored alloy of copper and zinc, similar to brass.</note> was discovered, Cyprian copper lost its value. He notes that for a long time, the highest quality was held in great admiration, but eventually it was no longer found as the earth became exhausted. Its quality was then imitated by "Marian copper," which absorbs a great deal of <term>cadmia</term> <note>Zinc ore or oxide used in the smelting process to turn copper into brass.</note>. Thus, it appears that this substance is both natural and artificial; one of these was perhaps that Babylonian or Indian bronze. This argues for the great antiquity of the chemical art <note>The author uses this to prove that alchemy (the "chemical art") has existed since ancient times.</note>. Lest you say it was merely natural, *Pliny* stands in the way, who in *Book 34, Chapter 17* denies that copper and lead are produced in India, but are instead traded there. But since the difference from gold could be detected by no judgment other than smell, was that bronze not perhaps turned into gold by the chemical art? Orichalcum is quickly proven false by many tests. As for the fact that orichalcum is no longer mined, could that be due to a change in the art of smelting, as happened with <term>electrum</term> <note>A natural or artificial alloy of gold and silver.</note>? The same can be gathered from the copper of the Mossynici <note>An ancient people of the Black Sea coast.</note> tempered with earth; that earth is found and smelted together with it, producing a very bright and white bronze, according to Aristotle.

### Suidas, Orosius, Constantine the Deacon.

**A**lchemy <note>original: *Chemia*</note> is the making of gold and silver. Diocletian sought out and burned the books of this art, etc., so that the Egyptians would not subsequently gain wealth from that art and rebel against the Romans.

**Suidas:** The Golden Fleece was actually a book written on skins, containing instructions on how gold ought to be made through alchemy.

Did the Argonauts not set out to the Colchians to learn the art, rather than to steal? The laws and conditions for taking the Fleece seem to be the documentation of the art. The watchful dragon is Mercury; it is not put to sleep except by Medea’s drug—that is, by "fixed sulfur" extracted from gold, which is instilled little by little and given to the dragon as if to be eaten. The fire-breathing bulls that had to be yoked, and the soldiers born from sown serpent teeth, represent nothing other than the progress of the alchemical work.

Why did Diocletian burn the books instead of kidnapping the craftsmen? Was it because they were so obscure that no one understood them, or because the Egyptians refused to interpret them? Just like that Indian man who could be compelled by no force to betray the secret of the root that induces "bloody sweat" <note>Likely a reference to a medicinal or alchemical botanical secret.</note>.

## PREFACE.

**T**here are three things in the discipline of minerals—which you might call metallurgy—that are quite ingenious and full of industry, and of no less necessity: the geometric description of mines (which is done with the help of the triangle, quadrant, magnetic table, etc.), the testing of metals, and the smelting. This was written long ago by Johannes Mathesius <note>A Lutheran pastor and friend of Luther who wrote *Sarepta*, a famous collection of "mining sermons" combining theology and mineralogy.</note>, a man of no common skill in mineral matters, and it is on the lips of almost all metallurgists. You might marvel at those subterranean <term>Pyracmons</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Pyracmon was one of the Cyclopes who worked in the forge of Vulcan; here Libavius uses the name as a poetic term for miners.</note>, who have devoted themselves entirely to digging out mountains and hollowing out the depths <note>original: *tartaro*; literally "the underworld," referring here to the deep recesses of a mine.</note>, living under the vast earth by paths, regions, dwellings, and roads almost as certain as those who walk in the Sun; and that they know the positions of east, west, south, north, and the angles, extensions, and curvatures, as exactly as if by the guidance of the Sun—

<meta>catchword: -dance [ductum]</meta>

## Preface.

->HH 2<-

...as if they had followed a path in the open light; and there are found those who, though they cannot distinguish the daylight outside so well, can nonetheless designate all their buildings in the belly of the earth with their chambers, streets, paths, crossroads, and meeting points, etc., so accurately on a map through boundaries that the upper parts correspond exactly to the lower. Some, indeed, if you show them a scraping of a vein, can point out with a ready finger the exact spot from which it was torn and in what part of the world it was born. 

But it is of no less wonder not only to recognize a dug stone—whether it be fertile with metal or not (for here practice even teaches the porters, so that just as a gardener knows the types of apples, they know how to judge a metallic vein by sight to some extent)—but also to clearly teach the granular difference: how much of this or that metal is within, how much of the mineral juices, how much of the mountain-rock, and whether the vein is mature or immature, whether it mocks the hope of the owners with a deceptive appearance or promises certain profit, etc. Indeed, they even prescribe the way and method to the <term>smelter</term> <note>original: *excoctori*, the craftsman responsible for extracting metal from ore using fire.</note> by which the riches embedded in the rocks can be carved out by the power of greater fires and, as it were, pressed out. For this reason, I would far prefer the <term>probatory</term> <note>The art of assaying; from the Latin *probare*, to test or prove.</note> art (as they call it—though we must accustom ourselves to this word, which has been accepted into the citizenship of this discipline by the prescription of long usage) to both the mapping of locations and the art of smelting. You would plunge into the earth rashly and describe towns there, as it were, in vain, unless the probatory art leads you by the hand. You would build furnaces and stretch bellows to no purpose unless the scout warns you how much it will cost to "cook" and in what manner you ought to do it.

Therefore, let us grant the higher place in <term>metallurgy</term> to this art, because it governs investigation—since one must follow where the fertile, non-deceptive, and sufficiently responsive vein leads—and also governs that which must be smelted, and how, as the nature of the matter in turn advises. The explorer <note>Here referring to the assayer as an "explorator" of the ore's inner nature.</note> makes both of these clear; indeed, he stands by and moderates almost every single stage: the meltings, the pourings, the roastings, and the mixtures. Without this, all metallic labor would tend toward uncertainty and could not direct itself to its proper end.

Nor is this merely a matter of discussing "dignity," for perhaps someone is considered more "worthy" whom the whim of the powerful wishes to be in greater honor, even if he has only as much metallic skill as a "sheaf of metallic stalks," as the saying goes among miners. We urge rather the necessity of the art, on account of which it also obtains the prerogative of dignity by our judgment. It is easy for any farmer, at any time of year and in any region (provided he is not a complete blockhead or a child in his discipline), to recognize apples and nuts, the seeds and fruits of other plants, and the offspring of animals—or at least to learn with such ease that, once shown, he recognizes them thereafter from the permanence of their face and nature. 

The knowledge of metals is not in the "bark," nor in external colors and shapes, but lies hidden in the depths. If you wish to make a judgment based solely on the appearance of the entire vein, you often cannot do so without hesitation, because from one vein a manifold offspring comes forth, dressed in such various ways that new ones occur daily. Here the metallurgist is compelled to perform the duty of <note>Aeacus was one of the three judges of the underworld in Greek mythology, known for his absolute impartiality and ability to see the soul stripped of its earthly body.</note> Aeacus: to look at the pure soul once the body is stripped away, so that he is not deceived by a garment more ornate or more filthy than is right, and thus pronounce a false judgment. He receives certain evidence from the assayer, by whose counsel both expenses are thereafter paid and profit is expected. 

For these two necessities invented the probatory art: namely, so that veins might be sought and dug up with fruitfulness, and separated and smelted with profit. Those who prepare the dug-up minerals by crushing, grinding, washing, roasting, in <term>smelting-places</term> <note>original: *vstrinis*, specifically referring to the calcining or burning furnaces.</note>, etc., follow the precepts of their own industry, to be sure, but by the judgment of the assayer, who can easily prescribe the method of those works—whether it must be roasted and how, when it must be washed, how the joined juices are to be resolved or <term>liquated</term> <note>original: *eliquandi*, the process of melting out a metal from its ore.</note>, and the rest—which cannot be so easily distinguished by the judgment of the eyes. Similarly, after preparation, he also advises the smelter in which furnace, with which fires, with what additive, and by what custom of the art the prepared veins are to be liquated. He also assists the refiner and the mint-master; he even catches and <unclear>if any</unclear> [deceit] of counterfeiters [creeps] from anywhere into metallurgy, minting, or <term>goldsmithing</term> <note>original: *aurifabrica*.</note>...

->Preface.<-

...have filled. *Necessity is therefore joined to dignity, and since the former is supported by the latter, it does not allow the assayer to be among the lowly.*

This discipline is a part of <term>chemical science</term> <note>Libavius uses the term *scientia Chymica*, which at this time encompassed both what we now call chemistry and the practical side of alchemy.</note>, and in ancient times it was in the power of the Alchemists. This will be easily recognized by anyone who has examined the records of that art and is well-versed in the ancient authors, especially those who use the rules of the <term>mastery of separation</term> <note>original: *magisteriorum segregationis*; these are specialized techniques for separating one substance from another, such as gold from silver.</note>. Therefore, even now, after it has passed to outsiders, a large part of the <term>probatory art</term> <note>Assaying; the systematic testing of ores and metals for purity.</note> is found within Alchemy. But it also adopts certain masterful processes of composition; and in its practice, it cannot do without physical experience, evidence, and Arithmetic. From this, it has become a specialized profession, just as usually happens in the practice of all arts. This can be seen in the faculty of Oratory, which has scraped together rules from everywhere—from the Dialecticians, Rhetoricians, Grammarians, Physics, Jurisprudence, Theology, and others. Hence that sentiment found in Cicero: that the Orator deals with many things and makes use of many branches of eloquence, even those for which he may not have his own specific rules.

Since, therefore, the Probatory Art is dispersed through many arts, and yet seems to require a common body of information for its esteemed use, no one is better suited for this function than the Chymist. He is the one who supplies the most important points from connected fields and gathers them from those that are scattered. So that my commentaries might not be incomplete, I wished to test my hand in this area as well—especially since I see that not only practical men deal with it, but even Philosophers consider it a point of honor to have worked strenuously upon it. I do not promise anyone my own inventions. The lasting arts can by no means be established solely on the experience and use of a single person. Instead, I will propose a completion of chemical matters based on what I have learned from distinguished craftsmen—both professors of Alchemy and Physicists, as well as those who have long been engaged in practice themselves, having been similarly taught and trained by their own masters. I have followed my own method of explanation, yet adding something of my own where I judge it serves the explanation. It will be enough for me to have wished to serve others when richer resources have failed in the actual result.

Moreover, **GEORGIUS AGRICOLA** <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555) is often called the "Father of Mineralogy"; his most famous work is *De Re Metallica*.</note> wrote most excellently and methodically on the Probatory Art; he is second to none in experience and metallic industry, nor in his diligence in writing. Recently, there has also appeared an excellent treatise by Modestinus Fachs, a master of the mint and a <term>weigher</term> <note>original: *Zygostata*; an official in charge of public scales or weighing at the mint.</note> of Anhalt, written in the German tongue according to the custom of this discipline among the Germans, and composed with great learning. Furthermore, there is the work of Lazarus Ercker, the Imperial Weigher and Master of Metals, which is full of learning and experience. Rennerus Budelius has some material in his books on coins and numismatics; he was himself a prefect of mints and the son of a mint master, and thus, having been nurtured in the discipline at home, he should not be considered among the least of the craftsmen. Among the ancients, Geber <note>An 8th-century Arab alchemist (Jabir ibn Hayyan), whose Latinized works were highly influential in Europe.</note> is the most prominent. Others have inserted bits here and there in their works, such as Pliny and others, along with a great number of Chymists and Arithmeticians who have occasionally sought to contribute something as an example. I shall use the craftsmen most of all. From the Philologists, I will sprinkle in "emblems" <note>Metaphorical or decorative flourishes of language.</note> whenever a convenient occasion presents itself—first proposing the rules, then providing concise illustrations and discussions. In this way, those who are to learn the art will not lack the evidence of axiomatic principles, and Philosophers may find things upon which they prefer to contemplate and debate among themselves.

Just as in other arts, which are perfected by practice rather than mere knowledge, some things are <term>theoretical</term> <note>original: *theoretika*</note> and pertain to the <term>preparation of instruments</term> <note>original: *paraskeuēn organikēn*</note> (in which the necessary aids and tools for working well are proposed); and some things are <term>practical</term> <note>original: *praktika*</note> and describe the form and method of working upon the subject itself. Thus, in the probatory art, the first part is to know the names, forms, and arrangements of the instruments. For upon these depends the practice that must be established according to the rules of the art.
