### Preface.

<margin>Synopsis of the probatory art.</margin>
So that I may set forth in a synopsis or table a certain [outline] of the whole of <gloss><term>preparation</term> <note>original: "sceuasticæ"; from the Greek "skeuasia," referring to the preparation of equipment and materials.</note> & <term>assaying</term> <note>original: "docimasticæ"; from the Greek "dokimasia," meaning the testing or examination of metals.</note></gloss>; let the first member of the probatory art be its own Preparation: the second, Assaying itself. In the study of preparation, the things of greatest consideration are the small furnaces, the hearth, the **ash cupels** <note>Small, porous bowls used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals.</note>, with their own small mortar and pestle, the **touchstone** <note>original: "lapis lydius"; a dark stone used to test the purity of gold by the color of the streak it leaves.</note>, testing needles, balances, weights, **nitric acids** <note>original: "aquæ fortes."</note>, fluxes, cements, coloring agents, and the scorifier: these are among the most essential. There are also others, greater in number, such as triangular crucibles, the blowpipe, bellows, the sighting-tube, the washing-trough, the casting mold or trough, small separating flasks with their tripod, brass brushes, hooks, clay, fire-tongs, the magnet, lye, golden shells, storage compartments, sieves, the mold for casting pellets, and other things adopted from general Chemistry and other foreign arts.

Assaying, indeed, besides the general judgment of minerals, is perfected by the exploration of metals and mineral media—principally the former, and the latter more cursorily. For this reason, those in the mining trade think this does not pertain to them, even though they are drawn in by the commonality of the precepts, nor should they be excluded from the essence of the art. It tests everything by fire and water: and metals, moreover, even by stone—either the touchstone or the magnet—and by similar, more specialized means, such as by mercury, weight, sound, color, sharp vapors, etc. (so that what was said of the smelting art—that he is a good smelter who can temper the four elements—is also true of the probatory art), about which it is customary to teach in its proper place. Furthermore, the distribution of the art is made from the nature of the subjects. For in metallic things, we explore either the veins, stones, or dross—that is, slag, furnace-crusts, or embers, ashes, and the like, some of which are mild and tractable, others refractory and stubborn, or some <gloss>easy</gloss>, some <gloss>difficult</gloss>, etc. Or, we examine pure metals, whether they are born thus in the veins and remain there, or are pushed out by the force of floods and storms, or are smelted, simple, or mixed. In these are various kinds of tin, such as **electrum** <note>A natural or artificial alloy of gold and silver.</note>, masses in cakes and loaves; wrought masses, coinage, the works of goldsmiths, artificial metals, and the rest; and these not only when solid, but even while they are still in flux during smelting or refining, and not only when finished, but even while still "under the master" <note>An intermediate stage of the metallurgical process before final refinement.</note>, so that the limit of perfection may be explored. From these things we understand that this art is of prompt benefit not only for the establishment and governance of the entire metallurgical industry, but also for political decrees concerning coinage and the metals to be mixed by goldsmiths; likewise for gold-leaf, and for various trades of metals or those things made from metals, or things coated or composed of them. From this, at the same time, counterfeiters can be confronted, and frauds detected and punished. The breadth of this art extends even into domestic economy and medicine. For when the <term>Paracelsians</term> <note>Followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus, whom Libavius often criticized for what he saw as chemical "magic" or deceptive practices.</note>—to whom this is almost innate—propose to us their gilded cups and foods, and it is established to what extent metals can be treated by them, and how they may even be recovered from juices, their falsehoods will be easily detected, insofar as it is permitted to this art. Thus, if anyone hawks sparrow-beaks and teeth covered with a yellow crust from "tartarean bile" as being golden, an industrious explorer can very easily restrain his audacity. Likewise, there is great use for gold, silver, copper, and iron in medicines. From them are made calces, liquors, flowers, oils, etc.; the probatory art certainly serves these. Those who cultivate **gold-making** <note>original: "chrysopœiam"; alchemy focused on the transmutation of base metals into gold.</note> and strive to know natural sympathies, antipathies, mixtures, etc., are led by this art as if by a right hand into the inner chambers of nature. Absolutely everywhere that metals and other minerals either are, or are said to be, this art holds its kingdom.

Furthermore, there are several classes of craftsmen, according as they are practiced in different materials. Goldsmiths, gold-separators, and the like, for the most part possess a maimed version of this art, since they have acquired some skill in gold, silver, copper, and perhaps also the remaining metals, but not in raw ores, nor in veins, slag, stones, furnace-refuse, hearths, and others—though even in these they see something more fully than a cow does, due to the relationship between the materials. Those who are employed at mines and smelting and casting workshops must be altogether the most shrewd...

And so, for the most part, they combine with the <term>probatory art</term> <note>The art of assaying or testing the purity of metals.</note> some aspect of metallurgical duty, so that the opportunity is not lacking to descend even into the mines themselves, and to behold in person the origin and <term>matrices</term> <note>The surrounding rock or "mother-stone" in which a mineral or crystal is embedded.</note> of metals. <term>Mint masters</term> have claimed for themselves the department of mixtures* <note>Referring to the alloying of metals for coinage.</note>. *Merchants have added the [consideration of] weight and the stone* <note>The touchstone, used for a quick assessment of gold purity.</note> *to their own established system for external valuation; and thus even this art has been pulled apart into various branches, lest it should not experience the same status as the rest. # ON THE ART OF ASSAYING
## PART ONE CONCERNING
### PREPARATION. <note>original: "Scevasia," from the Greek for the preparation of equipment or apparatus.</note>

#### CHAPTER I.
#### *What is the Probatory Art?*

<margin>Pliny, Book 33, Chapter 9: The art of discerning defects.</margin>

**I**T IS the art of testing minerals, and among these especially metallic ones, in order to determine the quantity of pure essence, their perfection, quality, and composition.
I call it an "art," although it owes its most important precepts to Chemistry and Physics. Even the branches of arts are themselves arts, possessing matter and form by equal right. However, the name of that category [art] fits it better than "science," since it is <term>practical</term> <note>original Greek: πρακτική (praktike); focused on action and application rather than pure theory.</note>. Its subject is indeed mineral things, but it is practiced more on metallic ones—by which word I include not only pure ones but also impure and mixed ones. And the distinction between the "mineral" genus and the "metallic" species was pleasing, although for Physicians, "metal" and "metallic" are almost the same as "fossil" <note>In the early modern period, "fossil" referred to anything dug out of the earth.</note>. The goals are distinguished by others into internal quality and external [value], which are set before the investigators; but they look most especially toward coinage. The examiner thoroughly investigates how much pure substance is in the ore and how much is foreign material. Then, [he asks] whether it is perfect or imperfect, burnt, whole, volatile, fixed, etc.; whether it is mild, harsh, <term>easy to use</term> <note>original Greek: εὔχρητον (euchreton)</note>, <term>difficult to use</term> <note>original Greek: δύσχρητον (dyschreton)</note>, etc. So also regarding the mixture: whether many metals are confused together or not, etc. From these things, he consequently concludes and pronounces on the profit, the method of purification, and other matters.

#### CAP. II.
#### *The Parts of the Probatory Art.*

**I**t has two members: one is the Preparatory <note>original: "Scevasticum"</note>, the other the Operational <note>original: "Ergasticum"</note>, which is the <term>assay</term> <note>original: "docimasia," the actual process of testing the metal.</note> itself. The Preparatory part concerns the apparatus of vessels and instruments necessary for that art.
This distinction is not idle in practical matters: it is most valid when tools are not sought from elsewhere as "adapted" instruments but are kept as proper ones, especially if they are not taught elsewhere—indeed, if their making is not even permitted. Thus, crucibles could be prepared by a potter, as could ash-cups <term>cupels</term> <note>original: "catilli cinerei," small vessels made of bone ash used to separate precious metals from lead.</note>, small furnaces, and other things. But skillful craftsmen keep such things among their secrets; they would rather borrow some labor from potters, masons, and other craftsmen as support for their art. Thus, <term>Fachsius</term> <note>Modestin Fachs (1534-1595), a noted German writer on metallurgy and assaying.</note> teaches about cupels at the end of his book and warns that the art of making them is a singular skill for masters. Thus, metallurgists build their own hearths and furnaces and do not take on the "foreign" labor of wall-builders and masons; a chemist would have to be very delicate indeed to entrust the sealing of glasses, the molding of furnaces, the lutes <note>Pastes used to seal joints in chemical apparatus.</note> themselves, etc., to outside craftsmen. Why not make it part of the primary discipline to grow accustomed to such "servile" [manual] tasks?
The most important of the vessels and instruments are: the small furnace, the melting hearth, ash-cupels, needles <note>touch-needles for testing gold purity</note>, lyes, clay, cement, fluxes, strong waters <note>nitric acid</note>, lead granules, and pellets. The method for making all of these is part of the probatory discipline. The rest are sought from elsewhere, such as the <term>dioptra</term> <note>a leveling or sighting instrument</note>, tongs, blowpipes, washing troughs, casting troughs, triangular crucibles, cone-shaped crucibles, the <term>touchstone</term> <note>original: "lapis lydius"</note>, the magnet, mercury, scales, weights, <term>cucurbits</term> <note>gourd-shaped glass vessels used in distillation</note>, cutting chisels, and whatever else there may be, the knowledge and use of which is necessary.

#### CAP. III.
#### *Concerning the Small Furnace.*

**I**t is twofold: fixed and mobile. And each, according to its shape, can be round, square, or square at the bottom and arched above. The fixed square one is built upon a hearth three and a half feet high, over which a chimney hangs. Its material is bricks, mortar, or clay. Its height is a cubit; its internal width a foot; its length a foot and two inches. It has an ash-pit and a hearth, which also serves as the workspace. The ash-pit begins from the floor on which it stands and rises five fingers, with a small door in the front part for removing ashes and letting in air; these are constructed from iron plate or pottery. Each has two oblong holes on the side and one in the rear part, so that space is left in the middle for placing a <term>straightedge</term> <note>original: "regula"</note>. If this plate is made of pottery, it is even made double so that its use is more lasting. Thus, two boards are bound with an iron band, and when one develops a defect, it is turned over so that the lower, intact one succeeds the damaged upper one. The small furnace ought to protrude a little bit to support the valves, coals, and whatever other things we are accustomed to place at the entrance. The iron plate is usually covered with clay and extends outside the furnace by a length of nine inches and a width of four inches <note>original: "dodrantis... palmis"</note>.

<summary>Libavius defines assaying as a practical art focused on determining the purity and composition of metals. He emphasizes the "Scevastic" part of the art—the preparation of specialized tools and furnaces—arguing that a true master must understand the construction of their own apparatus.</summary>
<keywords>assaying, metallurgy, furnace construction, cupels, crucibles, Modestin Fachs, chemical apparatus, mineralogy, touchstone, strong waters</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for the "Sceuasia" or preparation of equipment, specifically focusing on the varying recipes and purification methods for making cupels and tests, citing authorities like Agricola, Fachs, and Erker.</meta>

->Of the Preparation of the Probatory Art. Part I.<-

...They differ, however, in the choice of material and the diligence of preparation, and they contend over these points. Yet the method of shaping is the same everywhere, as far as I have discovered. In a certain manuscript book of Master Herdenius, the best <term>cupels</term> <note>original: *catilli*. These are small, porous vessels used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead.</note> are taught to be made from prepared hazelwood ash or <term>potash</term> <note>original: *clauellato*</note>; and the lime of bones from rams and castrated goats: to each part of which is added half a part of cuttlefish bone. Once mixed, they are worked with urine into a mass, and formed into a cupel as desired by accurate packing. The cavity is sprinkled with ground chalk, more thickly at the bottom and more thinly elsewhere. Once dried at the furnace, the cupel is kept in a warm place; and so that the rims do not break, they are smeared inside and out with salt water and dried. In use, when they have grown hot, a little <term>calf tallow</term> <note>original: *sebi vitulini*</note> is thrown in and consumed by the fire. From this, gold and silver are said to emerge in an excellent state.

Agricola teaches that the best cupels are made from ash that has been cleaned of coals, sand, straw, salt, fat, and other filth, then washed, cooked, and shaken out. He says the method of washing is the same as that for earths, until it no longer tastes of salt. Then, the water being poured off, it is dried in the sun. He commends ash from firm woods, such as beech, oak, holm-oak, etc. That which is made from soft materials like straw, brushwood, or willow is not suitable, because the cupels made from it break. However, if solid wood is lacking, he orders one to take whatever is available, provided it is purged as described and <term>reverberated</term> <note>fired or roasted in a kiln where the flames are deflected onto the material</note> in a baker's or potter's furnace. The older it is, the better. He records that praiseworthy cupels are also made thereafter from the burnt bones of animals, deer antlers, fish spines, burnt leather scrapings or shavings, etc. Furthermore, he teaches the compositions: such as one and a half parts of bone ash from the heads of animals; one part of <term>sorghum</term> <note>original: *sagini*</note> ash; a half part of the ash of burnt leather shavings. Or: equal parts of burnt leather shavings, sheep or calf skull bones, and burnt deer antler; let them be mixed with beer, water, or milk, etc., and the cupels formed. In workshops, ash is taken from the <term>refining hearth</term> <note>original: *foco fulminatorio*. Referring to the hearth used for cupellation or "brightening" of silver.</note> and cupels are made with bone ashes. The best are prepared from deer antler alone. These and many other things are found in Agricola.

Fachsius <note>Modestinus Fachs, a 16th-century author on assaying.</note> trusts in his own composition, but only with the most diligently prepared parts. First, he selects the ash that is driven to the edges of the hearth during refining, in which there is no lime or fat. If this is lacking, he takes whatever other ash is at hand; he shakes this through a sieve, extracts the salt with lye, and soaks it in constantly refreshed water until all <term>acrimony</term> <note>harshness or residual salts</note> has departed. This done, he adds much water and stirs. He draws off the turbid water and pours it through a hair filter or a very narrow sieve, and continues this until the ashes become sandy, which he removes. He collects the sediment from the pouring and, once the water is poured off, dries it gradually in the sun or at the furnace; the dried mass he reverberates in a pottery kiln and washes it again, lest the cupels made from it should crumble. He dries the washed material, powders it, and keeps it carefully so that no crumbs or urine fall into it, etc. As for the bones—most especially calf or horse bones—he first boils them so the fat departs; afterward, he calcines them in a pottery kiln, and having pounded them in a mortar, passes them through a narrow sieve. Then, by pouring on water several times, he washes away the acrimony; he dries it; the powder, divided into narrow jars, he reverberates in a pottery kiln; he washes it again with poured water and removes the <term>burnt smell</term> <note>original: *empyreuma*</note> at the same time. Finally, he grinds it and shakes it through a hair filter (some even smooth it on a marble slab) and orders it to be stored in a safe place. He dissolves ashen clay in plenty of water and washes it like earths, so that the sands are separated by pouring off the turbid part through a hair filter. He gathers the sediment into balls and dries them. Once dry, he crushes it into a fine dust and passes it through a narrow sieve.

<insert>Lazarus Erker <note>Lazarus Erker (c. 1530–1594), a famous Bohemian mineralogist.</note> is pleased by the calcined bones of the skull or forehead of a calf. Deer antler is judged less suitable. The jawbones and spines of fish are more appropriate. However, it is better to keep the smoothing powder by itself than in tablets.</insert> The <term>smooth coating</term> <note>original: *Lævor*. A very fine powder used to line the inside of the cupel to ensure a smooth surface for the metal bead.</note> to be sprinkled on the cupels is prepared by the same man in this way. He takes the hardest bones of the shins, once burnt, and calcines them again in a reverberatory furnace. Having pounded them, he washes them so the acrimony departs; calcined again, ground, and shaken through a hair filter, he pours water over them until the bitterness has gone. He grinds it on marble to an exact smoothness, mixes pure water with it, and once a sediment has formed, if anything yellowish or impure appears in the liquor, he pours it off moderately and puts in fresh water, ordering this to be repeated several times. Finally, having infused it with pure water, he stirs it and strains it through a narrow linen <term>Hippocratic sleeve</term> <note>A conical cloth filter used by early chemists and apothecaries.</note>, shaking it with a small stick so that the finest dust passes into the earthenware vessel placed below. He dries the sediment, crushes it, and shakes it through a sieve. That is the smoothing coating for cupels. It is also made from the bones or spines of fish, such as cod, <term>scallop</term> <note>original: *pectinis*</note>, and similar things, boiled, burnt, and prepared in the manner of bones.

Thus far Fachsius, whom it would have been enough merely to cite if he had written in the Latin language. Now it was necessary to consult several authors. Note that the cupels ought to be larger when much lead is to be put in, and smaller when little, so that there is a proportion between the vessels and the material.

## CHAPTER V.
### On Tests.

**T**ests <note>original: *Testæ*. Also known as scorifiers; shallow clay dishes used for roasting ore with lead.</note> are earthenware cupels made in the fashion of small pans, in which both the mixing of metals and the refinement of <term>refined grains</term> <note>original: *granorum fulminatorum*. Refers to the beads of metal resulting from cupellation.</note> to purity are carried out.

Their material is rich clay, the powder of old cupel fragments or bricks, or <term>Ybbs earth</term> <note>original: *terra Ipsensis*. A famous refractory clay from Ybbs in Austria used for high-temperature vessels.</note>, etc. They form them with a pestle and dry them.

According to Fachsius, the mixture is as follows: *One hundredweight of washed rich clay; fifty pounds of Ybbs earth or fragments from cupels; twelve and a half pounds each of ground flint and ground glass.* Let them be passed through a hair sieve and infused with water so that a mass is made for tests and cupels.

Commonly, the word "test" is applied to ashen cupels.

It emphasizes the removal of salts and impurities from bone and wood ash to ensure the vessels can withstand the high heat of the furnace.</summary>

# CHAPTER VI.
## On Muffles.

A <term>muffle</term> <note>original: *tegula*. In assaying, this is an arched ceramic cover that protects the sample from fuel and ash while allowing heat to circulate.</note> is a segment of a half-cylinder, hollowed out and oblong, shaped like a small oven. It is positioned so that it sits three fingers away from the back wall of the furnace while touching the front. On each side, it has two or three windows. The front part, which is also higher, is open; the back part is closed, though it is pierced with several holes. At the base of the back, there are either two or three semicircular cutouts, or it is pierced in a star pattern with five oblong little windows or two slits. All of these must have their own little doors or valves made of clay so that the work can be regulated.

Authorities describe the muffle according to their own measurements. <term>Agricola</term> <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "Father of Metallurgy" and author of *De Re Metallica*.</note> says it ought to be a palm and a half wide and one palm high near the opening of the furnace. Its length should be proportionate to the furnace itself, provided it remains three fingers away from the side and back walls. He sets the thickness to be like that of a clay pot, and orders the back part to be lower than the front so that the <term>cupels</term> <note>original: *catilli*</note> and roasting dishes can be more conveniently put in and taken out in turn. <term>Fachsius</term> <note>Modestin Fachs, author of a famous 16th-century guidebook on assaying (*Probierbüchlein*).</note> adapts it to his own scale, by which he also measures the circular furnace; he orders the internal capacity to be five and a quarter measures, the length seven and an eighth, the internal height three and a half, and the thickness one quarter. On both sides and in the back, he cuts out openings one measure high. However, these cutouts vary according to the materials being examined; for instance, Fachsius adapted his for silver specimens. Agricola looks to various needs and generally follows the size of the furnace, so that for a bright and large furnace, the muffle is made more spacious but with smaller cutouts, as I mentioned above.

Its use is to keep coals and ashes away from the material in the cupels and to prevent the excessive force of the fire, especially if it is not too heavily "windowed." For a muffle that is very open and low admits a great deal of heat; indeed, air enters through the holes and windows and tempers the fire. Therefore, valves or barriers are sometimes applied and sometimes removed, and occasionally they are adjusted to provide the appropriate grade of fire. Those vaulted chambers in glassmaking furnaces, which serve to cool the blown glass, provide a similar use. Muffles are not otherwise used for larger-scale work. Instead, large ash-basins are made, very similar to those used for <term>refining</term> <note>original: *fulminandum*. This refers to the final stage of cupellation where the silver "flashes" or "brightens" as the last of the lead is removed.</note>, but fixed in place. On a stone disc resting upon and supported by walls or masonry pillars, clay mixed with straw is placed to a height of three fingers; it is then driven down with a wooden rammer and thickened to the width of a finger. Then, a thin layer of ash is thrown on, moistened, and spread with brooms. Upon this, another layer of washed, damp ash is spread by hand and worked in; once thickened with the rammer, it is shaped into the form of a basin with a channel, over which dry ash passed through a sieve is scattered. They otherwise call this an <term>ash-bed</term> <note>original: *cineritium*</note>, as they do the assay performed within it, whether in large or small-scale work.

The remaining basins in the smelting and melting furnaces, as well as those attached to them on the outside, are made of charcoal-clay, but with a discharge outlet which they call the <term>eye</term> <note>original: *oculum*</note>.

More closely related to the ash-bed are the large roasting dishes of the refineries, in which they use "loaves" for refining almost to purity. These are ceramic, like the clay assay cupels, and are lined inside with almost the same powder as the ash cupels, once moistened. For the mixture is made of calcined bones reduced to powder and ash from the refining hearth, or brick dust and ash. These, forced into a mass with water, are pressed into the dish, but only in small quantities at a time; this is solidified with a toothed pestle, then another layer is added and forced down again, until the dish is filled. Finally, the basin is shaped with the help of a curved chisel, leaving a rim of three fingers. A smooth coating of bone-ash is sown on, in the same way as described for the cupels; once this has been pressed in with the pestle, it is dried with the proper heat of the sun or a furnace. Such dishes can hold thirty or more pounds, and are sometimes surrounded by iron hoops to hold the ash in place.

Otherwise, glassmakers' pots and goldsmiths' basins, called "golden shells," and other similar vessels correspond to these assay dishes.

# CHAPTER VII.
## On the Smelting Hearth.

The smelting hearth is set up before the bellows within an iron ring, fixed on all sides to the floor with clay so that it presents the appearance of a basin. This ring is cut away toward the nozzle of the bellows and reaches a height of two palms and a thickness of half a finger. The interior width (as Agricola says) is one palm and one finger. Its use is for melting, mixing, and purifying metals, and it frequently takes the place of a roasting dish in refineries.

The goldsmiths' furnace differs little or not at all from this hearth. Agricola calls it a "low furnace"; others call it a "wind furnace" <note>original: *ventosam*</note>, as <term>Budelius</term> <note>Renerus Budelius, a 16th-century legal expert and writer on minting and coinage.</note> also names it, because it is equipped with air holes and live coals. Agricola adds that a temporary arrangement is also made by craftsmen which is a "likeness of a furnace"—in the same way that we sometimes improvise temporary furnaces from arranged bricks in chemical distillations. In these, three bricks placed on each side and at the back complete the ash-bed. An iron plate is spread over it, which is again enclosed by as many bricks to represent the <term>workshop</term> <note>original: *ergasterium*</note>. However, exact assays should always be performed in a proper furnace. In improvised ones, the judgment is superficial, sought only when a vein or mass is offered to be examined suddenly and unexpectedly. Otherwise, those furnaces are usually described specifically by craftsmen. When, however, <term>nitric acids</term> <note>original: *aquae fortes*</note> are to be prepared by distillation, or when mercurial veins, sulfurous items, and pyrites are to be examined for vitriol, they take from the chemists ascending and descending furnaces, kettles, and so on; just as, in the absence of a furnace and under sudden necessity, they can take refuge even with goldsmiths, blacksmiths, etc. Those things which flow with a small fire, especially with additives, can also be managed occasionally on a table-top brazier, a thing which some take pride in when dealing with raw lead-silver. But it is easy to move to similar things by analogy.

# C A P. VIII.
->On Needles.<-

**P**robatory needles <note>original: *acus probatoriæ*; these are touch needles, small strips of metal with a known ratio of gold or silver used for comparison on a touchstone.</note> are metallic plates or thin rods, shaped like a wide, long needle, used for investigating mixtures and intrinsic quality by comparing the streaks they leave on a <term>touchstone</term> <note>original: *lapide lydio*, literally "Lydian stone." A dark, hard stone used to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak they leave when rubbed on it.</note>. They are primarily made in four sets, because four mixtures—of gold, silver, and copper—are most commonly in use. (They are specifically employed in the examination of the first two metals when they have been purified and smelted.) The first set is of gold and silver; the second of gold and copper; the third of gold, silver, and copper; and the fourth of silver and copper. The number of needles is adapted to <term>half-ounces</term> <note>original: *semuncias*</note>, or <term>pennies</term> <note>original: *denarios*</note>, or <term>carats</term>, according to how many of these units are in a <term>bes</term> <note>original: *besse*. A Roman unit of weight representing two-thirds of a pound, here used as the total weight of the alloy sample.</note>. For example, as there are sixteen half-ounces in a *bes* of silver, or twelve pennies, let that many needles be made for the mixture of silver and copper. Thus, the last needle should be of pure metal, and the rest of the mixture, mostly by half-ounces and pennies; sometimes also by <term>quarter-ounces</term> <note>original: *sicilicos*</note>, though if this is done, the matter is a little more complex. In the mixture of gold and silver, the number of needles follows the carats, so that the twenty-fourth is pure gold, while the first contains one carat of gold and twenty-three of silver. From copper and gold, <term>Agricola</term> forms thirteen, so that the first contains equal portions of both—namely, twelve of gold and twelve of copper—the second thirteen of gold and eleven of copper, and so on until pure gold. Other sets ought to be made similarly from copper, silver, and gold. But <term>Budelius</term> <note>Stephanus Bernardus Budelius, a 16th-century writer on minting and coinage.</note> is suspicious of varying the number. Therefore, in the needles with which gold is examined, he makes a mixture solely from copper, silver, and gold, such that one part is copper and two parts are silver.

The method of Budelius seems more clear to me, and better suited to common mixtures. [Ercker <note>Lazarus Ercker (c. 1530–1594), a famous Bohemian mineralogist and author of the *Treatise on Ores and Assaying*.</note> prepares sixteen needles for silvered copper and pure silver. He carefully weighs out what he wishes to mix. Then he melts them in a small new crucible, not allowing it to boil too much lest any metal be lost. But when it begins to smoke and be refined, he stirs it with a piece of wood and pours it into an oblong mold. From this he finishes the needles, on which he marks the value of each. See his work on page 53.] This is more adapted to common mixtures, but if there are more complex mixtures, they are more rightly referred back to the furnace. He depicts three sets of rods. The first is of gold and silver according to twenty-four carats, so that the last contains twenty-three carats of silver and one <term>keration</term> <note>original: *ceratium*; a small unit of weight equal to 1/144th of an ounce.</note> of gold, and so on until pure gold. However, let him mix the silver with half as much copper. The second set contains needles for testing silver, the mixture of which is of copper and silver up to twelve pennies, so that the twelfth needle has eleven pennies of copper and one of silver, progressing until pure silver. The third set is established according to the number of <term>lots</term> <note>original: *lotonum*; the "Lot" was a German unit of weight equivalent to a half-ounce.</note> or half-ounces in a *bes*, partly from a mass of gold and silver as above, and partly of silver and copper. <term>Fachsius</term> <note>Modestin Fachs, a master of the Leipzig mint.</note> in his judgment on mint gold and gold coins proposes three types of needles, each of which has twenty-four needles according to carats. The first type is of gold and copper, for coins, crowns, and others which have more copper than silver. The second is of silver and gold, for Hungarian coins and similar types with little copper. The third is of copper, silver, and gold, for the work of goldsmiths. According to this assessment, more sets will need to be established. We also use needles for <term>quartation</term> <note>The process of separating gold from silver by adding silver until the gold is only one-quarter of the mass, then dissolving the silver in acid.</note> in the separation of gold and silver to detect the pure intrinsic value. [When you wish to test silver by the needles, rub it on the touchstone so that it makes a bright, wide line, then compare it with the needles using water.]

# C A P. IX.
->On Lyes.<-

**L**yes <note>original: *lixivia*; alkaline solutions made by leaching wood ashes.</note> are juices percolated from abundant water through ashes or lime; they are useful in the assaying art for wiping away filth on the "skin" <note>the surface of the metal</note> and for making <term>alkali</term>.

<margin>-</margin>
Thus, a lye is usually made from calcined <term>tartar</term> <note>The sediment from wine casks, chemically potassium bitartrate.</note> to wipe away sulfurous vapors and blackness, and to restore the color to smelted metals, although some also use only an infusion or decoction of tartar. Salts for <term>fluxes</term> <note>original: *fluxibus*; substances used to promote melting.</note> are also made from <term>potash</term> <note>original: *cinere clavellato*.</note>, which others call "glass ash," because it serves to heighten and preserve the color of <term>woad</term> <note>original: *Isatidis*; a blue dye plant.</note> in cloths and to wash away stains; likewise from diluted and mixed juices and similar things, of which we shall speak in their place.

# C A P. X.
->On Lute.<-

**L**ute <note>original: *lutum*; a clay-based cement used to seal or protect laboratory equipment.</note> is a mixture of water and dry powders, composed of earthy mud or clay for the purpose of fortifying furnaces, crucibles, and other vessels.

It is composed in various ways and from various materials. Among practitioners in the assaying art, this recipe is especially commended: six parts of dry, lean clay passed through a sieve; three parts of <term>flock</term> <note>original: *tomenti*; wool or cotton fibers used to prevent the clay from cracking.</note> and finely ground sand; one and a half parts of iron filings or scales; a half part of clay <note>original: *argillæ*</note>, and the same quantity of boiled and skimmed dung. Add water and mix, and beat it thoroughly with an iron rod so that it becomes tenacious and ductile. When you have coated the furnaces with this lute and they have dried, smear them with this mixture: equal parts of quicklime and ground sand (or flint flour) incorporated with egg whites. Let them dry on their own.

There are generally two uses for lute. One is prepared for forming crucibles, hearths, and other vessels, and is a material in itself. The other is prepared for fortifying and <term>coating</term> <note>original: *loricanda*; literally "harnessing" or "armoring" a vessel.</note> thinner vessels so that they may resist the fire and hold the heat more reliably. However, both can also be used for filling cracks and repairing breaks. And the latter, when composed in a certain way, also serves as a glue for holding joints together and compensating for cracks in glass. For this use, Fachsius prescribed the following: one ounce each of chalk, wheat flour, and <term>Venetian glass</term>, a half-ounce of brick flour, and a little cotton flock; let these be powdered and mixed with egg white into the form of a paste, which is applied using a cloth.

<margin>-</margin>
Such compositions bear the name of "lute" by common usage, though they are otherwise called pastes, mashes, etc. Several compositions have been set down in the chemical <term>magisteries</term> <note>Advanced alchemical or chemical treatises.</note>, and a certain number cannot be defined. It is the task of the industrious craftsman to choose what will be appropriate for the work. Usually, many recipes are named so that in the absence of one, he may resort to another—

...we may be able to. Furthermore, what is described here belongs to Fachsius <note>Modestin Fachs (d. 1595), a renowned German assay master whose "Probierbüchlein" was a standard text for metal testing.</note>, and the mixture is not to be despised, although others might praise a mixture of iron filings with gypsum, brick dust, glass, brine, and urine, all collected and blended, as being excellent for the task. By the name of "dung," horse or donkey dung should be understood.

### C A P. XI.
### On Cement.

> *Cement <note>original: *Cæmentum*; in this context, cementation is a dry refining process where a metal is heated with corrosive salts to remove impurities.</note> is a mixture made of sharp and corrosive substances, prepared primarily for the purification and examination of the perfect metals.*
> *It is intended chiefly for judging gold, and is what they call "Royal Cement." It consists mostly of vitriol <note>original: *chalcantho*</note>, sal ammoniac, saltpeter, brick dust <note>original: *sarina laterum*</note>, verdigris, antimony, sulfur, and similar things, combined more or less abundantly in the form of a dry powder, after the gold has first been mixed with copper. That which is applied to silver is milder, and either lacks sal ammoniac, antimony, and sulfur entirely, or admits them only in small quantities; instead, a flux sometimes takes their place, consisting merely of alkali salt, glass slag, saltpeter, with added brick dust.*

Cement, flux, and "coloring paste" <note>original: *coloritium*</note> are closely related compositions. Therefore, they are sometimes even interchanged, so that we might use the coloring paste in place of cement, or likewise a flux, because it happens that the same material may have multiple powers and be used in different forms for various purposes. Regularly, however, they differ: cement includes brick dust, or flint, or similar non-melting substances, and takes the form of a dry powder or a paste. A flux is strictly a powder and should not receive anything "fixed" <note>substances that do not evaporate or melt easily</note> or non-flowing. For by its own swift flowing and catching of the flame, it ought to melt things that flow with difficulty—although usage has adopted a certain misuse of the term <note>original: *catachresin*</note>, so that the same name is also given to other additives which are mixed into fluxes for various goals. A coloring paste is a sharp paste, as will follow in the definition, and is used primarily on the small rods of a <term>touchstone</term> to "extinguish" <note>quench or treat</note> metals, to restore their perfect color to them, and so on. Sophists and impostors also turn cements and coloring pastes toward their frauds; they burn foreign colors into metals, increase their weight, and procure other signs of perfection. Otherwise, Chemists—without fraud—take delight in these things, admiring the analogies and sympathies of matter. He who desires more should consult the Chemical art and exchanges of letters.

### C A P. XII.
### On Flux.

> *Flux is a powder made from mineral substances that melt easily in the fire, prepared for the purpose of quickly liquefying metals. One kind is mild, for ores <note>original: *venas*</note> that are not very stubborn, and which can melt them without damage to the metal; another is sharp, which is added to those that are very refractory. Care must be taken, however, that in these assays we do not use fluxes by which the value of the ore might be increased or diminished. For a judgment from such a source is false, and a small discrepancy is the cause of great errors.*

A safe flux for silver-bearing ores: <margin>[*Bleyglas*, that is, glass made from lead. <unclear>Ore-</unclear> <note>original: *Erk-*</note> A flux is composed from one part white flint, calcined and exactly ground, and half a part of litharge <note>lead oxide</note>; place it in a crucible that is one-third empty, and spread salt or saltpeter to a thickness of 3 fingers; having put on a lid, seal it with lute <note>sealing clay</note> and melt it in a furnace with a strong fire. The glass from this is called "yellow glass," along with a lead grain that is knocked off, and the purified glass is saved.]</margin> Take two parts pure litharge (in which there is no silver) and one part white flint powder; let them be mixed and melted in a strong crucible in a reverberatory furnace so that slag is created and a <term>regulus</term> <note>a button of pure metal</note> of lead settles at the bottom. Remove it from the fire, and when it has cooled, break the crucible, separate the regulus from the slag, and having ground the slag in a mortar, shake it through a sieve; save it for the work, leaving the lead button behind. But if you nevertheless fear that some silver might be inside, test it; if you find any, it must afterwards be subtracted from the <term>refined grain</term> in the assay of silver or gold, or added to the weight of the mass. Of this flux, twenty-five pounds are usually added to a <term>hundred-weight</term> <note>original: *centupondivm*</note> of ore that flows with difficulty. According to Fachsius.

Another flux by the same author, for gold and silver, and also other metals: Mix saltpeter with twice as much tartar so that it becomes a fine powder; put this into a heated, unglazed earthenware pot, and having thrown in a coal, set it on fire. When it has finished burning, a black ash <note>original: *calx nigra*</note> will remain; while it is still slightly warm, immediately grind it in a mortar and pass it through a hair-sieve. Once passed through, keep it in a closed vessel in a warm place. Twice as much of this is usually added to the ore, such that a little melted salt or common salt is sprinkled over the mixture in the crucible.

For gold grains, an alkali is specifically made from one part each of potash <note>original: *cineris clavellati*</note>, salt, wormwood ash, and urine; two parts of quicklime; and half a part each of tartar and saltpeter. These are crushed and boiled in water in a cauldron; they are passed through a filter so that the same water is strained six times, and finally fresh water is added so that all the sharpness is separated. The solution is thickened into an alkali.

There is a great variety of fluxes, and almost every author commends his own. Fachsius was no ordinary craftsman in the assaying art. Therefore, I have gladly included those proven by him, among which are also these two: Let four parts each of saltpeter and tartar be mixed with two parts of borax. Also: Let two parts of calcined saltpeter, one of borax, and three of tartar be powdered and mixed. Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), author of *De Re Metallica*.</note>, however, is quite prolific in the composition of fluxes. I have chosen to transcribe one or two from him. Take half an ounce of ground white <term>fluor</term> <note>fluorspar</note> and two ounces of ground litharge of <term>gold</term> <note>original: *auri*; likely referring to the yellow-colored variety of litharge.</note>. Mix them under a tile in a crucible and melt for half an hour with fire applied. Once melted together, pour it onto a stone; it will turn into glass, which you should use after it is powdered. In place of litharge, he advises that lead ash made with sulfur can also be used. But if Fachsius feared lest the slag of litharge corrupt the <unclear>accuracy</unclear> <note>original: *axē-suas*</note> of a silver assay because of silver residues, one must see whether something similar might happen here too, especially since silver can be recovered from glass. This one is stronger: Equal parts of white wine tartar, common salt, and prepared saltpeter are calcined in a glazed pot; an equal amount of litharge is added to the ash. In use, twice the amount of the ore is added. The strongest: One <term>sicilicus</term> <note>a weight of approximately 6.8 grams</note> each of sulfur and glass gall <note>original: *fellis vitri*; the scum found on molten glass</note>; half an ounce each of antimony, salt of urine, melted salt, prepared saltpeter, litharge, vitriol, tartar, salt, <term>dead head</term> <note>original: *capitis mortui*; the residue left after distillation</note> of <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note>, and calcined alum; and one ounce of the "head" powdered with sulfur.

<meta>Catchword: Mix.</meta>

<summary>This page defines and provides recipes for "cements" and "fluxes," the chemical agents used to purify and melt metals during the assaying process. It highlights the technical distinction between dry refining (cementation) and melting aids (fluxes), drawing on the authorities of Fachsius and Agricola.</summary>
<keywords>cementation, flux, litharge, saltpeter, Fachsius, Agricola, gold refining, silver assaying, alchemy, metallurgy</keywords>

--- Page 48 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on chemical additives in metallurgy, transitioning from cements to the composition and selection of fluxes and other "additaments" used to separate metals from their ores.</meta>

<page-num>97</page-num>
<header>On Assaying, Part I.</header>

Mix them. In practice, one part—or a half part—is melted in a small clay dish or a crucible with one part of ore and two parts of lead, sprinkled with Venetian glass powder, so that they may be cooked for two hours. Once the <term>regulus</term><note>The "regulus" is the metallic button or lump that settles at the bottom of a crucible after melting.</note> is formed, it is purified through cupellation.

The use of such fluxes is not a matter of chance; they must be chosen according to the nature of the metal and the ore. Gold suffers less loss. Therefore, if its ore is stubborn, it can withstand even a stronger flux, unless the metal is delicate and soft. The same applies to iron. With silver, we must be more cautious. In other metals, although exact knowledge is desired, errors are not as costly. Fachsius <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century authority on assaying.</note> criticizes a flux containing equal portions of molten salt, glass gall <note>original: *fellis vitri*; the scum or impurities that rise to the surface of molten glass.</note>, borax, saltpeter, tartar, and a half-portion of sal ammoniac, because the ammonia, borax, and glass gall dissipate the metals; specifically, it makes copper degenerate and poor, which prevents a true judgment of its quality. Certainly, he does not say this without cause. If arsenic, sulfur, sal ammoniac, and similar substances were present in the ores, would we not work with all our zeal to remove them, lest they cause harm in quantity or quality? We must therefore be careful not to add them recklessly, especially since the <term>assayer</term><note>original: *docimastes*; a person who tests the purity of metals.</note> must pronounce judgment not only on the quantity but also on the quality and the method of smelting. It is well known what such minerals do to copper and tin. Therefore, the flux must be chosen diligently. For smelting iron, Geber <note>An influential 8th-century Arabic alchemist and metallurgist.</note> and others primarily recommend arsenic. All fluxes used with lead and ores in a dish or crucible are employed to produce a regulus in the testing process. In large-scale works, for the most part, "fluors" <note>substances that promote melting, often including fluorite or slag</note>, slags, litharge, and similar things—which are abundant and useful—are used, along with a "stone" or roasted pyrites, especially in silver ores. If necessity requires, salts, powdered glass, and the like are also sprinkled in, usually over mild coals, so that the flame can penetrate quickly. Large masses, such as those of copper and iron, when the metallic copper is being smelted from them, require something similar to cement. For they are layered and sprinkled in turn with powders made from glass, slag, realgar, litharge, and others. Likewise, in the smelting furnaces, alternating layers are observed, so that in the first place slag, <term>graphite</term><note>original: *plumbago*; in this historical context, likely referring to lead ore or a lead-based mineral like galena.</note>, crude pyrites, litharge, etc., are placed, and afterward the stone and the ore mixed with fluxes; then again slag, and so on. Sometimes these are even mixed together, with coals added.

# CHAPTER XIII.
## On other additives.

*Other additives are related to fluxes; some of these aid the power of the fire so that the slag is separated more easily and the metal is promptly received by the lead. Some protect the ores from the fire, so that the metal does not turn into ash; this happens even when the force of the fire and the added flux is diverted from the ore to something more solid. Some additives absorb and drink up the metals; they heat the ores and turn the violence of the flux upon themselves, such as iron scale, iron slag, or filings. Tartar, alkali, <term>caput mortuum</term><note>The "dead head" or useless residue left after distillation or sublimation.</note>, aqua fortis, and crystals from vinegar promote the fire for the sake of separation. Crude pyrites, pyrites baked into "loaves" (which they call "stones"), fluxes, glass gall, iron filings with their slag, blue vitriol <note>original: *chalcantum*</note>, and similar things protect the ores. Metals are absorbed mostly by lead, copper, graphite or molybdenum <note>original: *molybdena*; here referring to lead-like minerals</note>, litharge, and things related to these. The greatest power belongs to the stone and to lead, although in the testing process, fluxes are used instead of the stone if the situation requires.*

Most of these are excerpts from the book of Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "Father of Mineralogy," author of *De Re Metallica*.</note>, who, however, was looking not only at assaying but also at large-scale smelting. Although many things are common to both, there is some difference, such as with the "stone," which assayers do not use much, nor do they use molybdenum, even though it is suitable for melting. In large fires, however, they are common; the stone or pyrites is called the "master" by Mathesius <note>Johannes Mathesius (1504–1565), a mineralogist and clergyman.</note>, as it delivers the silver separated from the ore into the lead; and having received and defended it from the force of the fire, it commits the silver to the coolness of the lead, with which it is carried out and withdrawn from the flames. Just as I warned about the careful use and choice of fluxes, the same must be observed in other additives. It is well known that copper cannot be smelted to a pure state if a particle of iron falls into it, until that iron is consumed. In the meantime, however, some of the copper is lost. Therefore, the same care must be taken in the examination. Furthermore, Agricola also records mixtures, both for "defending" and for "separating," some of which it would be no trouble to list here. Equal parts of iron slag, white tufa, and salt, when combined, separate sulfur, orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentum*; yellow arsenic sulfide.</note>, realgar <note>original: *sandaracum*; red arsenic sulfide.</note>, etc., from the ores. Equal parts of iron filings and salt, melted with an equal amount of prepared ore, separate the regulus. Or equal parts of lead grains, molten salt, antimony <note>original: *stibii*</note>, slag, and iron may be mixed with an equal part of ore, etc. A certain mixture is said to protect metals from antimony: equal parts of sulfur, saltpeter <note>original: *halinitri*</note>, molten salt, and vitriol should be cooked in urine or lye for four hours until the smell of sulfur vanishes. Here you will note that other metals can also be purified through antimony, provided this "defense" is added. Some people gather clues from the smoke of the ores as to which additives are needed. Concerning this, Agricola instructs as follows: Let the ores be placed on glowing iron shovels. If they emit a purple smoke, they do not need any special additive. If blue, "the stone" must be added; if yellow, they require litharge and sulfur; if red, glass waste and salt; if green, the stone, litharge, and glass gall. If black, they require molten salt or iron slag with litharge and white limestone. If white, sulfur and rusty iron. If white within green, iron slag and flux-sand. If the middle part of the smoke is yellow and thick, and the outer edges green, they require flux-sand and iron slag. This same smoke also reveals the presence of "juices." Blue indicates the ore is infected with blue; yellow with orpiment; red with realgar; green with <term>chrysocolla</term><note>A green mineral, likely malachite or a copper-based soldering material.</note>; black with black bitumen; white with white; white in green, chrysocolla mixed with the same. If the middle is yellow and the edges green, sulfur is shown. Yet, even certain earths can produce such smokes. Thus far, Agricola.

But these matters are far from being a scientific necessity and are supported only by uncertain opinion. Therefore, no such thing is taught by others. Imagine that those smokes designate certain minerals, for the taming of which certain additives are useful. Yet it is better to be equipped with general principles and those things which have been proven by experience in the art. The judgment still wavers as to whether there is such a bounty of foreign matter and such stubbornness that it must be subdued not by fire alone but by aids; and whether the condition of the ore in other respects is such that they can cause no harm, or at least help. A small quantity of a substance produces a lot of smoke. If you hunt for clues from smoke alone...

...you capture; you neglect the non-smoking multitude. Volatile and rapacious <note>In alchemy, "rapacious" substances were those that "consumed" or carried away precious metals during heating.</note> substances might be argued this way, but not stony fixities, which are finally elevated and resolved only by a far stronger fire. What of the fact that some ores do not require additives, but rather a skillful method of operation? Sulfur, orpiment <note>Arsenic trisulfide, a common yellow mineral.</note>, and bitumen, because they can be melted by easy heat, are removed either by "torture" <note>likely referring to intense heat or specialized extraction</note> or, if the quantity makes it worthwhile, are collected by "descension" <note>A method of distillation where the substance melts and flows downward into a receiver.</note>; if vitriol, alum, and similar substances are present in abundance, they are removed by washing. So it is with the rest.

Therefore, that observation is rash or accidental, and cannot find a stable place among the rules. However, whether a vein of ore needs additives, and which ones, is usually investigated by other arguments. First, frequent experience has so instructed the master that, although Fachsius <note>Modestin Fachs, a renowned 16th-century assay master.</note> asserts the sight may waver due to the incredible variety of veins, he nevertheless recognizes the method of testing by the sight of the vein in common and familiar cases, and those of a related nature. Next, when he is assigned to a mine of a certain type, he ought to know its character, either through experienced miners or by inquiring of the smelters. Furthermore, preparations such as washings, roastings, and others indicate the conjoined minerals and their stubbornness in refining. During the roasting or burning, the constancy and odor of the fumes betray the nature of the vein. Even when the work is already in the assaying stage, signs show themselves by which it is immediately clear what must be done; for instance, if the metal does not immerse itself into the lead from the ore but instead bubbles, then alkali salt, "salt of art," <term>caput mortuum</term><note>The "dead head" or useless solid residue left after distillation or sublimation.</note>, and the like are required, concerning which we speak in the special assays. 

Likewise, if he has added a flux, yet fears the metal might be harmed by it, he adds iron filings. If, in a single operation during <term>fulmination</term><note>The final stage of cupellation where the silver "flashes" as the last impurities are removed.</note>, he notices from the very beginning—while it is smoking—various colors riding upon the surface like "flowers," he concludes that arsenic, sulfur, mercury, bismuth <note>original: *plumbum cinereum*, literally "ash-colored lead."</note>, antimony, and the like are clinging to it. Having discovered the matter, he will take counsel regarding the additions. He is entirely unskilled who approaches the work without being practiced in the various types of metallic veins according to their species, nor does he understand the art in which we see additives explained among the special rules for filthy, refractory, and rapacious veins of metals.

Finally, such aids are necessary not only in smelting ores into lead if they are stubborn, but also sometimes during fulmination, and even in a greater fire. In such cases, it is the rule to sprinkle the tin to be assayed (if the silver is separated from the lead with difficulty) with copper mixed with charcoal dust; or if impurity is contracted, with a mixture of tartar and Venetian glass, or with sal ammoniac, or with iron rust and tartar with a portion of saltpeter, and so on. While it is burning, it is also usually made purer by throwing grains of copper or lead into the <term>test</term><note>The cupel or shallow vessel used in assaying.</note>. When silver is being separated from iron, antimony is added, by which means a single trial of gold is also perfected; and specifically in separations, there is much use of assisting agents, of which we shall speak in their proper place.

## CHAPTER XIV.
### On Coloritio.

<margin>There is also a transformation as when a paste for cinnabar is made from silver filings and egg white, but this is not truly *coloritio*.</margin>
**C**oloritium <note>A technical term for a "coloring" or "touching" paste used to test the purity of metals.</note> is a moist mixture consisting of corrosive things and some liquid reduced to the form of a pulp, for the purpose of judging gold and silver. These substances are the same as those from which <term>aqua fortis</term> is made—namely vitriol, verdigris, saltpeter, alum, sal ammoniac, etc.—which are tempered with urine or vinegar for gold, but with water for silver, so that in the latter case sal ammoniac is either absent or present in small amounts.

Fachsius uses *coloritio* and *aqua fortis* on the touchstone <note>original: *lydio lapide*, the Lydian stone.</note> indifferently when jeweler’s gold, or something gilded, or something passed off as gold, is to be judged. Likewise, when a grain from a cupellation of ambiguous mixture is offered, you may explore whether it contains any gold or not. But it can also have various other uses, such as in cementing, quenching, coloring, fixing, increasing weight, etc., about which some things have been said before. Various formulas are prescribed. But the ingredients, as they call them, are chiefly those I have listed; and if you only mix alum, vitriol, and saltpeter in a lye and coagulate them again, you will discover the power of *aqua fortis*. Others also add alkalis, the *caput mortuum* of strong spirits, sulfur, antimony, arsenic, etc., especially when it is a paste for firing and <term>cementing</term><note>A process of heating metals with powdered reagents to purify them or change their surface color.</note>.

## CHAPTER XV.
### On Aqua Fortis.

<margin>See Ercker, page 62.</margin>
**A**qua fortis <note>Literally "strong water," referring here to nitric acid.</note> is a liquid drawn from corrosive minerals through distillation, used for separating lower metals from gold, and simultaneously for knowing how much of one is in the other. The minerals from which it is made in the assaying art are usually vitriol, saltpeter, and alum, from which it is prepared in this manner: *Eight parts of vitriol are calcined; the weight of the calcined material is noted so that as much water as was lost may be placed in the receiver to meet the spirits. Five parts of purified saltpeter and one of alum are added. Everything is ground to the size of peas and macerated in a stone <term>cucurbit</term> <note>The bottom part of a still.</note> in a cellar for eight days until they become moist. Afterward, having placed the alembic and the receiver (attached with a "rain-cover" <note>original: *pluviali*</note> as large as the weight lost by the vitriol during calcination), and having protected the joints with lute <note>Sealant clay</note> (leaving only one hole in the joint of the receiver and the beak to let out spirits if they are too strong, which hole should be plugged with a small stick), let the distillation be done in sand for two days. The distilled water is rectified and cleared by means of silver.* 

It is also tested in <term>quartation</term><note>A process where gold is alloyed with three parts silver so that the aqua fortis can dissolve the silver and leave the gold pure.</note> before it is put to use, lest it be too sharp; this is done by a thin plate made of one part gold and three parts silver. If the plate does not break, the sharpness is correct; if it breaks, it is tempered with fresh water, mixing half a drachm to a half-ounce until the strength corresponds. *This becomes **aqua regia** if it is tempered with sal ammoniac, or if it is distilled with it again or even from the beginning; by this, the constancy and deeper mixture of gold is seen, and sophisticated gold is examined, or even, if it is sharper, a tincture may be made from it.*

<margin>Preparation of saltpeter so that it does not break the vessels.</margin>
The description of *aqua fortis* is taken from Fachsius and is sufficient for the service of this art. He who seeks more methods should consult the chemical books. Calcined vitriol is called *colcothar* by the Arabs; it is made in an open pot over coals or burning wood until it becomes sufficiently red. However, lest you be unaware, vitriol is displeasing to others because it eats away at the gold. But Fachsius tempers it cautiously. Saltpeter is clarified by repeated solution, filtration, and coagulation. But here, such a preparation is not to be understood, but rather that which was mentioned above regarding fluxes...

# On the Preparation of the Assaying Art, Part I.

...is required, and its "fixation" <note>In this context, fixation refers to stabilizing the substance or making it non-volatile.</note> is named, or its separation from mixed salt, so that the niter <note>Potassium nitrate, also known as saltpeter.</note> remains pure. To obtain this, we dissolve and boil it in a copper cauldron to the proper consistency; once this is poured out, leaving the salt sticking to the bottom of the cauldron, we let it congeal into niter. Sometimes we also free it from "violent spirits" <note>Volatile or corrosive gases released during heating.</note> by fire.

For use as a flux, Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy."</note> specifically dissolves it in a lye made of quicklime and congeals it in a glazed pot; or he repeatedly pours it over and congeals it. For the salt in that lye either removes or inhibits its easy flammability. Thus, it is prepared if it does not catch fire when exposed to flame.

<margin>Clarification of nitric acid.</margin> The clarification of nitric acid <note>Original: *aqua fortis*, literally "strong water."</note> by means of silver is done in this manner: If you have a certain measure, pour it into a cucurbit <note>A gourd-shaped chemical flask used in distillation.</note>. Add a fourth part to a *sicilicus* <note>A small Roman weight, roughly a quarter-ounce.</note> of silver in a small flask. Dissolve it slowly over hot coals. Pour this solution into the previous three parts, and the sharp spirits will descend with the dregs, like buttermilk. When the sediment has settled for a day and a night, pour off the clear liquid. In a fourth part of this, dissolve another small bit of silver and pour it into the rest. If it becomes turbid, it is not yet clear enough. Therefore, repeat the same labor until it remains clear even when silver is added. It should be noted regarding nitric acid how much silver it leaves behind in the gold; 
<margin>How much silver the acid leaves in the gold.</margin> it is advisable to test this either in individual distillations or even in the examinations, lest you be deceived in your judgment, pronouncing it pure when a portion of silver still remains with it. Nor is it enough if you have tested a batch distilled only once. For if it is kept too long and becomes weakened, you would be deceived again, with a larger quantity being left behind than before. This residue is recognized if you mix a small portion of the purest gold (which is 24 carats) with triple the amount of silver. The mixing is done by melting them together, adding lead in a cupel <note>Original: *catillo cinereo*, a small porous bowl made of bone ash used to separate base metals from precious ones.</note> until the "flash" <note>Original: *fulmen*. This refers to the "blick," the sudden brightening of the metal bead when the lead is fully absorbed.</note> shines pure. Then flatten the mixture, roll it into a loose tube, and after pouring on a proper quantity of nitric acid, separate them; this is usually done with two pourings. What is not dissolved is washed with fresh water (after first pouring off the solution in which the silver is recovered by precipitation with salt water over a copper plate, and later reduced in a vessel with lead or flux). It is then dried and heated in a gold dish so that the vapors of the nitric acid depart. When this is done, the weight is checked. Whatever weight has increased beyond the original quantity is from the silver, and it usually amounts to two or three grains. These must later be added to the weight in the assay. If the acid is weaker, it leaves behind even four or five grains. If the gold comes out lighter, it was not pure or stable enough. For the best gold does not suffer loss from such acid, unless the acid was sharper than it should be. Furthermore, in "quartation" <note>The process of alloying gold with three parts silver so the nitric acid can penetrate and dissolve the silver, leaving the gold behind.</note> pure silver must be used, or any impurity must be compensated for by quantity. For that impurity is dissipated in the melting which is done with copper and lead.

From these things, it is gathered that in such an assay, gold refined to 24 carats is presupposed. And there is not only disagreement among the learned regarding exact purity; there is also a great question whether "gold-separating water" <note>Original: *aqua chrysulca*, another term for nitric acid or aqua regia.</note> separates all the silver. Budelius <note>Stephanus Budelius, a 16th-century author on minting and coinage.</note> fiercely resists those who deny that perfect gold can be found, arguing that at least a quarter-carat (three grains) of silver remains in everything—or a fourth of a grain, as Budé <note>Guillaume Budé, a French scholar.</note> says. Agricola maintained that one grain is left behind by the gold-separator. Budelius says that in larger masses 4 or 5 grains can indeed remain, but not in smaller ones.

Chemists do not struggle laboriously over this. Rather, they thoroughly purify gold that has been tested by nitric acid or *aqua regia* <note>A mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold.</note> by using antimony, cementation, and cupellation, so that Budelius's opinion is confirmed. However, regarding what is left behind in quartation <insert>Is that remaining part silver or the spirit of the acid? Ercker <note>Lazarus Ercker (c. 1530–1594), a famous Bohemian mineralogist.</note> answers in favor of silver.</insert>, it is correctly investigated according to Fachs <note>Modestin Fachs, a master of the Leipzig mint.</note> due to the diversity of sharpness in the acids: provided the craftsman takes care that the usual "separating water" is used, and not *aqua regia* (which also dissolves gold), and that the gold is not softer than it should be, or reduced to softness by some process. There are also other sharp waters or liquids used in testing, such as vinegar or urine, in which sal ammoniac, vitriol, and similar things are dissolved, by which metals or ores are quenched. Likewise the lye mentioned above. "Fixing waters" for ores and soft metals are sometimes from the category of "strong waters" and are made from astringents, about which we read in chemical books. Sometimes they are merely diluted. See the "Masteries of Fixations."

# CHAPTER XVI.
## On Granulation.

Granulation is the powdering of metals reduced into tiny parts through melting. In the art of assaying, lead and <insert><margin>See below.</margin> Granules are either round, which are used in "pagamenta" <note>Bullion or alloyed metal mixtures intended for coinage.</note>, or thin and hemispherical, which they seek for the separation of gold from silver.</insert> what are called "pagamenta" or monetary mixtures of metals, are prepared in this way. Lead, melted in a crucible, is poured into a wooden trough, and when it begins to cool, it is shaken until it breaks into powder. Alternatively, it is poured through a whisk into a tub of water. The water is poured off, and the lead is collected and dried.

Monetary particles, however, are mixed in a vessel that is first gradually heated; later, when it is not damaged by the heat (for it is placed among the coals in a wind-furnace up to the top and heated entirely), the fragments are thrown in with a trowel. When these have melted, carbon dust is thrown in, and they are mixed well with a hook, and afterwards poured over whisks placed in water, or a perforated board, like lead. These are called "Granalia."

Furthermore, since the highest purity is required in assaying lead (which is from Villach or Goslar <note>Famous mining regions in Austria and Germany known for producing high-quality lead.</note>) for exact examinations of silver, and yet some silver remains in every piece which cannot be separated without loss, it must be known how much that is before we adapt it for use. Therefore, since seven hundred-weights <note>Original: *centupondia*.</note> are usually used for "mild" ores and nine for "stubborn" ones, we test through the "flash" in seven and nine hundred-weights separately to see how much silver is contained; and this is later subtracted from the grain of silver that is smelted out of the ore.

We have explained the methods of reducing metals into granules <insert>In testing suspected or debased coins, granulation is especially observed.</insert> in the chemical "masteries." These methods are very suitable so that they can be mixed with the ore powder in the smallest proportions and immediately melted, if anything needs to be added during cupellation. Otherwise, since lead is not placed into the ash-cup at the same time as the ore, but the ore is put in when the lead begins to smoke, it is useful to have the lead either in small balls or broken into particles.
