<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for assaying from page 99, moving from the preparation of reagents to the physical handling of metals and the specialized tools required for the "docimasia" or art of testing ores.</meta>

<page-num>100</page-num>

->Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book V.<-

Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the author of *De Re Metallica*.</note> teaches a method of making pellets using tongs with a small mold, similar to those used for casting small musket balls. At other times, the metal is cast into "fingers" <note>Small rods or ingots.</note> or sheets and is cut up with shears or other instruments. Copper is granulated, or filed with a rasp, or drawn into thin leaves so that it may melt easily in the crucible. These granules of the alloy are made so that the mixture can be uniform and the sample provides a fair trial. For parts of unequal value must be reduced to equality. For this reason, mint-masters also sometimes do this to balance the consistency of the metal masses. Others simply extend the metal into leaves, especially with larger coins. It is also customary to break down other metals, such as when they are cast into a small trough to become rods or sticks (which they call "fingers"), which are later broken with tongs or another tool; a similar thing happens to stones or bread when exposed to great fire.

Ores are ground into powder, just as was said regarding fluxes. When the weight of lead is defined as seven or nine hundredweights <term>centupondia</term>, this is generally understood to be what is most often required for ores. Otherwise, when necessity presses, weights of eight, fifteen, or similar appropriate numbers are prescribed; in this way, Fachsius <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century authority on assaying and smelting.</note> joins fifteen hundredweights of lead to every hundred pounds of "black" <note>Impure, unrefined copper.</note> and degenerate copper. Agricola also adds a six-fold amount of lead to ore or refractory material, but with a flux. However, these things should be advised specifically in each individual trial.

A double table by Fachs serves this business, which is worth recounting here:

1. **In the trial of gold and silver:**
- To one hundredweight of easily-melted ore, add seven parts of lead.
- To difficult-melting ore, add nineteen parts.
- To a half-hundredweight of "white lead" <note>Likely tin or a lead-tin alloy.</note>, add fifteen hundredweights of lead.
- To one hundredweight of "copper stone" <note>Copper matte or pyrites.</note> for silver; to one of workable copper; to one of unworkable copper for silver; to one of bell-metal for silver; to one of gold ore for gold; or to one of gold grains: fifteen hundredweights of lead are required.
- To one hundredweight of "rough" copper for regular copper, add two hundredweights of lead.
- To one of leaded copper, add one and a half hundredweights.

2. **Addition of lead in marks <term>marcas</term>:**
- To one mark of granules whose value is from 1 to 8 *loth* <term>lothone</term> <note>A *loth* was a German weight unit, roughly half an ounce.</note>, add 20 marks of lead.
- To one mark of "workman’s silver" <note>Standard silver used by smiths.</note> whose value reaches 13 *loth*, and likewise to one mark of gold coins at 14 *loth*: add seven marks.
- To one mark of "refined" silver <note>Original: *argenti fulminati*, silver that has "brightened" during cupellation.</note> and to one of "burnt" silver: five marks.
- To one mark of gilded silver at 15 *loth*, and to one mark of gold from 12 to 24 carats: add five marks.
- To one mark of gilded silver at 13 *loth*: 7 marks of lead should be joined.
- To one mark of coinage whose value is from 10 to 12 *loth*: eighteen marks of lead are required.

# CHAPTER XVII.
## Regarding certain external tools.

**Dioptra** <note>A sighting board or face shield.</note> is a board with a handle, split or perforated lengthwise near the middle, so that the craftsman can gaze at the state of the work and the fire through it when held before the face, without injury to the eyes. (In the case of poisonous materials, one may also stretch out "the bladders of Dioscorides" <note>Protective masks made of animal bladders, mentioned by the ancient physician Dioscorides.</note> so that the virulent air is not inhaled, though most people protect themselves with antidotes.)

**Blowing Pipe** is an iron channel, or a two-foot tube about the width of a finger, through which the ashes that have fallen into the crucible are blown away.

**Washing Trough** is a hollowed-out "boat" or an oblong wooden dish shaped like an egg cut in half; it is used for washing ground ores with water to separate the light and fleeting parts from the metal by the movement of the hand. The value of slag, dross, and similar materials is also observed in the same way.

**Casting Trough** is a certain narrow, oblong iron box prepared for casting metals into rods or "fingers," and it is equipped with its own handle.

**Triangular Crucibles** are vessels made of firm earth and clay, with a sharper, rounded base and a wider capacity ending in a triangle at the top; they are designed for melting and mixing metals, and sometimes for purifying them. These are made in larger or smaller capacities, just like the "tests" <note>Shallow assaying dishes.</note>. Usually an iron tripod or another support is adapted for them so that the fire can be admitted from all sides. They also have various other uses in cementing, calcination, and several other "masteries" <note>Technical chemical processes.</note> performed by fire.

**Conical Crucible** is a metallic cup, most often made of copper, iron, or brass, with a wide round mouth ending in a cone; it is used to separate noble and heavier metals from lighter ones through passive cementing fluxes. When the metals have been melted in the triangular crucibles (which they also call *tigella*), they are poured into this conical cup, which has been smeared inside with tallow; by striking the rim with a hammer, the heavy metal is forced to the bottom. In this way, the "regulus" <note>The pure metallic button found at the bottom of a crucible.</note> is separated from antimony, and gold is purified by antimony, among other things.

**Small Mortar** is a brass mold for forming ash-crucibles <note>Cupels used for refining gold and silver.</note> in the shape of a wide circle or a pierced cup. They call it the **Nun** <note>Original: *Nonnam*.</note>.

**The Monk** <note>Original: *Monachus*.</note> is a pestle with a rounded hump and a wide, protruding base; by its strike, the hollow of the ash-cup is formed. These instruments are larger or smaller as the task requires.

**Hook** is an iron stylus curved at the tip and bent into a circle at the other end so it can be held; it is used for turning and mixing materials in the crucibles.

**Touchstone** <note>Original: *Lapis lydius*, or Lydian Stone.</note> is a certain black stone of uniform consistency and hardness, used for judging metals by rubbing them against it.

<margin>Some are black, others ashen, others greenish (they call it *verdellum*). It is considered a type of marble by Caesalpinus. Take care that the black is not softer or harder than it should be. Soft gold, such as Hungarian gold, is not correctly viewed on a hard stone. Scattered and "harsh" gold cannot be well judged by rubbing, for it always shows less than it contains.</margin>

The blacker it is, the more it shows the differences in colors, just as we see a rainbow appearing under the thickest and darkest clouds. It must also be hard so that it does not easily suffer damage from the "strong waters" <note>Nitric acid.</note> and coloring agents with which it is sometimes drenched. It is so smooth and uniform in consistency that it represents the metallic line evenly. It is usually fashioned into a four-sided shape an inch long. To clean it, they mostly use "white lead" <note>Tin oxide/calx.</note> with which it is evenly wiped and cleaned. It can also be scrubbed with lye and cloths. It is the companion of the "testing needles" <note>Standardized alloy needles used for comparison on a touchstone.</note>, which cannot be without it, although it does not alway...

# On the Preparation <note>original: *Scevasia*, from the Greek *skeuasia*, meaning preparation or the equipment needed for a task.</note> of the Assaying Art, Part I.

...the assayer requires these tools if the nature of the metal is known to him. The touchstone is used specifically for examining gold, silver, and their mixtures. But it does not always deserve our trust, as the history of Budelius <note>Joachim Budelius, author of works on coinage and weights.</note> testifies; he says he was once so deceived by a Sophist <note>Here meaning a fraudster or "wise-cracker" in the alchemical arts.</note> that, when he lacked the leisure for a more exact judgment, he purchased counterfeit or debased silver based solely on the touchstone. In the same way, the yellow coating of a tooth <note>Likely referring to a specific mineral formation or a deceptive plating.</note> deceived certain people on the touchstone, so that they thought it was gold, which was not the case at all.

Having learned from this, for the sake of greater certainty, skilled assayers drop *aqua fortis* <term>aqua fortis</term><note>Nitric acid, which dissolves base metals but leaves gold intact.</note> onto the gold lines, or smear them with a gold colorant; by these means, whatever is not gold is corroded or changed, so that it can be easily wiped away, or it vanishes, or is recognized by other traces. For silver, a "silver color," "water of tartar," and similar substances are applied. I judge that this same thing should be done even in the presence and comparison of needles <note>Touch-needles or "probing needles" made of known alloys used for comparison against an unknown sample on a touchstone.</note>. For a blend similar to the needles can be made with a simple liquid. Therefore, the "medicine of the art" <note>Chemical reagents.</note> must be applied both to the needle-strikes and to the metal sample; the conformity or discrepancy must be estimated from how both react. This is all the more necessary because the streak of the needles can deceive us, especially if there are triple alloys in the gold and many in number; the eye cannot sufficiently discern or choose the matching ones, which anyone can see is possible in such a variety of mixtures or alloys <term>liga</term> in coinage.

Other things they record about the Lydian stone <note>Another name for the touchstone.</note> may be sought from other authors. As for the question of whether it has a certain "magnetic familiarity" with gold, its vanity easily dismisses it, as it smacks of something Paracelsian <note>A dismissal of the more mystical/magical theories of Paracelsus.</note>.

The **Magnet** (which is also called the **Herculean stone**) is a rock that attracts iron, and with its other side points to the northern region. Its use elsewhere is extensive; in the assaying art, however, it distinguishes iron ores and indicates how much iron is in them.

Fallopius <note>Gabriele Falloppio (1523–1562), the famed anatomist and physician.</note> held the nature of the magnet, along with mercury and purgative medicines, to be among the wonders whose logic cannot be explained, but whose effects are to be admired with awe. And certainly, those three are of such necessity in human affairs that without them men would live much more inconveniently, and many disciplines would be crippled—as the magnet shows in metallurgy, navigation, and astronomy; medicine in purgatives; and various arts, especially metallurgy, in mercury. No creatures similar to them exist.

There is also **quicksilver** <note>Mercury.</note> among the special aids for examining gold and estimating metallic perfection, if the other factors agree.

Fachsius <note>Modestin Fachs.</note> calls lead the **"Mother of Metals"** because metals from ores are eagerly "drunk up" by it. But that name more truly fits mercury, since by his own judgment it is the material part of metals, and by it is received not only gold, silver, refined iron, copper, and tin <note>original: *plumbum candidum*, literally "white lead."</note>, but also lead <note>original: *nigrum [plumbum]*, literally "black lead."</note>, so much so that lead is believed to be imperfectly coagulated mercury; and all metals may be resolved into it.

**Charcoals** are to be chosen that have a moderate thickness, such as fragments of a medium egg. By smaller ones, the fire is suffocated.

<margin>See Erker, Part 1, page 34 in folio. <note>Lazarus Ercker, author of a major 1574 treatise on ores and assaying.</note></margin>
**Scales** in the assaying art are of three types. One is that by which the lead and additives are weighed: where eight ounces placed in the pans equal the moments <note>The smallest units of weight.</note>. The second is for weighing ores and metals, according to the smaller hundredweights <term>centupondia</term>, and it corresponds to the weight of the ore. The third is enclosed in a glass case or housing, and it is the most exact of all; it must be managed with the greatest attention and the "holding of one's breath" <note>A literal instruction: the scales were so sensitive that a person's breath could tip the balance.</note>, so that even the slightest differences in weight become known. To this scale are brought the "fulminated" grains <note>Small beads of precious metal purified by heat.</note> and those separated from ores by the magnet, mercury, or other aids. The weight of these must correspond to the smelting and refining in the great fire and in large portions.

Yet it is a marvel that in the refining of a larger fire, sometimes more comes out, and it exceeds by nearly a dram. At other times there are many causes why the results do not correspond, so much so that the value of a large quantity is very rarely predicted exactly. Sometimes the assayer <term>docimastes</term> errs, sometimes the smelter and refiner. Sometimes the material is unequal, and it cannot be reduced to an exact equality. Occasionally additives either take away or snatch something. It can also happen that a greater fire turns into a spark that which sustained a smaller fire, as usually happens with immature and "soft" metals, where the legitimate "fixation" <note>The process of making a substance resistant to heat.</note> is bypassed, but "rebound" <note>original: *repercussio*.</note> occurs, as Fachsius calls it. Likewise, if any residue remained in the dross <term>scotiis</term>, the stone, or the hidden cracks of the furnaces, it shows a richer ore in the great fire. But it can also happen that something stubbornly resisted the assayer, which nevertheless yielded to the smelter and refiner. For these reasons, the weights can be richer or poorer, and thus discordant.

Furthermore, those three scales are described by Agricola. Budelius places only the third hanging scale with its small case, and says of it that it is used for weighing everything. Otherwise, in contracts of sale and purchase, as well as in the business of the mint and the goldsmith, there are their own scales and weights, for which the commentaries of Agricola, Budaeus, Budelius, Mathesius, Fachsius, and others should be consulted. However, Agricola's teaching seems more appropriate, because scales are easily corrupted by outsiders and collect dirt, and thus lose their exact measurements.

To the scales belong the **pound-weights**, <insert>To the scales add the pans, which Ercker wants to be made of silver for the sake of cleanliness, and to be included in the cases. For these, silver plates of equal weight are required, which, when placed in the pans, support the grains or metallic powders. The grains are grasped with small tongs of a peculiar shape... with sharp feet.</insert> of which five types are necessary in the assaying art (according to Fachsius): the first is called the weight of the hundredweight, the use of which is for ores.

Its distribution is according to the parts of the hundredweight and the pound. The pound-weights according to the parts of the hundredweight are: 1. the hanging hundredweight; 2. fifty pounds, or half a hundredweight; 3. a quarter of a hundredweight, or twenty-five pounds; 4. sixteen pounds; 5. eight pounds; 6. four pounds; 7. two pounds; 8. one pound.

The **half-ounce weights** <note>original: *semunciales*.</note>: 1. sixteen half-ounces, which is called a **mark** and a **bes**; 2. eight half-ounces (or **lots**), which is half a mark; 3. four half-ounces, which is a quarter of a mark; 4. two lots; 5. one lot. And of this weight let there be two to complete a whole pound of 32 lots. From the com-

### Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book V.

By the positioning of these weights, one can easily calculate the remaining weights and their differences; for example, one who requires an eighth of a hundred-weight combines a mass of eight and another of four pounds with two-thirds of a pound <note>original: *besse*, a Roman unit representing two-thirds of a whole</note>, and so forth.

The second type of weight is that of **Grains**, the use of which is in examining coinage. It is divided according to **lots** <note>original: *lotones*, often referred to as a "Loth" in Germanic systems, typically half an ounce</note>, which are parts of a **mark** <term>mark</term><note>A "mark" was a common European unit of weight for gold and silver, roughly equal to 8 ounces, though it varied by region.</note>, and **grains**, which are parts of a lot, into double-sized masses. According to lots, the first mass is a whole mark, which is sixteen lots; the second is a half-mark of eight lots; the third is four lots; the fourth is two; the fifth is one. According to the parts of the lots, seven masses are made: the first is of nine grains; the second, six; the third, three; the fourth, two; the fifth, one; the sixth and seventh, a half-grain each.

The third type of weights or <term>characters</term> <note>original: *characterum*, here referring to the specific physical weights used in gold assaying</note> is used in testing gold. This is distributed according to **carats** <note>original: *characta*</note>, which are parts of a mark, and **grains**, which are portions of a carat. There are six masses of carats: the first is a whole mark, containing twenty-four carats of absolute purity. The second is a half-mark of twelve carats. The third is a quarter-mark containing six carats. The fourth is of three carats, which is an eighth of a mark. The fifth is of two, and the sixth is of one. Likewise, six small masses of grains are provided: the first is nine grains, the second six, the third three, the fourth two, and the fifth and sixth are one grain each, kept separately.

The fourth type is that of <term>denarii</term> <note>original: *denariorum*, often translated as "penny-weights"</note>, and is used for copper-bearing ores and gilded silver that is not intended for coinage. By its benefit, we can also know how many coins of any kind constitute an Erfurt mark, etc. The distribution of the masses is done according to lots, which are parts of a mark, and <term>drachmas</term> into which the lot is divided, and they correspond to the hundred-weight. For just as the pounds were distributed there from sixteenth to first, so are the lots here; and just as the lots were there, so are the drachmas with half-pennies <note>original: *halleris*, referring to the Heller, a small German copper coin</note> here. Therefore, there are five masses of lots: 1. is a mark of 16 lots; 2. is a half-mark of eight lots; 3. is four; 4. is two; 5. is one. In drachmas, the first mass has two drachmas, or 16 hellers; 2. has one drachma, or eight hellers; 3. has 4 hellers, which are two denarii (for a denarius consists of two hellers, and is taken here as a coin); 4. has two hellers or one coin or denarius. 5. and 6. each have single hellers, or little denarii, which are also called small coins. Some assayers <note>original: *Docimastae*, from the Greek *dokimastes*, a taster or assayer of metals</note> examine coins not in grain masses, but in Belgian denarii (according to the Netherlandish weight). And these are 14 half-ounces with 16 grains, the same as 10 denarii and 4 grains. If someone is working with mark-masses, let him take 16 pounds from the hundred-weight for one mark, and 8 pounds for as many half-ounces, so that there is 1 pound for a half-ounce, and so on.

The fifth type is also of denarii or coins, which can likewise be taken from the hundred-weight so that a mass of 16 pounds stands for one mark, while a mass of sixteen lots stands for a <term>sicilicus</term> <note>original: *sicilico*, a Roman weight equal to a quarter of an ounce</note> or a double-drachma. The small masses are designated in lots thus: the first has 16 lots for testing and is a mark; the second 8, the third 4, the fourth 2, the fifth 1. In coins or denarii, let the first mass be 8 coins or a <term>sicilicus</term>, which is two drachmas; the second 4, or one drachma; the third 2; the fourth one coin; the fifth a half or small coin; the sixth one quarter; the seventh one eighth.

They are also used for finding the value of coins, and then it is cut into fragments of lots and denarii, as <term>Fachsius</term> <note>Modestus Fachs, a 16th-century author of a famous handbook on assaying</note> shows, whom you may consult.

Furthermore, the calculation and distribution of the weight-parts is established differently for silver and gold. A silver **mark** has sixteen lots, and a lot has eighteen grains; or according to the people of Nuremberg, a mark contains sixteen lots, a lot four drachmas, and a drachma four small coins. Or according to the people of Cologne, a mark is divided into twelve denarii, and a denarius into 24 grains. Or according to the Venetians, the "bes" <note>two-thirds of a pound</note> consists of eight ounces, an ounce of eight drachmas, and a drachma of eighteen carats <note>original: *siliquis*, or "siliquae", the carob seed weight</note> or grains. A gold mark takes 24 carats, and a carat twelve grains; (for others, the carat is divided into 4 grains, and the grain into four tiny grains).

In both gold and silver, whatever is of 24 carats is here sixteen lots, or 12 denarii; that is of exact purity. Mixtures, however, are named chiefly by the quantity of the nobler pure metal (within certain degrees); for example, gold is of eighteen carats when it has that much pure gold in a mark, and the remainder up to 24 is silver, or copper, or both, which the test will indicate. Likewise, silver is of six denarii when it contains that much pure metal; the remaining part, namely also six, is of a foreign metal, such as copper or the like, although other minerals may be mixed in by "Sophists" <note>frauds or deceptive alchemists</note>. Thus gold of 23 carats and 9 grains is that which has three grains of mixture, by which it falls short of perfection.

In the weight-masses and the dimension of the weights themselves, there is no universal rule, except this: that the composition of the mass be made as many times as the money may be allowed toward the whole sum according to any part. Later, some achieve this more concisely, others less so. Thus, in establishing a certain measure and distributing the parts, the public law and the custom of the region must be followed. Since this is varied, it results in a varied number being assumed in special calculations as well, and we have declared that rule by way of example. The weights used are hundred-weights, lots, denarii, carats, and ounces in the Roman pound. Therefore, authors also look to these most of all, even though different ones may later disagree on the parts. However, the internal quality is not changed whether you calculate according to twelve denarii and 24 grains, or 16 lots and 18 grains. Thus in gold, the calculation can be set up by carats and lots. For they can be reconciled: since 24 carats are worth as much as sixteen lots, and one carat as much as twelve grains, there are as many grains in 16 lots as there are in 24 carats. From this it happens that 23 carats weigh as much as 15 lots with six grains, which the distribution clearly shows. For 23 carats consist of 276 grains. If you reduce these to lots by dividing by 18, there will emerge 15 lots with six grains remaining, etc. *Fachsius* also reduces carats to lots, drachmas, small coins, and their parts. The foundation is the equality of weight between 24 carats and 16 lots; likewise of one carat and a **sicilicus** with 1 ½ small coins or denarii, etc. You may consult the table set down by him.

In this way, denarii are reconciled with lots, so that 12 denarii are the same as 16 lots into which the mark is distributed, the weight being the same on both sides. Therefore, 24 grains of a denarius contain, along with the 18 grains of one lot, six additional grains; and two denarii will be two lots with 12 grains; three denarii will be four lots, namely a quarter of a mark on both sides. The word "lot" <note>original: *loto*</note> taken from the Germans indeed...

### Concerning the Equipment <note>original: *Sceuafia*, a Latinized form of the Greek *skeuasia*, meaning preparation or the physical apparatus of an art</note> of the Assaying Art, Part 1.

...indeed a twenty-fourth part of a Roman pound, or a thirty-second part of a civil pound in Germany. But in the present assay, it designates the sixteenth part of a **mark** <term>mark</term><note>A standard unit of weight for precious metals, usually equal to eight ounces.</note> of pure silver or gold (if its weight is reduced to **loths** <term>loth</term><note>original: *lotones*. A Germanic unit of weight, usually half an ounce; sixteen loths made one mark.</note>); so that silver of twelve loths—which in its total mass weighs sixteen loths to complete a mark—would contain twelve half-ounces of pure metal.

It follows from this that in arithmetic calculation, the **apprentice** <note>original: *tyro*, meaning a beginner or student</note> must not stray from the second rule of proportions. For example, if an assay indicated that in a hundred-weight of silver ore there are eight loths of pure silver, there will be the same proportion in a larger hundred-weight; and if there are many hundred-weights from several different pourings, they must all be gathered into one sum. If lead, gold, or another metal is present with the silver, that too is calculated in the same way according to the analogy. From this, the calculation according to the currency is afterwards produced, and the ratio of profit and loss emerges along with the expenses. In the case of granules, wrought silver and gold, and similar items, the matter requires a little more attention, because here the loss occurring during the smelting <note>original: *vrendum*, literally "burning"</note> must be calculated together with the cost of granulation and other factors that practical experience will advise in specific cases. 

(Other arts or even common usage provide many more instruments necessary for assaying. In the testing of gold, there is a requirement for a clean **cucurbit** <note>original: *cucurbitula*, a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</note> for separating; a small glass pouring vessel; glass dishes made of pure **Venetian glass** <note>highly prized for its clarity and chemical resistance</note> for washing; an iron or brass four-legged stand to support the cucurbit; a small, low tripod of iron or brass to hold the gold pan in which the **calx** <term>calx</term><note>The powdered remains of a metal after it has been roasted or chemically treated.</note> of gold is dried; a gold pan for drying or heating the calx to a glow; an iron plate with many small cups <note>original: *acetabulis*, small basins or cupels</note> so that the assays may be poured into it; a hammer and anvil for flattening the masses; forceps; a cutting chisel; a sponge for drying the **mercury** <note>original: *hydrargyrum*</note> after washing; shears for cutting metal foil; an instrument for drawing wire; brass brushes; files; fixed tongs; fixed probes; large and small ember-tongs; a casting cone; a granulating kettle; distillation instruments for **corrosive waters** <note>original: *aquarum causticarum*, referring to acids like nitric acid used to separate gold from silver</note>; separating flasks; and a funnel. Also a shade, a sighting-level, pokers, mortars and pestles of brass and wood, bellows, a blowpipe, a casting ladle, a scraper or shaving knife, stone jars, and many things of this sort.) So much for the equipment of assaying.

# THE SECOND PART OF THE PROBATORY ART
## CONCERNING DOCIMASIA <note>Assaying or the testing of metals</note>

->CHAPTER I.<-
->*What Docimasia is.*<-

> *Docimasia is the second branch of the assaying art, in which the actual form and method of testing is explained.*

->CHAPTER II.<-
->*On the manner of fire in Assaying.*<-

<margin>The more spacious and powerful the furnace and muffle <note>original: *tegula*, literally "tile," but referring here to the ceramic arch or "muffle" that protects the samples from direct coal contact</note> are, the stronger the fire—especially if the embers are scattered and plentiful. The more covered they are and the firmer the embers, the weaker the fire, until at last it is completely extinguished.</margin>
In this branch, although specific instructions sometimes present themselves, nevertheless all specimens can be examined by fire, the manner of which must be primarily maintained so that it suits the work. From this arise the "middle regimes" (one operation is done via a covered furnace, another via an open one. The former is employed by Ercker <note>Lazarus Ercker (c. 1530–1594) was a famous German metallurgist and author of a definitive work on assaying</note> for Baleris and florins <note>original: *Baleris & florinu*, referring to specific types of currency/silver testing</note>) and the tempering of heat. If the furnace is larger, it will provide a milder fire; if the muffle is larger and not cut away, or at least very little. It will likewise reduce the heat if the topmost opening is closed, which however must be done with such care so as not to suffocate the work in the cupel <term>cupel</term><note>original: *catillus*, a small, porous vessel used to separate precious metals from base metals like lead.</note>. Thus the small door of the ash pit must be closed.

The fire also tends to be less intense in humid or sweltering weather, or if there is another fire near the furnace in the same hearth. Therefore, in precise examinations, such arrangements are to be avoided because the same degree of fire is not required perpetually throughout a single work; rather, it must sometimes be increased and sometimes decreased. Sweltering air, or a southern wind, and a fire near the hearth take away the opportunity for this control. In the same way, rays of light or excessive brightness must be avoided, as they prevent you from judging the behavior of the fire. Therefore, black curtains are usually hung at the windows. It was also said above concerning coals that those smaller than what is proper do not provide heat and "bite," <note>original: *bitum*, likely referring to the intensity or "sting" of the heat</note> but rather suffocate it.

Moreover, the heat is intensified by throwing in medium-sized coals, and even some slightly larger ones, while keeping the door of the ash pit open and removing the ashes and small burnt bits from the muffle, replacing them with medium ones; and furthermore, by placing large embers in the opening near the muffle. If you require a more fervent heat, close all the exits of the workshop except the chimney and the one entrance where air enters; with no other exit found, the air exiting through the furnace into the funnel will blow the fire as if by a bellows. You shall decrease or increase the fire by degrees and step-by-step in this manner: If it is to be decreased, take an ember out of the upper opening (which you had placed there before during the intensification of the furnace); afterward, put back the top cover of the hole, leaving an open space or a crack the width of a finger. Thirdly, move its small valve to the door of the ash pit. (Remember, however, that the workshop must also be opened again, so that the air no longer builds up in the furnace, and rather that the entrance where it bursts in should be closed.) Fourthly, if you can make it even cooler, close the rear and side holes of the muffle with their own panels. Also, block the front part with a semicircular door, cut away a little bit at the bottom. Thus the furnace becomes so dark that the muffle and the cupels take on black spots. If, in turn, the heat is to be increased by degrees, remove the cover from the top so it is half-open, and pull the valve away from the muffle. If it is still too cool, remove the back panel from the muffle and put back the front door that is cut away a little bit. Thirdly, intensify the force further if you also take away the side closures from the muffle. Even more so if you remove the top cover entirely and place one or two embers at the front door of the muffle. Finally, it will become entirely hot when the lower obstacles are cast aside and the air is let in, as before.

->CHAPTER III.<-
->*On the Management of the Work.*<-

From here, the work must be begun in this way. Let the muffle be placed in the furnace. Let proper coals (from which the flame is constant and equal, and which do not leave behind a great deal of ash, by which the work is hindered) be thrown in and kindled. Let the cupels be put in so that the whole space under the muffle is occupied, even if you are not going to use them all (for in the meantime, the remaining ones can be more fully dried and more firmly solidified by the same fire. Sometimes shards are put in with the ash cupels). Move an ember to the opening of the muffle. Let the vessels be heated in this way (specifically the cupel <note>original: *copella*</note> etc., not the roasting dishes <note>original: *testae*</note> in which ore is cooked with lead) for half an hour. (For nothing ought to be committed to them unless they are thoroughly heated.) When you judge that they are sufficiently hot, blow away the ashes with an iron pipe if any have fallen into the cupels, and having removed the ember...

# On the Assaying Art, Part 2.

Using the fire-tongs, place the lead onto the cupel <note>original: *catillum*, a small porous dish used in assaying</note> situated in the lower part of the furnace, and watch if it jumps or crackles. If it does, the cupel has not yet been heated enough; it is necessary for them to glow more deeply with a longer stay in the fire until the added lead melts quietly.

That duration is indeed described as half an hour, but the time is indefinite, since it may be completed sooner or later depending on the size of the muffle <note>original: *tegulæ*, the ceramic arch protecting the samples</note> and the manner of the fire previously discussed. This heating of the cupels is called by the Germans **abgeadembt** <note>German: "tempered" or "steamed out"</note>, as if you were to say that the cold, damp air is drawn out like a breath, so that the vessel can receive the heat while dry. This same instruction must also be observed in large-scale works. For the Master, once the furnace is built, the crucible prepared, and the coals added, allows the fire to burn for half an hour, and furthermore waits for the tapping of the slag <note>original: *puncturam scoriarum*</note>, until it is thoroughly heated. This is achieved more quickly if he also smelted the day before or used the same furnace, which also applies to the assay furnace. For a vessel not used for a long time is more damp, while one that has experienced fire more frequently and recently is drier.

<margin>Why metals jump out of the clay and ash.</margin>
As for why lead and other metals jump out when the vessels are not thoroughly heated, they say the cause is the moisture of the clay and ash. They prove this by the nature of copper and other metals which, while being smelted to purity, if a little water or a damp object falls in, are thrown out with a great crash. It is well known from the tumult of burning objects when they are extinguished that watery moisture and fiery, vaporous dryness are adversaries to one another. But this opinion can be countered by pointing out the difference in conditions. For in the case where copper rises up, the whole mass is glowing hot; it does not suffer the same thing when it is still flowing and ignited but has less heat. This is similar to what usually happens in heated fats and oils when water is poured in, from which they boil over further because they then take on a completely vaporous <note>original: *spiritualem*</note> and fiery nature. They are suddenly forced from a thin state into a dense one, yet the vapors <note>original: *spiritus*</note> thus compressed into one, striving to yield to the pressing and narrowing suffocation, are forced into a violent flight, by which they carry away whatever they encounter. Nor can they be compressed so suddenly, but only by a slow motion, just as saltpeter <note>original: *halinitrum*</note> gradually learns to endure the fire which it could not withstand when encountered all at once. 

However, when cold lead is placed on cupels that are heated but not yet glowing through, there is a great diversity of causes. In the former case, one thing is boiling and entirely filled with fiery vapors; here, neither is boiling—indeed, if the cupel were boiling, the expulsion would not occur. Nor is the ratio of glowing metal to the cupel or clay the same. But why does it not happen with a hot cupel and cold lead as it does with hot copper and cold water? Does this show something of a mercurial nature? Either the mercury entirely flees from the fire, or it entirely settles. The former happens because of its volatility, when it is not yet thoroughly heated and brought to the nature of the fire, but retains something of its contrary cold and moisture; the latter happens when it has become familiar to the fire and has approached it most closely, being entirely inflamed. Therefore, even thoroughly heated metals jump back from cold moisture, even if only a small start of motion is received. It is necessary, however, that the cupel then match that same quality and glow equally. For it is known that they break otherwise, but by a dense, penetrating body working its way in and occupying the flight of the vapors. If, therefore, the glowing cupel dominates the injected material and changes it entirely, they endure each other, just as when both are cold and heat up together gradually. But if it cannot dominate because the heat is still diminished, and nevertheless the forces of the vapors are shut in, that which was put in is repelled; it does not jump of its own accord but is thrown out, so that here the opposite happens to what occurs in glowing metal, or oil, pitch, etc. 

We can also say that before thorough heating, the "spirits" of the clay, ashes, and indeed the vessels are still denser and cannot easily struggle out; when the lead is added, it immediately traps them as it melts, and even expands them further by thinning them. Thus they break out by force and carry the liquid with them, like a storm carries a cloud. But if the cupel is glowing, it emits thinned and fiery vapors which penetrate easily and overcome the trapping material, or they even move backward and escape; even if they thicken, they are not so restricted, since a small quantity can be made from a large mass, requiring little space. This sentiment can be illustrated by the nature of thin lightning, which easily escapes through thin spaces but strikes against solid ones, and if it does not yield, it breaks them, or if it is meltable, it liquefies it and thus makes it more vaporous. If you enclose quicksilver <note>mercury</note> in a narrow glass and block every exit, once turned into vapor over the coals, it shatters the glass into tiny pieces and rushes out with a crash. Raw pots not yet sufficiently dried, when placed on coals, not only break and jump apart into shards, but also shed scales from the bottom, inside and out, with a sound. But I return to assaying.

> *When you have correctly heated the cupels and the lead melts and begins to smoke, unless the metal is already with it, add it in the form of powder or grains cleaned from the ore, or even put them all in together mixed.* This is Ercker’s instruction. *On an iron plate, crush the ore into powder with an iron hammer. Add eight times the amount of granulated lead to this in a testing dish. Mix it. Place the dish in a pre-heated furnace. Move a coal to the door and smelt the ore into the lead with a more intense fire (**ansieden** <note>German: "to scorify" or boil down</note>); when the slag occupies the whole material in the dish, it is sufficiently smelted. Then stir and mix it with a glowing iron hook so that what sticks to the edge enters the lead. A little later, after the dish is removed, the alloy <note>original: *stannum*, likely referring to the lead-silver "work-lead"</note> is poured into a small pit in an iron plate. When it has cooled, the slag is knocked off. Meanwhile, an ash-cupel has been heated in the furnace for half an hour. The small mass of silver-lead is placed on this. A more intense fire is given until it smokes and separates. Then the heat is reduced so that the lead is consumed by a moderate fire and creeps into the cupel, with the grain of silver remaining.*

When we examine metals already smelted from ores or otherwise pure, we usually add them with lead; and sometimes they have already been melted with lead for a long time, even when we are looking at ores. For we first dissolve those in a dish or triangular crucible by smelting them with lead, so that a silver or gold alloy is made. This we then "refine with lightning" <note>original: *fulminamus*, referring to the 'blick' or flash of light when the silver becomes pure</note> in an ash-cupel, just as in a larger operation, except for the differences in dross and other external matters. But if we smelt the ores in the cupel, we either put the lead in first or put both in mixed together; the latter is easier, while the former is favored by Agricola and Budelius <note>Joachim Budelius, another metallurgical author</note>, which is nonetheless also observed in triangular crucibles, though not always. In a greater fire, the ore is added with molybdenum <note>likely lead glance/galena</note>, litharge, raw pyrite, smelted pyrite, and the rest. The lead, however, is placed in the outer cupel, though in a curved furnace it may be in the inner one. This instruction shows that lead can be put in first anywhere if it is not already combined.

# ## Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book V.

When the tin-lead alloy <note>original: *stannum*, here defined as a mixture of lead and another metal</note> already begins to smoke, moderate the heat, lest anything be harmfully consumed (this applies to silver or other metals, but most especially to silver and "soft" gold). And then also pay attention to the colors or "flowers," which indicate the presence of "rapacious" minerals, such as sulfur, arsenic, etc.

Furthermore, you can take signs from the lead as to whether the furnace should be intensified or dampened: whether it is running hot or cold. If the smoke rises straight up, it is hot; if it is reflected and wanders around the bottom, it is cold. If the alloy shines, the heat must be increased, unless that luster is left over from impurities. (Especially in a rich vein, this luster and the intensification of heat must not be neglected.) If the alloy is slow to smoke, and one or two coals are moved near the mouth of the vessel, the fire must be increased. In the same way, if the ash-cupel <note>original: *catillus cinereus*</note> turns black: and if it is surrounded by a dark, shiny ring, it is cold; work must be done so that it heats up again by moving a coal near the cupel and closing the ash-vent. But if it has cooled, and yet some alloy remains in the cupel, drop in a small ball of lead, and it will begin to smoke again; once this happens, the heat must be reapplied and the "flash" <note>original: *fulmen*, the "brightening" or "blick" that occurs when the last of the lead oxidizes</note> must be brought about, even though the weight of the grain may have decreased slightly due to the force of the lead. When he perceives that the flash is imminent, intensify the fire in the proper way, lest a "lead-flood" <note>an excess of molten lead oxide</note> stain the grain and make it heavier. After the flash, leave the grain in the furnace for a little while, with the coals removed from the mouth of the vessel; in this way, it comes out of the dish pure.

These instructions are primarily prescribed by <term>Fachs</term> <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century German master of the mint and author of a famous book on assaying</note>. The common method is called into question by <term>Ercker</term> <note>Lazarus Ercker, a renowned Bohemian mineralogist and author of the Treatise on Ores and Assaying (1574)</note>, because the slag harbors some silver, which results in the test not matching the truth. He therefore proposes such a method: Let a larger <term>cupel</term> <note>a porous vessel made of bone-ash used to separate precious metals from lead</note> in which copper is tested for silver be placed in the furnace and properly heated. Then let 16 hundredweights of lead be put in: let them be cooked to a boil. From here, let one hundredweight of crushed ore be added gradually in portions, enclosed in a paper wrapper. Then the lead is covered as if by an impure and harsh vein. One must proceed with a light fire at the start, then a stronger one so that the slag departs. Once this is done, another portion of ore is thrown in, and it is handled as before, and so on until the whole hundredweight is cooked in. Thus a mass mixed of silver and lead is obtained, which is then <term>flashed</term> <note>subjected to final cupellation</note>. But if veins were tested in the common way, the <term>assay master</term> <note>original: *docimasta*</note> would indicate one thing, while the smelting master would extract another. And although these instructions seem to pertain specifically to the silver test, they warn that it is appropriate for this to happen in the entire management of other metals as well, which for the most part require either lead or something else that performs the office of lead.

<term>Agricola</term> <note>Georgius Agricola, the "Father of Mineralogy," author of De Re Metallica</note> adds that the ore or grain ought to be placed in folded paper and not poured in by a spoon, because there is a danger of spilling. Neither should the order be perverted, nor the ore or metal be cooked before the lead. Also, so that it may be more easily received by the lead, they stir and mix it by using a sharpened coal. The slag is partly turned into ash and partly stands apart from the grain; and if they float on the lead, they are drawn off. The lead is also turned into smoke, or is drunk up by the cupels, or turns into glass and <term>litharge</term> <note>lead oxide</note>, just as in the "greater flash," where <term>molybdenum</term> <note>here referring to lead-based residues or galena</note> is also produced. If the clay cupels are not warmed before the imposition of the material, they break, or they make the lead tremble, or they cast it out; by which trembling the superior theory concerning spirits or breaths <note>the release of gases trapped in the porous cupel</note> is confirmed. If the lead or alloy leaps out, the experiment must be tried with new material. However, lest it tremble or leap out, it can be avoided and repressed by moving a coal near the cupel: from which the lead recedes once the spirits are released. <term>Fachs</term> also warns about removing slowness and accelerating the operation and the flash by means of a coal, as well as the black ring, etc. <term>Agricola</term> notes that it can also be done by a lighted torch moved near the cupel. From this it grows hot, the lead is consumed more quickly, and the flash follows. Yet a coal seems more suitable, lest the work be darkened by soot and a loss occur from an unequal flame. After the work has been restored by heat, <term>Agricola</term> says care must be taken that it has enough and equal heat to produce the flash.

The lead ought not to sit without motion, as if the material were covered by a skin. For then it is cold and must be heated. If it takes on a "tail" and does not become rounded, the union is being mixed. A tail occurs where the heat is more intense. Likewise, when the lead departs and fails before completion, new lead is added, but it must be pre-heated. Truly, as <term>Fachs</term> warns, this is done with fear of loss. Therefore, only as much slag is placed at the beginning as is enough. When the button <note>original: *regulus*</note> appears, which usually happens in three-quarters of an hour. (<term>Budelius</term> <note>Renatus Budelius, a legal and monetary scholar who wrote on the value of coins and metals</note> says it is rolled and rolled again, cooked in a glowing fire, and re-cooked, and thus purged through a quarter of an hour, so that finally nothing is there, nor can be seen, except a pure, clean grain.) And its face is shiny, with a cheerful and pleasing color, according to the nature of each metal. The small mass must be extracted while still hot, lest the ash stick to it when cooled;
<margin>q</margin> but if this happens nonetheless, it must be squeezed with tongs so that the impurity pops off, not scraped off, lest it incur damage. Furthermore, this work can also be divided so that the material is first cooked with lead in a triangular dish within a circle; afterward it is flashed under a muffle <note>original: *tegula*</note>. Some also perform both in the circle, but not as safely. Why lead should be used, especially in gold and silver and the rest in which there is some difficulty, was also explained above: namely, that some think the metal flees to the lead from the heat because lead is cold; others, because it is the "mother of metals." <term>Geber</term> <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous 8th-century alchemist</note> and others more correctly attribute it to a "mercurial kinship," so that if <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *hydrargyrus*</note> were more constant in the fire, or at least equally durable, it would be used more rightly. Now lead succeeds in its place, which is a "diminished" coagulated quicksilver, and is familiar to this and to other metals, except for impure iron, etc.

He who requires more certain tests ought to weigh and explore two or three specimens at once with one fire and effort. The grains are then compared to see if they are equal or not. If they are, the test is just; if not, it must be started again more carefully. Likewise, if something was lost from the specimen, foreign matter was present; if nothing was lost, it was pure and clean.

An exact result is rarely found unless the metal was first in a most skillful test. Thus if you hand over one part to one craftsman and another part to another to be judged, or try it with different fires or efforts, the same result rarely comes forth, because either unequal veins or masses are given, or the skill, vigilance, fire, furnace, and many other things are unequal. Therefore it is safer to use one good craftsman, with many specimens at once, and the same effort and fire. Effort must also be given that the vessels are not dirty, or smeared with slag and metallic filings. Therefore, even those which were previously used in another work are diligently wiped and scraped. Otherwise, the judgment is deceived.

On the Assaying of the Testing Art, Part 2.

# CHAPTER IV.

->The Division of Assaying<-

**A**ssaying <note>original: *Docimasia*, the art of testing the purity of metals or ores</note> is divided into the metallic and the mineral. (I use the term "mineral" specifically for spirits, juices, and other minerals which are called "intermediates," as no more suitable name occurs to me now.)

Metallic assaying is that by which metal-bearing veins and the metals themselves are tested. Hence, it is divided into the testing of veins and the testing of metals. Veins are either "mild" <note>docile and easy to process</note> or "harsh" (also called "wild"). Both can be smelted with their additives and judged; however, sometimes a harsh vein is reduced to a mild one through proper preparation—such as by washing, roasting, burning, quenching, and multiple fine grindings—and it is then tested in the same way. We achieve the same result through certain fluxes and other additives, whether it is smelted separately into lead in a test dish or a triangular crucible within a circle and later "flashed" <note>original: *fulminatur*, the "blick" or brightening seen when the last impurities are oxidized</note> in the ash-cupel; or whether both processes are carried out in a small ash-dish or cupel; or even if it is worked outside a small furnace.

There are also certain rich veins which are examined without any singular preparation; others are poor, which we separate as much as possible from rocks, sands, and other empty matter through washings, rinsings, or grindings—sometimes after a proper roasting has been performed, depending on the "wild" nature of the ore. To the poor veins we also add dross <note>original: *recrementa*</note>, slag, as well as furnace scrapings, ash, stones, and similar materials, and they are tested in the same way. Immature, volatile veins must first be "fixed" <note>made stable so they do not evaporate in the heat</note>.

The variety of metallic veins is inexplicable, because such subterranean mixtures are accidental and cannot be grasped by number. Thus, even the most skilled craftsmen sometimes encounter unknown veins never before seen in assaying work. Generally, however, all are distinguished in the aforementioned way: namely, that some are mild and others harsh—or, what is the same, some are "noble" and others "degenerate." You might call the latter stubborn, fierce, or "wild," because they are joined with harsh, sharp, corrosive, and fleeting minerals, from which they usually suffer damage in the fire, or are rendered entirely unfit for processing and are consumed. Furthermore, there are rich and poor veins; the latter are heavily mixed with mountain rock, stones, sands, juices, and so on. Therefore, they are often crushed and washed through sieves, troughs, layers, and other methods. Those that have juices soluble in water—such as pyrites, vitriols, and aluminous materials—are steeped in water or even boiled. Those with flammable fats, such as bituminous fissile stone, are burned off, or if the quantity makes it worthwhile, they are separated, such as sulfurous, cadmian, or arsenical veins, which are processed by "descension" <note>a method of smelting where the melted metal flows downward through a perforated plate</note> or other means. There is also another distinction not to be neglected: some are fixed and others volatile, which they call immature and soft. Unless these are made stable through proper "fixing waters" <note>original: *aquas fixatorias*</note>—made from vitriol, alum, gypsum, talc, iron slag, steel, or quenched glowing iron—they deceive the assayers and mock their hopes in a great fire, just as if they had been turned to ash by rapacious and corrosive minerals. Concerning slag, it should be known that they are sometimes empty and of no use, except that they can serve as a flux; however, in larger works, it is better to take slag that contains something rather than the empty kind, just like furnace scrapings, soot, and ashes. Those veins are judged to be metal-bearing if they stink while being drawn off. The stone named pyrites, when smelted, is called **Sterile:** <note>original: *Sterili*</note> it not infrequently carries some metal, such as gold, silver, or copper. It is smelted in a furnace kept perpetually open with vast fires into "loaves," so that it may be an additive for processing other veins. It is also used in its raw state.

Every vein must be taken from a selected and equally mixed heap, carefully weighed and ground, and protected so that no foreign matter falls in. Likewise, if something was lost during preparation, both the first weight and the second weight must be diligently noted, as well as the proportion of what remains.

Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "Father of Mineralogy"</note> orders hard stone to be burned so it can be ground and washed; if it is extremely hard, he douses it with vinegar before burning it. Soft stone he breaks with a hammer, grinds in a mortar, washes, and dries. Earth he washes in a trough and dries. A rich vein he only roasts in a closed pot over coals so that nothing is lost. A cheaper vein he burns even on a hearth placed over coals. But most of these instructions are to be understood as applying to the vein as it comes immediately from the mine, before it has been separated and selected.

Furthermore, one metallic vein is of gold, another of silver; of copper, of black lead <note>lead</note>, of white lead <note>tin</note>, or of iron; and it may be of a uniform metal, or multiform, containing several.

# CHAPTER V.

->On the testing of a uniform vein, and first, the golden one.<-

**T**here are two principal methods for testing golden veins: one by fire, the other by mercury <note>original: *hydrargyrum*</note>. If the gold vein is mild, quench it while red-hot in boy's urine <note>a common historical reagent believed to have unique tempering properties</note>; once ground upon a porphyry stone, weigh out one hundred-weight <note>original: *centupondium*, the standard unit of measurement in an assay</note>. To this, add a double amount of flux made from calcined tartar and saltpeter; place it in a covered triangular crucible in a wind-furnace, where it may gradually heat up. Afterward, intensify the fire with bellows, and when both have melted, add fifteen hundred-weights of pure lead. Apply a moderate fire with the bellows so that it begins to spit out the slag little by little. Mix and stir it with an iron wire. Finally, when the slag has emerged properly, remove it from the fire and let it cool in the dish (or crucible). This alloy <note>original: *stannum*, referring here to the lead-gold mixture</note> must be "flashed" in a thoroughly heated ash-cupel, using a sufficiently strong fire. Weigh the recovered grain. Do the same with a second sample. If silver is present with it (which the "little rib" with its coloring will indicate to you), separate it using *aqua fortis* <note>nitric acid</note>. The washed gold powder should be reduced in a clean gold shell <note>a small vessel for gathering gold</note>, where it is dried and ignited. If golden flint or another tender vein is to be examined, a little iron filings should be added to the flux, lest the gold be consumed by the violence of the flux.

The method described above is that of Fachs <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century master of the mint and author of a famous assaying manual</note>, who teaches first the physical mode of the generation of gold: that it consists of the purest mercury and the clearest, most fixed sulfur, most steadily mixed. (He agrees not with the common dregs of the "physicians" <note>likely referring to theoretical alchemists</note>, whose dreams are more important to them than any experiment, but with those who have proven the matter by certain experience.) Thus, gold suffers no loss in fire, nor in amalgamation with mercury, nor from the coloring of gold, sulfur, sal ammoniac, antimony, *aqua regia*, or the rest, although it may feel some loss from the vapor of lead. Afterward, he mentions that it is found in subterranean mines and in the sand of springs.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the assaying of gold, specifically focusing on the types of gold-bearing ores and the debate between masters of the craft regarding the best methods for extracting and testing them.</meta>

Commentaries on Alchemy, Part II, Book V.

of springs and rivers, produced by mercury and carried into the sands. The minerals, however, are copper-bearing stones, white flints with blue veins, marcasite <note>a term used then for various metallic sulfides like pyrite</note>, ochre, rust, and cadmia <note>often referring to zinc ores or furnace deposits</note>, in which silver and a little gold are found together; for this reason, they are called "gilded veins." The richest veins are those containing twelve carats. We could add here other things found elsewhere in nature, such as pure fossil gold in stone, gold in iron, or silver (either yellow or "fulvous") in white rock in Armenian stone, which is still stained with mercury (lest the unskillful deny that mercury is found in veins), and another type in ashen flint, and so forth. But these matters can be sought from the writers of metallic physics, especially **Kentmann**, **Gesner**, **Albertus**, **Agricola**, and many others. Closer to this art is the recognition of a true gold vein and its grains, which ought to be ashy or blue, and whose fracture looks like fresh and "mild" <note>easily worked or soft</note> galena <note>lead glance or lead ore</note>. Some can even be hammered out.

<margin>It seems a kind of red lead or cinnabar was once made from such things.</margin>
Indeed, those called marcasite and garnets not infrequently deceive the unwary with their purple, blood-red, or cinnabar-like color; but they must be quenched frequently in urine, especially the marcasites. For if their color remains constant and does not change, they contain gold; if not, they are barren. There are also certain veins of which the same **Fachs** <note>Modestin Fachs, a famous 16th-century master of assaying</note> says that they cannot be smelted by either a small or a large fire because of their "fugacity" <note>volatility; the metal evaporates before it can be collected</note>; these must therefore be "fixed" with strong waters <note>acids like nitric acid</note> and "reverberatory" agents, although this skill remains hidden from many assayers. Furthermore, certain disagreements among artisans are noted; for some think that golden veins require no other trial than the silver one, because gold, being highly "fixed" <note>stable and resistant to heat</note>, enters very readily into lead. But **Fachs** maintains that gold minerals must first be cleansed of filth and "intermediate" minerals—such as mercury, sulfur, and others—through fluxes, "reverberants," alkali salt, roasting, and so on, by which any volatile part might also be fixed. In lead alone there is little protection, for besides being volatile itself, lead is corrupted and dissipated by sulfur and mercury, so that it cannot sufficiently defend the "tender" <note>refined or delicate</note> gold from them. Once the gold is cleansed and fixed, however, lead is rightly added.

However, he seems to contradict himself regarding what he disputes in the preface about intractable and "degenerate" veins, against the opinion of others. He says that artisans will not allow themselves to judge correctly if stubborn veins are tested without a prior "coloring" <note>likely a chemical preparation or pre-treatment</note>. As a response, he adds that he certainly knows they must be burned once or twice. But since some veins contain tender and volatile gold and silver, from which something might be lost during the burning, and yet tender and fixed metals cannot be distinguished by everyone—and often that which should not be roasted is roasted anyway—he says he made no mention of the roasting but instead followed the common method, in which they are boiled or submerged in lead. He says it is also his custom, if the vein contains silver, lead, copper, or another metal (except gold) along with sulfur, arsenic, and antimony, to burn it; this is because he is certain that those impurities cannot attack the silver when there is another metal present for them to "devour." Nevertheless, he also tests such veins without roasting, immediately through lead, and usually finds the same value; however, the roasted ore is smelted more readily than the raw ore, which persuades many that the burned ore is better because it enters the lead more easily. This is the opinion of **Fachs**, who allows himself some leeway here. He burns fixed impurities and establishes a general rule that burned ores enter lead more willingly; although raw ones enter as well, yielding the same value in both cases, but with more difficulty in the latter. Yet, whatever is done more efficiently is also done more correctly. However, his thought that volatile parts might suffer some harm undermines the generality of his first rule. For the value will not be found to be exactly the same if something is lost somewhere. Furthermore, it is no small question whether the entire method should be changed because of the rarely occurring volatile gold or silver? And shouldn't another rule be set down instead, namely the one he has concerning correction through "fixation"? What use is such foresight in a small operation if it cannot be observed in a larger one, where it will be necessary to indicate a lot of metal but actually produce very little, thus misleading one into a false hope of profit when the matter cannot bear the expense. In such cases, perhaps a middle path would be to take one specimen with roasting, a second without, and a third with prior fixation, if indeed something volatile is detected. But enough on these matters.

The same author later judges that some people immediately pour the vein, once melted with lead, from the crucible into a matching mold; some smelt it in lead in a larger vessel in a small furnace, after which they finish the smelting in a "wind furnace" <note>anemia; a furnace without bellows</note>. But he himself judges it more advisable to smelt the vein into lead upon a testing-vessel (or in a crucible), from which, after cooling, the lead-tin mixture is removed and "flashed" <note>cupelled until the brightening point</note> in the cupel of the small furnace. In the preface, he proposes a certain axiom:
> *Golden grains should not be smelted into lead before they are fixed by their reverberatory agent; otherwise, no gold is found:*
This axiom is to be understood regarding "soft" and "tender" gold, which others call "immature," and which is mixed with volatile mercury, or whose sulfur and mercury are not yet fully fixed. It seems to me that the reasoning of **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola, author of *De Re Metallica*</note> is also explained, who orders a rich and mild vein of gold to be tested thus: <margin>Fachs' weights in such business are as follows.</margin> To a hundred-weight (minor) <note>a proportional weight used in assaying</note>—for in both cases, the measuring of the lead with the veins is understood—add an ounce and a half or two ounces of lead according to the larger weight. Mix by fusion in a small earthenware crucible. If it resists or "fights" the cooking, add a little roasted common salt, or a composite alkali salt; they will not produce much dross. Stir it often with an iron wire so that the gold goes into the lead and spits out the dross; once this is done, take out the mass, clean it, and flash it. So he says.

**Fachs** does not join it to the lead immediately, but first prepares it through quenching and flux, although **Agricola** meets the difficulty by adding salt; but it is to be feared lest some harm occurs first. To a skilled artisan, perhaps both methods are satisfactory. For in mineral matters, many effects are achieved in different ways.

### CHAPTER VI.

->*The pure gold vein that is degenerate and difficult to melt.*<-

The common people call it "Roanish Gold" (*Roanisch Gold*) when the vein is rough and hard, such as is found in rivers in a black color and in the shape of hairs (for they are grains); some are hammered out somewhat and are better; some fly apart. They are prepared thus:

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the assaying of gold, specifically focusing on the treatment of "stubborn" ores like marcasite and garnets, and the use of chemical fluxes and quenching agents like urine to reveal the metal within.</meta>

...of sulfur <note>original: "phuris," likely sulfuris</note>, one pound; enough tartar, 3 ounces; common salt, half an ounce; copper, 4 ounces. Let these be melted together over a moderate fire, so that the heat is stronger at the end. Grind the melted mass into a powder and divide it into portions <note>original: "lotones" - a specific measure used in assaying</note>. Cast these in order into ten pounds of molten lead; when one portion has been absorbed, add another until the last. Refine <note>original: "fulmina" - literally "to strike with lightning," referring to the bright flash seen during cupellation</note> the metal, and you will have silver and gold, which you should separate by quartation <note>a method of separating gold from silver by dissolving the silver in nitric acid</note>. Another kind of harsh gold vein is called Rebnicium or Rabnicium; it is black, hard, and full of sulfur and other "wild" <note>unrefined or stony</note> materials.]

<note>The bracket ']' and the preceding text represent the conclusion of a section from the previous page.</note>

**G**rind into grains the size of hemp seeds two hundredweights <note>in assaying, "hundredweights" refers to tiny, proportional weights used to represent larger quantities</note> exquisitely weighed in an earthenware crucible; roast and burn them so that the marcasites <note>a term for various metallic sulfides, often iron pyrite</note> glow with heat. While they are white-hot, extinguish them six or eight times in boy’s urine <note>urine was used historically as a source of ammonia and nitrogen to help break down ores</note> until the vein no longer smokes and becomes "mild" <note>soft and easy to work</note>. Reduce this to a fine powder and divide it into two equal parts; from one of these weighed parts, you will calculate how much was lost during the roasting. Note this loss <note>original: "detrimentum"</note>. Then mix that same part with a flux, as with the previous mild vein, but adding eight pounds of iron filings <note>original: "scobiæ ferreæ"</note> according to the hundredweight scale. Afterward, melt it into lead and refine it just like a mild vein, and you will find the true value in gold and silver.

**G**old-bearing garnets <note>referring here to garnet-rich ores or perhaps dark, red-colored minerals</note> that are pure, "wild," and rich are examined in almost the same way. Roast them in a dish with a lid so that nothing is shaken out or leaps away. Extinguish them with boy's urine, repeating this six or eight times. Once extinguished, grind them exactly and roast them again for a little while. Divide them into two parts (there were two chosen hundredweights) and note the loss on the scale. To one part, add double the amount of alkaline salt <note>potash</note> and eight pounds of iron filings. Place this at the bellows. If it swells up with bubbles in the crucible and appears unmanageable, sprinkle in a little fused salt <note>common salt that has been melted and hardened</note> and blow the fire with the bellows. When the whole thing is melted and the slag <note>original: "scoria"</note> has separated, pour it from the crucible into a heated cone-shaped mold <note>original: "coniformem"</note>; by striking the floor with a hammer, the metal will settle. When it has cooled, turn the cone-shaped crucible over and knock out the material; there will be a gold button <note>original: "regulus"</note> in the cone. Knock this off and refine it with lead in a cupel <note>a small, porous bowl made of bone ash used to separate precious metals from lead</note>. If the flux is too weak and the slag refuses to separate before the bellows, then in addition to the flux and salt, fifteen hundredweights of pure lead must be added, and the work carried out further as with gold marcasite. In this way, you can also examine washed gold scrapings <note>original: "ramenta auri elota" - gold dust or small grains recovered from sand</note>.

**T**he first method is for gold marcasites, which are generally stubborn and hard. However, it is sufficient that they be ground to the size of hemp seeds. Otherwise, during roasting, the smaller parts would exhale <note>vaporize</note> or at least be scattered and could not be entirely collected. **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola, the "father of mineralogy"</note>, since not every pyrite is gold-bearing, orders that the fertile kind be judged by roasting it three times and quenching it as many times in vinegar in which human urine or salt has been dissolved for three days. For if it does not break, nor change color, it contains gold. The judgment is the same if both the raw and the roasted material stain a touchstone <note>original: "coticulam"</note> the same color; or if, when it is washed and the scrapings (washed gold-sand) are cooked between two hollow coals, it melts easily, smells little, and remains beautiful. I have also placed the first part of this judgment in the preceding commentary from **Fachs** <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century assaying expert</note>. When he says the quenching should be repeated until the vein no longer smokes, it must be understood that with marcasites there is sulfur, arsenic, cadmia <note>zinc ore or furnace crust</note>, mercurial poison, copperas <note>original: "chalcanthum"</note>, and similar things, which are also proven by the corrosive waters <note>acids</note> made from them.

**T**he loss <note>detrimentum</note> must be noted so that the calculation remains complete afterward, and you may know how much impurity is present, how much will be lost in the preparation of a larger fire, and how much will remain. Iron is added so that the flux does not consume the vein, which has now been made tender. For it was said above that the flux acts principally on that which resists. Thus, it is turned away from the soft body; and yet while it acts upon it, it melts and purges it in passing. Anyone can see that the smaller "hundredweight" pounds or "assaying" pounds are to be understood here. From this process also comes **Electrum** <note>a natural or artificial alloy of gold and silver</note> consisting of gold and silver, which is separated by "strong water" <note>nitric acid</note>.

**G**arnets are more stubborn than pyrites. Therefore, they are compelled to endure a greater force. Furthermore, they are found to be "spirited" and quite nitrous, or at least mercurial, while they crackle and leap in the fire; so that they cannot be roasted and heated to a glow without a covered crucible. When they are roasted or burned again after quenching and grinding, it is noted that impure and stubborn spirits are mixed within; but they are not burned as sharply as before, lest any gold be lost now that it has been reduced to a smooth state. In place of the flux mentioned above, alkaline salt <note>potash</note> is used here, which he taught how to make from wood ash, quicklime, wormwood ash, salt of urine, tartar, and saltpeter; this composition is far stronger than that flux and is required because of the stubbornness of the grains, which are difficult to tame. Nevertheless, even so, the wildness is not tamed in all cases. Therefore, "fused salt" (common salt placed in a crucible and melted into a mass in a sharp reverberatory furnace, the kind of particles found in stone vessels where salt was sprinkled during burning) must be sprinkled into the blistering and boiling material. This cuts through the tough skin <note>surface tension of the molten slag</note> and dissolves and scatters the spirits. There is no need for lead to be added here, unless the salt is found to be too weak to cook the material. Thus, it is shown by such work that lead is not necessarily required everywhere, just as the chemical mastery of separation and cementation <note>a refining process using heat and salts</note> indicates. In truth, this operation is a chemical cementation; if it does not succeed correctly, the help of lead must be implored, and it must be taken in greater quantity the more persistent the material is. The "cone-shaped crucible" is the casting cone mentioned above. The edge or the "pavement" <note>the metal button at the bottom</note> is struck. The heavy metal will settle, just as when gold is purified by antimony. That button must nevertheless be refined in a cupel made of ash in a furnace under a tile <note>muffle furnace</note>, with lead added, so that the remaining impurity is removed and the gold is nonetheless defended from the violence of the fire. What is added regarding gold scrapings or washed sand should be understood not strictly as the immediately preceding method, but regarding the entire testing of gold according to the condition of each vein. If the sand is mild, it will mimic a mild vein; if not, a harsh one.

# CHAPTER VII.

## Gold vein dispersed through other minerals.

**L**et sixteen hundredweights of gold marcasite that is not pure, but dispersed through other minerals, be roasted, and once glowing, let them be extinguished in urine, dried, and ground. Once ground, let them be passed through a trough <note>original: "alueolum" - a washing cradle or sluice</note> and washed until they become metallic sand. Weigh this dried sand and note what was lost. Then roast it again and grind it so that the vein becomes thoroughly mild and can be melted by the flux.
