->Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book V.<-

- Take one hundredweight <note>In assaying, a "hundredweight" (centupondium) refers to a small, proportional weight used to represent a larger quantity for testing purposes.</note> of the material prepared in this way, and cook it thoroughly with flux and iron dross <note>original: "scabe ferri," the scales or oxidation found on iron</note> just as you would pure marcasite <note>a term used then for various metallic sulfides like pyrite</note>. In the same manner, process golden garnets if they are poor in gold: specifically, prepare sixteen hundredweights through the washing-trough and burn them, as has been said.

Thus far we have set down the instructions of Fachs <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century German master of the mint and author of a famous book on assaying</note>. Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola, the "father of mineralogy" and author of *De Re Metallica*</note> more briefly encompasses every stubborn gold vein and sets down a twofold method for testing it. The first is as follows: Roast the stubborn gold vein and quench it in boy’s urine in which salt has been dissolved; repeat this several times. Grind and wash it. To the dried material, add a triple amount of flux and a sixfold amount of lead. Cook it over a slow fire in a triangular crucible, increasing the heat gradually until the vein flows like water. If it resists and does not yet flow, add a little flux and an equal portion of golden litharge <note>lead oxide</note>. Stir it with a red-hot iron wire until the whole has melted. Having removed the crucible from the fire, finally strike off the cooled mass <note>the "button" of metal</note>, clean it, cook it in a testing-dish, and further refine it in a cupel <note>original: "fulmina in capella" — to "refine by lightning," referring to the bright flash seen when the gold is purified during cupellation</note>. The second method is: Cook a hundredweight of stubborn gold vein with a "greater weight" drachm of ox-gall <note>original: "felle vitti," likely meaning cattle gall, used as a surfactant</note> in a triangular crucible. If it resists, add half a drachm of burnt tartar; if it is still refractory, add a half-drachm of vinegar dregs or "dead head" <note>caput mortuum, the residue left after distilling aqua fortis/nitric acid</note>. A small mass will shine out in the crucible, which you should re-cook in a clay dish and refine the grain. These are the words of Agricola, although some things may seem rather obscure. Washing will hardly have a place in a pure vein. Neither is the end-point of the roasting indicated, nor is the loss of weight ordered to be noted; the addition of iron is also omitted. Since he likewise changes the flux so many times, he seems to provide nothing certain regarding the custom of such veins, especially since there can easily be a loss of metal, particularly with the addition of the "dead head," which will not spare the softened vein, especially if the gold is tender and soft. Chemists prefer to make the metal button in a matching copper crucible, just as Fachs instructs, because by striking it, it ought to settle into a point. Because of these and other matters of no small importance, the operation of Fachs seems clearer and more exact. Erker <note>Lazarus Erker, another major 16th-century authority on mining and assaying</note> does not approve of urines, roastings, and the like for gold, but is content with one general way, and for mild veins he uses 15 hundredweights of lead to 1 of the vein. If they are harsh, he adds one hundredweight of "lead-wine" <note>likely a specific flux or lead-based additive</note> besides.

### CHAPTER VIII.
## Examination of the gold vein by mercury.

**A** vein, or scrapings, or washed sand, is moistened with water and heated at the fire until it gives off a vapor. Then mix it with double the amount of mercury in a deep wooden basin (or wooden mortar) and work it in with a wooden pestle; grind it for two hours, having added a little urine, until the mixture thickens like a pulp and neither the mercury nor the scrapings can be distinguished. Afterward, wash it clean by pouring on lukewarm water. Then pour on cold water as well, and the mercury, having absorbed the gold, will settle. Separate the mercury by squeezing it through a piece of soft leather or a silk cloth bound with waxed thread. Scatter the remaining mercury <note>gloss: "n" — likely indicating the mercury is driven off as vapor</note> in a dish over hot coals. — Agricola.

This is the second method for testing a gold vein, but it is not suitable except for golden sand collected from "gold-washing" <note>original: "chrysophysiis"</note> in which flakes of gold appear. The methods vary. Some do not wash the mixture with lukewarm water, but drench it with a sharp lye with vinegar added, and allow it to rest in a jar for 24 hours in a warm place: they pour off the liquids with the filth and separate the quicksilver <note>mercury</note> through leather. Others drive the residue of it out "by descent" <note>a form of distillation where the vapor travels downward</note>, so that it is carried from an upper perforated jar into a lower one buried in the earth containing human urine, and this continues until the jar turns red, by which sign they recognize the completion of the work. If the cooled gold contains copper, they refine it by adding lead; if it contains silver, they separate it with aqua fortis <note>nitric acid</note>. <gloss>Note that if washed sand is soaked in "goldsmiths' water" or another sharp external liquid so that the outer coating is removed, it yields far more to the mercury than in the common way. Therefore some pour sharp liquor on the sand and, having added quicksilver, they cook it and stir it diligently with a wooden spatula, whence the gold enters into the mercury.</gloss> Others remove the mercury by subliming it into a "blind" alembic <note>a distillation lid without an outlet tube</note> whose top is perforated so it can be closed once the moist spirits have been emitted. Agricola thinks more mercury is lost here, and less there. Fachs rejects this whole method because the operation by fire is more certain. For mercury cannot collect gold from sand as purely or as solidly as flux and lead can. He also thinks something is lost in the separation through leather and fire. If you wish to remove it by evaporation, besides the troublesome odors and vapors, a loss of gold will occur. For mercury, finding nothing with the gold to consume, corrodes the gold and turns it into ashes. <margin>Gold becomes volatile through mercury.</margin> Fachs does not state this absurdly. I know by a certain experiment that not only are the thin parts of gold corroded and burnt by mercury, but they also pass with it through the pores of the leather and are lifted away. For when I once kept an amalgam in the fire, with the opening obstructed by a fairly thick layer of clay, the quicksilver escaped nonetheless, and took the gold with it, so that the largest part clung near the exit, and part even had to be recovered from the clay. Likewise, since mercury does not admit foreign bodies, whatever gold is within the earthy dust (which can be joined to very thin atoms, just as sulfur and mercury are in cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide</note>), that gold will not be taken up. Not to mention that by external conditions it can happen that the "familiarity" <note>chemical affinity</note> in the meeting does not appear, and the quicksilver stays away from the gold as if from a stranger. Therefore, this judgment is deceptive and does not satisfy the constancy of the art. Furthermore, there are other ways of collecting gold from a vein, such as by aqua regia <note>literally "royal water," a mixture of acids that dissolves gold</note>, etc., but they are as unskillful as they are uncertain. If a "golden magnet" <note>a hypothetical alchemical substance or device</note> were at hand, this separation would also have a place.

Furthermore, what has been said about testing the gold vein can be illustrated by the methods of smelting, of which two are in use. For when there is a small quantity of gold vein, or washed gold sand, the metal is drawn out in small vessels outside the smelting furnace; when there is a larger quantity, such as when pyrite contains gold, silver, copper, lead, etc. together and is abundant, large fires in smelting furnaces must be used. In the former method, some likewise call upon quicksilver and mix the gold scrapings into it, washing the amalgams with lukewarm waters and separating them. Others use aqua fortis, with which they segregate the mercury, and soak the remaining gold in water of calcined tartar, and cook it in a crucible with a flux consisting of borax <note>original: "chrysocolla"</note>, saltpeter <note>original: "halinitro"</note>, and salt, or they even subject it to quartation. But as I warned above, this method of separation is not exact enough, and can be used only when certain things are deliberately negle—

# Part 2 of the Examination of the Assay Art

...are neglected, even though this should by no means happen with such a noble metal. Why should such a laborious method be undertaken when the fire-based method is both faster and less expensive? If the ore is soft <term>soft ore|Latin: *vena mitis*. An ore that yields its metal easily through heat without requiring intense roasting or complex chemical additives</term>, it is melted in a ceramic crucible with added flux to form a metal button <term>regulus|A small "button" of concentrated metal found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</term>, which is afterwards refined <note>original: *fulminatur*. This refers to "fulmination" or cupellation, where the metal is heated until it "flashes," signaling it has reached purity.</note>, or "quarted" <term>quartatio|A process where gold is alloyed with three parts silver so that nitric acid can later dissolve the silver and leave pure gold behind</term> with silver, from which it is separated using "strong water" <note>nitric acid</note>. 

Agricola sets out several methods. One takes one pound each of ground gold ore, sulfur, and salt; a third of a pound of copper, and a quarter pound of tartar. These mixed in a crucible are cooked over a slow fire for three hours. After the fire is increased, they are melted and cast into molten silver, from which the gold is recovered. This is the same as is otherwise done in "quarting" (it is necessary for us to use these terms due to the custom of the discipline, which, having spurned the elegancies of Cicero <note>The author is apologizing for using technical "Jargon" rather than classical literary Latin.</note>, is better illustrated by its own names). Thus the washed gold dust <note>original: *fabulum aureum elutum*</note> is prepared. 

Another method melts the same ore with a half part of antimony <term>stibium|Antimony, used in this period to purify gold by reacting with and removing base metals like copper</term> and a small amount of copper. Lead is added to the molten mixture; when the scent expires or it smokes, iron filings are added to protect the ore. The mass is refined. The ratio of weights is: one pound of ore, half a pound of antimony, half an ounce of copper, two ounces of lead, and a little iron scale or filings. But as I warned in the assaying section, the nature of the ore and the flux must be carefully considered. 

If, however, it is silver, or a softer gold—such as is usually washed from sand—neither sulfur nor antimony will be useful. What madness is it to add those things to washed and purified ore which, if nature had added them, you would remove with the greatest effort and expense? Therefore, for a soft ore abundant in silver, I would use neither. Agricola indicates the same for smelting golden pyrite with double the antimony. But the aforementioned caution and the legitimate preparation indicated by the assay must not be neglected. 

Another method goes like this: one part golden pyrite, six parts copper, one part sulfur, and a half part salt. In a glazed pot armored with lute <note>a protective coating of clay and sand</note>, "burning water" <note>aqua ardens: high-proof distilled alcohol or spirits</note> distilled from wine dregs is poured over the mixture. They are macerated for six days in a warm place until the "living spirit" is soaked up; once done, they are cooked for three hours over a gentle fire. With lead added and the fire increased, they are melted and the mass refined. Burning water is added here so the mixture is disposed to catch flame within and melt easily—though sulfur also achieves this. If there is copper in the pyrite, the amount added must be decreased. Sulfur will have no place if copper, silver, and lead are present together, or if the gold is "tender" <note>pure or easily lost in the dross</note>. Clearly, the smelting method should be taken from the assay of Fachs <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century German mint master and author of a famous handbook on assaying.</note>.

The following methods, also from Agricola, are better, including this one: one pound of washed gold sand (whether from pyrite or river gravel, etc.), half a pound each of common salt and tartar, a third of a pound of glass gall <term>glass gall|Also called "sandiver," this is the salty scum that forms on the surface of molten glass; it was used as a powerful flux</term> (which however is more aggressive in tender ore than it should be), a sixth of a pound of gold or silver slag, and two drachms of copper. In a dark furnace <note>likely a small, enclosed assay furnace</note> previously heated, let them be melted gradually in a luted crucible, which takes 4 or 5 hours. Once the mixture is cooled and ground with a pound of litharge <note>lead oxide</note>, let it be cooked in another crucible. The purified mass should be refined. (It would be faster to add lead or litharge in the first crucible and pour the material into a conical mold <note>original: *catinum coniformem*</note> heated and smeared with tallow to form a metal button, which would later be smelted to purity by refining. See the rest in Agricola, including the method for mixing silver and copper, etc.; it is consistent that Agricola brought forward many methods so a skilled craftsman could choose according to the nature of the ore, and sometimes as a shortcut for quarting. But as I said before, I would advise looking back to the assay of Fachs.)

In a large furnace, a large amount of ore is not ground to powder but is smelted with litharge, molybdena <note>likely lead glance or a similar lead mineral</note>, and iron scale into "tin-like cakes," which are refined in the manner of silver-bearing tin. Smelting can be done in an "openable" furnace or even a "gaping" one—that is, one whose opening <note>original: *oculus*, or "eye"</note> is alternately closed and opened, or one that is always open—especially those of the first and second type in Agricola. Golden pyrite, or gold-bearing calamine <note>cadmia</note>, unless something prevents it, is first smelted into stone (that is, stone cakes) if it is a constant, solid, and mature metal. These are afterwards mastered by frequent roasting and made soft. Once this is done, the metal is smelted into lead in an open furnace, just like silver. The mixture is refined; if copper is joined with it, it is lost, but the gold and silver remain. If however the amount of copper is greater, a separation is established, as is usually done with mixed copper and silver through lead. Before the stone cakes are made, two parts of this pyrite are mixed with one part of raw ore and melted through the raw furnace, which is how stones are otherwise usually made.

<margin>Concerning the raw layer <note>German: *Über die rohe Schicht*. This refers to the initial "matte" or layer of sulfide produced in the first smelting.</note></margin>

If stubborn and "greedy" minerals <note>minerals that tend to absorb or "eat" the precious metal, causing loss</note> (either pyrites or others) cling to the gold ore, they recommend mixing six parts ore, four parts ironstone, two parts slaked lime, half a part of stone from copper-bearing pyrite, and one and a half parts slag. One trough of copper-bearing stone (smelted from copper pyrite by fire) is sent into the furnace first; the mixture is ordered to be sent in under it, and thus the smelting is performed. When the fore-hearth is filled, the slag is drawn off, then the stone, and finally the metallic mass. The stone is roasted and re-melted with lead. Its "tin" <note>an intermediate alloy</note> is refined. The metallic masses are either re-melted with an equal amount of lead and refined and separated, or if they are less rich, they are enriched by adding eighteen pounds of the mixture to forty-eight pounds of raw ore, three pounds of ironstone, and three-quarters of a pound of pyrite cakes. Once melted in the furnace and fallen into the crucible and cleaned of excrement <note>dross or slag</note>, it is sent to the refining hearth. One must understand here that the ore has been freed from empty rocks and other things separable by washing, roasting, etc., and if by chance it was found to be volatile in a smaller fire, it has been "confirmed" <note>stabilized or fixed</note> with iron-water, alum-waters, vitriol-waters <note>original: *chalcanthosis*</note>, etc. But enough on gold ore.

# Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book V.

Place the small mass into a thoroughly heated ash crucible <note>original: *catillum cinereum*. A cupel made of bone ash used to separate precious metals from lead.</note>, and having added coals to the furnace workstation, cook it with the ash-hole <note>original: *cineritio*. The aperture or ash-chamber of the furnace used to regulate airflow.</note> closed until the material begins to smoke. Then, with the ash-hole closed and one coal removed from the furnace door, allow it to "flash" <note>original: *fulminari*. This is the moment of cupellation where the silver suddenly glows brightly as the last of the lead oxide is absorbed, signaling purity.</note> with sufficient heat. The grain will shine with the bright color of the purest silver. Check its weight, subtracting the weight of the grain that was in the added lead, provided you used lead that already contained silver.

To this class also belongs the assay of stone or other metal veins containing gold that have been smelted, concerning which it is instructed as follows: take a half-centupondium <term>centupondium|A "hundred-weight" unit used in assaying to represent a large quantity of ore with a small, proportional laboratory sample</term> of ore rich in silver, ground very finely upon a clean stone, and mix it well with five times as much granulated lead. Cook this with a sufficiently strong fire in a furnace roasting-dish <note>original: *testa*</note>, so that the silver is gradually absorbed. This done, add eleven half-centupondia of the same pure lead, and increase the fire sharply so they are thoroughly mixed. If the melting is delayed, stir it with a clean, bright, red-hot iron wire, and thus force them together so they join into a solid mass. Pour out the large mass, or let it cool, and refine it <note>original: *fulmina*</note> according to the art. If there was any silver grain in those eleven half-centupondia of lead—which must be determined beforehand by the flame—subtract it from the grain produced by the ore.

If the smelted ore or stone is "poor"—for instance, if there is scarcely a drachm in a hundred-weight—weigh out four half-centupondia individually, and examine each separately as described. Weigh the four grains melted from them together, and after subtracting the lead's grain, you will find the value of two hundred-weights.

### CHAPTER X.

### Refractory silver ore and those difficult to melt, with their relatives.

Let one hundred-weight of finely crushed refractory silver ore be mixed with nine <gloss>Fourteen, according to Erker</gloss> hundred-weights of granulated lead of known value. Place it in a roasting-dish in the furnace; move the coals to the furnace door with the ash-hole open until the material begins to cook and smoke. Then close the ash-hole, remove one coal from the furnace door, and the silver is cooked into the lead. When it begins to spit out dross <note>original: *scoriae*</note>, reopen the ash-hole and put two coals back at the furnace door so the work reheats and is cleanly smelted. Refine the cleaned lead mass <note>original: *stanneam massam*. Literally "tin-like mass," referring here to the lead-silver alloy.</note> as is customary.

Certain ores take a long time to be absorbed by the lead and are merely scorched, floating like ash without being soaked up. For these, if you know their stubbornness from the start, mix in a suitable quantity (a small amount) of flux prepared for intractable ores; or if their "wickedness" was hidden until seen, add a quarter-measure of the same flux into the roasting-dish, increase the fire again, and it will be cooked and yield its dross.

If the ore is partly absorbed and partly gathered into a bubble among the dross, in which ore and dross are one, remove that bubble with a hook, grind it finely, and mix it with a quarter-measure of flux, taking care that nothing is lost. Put it back in the dish with the rest, and it will work its way purely into the lead.

If the ore appears to be "absorbed" <note>original: *incolla*</note> by sight, but when stirred with the hook it sticks to the dish and cannot be pulled away, add a little "dead head" <note>original: *capitis mortui*. The solid residue left after distillation.</note> of nitric acid ground finely, and place it in the dish; the ore will settle if you move it with the hook.

If the ore is indeed absorbed by the lead, but its metal fails during refining and is changed into dross so that no silver grain appears anywhere: remove it from the ash-chamber, shake off the dross, and cook it again in a roasting-dish; having done this, refine it again in an ash-crucible, and a pure grain will come out. Stubborn ores of this kind, when absorbed into lead, are not poured out but cooled inside the furnace in the dish; strike the floor near it lightly with a hammer, and it is forced together and densified; otherwise, it retains bubbles. Afterward, pull it from the dish and strip away the dross.

Silver in dross, embers, ashes, furnace sweepings, etc., is recovered by whichever of the said methods seems to fit. In cases where the ore is silver but contains more of another metal, it is smelted according to the custom of the predominant metal and examined in that later. Indeed, since much sulfur and arsenic or "realgar" <note>arsenic sulfide</note> is joined with these, you may flee to the artifice of maceration and washing in an alkaline lye, which is discussed in Chemistry.

<margin>
Consult Erker pages 3 & 4 in folio, Kentmann, Fabricius, Meier, and many others.
</margin>
The variety of minerals and ores that are of silver can be known by anyone even moderately practiced in metallic affairs. Some are very rich and "soft," such as raw leaden silver <note>native silver</note> which is ductile, in a hundred-weight of which there are often 170 marks of pure silver; raw red silver like a ruby <note>pyrargyrite</note>, often containing 150 marks of pure; raw pure white silver yielding 140 marks; raw horn silver <note>chlorargyrite</note>, and many others. Some are poor; some are found pure, but more are mixed with rocks, flints, cobalt, antimony, grey lead, galena, mud, and similar things, concerning which the books of the miners should be consulted. Nor has the genius of our people been so studiously occupied in almost any other kind of metal. Therefore, various questions and opinions regarding the assay and cooking of this metal are circulated, and one master is always more haughty than another, and one exercises his sharp-witted arguments against the others. Fachsius asks <gloss>Erker has the same question in the examination of copper for silver.</gloss> how it happens that when an ore is assayed—having first checked the weight of the roasting-dish, the cupel, the lead, and the ore—after the smelting is finished and the dishes, cupels, dross, and metal are weighed again, these latter are found to be heavier than the former, even though much of the lead and other impurities have been consumed by the fire.

<margin>
Question concerning the weight of the crucibles.
</margin>
He judged this question insoluble, and thus thinks he has thrown an invincible bone to the "know-it-alls" to stop their mouths and call their arrogance back to modesty. I, for my part, claim no singular knowledge of minerals, whose face appears so varied every day that no experience or knowledge can be enough; yet it seems the question is not so much inexplicable in itself as it is due to obscurity from omitted circumstances; nor is there time now to experiment. I judge that attention must be paid to the vessels: whether they are weighed immediately from the fire or when already sufficiently cooled. It is well known that it can happen just as with quicklime <note>original: *calce viva*</note>, which is light fresh from the furnace, but when held longer in the air it drinks in <term>moisture</term> and becomes heavier than itself—and even more so than before, if other things correspond—because it hungrily seeks it out and coagulates the moisture within itself.

<margin>
Pliny Book 34, Chapter 7, regarding Armenian Salt.
</margin>
Thus it is observed in subterranean caves that masses of salt are light, but where they have touched the air, they become twice or thrice as heavy. The same can happen to those cupels and roasting-dishes. Another reason lies in the density of compacted dishes, and in <unclear>instula</unclear>. By the spirits and <unclear>serimibus</unclear> carried off through smoke, the remaining parts become heavier; <term>especially</term> the ash crucible, after it drinks in the lead-dross <note>original: *plumbagine*. Here referring to litharge or lead oxide absorbed by the cupel.</note>, becomes denser and heavier, not only by reason of what is absorbed...

## On the Testing of the Proving Art, Part 2.
->KK 3<-

<margin>Question concerning cadmia.</margin>
...of the absorbed part, but also of the excluded air, which previously moderated the weight, just as a difference in weight is seen in porous woods and leaves. However, the question concerning cadmia <note>original: *cadmia*. In this context, it refers to zinc-bearing ores or calamine found in furnace chimneys.</note> and yellow marcasite <note>original: *marcasita*. Typically iron pyrites, often mistaken for or containing trace precious metals.</note> is more worthy of note. He says that pure, degenerate cadmia yields scarcely more than half an ounce of silver in a common assay, and it is exceedingly "greedy" <note>meaning volatile or prone to being lost to the fumes</note> in the fire. But since it is dissolved by *aqua forti* <note>nitric acid</note> and enters into it just like silver, he estimates that more profit lies beneath, and one must consider how it may be smelted out.

Nor are other signs of a silver-like nature lacking. For since there is impure arsenic and unclean sulfur present—and arsenic indeed tints copper with a silver color, while sulfur infects silver with a leaden hue so that it resembles crude leaden silver and mirrors the appearance of freshly fractured cadmia—he judges it consistent that silver is present more abundantly. But this latter reasoning is of no importance. For even if you join sulfur and impure arsenic, no silver is created; and these signs occur even in those substances in which it is certain that not even a speck of silver exists, such as in magnetite and others. The former reasoning also wavers. Even quicksilver <note>original: *hydrargyrus*</note> enters cadmia, and it has been detected elsewhere that silver-bearing cadmia was full of quicksilver. Therefore, if it holds any evidence, it hints at quicksilver, which can indeed be the "mother of silver" and is primarily suited for the artifice of the "silver stone" <note>an alchemical reference to a substance capable of transmuting metals into silver</note>; but it does not follow that one should expect a greater abundance of finished silver, unless it has been proven that the same thing happens with silver as with the Rebnicia gold vein <note>likely a reference to a specific mine in Rebnitz or a similar Germanic mining region</note>, which is soft and still smeared with mercury. In that case, a "fixing water" <note>a chemical solution used to stabilize volatile elements</note> would be excellently suited for both the tender and soft silver itself, and for the sulfur, quicksilver, and arsenic—as much as the nature of these things allows—lest they be so "thievish" <note>volatile</note> in the fire afterward. The Chemists could perhaps assist us by means of a "cement" <note>a dry chemical mixture used in a furnace</note> with filings of perfected silver, by which that which is volatile within is fixed. Regarding yellow marcasite, he says it carries with it a greedy and volatile sulfur, from which tender gold is dissipated; however, it also indicates something of hidden riches, since a third part of it rejects *aqua forti* and is not dissolved, but afterward is also smelted exactly with lead, and thus from a centupondium <term>centupondium|A "hundred-weight" unit used in assaying to represent a large quantity of ore with a small, proportional laboratory sample</term> there emerges half an ounce of silver, beyond what can otherwise be elicited by a common assay. He rightly attributes the cause of the more abundant metal to the "strong water" <note>nitric acid</note>, which, on account of the alum and vitriol, is simultaneously a fixing agent. And the deliberation is clear, if only the advice were commonly observed: but there would be too much expense in *aqua forti*. Therefore, a lye should be made from vitriol, alum, and iron ore, or copper pyrites, alum-vein, and iron rust. The ore, soaked in this, would acquire constancy, and no loss would be allowed. For that water or lye can be recovered: and it is established by certain experience that such a lye attains almost the power of *aqua forti*.

But here one must also consider a cement with a fixed body. Just as with orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide</note>, scarlet sand, sandarac, etc., it is done through gold, which are secrets of the Chemists, not to be revealed rashly to anyone. Pliny writes that the vein of gold and silver was also accustomed to be scrutinized on a touchstone with a method that did not fail, and by the same means, the amount of copper present was detected by a filing taken with a file. Even now, this can be tested in ores that have been washed and separated from stony foreign matter, provided a "morsel" <note>a small test sample</note> of suitable coloring is applied.

Furthermore, in examining silver veins, slag, stone, and similar things, certain unique precautions are repeated; specifically regarding stone, <term>Fachsius</term> warns that it should be ground on a well-wiped marble slab, lest any other or similar metal adhere to it, which would cause the assay of the grain to fail, as well as the <term>argyroplysia</term>. Next, he advises that granulated lead be taken from a covered box, lest any filing should leap in during the grinding or breaking. He also suggests that a large weight not be weighed on the assay balance, but rather a half-centupondium of the most finely ground stone, so that it may be smelted into the lead more quickly in the fire. He adds that in the small furnace, while the vein is being smelted into the lead, the fire cannot be too great—though I doubt this, unless it is understood to mean the breadth of the heat within the furnace workstation, such that when the vein is smelted into the lead, it can bear even higher degrees of heat. Furthermore, he orders that the iron wire with which we stir and gather the material in the crucible be scraped with a file after a rich vein has been worked with it, lest any adhering filing deceive the master's judgment.

Since there are also innumerable distinctions of veins and inexplicable varieties in silver, he indicates that one who is skilled in governing the fire and the flow, and who knows how to add the additives with the required skill, can easily and successfully examine even an unknown vein—something that cannot be done without observing such industry. The reader should be warned that an error seems to have been committed in the signs in the author’s German text: while writing on the assay of a free-flowing silver vein, it is written that during the "flash" <note>cupellation</note>, coals ought to be placed at the little door of the workstation and the orifice of the ash-chamber closed until it begins to boil; when this sign is seen, it should be opened and the coal removed from the door of the small oven. However, the opposite is prescribed elsewhere, and reason shows that in the beginning, when the cupel <note>original: *copella*</note> is already ignited and glowing, the heat must be strengthened until it cooks, since if the heat is lowered, this does not happen; but afterward, the cooking must be finished with a moderated fire, as is proper. Thus, the coals must first be increased and more air let in; but afterward, as the coals are diminished, so too is the wind.

<term>Agricola</term> is very concise in the assay of silver. Into a heated assay centupondium of a rich and "mild" <note>easily worked</note> vein, he puts an ounce of lead melted in a small ash-crucible and procures the "flash." For a poor or mediocre vein, he similarly smelts the same weight with an ounce of lead in a roasting-dish. If it does not liquefy easily, he adds a little flux (consisting of white spar and gold litharge <note>original: *lithargyro auri*. Lead oxide with a yellowish tint.</note>). If it still does not flow, he adds a little more until it flows and exudes slag; to make this happen faster, sprinkled powder is worked in with an iron wire. Once the roasting-dish is removed, he casts the mass into a hole or cavity in a fired brick. When it has cooled, he cleans it of slag and "flashes" it in a cupel.

<margin>Method for the larger work.</margin>
In the larger fire or "work" <note>industrial scale smelting as opposed to laboratory assaying</note>, the duties of the smelter are distinct from those of the cupeller. The finest vein is not committed to the smelting furnace, but is either immersed in a crucible with the slag removed from the rest of the material, or into tin cakes liquefied in the ash-furnace. A vein mixed with rocks and impure with stone, slag, and fluxes is smelted in a "closed-eye" furnace <note>a furnace where the tap-hole is kept plugged to allow metals to settle</note>, unless it is too poor and refractory. ...contracted into balls and enclosed in a pot with impurities, it is smelted; or, it is worked in a small furnace in a closed crucible with additives: three parts litharge <note>original: *lithargyri*; lead oxide used as a flux</note> and molybdenum <note>original: *molybdænæ*; likely referring to lead-glance or a similar lead-like mineral rather than the modern element</note>, half a part of lead-stone <note>original: *lapis plumbarius*; likely galena or lead ore</note>, and a small amount of salt and iron scale; the resulting mass is then cupelled <note>original: *fulminatur*; the final refining of silver by fire</note>. If the bismuth <note>original: *plumbum cinereum*</note>, antimony, molybdenum, lead-stone, slag, fragments of crucibles, realgar <note>arsenic sulfide</note> or soot, and furnace sweepings contain any silver, they are ground and washed in great quantity and smelted with other ores. 

If, however, there is a great abundance of pyrite, one takes three parts of roasted pyrite and one part raw; the washed scrapings and mixed slag are smelted in a raw state in an open furnace, and they are made into "cakes" <note>original: *panes*; ingots or circular masses of metal</note>, which are burned after being quenched in water. Four times the amount of the burned material is mixed again with one part of raw pyrite and smelted into cakes in the same furnace. If these are rich in copper, they are burned and re-smelted into copper; if they contain little copper, the burned cakes are smelted with fluid slag into leaden "tin" <note>original: *stannum*; here referring to a lead-silver-copper alloy produced during smelting</note>, with lead already placed in the receiving pot before the furnace. The floating pyrite is drawn off to be used for smelting copper. Silver-bearing calamine <note>original: *cadmia*</note> is roasted, mixed with raw pyrite and slag, and smelted into cakes, which are then roasted and re-smelted into lead in a closed furnace. The "tin" made from this is then cupelled. 

Flints, fluorspars, clay, and earth containing little silver are sprinkled onto raw pyrite or calamine and worked together, provided they are raw; but if they are roasted, they are added to the burned parts of the pyrite. Some, however, even in great quantity, smelt poor ores separately using a curved furnace <note>original: *curuam fornacem*; likely a blast furnace or one with a specific draft design</note>, where the expenses are lower. In all these matters, just as in the testing process, one must note the "stubbornness" <note>refractoriness</note>, harshness, volatility or immaturity, "greedy" minerals <note>those that consume other metals in the fire</note>, tenacity, and similar traits; therefore, the work must be advanced through additives so that the owners suffer no loss. 

Pure silver adhering to stones, or placed and mixed with them, could also be separated by the use of mercury <note>amalgamation</note>, and even drawn out from the ores by *aqua fortis* <note>nitric acid</note>, especially when it is in small quantities and tender, not yet hardened by the process of time; but the craftsmen prefer their fires. Chemists employ their cements and separations through pastes and fluxes in a crucible to produce a "regulus" <note>a small metallic button or ingot found at the bottom of the crucible</note>. 

However, I cannot pass over here without mentioning the "stone" <note>German: *Stein*; a metallurgical matte</note> or copper-bearing pyrite from Fachs <note>Modestin Fachs, a famous 16th-century assayer</note>, because he established two ways of testing the stone under different titles. One is general, regarding how all kinds of prepared minerals or ores and stones (by which we understand the German *Stein*, the cakes or ingots of pyrite smelted through a raw furnace) can be examined for silver, a method I proposed above. The other is a special method, regarding how copper-bearing stone is to be tested to find the value of the silver. Since this seems unique to me, it must not be omitted. It goes as follows:

If you wish to examine the (copper-bearing) stone [<margin>Copper-bearing stone; called *Ertz*, *Stein*, or *Schlackstein* by the Germans. It is made from marcasite or copper-pyrite (*aus kieß*), or it comes from the furnace in which a silver ore was smelted to which it had been added. It emerges in the third order. For in the crucible there is slag, calamine (*speiss*), stone, and lead with silver. Each is separated.</margin>]—whether it be raw or washed, removed from the furnace, or taken from the fore-hearth pot—break a small piece from each cake and mix them all together after grinding. Weigh out one hundred-weight <note>original: *centupondium*; the standard assay unit of weight</note> and add fifteen hundred-weights of granulated lead, mixing them well. In a small furnace with an open cupel <note>original: *cineritio*; a bed of bone-ash used for refining</note>, and with two coals placed at the tile-opening, cook it until the stone begins to boil and rise. Then close the cupel and remove the coal from the tile-opening; the stone is cooked over the lead and gives off its dross. If you notice that it is cooling too much, put the coal back at the tile so it reheats to finish the cooking. Move and turn it once or twice with a hook, as you see the slag depart cleanly or unclearly, so that it may be more quickly absorbed by the lead. Remove it from the furnace and let it cool in the vessel, just as you did with the refractory and harsh ores. Cupel it at a somewhat cooler temperature because of the copper. 

Thus says Fachs. He ordered so much lead to be added in no other ore; it is judged that this was done here because of the heat of the adjacent copper, so that the silver may be more protected, and so there is sufficient space for the consumption and separation of the copper. For copper is everywhere judged to be hotter in the work than other metals; and for this reason, it is also ordered here that the "tin" <note>the lead-silver-copper alloy</note> be cupelled more coldly. Otherwise, the silver would suffer some damage. It appears easy to see that this work is directed toward all pours, or the whole heap of stones. Yet what applies to the whole cannot be foreign to the part in homogeneous materials, except as pertains to the final report. Perhaps he judged that method to be more exact and suitable not only for copper stones, but also for others, since this one is adapted only to copper-bearing ones. 

It must also be observed in copper ores that before they are examined, they should be melted into a "stone." Fachs commands this to be done without roasting. For if they are roasted, he relates that the "stone" is scarcely found. Therefore, he mixes a hundred-weight of raw ore with half an ounce of flux made from calcined tartar and saltpeter, and they melt them in a closed crucible. Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola, author of *De Re Metallica*</note> also gives instructions on testing copper ore for silver. He roasts, grinds, and washes it; to the washed ore he adds a little gold-litharge. He cooks it under a tile <note>in a muffle furnace</note> in a vessel for half an hour. He knocks off the slag from the removed mass. He grinds the grain, and to one hundred-weight of it, he adds an ounce and a half of granulated lead. He smelts it into lead with a little compound flux added. Finally, he cupels the purified "tin."

# CHAPTER XI.
## On the examination of copper ore.

This is accomplished without lead, using fluxes or their own cements in a crucible, where after melting, a metallic button <note>original: *regulus*</note> appears in the cone, from which judgment must be made.

<margin>Rich and pure ore.</margin>
*The method of operation for rich ore according to Fachs is this: Mix a hundred-weight of finely ground ore with a double amount of flux made from litharge and flint. When placed in the crucible, put in a little salt, to the depth of a thumb's breadth. Cover it with its lid and heat it gradually in a draft furnace <note>original: *fornace anemia*</note> until the flux begins to crackle. Then work the bellows as strongly as possible for about an eighth of an hour, and if you fear the heat is too great, you may inspect the work by removing the lid. When the slag appears rising from the crucible, remove it and place it on the floor; strike the area nearby with a hammer so that the button settles. Having broken the crucible, weigh the removed button on the scale and judge its quality by sight.*

# On the Assay of the Art of Testing, Part 2.
## KK 4

A harsh and rebellious ore (*pure as pyrite, etc.*) must be crushed to the size of hemp seed. Two hundred-weights <note>original: *centupondia*; a standard unit of weight in assaying, representing a miniature hundred-weight</note> of it are roasted in a small furnace, but *without violence* <note>meaning without excessive heat</note>, lest it flow together and melt. Repeat this four times. Grind the roasted material more finely and roast it again four times. Finally, crush it to the finest powder and roast it once more until all its "wildness" is tamed, no stench or foul smoke exhales from it, and the color is a beautiful liver-red: indeed, it should have no roughness when being washed. When these signs appear, roast it one more time so that it more readily joins with the flux and is processed by it. Divide it into two parts. Discover how much weight was lost in the roasting: note the decrease, and from this, gather the method for establishing the metallurgy. Afterward, add to one part two hundred-weights of the superior flux and smelt it in a crucible, just like the previously mentioned mild ore. Judge the <term>regulus</term> <note>the small button of pure metal found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</note>.

If the ore is so refractory <note>stubborn or resistant to heat</note> that the flux is weakened or consumed before the ore is smelted, a little crude tartar or glass gall <note>original: *fellis vitri*; the scum or dross found on the surface of molten glass, used as a flux</note> must be mixed in. Do this immediately at the start if you know the nature of the ore; if you are ignorant of it, then do so when you see the failure of the flux.

Moreover, you shall recognize how much copper or bronze the melted pyrite or stone contains in the same way. Roast two hundred-weights of the finely ground stone, as was said in the preceding sections, so that it becomes entirely mild. Divide it into two parts. Weigh one, and record the weight. Mix it with the flux, and if it seems necessary, add a little crude tartar or glass gall. Cook it in a crucible in a wind-furnace <note>original: *fornace anemia*; a furnace that relies on natural draft rather than bellows</note> like copper ores to produce a regulus, and you will know how many hundred-weights yield how much copper.

If the copper ore is dispersed everywhere in rocks, and is so abundant that it compensates for the expense, there is no other skill for testing it except to wash sixteen hundred-weights of the finely ground material through a trough; dry the washed sand, weigh it, and note the loss. Afterward, take two hundred-weights of the same sand, prepare it by roasting, and smelt it with flux as before. From this you will declare: *first, how much pure ore is in the sixteen hundred-weights; second, how much impure and foreign material comes away; third, how much copper or bronze is in the washed ore; fourth, how many hundred-weights of raw mineral are required for one hundred-weight of copper; fifth, how much silver is in a hundred-weight of the washed ore.* Based on these things, you will be able to take counsel regarding the mine.

The best copper ore is azure or green, and often one hundred-weight pours out seventy pounds. After that, yellow marcasite, fissile stones <note>shale or slate</note>, pyrites, and other minerals—rich, poor, pure, mixed with rocks, clean, and impure—are found. And among these, some are even productive of silver; some have lead mixed in, others are full of <term>chalcanthum</term> <note>copperas or vitriol</note>; others are full of sulfur, etc. In testing all of them, the general method is this: after they have been crushed and reduced to pure and mild states (or found and selected as such), they are melted with flux in a crucible to a regulus. Skillful roasting mitigates the harsh ones; washing purifies those mixed with impure "mountain juices" or rocks. Here, however, one must note what I warned above regarding abundant *alum, vitriol, sulfur, etc.*—namely, that these "juices" must first be extracted in their own way, and afterward the ore is to be prepared for examination. Lead is not added, because it "steals" the copper and dissipates it. Likewise, one must avoid corrosive, sulfurous, arsenical, or antimonial fluxes, etc., by which the metal is also consumed. Fachsius <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century master of assaying</note> advised that the quality could also be judged by the color of the regulus; but he adds that quite often an unmanageable, spotted, black, and rough copper is drawn from mild ores, while a beautiful and ductile copper comes from harsh ones. I think the cause lies in the diligence of preparation and the frequent roasting, by which the clinging sulfur and other impurities are more deeply removed. And since "rapacious" <note>aggressive or corrosive</note> minerals are sharp, they also wipe away the filth and carry it off with them. If, therefore, even the mild ores were roasted, pollution would be prevented. This is proven afterward by the "ripening," by which such copper is smelted into a regular and pure state. In parching or roasting, one must therefore proceed gently, lest the ore melt and thus involve the filth within itself. This art must often be used in "fixation" through cements. For the moisture must be exhausted little by little; the volatile spirits withdrawn little by little; and therefore the powder is also turned constantly during roasting so that it does not melt together, just as is usually done in the calcining of antimony. But if we cannot prevent melting even in this way, as happens in sulfurous pyrites, either the sulfur must first be melted out by descent, or if melting has occurred, the crushing must be repeated, though it is then more laborious.

Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola, author of the definitive mining text *De Re Metallica* (1556)</note> teaches generally regarding copper ores that they must first be burned and roasted with a sharp fire for six or eight hours. Afterward, when cooled, they are to be ground, washed, dried, weighed, and the weight compared with the weight of the whole that was first selected. The sand or scrapings of the washed ore are considered as a "cake" (otherwise, pyrite or copper ore in a greater fire in a raw furnace is usually smelted into a cake which they call "copper-stone" <note>matte</note>). Three hundred-weights of this, with three units each of copper scale, saltpeter, and Venetian glass, are placed in a triangular crucible closed with a charcoal (which serves as a lid). They are first allowed to heat in a circle before the bellows with a gentle fire. Afterward, with the fire increased, they are melted until, the additives being consumed, the slag moves away. When the crucible is cooled and broken, the grain of copper is taken out and weighed. There is another method by the same author: the ore, once roasted, is washed, and three hundred-weights of the washed scrapings are joined with one hundred-weight each of common salt, burnt tartar, and glass gall. They are cooked in a three-cornered crucible. If the ore was rich, a copper grain is found; if poor, a copper-stone. This, once roasted, is crushed, washed, and smelted with "flowers" <note>sublimated powders</note> and saltpeter. The grain of copper remains, and once removed, it is judged. But although roasting might be granted even for mild ore, the confusion creates difficulty. And it is easy to judge that not all things roasted by a driven fire can or should be. Nor do I see to what purpose copper scale is added, unless to deceive the judgment. For if this is consumed, why not also the copper of the ore? But if it remains, the judgment is uncertain because of the greater weight. Fachsius more rightly orders us to strike for a regulus rather than to wait for the consumption of additives to produce a pure grain. There is also another method, suspect because of the glass gall, salt, and calcined tartar, which Fachsius rebukes in his preface, and not without just cause. In a larger work, pure ore (*green, azure, etc.*) is smelted in a furnace with a closed "eye" <note>tap-hole</note>, or in the first stage of an open eye. If much silver is present with it, lead is first applied to it in a crucible before the furnace, because the lead "drinks up" the greater part of the silver. The rest is left with the copper and is separated in a segregating hearth. If a small amount of silver is present, it is immediately cast into an empty crucible, and afterward, if it is worth the effort, it is segregated specifically. But if nothing is present, or so little that it does not compensate for the costs, it is finished immediately.

Harsh ore (containing rapacious minerals, such as pyrite, fossil metallic cadmia <note>likely cobalt or zinc ores</note>, iron-stone, etc.) is joined with raw fluxing pyrite and slag, and smelted into cakes. These are roasted as often as necessary,

# Commentaries on Alchemy, Part II, Book V.

& then the copper is melted out of them in the manner of a mild ore <note>original: *venæ mitis*; ore that is easily fused</note>. Indeed, the first smelting is done in a crude, wide-mouthed furnace; the flowing material is shaped into cakes which they call "loaves" or "stones." The roasting is repeated nearly seven times, and then the copper is finished in a furnace with a "closed eye" <note>a furnace where the tapping hole or observation port is kept sealed to maintain heat</note>. It should also be noted that when a copper-bearing ore contains more silver than copper, it should be processed in the same manner as silver ore. Bituminous and sulfurous fissile stone <note>likely oil shale or alum schist</note> is piled into heaps in the open air and burned for several days by placing bundles of brushwood upon them; for it catches fire because of the bitumen. What remains is smelted with <term>fluxes</term> <note>substances used to promote melting and remove impurities</note>, and "stone loaves" are made, which are roasted and smelted seven times after the slag has been removed. In the crucible, the material is separated into slag, stone, and a <term>regulus</term> <note>a small button of pure metal</note> pregnant with copper and silver. However, poor fissile stone is ground and pounded with pestles into a powder, washed, and shaken through a sieve. The washed sand is cooked into loaves, which, when properly roasted, yield copper through their cooking. If <term>chrysocolla</term> <note>a green copper mineral</note>, <term>lazurite</term> <note>a blue mineral</note>, yellow earth or ochre, or black earths are attached to it—in which there is copper with silver—it is not washed, but rather ground and smelted with fluxes. For indeed, the customs for smelting copper vary in different places, and various shortcuts are sought so that the silver may be called forth into a solid state.

## CHAPTER XII.
## On Black Lead Ore.

*A certain weight of this, whether naturally mild or brought to mildness through the proper roastings, is smelted in a crucible into a <term>regulus</term> with a light flux and a little iron sawdust—first over a slow fire, and then, after the signal of a "hissing" sound is given, suddenly under a strong heat in a blast furnace. The judgment of this regulus reveals the value and quality of the ore.*

**The explanation from Fachs:** <note>referring to Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century master of assaying</note> Mix raw, pure <term>galena</term> <note>lead sulfide, the primary ore of lead</note>, finely ground, in the weight of a hundred-weight <note>the relative unit used by assayers</note>, with double the amount of flux made from lime, saltpeter, and double tartar: add a little filed iron sawdust. Having placed these in a triangular crucible, sprinkle in as much melted or raw salt as the width of the bottom of the vessel; close the crucible with a fitting lid, and place it in the blast furnace before the bellows. Let it heat up gradually. When you perceive a hissing and crackling sound, blow strongly with the bellows, but not for long, lest it smoke away. Afterward, having removed the crucible from the fire, place it on the floor and tap near it so that the <term>regulus</term> descends into the cone. Leave it so that it cools on its own. Judge the extracted <term>regulus</term>.

*However, galena that is mixed with impurities and "wild" minerals—even if it appears pure and unmixed to the eye—must be pounded into minute particles. Two hundred-weights of these are roasted in a muffle <note>original: *testa*; a shallow clay vessel</note> in a small furnace once and again, depending on how much "wildness" they contain, which you will recognize by the persistence of the stench and smoke. During roasting, care must be taken that the ore does not melt from excessive heat and stick to the muffle. When it has been roasted enough, let it cool by itself, grind it finely, and smelt it with flux and sawdust just like the first.*

*If the black lead ore is scattered within useless rocks, flints, fissile stone, etc., grind a certain weight of it finely and wash it in a trough. Mix a hundred-weight of the washed and dried sand with half an ounce of flux made from saltpeter, borax, and tartar, or something similar, and smelt it well in a small covered crucible before the bellows. Weigh the grain.*

Lead ore, lead-stone (which Fallopius <note>Gabriele Falloppio, a famous 16th-century anatomist and mineralogist</note> elsewhere thinks is sterile and only so named from its similarity in color), or <term>galena</term>, or <term>plumbago</term>, etc., is found even though lead is joined with many ores of other metals, especially gold, silver, and copper. The same metal is also reduced from <term>molybdenum</term> <note>here referring to lead-glance or lead oxides, not the element molybdenum</note>, <term>litharge</term> <note>lead oxide</note>, certain ashes, and furnace scrapings. It easily transforms into quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, from which it originated, and is like an immature metal, or one imperfectly coagulated. Therefore, because of its "unclean sulfur" and "impure mercury," its nature approaches that of virulent spirits; it is related to mined <term>cadmia</term> (which they call **Cobalt**), **antimony**, ash-colored lead (or **Bismuth**), leaden **marcasite**, and similar things. For this reason, poisonous vapors arise during smelting, and the assayers and smelters are forced to protect themselves, just as they do against the malice of mercury, by drinking wine in which **Zedoary**, or **Pimpinella**, or **Angelica** root and similar herbs have been boiled or infused.

The examination of this ore is described quite clearly and diligently by Fachs. Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola, author of *De Re Metallica*</note>, as in other matters, is somewhat different here. He grinds and mixes equal parts of pure lead-stone and borax (such as half an ounce of each). Having placed them in a clay crucible, he melts them in a bed of burning coals. When the borax has crackled, he removes the coals and searches for the grain of lead in the bottom to be judged; when this is further refined by cupellation <note>original: *fulminatum*; purified by intense heat</note>, it also yields its silver. If the ore is impure and degraded, he burns, grinds, and washes it; he then melts one hundred-weight of this prepared material with triple the amount of composite flux in a clay crucible before the bellows within a circle of fire, and when it has cooled, he removes the slag.

Another method for the same: two ounces of prepared ore, five drachms of burnt copper, an ounce of glass gall <note>the scum from glass making</note>, and half an ounce of salt. These are ground and mixed in a triangular crucible and cooked over a slow fire so the vessel does not break. When it has flowed, the fire is intensified with the bellows; the crucible is then removed and allowed to cool in the air without pouring water on it, lest the metal remix with the slag if water is added. He also advises that iron sawdust should be added if it is difficult to smelt, because it will heat up and be purified more easily from that; he adds that the ore can furthermore be examined with fluxes or iron filings alone. There is no doubt that light is shed on these matters from Fachs' writings. When he uses a clay crucible for pure ore, one should see whether a triangular one might be more convenient, as it is better suited for covering and for depositing the <term>regulus</term>. Also, when it "hisses," the vessel should not be removed from the fire immediately; rather, as Fachs advises, the heat should be blown for a short while longer, with the caution he set forth. Likewise, the same author has explained more efficiently and significantly how the impure ore should be prepared. Not every ore should be washed after roasting, nor should every ore that is washed be roasted. It is washed when it is diluted by foreign materials, otherwise it is noble in itself and is not roasted. It is only roasted when it is "wild," otherwise it is pure in itself and is not washed; because fire, applied with skill, turns the fleeting spirits into flight in the form of a foul-smelling vapor. And so, one must roast according to the art until no stench appears. If it is degraded and yet also diluted by rocks, it is washed first and then roasted. In the method of smelting, the law concerning a sharp but brief fire must be observed, which we see has been omitted. In other matters, I fear lest the glass gall (though Etketus <note>possibly a corruption of a name or a less-known author</note> does not abstain from it), the burnt copper, etc., are partly too sharp for lead ore, and partly unnecessary. If...

<page-num>117</page-num>
# On the Assaying of the Proving Art, Part 2.

Indeed, if the proper preparation has been made, no other smelting <note>original: *excoctio*; literally "cooking out," the process of extracting metal from ore via heat</note> is required than that used for a mild ore. However, if you wish to melt down an unprepared ore and attempt to compensate for the labor of preparation with additives, error is close at hand. For the violent spirits released during smelting will hardly spare such a fleeting metal, even if iron filings are added; indeed, it can scarcely be smelted to a pure state with safety. Furthermore, iron is added to no purpose when the fluxes have other material besides the metal to consume. Agricola gives the reason why water should not be poured on: because the ore becomes mixed again with the slag. Fachs therefore orders the vessel to be closed with a lid, lest bits of coal fall in and renew the dross, thereby hindering the pure separation of the lead.

<margin>The reason for not quenching lead with water.</margin>
The reason for not quenching it with water is that in both white lead <note>tin</note> and black lead <note>lead</note> the <term>regulus</term> <note>the metallic button or lump that settles at the bottom</note> leaps out and is scattered. Agricola’s reasoning may coincide with this argument. Why these metallic buttons should leap away from water—while silver, gold, and copper do not (unless tin or lead is present with them), even though they themselves cannot bear moisture when they are at their hottest—is due to a more "spirited" nature and a certain "mercurial quickness." If you mix quicksilver with tin and move it toward the coals, it likewise crackles and is cast out; this happens specifically when both have not yet been thoroughly heated and ignited. No other reason appears than that the spirit mixed within, finding its path blocked—especially when moisture meets it from the outside and constrains it—cannot struggle free except with a crash and great force, just as is clearly seen in "Vulcan’s laughter" <note>likely a term for the popping or exploding of metal in a furnace</note>, thunder, and other such phenomena. And there is no crash without air or spirits. But why, when it begins to crackle in the crucible, must it be driven with sudden heat? Fachs says "sudden" so that the fleeting metal does not turn to ash through longer exposure; it requires heat so that it may separate purely from the slag and flow cleanly. Otherwise, it could not be properly separated from the slag by knocking it. This also occurs in chemical experiments, where certain things are melted by that same art, especially in fixing or transmuting <term>cements</term> <note>mixtures used to treat metals at high heat</note>, the reduction of tin calx, and others. In larger-scale operations, lead is smelted from <term>molybdaena</term> <note>lead glance or litharge</note>, pyrites, or lead-stone in its own furnace, usually by "descent" <note>a furnace design where the metal flows downward through the fuel</note>, although there is variety according to the customs of nations which abound in this metal; and since it is cheap, they do not care if some is lost. Some melt it first under the open sky, and afterward refine it in a hearth with a crucible.

<margin>Why iron is added to lead.</margin>
Others smelt it through a "raw furnace" with the "eye" <note>the tap hole</note> always open. Regarding these methods, let Agricola be consulted. The author here advises adding iron scales or slag to the hearth or the ore, because the lead is "driven together" by them; it was easy for a clever man to notice this, given the vitriolic constriction of this metal. But it can also be added as a means of defense <note>a better reason is that when **Galena** <note>lead sulfide</note> is present with **stibium** <note>antimony</note>, the force of the latter is diverted by the iron</note>.

<margin>Fachsius gives this reason.</margin>
For iron is used against these evils so that it turns the force and violence of the wasting flux upon itself, so that in the meantime the more tender metal can be smelted without loss. It should be noted, however, regarding the addition of iron, that it is not required in those ores which still contain some foreign impurity, but only in mild or pure and "tender" ores. For it is better that the flux be occupied in consuming those impurities (unless sulfur and antimony are present together) than in consuming the iron. Nor should one fear that it will bring any harm to the metal. It works upon the foreign matter, which is why Agricola’s previous instruction was confused.

When lead-bearing pyrites are smelted, Agricola notes that a white liquor first flows from the furnace, which is an "enemy" to silver, as it burns it away. This is poured out with the watery slag or pulled out with a hook once hardened. It even exudes from the walls of the furnace. Once this liquor has flowed down, the lead follows with its silver. From this, the slag is first drawn off—sometimes white—then the "stone," though it is not always present. Finally, the metal is poured into pits or crucibles to make "cakes for refining" <note>original: *panes fulminandi*; cakes intended for cupellation</note>, from which the silver is separated; and the litharge, re-smelted with the *molybdaena*, yields "impoverished" lead <note>lead from which the silver has been removed</note>.

<margin>Something regarding Bismuth.</margin>
He does not explain what he thinks that "white liquor" is. It is not far from the truth to say it possesses the nature of **realgar** and **arsenic**, since it erodes and burns silver and is found on the sides of furnaces; something similar is also found among the soot that grows in the fore-hearth and chimney. However, it is mixed with white flint, just as is the case with tin **marcasite**. But enough of lead.

## CHAPTER XIII.
### On the ore of white lead, commonly called tin.

**T**hat which is mild and pure is examined in no other way than the ore of black lead. If it is not pure but mixed with stone, a certain weight is crushed and washed in a trough. The loss is noted. A hundred-weight of the washed sand is burned two or three times, and afterward smelted like the former, but without iron filings. In the same way, the "tin-stone" <note>cassiterite</note> mixed with foreign matter is prepared, taking care not to burn it too much. It is smelted in a similar fashion.

The ore of white lead <note>tin</note> is mostly black, sometimes reddish-brown, gray, or yellow; some is even white, green, or stained with another color on the surface. It is found in mines in widened, heaped, or extended veins, mostly in white flint or red stone and similar materials. Grains are also washed out from the sand of springs and rivers. The black grains are called "tin stone," or *cassiteri* stone, which the Germans call **Zwitterstein**. Its assay in almost all points agrees with Fachs’s trial of black lead, except that in the case of washed sand he forbids the addition of iron, because the flux finds impurities to consume. But the same reasoning holds for similar ores of black lead. Therefore, I did not wish to declare a common precept using Fachs’s description. However, if anyone nevertheless desires the words of such a great craftsman, so that they may at least make a comparison with the previous ones, let him know the Latin reads thus:

<margin>Fachsius's description rendered into Latin. See Ercker page 121 in folio.</margin>
How the *cassiteros* (so I call the **Zwitter**) or tin stone is to be tested to know the value of the tin. To examine pure *cassiterum*, not false or adulterated, in which there are no foreign stones nor any void: Mix one hundred-weight, finely ground, with a flux prepared for copper ores. When placed in the crucible, throw in a little salt, as was done before with lead ore. Place it in the fire of a blast furnace and let it heat up slowly. Afterward, use the bellows and increase the heat; do not do this for long, but ignite it with sudden heat, lest the metal be consumed by the nearby flux. Then extract it and allow it to cool. Having broken the crucible, you will find its button. If the galena were mixed with stones...

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for assaying and smelting ores, specifically focusing on the methods for processing impure tin and lead ores. It compares the techniques of the masters Modestin Fachs and Georgius Agricola, particularly regarding the use of roasting, fluxes like borax, and the behavior of "spirited" metals.</meta>

<header>Alchemical Commentary. Part II. Book V.</header>

and not pure, proceed thus. Wash sixteen hundredweights (which are called *a hollow* <note>original: *eine Höhle*; a traditional German mining unit of measure</note>) through a trough as purely as possible. Gradually dry the washed sand. By investigating the weight, you will learn how much has been lost, and how much pure ore is mixed into those hundredweights. Roast <note>original: *crema*; the process of heating ore to remove volatile impurities like sulfur</note> the hundredweight of washed ore two or three times. Prepare and smelt it like the previous one; if any metal is within, it will remain. There is no need to add iron filings to this assay. For the washed sand retains enough foreign impurity, however studiously you wash it, that the flux will have business enough in consuming it.

->**How tin grains or impure tin stone are to be tested.**<-

Tin stone that is impure and weakened by rust or iron-stone must be ground very finely. Sixteen hundredweights of the ground material are to be washed through a trough. The washed material must be roasted once, but not too much, for it can be over-burned, so that the tin afterwards turns into lime <note>original: *calcem*; a powdery oxide or ash resulting from excessive heat</note>. Grind the roasted material again and wash it in the trough, and repeat this until the adulterating and sterile little stones have departed. Weigh the sand that has been washed, roasted, and thus purified, so that you may know how much pure ore is in the weakened tin. Afterward, mix one hundredweight with two parts of the recently mentioned flux, and proceed by smelting, as with pure ore. It can easily happen that it is burned away by excessive heat. In a large-scale work, the most certain proof is if the washed sand is gathered diligently, so that from one hundredweight of it, fifty pounds of tin—or half a hundredweight—are smelted. These are the words of Fachs.

There is a slight difference. In the case of tin, he makes no mention of the "noise" <note>likely referring to the "cry of tin" or the crackling sound made during certain stages of heating</note> which, when heard, signals that the bellows should be used. Furthermore, he gives a different reason for haste: namely, lest it be burned into lime by a longer roasting, whereas earlier he had said it was lest it be dissipated and exhale. He also omits that the area next to the crucible should be struck to settle the <term>regulus</term> <note>the concentrated metallic button at the bottom of a crucible</note>. What he interjects regarding impure galena <note>the primary ore of lead</note> pertains to the vein of lead; and the method of Agricola is clearly rejected here, as the addition of iron filings is forbidden. For if they were added, the impurities would be consumed more slowly, and thus the ore—with the heat occupied by a double obstacle yet suffering from it—would be burned or suffer loss; though in other cases, one should not prolong what can be completed more concisely. Regarding impure tin grains, there seems to be a difference in the roasting: he prescribes roasting once, then grinding and washing again, and repeating these in turn until we reach the purity we can achieve. Yet in the case of galena, he orders roasting only two or three times, without repeating the washing. But this disagreement is easily reconciled: where the mountain impurity suggests it, one must wash again even after the first roasting; where it is absent, the "greedy spirits" <note>volatile impurities like sulfur or arsenic that "carry away" the metal</note> are to be removed by roasting alone. He suggests the flux in both cases is the common one made from two parts tartar and one part saltpeter, calcined in one pot and ground. In the preface, he also designates another, made from two parts litharge <note>lead oxide</note> and one part flint, melted into dross. Elsewhere, he mixes and applies a flux of borax, saltpeter, and tartar—or borax, calcined nitre, tartar, and salt—specifically for grains of tin.

In these matters, it should also be noted that the same author, in another part of his work, sets forth a different way of examining tin grains, which at first glance seems contrary to the one I have just discussed. Weigh the tin stone (<term>Zinnstein</term>) or the vein of white lead <note>original: *plumbum candidum*; a common historical name for tin</note> (he names them indiscriminately); note the weight diligently; roast it well; wash the very finely ground material so that the sterile parts recede. Some stone must be roasted yet again. Dry the washed sand and investigate the weight, so you know how much tin is required for a hundredweight of pure ore or pure grains. Afterward, mix a little borax with it, moisten it slightly, and smelt it in the furnace. Or, pierce a small triangular crucible from the side, so that you can blow air into it from there. Take soft coals, reduced to the size of hazelnuts; when you have heated the small furnace or crucible, place the washed stone upon the glowing coals in alternating layers (layer upon layer), and the borax will not allow the stone to slip away or escape beneath. When you think it has melted, pour the small furnace (or crucible), inverted with the fire and the molten tin, into a basin of water; you will find the tin, which you shall collect and melt again upon a plate. It cannot be known with exact certainty how much is in a hundredweight, nor how many hundredweights will be smelted. This at least is certain and common: if you find tin in the grains or stone, and have diligently roasted and washed it to purity, half the weight of the stone ought to be smelted and become tin. These are his words. It is strange that he speaks so indifferently about any stone, whether it be weak or pure, mild or harsh, when he had distinguished them before. Furthermore, it is strange that he mixes it so freely with glowing coals, when it could easily happen that it is calcined. Moreover, although he specifically forbade pouring water on the veins of lead and tin, here he plunges the whole thing into water. 

But the first doubt will be easily cleared by a prudent man. For it is certain enough that a vein of tin is rarely so "mild" that it does not need roasting, except perhaps that which is found in <term>cassiterophyllia</term> <note>literally "tin-leaves"; perhaps a reference to very thin, leafy ore deposits</note>, which is even softer. But if it is found pure and noble, there is no need for that labor; the labor would be removed of itself. Second, the master's circumspection will prove it right; and since it is enough if you judge that half will turn out to be white lead <note>tin</note>, it provides a sort of handle for "dozing" <note>perhaps meaning a margin of error or a rule of thumb</note>. The third point is resolved by the headlong infusion. It is one thing to sprinkle or pour cold water to quench it; it is another to plunge the whole thing into water, from which such a small quantity will not escape, being overtaken by the multitude of water. As for what he says of borax—that the ore is moistened with it—I would take that to mean its dissolution in a humid place, as much as is required for dampness. But why can the art not attain certainty? Is the vein of lead more constant than that of tin? Or are the impurities more compliant there, and more stubborn here? Certainly, roasting, burning, grinding, and other preparations are more numerous and active in tin because of the stubbornness of the grains and the multitude of empty or sterile grains which, though they have no tin, yet compete with true grains in weight, constancy in fire, and color. Therefore, speckled and hard tin is often produced from them. Here it cannot happen without some of the good being dissipated along with it, for tin is very familiar with mercury and is full of "spirit."

Agricola has almost the same instruction, but what Fachs orders to be done in a crucible, he does in a coal. He teaches it thus: <margin>The assay of tin according to Agricola.</margin> Wash that ore and grind it. Mix a hundred and a half of this with a hundredweight of borax, and make a paste by sprinkling water. Take a large, smooth coal, which you shall pierce so that in the upper part there is a hole of three fingers' breadth, which ends in a narrow point at the bottom. Fit it to an earthen crucible. Apply coals and glowing embers. [missing text] the coal [missing text] the fire.
