<header>On the Assaying of the Testing Art, Part 2.</header>

# On the Assaying of the Testing Art, Part 2.

Once the fire has caught, place the paste into the hole and cover it with another wide, glowing charcoal. With several coals placed around it, a sharp fire should be stirred up until all the <term>white lead</term> <note>original: *plumbum candidum*; a common Latin term for tin</note> has flowed out of the hole and into the crucible. You can also coat that charcoal with clay so that when it grows white-hot, the ore does not scatter. Furthermore, make a small hole in the middle part of it (namely from the side, so that it reaches and ends in the large one); fill the large one with tiny coals, upon which you place the ore. In the small hole, however, place the fire, and stir it with a bellows by blowing through the nozzle of the bellows inserted into the same. It is also common to place it in a pit lined with clay. In this completed cooking, a small mass of white lead is found. These are the words of **Agricola**. **Fachsius** compensates for the charcoal and crucible with a single crucible: instead of a pit, he uses a draft furnace or a clay crucible within a ring. In 
<margin>Work of a greater fire.</margin>
larger-scale operations, the prepared tin ore is smelted in a high, narrow furnace with a gentler fire, so that the stones do not turn to lime or become glassy. When a shovel-full of ore has been thrown in, coals are immediately placed underneath, but these must be selected and washed clean of sand and rocks, lest the opening be blocked by their dross. The molten liquid flows through an open "eye" into a basin, which must often be sprinkled with charcoal dust so that the waste does not stick and so that none of the metal flies away. Small, medium, and large stones are cooked separately, lest they be melted unevenly by an equal fire, and meanwhile the tender parts perish while the more solid ones are still liquefying. In this way, both the furnace and the blast of air are adapted to the material, so that the furnace is narrower and the blast sharper for the larger pieces; for the rest, it is done in proportion, although this is not observed by everyone. Instead, in one furnace, the tiny ore is smelted first, then the medium is put in, then the thicker, and finally the more impure. The types of charcoal are also observed. Small pieces are put in dampened, and the furnace is filled with the material in alternating layers. It is a wonder that the stones from the <term>tin-washings</term> <note>original: *cassiteroplysarum*; from the Greek *kassiteros* (tin) and *plysis* (washing)</note> 
<margin>Tin from washings is nobler and softer than that from mines.</margin>
require a more vehement fire than the larger mined stones. But as the fire is greater, it is also shorter. If the stones are not sufficiently cleaned and roasted, or if more than the right amount are thrown in, they mix with the slag and flow out foully; sometimes they even settle so stubbornly in the furnace that they must be broken out after the work is finished. The dross is processed like "relaxed" ore <note>original: *vena remissa*; ore that is less concentrated or already partially processed</note> with much washing, as are the scrapings of the furnaces and the soot. During washing, the half-melted metal is distinguished from the raw and is washed separately, then smelted with the stones. So that those pregnant soots do not fly away, they are caught in chambers; from this, the volatility of this metal is understood.

## CHAPTER XIV.
### On judging iron ore.

**A** known weight of iron ore, ground very finely and—if it is impure—also roasted, is placed on clean paper and subjected to a strong **magnet**. The iron is attracted by this. [*So it is with steel, which the magnet does not attract as raw ore, but as roasted ore, so that it becomes similar to iron ore. They first test whether there is much iron in the stone by the rubbing of a knife. If much is rubbed off, they think much is present.*] This is wiped off and saved. By repeating the work, whatever is inside is collected: the weight is explored and compared with the previous weight and with the residue. Pure ore is melted in a crucible with a flux of saltpeter, etc., into a <term>regulus</term> <note>a metallic button or lump found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</note>, which, when subjected to judgment, shows the riches of the vein.

Iron is born in its own stone, and likewise in rusty clay; just as in **Styria**, it sometimes also contains gold, silver, copper, and tin. Authors generally agree on its testing by the magnet. **Fachsius**, however, does not further process the filings separated by the magnet, but leaves this task to the smelter. Furthermore, he disagrees with **Agricola** and others who wash it. For he says washing is not to be praised because the rust and iron-ochre are washed away at the same time, from which, nevertheless, good iron and excellent steel are made. He cites the master iron-smelters as witnesses. The magnet sometimes does not attract the scrapings unless they are roasted, just as it does not care for rust. Therefore, if the stone has been corroded by "sharp waters" <note>original: *aquis acutis*; likely acidic mine waters or mineral acids</note> and reduced to mud—as such a liquid is said to flow together in **Styria** and deposit rust in the lakes in which it is received, from which iron is nevertheless smelted—the use of the magnet will not be sufficiently faithful. In larger works, it is smelted in a crucible under a chimney, with alternating layers of charcoal and ore. The slag flows out through a hole at the side. The cooled mass is rolled out of the crucible and forged with wooden hammers. Ore that is loosened from the mountain and is hard to handle is selected stone by stone, crushed with dry pestles, and after being roasted, it is washed and cooked in a "closed-eye" furnace, similar to that in which rich and mild silver ore is processed, but larger and higher. Here too, mutual layers are placed, consisting of ore the size of nuts and charcoal. According to whether the ore is more or less impure, it is cooked once or even twice, and finally, the iron is finished in an iron-forge.

## CHAPTER XV.
### On the testing of ore of different metals.

**I**f there are several metals in one ore, it is tested according to that which prevails, either in quantity or in price, and in which the rest are preserved. From the produced mass, they are later segregated according to the method for examining metals, and the value of each one is indicated.

Such an examination is especially sought in those ores where the work can be made worthwhile, such as when silver or gold is present in copper, lead, iron, or tin; or gold in silver, or iron in copper. If no precious or abundant metal is present, even if it could be investigated for the sake of the art and the mode of separation shown, it is rarely required for the purpose of smelting the ores. However, because of coinage and other mixtures of pure metals, the investigation is necessary. For example, if a silver <term>pyrite</term> <note>a shiny, metallic mineral, often containing sulfur</note> has a little copper joined to it, the silver is sought and the copper is neglected, or at least only noted in passing. Thus, if in the lead of **Villach** <note>original: *Villacensi*; referring to Villach in Carinthia, known for its lead mines</note> there are very great quantities, but only a little silver is inside, the assayer indeed looks at the lead itself so that he may use it purely or at least without error in his testing, but for the sake of the silver, it is not subjected to examination except perhaps in the first specimen and for the sake of the art; where, nevertheless, the matter returns to the given rule. If a little iron is mixed into copper ore, an examination of both is not commonly established for the sake of preserving them, but so that, once the quantity of iron is known, the method of smelting is ready at hand. For it is established that if iron is within, the ore is very stubborn and does not turn out to be excellent copper unless the iron is consumed. But regarding these things, a more exact precept is found in **Chemical** <note>original: *Chymicis*; referring to alchemical or chemical texts</note> writings, as if in the principal art, from which those things that complete this section can be sought. This, however, I add: if there is a doubt whether it be...

...whether there is any metal in the ore, or none at all; and if there is, how much there is, with what substances it is mixed, and which one predominates. For the most part, I have established the examination according to the manner of the vein to which we judge the ore probably belongs. Thus, the testing is not undertaken as a primary purpose because of this or that metal mixed in the vein, but as if in passing, the primary question being whether any metal exists at all. Nor does the matter require any other instruction than what has been laid down generally regarding the <term>governance of fire</term> and the other things above, and what has been shown by example in individual cases, in imitation of which similar things can be worked out. Thus far concerning the examination of metallic veins: next follows the metals themselves.

### CHAPTER XVI.
## On the examination of metals outside their veins.
### And first, on those to be graded.

The <term>assaying</term> <note>original: *Docimasia*; the technical art of testing the purity of metals</note> of metals in themselves is when they are examined after having already been extracted from the veins. 
This is done in two ways: it is undertaken either to achieve a predetermined grade of quality, or to recognize the value of one metal within another.

*The first method is very common, first, in those metals which are found in mines—as the stories go—in a state of absolute purity, or in <term>lightning-refined silver</term> <note>original: *fulminatu*; silver that has undergone the 'blick' or flash at the end of cupellation</note>. It is also used in silver that has been further refined by fire after cupellation, as well as in hard tin. Next, it is used for spotted and unmanageable copper, and for those "loaves" of it which <term>Agricola</term> <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the 'Father of Mineralogy'</note> calls "disintegrating," and similar forms. Second, it is used for all adulterated metals which are called "graded" by the <term>Sophists</term> <note>A derogatory term for fraudulent alchemists who use "sophistry" to make metals appear more precious than they are</note>, and "transmuted" into the nature of gold and silver. To these are also added those which are colored for the sake of more ornate use without fraud, such as white copper, golden copper, and the like. General rules are handed down for all such things.*

*A metal is judged perfect if, through its examinations, it fulfills all the marks of quality without loss. That which suffers a defect in either quantity or quality is as far from perfection as the size of the defect, and is thus judged in comparison of the greater to the lesser. If, despite all things being correctly set up, a metal moves from better to worse while being examined, it is pronounced sophistical (fraudulent).*

*Specifically concerning gold: Gold is absolute if it withstands <term>royal water</term> <note>original: *aquam regiam*; a potent mixture of acids used to dissolve gold</note>, <term>cementation</term> <note>original: *cæmentum*; a refining process using salts at high heat</note>, <term>antimony</term> <note>used to purify gold by removing base metals</note>, <term>cupellation</term>, <term>coloring-agents</term>, and quenching in corrosive waters and sulfur; and if it receives no stain from the vapor of corrosives, and loses nothing of its weight, color, or the other prerogatives of its nature through all these. Another gold falls short of this only by as much as is lost, provided the distinction between nature and art is preserved. For that which is sought from nature and loses some of its substance while the rest remains unchanged is softer than it should be and requires <term>fixation</term>. That which decreases in its additives without loss of substance, but increases in quality, must be thought to have contained foreign spirits or other imperfect metals or minerals, the types of which are recognized by their own signs.*

*Silver is perfect in every way if it withstands a perfect <term>lightning-refining</term> <note>original: *fulmen*; see note above on cupellation</note> seven times, and suffers only a small loss in the cementation of gold. Anything else is either counterfeit, or not sufficiently fixed, or mixed with impure spirits, etc. It is the same for others, according to the nature of each.*

*But since one kind of quality is absolute and another is relative to use and public law, Chemistry follows the former with great exactness, while common assayers follow the latter—though even they are sometimes consulted regarding the highest perfection in matters of coinage, <term>quartation</term> <note>a method of separating gold from silver using nitric acid</note>, and other things. The examination of <term>lightning-refined</term> and <term>burnt silver</term> occurs quite often; likewise for unequal copper.*

### CHAPTER XVII.
## Examination of lightning-refined and burnt silver.

**T**his is performed as follows:
Two specimens from a "loaf" of silver, from above and below (<term>Ercker</term> <note>Lazarus Ercker, a renowned 16th-century assay master</note> cuts a sample of <term>burnt silver</term> <note>original: *Brandtsilber*; silver refined by fire</note> from the upper part, between the edge and the center; then he takes another portion from the lower part of the opposite side. On plates, he also takes the trial from above and below, even while keeping to the same side) are to be struck out according to the weight of <term>marks</term> <note>a unit of weight for precious metals</note>. Five times the weight of lead is to be assigned to each. Once the lead has been placed in a <term>sealed ash cupel</term> <note>original: *catillo cinereo seruestalto*</note> and begins to smoke, the metal must be submitted and <term>refined by lightning</term> until it is pure. Do the same for silver that has been both refined by lightning and burnt. If the value of the lightning-refined silver matches the value of the tin, and the value of the burnt or roasted silver agrees with the value of the lightning-refined, all has been done correctly. But if the values disagree, either an error was made in the cupellation or roasting—such that something escaped into the flue, settled in the ashes, or stuck to the <term>litharge</term> <note>lead oxide produced during cupellation</note>, which must then be investigated—or a theft has been committed. Likewise, since standard burnt silver ought to be 15 <term>loth</term> and 3 <term>drachms</term> <note>specific historical units of purity/weight</note>, a calculation must be made as to whether it was burnt beyond this law or below it, which the exact weight will indicate. For if you find it to be exactly a drachm, the refiner has hit the target; if it is less than a drachm, he has exceeded the limit (and then the mine owners must be compensated for this); if more than a drachm remains, he has not yet achieved his goal and is compelled to roast it even further. For this, however, several examinations are required: one to detect theft or error immediately after cupellation, another during the burning, and a final one after the burning. No certain limit is prescribed for lightning-refined silver. Therefore, the latter calculation does not apply to it, but only the former. However, a trial can be made based on estimation to see if, during the refining, it roughly reached the common and frequently experienced standard, or how far it is from it.

<margin>
Instruction of <term>Fachsius</term> <note>Modestin Fachs</note> on lightning-refined silver.
</margin>
It is not hidden that this operation is necessary to remove traps and to stimulate diligence. But since it is a matter of very careful judgment, I will add the accurate instruction of **Fachsius** as a declaration. He says this: Cut out the silver mass on both sides, in the middle between the center and the edges, with a semicircular chisel, so that when you have torn away a particle from one side, you turn the mass over and cut another from the previous spot, or from the region directly opposite. Wrap both portions separately in a paper envelope. Afterward, stretch it into a thin plate on a polished anvil with a smooth hammer, and turn it so that you can cut it with shears: weigh the pieces prepared in this way. First, place half a mark of the upper cut in the scale, and just as much of the lower. Join both and weigh them together as a whole mark. If you have weighed the halves carefully, they will correspond to the whole. After this, weigh two other half-marks in the same way and join them, so that there are two specimens, and one can be judged from the other. Assign five marks of lead to each mark...

<sig>LL</sig>

# On the Assaying of the Testing Art, part 2.

(Elsewhere he says seven, and a little further down he distinguishes between lightning-refined silver that contains lead and that which contains copper <note>original: *argentum fulminatum plumbiferum, & ætiferum*</note>, indicating that more is owed to the latter and less to the former.) These things being done, first place the lead in a well-heated <term>cupel</term> <note>a small, porous bowl made of bone ash used to separate precious metals from lead</note>; when it begins to smoke, place the weighed silver, wrapped in paper, upon the lead. When it has been absorbed, block the top hole of the small furnace with its lid, yet in such a way that a crack the width of a finger is left open; also close the little door of the ash-pit. Furthermore, place clay valves over the windows of the <term>muffle</term> <note>original: *tegula*; a clay housing that protects the metal from direct contact with the fuel</note> (at the sides and back), but not for long, for it is smelted quickly. When you see the cooking is nearly finished, remove the valves from the muffle along with the furnace lid, and add two coals to the door of the muffle. Thus manage the <term>flash</term> <note>original: *fulmen*; the "blick" or sudden brightening when the last of the lead oxide disappears, leaving pure silver</note>, though somewhat hotter than in other examinations, so that the grains do not retain leaden residue or smoke, which would make them stay heavier and deceive the judgment. Leave them in the furnace until they cool, for if you remove them suddenly the grains crack, and sometimes become lighter. Once cooled, take them out and explore the weight of both: if it is equal, it is well; and then weigh only one, and you will find the true value.

<margin>Why the ingots are sampled from both sides.</margin>
It should be known, moreover, that such a grain attains the highest purity of silver, as Budelius <note>Renerus Budelius (1530–1591), a jurist and expert on coinage</note> attests in many places. And although chemists may further roast the lightning-refined mass on a plate, this is not done because they judge it altogether imperfect, but so that they may remove anything perhaps adhering to the outside, or any leaden residue they think is left behind; and this indeed the assayer can also do if he detects anything. Fachsius <note>Modestin Fachs (1520–1595), an assay master and author of *Probierbüchlein*</note> illustrates his precepts with certain notes on roasted and lightning-refined silver. Of the former, he says its ultimate value is 15 half-ounces with three drachms; of the latter, that it is of unequal quality, since some silver is weakened by lead and some by copper, of which the latter is richer than the former. Next, it is necessary sometimes to add more lead during the testing of those which contain much copper than to others; otherwise, they would return a copper grain rather than a silver one in the crucible. Moreover, the use of this examination is also handed down here so that it may be known if anything has been lost. For however much the smelter transferred into the lead, so much the refiner ought to return in abundance; and however much here, so much the conqueror <note>the master refiner</note> at the completion of the refining. If the assay disagrees (in which, however, no error was made) with the value previously produced, one must search the <term>litharge</term> <note>lead oxide produced during cupellation</note> and the dross in the flash, and look for grains in the ash; otherwise, there is a suspicion of theft. Thus the defect of refining must be investigated in the cupel, which is prepared following the example of the lightning-refining hearth. Furthermore, as for why the ingots <note>original: *panes*; literally "loaves" or cakes of metal</note> are cut on both sides between the edges and the center, the reason must be thought to be the inequality that is often observed in such things. For the lower parts are more impure than the upper because the heavy parts sink, just like <term>diphryges</term> <note>a technical term for copper slag or residue</note> in copper. Sometimes, however, foreign matters float on the very top, though they are usually drawn off. Nor should it be sampled in the center, because in the lowest part there is a "lead pocket," as the metalworkers call it; in the top part there is almost exquisite purity; in the middle between the edges and the center, the mixture is medium and becomes equal if the top and bottom are joined. At the extreme edge, we also happen to be deceived in the equality: [silver recedes to the edges by the flight of heat in the middle of the ingots. Therefore, the sampling at the edges is enriched.] Thus it is not possible to establish exactly the equal value of the entire mass. As for why the weight of a <term>mark</term> is used in one place and a hundred-weight <note>original: *centenarii*</note> in another: the reason lies in the customary calculation. For they are not weighed by the hundred-weight: namely, whether the smelted metals are according to marks. Why half-marks and not whole ones are placed in the scales: the reason is both that the weight is thus obtained more exactly, and that the mixture of the top and bottom part occurs at the same time. The rest is manifest.

I think, indeed, that from the precepts concerning gold and silver, the common testing of goldsmiths and assayers can be sufficiently consistent for examining white, black, and green gold, etc.; likewise for silver that is furrowed, hair-like, thread-like, or powdery, etc., to be refined to purity. If ever these are found in the gravel of waters, being pure by nature and without rocks and other foreign materials, they are nevertheless infected by vapors; this must also be understood concerning the most noble grains of raw leaden, red, or white silver, etc. Such things are usually either refined with lead in a cupel and afterwards roasted in a clay crucible, or smelted with <term>borax</term> in a triangular crucible before the bellows, or reverberated with an added cement or coloring paste, as necessity requires. Gold specifically is also melted using <term>antimony</term> <note>original: *stibium*</note>, or if it is thread-like and powdery, it is collected by mercury and afterwards separated. Sometimes where there is only external residue, they flatten it with a hammer, make it white-hot, and quench it in urine diluted with salt, or wash it with water of tartar. Golden sands washed to purity are heated in a pan or burned on a plate. Indeed, if you have well perceived the method of smelting veins, you cannot be stuck on these, if only you remember that here there is no need for such great apparatus and sharp additives. As for those things which are <term>sophistical</term> <note>counterfeit or "alchemy" metals meant to look real</note>, although they are sometimes so tightly united that they withstand several flashes, they are finally judged by the fires, according to the examinations which are placed in the rules from Geber <note>an 8th-century alchemist, likely referring here to the Latin works attributed to him</note> and chemical experience. Some also see whether they turn black in the fire, whether they bubble, whether they endure quenching in urine, or quenching in vinegar with <term>sal ammoniac</term>, whether they are consumed by sulfur, whether they enter into mercury; and when they are melted with pure gold and silver, whether they mix purely, whether they sustain <term>quartation</term> <note>the process of separating gold from silver by dissolving the silver in nitric acid, requiring a ratio of 3 parts silver to 1 part gold</note>, whether they respond to needles on a touchstone, whether in the due quantity they are heavier or lighter, whether they sound like natural metals, whether they emit smoke, or jump out of the plate unlike other native metals, or whether they do not jump out if treated as those—although this is dangerous; and those judgments satisfy in full, not to mention anything of rust, dregs, grape-stones, or other things that might be applied.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

->Examination of impure and imperfect copper to see how much perfect metal it contains.<-

**COPPER** that is still raw and impure, with a certain weight of its own—namely a hundred-weight—is cooked moderately in a crucible within a circular hearth before the bellows with double the amount of lead (if indeed lead is not already in it) or one-and-a-half times (if it contains some). This continues until, the lead being consumed, the copper button <note>original: *regulus*</note> shines out. From the quality of this, judgment is made concerning the rest. It can also be purified to its own rule and perfection without lead on a plate.

In some places, copper is not worked to exact purity, but is sold in large masses after smelting,

<margin>On page 95 of the foreign editions, circumspect craftsmen command that several tests be made and that the judgment be drawn from the average of these. For in a single test, a deception often occurs, such that more is consumed in the furnace than was indicated by the sample.</margin>
...it is refined, and in other places it is re-cooked in specialized workshops. Likewise, the crumbling loaves of metal, from which silver has been separated by lead, are not yet uniform. Therefore, the Masters sometimes wish to learn from the <term>Zygostatae</term> <note>public weighers of metals</note> or the <term>Docimastae</term> <note>official assayers</note> how much hope of exact purity remains in a large heap or mass. This can be expedited in the prescribed manner. Sometimes, however, there is iron present, sometimes lead, and occasionally harsh and earthy minerals or darkening spirits, from which the copper becomes rough to the touch and brittle, or is defiled by spots; indeed, there is sometimes a defect in the very root of the mixture that cannot be corrected by common art. Hence, one may see copper that hardly bears the hammer and shatters under its blows, in which the <term>chalcanthum</term> <note>original: *chalcanthum*; copper-sulfate or vitriol</note> is too earthy and burnt. There is another kind that is lemon-yellow, and for amending such things, chemists have discovered excellent methods, though not all are profitable for use in workshops due to the expense. According to <term>Geber</term> <note>a legendary 8th-century Arab alchemist whose Latin works were foundational to European chemistry</note>, frequent metallic "descension" <note>a process where molten metal flows downward through a filter to purify it</note> purifies it, as does calcination, washing, dissolution, and reduction. It can also be dissolved into granules and washed frequently with water of tartar, and then reduced back to metal, especially if polluted sulfur clings to it. In the workshops, the "perfecting hearth" performs this, where the impure masses of copper or the crumbling loaves are melted in their own furnace and cooked before the bellows until their purity and softness in the iron rods respond to the worker's wish under the hammer. <term>Fachsius</term> <note>Modestin Fachs, a renowned 16th-century author on the art of assaying</note> undertakes a hard and dangerous province when he tests this by means of lead; for it is well known that lead consumes copper or bronze in the fire and turns it into ashes, as has often been learned from the preceding chapters, and he himself indeed foresaw this difficulty. Therefore, he strives to defend his opinion, but the best defense is Diligence, attention, and skill in the examination. I shall not be burdened to set forth his method and discussion in English words.

<margin>Of intractable copper.</margin>
There are various kinds of rough and intractable <term>copper</term> (he says). For some are held to be "iron-bearing," some "lead-bearing," and others are refractory because of harsh minerals. Those that are iron-bearing and rough from wild minerals he examines thus: coat the inside of a shell or earthen crucible with <term>litharge</term> <note>original: *lithargyrum*; lead oxide used as a flux</note>. Place a hundredweight of copper with double the amount of pure lead, and melt them before the bellows; when they are melted, blow the air gradually and circumspectly so that the lead is consumed, and diligently watch for the moment the lead vanishes, lest you lose the <term>regulus</term> <note>the pure button of metal found at the bottom of a crucible</note> of copper through negligence; for the heat attacks and scatters the copper. Prepare four specimens of these, as the gravity of the matter requires. Collect the four grains into a sum, and according to the proportion of the button from the value of four hundredweights of rough copper, conclude how much pure and regular metal is in the whole. This is the most certain way to find the value of perfect copper in the impure. And if some "know-it-all" should object that the copper is burnt and scattered by the lead and the heat of the fire: let him keep his opinion. Let him know, however, that even the smelters do not always hit the mark in perfecting copper, but sometimes produce more and sometimes less, and burn it during the roasting. Nothing is left to chance for the diligent man, etc. For lead-bearing copper, there is no need to add as much lead as for the iron-bearing and other refractory types, for it is already supplied with lead by its own nature. If you add a hundred and a half weight of lead to one hundredweight of copper, you will obtain a button of almost pure copper. Otherwise, the way of working is the same as in the former case. If at any time you cannot look into the material in the furnace and consider it diligently because of the fervor of the fire, pull out the crucible with cold <term>pyragra</term> <note>original: *pyragra*; fire-tongs</note>: quench the copper, and strike it in a mortar, or cleave it. By this very act, you can grasp whether it is sufficiently soft and workable or not. If not yet, put it back in the fire and blow. But if the lead fails before purity is reached, add a little more and cook it thoroughly to perfection. It is difficult and troublesome to complete or to learn this examination. For the brightness of the dross and the grain dazzles and breaks the sharp sight of the eyes. Nor is so much heat to be endured in any other work. These are the words of <term>Fachsius</term>. You see that he cannot deny that there is danger in using lead. But he excuses it by the equal error of the smelters. It suffices, however, if this is the safest way, in which we grant something to the assertion of a skilled craftsman who has performed his duty well, if he acted rightly according to the rules of the art, although he may not always lead the matter to the desired result because of the disposition of the material and other factors. It is better to finish with a minimal loss than to leave the metal crude. Nor do I see what way could be so safe that absolutely nothing is lost from the copper. There is something to be said for steeping and washing, but that does not remove all defects. A liquor must be found that spares the copper entirely but consumes or separates the iron, lead, and other impure mixtures. In other cases, they also use cements. But a more exact purity is proposed for Chemists than for the workshops. Therefore, the former can reach their goal while the latter cannot, since common copper, even when esteemed as perfect and regular, is still impure to the Chemists. And there is also some protection for them in transmutation.

Related to this work is the exploration of how much soft white lead <note>tin</note> is contained in the hard and spotted kind, and how much steel is in iron. The fire can reveal this. For it is customary in the workshops to re-cook hard tin so that the hard masses are melted through the "descending plates" of a notched hearth or sloping crucibles; and when the degenerate portion subsides, the nobler part is drawn off and cast into bars, leaving the tin-dross <note>original: *diphryge stanneo*</note> behind, which is also done in perfecting copper. Indeed, they judge that steel can be made from iron by its hardness and its fusion. <margin>The making of steel.</margin> That iron is fit for <term>stomoma</term> <note>original: *stomoma*; the Greek term for tempered steel or the "hard mouth" of a tool</note> which is <term>well-refined</term> <note>original: *εὔξηλον* (euxēlon); meaning well-worked or high quality</note>: ductile, and yet also hard, which qualities are likewise known by the benefit of the fire. This is the selection. The operation, however, is completed with fluxes and quenching, and by forcing it with hammers. For the iron is cooked with fluxes in a blacksmith's hearth with a crucible until the mass softens. This glowing mass is widened on the anvil and immediately quenched; once quenched, it is broken, and it is judged whether it has reached the perfection of steel. Broken into portions again, it is mixed with fluxes, re-cooked, and worked by quenching and the hammer until it responds. Thus can the experiment also be established in the "lesser art" <note>small-scale laboratory chemistry versus industrial smelting</note>.

### CHAPTER XIX.

-> On the examination of mixed metals, and how much of one is in the other. <-

**T**HE examination of mixed metals is that by which it is explored how much of some are in others, and it is completed through the skills of separating. The weights of the separated parts are compared among themselves.
Just as there are two kinds of mixtures, the natural and the artificial, so also can this examination be divided in a twofold way as first...

...first, the ratio of natural mixtures shall be handed down, as they are extracted from the ore, or as they are otherwise presented pure by nature; afterwards, the ratio of artificial mixtures in <term>pagamenta</term> <note>original: *pagamentis*; a term for bullion or base metal used for coinage</note>, as they call it, in coins, and in the works of craftsmen. In both cases, we must first consider those in which gold is sought, and afterwards silver, etc.

# CHAPTER XX.

## How much gold is in other metals.

<margin>Quartering.</margin>
**G**old is found either in silver, in base metals, or in mercury. That which is in silver—whether alone or mixed with some part of the others—is first <term>cupelled</term> <note>original: *fulminatur*; the process of heating an alloy with lead in a "cupel" to oxidize and remove base metals</note> with lead, a specific weight being taken. The resulting grain is weighed. The loss is noted and ascribed either to copper, or to other metals and impurities that were mixed in. Afterward, if the silver contains gold, it is separated with <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: *aqua forti*; nitric acid</note>. The gold left behind is washed with warm water, then cold; thirdly, it is roasted in a small vessel and weighed. The silver is recovered from the aqua fortis and cupelled in a crucible with lead, or melted in a basin with borax and evaluated by its weight. But if it is "silvered gold" <note>gold containing a high amount of silver</note>, one must test with <term>touch-needles</term> <note>original: *acus probatorias*; metal rods of known purity used to compare color against an unknown sample</note> how much silver is inside; or, if it is a coin or a craftsman’s ingot, the same must be learned from its legal value. Afterward, enough pure and unmixed silver must be added so that it is in a triple proportion to the gold—that is, one part gold to three parts silver—which they call <term>quartation</term> <note>original: *quartare*; the metallurgical practice of ensuring gold is only 25% of the alloy so that acid can penetrate the metal to dissolve the silver</note>. The resulting mass is forced into a tube and separated by aqua fortis. The weights of the separated metals are evaluated after subtracting the added amount; however, in both cases, one or two grains must be subtracted from the weight of the gold, according as you have learned the aqua fortis leaves behind, because that amount of silver remains in the gold.

If the gold is in base metals, it is smelted into lead and cupelled, and if silver is present, one proceeds as before. There is also a place for <term>cementation</term> <note>a dry refining process using salts and heat</note>. If it is with mercury, it is separated through leather and then set apart by aqua fortis or fire, in a vessel or by sublimation. Afterward, it is cupelled.

Lest you labor in vain in this examination, you ought to know beforehand whether there is any gold in the mass or not. [Gold in water is heavier than silver, even though their weight in air may be equal. Therefore, if you wish to know whether there is gold in the silver, <term>Ercker</term> <note>Lazarus Ercker (c. 1530–1594), a famous mining engineer and author of a definitive work on assaying</note> orders you to make equal masses in the air, one of pure silver, the other of the sample to be tested: then, using a small balance, lower them into water. The heavier one is indicated to contain gold. Testing is also done by drawing ductile wires. It is asked: what is the reason for this weight? Is it because gold "absorbs" the moisture? But gold is most compact. Nevertheless, those who cast many gold coins into a vial full of water without it overflowing offer this as the cause. This test seems uncertain, since the same metal, affected in different ways, may be heavier or lighter than itself.] Therefore, it is rubbed on a <term>touchstone</term> <note>original: *coticulae*; a dark stone used for testing the purity of gold by the color of the streak it leaves</note>, and aqua fortis or a coloring agent applied to it indicates the truth. You could also consult cementation, ignition and quenching in sharp liquids, and aqua fortis: but the touchstone is more efficient. Doubt occurs, however, when gold is hidden by other metals or a feigned color. Where gold appears immediately to the eyes, as in gold coins, unless the color is sophisticated <note>faked</note>, the matter is settled by itself. But a deception will appear if you apply a coloring agent to the hammered mass and make it white-hot, and afterward quench it in <term>mercury</term> <note>original: *viva*; short for *argentum vivum*</note> sharpened with <term>sal ammoniac</term>. In a mixture of gold and silver, as well as of other metals, this is usually observed: that <margin>When it is called Gold.</margin> a mass is called "gold" if it has more gold than four <term>lots</term> <note>original: *lothones*; a unit of weight equal to 1/16th of a mark, roughly 14.6 grams</note> per <term>mark</term> <note>original: *marca*; a weight of roughly 234 grams</note>. But if it is four lots or <margin>When Silver.</margin> below, down to three <term>denarii</term> <note>small weight units</note>, it is called "gilded silver." So also "gilded iron," lead, and <margin>Silvered gold.</margin> the rest. Conversely, gold also takes its name from what is mixed with it, being called "silvered," "leaded," etc.

The weight used here is almost always according to marks. In the business of moneyers, distribution is considered according to <term>carats</term>; in contracts of purchase, according to coins or denarii. For easy recognition of quartation, lest there be need for anxious calculation, <term>Fachs</term> <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century master of the mint and author of a book on assaying</note>, <term>Budelius</term> <note>Renerus Budelius, a legal scholar and expert on coinage</note>, and others present a table to the eyes. In this, once the value of the gold in a mark is known, the amount of silver to be added is easily found. For example, if in a mark of gold (which is estimated from five lots), there are five half-ounces, there is a need for two ounces of silver to be added. For the computation is made based on sixteen lots. If, therefore, there are only five in a whole mark, there will be eleven half-ounces of silver (either pure or mixed), and there ought to be triple the five—that is, fifteen half-ounces. Therefore, four are missing, or two ounces. It is the same in the others: for instance, if a mark has six half-ounces of gold, eight of silver must be added; seven of gold require twelve of silver; eight require one mark; nine, a mark with four lots; ten, a mark with eight lots; eleven, twenty-eight half-ounces; twelve, two marks; thirteen, two marks with four lots; fourteen, two marks and eight lots; fifteen, two marks with twelve half-ounces; <margin>7 carats of gold require 4 carats of silver; 8 carats of gold ask for the same amount of silver, etc.</margin> sixteen-lot gold requires three marks of silver, although it is then pure. There is a similar ratio for carats: except that carats must then be reconciled with lots; for example, gold of twelve carats requires twenty-four carats of silver—that is, sixteen lots, or a whole mark. The question is: why <margin>Why pure silver must be used for quartation.</margin> must pure silver be used in quartation and not mixed; and why is quartation estimated from touch-needles or coins, when it is established that they are mixed? It must be known that pure silver must be taken because the cause is distributed in the quartation. For the specimen was previously assigned to the cupel, so that it is sufficiently clear what was joined to the foreign material, or at least that it contains no gold. The things that separate after quartation are either of pure silver (provided pure silver was taken) or of impure; and if we wish both to be preserved, we shall labor. Otherwise, if the silver is recovered through the cupel, the copper will nevertheless perish, nor does it hinder the examination in any way. If, however, you were to set up the test without a preliminary cupellation, then a greater necessity would appear, because you would be ignorant of the value of the foreign mixture, unless you wished most laboriously to track down what portion is the mixture of silver to be added, and what portion is the larger amount separated from the mass by the acid. A more correct judgment is taken from the touch-needles after cupellation, if they are mixed from gold and silver alone. If these are lacking, we can also use others. For a small mixture of copper cannot greatly corrupt the judgment of the value of the gold and silver. Moreover, for quartation, the mixing of the silver and the small mass is done via the cupel. For by adding appropriate lead, we place them together in an ash crucible, and we mix those metals exactly through the smallest parts, and afterward we separate the lead in the same operation. In the separation of gold and mercury by aqua fortis, caution must be applied lest silver be present, which is not afterward easily separated—

...is joined by Mercury. Therefore, we will more correctly employ distillation through ascent or descent. In this way, even silver can be preserved. But afterward, the material must be <term>cupelled</term> <note>original: *fulminanda*; the process of heating an alloy with lead in a porous cup or "cupel" to oxidize and remove base metals</note>, and separated by <term>parting</term> <note>original: *per sortem*; the chemical separation of gold and silver</note>. ## How "gilded silver" should be tested.

If you wish to examine <term>gilded silver</term> <note>silver containing a small amount of gold</note> and know how much gold and silver a <term>mark</term> <note>a unit of weight, roughly 233 grams</note> contains: weigh out two marks compared against each other using the weight of coins. <term>Cupel</term> <note>original: *fulmina*</note> these with lead, as is done with used silver [lead, however, usually subtracts something from the silver] or worked silver. You will recognize how much lead you ought to add mostly from the <term>touchstone</term> <note>original: *coticula*; a small dark stone used to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak they leave</note>. If it is regular used silver, add five times as much lead; if worked silver, seven times; if it contains less pure silver than worked silver (which usually happens), eight or nine times as much lead must be added. Weigh the cupelled grains to see if they are equal. If they are, examine the weight of one, which is the gold and silver combined, and it should be noted. What was lost was copper or some impurity. Take two marks of this gilded silver; pour three <term>drachms</term> <note>a small unit of weight</note> of <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note> over one placed in a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original: *cucurbitula*; a gourd-shaped glass flask</note>, and close the glass well so the spirit does not escape. Place it on a tripod over gentle coals, and the glass turns yellow as the acid acts on the mass. Let it work for a quarter of an hour, and gradually increase the heat so the hand can barely bear the glass. When it becomes white again, and the water sends out large bubbles and sometimes leaps out as if jumping, it is enough. Remove the coals little by little, so the flask does not shatter from sudden cold. When it has cooled, pour off the first water and pour back about a drachm of new water. Dissolve as before, so that if the first was weaker than it should have been and had left some silver with the gold, it may be dissolved by the second. Finally, when the aqua fortis is entirely saturated with silver <note>The text says "saturated with gold," but in this process, the acid dissolves the silver, leaving the gold behind</note>, first pour over it warm water and wash it, then cold; and in a clean dish that does not crack in fire, or a golden shell, first dry it gradually, then heat it thoroughly until it glows, and it regains its native color; for before it was purplish. Weigh this gold, but in such a way that it outweighs slightly, because of the remains of silver which the aqua fortis did not corrode. This examination having been finished, perform the second on the other mass. Compare both completed results to know if anything was lost, which can easily happen. If you wish to reduce the golden powder or gold thus tested into a grain, wrap it in lead foil and cupel it. Compare this pure grain with the previous whole grain, and you will see how much gold and silver it contains; then pronounce on the total value.

<margin>The necessity of quartation.</margin>
You should also know that some people dissolve one of the cupelled grains, in which gold and silver are still together, with aqua fortis, and think they will find the gold in it just as well as in a mixed mark; but experience teaches that in this examination, the value of the gold is not found as exactly as in a mixed mark. <gloss>Therefore, it is helpful that <term>quartation</term> <note>the metallurgical process of adding silver to gold until the gold is only one-quarter of the weight, allowing nitric acid to penetrate and dissolve the silver</note> must be added: otherwise nothing different appears from the previous method. It is known from other sources that the cupelled grains must be flattened and shaped into tubes before they are placed in aqua fortis.</gloss> Moreover, the things placed here, he explains in another place in the same book in this sense: Regarding silver and gilded granules, likewise in copper, veins, and any others. Weigh one mark of very pure silver and the same amount of pure gold. Melt both together by cupellation with a certain weight of lead, using a sufficiently strong heat. Then you will find the constancy of gold and the inconstancy of silver. <gloss>Namely, if you dissolve it with aqua fortis to test how much silver is left in the gold: and afterward, proceed according to this judgment in a similar or the same mixture.</gloss> If the aqua fortis were weaker and did not attack the grain: gold is abundant in it. Therefore, add triple the amount of pure silver, and mix with lead by cupellation in a small dish. Form it into a tube, pour two drachms of aqua fortis over it in a small flask, and dissolve.

## How un-stamped "silvered gold" should be tested.

*Raw gold is tested by coin-weight for the sake of merchants: but by <term>carats</term> <note>original: *caracta*</note> in mints. The mass is cut above and below with a chisel between the center and the edges. The carved-out portion is compared with a golden needle made for carats by a line on a touchstone, so that we may examine the value. The value in carats is reduced to the value in marks, which are divided into <term>lots</term> <note>original: *lothonibus*; a weight unit where 16 lots make 1 mark</note>, drachms, and coins, so that when you have examined from the needle how many carats the gold is (it is known, moreover, that a mark is equivalent to 24 carats), you may then gather how many lots it is: as if it were nineteen carats, you would say, "24 carats make a mark or sixteen lots; how many lots will nineteen carats make?" 12 lots, two drachms, and two coins will result. You can also achieve the same thing immediately in a table prepared for this. Once the value in parts of a mark is known: triple the silver must definitely be added to the gold. But since that already contains, in the given example, eleven lots of silver with one drachm and two coins: you add only twenty-six lots with a <term>ficulicus</term> <note>a small fractional weight or scrap of metal used to balance the scales</note>. Make two specimens weighed against each other. Mix the silver with the gold in a cupel by cupelling quite hotly, with five times the lead added.* <gloss>By cupellation they are not only mixed, but copper and other impurities are separated.</gloss> *Weigh the grains. Note the loss. It was copper or similar things. Afterward, flatten the grains lengthwise like foils: and heat them until they glow quite often so they do not break; and when they have reached the thickness of parchment, they must be heated for the last time* <gloss>those heatings are done for the reason that they can be dilated and extended without a crack or break: therefore, after each time they must be struck again with a hammer</gloss> *and not shaken, so that the aqua fortis may act on them more promptly. Roll them into tubes, yet not too tight, so that the water can flow between and corrode. Afterward, pour an ounce of well-prepared aqua fortis, or according to the size of the weight, into a small flask. Take care that it begins to work gradually, and so increase the fire little by little for half an hour, until the glass becomes white. When the first water is poured out, put back half an ounce of new water, etc. (they agree in their instructions with the previous ones). Having poured in cold water, pour the tube out of the flask into a <term>sweetening bowl</term> <note>original: *concha dulcorateria*; a vessel used to wash acid from the metal</note>, and let the water remain for a little while. Then pour it out and dry the gold gradually in a golden pan. Then also dissolve the other tube in the manner described. Weigh them. If they are equal: you have not erred. Also examine the weight of one, once the remains of the aqua fortis have been removed. In the calculation, you first consider the weight of the gold: then of the silver added, then of the excess silver that was with the gold: finally, the loss in cupellation. It usually happens that in a needle rubbed on a touchstone, the exact value is not always apparent, and often one errs in quartation by an excess or defect of one unit. But such a small amount cannot spoil the test. (Why not? Indeed the value of gold...)*

...will be established, but the value for the silver will be as erroneous as the excess or defect was. What follows is plainer advice, although more laborious. <margin>From this, truly, loss will arise for the buyer or seller.</margin> If you cannot recognize the difference from the needle <note>assaying needles were tipped with known alloys to compare colors on a touchstone</note>: try in quartation without the needle, by conjecture, having added silver of a certain weight. (Add as much silver as will seem necessary to you: note its weight, however.) If it should likewise happen that the tubes break in dissolving: do not judge the assay lost, but collect the gold diligently: and thus a trial has also been made regarding a certain value according to which you can arrange the quartation.

## ->EXAMINATION OF WORKED GOLD.<-

Lest there be need for a troublesome testing or trial, have three types of needles ready: made of gold and copper; gold and silver; and gold, silver, and copper. Consult these, and arrange the quartation according to their indication. It is more advisable to follow the coin <term>alloy</term> <note>original: *ligam*; the legal standard of metal purity in currency</note>, as they call it, established by laws. From this, you easily recognize how much silver and copper is mixed in with the gold. (Provided, of course, the coin is regular. But if it is counterfeit: you are deceived. Therefore, one must return to the assaying proof.) And how much silver you ought to add. Indeed, you can also see whether the <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid, used to dissolve silver but not gold</note> detracts anything from the gold. Afterwards, <term>cupel</term> <note>original: *fulmina*; the process of heating an alloy with lead to oxidize base metals</note> the worked gold with a fivefold amount of lead so that you may notice the departure of the copper. Then <term>quart</term> <note>original: *quarta*; adding silver so the gold is 1/4 of the total mass</note> with silver, and mix both through a fivefold amount of lead in the cupellation. Dissolve as before. If the tube remains whole and turns purple <note>a sign of certain gold/silver reactions in the acid</note>, you will conclude that you have quarted well. Wash with warm water first, afterwards with cold; you can even place the tube on a clean linen cloth so that it may be better dried (unless gold filings or grains are present, which are not easily collected from linen). Thus finish the other specimen as well. You will subtract two grains from the tubes. If it is of 22 carats, it means that so much silver was left behind from the quartation, etc.

Moreover, those things which he taught separately concerning gilded silver, silvered gold, worked and unworked metal, are later repeated toward the end of the booklet, where nothing else worthy of note occurs, except that he declares the testing assay more clearly through an example. For he says this of it: Mix a <term>mark</term> <note>a unit of weight, approximately 233 grams</note> of mixed gold with triple the amount of pure silver (which is entirely free of gold) with lead through cupellation in a small cup. Dissolve the beaten and rolled-up grains into a tube for half an hour: do not care whether the tube breaks or stays whole. Wash the gold well with warm fresh water and dry it in a gold phial. According to the weight you find (having subtracted, of course, the weight of the silver added, and taking into account how much of it was mixed), arrange the quartation according to that. If the value of the gold is found to be up to seven carats: the mixture does not need quartation, for it has enough silver already. It must, however, be cupelled so that the copper may depart, and you can state the proper value of the silver and gold. Lead is increased in such cupellation according to the abundance of copper, for instance, a sevenfold or eightfold amount is added if there are four or five carats of copper, etc. <margin>Agricola’s assay in worked gold.</margin> Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy"</note> differs little from the method of Fachs <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century master of the mint and author on assaying</note>. He prescribes roughly thus: The value of silvered gold, or gilded silver (for he joins all such things) is explored on the <term>touchstone</term> <note>original: *coticula*</note> by the line of a rubbed needle. The silver that is detected is quarted, and let it be a mixture. A small ash cup is prepared in the furnace. Lead is put in: a little later half an ounce of copper [æris], or six drachms, is added if there is no copper in the mass; and this for the reason that the cup does not attack the gold and silver and consume some.

Finally, put in the specimen, or the small mass mixed of gold and silver, which you wish to examine. Boil until the lead and copper are consumed. Let the same be done in a new mass, so that you have two specimens. Bend the cupelled grains, beaten into thin sheets, so that a tube is made. Pour nine drachms of greater weight of <term>aqua fortis</term> of the third strength into a distillation vessel. The redder the water: the better it is. When bubbles like pearls adhere to the tubes, pour out the water shortly after, and pour in new. When white bubbles appear, let the tubes be removed and boiled in bubbling spring water. Afterwards, having been thrown into a gold phial held by the hand, let them be dried gradually over a gentle fire. Soon let the phial be placed on the coals and covered with charcoal, and let the fire be stirred by the breath of a bellows until a blue flame appears. Finally, let the equality of the weights be explored, and let each be weighed even alone. One four-grain weight [granulum] should not be counted on account of the remains of silver inseparable by aqua fortis. These are Agricola’s words: In which it is surprising why he adds copper to the cupellation. The reason regarding the "violence of the cups" is of no importance; for the cup must be prepared so that it retains no sharpness at all, nor can it detract anything. In a larger fire he advises the same, and adds: if a mark has more copper than five or six drachms, soon let the gold and silver be joined again. He separates there also through aqua fortis, <term>cement</term> <note>a refining process using salts and heat</note>, sulfur, antimony, composite fluxes, etc. In these, copper is more rightly added than in cupellation, aqua fortis excepted. If the coin is gold consisting of gold and copper, the assay differs not at all from silver coin; but if it also contains silver, the method is the same but with the addition of separation through aqua fortis; otherwise, needles and coloring are used. But enough concerning gold and silver.

## ->HOW MUCH AND WHETHER GOLD IS IN COPPER.<-

Fachs denies that there is gold in perfect and regular copper from which silver has been separated, as the Venetians are said to assert. But if some is indeed given, he orders it to be examined for silver, in that manner in which copper is otherwise usually explored. For since the gold is already fixed, and everything volatile is consumed through the smelting of the copper: it is not to be feared that it will flee. If likewise a grain exists there in the appearance of silver during cupellation: he thinks aqua fortis must be used to separate the silver from the gold, as has already been sufficiently described. (But the instruction should not be set down so much for separated copper as for a mixture made by any means. It will therefore be sound that we then elicit gold from copper by adding much lead, just as we do silver from copper. Then let us proceed through cupellation, and if necessary, even aqua fortis. Chemists, because the assay is done in a small quantity where loss is easy, would explore it more concisely immediately through aqua fortis: or cement, or antimony, or another flux, to draw it out into a <term>button</term> <note>original: *regulum*; a small bead of pure metal</note> in a conforming crucible. It might also be arranged in a triangular crucible through the consumption of volatile metals by fluxes, etc. No one perhaps melts gold into copper; yet if both were confused as in Corinthian brass, or gilded plates, or auriferous Indian copper, the art ought to show the protection of separation and examination.)

## ->HOW MUCH AND WHETHER GOLD IS IN BRASS.<-

It is recognized through aqua fortis. For the material is dissolved in it, and the <term>calx</term> <note>original: *calx*; a powder or oxide left after heating or chemical treatment</note> of gold remains, which is washed from the sharpness, and

It cannot be done through lead, since <term>zinc ore</term> <note>original: *cadmia*</note> causes damage to gold and silver if it is <term>blasted</term> <note>original: *fulminetur*; the process of cupellation where metals are heated until impurities oxidize</note> with lead.
(<term>Lumpy zinc ore</term> <note>original: *Cadmia glebosa*</note>, which they call <term>calamine</term> <note>original: *Galmiam*</note>, has volatile spirits. Thus <term>zinc oxide</term> <note>original: *pompholyx*</note> is born from it. Nevertheless, since it has for the most part been placed in the smelting of brass, and has reached an earthy consistency: I do not know if one should entirely agree with this claim. Certainly, it is sometimes used in <term>cementation</term> <note>a process of refining gold by heating it with salts</note> for fixing: and who would think zinc ore would harm gold as much as <term>antimony</term> <note>original: *stibium*</note>, which is the "final punishment of gold," as Philip Ulstad says? <note>Philippus Ulstadius was a 16th-century author of "The Sky of the Philosophers," a famous book on distillation</note> Nor should you think gold would then be volatile because it is cooked into copper, when it has sustained so many fires with it. If it sustains antimony without damage, why not lead and zinc ore and copper? If there is nonetheless fear, and you wish to act more securely, add some iron, as above.)

## Whether and how much gold is in tin, lead, or iron.

*Examine these metals according to the precepts for seeking silver in the same. If nothing remains in the blast: they contain neither gold nor silver. But if a grain remains, yet you do not recognize the gold: consult <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note>. There is no need for fluxes here, as in other gold assays: since while those metals are smelted, the gold is already fixed.*

<margin>To separate gold and silver from white lead while keeping all parts intact.</margin>
(It is well known that silver and gold are born in tin. But they deny an art has been found for separating both while keeping all parts intact. For its nature is so hostile to "perfect bodies" <note>gold and silver</note> that it takes them everywhere into its own nature and corrupts them, as some wish, or rather it is a friend, because it is so familiar with mercury—after gold and lead—it even admits them into its innermost chambers, and retains them, and does not let go unless it is destroyed. But perhaps it may not require such profound industry to find a water that only <term>calcines</term> <note>reduces to a powder through heat or acid</note> the tin, leaving the silver and gold behind. Moreover, the <term>calx</term> <note>the powdered residue</note> is recoverable, as Geber witnesses, even when it has flowed into a liquid, though not without skill in a descending furnace, lest it turn to glass. We see tin is easily calcined by dissolved <term>blue vitriol</term> <note>original: *chalcantho*; copper sulfate</note>, and from others also it turns into <term>ceruse</term> <note>original: *cerussam*; white lead pigment</note>, which they call "Spanish white," by which however gold and silver are little or not at all affected. Truly, that ceruse can be reduced is common knowledge, especially if it is mixed with melted tin, etc. Let effort be given entirely so that only the tin is calcined by any means, with the gold and silver unharmed, and let the powder be recovered. Craftsmen say the powder floats upon the lead and can be drawn off, etc.)

## Whether and how much gold is in mercury.

*Weigh by a hundred-weight, one or two units, according to the total weight. Squeeze firmly through a <term>soft leather</term> <note>original: *alutam*; a piece of chamois used to filter liquid mercury</note>. Collect what remained in it as diligently as possible, and place it in a pot so the mercury may slowly expire over a light fire. When the smoke has ceased, make it white-hot, and allow it to cool. Note the weight. Enclose the powder in a lead foil rolled up like paper. Blast it in a <term>cupel</term> <note>original: *capella*; a porous vessel for assaying</note>. Explore the weight. In the grain will be gold and silver. However much decreased during the blasting, that much was joined of copper and other impurities, and went into the winds. If it was copper, the small dish is blackened, since no metal darkens the ash-cup like copper. Note that loss. Separate the gold and silver through aqua fortis. If it does not dissolve, it is rich in gold; therefore wash the grain, and weigh out double the silver, and having melted both, commit them again to <term>gold-dissolving water</term> <note>original: *aqua chrysolca*; aqua regia</note>. Finally wash the gold, and weigh it after it has been ignited in a pot. You will find the value of the silver by subtracting that which you added. From this it will first be clear how much was pure mercury: Then how much gold, silver, copper, and other impurity remained within the leather: thirdly how much copper: fourthly how much pure silver: fifthly how much gold the hundred-weight contained.*

This investigation is usually instituted when mercury is found in rivers, or mines, especially in gold-bearing mountains: And the method of examination is almost similar if it contains other metals. Others more gladly <term>sublime</term> it <note>heat it into vapor</note>, or distill it through retorts. As for what is said about copper blackening the dish the most, so that one may decide from that whether it is present, we can refer this to the burnt sulfur, of which there is a greater abundance in blue vitriol. The neighboring colors—red, yellow, green, black—pass easily into one another through combustion. And <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: *ærugo*</note>, which is made copiously from copper, just like vitriol, on account of the sulfurous fatness which is joined to it—as shown by the "sweet oil of vitriol" which is made from the blue vitriol of copper—is readily stained. Copper itself attracts and sustains black filth. When therefore it is drunk up by the ash of the dishes, or the black and heavy smoke of the copper is reflected during the blasting and works its way into the cupel: that blackness emerges from it.

# CHAPTER XXI.

## Concerning silver with metals other than gold.

**S**ilver exists with other imperfect metals in two ways: For either it is abundant itself, such as <term>worked silver</term> <note>original: *argentum fabrile*; silver used for objects</note> and silver for coinage: or it is present in a smaller quantity, and that most especially in black lead, white lead, in tin, copper, and mercury, although sometimes several also run together.
Worked silver, and silver for coinage—whether it be in a mass and still raw, or already fashioned—is reduced to minute particles: it is mixed with lead and blasted to purity. The quantity of lead is smaller in the purer sorts, which have less copper. The minute particles are either grains, to which <term>billow silver</term> <note>original: *pagamentum*; base silver or currency</note> is usually reduced—or raw silver of the mint, and tiny coins, or small segments of foil, such as are accustomed to be made in smithing, and coins having a <term>drachma</term> <note>a small unit of weight</note> and more. Once the blast is done, if gold is present, it is also sent to this examination: if none, the calculation is made by weight, from which it is clear how much foreign mixture was present of copper, or white lead (which goldsmiths are sometimes accustomed to add) or black lead, etc. Having subtracted the grain of lead, however, and if anything happened during the granulation, burning, and melting, account is also held of that.
Silvered imperfect metals, which have a copious and sufficient amount of lead, after they have been cut and the samples lawfully mixed, are blasted. To the rest, lead is added according as they abound in copper and impurities, or if some lead in...

<header>On the Assaying of the Proving Art, Part 2.</header>

# On the Assaying of the Proving Art, Part 2.

*If they have [impurities] in their mixture. Lead is always more abundant where there was previously no tin, copper, or rapacious filth, or a great deal of it. If, during the tempering, something resistant appears, it is subdued by adding a flux. Then, the <term>blasting</term> <note>original: *fulminatio*; the process of cupellation where metals are heated in a furnace to oxidize impurities</note> is instituted according to the art. Silver with <term>sublimated mercury</term> <note>mercuric chloride, used here for purification</note> is purified with washes, then passed through narrow leather and sublimated. The silver is washed out at the bottom and blasted with lead.*

Both nature and art teach that there are various mixtures and temperings of silver with imperfect metals. Civil law allows minters and goldsmiths a mixture of copper at a certain <term>standard</term> <note>original: *pede*; literally "foot," referring to the legally defined ratio of alloy</note>. But these men sometimes also add <term>white lead</term> <note>often referring to tin in this context</note>, from which the silver becomes hard and brittle. <term>Sophists</term> <note>here meaning deceptive counterfeiters or "pseudo-alchemists"</note> mix a small amount of silver lime with arsenic, sublimated mercury, and similar things, and afterwards mix it with copper. Sometimes silver is added to bell-metal, which is tin mixed from copper and white lead; sometimes it is found naturally with iron and bismuth (or "ash-colored lead") and white lead. However, <term>assayers</term> <note>original: *probatores*; officials who test the purity of metals</note> do not usually give accurate instructions for every single tempering, providing only the rules for "unwrought" and "wrought" silver—namely, regarding masses, foils, "fingers," and so on, of raw monetary silver and raw artisan silver. Then they deal with the same materials when they have been worked, even though nature herself might have created the mixture. Afterwards, they likewise treat lead "cakes," or tin made from a mixture of silver and lead (whether rich or poor in silver), silvered copper, white lead containing silver, and specifically bell-metal. They refer the remaining mixtures back to those already mentioned, because they are rarely or never brought into their workshops—such as a mixture of bismuth and silver, which is referred either to the test for white lead or to silver-bearing <term>marcasite</term> <note>iron pyrite or similar sulfide minerals</note>. Likewise, the tempering of silver and iron approaches the rules for silvered copper, just as silver and mercury approach the rules for gold amalgam. Thus, if silver is mixed with antimony, the antimony is considered a rapacious mineral and is tested by the law of such an ore.

Pliny wrote that silver could be detected with red-hot iron rods: if the metal remains white, it is pure; if it turns red, it is rejected as black, although deception can be committed using urine. He also says it is judged good if, when a person breathes on it, the little cloud of moisture is immediately dissipated. But these are common, vulgar tests. Since experience has noted something peculiar even in these common and frequent mixtures, and the authors themselves seem to disagree among themselves—one surpassing the other in skill and the clarity of his instruction—I will add what is found in the works of <term>Fachs</term> <note>Modestin Fachs, author of a famous 1567 guide on assaying</note> and <term>Agricola</term> <note>Georgius Agricola, author of "De Re Metallica" (1556)</note> regarding each point. Where necessary, I will endeavor to compare and illustrate the opinions of both.

When masses of silver, silvered copper, or cakes are offered for examination, the first care is that samples be properly removed with a semicircular cutting chisel. <insert>From each cake of a single smelting, cut out samples from above and below, between the "navel" and the edges, according to the size. Melt the portions in a new crucible quickly before the bellows, etc.; consult <term>Ercker</term> <note>Lazarus Ercker, another definitive 16th-century metallurgical author</note>.</insert> Regarding these, Agricola says, using the example of copper: "Small masses are cut out from several cakes; from small ones, about the size of a hazelnut; from large ones, half a chestnut; from medium ones, a medium amount. They are cut, however, from the middle of the lower part of each cake." These are his words on copper. But they also pertain to other masses or cakes, of whatever kind they may be. One must think, therefore, that this is a general rule, in which the reason must first be sought as to why he seeks a specimen from each individual piece, and not from the whole heap of a single smelting. For if the batches are different, it is obvious that different tests must be instituted, not only because of the inequality of the ores, but also because of the smelting process itself.

<margin>Why a puncture must be sought from the masses of each smelting.</margin>
Next, why does he order the sample to be cut from the middle of the lower part? The cause for this is the unequal mixture of silver. For some cakes are richer, others poorer, though this is not apparent to the eye. Therefore, all must be reduced to an average. Indeed, in the masses of the workshops, the weight of hundredweights and pounds is observed simultaneously, lest any error creep in. Once the investigation is made, the value is pronounced for a single hundredweight as well as for all together, just as it is for the pounds. If several different batches are encountered, they can all be brought to a single calculation so that the owner's expectations are clear; nevertheless, each must be appraised individually by itself. In the second question, neither logic nor experience is satisfactory.

<margin>Agricola's sampling is less certain.</margin>
Thus, it is clear that the cutting should not be done in that way. For in the middle of the lowest part, there is usually less pure metal, and in the upper part, more. For example, if you look at copper cakes, the lead rather floats with the silver during the cooling. In masses of copper, there is likewise more filth and emptiness at the bottom, as also tends to happen in silvered lead. Therefore, far less silver would be produced if you only wanted to explore the bottom parts.

<margin>Fachs's sampling.</margin>
Fachs gives these instructions on the method of cutting: "Some copper contains much lead, and when it is roasted or burned in the furnaces, the lead emerges and floats on the discs. If, therefore, it flows together anywhere and is caught during the carving out of the sample, this specimen will be far richer in silver than the remaining parts." Therefore, you ought to cut as deeply as you can into each cake from both sides, in the middle between the center and the edge. He also warns of this in the preface of his book against the custom of the Mansfeld miners, and adds the reason: that by cutting from both sides in this way, the whole cake or mass reaches a median mixture and does not deceive the craftsman. He orders the same to be done also in masses or cakes of silver-lead, or tin for blasting, silver for roasting, and similar materials. From this, we easily understand that the same craftsman wants this to be observed in all masses or cakes. Nevertheless, a doubt seems to remain, which even so might not allow us to reach an exact result. For it is possible that what is richer has moved toward the margin, or is stuck somewhere else, as there are different and fortuitous moments of flow while the masses, discs, or cakes are being made. Where this is observed, it will be reduced to a temperament in a similar way, or at least the remedy will be the individual cutting of every cake, since it can hardly happen that such an aberration occurs in many or all of them.

<margin>Selection of specimens in foils.</margin>
Foils, thin plates, or coins have their own way of selecting specimens. Since it is consistent that the mixture is equal in plates and foils, a <term>drachma</term> <note>a small unit of weight</note> is taken from all over, beaten out, and cut into small pieces. But if we suspect fraud—since counterfeiters are accustomed to enriching the outer edges while adulterating the middle more heavily—this must first be investigated by scraping the surfaces. Sometimes a part must be cut from the "poor" region and a part from the "rich" region, if we are seeking the value of the whole together; but if only of a part, it is enough to take that part for judgment.
