The same logic applies to larger coins, where one must likewise observe the richness of the edges and ensure no <term>adulteration</term> <note>the practice of debasing coinage by adding cheaper metals like copper</note> has been committed. Usually, however, they are cut through the middle, flattened, and chopped up. With small coins, when a pile is presented, they usually select some from the middle and the edges, and after something has been trimmed off the margin (such as a fourth part), the remainder is chopped up. Weights are taken according to marks, grains, or even <term>denarii</term> <note>a unit of weight used by assayers, not just a coin</note>, especially in contracts between buyers and sellers. In other cases, grains provide a more exact judgment.

Furthermore, the selected parts are reduced to an equal mixture according to the proportion of each, regarding which Fachs says the following:

## HOW MUCH SILVER IS IN THE LEAD CAKES, WHICH YOU MIGHT CALL <term>FULMINATING TIN</term> <note>original: *stannum fulminarium*; here referring to a silver-rich lead or lead-tin alloy prepared for the cupellation process</note>.

*To examine <term>fulminating tin</term> smelted in a single operation from mild ores: cut out pieces from the lead cakes above and below, following the midpoints between the center and the edges. Melt these small sampled masses in a little furnace upon a <term>cupel</term> <note>original: *testa*; a shallow, porous vessel used in assaying</note> or a clay dish, and when you see smoke rising from it, immediately mix it with a heated hook, draw it out, and when the mass has cooled in the dish, pull it away. Inquire how much that tin-smelter has produced; weigh out that much according to your weight of a <term>hundredweight</term> <note>original: *centupondium*; a standard bulk weight for ore</note> and pounds, and <term>blast</term> <note>original: *fulmina*; the process of cupellation where lead is oxidized to reveal silver</note> it in an ash dish while it is sufficiently cold, and you will find the value. Likewise, if you find the tin already melted in the crucible before the furnace of the smelters, take a spoon and draw out a little from deep in the middle: and according to the hundredweight scale, take as much as weighed in the larger weight after it has cooled. Blast that: in this is a shortcut for cutting and melting.*

By the weight and method of cutting—or if it is already liquefied, by drawing it out—this differs from the common examination of lead, provided that no <term>rapacious ores</term> <note>ores that "consume" or waste precious metals during the smelting process</note> or stubborn impurities have adhered to it. Therefore, one must only note the method of sampling, which is the same as with copper; then the weight of each mass according to hundredweights and pounds. The author also warns that if you wish to test the value in a single hundredweight and afterwards pronounce judgment on all by calculation, you will not achieve an exact judgment. However, the reason he adds nothing regarding tin from "harsh" ores is, I believe, because it makes no difference, except that fluxes must be added and the fire must be managed in the same way as is abundantly prescribed for <term>galena</term> <note>lead ore</note> and other veins. This teaching can therefore be sought from there. Agricola commands that it be melted in an iron crucible over a burning furnace. Then, pour it into an iron mold so that it emerges as a "finger" or rod. This he flattens into a foil with a hammer. Then he blasts it for half an hour without a violent fire; for this, it is not necessary to cover even half the furnace with a lid, nor to close the little door. Through these steps, those things can be clarified, although in such a fluid metal, there is no need for casting into a rod or special flattening.

<margin>The <term>blasting</term> <note>cupellation</note> of rich tin in large-scale operations.</margin>
In large-scale operations, the "greater blasting" corresponds to this. For there, too, after the <term>ash-bed</term> <note>original: *cineritio*; the hearth of a cupellation furnace</note> has been prepared by its own art, the tin masses of a certain weight are placed upon it with glowing coals and charcoal. The work is governed by mixing, purifying, diverting the <term>litharge</term> <note>lead oxide</note>, adding fluxes or other refractory materials, and managing the fire entirely as in a small furnace, except that there is no need for a special melting together of the cakes. For it is done in the same operation. Agricola has explained this labor more copiously, and some light can come from there to this treatise, especially regarding tin from intractable metals. I will therefore contract what he has into a summary and present it here to the eyes. Sixty or seventy hundredweights of tin or small cakes (to be blasted) are placed in this way. Three bundles of straw are arranged in the dish so that the lead does not stick. From here, the master inserts some cakes through the hole of the channel, and also some at the sides through the rear opening. Soon, lighting the fire in the dish through the upper hole of the cover, he places the cakes, handed from the left in a circle, near the cap. Rising again, he also places some in the dish. If anything remains, he later places it on the burning wood with a fork. With the cakes thus arranged, he adds charcoal, and having moved the glowing coals at the proper time, he rouses the fire with bellows, also throwing in small pieces of wood. The cakes melt in the space of an hour, and then wood is put in, resting on its supports or stools: and then finally the remaining cakes are brought in with a fork: and if there is also any pure raw silver, it is nevertheless first chopped up and heated in iron dishes. The lead, thus heated for two hours, is stirred with an iron hook so that it becomes thoroughly hot. If it is separated with difficulty from the silver, copper and charcoal dust are thrown in. If the mixture of silver-bearing gold with lead has contracted any impurity from the ore, equal parts of tartar and Venetian glass are thrown in, or <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride, used as a flux</note>, or equal parts of Venetian glass and Venetian soap, or two parts tartar and one part iron rust, etc., so that the additive is eight, twelve, or sixteen ounces, depending on the greater or lesser impurity, for every hundred pounds of material. The lead mixed with charcoal produces a sort of "skin," which must be extracted with a shovel through the channel. Afterwards, for a quarter of an hour, the dish absorbs the lead, and then it jumps and boils. The master draws out a little with an iron spoon and explores how much silver is in that entire mixture. After this, he extracts the "silver foam" with a rag, which is made from the burnt lead and copper, if copper was present. If the silver pours itself out with the litharge, a sharp wedge made of clay is placed in its path. When the silver <term>brightens</term> <note>original: *resplendet*; the "blick" or flash of silver indicating the process is complete</note>, white spots appear, and a little later it becomes altogether white. Soon the bellows are stopped, and a few small vessels of water or beer are poured in so that the <term>regulus</term> <note>the button of pure metal</note> may cool and become whiter. However, he does not pour it directly onto the cake immediately, but into the hearth through an inserted channel: then he lifts the cake with a wedge and cleans it of <term>molybdena</term> <note>here meaning lead dross or residue</note> and litharge. These are the words of Agricola. Such blasting is common to masses of gold, silver, and <term>electrum</term> <note>a natural alloy of gold and silver</note>, although otherwise, "blasting" is proper to silver. The additives he has placed are not suitable for everyone. Therefore, they must be chosen from the above with great judgment, especially for the work of the small furnace. Furthermore, chemists can also complete the same examination through <term>cementation</term> <note>a process of refining gold by heating it with salts</note>, "sharp waters" <note>acids like nitric acid</note>, and similar things, but these must be specifically intended and selected so that no harm comes to the silver. He retains the proven blasting as being safer.

<header>On the Assaying of the Art of Proving, Part 2.</header>

## HOW MUCH SILVER IS IN WHITE LEAD <note>original: *plumbo candido*; in this period, "white lead" refers to tin</note>.

Melt one <term>hundred-weight</term> <note>a standard unit of weight for assaying, not necessarily 100 pounds</note> of copper in a clay crucible before the bellows. When melted, cast in half a hundred-weight of white lead <note>tin</note>. Blow with the bellows so they act upon each other and are mixed. Afterward, add fifteen hundred-weights of black lead <note>common lead</note>; the white lead is "tamed" by the copper, and the copper is most vigorously "revived" by the black lead. Blow a little longer, but not too much, lest it boil over or rise up. In this way, you have mixed these three. Transfer it from the hearth into the small furnace and let it be heated for a little while. Then close the little door of the <term>ash-cupel</term> <note>original: *cineritij*; a vessel made of bone ash used to absorb base metals</note>, so that the white lead and the impurities are consumed and burned away above the black lead. But if the impurity is too stubborn, sprinkle in a little <term>flux</term> <note>a substance used to promote melting and remove impurities</note> made for persistent ores, and let the dross become pure. When you have added the flux, open the lower door of the furnace and increase the heat. After it has entered purely, mix it and tend it with a hook. Once the tin is extracted from the furnace, let it cool; it remains together and is neither scattered nor spread. By this labor, you have "extinguished" <note>transferred</note> the silver of the white lead into the black lead, and you have produced a small mass of tin which still contains copper. <term>Refine</term> <note>original: *fulmina*; literally "to flash," referring to the moment of "brightening" in cupellation when the silver becomes pure</note> it in a well-heated ash crucible and provide a weaker fire, or one cool enough that the silver is not dissipated by the copper. Weigh the grain that comes out of it. Lest you be deceived, you must know beforehand how much silver was in the hundred-weight of copper you added and in the fifteen hundred-weights of lead. Subtract this from that grain.

There are three stages in this work. The first mixes or melts the three metals together. The second cooks out the silver extracted from the white lead through the copper into the black lead, by which the <term>calx</term> <note>the powdery oxide formed by heating a metal</note> of the white lead and the impurities are separated. The third leaves pure silver through the "flash" <note>cupellation</note>, where the fire ought to be milder because copper is a harsh, hot, and burning metal that would easily destroy and dissipate the silver. Sometimes white lead tends to boil up and not enter the mixture immediately, and so flux is added. But another method is more concise, which the same Fachs <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century expert on assaying</note> recorded twice, and which is read in Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola, author of the famous mining text *De Re Metallica*</note>, being the third in this examination. Fachs’s method first <term>calcines</term> <note>burns to an oxide or ash</note> the white lead and proceeds further in this manner: Calcine one hundred-weight of white lead, beaten into a thin plate, upon a clay crucible in the furnace, specifically with the ash-hole open and coals placed on the tile; it will become a white ash. To this, add fifteen hundred-weights of black lead and cook them together like ores, so that the silver moves into the lead; and if it boils up and refuses to enter, add a little flux, and it will be received purely. Finally, refine it <note>by cupellation</note> as was said before. This method is repeated almost at the end of the book, nor does it differ except that instead of a full hundred-weight of white lead, he uses a quarter, and orders two samples to be tested and calcined for a long time in a strong vessel. He cooks the calx with "impoverished" lead <note>lead already stripped of its own silver</note>, as before, after the dross is drawn off. He warns that if it rises into a bubble above the lead, it can be drawn off with an iron wire onto an iron plate, ground upon a stone, mixed with borax, and joined again with fresh lead. However, he requires four times more lead for a quarter-hundred-weight than other tests do.

How does Agricola instruct? Put black lead in a clay crucible until it begins to smoke. Then cast in the white lead. For if it were cast in first, the silver would be consumed—which itself must be noted: if the white lead is in some alloy (such as in bell metal), the silver may separate into the lead during the cooking. Indeed, the white lead boils and turns into ash, which is removed with a thin piece of wood.
<margin>Note this: if you reduce this by the art of Geber <note>an 8th-century alchemist, or the 13th-century "Pseudo-Geber," known for metal reduction techniques</note>, you will recover the tin.</margin>
Refine the remaining mass in an ash crucible. This is Agricola’s method. If I understand anything in this matter, the first method seems better to me. For since tin is the "corruption" of silver and has swallowed it deep within so that it does not suffer loss in substance unless the silver is lost at the same time, the copper is rightly added; by it, the force of that "greedy" metal is diverted from the silver, and the silver takes refuge in the copper, just as if in a stone from the ores in a smelting furnace. Afterward, the separation is made by the "flash." It is almost incredible that white lead can be calcined by another strong fire without the loss of silver, and for this reason, Agricola also avoids it.
<margin>Why tin is calcined faster than lead.</margin>
But his method should not be passed over without judgment. We know the "familiarity" <note>chemical affinity</note> between white and black lead. They mix easily; but since the white is drier and hotter than the black, it is easy to estimate that the former is calcined more quickly than the latter and is spat out when reduced to calx. Silver, however, since it is more "fixed" <note>resistant to fire</note>, remains with the black lead, which it "loves" to stay with as a companion; thus, while the white lead perishes, the black lead defends itself with its moisture, and the silver by its constancy. But since there is some "prerogative of perfection" in white lead—which is apparent from its very easy mixture with mercury and its tinting, and moreover because it has drunk in the silver intimately—it is consistent that even if a grain of silver is produced, not all the silver can be brought forth.
<margin>Spanish White.</margin>
Agricola says that white ash remains. That is "Spanish White" <note>likely bismuth or a high-quality tin oxide</note>, which can be reduced back into white lead by a certain artifice. If the same thing happens in a great fire, the reason for the separation of silver and white lead appears quite clear, provided the trial is made by those who are prudent and experienced. Geber, however, teaches that reduction. Furthermore, lest Fachs's calcination be entirely condemned, I think it serves that white lead in which there is both gold and silver, where one is defended by the other. When he orders flux to be added to stubborn things, one wonders why—in the case of gilded tin, which he ordered to be tested by the same examination as silvered tin (tin here being white lead)—he denied the need for fluxes, adding the argument that when the tin was smelted, the gold reached its own perfection. Has not the silver in the tin also been so smelted that it is no longer foreign to the lead, since we see that any tin is easily drunk up by lead? Surely calcined tin is closer to refractory minerals or <term>marcasites</term> <note>iron pyrites or other brittle metallic minerals</note>. Therefore, if it does not enter the mixture, it must be forced by flux. That it is of some substance is shown by its vitrification <note>turning to glass</note> and the nature of white lead pigment. I think a similar labor is owed to ash-colored lead, although it may also suit marcasite.

## HOW MUCH SILVER IS IN BELL
## METAL.

From the individual masses or fragments, <unclear>extract</unclear> or knock off a small part and crush them all like poppy seeds. Weigh out two hundred-weights against each other. To each also add fifteen hundred-weights of black lead <insert>[Ercker <note>Lazarus Ercker, a prominent 16th-century metallurgist</note> adds: or 16 hundred-weights of lead to a half-part of tin. For it is smelted more fervently and slowly. Otherwise, the assay is the same as with impure and harsh copper.]</insert> Place the tin in the small furnace upon a clay crucible and, with the fire moved near, heat it sufficiently, yet not so much that they

<meta>Catchword: Nothing</meta>

*...let the grains flow together and melt. Then add the black lead <note>original: "plumbum [nigrum]"; common lead used as a solvent in assaying</note> gradually, so that the tin <note>original: "stannum"; here referring to the white lead mixture</note> does not cool down. When it begins to boil and emit smoke, close the ash-cupel <note>original: "cineritium"; a shallow vessel made of bone ash that absorbs base metals</note>, and let it cook for a while. Then revive the fire, removing the little door from the mouth of the cupel once more, and use other methods to increase the heat. Boil it down for a long time in this way until the white lead <note>original: "plumbum candidum"; tin</note> and other impurities are consumed. Indeed, it is boiled into the lead with great difficulty and persistence. But if its wildness resists, sprinkle in a little flux made for impure veins, so that it may flow more readily. Mix it and stir it well. After mixing, keep it in great heat for a little while so the material settles. Finally, extract it and let it cool in the crucible. Refine the leaden mass by the "lightning flash" <note>original: "fulmina"; the sudden brightening of a bead of silver at the end of cupellation</note>, just as you would with silvered copper.*

*Regarding bell metal <note>original: "stanno campanario"; a high-tin bronze alloy used for casting bells</note>, there is nothing in the works of Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), a famous mining author</note>. Its testing partly agrees with the first method for silvered white lead, where copper was added, and partly with silvered bronze; for this reason, Fachs <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century master of the mint</note> placed it under the investigation of "intractable" copper containing silver. However, the treatment is quite clear. When he gradually adds black lead to the glowing grains, with a warning not to let it cool, he implies it should be put in bit by bit, either pre-heated or even molten. For the coldness of the lead and the heat of the glowing metals do not tolerate a sudden meeting. Meanwhile, while it grows hot and the lead is added, the lower door is open so that the breathing air may intensify the fire. Then, when smoke appears, he orders it to be closed and cooked with a gentler heat because of the copper, which otherwise, spurred on by the black lead, would consume the silver. How the heat may be increased again is clear enough from the general management of the furnace, discussed in its own place. On account of the stubbornness of foreign elements, the heat must be increased again, and flux should also be added—made from borax, saltpeter, and tartar; or others made from borax, calcined saltpeter, tartar, and salt; or even that made from the dross of litharge <note>lead oxide</note> and flint, which he says is intended for copper ores. This operation corresponds to the smelting of ores in large or small fires where copper is present. Therefore, afterward, the tin-like mass, with which the silver, copper, and more are mixed, is separated by the "lightning flash" refining, as the copper and lead perish. It should be noted here that white lead <note>tin</note>, because of its softness, perishes more quickly than copper, although both are volatile and are dispersed by the black lead. We shall soon hear from Fachs how silvered copper is refined. If gold is mixed with the bell metal along with the silver, there is no other way to test it except that the refined grain must finally be separated by <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid, used to dissolve silver while leaving gold behind</note>. But if it contains gold without silver, then this method is valid, as are <term>royal cement</term> <note>a dry refining process using salts and brick dust</note>, antimony, aqua fortis, and similar things. Furthermore, because many base metals are confused here with one or both of the precious metals, this method will also serve for judging other such mixtures. Indeed, since white lead is almost considered a "rapacious" mineral <note>one that "steals" or consumes the precious metals during smelting</note>, we can even adapt this for "sophisticated" <note>counterfeit or imitation</note> silver, especially if it is made from silver, copper, magnetite, mercury, arsenic, and similar things.*

## HOW MUCH SILVER IS IN MALLEABLE COPPER.

*The copper must be skillfully cut and cast into rods. From these, the end portion is cut off, and another piece is broken off, which is drawn out with a hammer and broken into small bits. Two <term>hundred-weights</term> <note>specific small weights used in assaying</note> of these are weighed against each other, separately, from one kind of copper. Assign fifteen hundred-weights of black lead to each. First, melt this in a well-heated ash crucible, with two coals placed at the opening of the tile and the cupel closed; when it begins to smoke and heat up, add the specimen for testing. When it has been "drunk up" by the lead, remove the coals from the mouth of the hearth, block the cupel, and cover the hole of the furnace with a lid, but leave a crack the width of a finger so the fire is not choked but can still work. Afterward, place a semi-circular valve at the back part of the tile. Also move the side doors and the half-cut door to the front; and in this way, "cook it coldly" <note>refine it at a lower temperature</note>. For copper is a "hot" metal; therefore, in the refining flash, it tolerates more cold than the others. When you see almost half is consumed, gradually revive the small furnace and restore the heat; if the smoke rises straight up, the heat is too much; but if it falls back into the crucible, the work is too cold; therefore, strive for the middle of these signs. When more than half has evaporated, because some of the copper has been dispersed, it does not withstand as much cold as before. Therefore, remove the back valve from the tile, leaving the others. When it has proceeded further and now less tin remains, remove the side obstacles; and if it is still too cold, move the lid or take it off entirely, as the assay requires. In this way, the fire is revived step by step without the addition of more coals. For if you were to throw in charcoal, you would choke the fire. If you cannot do without them, first place some at the sides of the furnace until they glow, then push them in in order.*

<margin>A hole lowered into the rule.</margin>

*Furthermore, with a hook or iron wire inserted through the hole above the mouth of the hearth, remove the ashes from the tile so the furnace gradually reheats. And although near the end the heat may be somewhat more violent, nothing is lost, as would have happened at the beginning while much copper was still in the material. Therefore, attend to the fire and the material in the crucible, and with sufficiently intense heat, bring about the lightning flash. Once the flash has occurred, remove the coals from the opening of the tile and keep the grain in the furnace for a little while longer, so it can be pulled away cleanly from the crucible. Finally, extract it and pull it away; seize it with forceps and squeeze it so any adhering foreign matter falls off. Wipe the same with a bristle, and since there are two, weigh one against the other. Equal weight proves the completion of the work; unequal weight warns that the process must be repeated until the grains come out equal. From the weight of one, you perceive the true value, which you note on the copper bar from which the specimen was taken, and you pronounce judgment on the whole lot. If you manage the fire as has been said, you will find more silver, and you can trust your art.*

## ASSAY OF DARK, INTRACTABLE, OR RUSTY COPPER, TO FIND HOW MUCH SILVER LIES WITHIN.

*Cast the pieces into small rods. Break off and crush the specimens; from the crushed pieces, weigh two hundred-weights, each placed separately in a shard or earthen crucible. Also assign fifteen hundred-weights of black lead to each. Place the shard with the copper in the furnace, with the cupel open and two coals moved to the mouth of the tile, until the copper in the crucible glows. Afterward, put in its lead; when it begins to work, close the doors of the cupel and remove one coal from the entrance of the tile, so that it may be "cooked in" and spit out the dross. Then reopen the cupel and put back both coals at the tile so it reheats. Stir and mix it thereafter with an iron hook, and watch carefully to see if anything sticks stubbornly in the crucible. Extract it immediately after mixing (specifically, when you see nothing sticking, and let it cool). Pull away the mass and refine it by the flash in the manner previously described for malleable copper.*

# Part 2: On the Art of Assaying <note>original: "Docimasia"; the technical term for the process of testing or assaying metals to determine their purity or value</note>

<margin>Method for melting the samples together.</margin>
In my opinion, Fachs <note>Modestin Fachs, a 16th-century German master of the mint and author of a famous book on assaying</note> has left no stone unturned here. He even repeats general principles and adapts them specifically for the understanding of apprentices, even though such details might normally bore a master craftsman. First, he advises on the skillful sampling <note>original: "expunctura"; the process of taking small drillings or "points" of metal for testing</note> of copper, which he judges is best done if it is performed above and below, halfway between the edges and the center. Afterward, he orders the samples <note>original: "puncta"; literally 'points,' referring here to the small bits of metal taken as a sample</note> to be melted together so that they form a rod or small stick, which they call a **finger**; this too must be done with careful attention. The samples are placed in a triangular dish or crucible <note>original: "testa seu catino"</note> and melted before the bellows. Here, one must be diligently careful that nothing is lost from the leaded copper due to the heat once it has melted; for with too great a fire, the lead is transformed into **litharge** <note>original: "lithargyrum"; a lead oxide byproduct that forms when lead is heated in air</note>. Consequently, in the final judgment of the assay, because the quantity of the whole was diminished compared to the previously weighed specimens, the copper is judged to be richer than it truly is, and the buyer is deceived by that judgment. However, in those masses of copper where little or no "black lead" <note>original: "plumbi nigri"; common lead</note> is present, errors are not so easily made during the melting. In either case, one must ensure that as soon as the samples are melted, the bellows are stopped and a dried wooden rod is dipped into the crucible to mix the material thoroughly. This is the skill of melting the samples together. It is easy to understand that if a sluggishness or obstacle is felt while mixing, the whole has not yet melted, and the fire must be renewed until it flows completely.

<margin>Casting the fingers.</margin>
The **fingers** <note>small, rod-shaped ingots used for further testing</note> are cast in this manner: an oblong iron channel with a handle is smeared with a little wax and allowed to warm up slightly. Afterward, the molten metal is poured from the crucible (which we pull from the hearth with tongs) with such care that the rod is formed with a uniform shape. Sometimes fibers or scraps tend to break off from this rod or cling to its outside, containing lead rich in silver. These must not be removed, nor should they be scraped off with a tool; for this reason, they do not usually wipe the "fingers" or strike them with a hammer, lest any of those rich fibers, scales, or sparks be lost.

Furthermore, that **finger** is broken at the tip before a specimen is taken. One might think this is done for the same reason mentioned regarding sampling—namely, because there are more impurities in the first part that flows out (for dross <note>original: "scoriae"</note> tends to rise to the top and the metal settles behind it, appearing first in the mold), just as in a lead "pocket" or **regulus** <note>original: "regulo"; a metallic button or mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible</note>, as the miners call it, and on the middle of the surface. However, it can also happen that very little impurity is present, and the lead flows out immediately with the silver. This very reason is given specifically regarding the "fingers": that the tip is broken off because the silver flows out first, and the tip is richer in it. I would prefer to granulate the whole <note>original: "totius granalia"; turning the entire sample into small grains</note> so that the value is equal everywhere. Thus, this task will require close attention.

Regarding the second portion, Fachs adds that it ought to be stretched and thinned with a hammer. It should be understood that nothing should be done here that goes against the rule about not striking the leaden "fingers" or those from which fibers have broken off. Therefore, if the mass is of that sort, the thinning must be done cautiously, and granulation may also take place. However, his instruction here to take two **hundredweights** <note>original: "centupondia"; a proportional weight used in assaying, not necessarily a literal 100 pounds</note> contradicts another passage where he prescribes only one. In that case, there would be only a half-hundredweight in one specimen, so that a mass of a hundredweight corresponds to a **dram** <note>original: "drachmae"</note>, and a half-hundredweight to a half-dram. This is done by choice, however, and not by necessity of the craft. For in either case, if you act correctly, you will achieve the same result, except that a smaller weight is taken when a more exact examination is required, or when the material is more stubborn, and the scale or balance is more precise. There is also variation in the addition of lead. Here he takes a fifteen-fold amount, elsewhere sixteen-fold, which might seem strange to some, since a smaller quantity is consumed by the fire more quickly than a larger one; from which it follows that less lead would be required there. But there is little difference in a single hundredweight: and we know that more is required where the stubbornness of the metal is greater, and the "acting cause" <note>the lead/heat</note> must be adapted to the "patient" <note>the copper being treated</note>. A specimen must be taken from one kind of copper, namely from a single smelting, which is also observed in silver-bearing tin, as we said the reason for that earlier. But if there are various smeltings, each proved separately, they can be reduced to a total sum by industrious calculation. Likewise, if the total quantity does not end exactly in hundreds, the added pounds must not be neglected. The rest is self-evident.

We should remember, however, that even the grains of a broken specimen must be carefully collected, wrapped in paper, and placed in the small crucible, lest anything be poured out by accident. It is customary to mark the value on the "finger"—namely, that in the present kind of copper to which that finger belongs, and which weighs 20, 60, etc., one **hundredweight** contains as much silver value as was found. From this, the remaining hundreds are estimated. The assaying of "untreatable" copper is almost the same as that for **bell metal** <note>original: "stanno campanario"; a high-tin bronze</note>, and does not differ from the judgment of "tractable" copper except by the addition of one extra labor. For, as if it were being smelted anew from ore into lead, it is first heated in a dish, then lead is added and it is gradually cooked in, so that the iron impurities (which made the metal untreatable) may seep out like excrement and be rejected. The pure copper, meanwhile, is absorbed into the lead along with the silver. But if it resists and clings tenaciously to the dish, or resists in another way, one must resort to salts and other **fluxes** <note>original: "fluxus"; substances added to promote melting</note> or additives, which, when added skillfully, make the matter succeed. And that is how the teachings of Fachs stand.

The rules of Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola, author of the mining classic 'De Re Metallica'</note> differ somewhat from those in certain details. But because they can bring some light to what has been said, I will include them. Cast the cut portions into a triangular crucible, adding a small slip of paper <note>original: "schedula"</note> on which is written the type of copper the portions were taken from—for example, that this copper is from the heap that weighs twenty hundredweights. Then let a circular hearth be prepared, with coals and embers cast in a circle, and the fire is blown. When it has gained strength, the crucible is put in, with the slip of paper removed and set aside for a moment. Heat is applied gradually for a quarter of an hour until it glows; then it is intensified with bellows for half an hour until the samples melt and flow, although leaded copper flows even faster. Removing the embers, and using a thin wooden rod held by tongs, the melted material is stirred and mixed. If it moves with difficulty, it is not fully melted. Therefore, replacing the removed embers, a large coal is also placed on the crucible itself, and the fire is blown with the bellows for a short time, by which we ensure the melting is complete. Once it has melted, one must stop using the bellows, lest anything be lost and the residue appear richer than it is (a caution which applies properly to leaded copper, but is also observed generally for the sake of greater circumspection). When melted, it is poured into a small iron channel of the proper capacity (according to the quantity...

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on melting copper samples into 'fingers,' this page describes the cooling and granulating processes before moving into specific assaying recipes for copper, iron, and coinage alloys according to the methods of Fachs and Agricola.</meta>

### Commentary on Alchemical Assaying, Part II, Book V

...that is, of the molten material. (There are indeed large, medium, and small sizes, as the use requires.) When the copper is poured in, that channel is immersed in a nearby tank of cold water, which cools it. (Fachs, however, did not advise this, and perhaps not without reason, for it can easily happen that some of the grains are lost. But careful caution will be the remedy, just as when the same metal is granulated and broken up with a hammer.) When it has cooled, it is dried, and the tip is broken off with an iron wedge. Others mix the molten copper with linden charcoal and granulate it by pouring it through brushes, straw, or over a stone placed in water, or even by agitation in water; it is necessary that it either be stretched into thin plates, reduced with a file, or granulated. Otherwise, it will not flow in the ash cupel <note>original: "catillo cinereo"; a small, porous bowl made of bone ash used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals</note>.

Copper prepared in this way, if it is rich in silver and free of iron and lead, is joined with lead by adding to the assay hundredweight (which is about a drachm) one and a half ounces of the larger weight of black lead <note>original: "plumbi nigri"; standard metallic lead used in the cupellation process</note> (which would be twelvefold). If it contains lead, one ounce of black lead is added (eight parts); if it contains iron, two ounces (sixteenfold, according to the teaching of Fachs for "untameable" ores, although he prescribes fifteenfold black lead for both wild and "tame" <note>refined</note> metals). The lead is first placed in the ash cupel of the furnace. When it begins to smoke, the copper is added (understand this to mean workable copper). The **lightning** <note>original: "fulminatio"; the "flash" or "brightening" that occurs at the moment the silver becomes pure during cupellation</note> is completed in five-quarters of an hour, although the work is finished more quickly in a wind-furnace where a breeze is blown in. But it is sufficient to cover the upper part of the furnace halfway with a lid, place the windowed doors at the opening, and close the window with a piece of charcoal or a small bit of brick. Unworkable copper, which is difficult to separate (and which stubbornly retains silver), is prepared thus: Lead is placed in a clay dish. Then the copper is added with a bit of roasted salt so that the lead may drink in the copper and the copper may be purged of its dross. So says Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola, author of "De Re Metallica," the most famous early work on mining and metallurgy</note>. But in most matters, he is briefer than what a beginner can grasp, especially regarding unworkable copper, where he also acts differently than Fachs—namely, he does not put the copper in first, but the lead; perhaps because the same thing can be done either way. However, in Fachs’ method, the reasoning is easier, since the pre-heating of the copper is like a roasting by which the harsh minerals are tamed. Therefore, salt does not need to be added later except in cases of great stubbornness. Agricola compensates for the roasting by adding salt immediately, presumably assuming knowledge of that metal’s behavior, which nonetheless cannot be entirely certain from the start. Thus far regarding copper.

# HOW MUCH SILVER IS IN IRON.

*Take a quarter-hundredweight of finely filed iron, and another quarter against it. Add lead to it according to the ratio of a half-hundredweight. For if you wished to follow the quarters, you would take less lead. Cook and perform the lightning <note>cupellation</note>, as in other assays.*

This examination does not occur easily. However, Fachs did not omit the precept of the art, though he was quite concise. It must be known that it is not easy to elicit silver from iron and white lead <note>tin</note>, because in the former there is an iron-like stubbornness and the greatest difficulty in melting; in the latter, there is rapacity <note>referring to how tin can "consume" or ruin an assay</note>. Nevertheless, in both cases, something must be attempted by ingenuity, albeit with the risk of losing one or the other. The iron is reduced exactly by a file, and properly wiped and cleaned by washings. Afterward, it is weighed and divided into two specimens, but of a smaller weight—namely, the fourth part of a drachm, or the assay hundredweight—and this is because of the stubbornness, on account of which the same author also reduced the copper. Lead is assigned to it as if it were a half-hundredweight, that is, eight hundredweights, so that there is thirty-two times as much lead as iron; this is because iron is overcome and dissipated slowly. Indeed, even then, if it is refractory <note>stubborn/heat-resistant</note>, we cannot do without fluxes. The method of the work is to first cook it in lead and purge it of dross: the tin-like mass is afterward subjected to the **lightning**, and indeed the same process can be observed as in unworkable and bell-metal copper. The same could be done with a lunar cement <note>a chemical mixture used for refining silver</note>. The iron could also be pre-softened or changed into copper according to its own masteries.

# ON MONETARY SILVER AND COINS, FROM FACHS.

<margin>In granulating, something is lost.</margin>
*Monetary alloys, which they call bullion <note>original: "pagamentum"; the mixture of silver and base metal used for coins</note>, must be melted together and poured into grains; in this work, there is a loss of one drachm in a mark. Of the grains, weigh out two equal specimens according to the weight of the coins or denarii, so that each is one mark. Assign to them an equal number of masses of black lead, each of which should be twenty times the weight. Choose ash cupels of analogous size and capacity, and with the furnace properly heated, place the lead in the cupels; when it begins to smoke, submit the grains contained within a paper wrapping onto the lead. When they have been "drunk up" <note>absorbed into the molten lead</note>, close the door of the ash-furnace and remove the coals from the entrance of the tile. Also, cover the top hole with its lid. Close the side and rear windows of the tile and its orifice with their doors, and thus allow it to cook. If signs of cold appear, such as a lack of shine or others, remove the rear bar of the tile along with the side and front valves, so that the furnace is breathed upon to work. Afterward, remove the valves entirely and replace the front one. If it is still not sufficiently heated, also remove the lid as much as the work requires, and finally, place two coals at the door of the tile, and thus throw the **lightning** with enough heat. Once the lightning has passed, keep the beads in the furnace for a little while, and they will be pulled away from the ash cupel more readily. Extract them, pull them away, and explore the weight of one against the other. Equal weight indicates the end of the work. If this is so, the value of one proves what was sought. Other grains are to be tested in this way, unless perhaps they equal professional-grade silver or are even richer. From this value of one grain, you will calculate how much is in one mark of the same kind, and how much in all of them, always subtracting the drachm lost during granulation from the mark. You can also state the value in coins, after subtracting the cost of labor and knowing the selling price of a mark of pure silver.*

<margin>Pliny records that this art arose in Rome by the law of Marius, for whom the common people...</margin>
This examination concerns both worked and unworked silver in monetary alloys, although the author later separately delivers the method for testing poor <note>low-purity</note> coins, and reserves some even for the examination of silversmith's silver. The difference is that in the prescribed manner, any bullion can be examined whose silver value or intrinsic goodness in one mark does not reach or exceeds ten **lots** <note>original: "lothones"; a unit of weight where 16 lots usually equaled one mark</note>. That which is from ten lots up to fourteen, consider separately...

# On the Assay of the Proving Art, Part 2.

...is observed, in which, however, nothing peculiar is prescribed, except that if that silver has not been reduced into granules, a drachm of it must be flattened with a hammer, and two marks weighed out according to the weight of coins, and seven times the amount of lead assigned to each. 
<margin>
For this reason, they said the whole state was corrupted when Mark Antony the triumvir mixed iron with the silver denarius, and thus debased the currency.
</margin>
In the case of small coins, in which a mark contains less silver than ten lots <note>original: "lothones"; a unit of weight where 16 lots typically equaled one mark</note>, there is no difference, except that sixteen-fold lead is taken by reason of the more abundant base metal; and yet elsewhere this same quantity is assigned even to granules, so that it appears this matter (concerning sixteen and twenty parts of lead) is almost arbitrary, or according to the rule that more lead is required when tin or more copper is mixed in the silver. Although small coins can also be granulated, they are sometimes merely cut into small pieces after the edges have been broken off. But so that there may be less error in these matters, I will interpret the individual methods of the author himself. Regarding the granulation of bullion <note>original: "pagamento"; scrap silver or mixed coinage intended for melting</note>, he discusses it thus:

<margin>
Bullion.
</margin>
<margin>
The method of granulating bullion.
</margin>
By the term "bullion," he says, is called any coinage or undervalued silver for which a certain assay cannot be established unless it is melted and reduced into granules. And although the coins might be of one kind and uniform, the portions are nevertheless unequal in value, and some are richer in silver than others. Therefore, through granulation, they must be brought to equality in this manner: Determine the weight of the bullion in marks and lots, and record it. Afterward, place a triangular crucible <note>original: "catinum triangularem"</note> upon a stand packed with ashes in a wind-furnace <note>original: "anemia"; a draft furnace used for high heat</note>, and close it with an iron lid. Fill the furnace with charcoal up to the lid of the crucible. Place ten glowing coals around it, over which you should again throw charcoal, so that the crucible is gradually heated from above and becomes white-hot. Then observe that no rupture or crack opens up. If it is solid everywhere, put in the bullion taken up with a spoon until it is full. Replace the lid and pour in glowing coals, so that the melted material settles; once this is done, add the rest until it is all in the crucible. When it is all melted and boiling so that it almost smokes, turn and stir it with a larger hook. Remove the scum floating on top with a skimming spoon. Throw in a handful of charcoal powder. Stir well with the hook so they are perfectly blended. Cover it for a little while longer so the material reheats. These things being finished, seize the melting crucible with tongs while it is glowing and pour out the melted bullion over a basin of water, with an assistant standing by and beating the liquid with brushes. When it is no longer possible to pour, take the crucible itself out of the coals, turn it over, and pour it over the brushes into the water; thus come out small grains, called "Granalia." Carefully drain the water so that none of the granules are lost. Transfer them from the basin into a bronze bowl and wash away the charcoal. Once washed, dry them by the fire. When they have cooled, weigh them, and notice that a drachm has been lost from the mark. From the remainder, take a drachm for a sample, and assay it thus: Weigh out two equal marks according to the weight of denarii <note>original: "denariorum"; refers here to a specific weight system used for coins</note> in a balance, etc., as I have recounted above.

<margin>
The assay of granules.
</margin>
Near the end of the booklet, as if by a universal rule concerning mint granules and common silver—whether in masses, thin plates, or "fingers"—whose value extends up to fourteen lots, he writes thus: To such silver, add sixteen times the amount of lead for the mark weighed. Here you see the twenty-fold quantity is not observed; and although he had said before that mint silver cannot be assayed except in granules, he now does not exclude other forms. As for why he assigned twenty-fold lead to it, he says elsewhere that this was done because granules are often impure and have white lead <note>tin</note> coins mixed in, which are not consumed by a small amount of lead. If only sixteen parts are commanded, it happens because the material was purer. Similarly, in inspecting silversmith's silver <note>original: "argento fabrili"</note>, which he joins with common silver, likewise in granules, "fingers," or masses, whose silver value is from ten to fourteen lots, he has these instructions: Silversmith's silver (which goldsmiths use), if not in large masses, such as used silver, assay it thus: Flatten a drachm of it into a thin plate <note>original: "bracteam"</note> and cut it into small pieces. From this, weigh out two marks equal to each other according to the weight of denarii, and to each add seven times the amount of black lead. Afterward, proceed in the work just as in the assay of granules, except for this: that the "lightning" <note>original: "fulmen"; the 'blick' or flash of light that occurs when the silver becomes pure at the end of cupellation</note> appears more quickly, and thus one need not linger long over it. For a little lead reveals pure silver more swiftly.

<margin>
Why the tip of the "finger" must be cut off.
</margin>
But if you take a "finger" of silversmith's silver to be tested, break off the tip. For it often happens that the silver projects and sticks out there. Then file off another portion, which you weigh and assay. These are his words on silversmith's silver. He suggests that this too can be tested either in the form of granules, plates, or "fingers." However, if it is poorer than ten lots, more lead will be required, and the labor will be prolonged. It is a wonder why they perform the assay on the broken-off tip in the following section, since it is necessary that if the silver flowed to the tip, the rest must be impoverished. Therefore, the judgment will be more correctly completed in granules, where everything is equalized, even though some small portion of the additives is lost.

<margin>
Assay of poorer bullion.
</margin>
<margin>
The margins of coins must be cut off.
</margin>
If the coins have less than ten lots in a mark, or do not even exceed this, he proposes these rules: Take those coins, about eight in number, and trim the margins of each one by dividing it into four parts, or cut off a fourth part, which you set aside. For because of the rims and edges, it is richer than the middle. Afterward, cut two segments from each coin; these you will weigh according to the weight of grains, so that there are two marks equal to each other. To each assign sixteen times the amount of black lead. Perform the "lightning" process <note>cupellation</note> as diligently as with granules. For the poorer the coinage is in silver, the lower the heat ought to be, because of the boiling of the copper. Here the author is at odds with himself. For how is it that sixteen times the lead is to be added to silver up to fourteen lots, when that same quantity is owed to silver poorer than ten lots, and for silversmith's silver so rich, only sevenfold is reckoned? Why is like lead not assigned to like metals? We cannot flee to the excuse of "stubborn" <note>difficult to refine</note> ores that might cling more to one than another. For both are already smelted and remixed. Next, regarding the system of weights, it should be noted that in the assay of silversmith's silver he uses denarii or coins, but in mint silver he uses grains. There, he surely looked more to marketplace contracts, for which the coinage weight is more suitable, lest the buyer be pressed too exquisitely. But in this, a fraud will be committed against the seller unless it is so agreed. The standard of the minters must also be examined exactly. Therefore, here one should not take the weight of denarii, but of grains. Altogether, the perfection of the art rejects marketplace contracts. Fachs warns, however, that it was customary for coins to be tested by denarii, since it is a matter of small importance, as when a mint master buys coins as material for new coinage. The first cause is so the buyer may have some profit; the second, because it is for the public good...

<header>Commentary on Alchemy, Part II. Book V.</header>

of custom in pure silver and fragments of coinage; thirdly, because a mark in coins does not extend beyond 236 parts, but in grains, it is extended to 288, and exceeds the former by 52 parts. For this reason, this assay is more exact. But if you set aside custom—which carries the force of law—those arguments have little weight; and custom itself is of no importance where the nature of the matter is concerned and the sincere judgment required in chemical affairs.
<margin>Agricola’s method for testing coinage.</margin>
But let us return to the fragment of his work and to <term>Agricola</term> <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy," whose work *De Re Metallica* standardized mining and assaying</note>. He takes silver coins from the bottom, the top, and the sides of a heap, cleans them well, and either granulates them or flattens them into small sheets; larger ones he thins out from a drachm to an ounce. Afterward, he wraps two marks individually in paper and places two small pieces of lead into an equal number of ash cups <note>original: "catillos cinereos"; these are cupels used to separate noble metals from base metals</note> that have been previously heated. He does this in such a way that the more precious the coinage is, the less lead it receives; but it receives more the cheaper the coin is. For example, if there is a half-ounce or an ounce of copper in a mark of silver, a half-ounce of greater weight of lead is added to the assay mark. Where the silver and copper are equal, an ounce is applied. If there is a half-ounce or an ounce of silver in a mark of copper, a unit and a half of soft lead <note>original: "plumbi nigri"; literally "black lead," used historically to refer to common lead as opposed to "white lead" or tin</note> is weighed out. This is the rule for the addition of lead. When the lead begins to smoke in the ash cup, the mixture wrapped in paper is thrown in, one into each cup. The mouth of the furnace is blocked with coals. The <term>brightening</term> <note>original: "fulminatio"; the sudden flash seen at the end of the cupellation process when the silver becomes pure</note> is carried out with a slow fire. For copper, by its own heat, might drive the silver with some particle of lead into the cup, which would cause the experiment to fail. The "lightning grains" <note>the silver beads left after the flash</note> are cleaned and weighed against each other. If they are equal, they complete the work; if unequal, they force a repetition. This is generally what Agricola holds. But in my judgment, the instruction of <term>Fachs</term> <note>Modestinus Fachs, a 16th-century master of the mint and author of a famous handbook on assaying</note> is richer and more illustrious; where two weights of lead can be observed: sevenfold in silver-rich samples, and sixteenfold in poor ones. It happens sometimes that foreign minerals are mixed into the coins; these will depart in the cup, and if they are stubborn, the help of fluxes or <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note> must be sought. Chemists also extract all the copper from coins using sulfur, leaving only the silver with its mark. This is done in its own cement, sometimes with salts added. Nor is it difficult to achieve the same through "sharp waters" <note>acidic solutions</note>, by which the copper alone is consumed while the silver is left behind. <term>Budelius</term> <note>René Budel, a legal scholar who wrote on the laws of coinage and metallurgy</note> also mentions this, but assayers do not use it.

## CHAPTER XXII.
->*On the mixtures of imperfect metals among themselves, etc.*<-

**F**inally, after the mixtures of perfect metals with each other and with imperfect ones, we find the proportions of imperfect metals mixed together—for instance, when copper is joined with lead or iron; likewise when other minerals are joined with copper, as in brass <note>original: "orichalco"</note>, <term>cadmia</term> <note>a zinc-rich ore</note>, white bronze, and so forth. The assays of these agree with the ones above, and for the most part, smelting removes that which is more volatile. If, however, some lead remains in the copper, it is investigated according to the law of "leaded copper," mentioned above. Brass is examined by the proofs for impure copper, and so with others, although there is no inquiry into these unless they are prepared for the purpose of deception, just as sophisticated gold is examined by its own art, and silver by its own. If iron is mixed with copper, the law of degenerate copper is observed, which will be discussed in its own place. Bell metal and other such mixtures, created by exuberant minds for the display of art, can be brought to assay when we inquire whether the legitimate proportion was made without fraud; and then we likewise look to the law of impure copper, which we smelt with lead and "brighten" to a copper button. At other times, it is examined for silver or gold. And so much for the assaying of metals.

## CHAPTER XXIII.
->*On Mineral Assaying.*<-

**M**ineral assaying is that by which those minerals are tested which, though devoid of metal, are endowed with "mineral juices" or spirits suitable for conducting life. The series of these is numerous and the species very many, but those more frequently offered for examination are: the vein of mercury or quicksilver; the marcasite of white lead (which they call <term>bismuth</term>); the vein of antimony <note>original: "stibij"</note>, and also antimony itself for its metal button; the vein of sulfur; the vein of vitriol, nitre, saltpeter, and similar substances (to which can be added cinnabar, sublimated mercury, and things of this kind).

## CHAPTER XXIV.
->*On the examination of native Minium, or the vein of quicksilver.*<-

**T**ake a certain weight of the ore, such as a hundredweight, broken into small parts, and either sublimate it with tartar, or distill it by descent or inclination. [ <gloss>Through a retort into a receiver in which there is water. It may also be driven into a blind alembic, whose rim is wide and contains water. The receiver must be kept cold if possible.</gloss> ] The quantity of quicksilver drawn out will indicate how much is in one hundredweight, and so on for others of the same kind.
<margin>Pliny, Book 33, chapters 6 and 8.</margin>
The vein of quicksilver is mostly native <term>cinnabar</term> <note>original: "minium"; in this context, it refers to the red ore of mercury, not lead-based red paint</note>, which is called secondary minium; according to Pliny, it is also called a certain "silvery stone," or metallic silver-bearing cadmia, in my opinion, from which he established the distinction between quicksilver and mercury <note>original: "argentum vivum & hydrargyrum"</note>. Sometimes it also adheres to veins or grains of gold and silver. Frequently it is also drawn out from pits and gathered in the gravel of wells, springs, and rivers. There are those who say it has been extracted from old sewers. Therefore, its discovery in common workshops is threefold: while it is found by itself, or in its own vein, or in metallic veins (especially silver and lead ones); sometimes it even adheres to gold, and when these veins are smelted and roasted—as Dioscorides also testifies—it often drips from the vaulted chambers. But regarding its birthplace and veins, we discuss this more copiously elsewhere.
Chemists add a fourth method, by which it is produced from resolved metals, a method which does not concern assayers, just as the one by which pure or naturally "living" mercury is collected. Whatever the vein may be, it is tested in various ways...

<page-num>135</page-num>
<header>On the Assay of the Art of Testing, Part 2.</header>

# Part 2: On the Assay of the Art of Testing.

It can be examined in many ways, just as it can be smelted. <term>Fuchs</term> <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a German physician and botanist whose works often touched on the medicinal and chemical properties of minerals</note> describes three methods, one of which is distillation by inclination—which they also call distillation by **retorts** because of the type of narrow and curved-beaked vessels used—and the other two are by "descent" <note>A method where the vapor or liquid is forced downward into a receiver</note>. <term>Agricola</term> <note>Georgius Agricola, the mining authority mentioned on the previous page</note> sets down one method, which is similar to the descent that occurs in "cementing" by protection. He also makes mention of "ascent" <note>standard upward distillation</note> and "descent."

*The first method of Fuchs using retorts is this: Reduce the mercury ore (they call it native cinnabar, which is reddish and sometimes dark) into tiny particles. Weigh out a pound of these fragments using the "greater weight." Put them into one retort, and insert its curved beak into another retort that contains a third or fourth part of water. Close the joints with <term>lute</term> <note>a clay-based sealant used to make vessels airtight</note>, though leave a small air hole that you will block with a piece of wood so that, when necessary, you can open it to vent the work. Place the retort with the ore over hot coals and pile charcoal around it. Place the other retort with the water in sand, so that a brick partition stands between them to prevent the receiver from being damaged by the heat of the fire. Apply the fire in stages until the pot finally glows white-hot. The smoke creeps from the first retort into the second, and the charcoal poured over it turns into quicksilver. Weigh this sample with the greater weight and calculate according to it, so that you may see how much is contained in a <term>hundred-weight</term> <note>original: "centupondio"; a standard bulk unit for ore</note>. But watch yourself carefully against the breath of the quicksilver.*

This method is not exact enough. Even with the smallest air hole provided, the mercury flies away. Therefore, a path must never be given before the process is finished. To avoid the breaking of the vessels, larger and stronger ones are preferred, or the work should be carried out through upward distillation. But it seems that Fuchs, in dealing with larger weights, ignores that tiny quantity which might escape, since in a larger fire not everything can be managed so precisely.

*The second method: Put the ore into the bottom of a pot pierced with tiny holes, and fit and glue it to another pot which is buried in the earth up to the rim of its opening and contains water. Once the joints and the opening are carefully blocked—leaving a small air hole as before—apply a circular fire, and the smoke of the mercury descends into the water. The weight of the ore must be known so that you can calculate accordingly, as in the previous work.*

*The third method is likewise by descent. Put the ore, weighed out by the assay weight, into a triangular melting crucible perforated at the bottom. Fit this to a small pot holding a third part water and glue them together; place this in the sand of a bronze pan up to the crucible. Afterward, stir up a circular fire in the sand around the crucible, and the mercury descends.*

This method is truly "docimastic" <note>relating to assaying or testing</note>, as it is done following the example of large-scale work but with a small weight. The method of descent is easily understood. The crucible ought to be pierced with three or four holes and protected with a lid. Instead of a bronze pan, a sand-bath crucible or a copper kettle can be used.

*Agricola's method: Take one part of the fragments of quicksilver ore, three parts of charcoal powder, and one handful of salt; place the mixture in a covered crucible coated with lute over hot coals and smelt it. When a burnt color has settled upon it, remove the crucible, and when it has cooled, you will find the mercury at the bottom. Take care not to cook it too long, for it flies away. It can also be distilled by ascent into the water of a receiver, or by descent, by which means it is also smelted.*

<margin>Large-scale smelting of quicksilver.</margin>
This is the "cementation" method, as I said. Alchemists otherwise also distill it with tartar. In large-scale operations, the vessels are made of strong potter's clay: one shaped like a <term>urinal</term> <note>original: "matula"; a flask with a rounded body and wide neck</note>, the other like a smooth crucible, and many of them are used. The broken ore is placed in the flask, the mouth of which is blocked with moss so it does not fall out. Then, inverted, it is fitted to a pot or crucible buried in sand or a mixture of earth and crushed charcoal, so that the flask sticks out by a palm’s breadth. The joints are glued with lute. A great number of these vessels are placed in the same area and surrounded by stones upon which small troughs are placed, so that they do not touch the pots; they are set on fire, and they melt out the ore.

<margin>A sweetness exhaling from quicksilver ore.</margin>
<margin>Fallopius also mentions this.</margin>
That the quicksilver is escaping is signaled by a breath hitting the sense of smell with a great sweetness; the smelter performs his work facing away. Another method of smelting is through <term>cucurbits</term> and <term>alembics</term> <note>standard distillation equipment consisting of a boiling flask and a cooling cap</note> arranged in a long furnace with the fire applied below and receivers nearby. A third method is performed in a vaulted chamber with broad-leaved branches arranged in the middle and hearths around the perimeter for the cucurbits or pots containing the ore, with a fire lit below. The collected quicksilver partly flows down onto a concave floor and is partly shaken down and wiped off the branches. Agricola also recounts a fourth method, which is by sublimation. It is done in a cucurbit or pot with a "blind" alembic <note>an alembic without a discharge beak</note>, so that sand two fingers thick is placed between the ore and the alembic. The mercury, smoking out through this, is collected in the alembic and on the surface of the sand, from where it is later recovered and separated by washing. If the quicksilver ore contains another metal besides, it is further processed in its own way. If it contains nothing else, it was once turned by <term>reverberation</term> <note>heating in a furnace where the flame is deflected onto the material</note> into "secondary minium" <note>red lead or cinnabar pigment</note> for pigments. Lead, by a similar art using a retort, pours out quicksilver if tartar is added; about which we will speak in its proper place. Small alluvial deposits sprinkled with grains of gold or tin are ignored. <term>Moffett</term> <note>Thomas Moffet (1553–1604), an English physician and naturalist</note> reports that mercury is in every metal-bearing place and can be recovered by making pits and placing damp hay inside, to which the mercury adheres. Sometimes <term>cadmia</term> <note>a cobalt or zinc-rich ore or furnace deposit</note> is so pregnant with quicksilver that it falls out by a mere push, or sometimes it exits easily when heated. Some try to summon it out with vinegar or "water of tartar"; <term>Pliny</term> indicates the former of these, which is performed by grinding the ore in a mortar with vinegar.

***

->### CHAPTER XXV.<-
->## Bismuth Ore.<-

*The assay of this ore is close to that of lead ore, and is performed in the same way. For a quick test, it is merely melted in a small crucible. While the slag remains on top, the <term>regulus</term> <note>the pure button of metal found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</note> is at the bottom.*

Some consider this a type of lead. Others remove it from the class of metals and place it among the <term>marcasites</term> <note>in this period, a term for metallic minerals like pyrite or ores that weren't fully "perfected" into metals</note> and "spirits," just like antimony. If its ore contains silver, which makes it more worthwhile, it is smelted like "raw" silver ore that has been sprinkled. Fuchs encompasses the ore of bismuth and lead in a single process, which

<margin>The assay of Fuchs.</margin>
proceeds as follows: Bismuth ore mixed with flint, shale, or other empty mineral must be ground into tiny pieces. After a certain weight of the best parts is selected (though you can also take a specific weight after grinding), the crushed material is washed in a small trough. The washed material, whatever it may be, is weighed again (to establish how much waste has been removed). A docimastic "hundred-weight" of this is joined with a half-ounce of **flux** (which is made from borax, saltpeter, tartar, salt, or thereabouts), and placed in a small closed crucible, it is melted before the bellows, and...

<margin>Large-scale smelting of bismuth.</margin>
in that case, the method of <term>Agricola</term> <note>Georgius Agricola, the famous mining author</note> can be used, which he describes as follows: fragments of bismuth ore placed in a clay crucible under the roof-tile of a burning furnace will, when heated, yield a lead-like mass from which the value is estimated. In a larger operation, the crucible should be as deep as a copper kettle and built out of charcoal-clay. Dry wood is arranged over it and the bismuth ore is thrown in; as it burns, the metal flows down into the crucible, from where it is drawn out and re-cooked until pure. Its masses are mostly sold in the form of cakes under the name <term>marcasite</term> <note>In this period, "marcasite" was a general term for various bright, metallic minerals, including bismuth</note>, sometimes with an addition of tin. It can likewise be smelted in an iron-ore hearth and by many other methods which Agricola recounts.

## Chapter XXVI.
### Antimony Ore.

**W**hen melted in a crucible, it separates its <term>antimony</term> <note>original: "stibium"</note> just like bismuth. It can also be driven "by descent" through a perforated crucible into a pot placed beneath. [*By descent is the method favored by <term>Ercker</term> <note>Lazarus Ercker (c. 1530–1594), a renowned Bohemian metallurgist and author of "Treatise on Ores and Assaying"</note>. The lower pot must be protected from the heat; the upper one is heated by degrees until it glows. The antimony flows down through the holes. When it has cooled, it is removed and weighed.*] The <term>regulus</term> <note>the purified metallic part of the ore</note> is elicited through melting with <term>nitre</term> <note>saltpeter</note> or salt of the rock and iron filings. When it is melted, it is poured into a matching crucible, and by striking the edge or the floor, a tin-like "regulus" settles, sometimes in the shape of a star, other times as a globe or cone.

The assay of this is not laborious and matches the work of mercury, or lead and bismuth. Therefore, authors have prescribed nothing unique regarding its judgment. It is helpful to understand, however, that this too is either pure or mixed, either with metallic veins, or rocks and other minerals; these must be accounted for in the assay in the same way as in lead and similar metals. In larger works, it is separated by descent, like mercury. In the lower pot, masses or "loaves" are found and extracted once cooled. They are said to consist of sulfur, mercury, and arsenic: and indeed, from the *regulus*, Chemists even produce <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>. The sulfur reveals itself by its smell, its flow, and its flame. To the arsenic they attribute a poisonous power and a heavy smell. It does not differ much from bismuth and hard or degenerate lead. Thus, they say both can be turned into lead by the <term>chemical mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterio chymico," referring to a transformative laboratory process</note>.

## Chapter XXVII.
### Sulfur Ore.

**S**ulfurous earth is melted out like antimony, and <term>pyrite</term> or other crushed stone is processed "by descent." *The judgment is made from the pure substance that has been separated.*

The method for examining such things is easy, provided the weight and the analogy of the larger work are observed. However, sulfur requires greater attention than antimony, bismuth, etc., because of its easier flow and because it catches fire quickly. Therefore, the vessels must be carefully blocked up and a gentler fire applied. Commonly, they thicken sulfur that floats on water by boiling it. They distill sulfurous earths and extract pyrite by descent. Concerning these, see Agricola and *The Alchemy*. [*It is tested either by combustion or by distillation through a retort. The residue of the ore shows how much sulfur it contained.*]

## Chapter XXVIII.
### Ores of Nitre and Halinitre.

**T**hey are dissolved in water if they are earthy; if they are stony, they are crushed and strained by pouring water over them as often as possible. *The strained liquids are coagulated in glass vessels. If water is allowed, the filtration and coagulation of the juice is sufficient. The same is done in brine, and with ores of common salt, <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>, and other minerals. [First test how much congealable juice is in the ore. Then see whether it is pure saltpeter or another juice mixed in. If such juices are in stones, a roasting is performed first, etc. It is known by taste and by hot coals whether salt, <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "chalcanthum"</note>, etc., is present together. Pure saltpeter feels cold to the teeth and does not crackle on hot coals; salt crackles and bites the tongue. <term>Halonitrum</term> <note>a soda-like mineral</note> is entirely consumed by fire, while mixed salt resists it, etc.]*

## Chapter XXIX.
### Alum and Vitriol.

**T**hose mixed with water are processed like diluted salts. *Earths are boiled in kettles and often strained into a <term>lye</term>, which is then coagulated. Rocks and pyrites must first be "reverberated" <note>heated in a furnace where the flame is deflected onto the material</note> in open crucibles, then extinguished with water so they soften. Finally, they are diluted, boiled down, and strained to make a lye, which is coagulated in the previous manner. Whether it is <term>vitriol</term> <note>iron or copper sulfate</note> is proven by the taste, and by <term>gallnuts</term> <note>growths on oak trees used to make ink and test for iron</note> and iron, which is reddened by it.*

->How much salt is in the halinitre.<-

->This is indicated by the boiling of the solution in a copper kettle. For the salt settles at the bottom. The nitre, poured off with the water, coagulates.<-

->How much vitriol is with the alum.<-

->Let the urine of a boy be poured into a dilution of these, and the vitriol will settle to the bottom. The alum, drained off with the water, coagulates.<-

Specimens of this kind are made in imitation of larger works through solutions, strainings, and coagulations; the logic of all of them is nearly the same, except that hard and stubborn materials must be prepared through reverberation, grinding, and soaking. Chemists also consult their distillations and other matters, which have been sufficiently discussed in the book on the judgment of mineral waters. But even in the chemical art, there are specific precepts regarding these things.
