<header>On the Assay of the Art of Testing, Part 2.</header>

In the case of <term>nitre</term> <note>saltpeter</note>, alum, and <term>vitriol</term> <note>metal sulfates</note>, there is no need to wait for a long period of <term>coagulation</term> <note>the process of crystals forming out of a liquid</note>. Once the boiling has reached a certain thickness, evaporate the rest gradually in glass pans using the heat of the furnace. For here, such an exact refinement is not required. If impurities <margin>The impurity of saltpeter is recognized from the heavy ash remaining after its combustion.</margin> cling to the first samples, they are easily removed by repeated dissolving, filtering, and crystallizing.

## CHAPTER XXX.

->On the judgment of brine: how much salt it contains.<-

**W**hether water contains salt is easily explored by taste; however, how much salt it contains is revealed by the crystallization of a fixed measure, which must be conducted so carefully that nothing is lost. Therefore, a measure of <term>brine</term> <note>original: "muria"</note> is usually distilled in a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "balneo", a gentle heating method using hot water</note> until it reaches a syrupy consistency. The remainder, poured out and distributed into glass shells or small pans, is finished by drying and thickening with gentle heat. The weight is then checked on a scale. Regarding this matter, we read in the works of <term>Thölde</term> <note>Johann Thölde, a 17th-century chemist and author on salt production</note>—to recount it at least briefly—that there are various ways of examining brine. One method takes a certain quantity collected by weight or measure, boils it, and crystallizes it; from this, one estimates how much fresh water was mixed with how much salt. Another weighs both fresh water and brine in equal silver or glass shells, and from the greater weight of the brine, calculates the abundance of salt. A third method is performed by a "spindle" marked with points. Because thicker water, such as salty water, supports weights better and does not let them sink as much as thin, fresh water (a fact also shown by sailing in the sea versus rivers), they construct a spindle divided with half-ounce marks; by immersing this into the brine, they recognize how much salt is within. The spindle is prepared thus: Take fresh water, free of all salt. Lower the spindle into this, weighted at the tip with a lead knot, until it reaches the bottom (care must be taken that it just barely touches the bottom and balances there, without sticking as if fixed). Then add half an ounce of salt and observe how much the spindle is raised. Mark the place with a point. Add another half ounce; and mark its elevation as well, and so on as you wish. This spindle will afterwards easily manifest the value of any brine. In place of a spindle, there is another instrument consisting of mass weights, built upon the same principle. For without weight, it reaches the bottom of its own accord in fresh water. But if an ounce of salt is present, it is counteracted by an ounce weight; if a pound, by a pound weight, and so on. The form of the instruments is as follows:

<margin>
The Spindle.
</margin>

**a.** The Base. **b.** Spaces filled with lead. **c.** Points for weights. **d.** A lead weight, of such a mass that the spindle can be lowered exactly to the bottom of the vessel and rest there in equilibrium.

**a.** The weight protruding from the water and, as it were, floating. **b.** The shaft. **c.** The knot or "egg" where the sections meet. **d.** Spaces weighted with lead. **e.** Ounce weight, half-ounce weight, etc.

So much for the Assay of minerals and the art of testing. Indeed, in every part of nature, as in other sciences, "the straight is the judge of itself and of the crooked" <note>original Latin: "rectum iudex sui & obliqui"; a philosophical maxim meaning that knowing the truth/correct standard allows one to identify errors</note>, so that the power of a universal testing art is scattered through all things; yet in many matters, special wisdom, knowledge, and practice are required, which not infrequently require specific instructions. We have wished here only to treat metallic matters, and those brought into this art by practical experience. For gems, one may consult <note>The author lists classical and Renaissance authorities on gemstones and mineralogy</note> the last book of <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder's Natural History</note>, specifically the final chapter; later, <term>Cardano</term> <note>Girolamo Cardano</note>, <term>Battista Porta</term> <note>Giambattista della Porta</note>, and others who have handed down many things regarding their identification. Likewise, the same Pliny has much to say on pigments and other things. In truth, from no art is there a greater abundance of proofs than from <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: "Chymia"</note>. Therefore, he who has learned and practiced this will not be left wanting for the rules of judgment.

# ADDENDUM.
## Aristotle in *On Marvelous Things Heard*, Number 60.

**I**t is a thing of wonder why such things occur among the Indians concerning the lead found there. For when it has been melted into cold water, it is held there for some time, and at last it leaps out from the water. 
   Is this a fable, since in our times nothing of the sort is heard of, especially in well-frequented places? Or does it happen because the <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; in alchemy/early chemistry, these were volatile substances or gases trapped within matter</note>, being slightly repelled, remain in the water until, having been gathered and increased, and made stronger than themselves, they break forth with force and expel the lead?

## Number 48.

Celtic tin is written to melt much more quickly than lead. The proof of this melting is that it is accustomed to melt when placed in water, as is well known. Therefore, it colors [the water] easily. However, it melts in extreme cold and frost, when its innate heat is shut up within and is compressed because of its weakness.
   The Greek is clearer when he names it <term>tin</term> <note>original Greek: "κασσίτερον" (kassiteron)</note>, and instead of "as is well known," he says <term>as they say</term> <note>original Greek: "ὥς φασι"</note>. In the phrase "it colors easily," he interposes <term>as it seems</term> <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἔοικέ"</note>. For "extreme cold," he says: <term>in the cold when frost forms, as they say, the heat existing within it is changed or compressed because of its weakness.</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐν τοῖς ψύχεσιν ὅτε γένηται πάγη, ἐξαλλαττομένου ὥς φάσιν ἤ συνωθουμένου τοῦ θερμοῦ ἐνυπάρχοντος αὐτῷ διὰ τὴν ἀδύνειαν."</note>
   He undoubtedly means that white Celtic lead <note>The Romans and Greeks often called tin "white lead" (plumbum album)</note> melts more quickly in fire than black lead, although elsewhere this flows more easily due to its greater moisture and the weakness of its composition. He seeks proof of a faster flow from a certain reaction of it in water; yet he does not state this simply, but says it "seems" to color quickly, which swift staining of the water is an indication that this lead is also quickly dissolved. He reports that the same thing happens in freezing cold due to the heat being united inside through <term>antiperistasin</term> <note>An Aristotelian concept where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat concentrating in the center of a body when the outside is chilled.</note> of the cold. A wonderful nature of tin, and not absurd to a Philosopher who listens to reason. But is it still found today among the Celts? What if <term>Bismuth</term> <note>original: "Bismuthum"; a brittle metal often confused with tin or lead in the early modern period</note> is to be understood, and that as a native metal, not yet mature? <term>Mathesius</term> <note>Johannes Mathesius, a 16th-century clergyman and author of "Sarepta," a famous work on mining and metallurgy</note> reports that it certainly flows in vats and solidifies. Nor is the argument of cold compressing heat inconsistent. That vein of ore is very hot and fleeting. Therefore, it ferments within itself while the cold stands around it, just as balls made of quicklime, gunpowder, naphtha, camphor, etc., are ignited when thrown into cold water.

## Number 46.

<term>It is said that there is a certain unique origin of Chalybian and Mysian iron; for it grows together, as they say, from the sand brought down by rivers. Some say they simply wash this and smelt it in a furnace; others say it is the sediment that forms, since the nature of the sand is washed many times. They add the so-called fire-resistant stone, of which there is much in that region. This iron is much more beautiful than others, and if it were not burned in a single furnace, it would seemingly differ in no way from silver. They say it alone is rust-free, or does not become very much so.</term> <note>This entire paragraph is a translation of the Greek text provided in the source: "Λέγεται ἰδιαίτερόν τινα εἶναι γένεσιν σιδήρου..."</note>

<margin>Silver-like iron, as in Babylon, and gold.</margin>
   He says iron is produced in the region of the <term>Chalybes</term> <note>An ancient people of Asia Minor famous for their early mastery of iron-working and steel</note> and Mysians from the sand of rivers. He reports elsewhere, indeed, that copper floated in the sea and was collected from there; and <term>Geber</term> <note>Likely referring to the works of Pseudo-Geber, a highly influential 13th-century alchemist</note> mentions that scales of copper pushed along by a river finally yielded gold. But there is nothing absurd in ferruginous water providing iron-mud, as in marshes, which is smelted entirely with <term>pyrite</term> <note>an iron sulfide mineral</note>, or washed beforehand. When he says it differs in nothing from silver, <insert>Think of <term>Azzalo</term> <note>An early term for high-quality steel (from the Italian "acciaio")</note>, Indian or Seric iron, which some call Chinese, and wish to have perished,</insert> if it be more frequently refined in many furnaces, he seems to indicate that silver can be made from it, either by separation or by transmutation, just as it turns into copper and lead.

->THE END.<-

->To God, the Best and Greatest, Our Protector<- <note>original: "D. O. M. A." (Deo Optimo Maximo Auspice)</note>

# COMMENTARIES ON ALCHEMY
## BY ANDREAS LIBAVIUS, M. D.
### Part II.
### THE SIXTH TREATISE.

*Containing three books on the assessment of mineral waters—Physical, Chemical, Medical, and Philological—carefully composed by the same author.*

A related and indeed specific argument is contained in the fourth volume of Libavius’s *Miscellanea* <note>original: "Singularium"; a collection of specialized scientific or medical essays</note>, explaining in two books the nature of the wild baths <note>original: "ferinarum"; likely referring to the *Wildbad* or natural thermal springs</note> of Rothenburg on the Tauber <note>original: "Rotemburgensium ad Tubarim"</note>, concerning which the last letter of the third volume of *Chemical Letters* also deals, which may be referenced here.

# ON THE ASSESSMENT OF MINERAL WATERS.
## PART ONE.

<margin>Preface.</margin>
*Indeed, there exist many very learned commentaries on mineral waters by highly skilled men, and they are found in the hands of almost everyone—even commoners who have barely looked askance at the first steps of literature and the elements of reading and writing. Thus, it is a wonder what could drive anyone to philosophize about them anew. However, a certain logic in my own plan led me to touch upon this part of natural philosophy as well. I do not promise anyone anything more perfect than the labors of the greatest minds, nor do I strive to snatch away the praise of others through the disease of envious ambition. This contemplation is also held within Chemical matters. I have endeavored to cultivate Chemistry <term>Chymia</term> <note>In the 17th century, the terms alchemy and chemistry were often used interchangeably for the study of matter and its transformations</note> thus far. It is not right for me to fail in this, in which there is such an abundance among others: although there is no equal consistency amid such difficulty in the subject, and such a wondrous variety of minds and opinions. But if an addition to the completion of the art is made from this treatise, it is enough. Any good that comes of it beyond expectation will be counted as profit.*

## CHAPTER I.
### Which waters are called mineral.

*We have been accustomed to call those "mineral waters" which, departing from the simple, common, and pure state, have joined with some subterranean mineral, and are either <term>spiritually</term> <note>original: "spiritualiter"; in this context, it refers to waters impregnated with volatile vapors or gases rather than solid matter</note> tinted, or <term>corporally</term> <note>original: "corporaliter"; mixed with physical, solid mineral particles</note> mixed. Some deny that simple and extremely pure water can even be found in the realm of mixtures, for the sake of the health of living things. Yet, there are, as it were, images of it in those waters which appear to the senses for the most part unmixed and <term>Lyncean</term>.* <note>original: "lynceae"; a classical reference to Lynceus the Argonaut, famed for his supernatural keenness of sight; used here to mean "perfectly transparent" or "crystal clear."</note>

<summary>This page introduces Libavius's treatise on mineral waters, establishing his intent to categorize them chemically and physically despite existing literature. He defines mineral waters as those containing subterranean substances either as volatile "spirits" or physical mixtures.</summary>

<keywords>mineral waters, Andreas Libavius, Rothenburg on the Tauber, natural philosophy, medicinal springs, chemistry vs alchemy, spiritual vs corporal mixtures</keywords>

--- Page 91 ---
<meta>This page continues Libavius's discussion on mineral waters. It moves from the introductory remarks on page 139 into definitions of what constitutes "mineral water" versus "pure water," classifications based on taste, and the geographic locations of famous mineral springs and rivers.</meta>

Commentaries on Alchemy, Part II, Book VI.

...just as there is pure spring water, formed by the consistency of vapors without the influence of any mineral, which the tongue, eyes, and other senses judge to coincide most closely with the simplest elementary form. An example of this is also found in common distilled water, and rain water—which mimics distillation—and similar types. But we do not call those "mineral" which carry the debris of dirt, gravel, or mud, nor do we so name river water. Those waters which proceed or are drawn from living things, and are characterized by their own temperament <note>original: "crasi sua"; the specific mixture of humors or qualities</note>, are of the same judgment. A **mineral** <note>original: "Minera"; Libavius is formalizing the use of this term</note>—which word is now sufficiently common that it is not absurd to grant it "Latin citizenship," as there is no clearer term for the thing—is a subterranean <term>matrix|a place or environment in which something develops; a "womb"</term> in which any effective fossilized substance <note>In this period, "fossil" referred to anything dug out of the ground, including metals and salts</note> of a mixed nature can arise, whether it be a metal, a stone, a juice, or a clod of mineral earth. If the offspring of this matrix combines with water that is otherwise pure, or with the "principle" of water, and is mixed—either at its place of birth or during its course—in the form of a breath, vapor, spiritual tincture or quality, or a physical dissolution, or even if several of these occur together, it produces **mineral waters.**

When we call these waters to examination, together with their related mixtures—whether nature mixed them within living beings, or whether art or fortune mixed them outside of nature—and when we explore their mixtures, temperaments, principles, and effects, there arises the discipline upon which we are now laboring. This is the primary study of minerals; the rest follows from the affinity of their temperament and knowledge.

### CHAPTER II.
### *The Species of Minerals.*

**J**ust as there are innumerable mixtures and varieties exceeding the industry of all men, so too are there immense species of mineral waters. Their discrepancy is even greater because they do not follow a certain, defined origin established by nature, but are subject to the accidental encounters of things, preserving the condition of imperfectly and inordinately mixed substances. In such cases, if inordinate species behave like numbers—increasing and multiplying by the addition of a constant unit rather than by chance—it certainly happens much more so when fortune and accident have power over them. The same water from the same source may emerge at different points in time, or through the flow, arrival, and departure of matter, looking unlike itself and belonging to a different species. But the most powerful ones, which have obtained the prerogative of our contemplation, are those they call **thermal-springs** <note>original: "Therothermas"; specifically hot or medicinal springs</note>, which are not altered by a simple quality, but have simultaneously attained a tempered mineral state. Related to these are the **salty waters** (varying according to the different kinds of salts), the **acidic**, the **bitter**, the **slightly sweet**, and the **sharp** waters—distinguished primarily by their tastes. Added to these are those noble more for their effects and other virtues than for their taste, since many things in minerals lack taste, yet preserve or mimic the nature of metals, gems, mercury, or others.

### CHAPTER III.
### *The Forms of Mineral Waters.*

**T**he forms of springs and sources are mostly seen on the outermost part of the earth. For they break out from hidden recesses through the cracks and fissures of mountains, caught in their own channels. But they also expand into the breadth of lakes, and when mixed with rivers, they render these mineral as well. Thus, although most people believe the sea to be the origin of its own nature, there is perhaps nothing far from the truth in the idea that it became "natural brine" through the embrace of salty minerals, or the confluence and detention of such springs—or at least by a process such as occurs in lye through combustion and percolation. They report that in **Gothland** <note>Southern Sweden</note> there is a hot and sulfurous lake near the city of **Växjö** <note>original: "Vexionem"</note>; another at **Trondheim** <note>original: "Nidrosiam"</note> in Norway; another near **Aran** <note>original: "Haranem"</note>, a fortress of the West Goths. Nor is Lake **Velino** <note>in Italy</note> lacking a mineral nature. Aristotle and Pliny were ignorant of **Lake Ascanius**. Nor are the **Moravians** <note>people of the modern-day Czech Republic</note> without their own medicated lakes and marshes. Of the rivers, they say the **Nile**, the **Choaspes** <note>The Karkheh River in Iran</note>, and the **Euleus** <note>The Karun River in Iran</note> are slightly sweet at the surface but salty or slightly bitter at the bottom. In **Spain** there are mercurial rivers made of **cinnabar** <note>original: "minio"; mercuric sulfide, the primary ore of mercury</note>. They say the **Tiber** is of the same kind because of the white waters it receives, as is the **Nera** <note>original: "Narnim"</note>, the **Cydnus** of Cilicia, the **Thermōdōn**, and others. But whether there be much water or little, in the form of a sea, a pond, a lake, a pool, a river, or a spring, it makes no difference to our business.

### CHAPTER IV.
### *Concerning the Efficient Causes.*

**M**ineral waters can arise either within a mineral source, or from it, or nearby, or during their progress, in various ways. It is certain that the power of the stars, and especially of the **Sun**, can naturally do much in these lower realms. Thus, it seems to some that they hold dominion over the generation of metals and gems, which they say is perfected by heat, since heat is primarily generative, while cold, by contrast, is destructive. And to tell the truth, the matter does not seem clearly judged to me, although arguments more evident to the senses oppose the heat of the celestial bodies. The strongest of these arguments is that heat does not penetrate all the way to the mineral sources; for where the rays of the sun burn most fervently, just a little beneath the "skin" or crust of the earth, a coldness is found to prevail that is adverse to generation. But this can be countered by a different fact: the earth is not prevented from being warmed by the sun just because cold dominates in the vicinity of the ether, or further from the earth on the highest mountains and in the middle region of the air. No less is the **Moon** the arbiter of waters in the remotest parts of the earth as on its surface. Certainly, the miner near the seat of shadows will complain just as much about the power of the full moon upon the humors <note>The bodily fluids, which were believed to be influenced by the moon just like the tides</note> he carries with him as if he were under the open sky. And who...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature and classification of mineral waters, specifically moving from general definitions to the physical causes and "matter" behind their generation within the earth.</meta>

->On the judgment of mineral waters, part 1.<-

It has been proved that the locations of minerals, though they may seem deep in some places, are less deep in others and have their own vents, entrances, and recesses, so that they can be joined with the daily air—which is surely the vehicle for the powers of the heavens. And what vein reaches the total depth of the sea? It is said to obey the moon from the very bottom. Therefore, one should not think that the case regarding the power of the stars over subterranean things is entirely defeated and judged as either nonexistent or meager. But we must philosophize through things closer to us; through these, those celestial influences do not seem entirely empty, and yet the subterranean cause of generations and corruptions is more powerful: the very nature of the lands and the place, whose movement is neither accidental nor violent, but comes from an internal principle and is distributed by an innate assistance within the bowels of the earth. It is not, indeed, absurd to suggest that all remaining heat is derived from a primary source of heat, which is afterward certainly defined and determined by the nature of the individual thing it assumes and follows, becoming intimate with it by applying itself to it. But it is also not absurd that nascent things have their own heat, which, just as it could be taken from that common source, so also can be engendered individually by the powerful Author of all things. Therefore, let heat not be sought only in the ether, nor in the regions of the moon, but also in the bowels of living things and even the earth. Through the operation of this heat, alterations, digestions, solutions, putrefactions, concretions, definitions, and other varied effects occur, especially as the force of cold and other qualities hangs over them, and as the dispositions of the matter and its principles allow.

### CHAPTER V.
#### On Matter.

<margin>The first mode of generating mineral waters is from the gathering of mineral vapors and breaths.</margin> When digestive heat acts upon moisture, whether actual or potential, and simultaneously exercises a dissolving power, breaths, vapors, and smokes are stirred up. In these, if a watery nature excels—whether in the mineral itself (which is fit for the work and allows for a certain cavity) or in other receptacles to which they are carried, rolled forward, or otherwise emitted and thrust out—a coagulation can occur through a proportional cold. From this, the collected humor, continued in a just quantity and by a perennial succession and the "fostering" of the mineral, finally finds an exit for itself into the light. In this way, nature procreates mineral water or a medicinal spring: namely, when the mineral breathes out and evaporates at the same time, existing as one with it. Sometimes the <term>mingled|original: συγχυθεὶς; poured together or mixed</term> breaths of a single mineral, which run together, thicken into a mineral liquor. Sometimes <term>each of the two|original: ἑκάτεροι; referring to two distinct types</term> smokes of one mineral rising up are associated with the vapors of another, near or far. Occasionally it happens differently: a vapor elevated from a pit licks up spirits hanging somewhere on the way, or those still fresh; experience confirms that both usually happen. For breaths not yet coagulated, especially the more tenacious ones, halt at obstacles, and unless they are moved, they finally unite into a body. It is obscure to no one that vapors intervene with these and thicken with the things they have taken up. Thus, before they settle and turn into a liquor or a body, the moist and dry spirits can unite and constitute mineral water. A testimony to these things can be what we see happening around chimneys, where especially moist wood is burned with dry wood, with minerals added. For a humor related to the minerals drips from there, especially if the vapor predominates. But the experiments of the Chemists <note>original: "Chymicorum"; referring to early modern alchemists and chemical physicians</note> are more ingenious and less polluted. For if you mix vaporous things with breath-like things, and having instituted a proper maceration, you procure a distillation: not simple water, but medicinal water will come forth—and all the more so if the heat was more active and also raised the dry spirits. The same will happen if you place a breath-like substance at the bottom of a vessel and a vaporous one where the exit is—such as incense at the bottom, and a cup of simple water near the neck—or water at the bottom and a breath-like substance near the lid where the spirit must proceed. Thus, if different materials are placed in different vessels, and yet all are gathered either by a common lid or a channel, a medicinal liquor results. This is the conspiracy of dry spirits with moist ones, inexplicable in the quantity of matter and the degree of virtue.

### CHAPTER VI.
#### Diverse vapors for one water.

Afterward, one may consider that different species of one kind and of different virtues are confused; for instance, when two or more vapors affected in different ways meet, and likewise exhalations and smokes. For although every vapor is similar to itself and possesses a watery nature—so that by this name it would not seem to produce anything beyond simple water <term>by composition|original: συνθέσει; through the synthesis or putting together of parts</term>—we do not now take it so nakedly, but rather that in its prevailing vapid nature it contains something of a breath-like affection or an "alluvion" <note>An overflow or washing-up of mineral matter</note>, just as we do not understand a "breath" to be of such great simplicity. Therefore, various species of vapors can be established without absurdity. But they can also be altered both by reason of the matter and by the "matrix" <note>The womb-like environment where minerals form</note> and the paths and other things they encounter. It is likely, therefore, that mineral waters also arise from here. An example perhaps would be if you allowed the must of wine in one vessel, the phlegm of vinegar in another, and the whey of milk in a third to evaporate and distill into a common lid. A modified water will emerge from there, such as nature might produce in its great earthly vessel through its own "cookings." The same judgment applies to exhalable and smoky things.

Sometimes the same vapor, or breath, partly condensed and partly still dissolved, is altered by effective qualities; once altered, it is changed further, having received a principle of mutation which, progressing like a contagion, causes either the whole or the most significant part to take on a mineral character. It has been discovered that vapors and breaths enclosed for a long time have acquired a varied nature, just as they tell of a small chest not opened for many years; and Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the preeminent German scholar of mining and mineralogy</note> records that caves closed for a long time exhaled a pestilential spirit when they were reopened. Such is the power of a septic principle when it has taken root.

<meta>This page continues the alchemical discussion on the origins of mineral waters, transitioning from celestial and internal heat influences to the specific chemical and physical processes—such as distillation and the mixing of "spirits"—that create various types of medicinal and mineralized springs within the earth.</meta>

Commentary on Alchemy, part II. Book VI.

# CHAPTER VII.

<margin>The second mode.</margin>
**T**he resolutions of substances thinned by the vehement heat of fires suggest to us another mode for the generation of mineral waters. This belongs partly to spirits and partly to bodies, according to the way chemical artists use these terms. For when thinned *calces* <note>original: "calces"; these are the powdery metallic remains left after intense heating or "calcination."</note> are brought to the nature of salts, they readily dissolve into waters or liquors in moist air; this should be thought to happen for no other reason than when the moist air is absorbed, it coagulates and melts the *calx* together by a certain appetite for its opposite. For once the watery part is again drawn off into vapor, the original *calx* returns. This same artistry has produced for us "coagulable spirits" and oils, which, while driven from metallic substances by the power of the most vigorous fires into the cold part of the vessels, join there with the air and become liquors. Thus, if you elicit a sharp spirit from flint with sublimated mercury and antimony, or lead, and others, the coagulation—achieved by injecting water, spirit of wine, or similar substances—shows that those very principles consisted in that way. What art performs in smaller vessels, the "Daedalian and Vulcanian" <note>This refers to the "artful and fiery" power of nature, named after Daedalus the master craftsman and Vulcan the god of the forge.</note> nature performs in similarly arranged large ones, as the consensus of the wise has confirmed that nature procures these things through the same or analogous agents. But minerals of this kind rarely pour out pure waters, because they are easily absorbed and coagulated again. If, however, moisture flowing from elsewhere either receives those spirits (as happens in *aqua forti* <note>Nitric acid.</note>, for which common water is placed in the receiver) or washes them away after they have been absorbed, then flows and springs are formed. This reasoning differs from the former in that here the things are more "spiritual" and like fiery concretions, whereas there they were more corporeal. Therefore, even if such dry spirits, separated by Vulcan <note>the fire</note>, have settled somewhere and afterward were dissolved into liquor by moisture, the result is the same.

# CHAPTER VIII.

**N**ext to these is the procreation from parts that are bulky on both sides, whether both are actually liquid or potentially so: or at least from a bulk of liquor that receives a "spiritual tincture." First, we must place water in the subterranean regions, whether it has sent itself down through visible cataracts, or having been drunk up gradually, has flowed together from everywhere, or was commanded to be there by its primeval origin and the stable law of nature—staying still at times and at other times running through rivers like veins, just as the "lesser world" <note>The "Microcosm," or the human body, which alchemists compared to the Earth (the Macrocosm).</note> of an animal has its own seat and channels for waters within itself. This water may have been born within, or gathered by the sea insinuating itself everywhere and, as it were, pouring through. For it is not a rash thing that Ecclesiastes says: "all waters come from the sea, and return to the same place" <note>Ecclesiastes 1:7.</note>; just as in the second book of the *Meteorology*, Aristotle says, <note>original: "ἀρχὴ δὲ καὶ παντὸς ὕδατος θάλασσά ἐστι"</note> "the sea is the origin of all water," an opinion that is not foreign to Plato's *Phaedo*, nor to Homer and others (though Cardano, in his arrogance, made himself its first author). No one is ignorant of the fact that there is no small supply of such waters in the gulfs of the earth, unless they have no knowledge of metals and minerals in the bowels of the earth. It is also established that very large lakes have been seen in vast and horrendous abysses, so that Plato's "Tartarean Ocean" in the depths of the earth might not seem fabulous, nor the fictions of the Poets: Styx, Phlegethon, Acheron, Cocytus, and Lethe <note>The five rivers of the Greek underworld.</note>. Water must be placed beneath because it constitutes the "body" of mineral flows or waters; it is usually elicited from all things in greater quantity and has the form of a flow with thinness. However, in some it is so weak and volatile that it quickly evaporates into the air from a little digestion and leaves behind the solid body it carried, as history testifies regarding the *Albula* <note>Sulfurous springs near Rome.</note> and certain Hungarian waters. Pure "mineral juices" can also exist and flow, but we do not call them "mineral waters"; such are Petroleum or Naphtha, liquid amber, and things of that sort. The same reasoning applies to those things which, in the estuaries of the earth, either flow or are spat out as molten substances, such as the *Pyriphlegethontes* <note>literally "fire-burning" rivers</note> vomited by the fires of Etna, liquefied metals, juices, stones, etc., which in the *Timaeus* are called "fusible waters."

# CHAPTER IX.
### How water is tinged.

**F**urthermore, that elemental water receives either a "spiritual" or a "corporeal" tincture, according to the way the Chemists (in whose marketplace we now find ourselves) are accustomed to speak. By "spiritual tincture," they understand both alterations and the mixtures of essential spirits summoned from bodies, whether they have already settled and coagulated or not. By "corporeal tincture," they mean if the whole substances, or at least the remains of extracted things, are tempered together. We respect this use of terms now, although among corporeal things we also have thicker juices elicited by nature from their matrices.
Through a spiritual tincture, therefore, common water becomes mineral when it is altered by the powerful forms of effective minerals—either while it stays and dwells upon them for a long time, or is carried past them over a long stretch—though this can also happen in a short time by great force, which otherwise would take a long time by a lesser force. In this category are the excellent thermal baths (*thermae*), and some which are, conversely, extremely cold, as well as lukewarm ones. Then there are those that receive "third powers" and the forces of the whole substance, examples of which we have in the "masteries" of substance: such as lime water, water of extinguished metals, and purging antimony water—because either the substance was boiled in it, or glass of antimony was macerated in it. It is clear that these acquire new powers without a communion of the substance itself, a thing which even the common people experience in rain water, or other water kept for a long time in copper vessels, and much more so in wine, must, and other such liquors. They are "spiritually tinged" in another way when a spirit exiting the substance brings a virtue along with it; it does not merely alter by contact, but while it insinuates itself, it coagulates and, as if acquiring a body, is mixed by this very act. However, such a concretion is sometimes not very fixed or stable because of the volatile nature of dry spirits, which assist the mixture in a somewhat congealed state rather than being fully tempered. Thus, in the caves of mines, when virulent breaths are resolved from mountains and minerals by the power of fires, because they seek coldness, they settle upon the waters...

On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part I.

...they are sometimes even accustomed to standing quite thick, but once they are agitated, they soon fly back; however, by their settling, they make those waters deadly. But if they are forced into a narrow space, such as when they are compelled to exit with the water through common cracks or channels, it is natural for them to unite more deeply. Thus, the waters of <term>mine tunnels<note>original: "cuniculorum"; refers to the drainage or access shafts in mining operations.</note></term> are not without mineral power, both for other reasons and for this one. This happens more quickly from mineral vapors and fumes because they are more akin to a watery nature and consistency, and are thus more easily admitted, coagulated, and held fast. This is a matter of common experience, as when fumes are mixed into broths during cooking; neither cooks nor <term>chemists<note>original: "Chymici"; in this period, the term covers both practical chemistry and alchemy.</note></term> are ignorant of this when they imprint the <term>empyreumata<note>original: "empyreumata"; the "burnt" smell or taste resulting from the chemical transformation of organic or mineral matter by fire.</note></term> of roasted or burned things onto waters. That stench, or rather the spirit emerging from scorching during boiling, belongs to the category of smokes.

But if anyone denies that mineral waters emerge from a fellowship of spirits, he has neither contemplated arterial blood mixed—or rather confused (for such mixtures are imperfect, and like unstable fellowships or placements)—with vital spirits, nor does he consider that where a mineral spring breaks forth, a great abundance of spirits appears. These are so potent that they bring on dizziness and fainting to those who gaze upon them too intently or for too long, though as they vanish in the stream's course, they abandon the water and leave it alone.

## CHAPTER X.
### Powers arising from the meeting of substances.

**T**o these "spiritual tinctures" one may also refer those powers which, having been detected in no single part before the mixing, only then emerge when they are combined. Thus, cold metals poured into equally cold <term>aqua fortis<note>original: "aquæ forti"; literally "strong water," referring to nitric acid.</note></term> will effervesce upon contact. This also happens with fresh quicklime, in "strong water" and water of tartar, and even when two different "strong waters" are mixed, or in the sharpest spirit or <term>oil of vitriol<note>original: "oleo acerrimo vitrioli"; concentrated sulfuric acid.</note></term> and simple water, and many others, according to their mutual affection or <term>sympathy and antipathy<note>A common Renaissance idea that materials have natural attractions or repulsions to one another.</note></term>, such as the power communicated to iron by a magnet. For those who contend that what was not in any part before the composition cannot be in the composite do not argue with enough consideration—as if a body cannot be heavy or light, even though neither the matter nor the form are such when we imagine each in isolation. That such a thing happens not only in the "Vulcanian" <note>Referring to the workshops of craftsmen and chemists.</note> arts but also in the workshop of nature has already been said several times. It has long been asserted that vapors can putrefy with exhalations; for although each is named separately, they are not entirely simple, and thus by coagulating they constitute a mineral flow. The same must now be established regarding water, and indeed it is likely that a certain variety exists here according to the various disposition and degree of putrefaction. If you consider that these modes of spiritual tincture can coincide in many ways in different places in the same water before it ever sees the sky, you will understand how unexplored the certainty of such things is in individual cases.

## CHAPTER XI.
### The physical mixing of minerals.

**T**hose things which meet with water physically are usually in the form of liquors, or juices, or limes soluble in moisture, although "flowers," tinctures, and other things can have a similar nature, as is explained in the chemical "magisteries" and essences; these have already acquired a body through coagulation, although some of them are also counted among the spirits in their own way. It matters nothing to the mixture whether all the juices have matured, or are still in motion toward maturation, or whether they are more or less thickened, coagulated, or frozen, as they say; nor does it matter if they are together or dispersed through the earth and mountains, though this makes a difference in terms of their powers and variety.

<margin>4. On the Senses.</margin>
> Concerning these things, the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle.</note> long ago commented thus: "Wherefore" (he says) "many of the ancient physiologists also say that water is of such a kind as the earth through which it passes; this is especially clear in the case of salty waters. For salts are a kind of earth. Therefore, those things filtered through ash hold a bitterness and make the juice bitter; and so it is with others. There are many springs, some bitter, some acidic, and others having all sorts of other flavors," etc. <note>original Greek: "Διὸ καὶ πολλοὶ φάσι...".</note>
>
> Similar things are read in the second book of the *Meteorology*: "Other qualities," he says, "exist through a certain mixing of the water itself, and whatever the substance mixed in may be, it creates such a flavor." Likewise: "Whenever there are salty flows of rivers or springs, one must think they were once very hot; then the source of the fire was extinguished; but the earth through which they penetrate still remains like <term>lye and ash<note>original Greek: "οἷον κονίαν καὶ τέφραν".</note></term>. There are, however, in many places both springs and river flows having various flavors of every kind, the cause of all of which must be placed in an existing or ignited power of fire. For when the earth is burned out to a greater or lesser degree, it takes on various forms and <term>colors<note>original Greek: "χρόας".</note></term> of <term>juices<note>original Greek: "χυμῶν"; here meaning flavors or mineral fluids.</note></term>. For it becomes full of the powers of alum and lime and other such things, through which the sweet waters that are filtered are transformed." These are the words of Aristotle.

<margin>The generation of alum and other juices.</margin>
It seems indeed that he attributes the miraculous generation of <term>alum<note>A naturally occurring mineral salt used in dyeing and medicine.</note></term> to burnings, which does not correspond to the experience of craftsmen; rather, there is a primal creation of such juices, and afterwards a continuation through generation from a <term>seminal virtue<note>The "seed-like" power or blueprint believed to exist within matter that allows it to grow or change into specific substances.</note></term>. But let us not think the greatest Philosopher's opinion so childish as to suggest that he wants such juices to be produced from mere earth by the power of fire. We must think he presupposes stones and earth that are mixed and endowed with the potential or "nursery" of alum, <term>vitriol<note>original: "chalcanthi"; specifically copper or iron sulfate.</note></term>, and the rest; while the power of fire or arranged heat works within these, the juice is perfected, matured, and brought into action through certain <term>digestions<note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow heating of a substance to mature or transform it.</note></term>. This is called the essential principle. In this way, he should not be believed to have been such an infant in the generation of metals as to think they are born solely from watery vapors and exhalations.
<margin>Division of mineral exhalations.</margin>

The experience of craftsmen also confirms this exposition. For the veins, or stones, and earths of vitriol, alum, and similar things are either softened by "open-air digestion" through heat, rain, and other weather, or are further subdued by the power of fires, so that they may afterwards pour out juices which before were sought in vain...

Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book VI.

...you would not bring it forth by washing or boiling. Nor indeed can you extract salt by any fire from a thing in which there is naturally no principle of salt.

<margin>Spiritual tinctures are not present in mineral waters.</margin>
By this kind of generation, the opinion of those who can attribute nothing to mineral waters—such as <term>acidulae<note>original: "acidulis"; these are "acidic" or "sour" mineral springs, highly valued for their perceived medicinal properties in the early modern period.</note></term> and the like—except for spiritual mixtures and immature seeds, or "first entities," is refuted. These theorists believe that before these substances can coagulate and take on a form, they are prematurely taken up by the waters. It must be admitted that this can happen; however, it should not be held as a universal rule, since <term>the Art<note>original: "ars"; specifically refers to alchemy or the "spagyric art," which sought to replicate and accelerate natural processes.</note></term> itself often draws out these juices, perfected in their substance, from mineral waters through coagulation. To deny that such waters contain minerals is the mark of a very narrow mind, too fond of its own ideas. Truly, who can name and show a "metallic water" that carries the "first matter" of metals before it is solid—before it has a form or the virtues of a perfected metal? How can they call this water "iron-bearing" or that one "copper-bearing" if they have never known the qualities of the first matter of each individual metal? All things can be reduced to <term>mercury<note>original: "hydrargyrum"; quicksilver.</note></term>; from all things, salt and <term>vitriol<note>original: "calcanthum"; a term for metallic sulfates, often blue or green in color.</note></term> are extracted. Who shall distinguish these in their first beginnings and raw state? More probable is the opinion of our Philosopher: that these things happen through resolution, either into the "spirits" mentioned above, or into soluble juices or <term>calxes<note>original: "calces"; the powdery residue left after a metal or mineral has been roasted or "calcined."</note></term>. For the Art bears witness that calcined metals are dissolved into liquids, and other juices are drawn from them and washed away by percolating elemental waters. Indeed, they are even corroded by sharp things (strong waters, <term>cementing powders<note>original: "caementis"; refers to the alchemical process of "cementation," where metals are refined using dry mineral powders and heat.</note></term>, coloring agents, etc.), and this corrosion is mixed with the waters so thoroughly that it is not visible until after coagulation—just as the essence of many things remains in very clear wine, the juice of boiled things in purified decoctions, or metallic filings in <term>aqua fortis<note>original: "aqua forti"; literally "strong water," refers to nitric acid.</note></term> and soluble juices in solutions.

# CHAPTER XII.
## Analogies of Minerals.

**T**o this class of "corporeal mixtures" one may also refer those waters which acquire nothing at all within the mineral vein or the caverns of the earth, but rather carry with them a power already mixed at the earth's surface. Thus, if the sea were to enter a gap in the earth and burst forth again at another opening, it could be considered a mineral spring. Likewise, if rainwater, river water, stagnant water, or marsh water, having taken on power from plant juices, animal excrement, or other things, were to descend somewhere and emerge again affected in the same way, or at least changed somewhat from that original principle. It is well known that where herds of animals stable, the places soaked in excrement receive the beginnings of <term>saltpeter<note>original: "kalinitri"; refers to potassium nitrate or nitre.</note></term>. If these are then soaked up by a stream creeping here and there and finally emerging as a single spring, the water will turn out to be what should be called "nearly mineral." It is also known that various things, especially animal and vegetable matters, can rot in stagnant waters. From this, too, an origin representing a mineral will arise.

# CHAPTER XIII.
## The Opinion of Paracelsus.

<margin>The first matter of metals.</margin>
**P**aracelsus <note>The famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist (1493–1541) who pioneered the use of chemicals in medicine.</note> was also taught this by his teachers and the evidence of experience. For although he sometimes attributes a unique and primeval nature (existing since the beginning of the world) to mineral waters, saying that mineral waters were once one and the same as simple waters but were later separated and flowed apart for the health of animals and plants; nevertheless, he either corrected this opinion or changed it later (consistent with his usual inconstancy or Socratic uncertainty). He left written that cold mineral waters arise either from <term>alum<note>original: "alumine"; a specific type of mineral salt used in dyeing and medicine.</note></term>, salt, or <term>vitriol<note>original: "atramento"; literally "ink," but in an alchemical context, it refers to "atramentum sutorium" or ferrous sulfate.</note></term> that are immature and unmixed in their vein—does this mean that no elemental water is added, but those very immature, uncongealed substances existing in the form of a liquid emerge purely and establish a mineral spring with a perennial flow? (If this is so, an immense force must be collected in vast reservoirs or spaces for the flow to last a long time; otherwise, Nature is frustrated in her attempt in that place, emitting nothing but imperfect abortions into the light). Or, he says they arise from the <term>Three Principles<note>The alchemical triad of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which Paracelsus believed were the components of all matter.</note></term> of the seven metals before they solidify. If a rush of water runs through and "corrupts" them so they cannot be perfected—or at least from the first matter of these three in each metal, both simply and mixed—as if the operation of nature were overtaken by the influx of elemental water, dissipating the salt, sulfur, and mercury of gold, silver, tin, lead, iron, copper, and quicksilver that were about to coagulate. Yet that thing cannot be called "first matter," since it is nothing other than dissolved salt, uncongealed sulfur, and unsolidified mercury. The true "first matter" of these is either a vapor and seminal breath having the potential for those things, or a viscous principle fertile with such a spirit. If this is snatched away before its maturity and diluted by waters, it can in no way imprint a metallic nature upon the waters, since it possesses it not in act, but only in potential—just as if the <term>fluid of a chicken egg<note>original: "gallinacei liquor"; literally the "liquid of a hen." The author argues that a raw egg yolk mixed in water doesn't have the "nature" of a chicken yet.</note></term> were scattered and diluted in water, it would not take on the nature and powers of a hen, nor could it even be recognized as such. Moreover, it is ridiculous that such a principle could flow out simply, since it is established that in a mine it is enclosed and matures like the fruits of plants and animals; if it flows together, it is either not that principle, or it has already taken a form in the mine, lacking only the proper coagulation which it finally acquires in its pool. It is certainly easier to imagine such a thing than to show it. However, it should not be denied that metallic waters arise in some way through the mixing of "wild" waters with the immature beginnings of metals, whether they be spirits or liquids. But if you also add that those three principles are to be understood separately, so that <margin>Doubt concerning metallic origins.</margin> twenty-one mineral flows could exist from them, you will be raving even further. For they do not exist separately, nor are metals made by a composition of those separate parts, but they are brought forth as if from a seed, in which those principles were together in potentiality—if indeed they are to be held as true principles, and not rather as "chemical masteries" elicited by art from metals affected in different ways. In this way, we can make vitriol, flowers, calxes, and liquids from the same metals, which nevertheless are not considered true "origins." Or, they arise from the spirits of the three metallic principles. (The same is said: for it matters not whether they appear outwardly in the form of spirit or liquid, if they are imperfect within. We can, however, also understand the breaths of resolved things, and take those "principles" <term>figuratively<note>original: "catachrestice"; a rhetorical term for using a word in a forced or improper sense.</note></term> for salt, sulfur, and mercury—not those which are the beginnings of the composition or generation of things, but things perfected in themselves, just as we consider the elements in themselves, insofar as they are simple bodies per...

<summary>The author refutes the idea that mineral waters are merely "spiritual" seeds, arguing instead that they contain physically dissolved mineral substances. He critiques Paracelsus's theories on the "Three Principles" (Salt, Sulfur, Mercury) as the origin of mineral springs, suggesting these theories are more imaginary than observable.</summary>

(existing separately) or from the liquids of gems: (either before they harden, or after they have been dissolved, or while they possess only a seminal existence in their <term>matrix<note>original: "matrice"; in early mineralogy, this refers to the surrounding rock or "womb" in which minerals and gems were thought to grow like embryos.</note></term>) or from the viscous substances from which pearls, shells, and similar things are born: (*which viscosities are, however, determined toward a specific thing, and are found beneath certain plants as well as animals, and even in some souls*) or from the juices of plants, by which they are colored (*from which they are called "mineral" only by name or through a metaphorical transfer of the word*) whether before they become solid, or when they are dissolved (*though this dissolution is more an extraction, unless you prefer to understand it as a departure through putrefaction*) or from the waste of animals dwelling in one place (*as is the case in fishponds and preserves; similarly the sea and fish-filled subterranean lakes are changed. In some places, marshes or rivers going underground have left the seeds of fish, or the small offspring themselves, clinging there as if in sluggish mud; if rainwater or spring water flows through these, they take on a mineral character. Thus, if worms, frogs, and other creatures dwelling in the hiding places of the earth infect it with dung and other excrements, the waters draw in that taint, etc. If these waters are considered "mineral," then every river flowing past human settlements or nourishing fish and frogs would be included in that category.*) or from manure-pits and parts of plants rotting in the earth: or from various types of earth: (*There are various boles, clays, muds, etc., within the earth and in its crust; if waters absorb and carry away their subtle juices which have a mineral nature, and are altered by them, they truly become mineral. In this way, if a mound of earth cast out from pits and trenches is dissolved by the force of the air and rains, or dried out by the heat of the sun, and afterwards deposits something mineral into the waters it meets, those waters become mineral. No one, however, calls the pools of manure-pits "mineral," although if they penetrate into the earth and are filtered, they can nevertheless take on something resembling minerals.*)

These things are found in the writings of Paracelsus, or rather in the transcriptions, though they are less "Paracelsian" in style. Otherwise, it is a wonder why he does not make mineral waters the mere, orderly, and constant offspring or fruits of nature, just as he trifles about those things produced in the air. It is likewise a wonder why he did not say they were made by the stars within the earth, or concede that certain rains—the excrements or constructions of certain constellations—should also be counted among minerals. He also showed little favor to his own gods, <term>Ilech<note>A Paracelsian term referring to a primordial supernatural power or the "First Matter" of the cosmos that governs the formation of things.</note></term> and the rest of his dreams, which he places in charge of his ministries in every birth of nature.

---

## CHAPTER XIV.
### *The most frequent minerals found in mineral waters.*

**B**ut setting those theories aside, it can be somewhat clear to the investigator of mineral waters from such a history of generations that their origin should be attributed not only to the elements and their primary qualities, but also to things constituted from them later—whether immediately at the beginning through creation, or afterwards through established causes like generation, mixture, and natural alteration. Indeed, the minerals of metals, stones, juices, earths, vapors, and exhalations dominate here: whether you consider them before they reach consistency, or in their coagulation and perfected form, or in their dissolution and extraction. Those waters are similar to minerals which emerge from the company of animals and plants, and from various works and "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" refers to the ways substances are acted upon or changed by external forces.</note> in many types of movements. But if anyone demands the names of these things in specific detail beyond these general categories, it is hardly possible to explain every single one to him, let alone their mixtures and combinations; however, let him know that among metals, *copper, iron, lead, and mercury* occur more frequently; while *gold, silver, and tin* occur more rarely. (One must understand these not only as the pure metals themselves, but also their veins and mixtures; and not only the perfected forms, but also the imperfect ones when they are still in their "first matter"—metallic yet determined—and even their dissolved states.) Among the "middle minerals," one must turn one’s mind to *salt, vitriol <note>original: "atramentum"; literally "inky substance," referring here to metallic sulfates like green or blue vitriol.</note>, alum, sulfur, bitumen, amber, orpiment with sandarac and arsenic; furthermore antimony, antimony-lead <note>original: "plumbum cinereum"; likely bismuth or a specific lead-antimony alloy.</note>, magnetite, and various pyrites, which are also called marcasites: golden, silvery,* Gelfum (*pale marcasite*), Zinc (*brassy marcasite, as if a false copper, white or red*), *chrysoccolla,* etc. Among the types of earth, one must look at *various boles, ochre, rusty earth, and lumpy cadmia, which they call calamine stone,* etc. Among stones, *stony cadmia, tufa, gypsum, marl, shale, coal <note>original: "lithanthracem"; stone-coal.</note>, Armenian stone, blue-stone,* and various others; among which gems excel, and the "false gems" which they call *fluors*, from which come the *crystalline, magnetine, amethystine, adamantine, and carbuncular types,* etc. Add to these the many *kinds of marble and limestone.* Nor should we omit those things that arise from them or are found with them, such as *dross <note>original: "recrementa"; the waste products of mineral formation or smelting.</note>, in which are soot, exhalations, vapors, slag, cadmia (both cadmia and realgar), sterile veins of metals, juices, and stones, lime, liquids, minium, white lead, verdigris, iron-rust,* and almost infinite things similar to these—to say nothing of the species that fall under those categories, such as *sal ammoniac, rock salt, nitre, saltpeter,* etc. *blue, green, white, yellow, and red vitriol (that is, sory, misy, melanteria, vitriol, and chalcitis),* etc. *liquid alum, solid alum, flaky alum, round alum, etc. white, yellow, and lemon amber, ambergris, jet: black and yellow bitumen, asphalt, liquid and solid, etc. fertile, sterile, brassy, golden, silvery, aluminous, and vitriolic pyrites, etc. red, black, and yellow sulfur,* etc., all of which are explained more fully in the history of natural things.

---

## CHAPTER XV.
### *The dullness of the human intellect.*

**I**t is evident from the stated variety that hardly anyone can promise himself an exact knowledge of the mixtures in mineral waters, and many things must be left among the "marvels." Yet one must attempt something rather than nothing; and since it is clear what the nature of the mineral <term>matrices<note>The geological environments or "wombs" where minerals are formed.</note></term> is, and what sorts of things happen within them, the labor spent on this contemplation will not be in vain. It is a mark of torpor, laziness, and a shameful contempt for miracles to be unwilling to test the powers of the intellect even in the smallest matters. Yet it is a mark of foolish confidence and insane arrogance to pronounce the exact differences and measures of the ratios of mixtures as if with a pointing finger, since it is certain that this is beyond human grasp. This is something <term>Jordanus<note>Refers to Thomas Jordanus (1539–1585), a physician who wrote extensively on the medicinal properties of waters and the plague.</note></term> also frankly admits, and the difficulty of judgment is clear from the disputes of the most learned men, since you will hardly find two who, relying on their own experience and not the decree of another, agree on the same water...

...must be judged by consensus, just as you may see occurring with the baths of Abano near Padua <note>original: "balneis Aponi Patauini"; the thermal baths of Abano Terme have been famous for their healing properties since Roman times.</note>, concerning which Montagnana, Savonarola, Dondi, Falloppio, etc. <note>These are all prominent Renaissance physicians and medical writers who wrote on balneology, the study of medicinal springs.</note>, each established something different from the next. Falloppio corrects Montagnana and Savonarola, and he in turn is chastised by the censure of Bacci. Paracelsus, in his usual audacity, seemed to pluck at them all, and after him Tabernaemontanus spared few. It will be enough for me to have investigated those things which reveal themselves by evident arguments, and those which stand out in the mixture. I shall not advise anyone to name every single ingredient that concurs or their specific degrees. Likewise, since the specific springs have been commented upon quite accurately by many in detail, I shall touch only upon the general headings of this judgment. I do this with confidence in several arts—since this matter does not belong to one alone—but especially in physics and medicine, to which Alchemy <note>At this time, "alchemy" referred to the chemical extraction of medicines and the study of mineral transformations.</note> is subject and serves as a handmaid, bringing the most powerful aids to this investigation. If the astrologer, the geometer, the arithmetician, the cook, the plowman, the gardener, the metal-miner, or even any common neighbor who turns that mineral water to the uses of life can supply something—or even what hunters and woodcutters, who are familiar with the mountains and valleys and are in some way endowed with the gift of judging nature, might contribute—these things are not neglected.

### CHAPTER XVI.
### The distribution of this contemplation.

Therefore, for one intending to investigate the nature of mineral waters, the mind must first be directed toward those things which are outside, around the spring, whether they are joined to it or surround it, or in whatever other way they relate to it. Then, the nature of the water itself as it gushes from the spring must be diligently contemplated. These two headings seem especially necessary for a slightly more refined certainty, and they have not been overlooked by those who were engaged in this same matter before us.

### CHAPTER XVII.
### The virtue of the heavens.

Among external factors, the first in dignity is the heaven, whose stars have a manifest right and power over the elementary region. It is certain that the nature of places varies by their different position relative to the sun, so much so that even in the innermost parts of the earth, miners are persuaded that no small momentum of good hope depends on this. Yet we do not approve of the dreams of superstitious astronomy or "astromancy," although those foolish prophets are greatly offended by the contempt shown for it. We do not want those silly fantasies about Saturn as the progenitor of lead, or Mars as the parent of iron, or those certain "conjunctions" spewing forth subterranean cataclysms and an immense force of waters in a "watery trigon," or the fictional houses of the heavens, and other follies of those sleeping and dreaming in the Cave of Trophonius <note>original: "antro Trophonii"; an ancient Greek oracle where consultants experienced vivid, often terrifying visions; here used to mean a place of delusions.</note>. What the Sun, Moon, and other active stars effect—whether by heat, or by the influx and motion of the virtues contributed to them—in the place upon which they rest and which they strike with straighter and more concentrated rays, is before the eyes of everyone. And the causes of certain events in mineral waters and other things are to be referred to these.

<margin>
The Fountain of Cyane.
</margin>

Both ancient and modern authors report that the Fountain of Cyane at Syracuse increases and diminishes with the Moon. It is not obscure that this depends on the force of that star. If the Moon has such power in this instance that it proves its cause by manifest motion, it will undoubtedly also engender other powers, and obtain power over the matter of the water to be poured out or absorbed. In the torrid zone, and throughout the tract toward the south,

<margin>
In the torrid zone: salty and bitter.
</margin>

one finds more salty and bitter things; there, sandy salts and <term>nitre<note>original: "nitrosi"; likely referring to natron or saltpeter, commonly found in arid regions.</note></term> are also frequent. If the waters there are salty and bitter, the cause is at hand. Toward the north, things are more vapid, raw, and tasteless (at least regarding the waters). In both places, the air is disposed similarly, and those things which enjoy its benefit or feel its harm are affected accordingly. Therefore, if the source and flow of the spring turns toward the Sun and endures it all day, the waters will be less raw, and not so subject to vapid spirits. The mineral principle will be indicated as steamy, more well-digested, mature, hotter, etc.; conversely, if it faces the north. The east and west promise moderate qualities. The more particular dispositions of the sun in the signs of the Zodiac also contribute something, whether considered individually or by the quarters of the year. Nor is the phase of the Moon without effect. Sirius, the Pleiades, Orion, etc., also have power. The Philosopher <note>Usually a reference to Aristotle.</note> used to recall the perennial durations of rivers and their interrupted paths to the periods of the heavens; just as the ages of animals and the continued series of their kinds depend on these, so too do those of rivers and springs. Thus, the flooding of the Nile and other rivers are judged by some to follow the stars, just as some flowers also seek the favor of the Sun. But enough concerning the heavens.

### CHAPTER XVIII.
### The judgment of the Air in minerals.

After the heavens, the contemplation of the air is necessary in this judgment. The air, being most closely subject to the heavens, is believed to be the first to receive the force of the stars, and then to communicate that force, once overcome, to the things placed below it. Some even maintain that by the powerful impressions of the constellations, the air is disposed toward certain effects, so that it afterwards exhibits not only unprecedented changes but even portents. In this way, it would serve as a judgment for a place or mineral water that is about to suffer something, rather than describing how it is currently affected or what the internal digestions of the earth are producing. But we are distant from this opinion; we say that while the air is indeed subject to the operations of the stars, it does not always follow the action, because the contact is not admitted due to a lack of "disposition." For the actions of agents occur in things that are disposed to them; in this way, though the Sun is burning, it does not have the action of melting upon wood or stone. Furthermore, the heaven does not induce impressions into the air itself, nor does it prepare the air peculiarly for its own service. For the air does not suffer similarly in its highest, middle, and lowest regions; but at the boundaries of the lands and waters, it is subject to the disturbances of breaths and vapors, with the cause acting either in the outermost part of the earth or its...

It highlights that geographic location and the orientation of a spring toward the sun significantly alter the water's chemical "maturity" and flavor.</summary>

<header>On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 1.</header>

# On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 1.

...or from its innards. For from here arise exhalations, vapors, and fumes; from here, the water is altered by the quality of the body it contains; and not infrequently it receives motion from sea currents <note>original: "euripis marinis"; referring to the Euripus Strait, famous for its strong oscillating currents, used here as a general term for tidal movements</note>, from storms, from subterranean fires, and other causes. The stars find these elements and afterwards disperse them by their own power rather than generate them, so that they might be placed over the elements for the sake of health and not for destruction—although during the struggle various impressions may occur. This is much like when the sun dissipates mists vomited up from the abyss <note>original: "tartaro"; literally 'Tartarus' or the underworld, used here to mean the deep, dark interior of the earth</note>, and occasionally produces winds, rains, and other effects on the same occasion, or when it dries out moist lands or melts winter snows and ice; in such cases, clouds and rains arise <unclear>excessively</unclear>, though not as the primary act of the sun. 

Things being as they are, one must consider the air of the place where the mineral water is submitted for judgment, which is contained either within that whole region of its origin or a large part of it (for some springs come from far away). If the air is vaporous, misty, or rainy—and it produces similar qualities in the bodies existing within it, pouring out from itself the nourishment for clouds, as we see in dense and humid forests—we may infer that the "wild" mineral water is gathered in the vicinity. If it is present in great quantity, it will make the medicinal power more diluted. For by a reciprocal motion, moisture rises from the pits of the earth and from the volcanic baths <note>original: "balneis Vulcaneis"; refers to the subterranean heat or "fires of Vulcan" that warm the waters</note>; once condensed, it is returned to the same place, so that it is necessary for frequent springs of water to not be lacking in those locations. 

However, if the air is more often foggy than vaporous, and is vexed more by winds than by rains, and if dryness, clear skies, and parched conditions follow more frequently, then the things contained within that region will behave similarly; we shall then judge that the mineral power prevails in the caverns of the earth. It is easy to judge whether such things arise there or are brought in from elsewhere by the movement of the air. For those conditions that are somewhere in the middle, the judgment is likewise middle-of-the-road. 

There are also more specific observations of these things, if they are referred to the points of time and the rising and setting of the stars. For it must be seen whether the winters, summers, springs, and autumns in that place behave in the usual manner as in other places lacking mineral springs, or not. One should observe whether humid mists appear during full moons; whether the air thickens with rain coming from afar, or if it is only destined to occur in those specific places. If there are high mountains in the circuit or vicinity, we shall easily recognize from their peaks whether the storm is local to the place or general, which the movement of the winds will also prove, as it precedes and follows the storm. 

Furthermore, if the region is to be evaluated, we shall observe whether the breeze is open and free-flowing, or enclosed and stagnant in a narrow space, lest we perhaps blame the spring for any evil arising from the air—although some influence can also be communicated from the air to the earth, which, when washed by rains, might further change the spring. The air reveals its nature and that of the place also by its smell and by its effects on living things. A smell that is sulfurous, bituminous, metallic, aluminous, inky <note>original: "atramentosus"; referring to vitriol or the metallic salts used to make ink</note>, or parched—appearing most strongly when the south wind blows—betrays minerals of that kind. And if the exhalations proceeding from there should condense and catch the beginning of a flame, then ignited meteors <note>In the 16th/17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including lightning, swamp gas, or "will-o'-the-wisps."</note> are commonly seen either on the surface of the earth or even higher up. 

Thus, one must see whether the health is inconvenienced by the general air of that tract or by certain specific places, such as villages, pools, cellars, pits, openings in the earth, mines, caves, and wells, or even in the border and the spring of the fountain itself, the river, or the marsh, etc. Heavy metallic breezes sometimes even extinguish candles, or at least change the brightness of night-lights or lamps in mines; they cause "fungi" <note>clumps of soot or carbon</note> to collect on the wicks, exhibit rainbows or halos, and sometimes fires, even when no such material has been used for fuel or kindling. Nevertheless, they vary the light and the smoke so that paleness, greenness, or redness appear, just as if metals were being smelted. 

But let us not allow ourselves to be deceived by accidental things. For it can happen that the air breathes something pleasant because of metal workshops in the vicinity, or because of smoke from chimneys, dung-heaps, ponds, charcoal pits, and similar things. <margin>Manna</margin> Manna, or "aerial honey," is a certain offspring of the air, affected in a specific way by fumes, vapors, and exhalations; although it is not always local or native, but can be a traveler. Birds also can provide signs regarding the air. Once all these things have been accurately inspected, we shall come more readily to a judgment. The closer the atmospheric storms are to the head of the spring, the more certainly we can pronounce upon its nature. From there, a "spirit" <note>A volatile gas or vapor</note> sometimes bursts out into the air with a manifest sign and harms animals. But let us leave the air aside.

***

# CHAPTER XIX.
->Conditions of the Earth.<-

It will not be irrelevant to bring the disposition and external face of the earth into the same business. For in this way, miners <note>original: "metallici"; those who work with metals or prospecting</note> at first glance either take hope from the site or set it aside. [In flat places, they say waters are rarely found unless they are medicated, such as salty, aluminous, or nitrous <note>containing "nitrum," a native soda or saltpeter</note> waters, because the rays of the sun constantly beating down resolve the sweet water into vapors, leaving behind an earthy filtration; these things can be granted regarding those places close to the sun's power and path, such as Ethiopia, Libya, Arabia, etc., unless the veins are so deep that the heat cannot penetrate to them.] 

If the place is wide and flat, either the water is propelled into the light from the deep by force, or it comes from far away, provided that no mineral is found in the open. For where there are sandy fields, as in Egypt and Libya, they abound in nitre, salt, alum, and similar juices, which either the rivers drink up, or the small springs, torrents, and rains wash away and carry into a fountain or a channel; in such cases, the reasoning is different. 

A mountainous tract, or one crowded with frequent hills; where there are also deep valleys, and sometimes ridges extending in a long series, or sometimes coming together in a circle to enclose valleys: this gives hope of a mineral in the vicinity. If we track this down, we shall be led closer to the nature of the spring. For knowledge from this is more certain than if the water flows from afar. Sometimes the earth gapes open at least with cracks and chasms, even where there are no mountains or hills. Here is a handle for singular consideration: whether the mineral water belongs to those fissures or not. Also, the perennial course of rivers carves out the earth and makes lagoons. Nor do plowmen, winds, rains, beasts, or diggers contribute nothing to our knowledge. Certainly, such caverns must be visited, and one must contemplate what is found in pits, crypts, cellars, trenches for drinking, the channels of rivers, the hollows of pools, the dens of beasts, and the caves of wild animals. Meanwhile, both the solidity and the concavity—or at least the thinness and thickness of the earths—will offer themselves, from which we may infer whether the rains penetrate or flow past, whether they are held back or have outlets. Echoes also reveal cavities, as do the murmuring of winds, the hiding places of beasts, the shaking of the earth, the sinking of rivers, and whirlpools that do not return the water but swallow it up.
