### CHAPTER XX.
### Bareness, etc.

<margin>Whether bare or forested mountains are more watery.</margin>
**N**akedness of the land and the presence of forests are also external factors to consider. It matters greatly whether mountains are shorn of growth and exposed to the sun, or planted with the trees of groves and woodland thickets; whether they are grassy or sterile, humid or dry, cultivated or wild, inhabited or deserted, and so forth. Shorn mountains, because they lie open to the air and sun, become drier in themselves. For they cannot nourish the moisture that feeds them. Therefore, even "wild water" <note>original: "aquæ syluestris"; referring to naturally occurring, unrefined surface water</note> does not much disturb the source of the mineral vein. Some scholars argue otherwise, thinking that bare places are more watery and that hills stripped of their thickets pour out more springs because the moisture is not being consumed by plants. However, immediate experience proves them wrong. If, therefore, in such a location, there is nonetheless much wild water along with a mineral; that water does not come from the outside or from the surface, but either arrives from a distance, or a specific vein converges there, or there is a fertile <term>vaporarium</term> <note>a "steam-room" or pocket of hot subterranean vapor</note> in the depths, or it is fed by some stagnant abundance. In misty, humid places prone to fogs, the matter is self-evident.

### CHAPTER XXI.
### Animal Shelters.

**T**here are also gatherings, societies, and stables of animals both within the earth and upon it. Just as there is a frequency of men in villages, towns, and huts, so too are there flocks of sheep, herds of cattle, and abundances of wild beasts. There are places where great cohorts of rabbits hide in their burrows; there are also dens of dormice, badgers, serpents, and the like. In some places, owls, bats, and similar light-shunning birds nest in caves; from the droppings of all these, <term>nitrous</term> <note>saltpeter-like</note> and <term>chalcantous</term> <note>original: "chalcantosa"; relating to chalcantum, a term for vitriol or copper sulfate</note> concretions arise. [It is known that crabs reveal the veins of water; indeed, even "fossil fish" <note>likely referring to fossilized remains found in mineral-rich strata</note> do the same.] There are also times when wild honey is gathered by bees and wasps in the cracks and caverns of mountains, and there are fish ponds, etc., which ought not to be overlooked.

### CHAPTER XXII.
### Plants, etc.

**O**n the surface of the earth, there is also a great diversity of sown crops as well as those that grow spontaneously; and yet, a small spring can be tinted by them. Thus, where great decays of plants, animals, and such things occur, "tinctures" <note>discolorations or mineral infusions</note> can arise. But it is easy for anyone to observe what the earth carries on its surface. Reeds, clover, and brambles are judges of sweet waters, according to the testimony of <term>Democritus</term> <note>an ancient Greek philosopher; here cited for his observations on natural indicators of water</note>.

### CHAPTER XXIII.
### Contents within the Earth.

<margin>The investigation of veins.</margin>
<margin>The investigation of springs.</margin>
**R**egarding the things within the earth itself—both its nature and its contents and what is generated therein—not all are equally evident; they sometimes require expert judges. However, perhaps public rumor or the experience of farmers will show whether a place is common and sterile of minerals, or whether it possesses metallic, sulfurous, aluminous, vitriolic, bituminous, salty, or nitrous minerals, and so on. One must see if the type of earth is tenacious and fatty, or gravelly and sandy. If nothing can be explained by the farmers, it must be tested: pits and crypts must be made; one must crawl into caves; and especially wherever there are rivers, streams, torrents, and springs, one must inquire into the sand, gravel, or mud. Some evidence should also be taken from things growing or efflorescing <note>original: "efflorescentibus"; the formation of powdery mineral crusts on surfaces</note>, or even from crusts scattered outdoors. Thus, in some places, filings of metals or metallic veins are found in the sands; in others, salts or sprinklings of salts, marl, gypsum, etc. Elsewhere, flames or smoke break out, whether ignited spontaneously or by chance by peasants—by which method a vein is often detected while the wild nature of the fields is being tamed by fires, while the earth is plowed for the sake of crops, or while pits are dug for plants. 

Wherever miners investigate veins, they also consider dews, frosts, and snows. For where a vein stretches or is compressed, the breath <note>original: "halitus"; subterranean vapors or "exhalations"</note> sent out like the heat from the mouth of a furnace does not allow frost to form, even when the neighborhood is white with it. Likewise, in those spots, dews are dissipated, snows melt more easily, and the earth does not freeze deeply. In the same way, they detect humid spirits if vapors and mists rise from there, if the grass and leaves of trees are frequently wet, if stones drip, and so on. In the growth of plants, a vaporous vein is betrayed if they do not reach their proper height, if they are juiceless and wither quickly—either entirely or just at the tips—or if they divide into many branches near the ground. If in May and Autumn the herbs are shorter than others and discolored; if the trees turn black; if they have metallic "sprinklings" on their leaves; if they are bent toward the ground; if they are not deeply rooted and easily succumb to the winds. Even beasts flee those vents and breathing-holes if they are a little too heavy <note>referring to toxic volcanic or mineral gases</note>, just as, conversely, when the air is freezing outside, they gather in those same places because they are milder. But who could run through every single detail? Let it suffice to have set down the signs and shown the entrances, especially since knowledge of the earth from its color, smell, taste, and touch agrees with the judgment of the minerals found within them, concerning which more is said below.

### CHAPTER XXIV.
### The Contemplation of Waters.

**W**aters in the whole region, beyond the mineral spring itself, reveal the nature of the earth and make the conjecture about the source of the spring a little more evident, especially if they have something notable in common with the spring. We shall contemplate here first their presence, absence, abundance, and scarcity; afterward, if any are present, whether they are near the source or far distant, and whether they communicate by origin or confluence, or not. Likewise, their strengths...

->On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part I.<-

The circumstances will likewise reveal a connection or a separation. If the neighboring waters are not mineralized, but the main spring is, it easily appears that they either do not share a common origin or confluence at all; or that the mineral vein <note>original: "mineta"; a site where ore or minerals are formed</note> exists in only one of the streams, or that an inflow occurs from elsewhere, and so on. If they are indeed mineralized, but not of the same kind as the main spring, we will recognize the varied nature of the locations, or a source existing elsewhere, or a non-uniform mixture. However, there remains a suspicion of a common connection, the exact mark of which may be hidden by a different "temperament" <note>original: "crasi"; the specific mixture of qualities or minerals in the water</note>. 

If, therefore, metals, gems, or other minerals are collected from waters in the vicinity; if sulfur, bitumen, alum, vitriol <note>original: "atramentum"; literally "inky substance," usually referring to ferrous sulfate</note>, salt, and so on are boiled down; if they deposit lime after boiling, we may conjecture that it is possible for the spring to carry something of the same nature, or at least to be "spiritually" tinged by them and their vapors. But if they are affected by external things such as dung heaps, the decay of animals or plants, or the juices and liquids of the earth—especially if the land is porous and cavernous in a higher elevation—we shall judge that some part of this is shared. We can speak similarly of heat, cold, and contents. 

We should not only inspect these waters that are under the open sky, but also explore wells in the deepest recesses; we shall survey vaults and tunnels, and sometimes, if they are not already present, wells must be dug in the vicinity and in the direction we judge the stream to tend and the source to come from. If water does not come forth from there, one may still pour in simple white clay <note>original: "allam"; likely a type of earth or pigment used as a tracer</note> and observe how it is colored from that point. From this, there will also be some evidence concerning the proximity and diversity of the mineral veins. For if different minerals gush forth from many dug wells, which when mixed produce the one we are investigating, it will be persuasive that our spring does not flow from or be affected by a single mineral vein. But if one well pours out a similar or identical water, unless the source of both comes from far away and the nature of the places and soil corresponds, we shall judge it to be the same mineral. If the mineral power fails in a cave or ditch dug far away, there will be some conjecture of a nearby mineral, unless it comes from secret and deep abysses. One must also inquire about the constancy of those waters, whether you look at their abundance and duration, or their strength, or the fish and other contents. But here too, many things are common regarding odors, colors, tastes, and effects, which will be discussed in the formal assessment of the mineral water itself.

## CHAPTER XXV.
### Factors Brought from Elsewhere.

**A**fter the entire region has been considered in this way and the whole vicinity surveyed, we shall also turn our minds to more distant things. For it has often been noticed that the causes of certain things in waters must be sought far away, just as when storms and "battles and whirlwinds" <note>original Greek: "μάχας, δῖνάς τε"</note> come from elsewhere, bringing foreign qualities of the air and location; whereby, after the whole region is tainted, the mineral waters must necessarily become worse. Thus they say that long ago a plague from Africa took hold in Italy; and thus the ashes of the burning Mount Vesuvius were carried as far as Egypt. 

Furthermore, subterranean passages sometimes continue for a long distance, from which rivers, entering the earth, break out again after long distances. They recall that the spring Arethusa penetrates through the sea from Achaia into Sicily; and that the coastal regions of the Tyrrhenian Sea and the neighboring islands, such as Procida and Ischia, are connected through caverns under the sea. The sea itself, driven by the force of storms, pushes winds and waters into the most remote spaces, where finally, having excited an earthquake, they break out. Nor is there any lack of springs, both on the seacoasts and even further inland, which observe the ebbs and flows of the sea. 

Many things are also carried by rivers, lakes, and the sea from a foreign world into our climate, as histories testify regarding amber, ambergris, bitumen, and certain fatty substances, and other such things that are later collected on the coasts and at the heads of rivers. Certainly, even in the channel of the earth, rivers and streams have been found flowing with continuous waters through excavated paths of veins, with which it is consistent that minerals are snatched up and transferred. Thus, in some places, scrapings of gold, tin, silver, etc., are read about in the sand of rivers, even though nothing metallic exists in the entire vicinity. Likewise, if flows are drawn down through extended tunnels or the streams of metal-working shops (in which ore veins are prepared by washing), something mineral is supplied even in remote places, especially if it was moved violently by strong cataracts or floods. Therefore, things remote in location should not be neglected if they have some connection through such progress; and not infrequently, the mineral of that which was found near Alexandria, Memphis, or Pharos must be sought in the most remote sands of the Nile and the Ethiopians, and its nature must be explored in the Alps for that which was perhaps collected in the Black Sea <note>original: "Ponto"</note>.

## CHAPTER XXVI.
### The Harmony of Causes.

**S**ince, however, some things do not belong to just one of the factors mentioned, but to all or many of them—some acting as principals, others as partners or helpers—the powers of the sky, air, water, earth, fires (both arriving from outside and domestic) must be coupled together, and a comparison established among them. This is done so that it may be clear what contributes more or less to the nature of the mineral water or promotes it. Those things which are in the water itself will be described in their proper place. But in the surrounding circumstances, the favorable or adverse conditions of minerals, plants, and animals can be considered; and since minerals are more internal, we shall now say only a few things about plants and animals. 

<margin>Concerning plants and animals.</margin>
The mildness and kindness of the sky indeed blesses the nature of a place and those things dwelling in it, but the soil must not be stubborn or ill-disposed. For the general power of the sky seems to be such in its action as the soil is with the air, water, and the remaining things that are to be acted upon. And the air in our vicinity is sometimes changed more powerfully by the underlying natures than by the overhanging ether. Where, therefore, plants and fruits grow successfully, where animals are well-kept, the harmony of these things is auspicious, and the mineral veins are either mild or non-existent. For it is well known that minerals and mineral waters about to be born pour out juices and vapors adverse to life and to the good constitution of such things, by which the air, food, drink, etc., are similarly changed. Hence it happens that those places which produce the most metals, alum, sulfur, vitriol <term>chalcāthum</term> <note>a green or blue sulfate mineral, often copper or iron-based</note>, etc., either produce malignant fruits or are almost sterile, and those who would live there more comfortably are forced to bring in outside supplies. Even one skilled in these matters easily distinguishes mineral locations from other sterile ones. If in a fertile soil...

<header>Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book VI.</header>

If the sources of potent minerals appear, they come from afar or from the deep. If the surrounding areas are seen to be raw, wild, and "undigested" <note>original: "indigesta"; in alchemy, this refers to minerals that have not been fully refined or matured by the earth's heat</note>, and the people are discolored, in poor health, and subject to some endemic or local disease—whether this condition is constant or periodic—minerals are usually indicated. These minerals are often spiritless if the rawness is excessive. Other minerals are known by their own specific signs. However, it can also happen that enclosed, cloudy, and damp places, combining with the local air and diet, may afflict the inhabitants by blocking out the kindness of the sky through the height of mountains, the density of forests, or an unfavorable position. It may also happen that some harm is brought in from the sea, marshes, or other sources. Filth, as well as sharp and hot vapors, betray themselves by their own evidence, and they suggest the presence of vaporous minerals if other signs agree. Thus, the regions of Etna, the coasts of Campania <note>The region around Naples, known for the volcanic Phlegraean Fields</note>, and similar places that pour out sulfur, bitumen, and the like, provide evidence for judging the rest. The Libyan and Ethiopian sands, scorched by perpetual suns, conceive salty and nitrous principles (previously arranged by nature), and they tint the waters that filter through those juices. Here you may see all of nature working in harmony. Around the Nile where Memphis and Alexandria are, animals and plants thrive not only by the kindness of the sky, but also from the Nile itself, which is mineral in nature due to the nitre <note>original: "nitrum"; likely referring to natron or saltpeter</note> and sal ammoniac <note>original: "salem ammoniacum"; a salt traditionally collected from the soot of camel dung fires in Egypt</note> it carries. This is proof that the mineral composition is not born there, but comes from elsewhere. There are regions where venomous creatures cannot live; there are places where the earth does not produce insects, snakes, frogs, and so on. Even plants grow poorly over mineral veins. Certainly, by the metallic fumes of the workshops—whether the veins are being smelted, roasted, or burned—the flowers of herbs, shrubs, and trees are destroyed. Suspicion will arise where similar effects exist that similar causes are present; and since the production of such things is aided by many factors, we will easily find the principal acting cause by making a comparison. Mine workers use waters in the caves that are suspect and breathe air that is inconvenient to life; therefore, they are eventually afflicted by asthma, consumption <note>original: "phthisi"; a general term for wasting diseases of the lungs</note>, and pains of the joints and nerves. If an entire region suffers similarly in many people—especially those who live off the local air, waters, and fruits rather than imported ones—and they are constitutionally similar to metalworkers, why should there not be a suspicion of a mineral source? But such things must later be compared with those signs taken from the source itself, its contents, and its associated materials.

# CHAPTER XXVII.
->On things associated with the spring.<-

**HAVING** dwelt long enough on the more remote signs, we now come to those things that are connected to the source—clinging to it, sitting near it, or joined in any other way—though they are not essential parts of the water itself. Some things flow into mineral waters by nature, others by art <note>original: "artem"; human intervention or industry</note>. These materials either stick in the common channel, the bed, or the veins, or they are pushed along floating or submerged. What kind they are must be sought from their own signs, by which mineral and non-mineral things are judged; this part of the investigation is shared with the judgment of the essential qualities of the water. First, one usually considers the sand, gravel, mud, stones, and so on, which exist either in the water's bed or in the vicinity along its path. Therefore, pits are dug in the surrounding area and tunnels are driven into the interior of the mountain—if indeed it is a spring breaking out into the light—taking care, however, not to scatter the origin and meeting-point of the flow and thus lose the "head" of the mineral. In these matters, sight, smell, and taste must be consulted so that we may know if there are metallic veins in the pits, tunnels, or water channels—whether they be pure metals, dross <note>original: "recrementa"</note>, or the sorts of things usually found with them, such as gems, rocks, pure gravel, sulfurous or bituminous mud, decays, sprays, salty concretions, ashes, limes, and other related things. In this way, coals and lime come forth in the springs of Aponus <note>Modern-day Abano Terme in Italy</note>; fire and water together in the springs of Puteoli; in others, ochre; in others, chrysocolla <note>original: "Chrysocolla"; a green copper mineral</note>; and in others, something else. Sometimes, soot or white concretions and other things are found hanging from the parts of caverns. In exploring these things, we shall use the skill of miners and chemists more diligently; and after we have contemplated those things by themselves—whether they are liquid bodies, earthy, muddy, or solidified juices soluble by moisture—we shall drench them with plenty of water, wash them, and after the sediment settles, we shall taste the water, coagulate it, cook it, or collect the filtered liquid like lye through evaporation. We shall likewise examine the remains of whatever we have produced by cooking—just as alum, vitriol <note>original: "atramentum"; literally "inky substance," referring to metallic sulfates</note>, salt, sulfur, bitumen, and so on sometimes come out coagulated—by sight, taste, touch, and smell, either by themselves or washed, separated, or acted upon by fires. In both cases, distillation, sublimation, roasting on a metal plate, quenching, melting, calcination <note>reducing a substance to powder by heat</note>, and other operations are effective, about which we speak below. Things we suspect to be metallic we shall place into small furnaces and cupels <note>original: "testæ"; shallow porous vessels used in assaying</note>, either alone or with additives; here, on pure filings, the touchstone or quicksilver <note>original: "hydrargyrum"; mercury</note> sometimes has a place, although they may be recognized immediately by experts.

Some things are also dissolved by boiling water or oil, and they could have been melted in the heat-vents of the earth or around them, only to be solidified again once the waters cooled. It is indeed difficult to recognize the matrices <note>the surrounding rock in which minerals are embedded</note> and the rudiments of minerals—even the "first entities" or "prime matter," as they call them—yet if many signs are gathered together, the judgment will be less obscure. Therefore, we sometimes even scrutinize the effects on plants and animals when such things are given or applied to them.

Things that are combustible <note>original: "cremia"; dry fuel</note> and catch fire reveal themselves by their vapor, the manner of their flame, their noise, and other signs, where again we consult multiple senses. Sometimes we pour on sharp liquids, such as urine, distilled vinegar, "strong waters" <note>original: "aquas fortes"; usually nitric acid</note>, or spirits. From their mutual reaction and change, we also grasp some evidence. For those whose thickness prevents examination, if there is something of importance in them, we break, rub, grind, and smooth them; and once the worthless mountain-matter is separated by a trough or other washings and siftings, we consider the noble part in the manner of miners. But however such things behave, a comparison with the essence of the water must not be omitted. For it must be seen whether those things are accidental—such as the many things pushed out by the force of rivers from torrents, the inflow of wild waters, or brought in by other means, even placed there by animals or cast by winds—or whether they truly belong to the nature of the water itself, whether they concurred in its generation or were further excreted and separated from it.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.

### On Things Floating on the Surface.

<margin>Mention was made of these above in consideration of the whole region and its surroundings. Fish in hot waters.</margin>
**A**nd so much for the things connected to the tables. Some things float and must be investigated within the water itself, occasionally even living creatures, just as we see in the sea and its pools that certain plants and fish exist; yet this is also common in various mineral sources. How fertile in such things is the nitrous Nile! The waters of Buda, <note>Modern-day Budapest, famous for its thermal springs.</note> though hot, also nourish fish which die if moved to cold water, according to authors such as Wernher, Agricola, <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), often called the "father of mineralogy."</note> Mattioli, Bacci, and others. Some of these authors assert the same regarding the aluminous thermal baths at Zuglio <note>original: "Iulium Carnicum," a Roman town in the Alps.</note> and in Tuscany at Vetulonia, as Pliny also relates, adding that frogs are found in the Caldana springs of Pisa. But it is no wonder they exist in thermal baths, since frogs have been found enclosed on all sides in millstones, and fish are dug out of muddy earth with mattocks and shovels; some creatures live in the midst of fires or snows, and they do not even shun poisoned waters. In this way, they record that there is fishing in the Stygian water of Arcadia, in a certain spring in Armenia, and in the pool of the Nymphs in Lydia—though the catch is venomous.

Even humans can be saturated with poison, and many poisonous things are consumed by beasts, in whom the power of the poison is "concocted" <note>An alchemical term meaning refined or matured by heat.</note> so that it does not later remain an unhealthy food for man. It is no wonder that even the "mute herds" <note>A poetic reference to livestock or animals.</note> fare well in Stygian waters. Nevertheless, if such things are seen in mineral waters and are harmless to human strength, we may promise ourselves that the water is healthful—provided the trial is made cautiously. For the varying sympathy and alienation of different natures makes for an uncertain agreement. We will be more certain of the thinness <note>In this context, "tenuitate" refers to the purity or lack of heavy mineral saturation.</note> of the mineral if fish or frogs released from common ponds survive. If they die, they prove the presence of powerful "tinctures" <note>Chemical infusions or concentrated mineral properties.</note> or mixtures, and all the more so if they also kill living animals on dry land. The most important parts of this study come from experience itself, which brings forth edible fish from the sea, even though perhaps no one could drink its salty water without immediate harm. But for that reason, it is not to be condemned for external needs such as washing, swimming, and so forth.

Of plants, some do not float but are attached to the margin or the bottom. Most indicate that "sweet nourishment" <note>original: "alimentum dulce," meaning fresh or non-corrosive nutrients.</note> is not lacking, although they seem to make that axiom suspect (namely, that living things are nourished by sweet juices), both the fish I mentioned and plants born from salt waters that taste of salt—unless "sweet" is the same as "pleasing," just as perhaps the bitterness of willows is a kind of sweetness and delight to goats, as "bilious" fodder is to swine.

<margin>Fatty substances and those that float.</margin>
Certain fatty substances also float, such as the oily liquid at the Petriolo baths <note>Ancient thermal baths in Tuscany.</note> near Rosserus, which coagulates into sulfur; liquid bitumen in the sea; asphalt in the Judean Lake <note>The Dead Sea.</note>; liquid amber <note>original: "succinum liquidum," likely referring to a resinous or oily mineral output.</note> elsewhere; and if it is something different from bitumen, then also naphtha. Thus they say that the cold waters between Bologna and Florence (lest you say the resolution was caused by heat) and likewise the bath at the fortress of Vinadio in the territory of Turin near the Alps, carry fatty substances. At the head of the Nile, on sea shores, and in the pools of Adarce, <note>A salty efflorescence or froth found on reeds in marshes.</note> "spermaceti" <note>Historically used to describe various waxy mineral or biological substances found on shores.</note> and similar things are commonly seen. The nature of these "greases" will also reveal, in a way, the constitution of the water itself. For even if they happen to contribute nothing to the essential composition, they will nonetheless alter it and impart a spiritual tincture. Indeed, they lead the observer to the interior mineral and, during the process of resolution, they provide some warning regarding limestones, ashes, filings, vapors, "coagulated spirits," juices, and the like.

<margin>Films and foam.</margin>
Regarding those things which may be thrown in or swept away and stand out or flow on the surface, such as wood, straw, leaves, feathers, etc., there is no need to give warning. One must think more diligently about "pellicles" <note>Thin films or skins (cuticulæ).</note> and subtle shavings, marshy growths, foams, and so forth, which are accustomed to rest upon waters whether they are still agitated or quiet, hot or cooled—whether they have emerged through separation from the body of the water, or have coagulated in any way on the surface, or were even carried there by the force of the flow. There is no method for investigating these other than that used for other contents and things joined to the channel. Therefore, at least the history will pertain here. Such films, foams, and dusty secretions are sometimes the "smoothness" of metals or very tiny, gold-like filings. For it has been found that gold, silver, etc., when thinned into "minium," <note>Usually refers to red lead, but here likely refers to a finely powdered state.</note> can rest upon waters, and they can cling for a long time especially in foams. Sometimes they are webs made from dispersed mercury <note>original: "hydrargyro."</note> or its vapor. Occasionally, "resolved juices" produce such a thing: it is when things are extinguished by the waters while their spirits are suffocated by the water, showing them as concretions on the top, just as metallic fumes, raised by heat, settle upon the waters like a storm. Not infrequently, white, black, red, yellow, and multicolored foams ride upon the surface, produced by ashes, lime, tufa, sulfur, bitumen, and the like. But enough regarding those things which nature joins together. They will be judged better if the history of the following things is known, as well as those things internal to the water, about which more exact instructions are given in their proper place—since that contemplation is the genuine focus of this treatise, while this is rather preparatory.

## CHAPTER XXIX.

### Things Applied to the Waters.

**T**hose things which art has applied, or which the judgment of men throws in for the sake of exploration, do not belong here insofar as they have their own nature, but rather insofar as they are affected in a certain way by the water, whereby its condition becomes known. In this category are the planks and boxes by which the head of a spring is enclosed; the channels by which it is usually led away; the cauldrons in which it is boiled, and so forth. If the material is metallic and remains unchanged, except for what usually happens from common water, then no sharp minerals are present. We know how iron is reduced to "saffron" <note>original: "crocum"; here meaning iron oxide or rust.</note> by salty waters, and lead and tin are turned into "ceruse" <note>White lead, a byproduct of lead corrosion.</note> by acids and other substances. But usually, the damage prevents the use of metallic vessels, although the law of necessity is harsh; in boiling salt, alum, vitriol, etc., bronze or lead cauldrons are preferred, though they do not last for long use. Sometimes even stone receptacles are worn away; but then, upon these, as well as upon wooden channels, pipes, and metallic cauldrons, there grow certain stony, juicy, or "flowering" substances, which by their own law...

...will be judged: now at least they teach of a thicker mixture of water. If wood rots easily, turns black, attracts mold, suffers decay, or conceives and nourishes fungi and plants—or even if wood-worms <term>cossi<gloss>larvae of wood-boring beetles</gloss></term> are generated in the holes and hollows of rotten things, as usually happens in the planking of ships and other things falling into the sea (like the fruits of the Scottish tree, from which first worms and then birds are generated) <note>original: "Scoticæ arboris fructibus." This refers to the medieval myth of the Barnacle Goose, which was believed to grow from barnacles on driftwood rather than laying eggs.</note>—judgment shall be made of them according to the nature of each effect. And indeed, the "raw" <note>Unprocessed or untreated</note> waters of wells cover their sides with moss, or a black, blue-gray, or green coating and decay. Where this occurs in a mineral spring, the mineral power will be judged weak, since a strong power instead wards off rot, as we see in salt, alum, sulfur, etc. In the sea, those things which rot do so not because the water is salty, but because while that thick saltiness is kept on the outside, the "sweetness" <note>Internal moisture or fresh water within the object</note> works its way in and receives nourishment from external heat, and so on.

### CHAPTER XXX.
->*On those things which are thrown into waters.*<-

**B**ut let us run through things thrown into the water. That heavy things sink and light things float contains nothing new, unless they are compared; just as if a ship floating in the sea were to be submerged in a river: here the water is proven to be thinner, and there thicker <note>The author is discussing buoyancy: salt water is denser than fresh water and provides more lift.</note>. But neither should a proper amount of water be lacking, nor should any external shape or force interfere, as happens differently with broad and sharp objects, etc. If anything happens beyond common knowledge, or alien to the custom of ordinary water, it demands special consideration. In Lake Avernus <note>A volcanic crater lake in Italy, traditionally the entrance to the underworld.</note>, though it is bubbling and heavy, nothing floats, not even the leaves of trees. They say the same of the violet spring of the Ethiopians, and they attribute it to "weak" water. Such a lake is also said to exist in Ethiopia: a pool in India, and the one they call the Alcyonian Lake, etc.

But it should be thought that this happens not always because of a weakness in supporting weight, but because of a nature of swallowing and sinking things, which we see in waters that are very easily divided, or very "thin," having little or nothing of a viscous body; these we can call "weak." Sometimes this is due to sharp spirits <note>Corrosive or acidic vapors.</note>. Therefore, one might more rightly call them "sharp, coagulated spirits," which by their penetrating and breaking sharpness immediately attack or scorch the object, and once paths are opened, they expel the airy breaths <note>Air bubbles or internal air pockets.</note> and soak or drink up the whole thing; this is what happens in less penetrating waters over a longer time. For experience testifies that even in ordinary water, wood, stalks, flowers, etc., sink once they are thoroughly soaked and the air contained in their pores has been driven out. But thin and sharp waters achieve this immediately. Thus we judge the "spirit of wine" <note>Distilled alcohol or ethanol.</note> to be most subtle, since it immediately swallows an injected downy feather so that it seeks the bottom. By the same judgment, "heavenly mineral waters" <note>Potent distilled mineral acids used in alchemy.</note> are categorized.

<margin>Asphaltites <note>The Dead Sea.</note></margin>
There are, however, some "airy" and "fiery" liquids so light and thinned out that they stand out like air and fire, such as certain oils and what they call "quintessences," etc. In contrast to Lake Asphaltites, it is said that everything floats there because of the tenacity from the mixture of bitumen and a salty thickness, which resembles the sea or even mud. They say the same of Arethusa, and a lake in Lesser Armenia, and others which have the consistency of thick lye, containing much saltpeter, bitumen, or some combination of these.

<margin>Disagreement regarding Lake Asphaltites.</margin>
<margin>According to Pliny, nothing sinks in it, with even elephants and bulls floating.</margin>
It is strange that historians disagree regarding Lake Asphaltites; some report that everything sinks there except things smeared with alum. Certainly, any objects staying for a long time in nitrous <note>Rich in saltpeter or sodium carbonates.</note> waters will sink. However, this lake is said to be so nitrous that it sprinkles those washing in it with much salt. The disagreement can be reconciled by the factor of time. In a short stay, nothing sinks (of those things which sink in other waters, though perhaps not everything has been tested); but over a longer time, everything sinks because it is drawn down, weighed down by the saltpeter, as in Lake Ascania. Some things thrown in turn to stone <note>Petrification.</note>, others suffer something else; since these also pertain to the judgment of the water's effects, they will be discussed below in their proper place, as will the substances that are separated out by means of thrown-in stalks, sticks, and other things. Thus far concerning external matters.

->THE END.<-

On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 2.

# A TREATISE ON MINERAL WATERS
## PART TWO.

### CHAPTER I.
### The apparatus for the separation of waters.

<margin>A</margin> Water itself is considered either as a whole in itself, or as separated into its component parts, each of which is then viewed on its own. In both cases, many things are held in common. We will first examine those things which are closer to the senses; then those which belong more to reason, that is, the effects: before which we will place the methods of separation that are usually adapted to this matter.

So that we may arrive at a knowledge of the component parts through separation—for every mineral water is of the category of "imperfect mixtures"—a certain quantity must be drawn from the spring itself at the time when it is most truly itself, strong in its power, and free from elemental disturbances, from the harm caused by animals, and from similar external factors. This is judged to be possible during a long period of clear weather, shortly before autumn, at dawn, when the spring has rested enough from those drawing or drinking it, and when the winds are not raging, etc. The separation should be established not far from the spring, lest it suffer a loss of certain spirits <term>spirituum<gloss>volatile components or essences</gloss></term> while being carried further away. The vessels should be of glass or stone, impenetrable to vapors or corrosive juices, unless the nature of the examination requires or even permits metallic, wooden, or earthenware <term>figulina fara<gloss>pottery vessels</gloss></term> ones, etc.

### CHAPTER II.
### The separation of spirits.

<margin>A</margin> Once a certain weight has been measured, let it be immediately put into a cucurbit <term>cucurbitam<gloss>a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</gloss></term> with an alembic <term>alembico<gloss>the cap or head of a still</gloss></term>, whose beak should pass through cooling systems, or let it be covered with cooling cloths, etc. Let a receiver <term>excipulus<gloss>a vessel to catch the distillate</gloss></term> be attached, and let all the joints be blocked as precisely as possible with tenacious mastic <term>maltha<gloss>a cement or putty used to seal laboratory equipment</gloss></term>. Let the cucurbit be placed in gentle dung <note>Dung was used as a source of low, steady heat for "digesting" substances.</note>, or a vapor bath, or at least a lukewarm water bath <term>balneo maris<gloss>literally a "bath of the sea"; a bain-marie</gloss></term>, so that the most subtle spirits may be drawn off. Let these be examined one by one, as well as the water left in the cucurbit. Afterward, let them be compared, so that it may be clear in which part the power is more potent. Both can also be reduced to their weight. But if none or very few are drawn out, it must be judged that the mixture is rather "corpulent" <note>Thick or heavy</note>, or, if you prefer, that the spirits are more earthy, like juices dissolved in the liquid.

### CHAPTER III.
### Separation of the wateriness and the contents.

<margin>S</margin> But whether something has come forth or nothing, let the vessel be transferred to the ashes <note>A sand or ash bath allows for higher heat than a water bath.</note>, and let the watery part be provoked until it reaches a honey-like consistency, if such is judged to be appropriate. Let the parts be viewed separately likewise, and then compared with one another. What remains should be drenched with some part of the extracted water (if indeed a certain thick consistency is judged) and allowed to soak. Afterward, let it be poured off. Let the poured-off liquid be coagulated to the thickness of lye, alum, and similar juices. Then let either straws, or small cords, or little rods, etc., be placed into both parts. And let coagulation be expected, or else let evaporation <term>diuaporatio<gloss>slow evaporation by heat</gloss></term> occur in a glass shell gradually by the heat of the furnace in a closed vessel. The contents will be at the bottom. If no thickness appears after the greater part of the subtle matter has been exhausted, let it be set to "putrefy" <note>In early chemistry, this refers to a slow digestion or fermentation process, not necessarily rotting.</note> for a month. If even then no sediment <term>hypostasis<gloss>a deposit or sediment</gloss></term> is found, let it be distilled or evaporated entirely. For where no separation occurs and no remains are found, the entire mixture is of a spiritual nature, and its power and nature will be estimated from the distillate and the residue through mutual comparison. Note, however, that where you have separated the thinnest spirits by the gentlest heat, in the second distillation over ashes, with the receiver changed and kept movable during the distillation, the drops should be observed and tasted more frequently. For if they taste of the same mineral power, or exhibit a new one, or are even tasteless like water, you will be able to determine the method of separation more exactly, and receive different liquids in different vessels. It is also possible to note by sight when the invisible spirits cease and are succeeded by watery ones. For then the alembic "sweats" and is marked by little streams. By this method alone, if you act skillfully, you will be able to draw out the most essential parts. For the first operation provides the spirits; the second, the heavier waters, whether mineral or tasteless and pure. The third separates the solidifiable juices from the "limes" <term>calcibus<gloss>residues left after calcination or evaporation</gloss></term>, and indeed alum from vitriol <term>attramento<gloss>literally "ink," often used for vitriol or copperas</gloss></term>, salt from niter <term>halinitro<gloss>a natural saltpeter or soda</gloss></term>, etc.

### CHAPTER IV.
### *Separation of Sediments.*

But if you are not able to work skillfully in these matters, or even if sediments and coagulations of various natures still appear, you can call upon other techniques for help. One of these is sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again on a cooler surface, used to purify chemicals.</note>, whether into a "blind" alembic <note>original: "alembicum caecum"; a distillation vessel without an outlet tube, used to collect solid vapors.</note> at a greater distance, or into a dish, or a half-sphere lid, or simply onto the surface; let this be done in the manner of "cementing" in a reverberatory furnace <term>reuerberio<gloss>a furnace that reflects heat onto the material being processed</gloss></term>. Then, the sublimated material and the "dead head" <note>original: "caput mortuum"; the useless residue left in the vessel after distillation or sublimation.</note> should be examined individually.

Another experiment is performed with a cloth, along with boiling and exposure to the sun. We cast a clean cloth of a known weight into the mineral water until it is thoroughly soaked. We hang this over a vessel so that it may drip and dry on its own. When dry, we observe whether it has acquired any spots; we likewise investigate whether it has become heavier. If the weight is the same as before, there is a suspicion that no "bodily" <note>Physical or solid mineral content.</note> matter is present; the judgment will be more certain if it is immersed and dried again and again and keeps the same weight—provided that no force from fire or wind was used during drying. For thin crusts are easily scattered this way. If it is found to be heavier, and this is not due to moisture (especially if spots appear at the same time), we conclude that solid solutions are present in the water. We then boil the water if we think the volatile spirits should be ignored (for this is done primarily for the sake of exploring the "body" of the water), or we distill it if we wish to save them. When we have reached the consistency of oil, we expose the remaining scraps to the sun until dry. If the intention is to separate this further, we proceed in the manner described above by pouring in water, draining, and coagulating; or we sublimate it, or we drive off strong spirits through a retort with a strong fire. Or, if any fatty or mercurial matter is present, we even use "distillation by descent" <note>A method where the vapor is forced downwards into a receiver.</note>. Sometimes we use a reverberatory furnace and calcine the material; we then dissolve the ashes through "deliquium" <note>The process where a salt absorbs enough moisture from the air to turn into a liquid solution.</note>. But in that case, the researcher must be knowledgeable in many things, so that he knows what is produced from what through such violent examinations, since nothing happens without corruption and alteration in many substances.

### CHAPTER V.
### *Separation by Descent.*

There is another work performed by letting the water settle in stillness, by which we also wait for things that float. Once these are removed, we pour off the clear liquid, and we test for coagulations and the rest in the residue just as we did in the poured-off part. If the eyes immediately detect something solid, filters are also employed. Whatever is caught in these, we do not hesitate to burn, roast, and if possible, melt—either by itself or with additives. However, if there is a suspicion of metallic filings, we immediately follow the roasting with a washing in a small trough. Roasting is likewise done on a glowing plate, in a shell, or similar vessels. If, meanwhile, a flow like wax or lead is seen, or if a flame is caught, or an odor or fumes exhale, we use our own judgment.

### CHAPTER VI.
### *The Boiling of Water.*

Sometimes we perform distillation on one portion of water; on another, settling and skimming; and on another, boiling, which we also manage specifically in this way: In a glass vessel, or a firm earthen one (for in porous ones, salt ammoniac <term>sal ammonius<gloss>ammonium chloride</gloss></term>, the thinner part of common salt, sublimated mercury <term>hydrargyrus sublimatus<gloss>mercury(II) chloride</gloss></term>, and portions of vitriol and sulfur etc., escape), we set up a "double-boiler" <note>original: "diploma"</note> or even a "triple-boiler." The foam is removed and set aside for special study. When the liquid has been reduced to a half or a third, we examine the weight and compare it with the total quantity we put in; this reveals to us whether the volatile spirits or the solid juices are more numerous.
<margin>Clear medicinal water of equal weight, etc.</margin>
For the thick and mixed part is heavier than the spiritual part and fresh water—though it seemed a most wonderful thing to Andrea Bacci <note>A famous 16th-century physician and writer on baths and wines.</note> that some medicinal waters were found to be either acidic, sharp, or purgative, yet remained clear and of the same weight as simple, clear waters. But the difference is made by the spiritual or solid mixture and "tincture." Furthermore, the decoction reduced to a third is poured through a sieve, and thus the scraps are separated; the sieve is sometimes of linen cloth, sometimes of folded paper. The strained liquid is left to rest for three days. Then we pour it into glass shells or wooden vats, according to our judgment of which juices are inside (in which case it seems that sometimes copper or lead vessels might be required, where scraps of silver and gold are present), and we wait for crusts to form around little sticks. If nothing more grows on them, the lye <note>The concentrated mineral solution.</note> is boiled to a greater thickness, and a second coagulation is attempted down to the dregs. Sometimes we boil in a copper vessel if we suspect salt and "halinitrum" <term>halinitrum<gloss>saltpeter or potassium nitrate</gloss></term>, or a mixture of this and "atramentum" <term>atramentum<gloss>a term for vitriol or ferrous sulfate</gloss></term>. For salt sticks to the bottom, while saltpeter is poured off with the water. In the same way, vitriol also stays behind. Yet it is easy for an expert to distinguish them even if saltpeter, vitriol, and alum are present together. For the most part, each settles and coagulates by itself and can be recognized by its own signs. It should be noted whether the salt is bituminous, such as Sicilian salt, which thickens with water and dissolves with fire. There is also a method where, in the second coagulation, the remaining moisture is drawn out through strips of cloth. Once the crystals are removed, the dreg is dried out, though care must be taken not to burn it. But the "double-boilers" should also be checked, for as the water gradually fails during boiling, it leaves deposits in them. When this is finished, we make a comparison between what we produced by distilling and what we produced by boiling and settling.

### CHAPTER VII.
### *Putrefaction.*

If we wish, we can add a fourth experiment through mutual putrefactions and distillations, by which method the Chemists extract the elements.

## CHAPTER VIII.
### Sun-Exposure.

**S**ometimes, without any reduction in quantity, we simply digest the waters enclosed in glass in the sun, though occasionally leaving a small breathing-hole <term>spiraculo<gloss>a small vent or opening</gloss></term> so that the stirred-up vapors do not break the container. By this sun-exposure <term>apricatione<gloss>the process of exposing something to the heat/light of the sun</gloss></term>, oiliness is sometimes revealed, and sediment is collected.

## CHAPTER IX.
### Infusion.

**T**here is also a method where we soak the dregs or dry contents in spirit of wine <note>High-proof alcohol/ethanol.</note>, and after drawing that off, we replace it with another, thus learning the nature of the thing more deeply. There is another method where we use strong waters <term>aquas fortes<gloss>powerful acids like nitric acid</gloss></term>, or sharp spirits of vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid.</note>, sulfur, salt <note>Hydrochloric acid.</note>, tartar, vinegar, and the like. Sometimes separation is achieved through infused juices or specific waters, whereby water that was previously clear becomes turbid and separates into parts, as seen in solutions of metals, strong spirits, and many other things that are coagulated by vinegar, fresh waters, spirit of wine, salty waters, or salt itself. Indeed, even a thicker spirit, once the thinner part is removed and it is slightly agitated by the heat of fire, will coagulate if it is poured back and becomes more watery. Those things commonly known to be condensed by coagulants, such as "Medusean salt" <note>original: "salem meduſaeum"; likely a reference to a specific crystalline mineral or chemical agent used for solidification.</note> and similar substances, are well-known. However, there are some things that cannot come together unless they receive a "body," such as certain inky waters <note>Chalybeate or iron-rich waters.</note>, to which a small amount of iron must be added. Nor does a solution of copper in strong water coagulate if it has been filtered many times, although otherwise vitriol <term>chalcanthum<gloss>copper or iron sulfate</gloss></term> might crystallize from it. Therefore, take care not to be deceived into thinking nothing solid is present when, in fact, a great deal is bound within. In Italy, there are many nitrous waters, but nitre <term>nitrum<gloss>saltpeter or native soda</gloss></term> cannot be made from them because the art of coagulation is lacking. In Italy and Spain, they pack vitriol by adding copper or iron, etc. They also say that sulfur "steals itself away" <note>evaporates or escapes</note> during coagulation, which is likely when it has a spiritual <note>volatile or gaseous</note> nature.

## CHAPTER X.
### Diversity of contents in various separations.

**N**or should you be deceived if different dregs appear in distillation or a double-boiler <term>diplomate<gloss>a water bath or bain-marie</gloss></term>, others in boiling in a pot, others emerging after evaporation; others grow together in the pipes. For example, in the Baths of Abano <note>original: "Aponi balneis"; famous thermal springs near Padua, Italy.</note>, the sediment from spontaneous evaporation or clarification is—according to Baccius <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), a renowned Italian physician and author of a definitive work on thermal baths.</note>—greenish and like grass; in the pipes, it is grayish, muddy, yellowish, etc. It is easy for accidental additions to be changed by different conditions. The true investigator of things hunts for the essence and is well-acquainted with the habits of natural Proteus <note>A reference to the shape-shifting sea god, here a metaphor for the changing states of matter.</note>. But many more modes of separation will be supplied both by chemistry and by the industriousness of other arts.

## CHAPTER XI.
### Fuller preparation of separated substances.

**T**o better judge separated materials, they are often prepared further, some methods of which we have already touched upon in the section on segregation. For some are "reverberated" <note>Heated in a furnace where the flame is deflected back onto the substance.</note> in crucibles or in a "physical globe" <note>original: "globo phyſico"; likely a spherical laboratory vessel.</note>, some are merely exposed to the sun, and these are sometimes even brought to a perfect smoothness. Poured over with very hot water and dissolved, they are passed through a chemical filter made of paper with a linen cloth underneath; what has passed through is allowed to coagulate. But it must be noted that certain juices, while raw, can be both dissolved and filtered; but if they are reverberated by fires, they turn into the nature of stone, such as nitre, alum, vitriol, etc. In this way, they say that "Tibur stone" <term>lapidem Tiburtinum<gloss>travertine limestone</gloss></term> is born from liquid alum even without intense heat. By sublimation, not only are "flowers" <note>Volatile solids that condense into powder.</note> and soot separated from the fixed part, but a preparation is also established for a clearer judgment. The same is true of roasting, burning, and similar processes. Since iron in sharp waters of its own kind produces rust <term>ferruginem<gloss>iron oxide</gloss></term>; copper produces verdigris <term>aeruginem<gloss>copper carbonate/acetate</gloss></term>; types of lead produce white lead <term>ceruſſam<gloss>lead carbonate</gloss></term>; and silver produces Azure <note>original: "argentum Lazurium"; likely a blue byproduct of silver reacting with specific acids.</note>, the ores of such metals can be tested using those waters. Many, however, deny that the substances of metals are communicated to waters, and perhaps they deny it rightly if they mean in their own form or as known to common folk; but they are wrong if they mean in the finest filings <note>original: "ramentis"; microscopic particles.</note> whose external quality has changed. For it is known that they can be dissolved into the clearest waters and then reduced <note>Returned to a solid/metallic state</note> by their own arts; and as this happens in the "lesser Vulcan" <note>The chemist's laboratory furnace.</note>, so it can happen proportionally in the "greater" <note>The natural geological heat of the earth.</note>. Indeed, the dissolved powders <term>calces<gloss>the powdery residue left after a substance is heated or oxidized</gloss></term> settle back down when fresh water is added in abundance; but since they emerge and are swallowed as a single flavor in turbid and stirred-up waters, and since the full quantity does not always come into view, their presence cannot be denied. Certainly, if the ashes of limestone, tufa, pumice, and other things that usually grow in large, heavy, and solid masses in the pipes are admitted to be hidden and imperfectly mixed in such waters, why should the solutions of metals be denied? These too can be ground into a finer meal, powder, and perfect smoothness, as witnessed by mercury, minium <note>Red lead.</note>, cinnabar, sublimate, etc.

**T**hese filings <note>original: "ramenta"</note> are not only well-disposed for judging with sharp waters, but are often reduced in their own ways, as is said in books on chemistry. Care must be taken, however, lest they turn into glass through violent melting; if this happens, although a skilled person can still draw some judgment about the metal from it, it is more obscure because the similarity to other things may deceive us. Certain manifest things are held on a glowing plate and allowed to smoke or burn, so that a conjecture may be formed from the flow, consistency, smoke, vapors, appearance of the flame, sound, coals or dregs, and other signs. The smoothed dregs, reduced into a mass, are spread over a plate so that the sun may reveal false parts through their shine, elevation, and other traits. Some are extended [by] animal...

It argues that even if metals are not visible in their common forms in water, they exist as microscopic particles that can be recovered and identified through chemical "arts."</summary>

...fed to animals with their food: and for this investigation, the water itself is also used, which is either given as a drink, or boiled or soaked into the food. But not every preparation is suitable for everyone. It can easily happen that from an improper preparation you might conclude there is a mineral salt in the water when there is not; because through an unskilled burning <note>original: "vstione sinistra"; literally "left-handed" or "unlucky" burning, implying a technical error in heating</note> you produced the taste of salt in the sediment. In the same way, you might judge that rust <term>ferruginem<gloss>iron oxide</gloss></term> or red lead <term>minium<gloss>lead tetroxide</gloss></term> is present, when you have merely turned verdigris <term>æruginem<gloss>green copper carbonate/acetate</gloss></term> red by heat. Therefore, do not be content with one sign alone, but be certain you have explored what is added to the matter by any given preparation.

### CHAPTER XII.
->*On the judgment of the senses.*<-

But let us come to the judgment based on the senses (even though both the ancient Platonists and the recent Pyrrhonians <note>Skeptics who doubted the certainty of knowledge; here the author is criticizing the followers of Paracelsus</note> from the herd of Paracelsus, who wrongly emulate them, reject this). Here it must first be known that we do not simply use the sense as it is found in brute animals, but the human sense, and that as a servant to the inner principle, which is the mind and reason; so that the most important parts of judging belong to the intellect, which is awakened by things perceived through the senses. Nor indeed does just any intellect have a place here, but one that is equipped with the use and experience of things, and is able to judge them with integrity, as far as is fitting for a human. For it is not enough to have perceived a red color, and even to have declared it to be redness; but the observer—once the remaining signs have been collected together and compared with a collection of similar things—must be able to say of what thing it is, such as rust from a mineral, orpiment <term>auripigmenti<gloss>arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral</gloss></term>, sulfur, and so on. In such examinations, we primarily use sight, taste, and smell to present sensory data to the intellect, which Galen also chose; after these, some authority is also given to touch, as Agricola, Baccius, and others have employed it. We shall not even reject hearing; gathering from every side whatever can contribute to some degree of certainty.

### CHAPTER XIII.
->*On transparency.*<-

As far as sight is concerned, since its specific function is to perceive colors (among which we also include light) and to offer them to the common sense to be discerned and to the mind to be judged: and since color is the act of light terminated in a transparent medium: it will also consider the transparent and the opaque <note>original: "τὸ διαφανὲς & ἀδιαφανὲς"</note> together. For darkness is useless for this task. If, therefore, mineral water (for we shall primarily call it this, determining the rest by analogy) flows from a spring transparently, and that transparency is more "airy" than "watery," we will suspect a spiritual mixture <note>A mixture involving "spirits" or volatile, gas-like substances</note> lies beneath it, or a substance of bodies so thinned out that, being exactly mixed with the water, it does not block the sight: or perhaps similar mixed juices. Which of these it may be, other arguments will reveal. For the opinion of a spiritual mixture is confirmed if the transparency is constant in every experiment; if it is inconstant, we turn our attention to the remaining signs. There is, however, a very great variety in such things. For some things are translucent while the actual heat is still joined to them; but when that heat is removed, they become dense. Some undergo the same when a spirit is present or departing. For it is the nature of both heat and spirit to disperse thick matter and to keep parts separate, which then collapse and become opaque when those factors depart. They depart either by spontaneous evaporation, or by the pressure of external heat, or by something dissipating them through motion, or by consuming and defining them; just as we see in brine <term>muria<gloss>saturated salt water</gloss></term> coagulated by fire; in oils thickening; in the curdling of milk; in solutions of metals, decoctions, etc., through the spirit of wine, vinegar, salt water, and similar things being frozen or solidified. Some things become solid due to cold, but remain homogenous. Thus, this does not contribute much to establishing this judgment. It must also be seen whether the transparency is such that an exact image and size of objects placed within it are represented, such as the water of the Bath of St. Ladislaus in Hungary is said to be; or whether the object appears smaller or larger, <margin>An object is not always larger when seen through a denser medium.</margin> or the appearance is duller. For if there is to be any judgment regarding the mixture, one might take as an axiom what they say: "an object is seen larger through a denser medium"; unless spectacles <term>perspicilia<gloss>early lenses or eyeglasses</gloss></term> had refuted that, which present a thing to the sight even smaller than it appears through the air. One must pay attention, however, to where that opinion holds true.

### CHAPTER XIV.
->*On turbid waters.*<-

Those waters which are opaque and turbid immediately argue for a "corporeal" <note>Solid or physical rather than volatile</note> mixture; and sometimes they even deposit it by settling, and then the part that is watery becomes clear. The same also happens to those that are made turbid by boiling, by the injection of medicines, or in another way, but later become clear, like the whitish aluminous and marble-like waters; the Fiderius well in Rhetia <note>Fideris in modern Switzerland</note>, which is acidic and aluminous, and similar ones which are clear at first, then grow thick, and thereafter, having formed a sediment, show a transparent liquor again. It can happen, however, that even here something corporeal remains in the liquor. It is a matter of great judgment to indicate something certain from transparency alone, since we see that not only hard, concreted bodies like glass, Muscovy glass <term>lapidem specularem<gloss>transparent mica or selenite</gloss></term>, crystal, many gems, marble, also alabaster, certain "tears" <note>Resins or sap droplets</note>, juices of alum, borax, and salt, and certain metallic veins, such as raw red silver <note>pyrargyrite</note>, red sulfur <note>possibly realgar</note>, etc., are transparent, but also those bodies hidden in waters regarding the obstruction of the transparent medium, and filtered through double or triple papers, as is evident in brine and solutions of many minerals through "strong waters" <term>aquas fortes<gloss>acids like nitric acid</gloss></term> and others. If you reach the point where you can discern a spiritual mixture from a corporeal one, or rather divine it, you have achieved something worthy of your talent. For it is impossible to pronounce with certainty what the mixture is, or to which body it belongs, from transparency, opacity, or turbidity alone, unless a certain property and a color pertaining to a specific thing is joined with it.

On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 2.

### CHAPTER XV.
->On colors.<-

**So** doubtful is the evidence of colors themselves for expressing things definitively, that hardly anything stable can be found in them when you look at minerals. It can happen that what belongs to <term>sandarac<gloss>red arsenic sulfide or realgar</gloss></term> may look like <term>minium<gloss>red lead</gloss></term>; what belongs to golden <term>fluor<gloss>fluorite or flux-stone</gloss></term> looks like gold; what belongs to Spanish white looks like <term>ceruse<gloss>white lead</gloss></term>; what belongs to silver looks blue; what belongs to <term>salt gem<gloss>halite or rock salt</gloss></term> looks like alum; what belongs to "fern" <note>likely referring to a fern-like dendritic mineral growth</note> looks like crystal; and what belongs to transparent red sulfur looks like translucent red silver ore—and so on almost to infinity. Therefore, craftsmen say that judgment taken from these regarding the nature and qualities of mineral waters and their contents is the weakest of all. But many things are useful here that do not help when taken individually, especially if industry is not lacking in recognizing specific traits, by which we can somehow discern the green of copper from <term>chrysocolla<gloss>a green copper mineral, often malachite</gloss></term>; a rusty color from <term>corallate mercury<gloss>red mercuric oxide</gloss></term>; silver from English white lead; and so with others. However, those accidental factors and "emphases" <note>visual distortions or highlights</note> must first be removed, by which a thing is thought to have a certain color when it does not—such as when waters are believed to be green because of green mud or sand at the bottom, or red because of red sands, or because of herbs, flowers, trees, floorings, and other things communicating their own color to them through the reflection of light. Next, care must be taken that depth does not deceive us, and that a foreign appearance is not given to the contents extracted from there—or if that happens, it should be noted by what means it occurs. One must ensure that no more radiant light falls on it than allows the color to be viewed purely, that the light is not malicious and dark, or deceptive like candlelight, and many similar things worthy of observation.

### CHAPTER XVI.
->On judging black substances.<-

**That** water which is black when drawn in the hands or in glass—depending on the variety of blackness, which is sometimes diluted, sometimes thick, sometimes leaning toward reddish-brown, etc. (*For dense red, as well as thick green, are perceived as black, such as balsam of sulfur, non-translucent glass of antimony, bunched green glass, etc.*)—indicates either various things or a various mixture. For there may lie beneath it a juice affected by fire, or a breakdown of matter: just as the stone of minium turns black when the mercury is drawn out. Mercury itself is also found in the form of black soot, and it is well known that condensed vapors dissolved in water stain them black; and in animals, blood is sometimes black from "scorching" <note>adustio: a medical term for an imbalance of heat</note>; in plants, and indeed in almost anything, a black wash-out occurs from scorching, as in charcoal and unburnt bones, etc. Or there are things black by their own nature, whether scorching has occurred or not, which when confused or mixed with waters bring blackness to them. Examples include <term>pnigitis earth<gloss>a black, greasy clay</gloss></term>, <term>bitumen<gloss>mineral pitch or asphalt</gloss></term>, <term>lithanthrax<gloss>stone coal</gloss></term>, <term>lapis fissilis<gloss>slate</gloss></term>, certain metallic <term>cadmia<gloss>zinc ore or furnace soot</gloss></term>, black sulfur, black gypsum, black chrysocolla, <term>gagates<gloss>jet</gloss></term>, black <term>boles<gloss>medicinal clays</gloss></term>, <term>cotes<gloss>whetstones</gloss></term>, and what they name from bear's oil <note>original: "ab vrsi oleo"; likely a cryptic name for a form of antimony or stibnite</note>, antimony, the magnet, soot of amber and similar things, black <term>Sory<gloss>a copper/iron sulfate mineral</gloss></term>, black <term>melanteria<gloss>ink-stone</gloss></term>, and the blackness of metals—especially of copper, mercury, lead, iron, etc.—and most especially if mercury has "devoured" gold or silver and reduced it to a black earth. Or, sharp juices mixed with waters that contain plant juices turn black together, which happens if types of ink are tempered with yellow or dark decoctions or infusions. [It happened once that water from the spring of Langenschwalbach <note>a famous spa town in Germany</note> was carried in fresh oak vessels to the Count of Hohenlohe <note>Alta-flania</note>. During the transport, it turned black as shoemaker's ink. This is a sign that those waters consist of much physical <term>chalcanthum<gloss>green vitriol or iron sulfate</gloss></term>, which is also proven by a crimson "flower" or precipitate. But a mineral of iron is also indicated. For by this, as well as by the vitriol of copper, waters are blackened. See Johannes Bauhin <note>a famous 16th-century physician and botanist</note> on the Boll spring <note>Bad Boll in Germany</note>, pages 16 and 37.] That writing ink is made this way is common knowledge: thus shoemakers make their ink from soaked old iron, a decoction of barley, or whey. To this also belongs the confluence of various waters that carry staining juices with them, or which are changeable into black by certain agents. Thus we see rivers blackened by the influx of abundant marsh waters; and the banks of the Nera River <note>Narnis</note> are believed to be stained with blackness by the juices received from medicinal springs.

**Some** things also turn black when soaked for a long time in simple waters, and sometimes even deposit their juice into them, such as oak wood, alder, galls, and the like. From this it is clear that waters in which many alders grow, especially marshy ones, are stained black or dark brown. Certain waters are infected with the same color by the wash-out of watery vapors which settle and conceive some putrefaction, as is visible on stones and the walls of wells. But in minerals, we generally suspect something inky or metallic, which is nevertheless also referred to the nature of <term>chalcanthum</term>—besides scorched sulfur—since it is known to be present in metals. Thus, if you wish to coagulate ink dissolved in water in a green glazed pot—the kind of color that usually arises from <term>litharge<gloss>lead oxide</gloss></term> and especially from copper—the liquid turns black. If you throw a solution of copper into a decoction of herbs, it is darkened. It is common knowledge that vessels made of white lead <note>likely tin-plated lead or pewter</note> contract a black stain if the juice of grapes lingers in them. The Volaterran water <note>from Volterra, Italy</note> is written to be thick and black. Experience proves it is mixed with ink, for it is produced from that boiling. Lake Avernus in Campania is said to be black, but they say it is a diluted form of <term>chalcite<gloss>a copper/iron mineral</gloss></term>, <term>Sory</term>, or <term>Misy<gloss>a yellow vitriol mineral</gloss></term>. Likewise, Venetian earths are mostly found with some appearance of ink, such as <term>melanteria</term>, <term>misy</term>, <term>sory</term>, etc. To black also belongs a livid <note>bluish-gray</note> color, which they attribute to lead and its vein. But certain sulfurous and bituminous waters also turn livid, especially if they consist of putrid mud mixed with sulfur or bitumen. Veins of livid color and leaden raw silver, and many other things, are also found in inky hills. <term>Melanteria</term> is also believed to turn black or livid upon contact with water—at least the kind that is sulfur-colored. For when I made a trial on the gray or ash-colored variety, the experiment did not respond.

### CHAPTER XVII.
->On Browns.<-

**The** brown color is close to black and reddish-brown, and in most cases designates an affection by fire—either actual or potential fire. For we see that woods become brown from flame before they reach blackness, just as when
