We see this same color on the fingernails of fullers <note>Fullers used harsh alkaline substances to clean and thicken cloth, which stained their hands.</note>. The same logic applies to why wood becomes dusky or reddish when it is drenched in <term>strong waters<gloss>nitric acid or other corrosive mineral acids</gloss></term>. In animals, too, when yellow bile is overly "burnt" by heat, the fluid becomes dark; it is no different in minerals, where we find dark sulfur, bitumen, burnt ochre, roasted <term>red earth<gloss>rubrica</gloss></term>, <term>colcothar<gloss>the brownish-red iron oxide residue left after the distillation of vitriol</gloss></term>, certain types of <term>chalcitis<gloss>a copper-bearing mineral, likely a sulfate</gloss></term>, and so on. Some minerals acquire a dusky color from black "tessellated" juices—not just any black, but those closest to red (for compressed red appears black, and if it is scorched further, it undergoes the same change), or those which are congealed from a diluted reddish hue. It is as if one were to dissolve and dilute the hardened smoke or soot from wood-burning furnaces in a great deal of water. A similar thing remains in ashes; thus, the <term>lye<gloss>lixivia</gloss></term> made from them turns out tawny or reddish. If the serum in animals is diluted with burnt bile, it takes on the same color. The same emerges from mixtures of dark bodily substances, such as <term>jet<gloss>gagate</gloss></term>, bitumen, and the like. For that dye comes closer to the <term>spiritual<gloss>in alchemy, "spiritual" refers to volatile or subtle substances that can be sublimated or evaporated</gloss></term> ones, as the Chemists call them. Some things, while they are fermented or soaked together, display the same appearance—as when iron, alder wood, or oak is infused in water, the liquor is judged by this color before it turns black. For it becomes dusky before it reaches blackness. Sometimes it precedes redness and whiteness, specifically when it arises from an overflow of "sooty spirit," and this happens more in dry things, although the variety in individual cases is beyond explanation. In minerals, therefore, it signifies either an affection caused by fire, or fermentation, or a mixture that is either spiritual or substantial.

### CHAPTER XVIII.
#### On violet colors.

<margin>Hence the rusty hyacinth.</margin>
**V**iolet is close to black (just as "black violets" are described by the poets); it is also close to green. Therefore, in the mineral kingdom, it mostly arises from black, leaden-grey, and green substances; indeed, it is also related to blue. Whence <term>lapis lazuli<gloss>filazucium</gloss></term> is scorched a little, it turns violet, just as stag’s horn roasted in a covered vessel turns partly black and partly violet, specifically where the whiteness excels within the blackness. That fire, or fire-like states, are sometimes the cause of this condition is proven by a polished iron plate moved near flames, or even if the smoke of certain ignited things is absorbed. However, its power is most excellent in iron, as witnessed by the <term>violet crocus of Mars<gloss>an iron oxide pigment</gloss></term> which is prepared from it, though not without a specific method of firing. Clays and boles of the same color are also found, as are marbles, gems, and other things. <term>Baccius<gloss>Andrea Bacci, a 16th-century physician and author of a famous work on thermal springs</gloss></term> teaches that at the district of Monte Gibbio in Italy, when a spring of liquid bitumen failed and the veins were dug out, a honey-like liquor appeared in the bowels of the mountain, and next to it, violet water. He notes that the clods from which the vein is extracted are chalk thick with fatness, greenish, and sprinkled with a violet luster. It seems, therefore, that such things turn violet from bitumen that has been diluted and mixed with putrid vapors—unless perhaps it happens by an optical illusion, such as is seen on the necks of pigeons. But it is not absurd that white clay, abounding in raw vapors or thicker watery ones (as if covered with mold), becomes violet while it ferments. We see such a thing exist even in the moldiness or decay of bread, and the sides of wells show a violet tint between black and green. The "Carolina Pitch" <note>likely a type of bitumen or mineral resin named after a location</note> which is dug up near hot springs has a violet color among others, for no other reason, it seems, than a vaporous breath or a "spiritual" tincture. Nevertheless, some waters are also diluted by such juices, like the chalybeate <note>iron-bearing</note> waters near Naples, at the Villa of Lucullus, which when still are said to shine with a violet luster and even imbue stones with it. This would likewise happen if boles and the dissolutions of amethyst flowers were mixed with water. At Peloro in Sicily, the salt is violet. From this, it can communicate its tincture to watery liquids. <term>Eretrian earth<gloss>a type of medicinal clay from Eretria</gloss></term>, when rubbed on bronze, induces a violet color. Let the violet color therefore be, according to the nature of the things involved: either from fiery breaths, or putrid and condensed vapors, or juices dissolved in liquid, or mostly from diluted violet boles; unless the ore itself proves to be green, leaden, blue, or clay-like, such as iron, lapis lazuli, bronze, <term>flower of copper<gloss>verdigris or copper flakes</gloss></term>, marble, gems, <term>fluorspar<gloss>gemmeus fluor</gloss></term>, salt, blue sulfur, or violet clay.

### CHAPTER XIX.
#### On glaucous and blue colors.

**T**he judgment is almost the same for glaucous <note>a pale sea-green or bluish-grey</note> and blue, for waters and minerals of this kind are found, such as the glaucous water at Thermopylae, the river called the Blau <note>literally "Blue"</note> from its appearance, the Isar likewise, and a certain blue lake in Armenia. So in the veins there are lapis lazuli, boles, sulfurs, and other blue things. Blue arises readily from <term>verdigris<gloss>ærugine</gloss></term> or the green "flower of copper," likewise from brass and Hungarian vitriol, and sometimes even from the veins of iron, copper, and silver, and even gold. Blue ink shines wonderfully. A certain bitumen is also somewhat blue. <term>Chrysocolla<gloss>a green copper mineral</gloss></term> also turns into blue. Craftsmen extract an excellent blue from silver, and a certain mixture of <term>sal ammoniac<gloss>ammonium chloride</gloss></term>, mercury, and sulfur turns blue through sublimation. Lime water in which sal ammoniac has been dissolved is dyed the same color when placed over brass. But in minerals, the veins of copper and silver take the most important part of the judgment. For an excellent blue is also dug from these, as in the copper mines of Cyprus, and copper is sometimes smelted from blue ore. Where the veins of these metals (whether mature or immature) are missing, the suspicion is that such a clay or bole lies beneath, or a certain greenness affected in a specific way, or a visible "image" <note>an optical effect</note>. In this way, the water of Petriolo is greenish in color but blue at the bottom, because <unclear>falling</unclear> into the deep, with a certain defect of admitted light, it appears blue to the sight—or a clod of green or blue sulfur exists there. In limestone quarries, a earth similar to Eretrian earth is sometimes found, of a grayish-blue color. <term>Diphyges<gloss>an ancient term for a mineral that is "of two natures," often a copper slag or dual-colored ore</gloss></term> sometimes becomes blue if water remains on it. Indeed, some things scorched by fire take on such a tincture, especially where sulfurous, antimonial, or lead-based spirits are joined.

# On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 2.

### CHAPTER XX.
->On Green Colors.<-

**G**reen color is also frequent in the judgment of mineral waters and soil, and it primarily indicates green clay, such as <term>Chrysocolla<gloss>a green copper carbonate mineral, often malachite</gloss></term>, or dissolved copper, or a vein of copper, or a dilution of vitriol, or fossil verdigris, marbles, gems, green fluors, stones, and the green chalk which they call <note>original: "Theodofion"</note> Theodosion, etc. Wherever Chrysocolla is found, a vein of copper is indicated. In Hungary, near the town of Banská Bystrica <note>original: "Bistriciam"</note>, where there are very rich copper mines, a certain tunnel yields green water, from whose sediment Chrysocolla is collected. The baths of Avignon, which turn green where they flow under the sun, are tinted with <term>chalcanthum<gloss>blue vitriol or copper sulfate</gloss></term>. In Persia, there is a green water derived from copper, although they also boil salt out of it, as it is salty and bitter. If the greenness comes from copper, it turns black when exposed to fire or the heat of the sun. It can also be caused by sulfur, or it can be communicated to the waters as a visual illusion due to the bottom of the pool or surrounding green objects.

### CHAPTER XXI.
->On Blood-Red and Red Colors.<-

**T**he color of blood is present in many minerals, and it seems in most cases to be the end result of all other colors if the substances are subjected to the forces of fire. Such things found include native <term>cinnabar<gloss>mercury sulfide, referred to here as "minium"</gloss></term>, hematite stone, certain types of rust, <term>red ochre<gloss>rubrica</gloss></term>, blood-colored <term>bole<gloss>a medicinal clay</gloss></term>, sulfur of that sort, mineral <term>sandarac<gloss>red arsenic sulfide</gloss></term>, <term>schist<gloss>here referring to a type of hematite or fissile stone</gloss></term> in iron-bearing hematite mines, silver veins (or raw red silver), the ruby gem, and similar things. But the juices of plants also sometimes tint waters with a blood-red color, as if you had infused red sandalwood.

At a lower intensity is a diluted and shining redness; the color purple, which is close to black like clotted blood, exceeds it slightly. Mostly, redness arises from a certain ferruginous <note>iron-bearing</note> earth or ferruginous clay, just as in the Thuringian Forest in certain iron mines everything is red, and the very stone that is dug up has a violet tint, which, when crushed and diluted with water, turns red. There is also red bole, <term>sory<gloss>a mineral related to vitriol</gloss></term>, cinnabar, sandarac, <term>orpiment<gloss>yellow arsenic sulfide</gloss></term>, and those things we recounted among the blood-reds. (For the blood-red color differs from red and crimson only by degree, and not rarely red, rosy, liver-colored, crimson, purple, and blood-red are produced in one and the same thing under different conditions.) Likewise, there is Sinopian earth <note>a famous red earth from Sinope</note>, red mountain salt such as is found in Sardinia, and formerly near Memphis and around the Oxus River, which was reddish—just as it is saffron-colored in Cappadocia, purple in Sicily, etc.—gypsum and reddish marble, red emery, <term>chalcitis<gloss>a copper-iron sulfate</gloss></term>, saffron of iron <note>iron oxide</note>, and so on. They say it is a sign of iron veins if the silty redness has a ferruginous taste, from which drops sometimes distilling in caves form columns and cones <note>stalactites and stalagmites</note>. The waters near Narni <note>original: "Narnia"</note> are said to turn red from ferruginous dross. Pliny states the same regarding the spring of the Tungri near Liège <note>original: "Leodium"</note>, whose water becomes turbid when moved toward fire, and afterward returns to a reddish color with a ferruginous taste.

But how many things turn red by fire or "sharp" <note>acidic</note> waters? Artisans indeed experience this with mercury, antimony, orpiment, gold, copper, verdigris, vitriol, and many other things; but it is consistent that the power of subterranean heat is no less, just as they think <term>sandix<gloss>a bright red pigment</gloss></term> is made from burnt silver-bearing stone. It can happen that into lakes and pools steeped in plant juices, a certain sharp vein flows, which changes that water into a red juice like blood. Thus, the common people think blood has suddenly appeared and they regard it as a miracle. However, it is evident that sharp juices can produce that color in prepared substances from the example of sharp lye, in which if you soak antimony and then pour in vinegar, a redness will emerge. Likewise, human skin turns red by a solution of mercury in <term>strong water<gloss>nitric acid</gloss></term>. Sometimes mere heat and power bring redness into action; this we have observed in a certain sharp water which flowed cold, but when heated became turbid and turned red, just as Pliny writes of the Tungri spring. This happens in solutions of <term>Mars<gloss>the alchemical name for iron</gloss></term>. Therefore, it is no wonder if in hot summers certain pools not far from iron veins suddenly turn red and later lose that same color again.

### CHAPTER XXII.
->On Yellow Colors.<-

**C**ertain waters are yellow, like the Grotto of Viterbo; some have yellow sediments, like the "Holy Water" near Alcalá, which, if silver coins are thrown in, tints them yellow shortly after; some push out such filings, etc. In minerals, the yellow color belongs to yellow arsenic, sulfur, yellow bole, yellow sand, the lumpy <term>cadmia<gloss>zinc ore</gloss></term> which they call <term>Calamine<gloss>Galmiam</gloss></term>, a certain copper, iron veins, and what is called <term>Zinc<gloss>Zinkum</gloss></term> (though not all of it), pure bitumen, pure amber, tripoli ochre, sparks of mercury, certain fossil <term>plumbago<gloss>here likely meaning a lead or graphite-like mineral</gloss></term>, the solution of copper which settles, likewise what settles in dissolved vitriol, and those things which are called "golden," <term>ammoschrysos<gloss>gold-sand stone</gloss></term>, orpiment, <term>misy<gloss>a yellow vitriolic mineral</gloss></term>, and similar things. Some things turn yellow when diluted though they were red when solid, such as saffron, a juice which the schist stone also yields when rubbed. Waters turn yellow primarily due to the mixture of saffron-colored clay, or earth and ochre, with which they are also accustomed to tinting tiles. Other things also turn lemon-yellow by fire or sharp waters, such as antimony (from which a yellow earth is produced), the mercury called <term>Turpeth mineral<gloss>a yellow mercury sulfate</gloss></term>, lime of tin, toasted white lead, and verdigris toasted slightly—though it also contains whiteness and yellowness within itself, as if it were a mixture of lemon, white, and blue parts.

### CHAPTER XXIII.
->On White Colors.<-

**A** milky white color indicates clay, marl, lime, marble filings, and many such things. There is also white and pale Chrysocolla, gypsum, white lead, dissolved mercury, dissolved litharge, and silver...

# CHAPTER XXIV.
## On Various Colors.

**I**n general, those whose tinctures are spiritual and volatile perish easily; those whose tinctures are spiritual and fixed are introduced through an <note>In this context, "abort" likely refers to a failed or interrupted natural process in the earth.</note>abortion or through powerful mutations. Corporal tinctures are more lasting, unless the body itself is large and fleeting. Thus, colors are recognized according to the experience of individual cases in every genus. However, one must not immediately pronounce judgment on the essence of a thing from a single color. For nature "luxuriates" wonderfully in this area. Thus, a beginner would not deny that a substance is chalk simply because it is not shown to be white, since it can also be black, green, ashen, and even red. Likewise, <term>saltpeter<gloss>halinitrum</gloss></term> is found white, yellow, reddish, and ashen; similarly, <term>soda<gloss>nitrum</gloss></term> can be rose-colored, dark, white, or purple within white. There are various <note>Fuller's earth, used for cleaning wool.</note>fulling earths, various clays, marls, etc. So too <term>vitriol<gloss>chalcanthum</gloss></term> can be white, green, hyacinth-blue, red, gold, ashen, etc. In the same mine, diverse colors are found, as around the lagoons of <note>Volterra, Italy, famous for its salt and sulfur springs.</note>Volterra where the waters seethe; one may find livid, oily, and blue clods, though the innermost mineral is sulfur with particles of iron and vitriol. [<insert>Bitumen also produces violet and other variously colored hues.</insert>] Therefore, where variety occurs, there is either a mixture of various things, or a different tincture of different parts, or a varied affection from the same cause operating more or less according to the disposition of the material and the progress and communication of forces. Certain things are colored differently at different times, like the <note>The Dnieper River.</note>Dnieper <gloss>Borysthenes</gloss>, which sometimes flows tinted with verdigris.

<note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), a famous Italian physician and author of a major work on the history of thermal baths.</note>*Baccius* says that the iron-rich bath in *Bellicano* changes color by the hour from gold to black and turbid due to heterogeneous vapors. In the waters of Abano, in the Royal Bath, and the *Cornelian* bath at Aachen, the color changes even when no one is disturbing it; although the water may be very clear, it sometimes becomes greenish, bluish, or whitish, and this happens most especially around changes in the weather. The water in the springs of the <note>Tongeren, in modern-day Belgium, famous for its mineral springs described by Pliny.</note>Tungri is at first not red, but later, as we said before, it turns red when fires are placed beneath it. Some vary when different things are thrown in, where neither of the items had the color that emerges. In some there are certain successions of colors by which they are recognized; for instance, when <term>white lead<gloss>cerussa</gloss></term> is made from livid lead, it later turns yellow, and finally becomes <term>red lead<gloss>minium</gloss></term>. The nature of *mercury* <gloss>hydrargyri</gloss> is wondrous. Precipitated with nitric acid it turns white, then yellow, and finally red, sometimes by fires, sometimes by waters. I had a precipitate that was a dark red; I poured nitric acid over it, and it recovered its whiteness, and the part that was less <note>original: "rosa" - perhaps referring to a pink or rosy hue.</note>red, or where a weaker water was poured, it turned lemon-yellow, so that there is not only a progression of colors here, but also a regression. That <note>A famous medical hoax of the 1590s involving a 7-year-old boy in Silesia who was rumored to have grown a natural gold tooth. It was later found to be a clever gold crown.</note>boy to whom a golden tooth was said to have grown (though falsely) has a golden casing around it, which they say changes color according to the quarters of the moon. It appears, therefore, that various causes can underlie such things: namely, either a varying agent, or the same agent but different in power and strength, or a subject unequally disposed, or new spirits and habits which, while moved unequally, stir up something from the bottom and the spring, or new inflows. Thus cold, heat, and other qualities affect things in various ways, from which a change of color follows, just as when cold constricts vapors and makes them denser, the water becomes turbid, etc. We have already spoken of sharp juices that dissolve, coagulate, and define. Nor is there no power in the periods of the sun and moon. Let it be observed, however, where the change occurs: whether in the spring itself, or in its progress, and how far away; what things are mixed, what are removed, what are the agents; likewise, whether it is the water itself, or the filings and contents within it, and what things are produced from it. But enough for now regarding color.

# CHAPTER XXV.
## On Odors.

**T**he power of odors resides mostly and principally in the spirit. But since this spirit is either innate or foreign—which nevertheless easily insinuates itself and adheres to things in which no part of the substance from which the odor came exists—it not infrequently deceives the investigator. Nevertheless, there is some evidence to be gained from it. For if it does not come from the mixture of the stone, it has been acquired from elsewhere, either from the affection of powerful qualities in fire and the like, or from the passing through of spirits brought from afar out of the vents of the earth; what kind of thing that may be, we can investigate further.

However, some things are clearly odorless, such as the simple elements in themselves—air, water, earth, etc.—and those things occupied by the dominion of cold, like snow, ice, etc., and those which emit very little even after fires, such as metals, salts, pure stones, etc. Some are odorless in action, but when a little heat is applied they emit effective spirits, such as horn, hair, pitch, amber, etc. Some smell immediately, such as ambergris, liquid <note>Likely a reference to a liquid bitumen or resin.</note>faccinum, <term>serpentine<gloss>ophites</gloss></term>, and similar things; but most of all those whose decay is in action, such as stagnant lakes, heavy mud, etc. In the examination, they are tested in various ways—

the act of testing must be attempted through methods such as friction, burning, roasting, boiling, and so on. In these processes, heat dominates; its role is to release the <term>spirits<gloss>volatile vapors or essences</gloss></term> and carry them to the sense of smell. Furthermore, if the odor vanishes immediately, it is usually because the spirits are either thin and easily dissipated, or they barely sit upon the surface, or they are quickly congealed by the cold. From these signs, one might argue whether the odor is primary to the substance or not, which can also be shown by comparing species of the same kind. An inherent odor lasts longer, depending on the nature of the substance and how it is handled.

### CHAPTER XXVI.
### On odorous things.

**O**dor must be hunted for not only in the mineral water itself, but also in the air, both nearby and further away in that region—even in the course of the stream, the types of earth, and the nature of the contents and extracts. One must take care that there is no powerful chimney or <term>vent<gloss>æstuarium</gloss></term> in the vicinity, such as a metal-working shop, a cave, a mine-shaft, a <note>original: "scrobs Chæronea." A reference to Plutonian pits or mephitic caves near Chaeronea in Greece, known in antiquity for exhaling deadly vapors.</note>Chaeronean pit, a rotting pond, or decaying vegetables, which could corrupt one's judgment. One should observe whether the same odor is present when the water is in motion as when it is still, and in what abundance and intensity. Likewise, note the smell before and after boiling, friction, roasting, and burning. Sometimes the substance must be chewed (unless there is danger in doing so) and the exhaled breath judged; occasionally, even a <term>burp<gloss>ructus</gloss></term> reveals the nature of the thing by its smell, especially after drinking the waters. However, this can be deceptive, as something smelly could have been lingering in the stomach, which, when mixed or released, spoils the "lyncean" <note>A reference to Lynceus, the Argonaut famous for his sharp sight; here used metaphorically for sharp or keen senses.</note> purity of the odor; similarly, any foulness lingering in the mouth can corrupt the test.

### CHAPTER XXVII.
### On the types of odors in minerals.

**F**urthermore, the odors of minerals are either reduced to simple types or are expressed by the nature of specific things. In the first category is the "foul" odor, under which can be grouped the putrid and the heavy; there is also the sweet, the acidic, and others. In the second category are the sulfurous, bituminous, <term>inky<gloss>atramentosus</gloss></term>, violet-like, camphor-like, myrrh-like, wine-like, and musty odors, as well as horny smells and similar ones. Some of these also fall back into the first category, as they are all either pleasant or unpleasant.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.
### On foul odors.

**F**oul odors (which are also called rank, noxious, troublesome, heavy, putrid, and so on; though to those who consider the matter more scrupulously and exactly, a "heavy" smell is not the same as a "foul" one) are mostly detected in decaying mineral matter, where sulfurous, bituminous, or inky mud is fermenting. Thus, those rank spirits sometimes congeal together and cling inside, so that even after a mixture is made—even when the decay, fermentation, or digestion has ceased—wherever they are provoked by fire, they create distress. This can be seen in sulfur, which, when dissolved or set on fire, smells more foul than human sewers, or at least no less so; for which reason it is known that dung is also sulfurous and can be set on fire. Hence, any sulfurous, bituminous, or inky substances betray their principles more or less, as is evident in the smelting or roasting of metallic veins, such as in veins of lead, <term>bismuth<gloss>bismuthi</gloss></term>, fissile stone <gloss>shale</gloss>, coal, <term>metallic cadmia<gloss>zinc ore</gloss></term>, antimony, native <term>cinnabar<gloss>minio nativo</gloss></term>, <term>virgin sulfur<gloss>sulphure vivo</gloss></term>, and many others. <term>Sory<gloss>a dark, vitriolic mineral</gloss></term> gives off a heavy and nauseating rankness. <term>Nitric acid<gloss>aqua fortis</gloss></term> does not forget its origins—namely, alum, <term>blue vitriol<gloss>chalcanthi</gloss></term>, and saltpeter—combined with a burnt smell; however, the strongest qualities belong to the vitriol, for the sake of which both metals and their veins exhale something heavy in the fire, since it can be extracted from all of them by art. A rank odor is also found in <term>red arsenic<gloss>sandaracæ</gloss></term>, arsenic, <term>orpiment<gloss>auripigmento</gloss></term>, and similar substances when they are burned or roasted. The odor of orpiment, however, is closer to sulfur than that of red arsenic, whether they are just carried in the air or burned. And it is very well known from the workshops—where metallic dross and ingots are quenched in arranged basins—that these odors are communicated to the waters in which the scorched or melted materials are extinguished or washed while they are in fermentation. For the waters themselves smell of the same rankness, though blunted, because the congealed mineral spirits are precipitated by the abundant water. The same happens when they are boiled in certain liquids and when they are dissolved in spring waters, though there is danger in the experiment. For such foul stenches dissipate and choke the animal and vital spirits, and sometimes corrupt them with a poisonous quality.

### CHAPTER XXIX.
### On pungent and similar odors.

**T**o the foul odors, pungent and acidic ones are sometimes added. For these are also heavy and troublesome, though they should not be considered among the truly stinking so much as simply unpleasant. Something acidic and pungent is exhaled by the spirits of vitriol and sulfur, which are also observed in the smoke of sulfur and in putrid mud, in which (if it is indeed mineral) one mostly finds vitriol, sulfur, and bitumen. This same acidity is abundant in veins or caves of iron, alum, and copper. For here too there is a bounty of vitriol, just as in rusty materials and the places from which acidic springs flow. Thus Galen says that in the caves of Cyprus there was a suffocating odor that could hardly be endured, representing <term>chalcitis<gloss>a copper-iron mineral</gloss></term> and <term>verdigris<gloss>æruginem</gloss></term>; we can count this among the pungent and sharp smells, as we do the odor exhaled by strong acids. In some, an added burnt smell sharpens the pungency, as with the spirit of salt. There is also a pungent and heavy odor in dissolved amber, <term>naphtha<gloss>naphthæ</gloss></term>, and <term>petroleum<gloss>petroleo</gloss></term>.

### Odors named after certain things.

**T**hese also explain the foul sulfurous odor, especially if it is in putrid mud, as well as the bituminous, inky, and salty odors in fermented decay (as can be seen in salt-works, where although salt resists decay,

From some, flames emerge, and together they emit a heavy sulfurous or bituminous odor. <term>Sory<gloss>a dark, mineral substance containing metallic sulfates</gloss></term> usually mimics a thunderous or "lightning-like" breath. Chemists easily recognize the smell of <term>stibium<gloss>antimony</gloss></term>, cinnabar, cadmia, and other things with which they are frequently familiar; thus, for them, judgment is easier.

## CHAPTER XXXI.
->On pleasant odors.<-

<margin>Musty odor.</margin>
**T**here are likewise many species of pleasant odors defined by certain substances. A musty and wine-like odor is moderately pleasant, but when immoderate, it is heavy—as is seen after digestion in the stomach, which can be observed from the breath of drunkards, and from belches and the jars in which wine has stayed overnight. Those who drink from <term>acidic springs<gloss>acidulae</gloss></term> mostly belch a musty scent; it is likely these waters carry sulfurous, inky, or aluminous spirits in a certain proportion. For sulfur-treated wine also belches something musty. However, bitumen can also contribute to this.

<margin>Odor of camphor.</margin>
There are those found that express the vivid odor of camphor; regarding this, *Baccius* says: *In the territory of Modena and Parma, the bitumen is fatty and sometimes, especially in the waters, produces an odor rivaling camphor. Thus Savonarola*
<margin>The power of camphor in amber.</margin>
*wrote that the salt waters at the Italian spa town smell of camphor, where the nature of the earth is similar.* *Avicenna* maintains that an odorous power of camphor exists in <term>succinum<gloss>amber</gloss></term>, which is confirmed by experiment. For if anyone, while <term>oil of amber<gloss>oleum succini</gloss></term>
<margin>Camphor is not the "flower" of amber.</margin>
is being made, places a cotton cloth moistened with water over the <term>alembic<gloss>the cap of a still</gloss></term>, it will emit a smoke smelling of camphor. Hence *Agricola* wished for camphor to be the "flower" of amber, or of Arabian bitumen, extracted by <term>sublimation<gloss>turning a solid into vapor and back to solid</gloss></term>, which nonetheless *Garcia* proves to be false. To some, there is a violet-like odor, such as the Spring of the Macrobii,
<margin>Odor of violets.</margin>

It is consistent that this is a tincture from violet-colored marble lime, or some such mineral, which *Agricola* describes: [the spirit of vitriol can be circulated until it smells of violets.] The "Earth-stone" <term>Geodes</term>, he says, found in Meissen, breathes out this odor when broken: *Likewise a fragment of rock from Aldenburg, and the stone of Berninger to which moss clings with its fragrance. <margin>Odor of myrrh.</margin>

Ancient authors state that from the Cratea spring near Carthage, a black bitumen flows out which has the odor of citrus. They also refer the springs of Arabia Felix to bitumen, which pour out liquid amber; both in odor and substance, but of a yellow color. Those waters that take their odor from their contents or things growing in them—such as fish ponds that smell of fish, or lakes that mimic the smell of herbs, trees, reeds, etc.—judgment of these is not difficult.

## CHAPTER XXXII.
->On tastes.<-

**T**astes are analogous to odors. For everything odorous that can be dissolved is flavorful, although not everything flavorful is odorous, such as salts, etc. Here the sense of touch also coincides. For taste is a kind of touch. Thus we judge not only sweet and bitter, fatty and salty, sharp, acidic, and harsh with the tongue, but also the piercing, the stinging, the penetrating, the blistering, the watery, the earthy, the hot, the cold, etc.—about which, however, we will speak individually under "touch." Although most minerals are tasteless, and this sense belongs rather to vegetables, mineral juices are not entirely lacking, which you may judge by this very means; just as the impressions of metals in waters—in which they are extinguished while glowing hot or in which they linger for a long time—are perceived by a certain metallic viscosity. But even a lack of taste proves something. For those things which are certainly mixed, we gather are composed of such parts if they are tasteless; things which by their nature lack taste, or being overcome by earthy portions, hide it—as happens in copper, which is tasteless, yet its vitriol and its <term>verdigris<gloss>the green pigment/rust of copper</gloss></term> do not lack taste. This happens if the <term>calces<gloss>powdery oxides left after heating</gloss></term> of metals or other minerals, having been washed, are mixed into waters. It should be noted that if the taste does not appear at the very first trial, it must be sought in resolutions, in dross, in congealed smokes, in clay, in sand, in lye, in roasted or scorched things, and in whatever other ways it can be called into action.

...can be called. It often happens that a juice diluted by much water affects the taste so weakly that it does not seem to be perceived. Then, coagulation will gather it together and make it manifest. One must see, however, that through improper operation we do not introduce something foreign, just as almost all things become false through **reverberating calcination** <note>original: "calcinatione reuerberante"; a chemical process where heat is reflected onto a substance</note>, nor can that salt be well discerned. Furthermore, it must be noted whether the thing is equally flavorful—for example, in a mineral water, whether it is of equal taste at the top, middle, and bottom, or different in kind or degree. Let it also be observed whether the same remains or fades away, by what things mixed in or applied it is changed, and into what; for instance, whether the taste of the water is changed by rains, winds, clouds, or a cloudy or clear sky; whether it is constant and perennial when the sky changes, during the cycles of the Moon and Sun, likewise by heating and cooling, in motion and at rest, with spirits and without them. For we see that certain waters lose the grace of their taste through carriage or transport, and finally even become tasteless or <term>putrilaginous<gloss>decaying or rotted</gloss></term>, while some endure even when exported far away. Some also have a completely hidden cause for this change, while either the internal heat-source varies, or a new juice flows in, or the mineral becomes more abundant, or something is withdrawn. From such observations, however, we can know whether the taste is from a spiritual tincture rather than a bodily one—that is, from the presence of spirits—or from the dilution of resolvable juices and other bodies. If the taste fades through carriage, with no other force applied, or likewise by exposure to the sun, light boiling, and similar things, it must be attributed to spirits <note>In early chemistry, "spirits" referred to volatile substances that could easily evaporate</note>. Nor, however, should it be thought that in all cases every mineral power perishes when the taste is lost. For in some, an internal tempering remains, and spirits are recalled from the coagulated juices. That water should be judged useless which has only a temporary presence of spirits, such that all efficacy depends on this. For once the spirit is lost, it becomes like a corpse when the soul departs, and promptly putrefies, and instead of an <term>alexiteric<gloss>a protective remedy or antidote</gloss></term>, it produces poison.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.
### On sweet taste.

<margin>Sweet and bitter.</margin>
The types of tastes in mineral waters and juices, just like odors, are considered first generally, and afterwards specifically. In general, they are found to be non-putrid, putrid, sweet, fatty, bitter, salty, acidic, and acrid. For the "austere" and "harsh" tastes belong to fruits and juices from plants, unless you misuse the terms. Specifically, there is the taste of garlic, fishy, dung-like, <term>nitrous<gloss>tasting of nitre or saltpeter</gloss></term>, aluminous, metallic, etc. And from material effects: styptic, <term>pontic<gloss>a sharp, sour, or astringent taste</gloss></term>, etc. Likewise from formal effects: piercing, stinging, burning, etc. A sweet taste in water is understood in two ways. First, we call that water sweet which has a taste not foreign to common spring water, so that it is close to or the same as ordinary drinking water, even if it is otherwise tasteless. Secondly, this is also called sweet which moves the sense of taste not by a lack of flavor, but by an actual act of sweetness, in the same way we call honey, sugar, and milk "sweet." Thus, near the town of Glaucha, the warm water of Cardia is sweeter than milk. It is likely that sweetness of this kind exists either from a thickening of the air, or by cooking, or by the mixing of juices or bodies that are either sweet in themselves or bring about sweetness by their meeting, or even by an alteration made by things dwelling within. Thus we find in <term>chalcanthum<gloss>blue vitriol or copper sulfate</gloss></term> along with its astringency and sourness, there is a marvelous sweetness, which can even be separated by art. There is also a certain sweetness in sulfur; it is in lead. Therefore, sweet oils, sugars, and similar things are made from them. **Vitriol of Venus** <note>copper sulfate</note> and **verdigris** likewise carry a remarkable sweetness along with an astringency; less so the vitriol of iron: even more so lead and **ceruse** <note>white lead</note> and **litharge**, **molybdæna**, **plumbago**, **galena**, and similar things. And so we also notice that wine kept for a long time in metallic vessels takes on that sweetness—which is, however, metallic and nauseating—and water conducted through lead pipes, as well as the liquor of wormwood distilled through such vessels, becomes sweet. *Jordanus* says that the waters of Lossinum are sweet at first, then become bitter. He attributes to them a mineral of sulfur. If you mix <term>aqua fortis<gloss>nitric acid</gloss></term> with much simple water and taste it, you may perceive a sweetness, though a stinging one; indeed, it is usually prepared from alum (which itself has something sweet joined with much sourness), vitriol, and saltpeter. 
<margin>The sweetness of the Nile.</margin>
The sweetness of the Nile is highly praised. It can be from the temperateness of the air, its own thinning and "cooking" while it is carried through hot places, and it is even tempered by certain juices, or it takes on the nature of the earth, which is benign in Egypt—as evidenced by the sweet reeds and other things growing on the bank of the Nile. 
<margin>Milky sweetness.</margin>
A milky sweetness seems to come from lead and leaden things or sulfur: sweetness with a greenish tint, or other signs of <term>atramentum<gloss>a black mineral substance, usually iron sulfate</gloss></term>, comes from this very thing: for redness, blackness, whiteness, and yellowness, etc., can exist together. 
<margin>Fatty sweetness.</margin>
Fatty sweetness is indicated by oiliness, such as comes from the most noble **bitumen**, or liquid amber, fatty **marl**, somewhat fatty atraments, jet, or liquid alum. And oiliness of this kind is sometimes even separated when at rest; and other fatty things in the vicinity show it to be present. Moreover, there is nothing absurd in oiliness being mixed with thicker waters. For it is so in milk, in wine, rose water, cinnamon water, rosemary water, spirit of sulfur, spirit of vitriol, etc., from which it is finally separated—not to mention anything of the sea, the **Asphaltite Lake** <note>the Dead Sea</note>, and similar things. Indeed, it is certain that liquid bitumen, liquid sulfur, and such things gush forth with water from springs.

### CHAPTER XXXIV.
### On bitter things.

A bitter taste, such as is found in many springs of Libya, Africa, and Arabia, is judged to come primarily from **nitre** and **saltpeter**. For although nitre is also salty, it nevertheless has a remarkable bitterness and pricks the tongue with a kind of suction; and the purer the nitre is in the waters, the more bitter they are. *Jordanus* testifies that he boiled down a great deal of nitre from the bitter Ceicensian lake. There is also black bitumen, somewhat bitter in taste, because it is tinged with acrid soot. For it is known that smokes are bitter and acrid. So it is with asphalt and **Sodomitic salt** <note>salt from the Dead Sea</note>. Nor is <term>sal ammoniac<gloss>ammonium chloride</gloss></term> devoid of bitterness. Thus, since this is frequent in Libya, Arabia, Egypt, and Ethiopia, and it is made artificially from urine, then the bottom of the Nile and other springs is more bitter, and urines become bitter. The same logic applies to Lake Ascanius, where nitre is not lacking, and histories testify that Egyptian nitre is dark and bitter. But truly I count also some sweet...

...sweetness seems to be present, which is also detected in <term>halinitre<gloss>a natural mineral soda or saltpeter</gloss></term>; if you taste it, it is somewhat bitter at first, but later resolves into sweetness. They record the same about Lake Asphaltites <note>The Dead Sea</note>, that although it is very salty and <term>bituminous<gloss>containing asphalt or tar-like substances</gloss></term>, it is nonetheless slightly bitter. Indeed, the bituminous "fatness" tempers the bitterness with a subtle sweetness. From this, perhaps, one reason may be sought for why the upper parts of the Nile are sweet, a matter discussed elsewhere. Furthermore, certain other salts are somewhat bitter, especially the smoky ones. If you dissolve <term>salt of the rock<gloss>saltpeter</gloss></term> and <term>vitriol<gloss>metallic sulfates</gloss></term> in water, it becomes bitter, astringent, sharp, and green. Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "Father of Mineralogy"</note> says that when the flavor of copper infuses into a liquid, it reminds the taster of bitterness. Iron is not far removed from the bitterness of copper, and he wishes the cause to be the "burnt earth" which these metals share. We might say more accurately that a mixture of <term>chalcanthum<gloss>blue vitriol or copper sulfate</gloss></term> and halinitre concurs in them. Both are found joined together not infrequently in copper and iron <term>pyrite<gloss>sulfide minerals, often called "fool's gold"</gloss></term>. Hence, if waters are strained through raw veins or the "principles" of such minerals, or if they sit upon them, they will become bitter, just as waters long contained in copper vessels are seen to become. The Hypanis river is said to be made bitter by a spring of <term>sandarach<gloss>realgar, a reddish arsenic mineral</gloss></term> flowing into it; there will therefore be some cause from this mineral as well. The bottom of the sea is more bitter than it is salty, due to the abundance of salt—not a simple salt, but of various kinds—and other juices that flow in with the rivers. In Asia, there is said to be a lake that is stained with bitterness by the abundance of <term>wormwood<gloss>original: "abshynthii"; a notoriously bitter herb</gloss></term> growing around it. Where there are subterranean vents and vapors are washed away and carried into the waters of the mines, it is no wonder that they become bitter.

## CHAPTER XXXV.
### On salty things.

**S**alty is so neighborly to bitter that both flavors are often present in the same thing, as in <term>nitre<gloss>sodium carbonate or saltpeter</gloss></term>, halinitre, <term>salt ammoniac<gloss>ammonium chloride</gloss></term>, salt of urine, etc. This saltiness undoubtedly argues for the presence of spirits, tinctures, and juices. There is also something salty in congealed soot; it is in <term>limes<gloss>calcium oxides</gloss></term> created by the force of storms and subterranean vents; and it is in parched sands. From these, therefore, "salt-sweet" waters are made, as the water washes away the juice or receives the spirit. However, which kind of salt is in which water or mineral will be indicated by specific signs sought from natural history or experience. Taste shows that common salt is "sincerer" <note>pure or unmixed</note>. Those salts made by the force of fire taste of <term>lye<gloss>original: "lixiuiale"; an alkaline substance</gloss></term>, just as the salt of urine is sharp and sub-bitter; so too are halinitre, nitre, etc.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.
### On acidic things.

**T**he acidic taste—from which <term>acidulae<gloss>naturally acidic or sparkling mineral springs</gloss></term> are named—sometimes comes from rot, when stagnant waters diluted with the juices of plants or other suitable things begin to decay and turn sour, just like diluted apple juice, grain decoctions, wines, and similar things. Furthermore, just as certain plants are naturally acidic and stain other liquids with their juice, so it is in the minerals of the earth. Hence <term>alum<gloss>an astringent mineral salt</gloss></term> is found among the chief causes, which, when dissolved in waters, makes them acidic with an astringent quality. For this reason, the "white acids" are judged to be aluminous.

Vitriol follows alum, in which there is not only the virtue <note>essential power</note> of alum but also its body. Therefore, they are sometimes boiled out of common pyrite, and aluminous spirits are separated when "oil of vitriol" <note>sulfuric acid</note> is made; and that oily liquor of chalcanthum is so acidic that it sets the teeth greatly on edge and even surpasses vinegar. Hence, someone wrote that the *acidulae* are from vitriol when it is resolved into its first matter, since they think the solutions of art indicate those which occur in nature. These two minerals possess the greatest powers, and they include both their own veins and those to which they adhere and from which they are drawn—just as vitriol is primarily from iron and copper, so the metals of iron and copper, and all <term>verdigris<gloss>the green pigment/crust on copper</gloss></term> and other similar things are disposed, such as <term>chrysocolla<gloss>a copper mineral</gloss></term>, blue-pigment from verdigris, iron-ochre, inky ochre, copper-ochre, etc., which act in the same way. In lead also there is some power of sourness because of the chalcanthum, but it is obscured by an abounding sweetness. Sulfur claims the third place for itself, whose spirit made "by the bell" <note>original: "per campanam"; a method of distilling sulfur by burning it under a glass bell to collect the acid</note> differs little from the acidic oil of chalcanthum. Therefore, whether before it coagulates, or after it is resolved by the force of the weather, and while it is burned, it sends out acidic spirits; it can produce *acidulae*. There is indeed a great kinship by reason of this acidity between chalcanthum and sulfur; both are found in one and the same mineral, and even in one and the same metal; so that you might not undeservedly judge that chalcanthum is contained in sulfur. Yet when held back, its appearance differs greatly; the acidity of sulfur also comes with a more evident "fatness," which is more obscure in the oil of vitriol but is abstracted by art. What if that fatness belongs to the sulfur in both, the acidity to the alum, and the earthy stypticity <note>the quality of shrinking or constricting tissues</note> is specific to the vitriol? Nature, then, would have composed these three almost from common principles, assigning more thick earth to one, more air to the second, and more water and purer earth to the third. Some assert that nitre also contributes something to sourness, as in the "Puteolan acids" <note>springs near Pozzuoli, Italy</note>, which they judge to be "nitrolas." But however much nitre may be joined to them, the acidity does not principally come from here. Some add <term>rubrica<gloss>red ochre</gloss></term>, gypsum, and others: but these can provide acidity either by the protection of the aforementioned juices or by putrefaction. This taste is usually so fixed in waters that it does not exhale during boiling, distilling, or parching, etc.; this fact shows that it resides in the body or juice rather than the spirit, or as Jordanus says, in the "earthy substance."

## CHAPTER XXXVII.
### On the vinous taste.

**A** kin to the acidic is the "vinous" vapor, such as the spring that once existed near Paphlagonia, on the island of Andros, and in Naxos; in our times, however, the one at <term>Macros balbaci<gloss>Bad Schwalbach in Germany</gloss></term> is celebrated. Baccius <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), author of a famous work on thermal waters</note> is persuaded that this taste comes especially from alum, and then from iron, copper, and bitumen being present together, but in a milder form: just as at Koblenz <note>original: "Confluentiæ"</note> among the Belgians, the wine-like and astringent water is attributed mostly to alum. Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus <note>16th-century botanist and physician</note> established that the spring of Macros balbaci is a mixture of water, much iron mineral, <term>misy<gloss>a yellow mineral, likely a basic iron sulfate</gloss></term>, <term>jet<gloss>original: "gagate"; a hard, black coal-like mineral</gloss></term>, rock salt, and liquid amber, to which a little sulfur is added to temper the acidity...

# On the Assessment of Mineral Waters, Part 2.

**T**herefore, it produces a pleasant effect, such that a wine-like flavor and a musty <note>original: "musteus," referring to the scent of fresh grape juice or new wine</note> burp arise from it. He offers arguments of this sort for his judgment: Iron-rust <note>original: "Ferrugo"</note>, he says, is detected by the taste; from there, a crystalline salt floats upon the surface in a state of rest, along with a subtle oiliness, which the taste also detects at the beginning; it consists of a small amount of white amber and <term>mountain camphor<gloss>likely a solid bitumen or mineral resin</gloss></term> (<term>liquid ambergris<gloss>ambate liquido</gloss></term>). In other springs, a certain oily film is seen when the water is still, resembling a spider's web or plucked flax, of various colors such as green, lemon-yellow, or crimson, though it lacks taste and smell. The flavor often changes daily, especially when the sky is cloudy or rainy. Accretions <note>mineral deposits or crusts</note> change from a bright red to a pale yellow or whitish hue. The taste loses its charm when the midday sun's rays are cast into the spring, or if the water is carried about for too long. Those red or yellowish-red accretions are from iron ore. These things and others he mentions.

**I**t is consistent that here too the spirits of <term>chalcanthum<gloss>blue vitriol or copper sulfate</gloss></term> are not lacking, whether they emerge from iron ore or from ferruginous ochre. These, washed by much water, cling only to these parts and leave behind the ochre or rust, unless the ochre is mixed with <term>chalcitis<gloss>a copper-bearing mineral</gloss></term> or red <term>colcothar<gloss>iron oxide residue from vitriol distillation</gloss></term>, so that it turns from yellow to red. Furthermore, art <note>meaning alchemy or chemistry</note> teaches that there is a tempering or repression of acidity by sulfur, and that oiliness can be attributed to sulfur rather than to liquid amber, especially since such a film—lacking the odor and taste by which amber would perhaps reveal itself—rests upon the spirit of vitriol and sulfur after a long period of stillness. The astringency of iron is also found in vitriol, copper-rust <note>verdigris</note>, copper, and similar things, although **Mars and Venus** <note>Alchemical symbols for Iron and Copper, respectively</note> are mutually transmuted into one another; Venus may be made from Mars when the copper-bearing <term>chalcanthum</term> is increased from copper <term>pyrite<gloss>sulfide minerals, "fool's gold"</gloss></term>. The spirit of vitriol coagulates into an acid salt that is both astringent and simultaneously sharp and piercing. This spring should be categorized with rock salt <note>original: "sale gemmeo"</note>. It is necessary, however, for the <term>estuary<gloss>here meaning a subterranean heat source or volcanic vent</gloss></term> to be remote: by its dissolving and reverberating action, such things are made by <unclear>cleansing</unclear>. Such a sudden change argues that the spring originates or emerges not far from the turf, or at least that the earth is loose and cavernous. Stirring winds, or even moderately pushed air and fallen rainwater, scatter the spirits, drive them elsewhere, and dilute those that have coagulated. There is also another cause for this variety: namely, the inequality of digestion <note>the alchemical process of heating/maturation</note> in the subterranean heat-chamber or "vaporarium." From there, the erupting spirits, diverse in quantity and quality, can change the water. But enough regarding the wine-like flavor.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.
### On Sharp Flavors.

**A** sharp taste—one that is piercing, lancinating, blistering, and biting, as found in <term>strong waters<gloss>mineral acids like nitric acid</gloss></term>, ink, and similar substances—is indicated to come from corrosive minerals. These include efflorescing <term>melanteria<gloss>a natural iron sulfate</gloss></term>, sometimes from pyrite, sometimes from bituminous <term>cadmia<gloss>a zinc-rich ore or furnace deposit</gloss></term>, amber, and others. Furthermore, there is inky pyrite, the **flower of the Assos stone** <note>original: "Asii lapidis flos," a mineral efflorescence from the Troad region known for its caustic properties</note>, fossil <term>spodos<gloss>mineral ash or metallic oxide</gloss></term>, powdery nitre exuding from mountains, and the very sharp soot or ash of black bitumen, similar to <term>salmirhaga<gloss>an obscure alchemical mineral salt</gloss></term>, etc. To these, some add ochre, rust, sandarac <note>red arsenic sulfide</note>, orpiment <note>yellow arsenic sulfide</note>, the sharp blue of astringents, rock salt, the sharp juice produced from cadmia, the slightly sharp Armenian stone <note>azurite</note>, cinnabar, quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, etc. But regarding ochre and rust, I can hardly be persuaded unless chalcanthum is added. A mixture of alum, vitriol, and <term>halinitre<gloss>natural soda or saltpeter</gloss></term>, when dissolved and coagulated, almost attains the power of "strong water." Quicksilver might indeed corrode imperceptibly, but I doubt whether it can produce sharpness in the taste by itself. However, its solution in corrosive waters and its precipitate are sharp and biting unless washed away. They claim there is a sharp spring on the island of **Elba** <note>original: "Ilua"</note> originating from quicksilver and cinnabar, but it is more likely from pyrite.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.
### On Sour Flavors.

**A** sour <note>original: "acerbus," meaning harsh or tart like unripe fruit</note> taste is characteristic of immature plants. Therefore, when **Baccius** <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), author of a famous work on thermal baths</note> writes in Book 6, Chapter 12 of *On Baths* that it is caused by quicksilver, he seems to have spoken metaphorically, or perhaps used "sour" in place of "sharp," although neither is detected in quicksilver by itself.

## CHAPTER XL.
### On the Putrid and Pontic Tastes.

**A** putrid taste reveals itself by a rancid quality and its peculiar nature, bringing about loathing and nausea. The **Pontic** <note>A classical term for a harsh, astringent flavor, like that of certain berries or minerals</note> and astringent taste belongs primarily to vitriol, or certainly to inks. After that, it also belongs to alum, a certain salt, etc.; hence to copper, iron, copper-rust, etc., and even more so to minerals of that kind.

## CHAPTER XLI.
### On the Flavors of Specific Things.

**T**here are also other tastes of waters, such as the ferruginous <note>iron-like</note> flavor in the waters of **Tongeren** <note>original: "Tungri," a city in modern-day Belgium famous for its mineral springs</note>, or flavors of alum, copper-rust, ink, etc., such as are made if these things are diluted in water. In **Baiae** <note>The famous Roman resort city</note>, a spring is said to be "sacristy-like," with the flavor of **broth** <note>original: "Brodii"</note>.

## CHAPTER XLII.
### On Various Flavors in One.

**W**aters are found that exhibit various tastes, such as salty and bitter, or salty and oily, etc. The **Fountain of the Sun** is said to be sweet and cold at noon, but bitter and boiling at night, which happens according to reason. For when it is at rest, the salty and bitter parts settle; when it boils up, they are driven from the bottom. The heat and cold are partly due to the environment and partly to the subterranean heat source, coinciding with the winds and the cycle of the sun as it shines and recedes. Among the **Troglodytes** <note>A legendary or historical cave-dwelling people</note>, they say a fountain changes its taste three times a day, becoming bitter, salty, and sweet, which is the same cause as the preceding one. At **Stalbach** <note>original: "Sbalbaci"</note>, the spring is unstable in flavor, as said before; it results from diverse mixtures, whether you look at the breaths and vapors, or the waters, etc. Furthermore, what is told primarily of waters ought to be understood also of the clods of earth. Thus, let these be dissolved and diluted by pouring water over them, and let the parts be separated. Afterward, a judgment can be made regarding the taste, if one wishes to apply them to the tongue.

### CHAPTER XLIII.
#### On Sound.

**T**here are few signs derived from sound, and here we primarily observe whether the water proceeds, breaks forth, or makes noise in a quiet or silent manner. Afterward, we check if the caverns within "roar"; then, whether waters cooked by fires "hiss." Furthermore, we observe whether dry things—whether they are saturated with waters, mixed in and produced by them, or surrounding them—resound, clatter, hiss, or "thunder" when exposed to fire. Likewise, we note those things that sound when they are shaken, rubbed by the hands, ground with the teeth, or scraped with fingernails or a knife, etc. If whirlpools murmur when wind is let in, it is not so difficult to explain; when a stone is thrown in and a thundering is excited, the sluggish beginning of the vapors has been given an impulse. One must assume that many "clinging vapors" <note>original: "halitus," often referring to spirits or gaseous exhalations</note> lie beneath, although when movement occurs, the bottom of the craters often effervesce, just as if someone had poured <term>aqua fortis<gloss>nitric acid</gloss></term> onto tin, or even because an adverse quality has been introduced, producing the same effect seen when water or another moisture is poured onto glowing hot metals.

<margin>Why it happens because of a contrary quality and trapped spirits.</margin>
The <term>Caroline waters<gloss>the hot springs of Karlovy Vary (Carlsbad)</gloss></term> struggle through narrow openings with great noise and "hiccuping." In Hungary near Spiš <note>original: "Zepusium"</note>, a spring murmurs greatly within before it exits, which can be perceived if an ear is pressed to it. It eventually coagulates into stone; indeed, the spirits and the waters "wrestle" with the twists and turns of the earth. Sometimes sharp waters rushing into dry things (like vinegar onto chalk, lime, marble, etc.) or flowing over them excite a hissing sound, but even then, spirits are created by the <term>resolution<gloss>the process of dissolving or breaking down a substance</gloss></term>, just as in common baths, which they call "dry stoves" or <term>vaporaria<gloss>steam rooms</gloss></term>. <term>Atramentum<gloss>vitriol or metallic inks</gloss></term> and those things in which metals have been dissolved, or similar substances, hiss during boiling after the thinner parts have been dissipated. Fat and oily substances flow and fall more softly if they are poured into water or oil, whereas other liquids clatter more loudly. Salts are assessed by the same evidence, but the reasoning is not the same for all. Compact and thick salts crackle and leap in the fire, especially the man-made ones, in which the oiliness is very thin and the hidden spirits are most vehement; the <term>native<gloss>naturally occurring</gloss></term> salts are milder. <term>Agricola<gloss>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "Father of Mineralogy"</gloss></term> denies that true <term>nitre<gloss>likely referring to sodium carbonate or soda in this context</gloss></term> crackles and leaps in the fire, since the native kind only melts and swells up deeply, like Egyptian nitre and <term>chrysocolla<gloss>a gold-soldering mineral, often borax or malachite</gloss></term>. <term>Baccius<gloss>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), a physician who wrote extensively on thermal waters</gloss></term> says the same: Nitrous waters leave a thin, small, and transparent sediment which, when thrown into the fire, does not leap, etc. Man-made <term>saltpeter<gloss>potassium nitrate</gloss></term> is greatly agitated by fires, whereas the native kind is more modest. However, its substance catches flame. How it "thunders" if ignited in a narrow place and vomits spirits is well known from the <term>torments<gloss>artillery or cannons</gloss></term>. There is a fossil saltpeter in Calabria, in the village of Altofonte, which neither leaps nor crackles when thrown in the fire. There is a Sicilian salt from Foranga which is dissolved by fire and thickened by water and crackles; Pliny attributes something similar to the salt of Agrigento when jumping out of water. Cones of saltpeter, when held in the hand and feeling its heat, burst with a sound. Boiled, small, and thick salt only crackles in the fire; sea salts do not experience this, and they mostly consist in lakes by the heat of the sun. True <term>sal ammoniac<gloss>ammonium chloride</gloss></term> crackles and jumps in the fire, and if it is enclosed, it even breaks the vessels. Indian salt and man-made sal ammoniac do not crackle but are entirely consumed. There is a Tusculan flint which bursts when fire is applied, due to a "poverty of moisture," as Agricola says. If the moisture is salty or nitrous, it bursts with a great sound, like <term>spar<gloss>crystalline minerals like calcite or fluorspar</gloss></term> or metallic flint. Concerning the noise of "extinguished" things <note>substances cooled or quenched in liquid</note>, and the "thunder" of metals leaping to the roof from crucibles when cold water is added, that is another discourse. Some things are drenched in vinegar or aqua fortis, but from their hissing, only certain general facts are evident: that the thing is dry and spirited, like burnt deer horn, chalk, "crab stones" <note>calcium deposits from crayfish, used in pharmacy</note>, etc.; or that the aqua fortis finds something predisposed to it, like marble, metal, or the like. <term>Alum<gloss>a sulfate mineral</gloss></term> rises in bubbles over coals like nitre, and if it is roasted in a pot, it loses some of its substance. "Fat" vitriol also swells; the "lean" kind is merely dried during roasting. Things that sound when rubbed by the hands indicate a thicker, dry, rough, and earthy consistency. For fine flours do not sound. Dry and "lean" things ground by the teeth crackle, while oily and moist ones do not; such is the nature of salts and similar things.

### CHAPTER XLIV.
#### On Hot Waters.

<margin>The delirium of Paracelsus.</margin>
**I**n the assessment by touch, the primary qualities first mentioned are encountered, and in these, <term>recognition<gloss>original Greek: ἐπίγνωσις (epignosis)</gloss></term> involves a more abstract and difficult investigation. For we are not content with only the knowledge of <term>the fact that<gloss>original Greek: ὅτι (hoti)</gloss></term> it is so; we seek <term>the reason why<gloss>original Greek: τὸ διότι (to dioti)</gloss></term>, so that we may come closer to the mineral and its power. Always, however, the excesses of heat and cold are more wondrous; while we might easily provide a reason for moderate heat, we promptly seek the cause of cold from the water’s own nature and its "coagulated" components, unless the cause is manifest in the external air. Nor does dryness argue for anything other than a state brought about by heat or cold, with the moisture evaporated and consumed, while humidity argues the opposite—unless, however, something unusual occurs in these as well. But let us first dispute concerning heat and cold. Agricola teaches that certain metallic veins, when brought out into the air, grow hot, though they were cold inside—just as salts are found light in their mine but heavy outside. Thus, he says certain clods are endowed with mild heat inside, but when they come into the external air, the heat becomes heavier, so much so that they even burn with pain. It is easy to dismiss these "passions" as <term>antiperistasis<gloss>the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, like heat being compressed by cold</gloss></term>, where the spirits trapped inside are united, and thus increased and strengthened, they burst forth more violently. But it must also be considered whether something happens there such as occurs with lime, <insert>here, when burnt deer horn, pearls, crab stones, etc., are <term>calcined<gloss>heated to high temperatures to produce a powder</gloss></term> with spirit of vitriol. Likewise with iron filings, antimony, tin, etc. In a "gradatory" gourd <note>a chemical flask used for increasing the "grade" or strength of a substance</note>, heat is produced without any actual fire, </insert> when it is quenched, or in tin when drenched with aqua fortis. We think this happens when different spirits encounter one another and, by the friction produced, thin themselves out and turn into fiery spirits—a reasoning which also pleased the <term>Philosopher<gloss>usually Aristotle</gloss></term> when he discussed the heating of air. However, it is necessary that the thing be "spirited" and disposed to conceiving heat, such as those things from which "pills" <note>chemical pellets or masses</note> are made, which, when thrown into water, conceive fire or heat. But what heats waters to such a degree is more questioned. For men think that in dry things a "kindling" of sulfur, bitumen, or similar things can easily exist, but in waters, which are by their nature cold, this has no place. <term>Paracelsus<gloss>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous and controversial Swiss physician and alchemist</gloss></term>, as he is foolish and uncertain in many other things, so also here he writes ravingly that the Hot and Cold Springs were confused at the beginning of creation and later separated, as if both were thus primeval, or first...

Its primary nature is such, not from a coincidental condition, which he calls "fixed." Others he names "transmuted," which have acquired their quality from outside. Among these are first those which heat up from the limes of various minerals, and afterwards those which pass through unquenched estuaries <note>The author uses "estuaries" here in the classical sense of "aestuaria"—passages or vents where heat and vapors surge up from the earth.</note>. [This reasoning also pleases the learned because the waters run through the "fire-rooms" and "winding pipes" of the Great Mother <note>A poetic reference to the Earth's internal geothermal systems.</note>, or through vast mountains of embers from the world's fires—periodically renewed and sufficient for eternity] as seen in bituminous substances, which are not extinguished by water. Therefore, as they perpetually flow past, they heat the water. Furthermore, there are those that are mixed with certain mineral juices, just as <term>aqua fortis<gloss>nitric acid</gloss></term> is mixed with strong water, or <term>spirit of tartar<gloss>a solution of potassium tartrate</gloss></term> with strong water, or fresh <term>red oil of vitriol<gloss>sulfuric acid</gloss></term> <note>original: "oleum rubeum chalcanthi"</note> with simple water, and so on. Finally, heat arises when minerals are ignited by the air and the passing waters grow hot. We certainly cannot deny that such things sometimes occur in smaller, momentary artificial processes. For it is well known how much nitric acid heats up when poured over antimony and tin; it is also known that certain things piled up in the open air ferment and boil, such as veins of <term>atramentum<gloss>ferrous sulfate or "ink-stone"</gloss></term>, alum, and bismuth, especially if they are irrigated with water—just as manure, hay, and the like do. And when cold persists, it drives the heat to the interior, where if there is a principle of fermentation, digestion, or putrefaction, a great heat arises—who does not know this? Thus we admit this regarding the "manure" of the Chemists <note>A reference to the *balneum mariae* or gentle heat sources used in alchemy.</note> when irrigated with water. But if you survey each of these causes, you will find they are not sufficient for the eternal nature of thermal springs, nor for their abundance and safety. Nor do they correspond to the experiments noted in the use and handling of things, even though they might happen in small chemical furnaces and glass vessels. Who, I ask, could imagine such a great force of metals and nitric acid that could sustain the <term>Caroline springs<gloss>the famous hot springs of Karlovy Vary (Carlsbad)</gloss></term> forever? If you say that much cold water is added, you overturn your own experiment. For it does not happen that way if you pour cold water into a metallic solution, nor could that water be drunk because of its bitterness. The same is true for the spirit of vitriol, for lime, and the rest. Indeed, even things piled in heaps that ferment are eventually extinguished, even if you imagine the mountains to be as large as possible, unless you supply a living fuel of sulfur or bitumen. Therefore, <term>Paracelsus<gloss>a famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</gloss></term> will hardly maintain his second method, and even that is imperfect if he only proposed bitumen and things unquenched by waters. An eternal hearth and a perpetual Etna-like forge must be furnished with actual fires, where the fuel is bitumen, sulfur, naphtha, saltpeter, and veins of these things—various types where the cause does not fail, which, when consumed, would be restored and endure. Thus, while "wild" waters are carried through the vent itself, or are joined to flames and heat on their path, or run through channels near or above them for long enough to be heated, thermal springs exist, differing in degree according to the intensity or mildness of the heat; likewise by proximity, distance, delay, or swift progress. Whence it happens that some are lukewarm, some hot, others surging and boiling; some even, having retained their heat through a long journey through cold regions, come out cold again. That a volcanic vent must be established is argued not only by the aforementioned, but also by the evidence of the matter around Mount Etna, Enatia, Vesuvius, Puteoli, etc., where fiery breaths and flames emerge along with the water. In Puteoli, where the water is a "Bubble" <note>Referring to the *Acqua della Bolla*.</note>, <term>Baccius<gloss>Andrea Bacci, a famous Renaissance physician who wrote a definitive history of baths</gloss></term> says that if anyone digs a trench and pours in cold water, it quickly grows hot. In Italy, Spain, Calahorra, etc., steam-rooms are attached to the thermal baths. Therefore, the waters grow hot as if through "stoves," as they call them. If they are enclosed, they boil so much that they become intolerable. Therefore, heat-vents lie beneath.

Nor does the standard comparison from small things to large things have a place here, because of other qualities and unequal effects. It is not the case that if a little lime heats a little water, one must imagine an infinite amount of lime inside to heat an infinite amount of water, since that thing could not be long-lasting; lime itself, easily moistened by vapors, would gape open and no longer heat, unless there were a perennial fuel-source of actual fire. Lest the fires lack nourishment, Baccius thinks it is restored by the sea, which we do not deny; but it can also happen that different minerals and confluences succeed one another, so that what is once exhausted is repaired in the meantime while another region burns. This is especially true since sulfur, bitumen, and similar things contain within themselves a "seed" and eternal balsam unconsumed by fires, which, while it is transferred through soot, embers, and fatty breaths from one matter into another receptive one, fertilizes it again. Thus we certainly see oils preserved in distillations, which would be dissipated into the air by visible fires in the form of a fiery breath. For fire does not act upon nothing, but toward something like itself, which, when coagulated, again reflects the nature of the original, though in a nobler and purer essence, unless it is polluted again by seeded matter.

Besides the stated method of heating waters through vents, there is another, but not without a hearth. For we see from a boiling cauldron that the hot vapor is collected on the lid and likewise coagulates into hot water. Let there be placed, therefore, even under the earth, a great vessel with a hearth and a vaulted arch, the exit of which is some path where the flow can go: thus they will also be hot. Furthermore, it has been observed that some waters grow hot at night which are lukewarm during the day, either because <term>antiperistasis<gloss>the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat concentrating inward when the air turns cold</gloss></term> increases the heat within (for in these regions where this is observed, the nocturnal cold is intense), or because the breaths of the vent, even if hidden there, are restrained and make the waters boil. For they are frozen by the cold and stick sluggishly; when the sun returns and the air flows more subtly, they are dissipated and abandon the water, which therefore also cools more readily because the influx of cold water is continued. Does the sea drive in hot conditions and relax them alternately? Those rivers in the open air in torrid regions that grow hot while they are carried through burning sands and a parched atmosphere ignited by solar rays have an obvious cause, but one which confirms the existence of the subterranean vent. And that is enough regarding heat.

### CHAPTER XLV.
## On Cold Waters.

**S**ome waters are intensely cold, whether you explore them with the hand, tongue, teeth, etc., or breathe in their quality by drinking. <term>Athenaeus<gloss>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian</gloss></term>, citing <term>Ptolemy<gloss>Ptolemy VIII Physcon</gloss></term>, describes such a spring near Corinth as "water that generates cold" <note>original: "ψυχρογενέειν ὕδωρ"</note>, from which many do not drink because they seem to freeze themselves. Likewise, from <term>Homer<gloss>referring to the Iliad, describing the springs of Scamander</gloss></term>, he mentions others which in summer "flow like hail or cold snow, or ice from water" <note>original: "ῥέει εἴκελα χαλάζῃ ἢ χιόνι ψυχρῇ, ἢ ἐξ ὕδατος κρυστάλλῳ"</note>. The Melas and Cydnus rivers are also reported to be very cold; likewise the Aqua Virgo in Rome. The Bath of Agnano in the Pisan territory brings shivers to some because of its coldness. The water of Nansei in Viterbo has one of its veins that is scarcely tolerable because of the frost. The water of the Styx in Arcadia, by which they say Alexander the Great was killed, is said by <term>Pliny<gloss>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</gloss></term> to be [lethal] because of excessive cold...
