<meta>This page follows the discussion on the causes of heat in mineral waters. It shifts focus to the opposite phenomenon: extreme cold. It investigates why certain springs freeze while others remain liquid, and examines the inherent properties of substances like mercury and gypsum in relation to cold.</meta>

<page-num>168</page-num>
<header>Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book VI.</header>

Harmful cold is said by *Theophrastus* to be extremely frigid, although *Seneca* makes it like gypsum <note>Latin: "gypseam". Plaster-like or sulfate-rich.</note>, which causes stones to form and binds the internal organs. It is worthwhile to investigate what might be the cause of such great cold.

Indeed, philosophers establish, in the comparison of elements, that simple elemental water is the coldest of all, and the center of the world is cold for this reason: because it is <term>immobile<gloss>original Greek: "akinēton"</term>. However, since simple water is rarely found in its natural place due to the processes of generation, and we are now dealing with mineral water—which is not simple—we find enough support there to believe that water can, by its nature, be cooled to the highest degree. This potential is sometimes near at hand and sometimes more remote, though we do not rely on that cause alone. 

Furthermore, it has been observed that in all things regarding an excess of cold, there still remains some heat by which the substance does not freeze. (For when we speak of elements, one should not think of the exceeding heat found in a flame, nor the overmastering cold in ice that destroys the element’s nature). This internal heat is mostly dissipated by boiling, other heating, or even by putrefaction in mixed waters, so that any water that has been "cooked" becomes weaker and resists encroaching cold less than "uncooked" water. Thus, the Philosopher <note>Usually a reference to Aristotle.</note> said from experience that pre-heated or boiled water freezes faster than water that has not undergone such a process. 

We might also think such a thing can happen in subterranean vaults from boiling vapors which are later abandoned by their heat-giving principle; or when subtle spirits are mixed in, which resemble air in their nature and rarity. Because of this, just as very clear winter air—when moved from the north or east—most readily receives the extreme frost, so too when waters are thus disposed and a cause of cold is introduced, it is easy to see why they take on such intense frigidity. 

Cold is brought in by air or other surrounding matter, as is manifest from what happens outdoors. For air cooled in the winter months so affects the liquids it touches that they freeze. Even snow cannot do this everywhere, since plants live beneath thick snow without freezing, and worms are said to be born in the perpetual snows of the Alps. The power of the "airy spirit" is that great, more so than any other body. And although ice, packed snow, frozen stones, and intensely cooled metals also communicate a vehement cold to bodies moved near them, it is not so much through their thick substance as through the spirits and the changed air in their circuit. This air, being most subtle and highly changeable, is the most penetrating (excepting fiery spirits), allowing it to make powerful impressions, as is also testified by the dry northern winds. 

Thus appears the reason why outdoor air, changed by snows, ice, frost, and "frosty spirits," is cooled to the highest degree and induces rigor in things. But another cause must be considered: when it suffers a <term>privation<gloss>original Greek: "sterēsin"</gloss></term> of heat. They claim this happens in the middle region of the air, as evidenced by the cold breeze and air on the highest mountains, and the clouds, hail, and ice pellets existing in that same place. The greater this privation is, the more powerfully it excludes the action of heat, and thus intensifies the maximum cold in the air, which is naturally prone to freezing. For the privation of heat is not "naked," but comes with an opposing active force. The compliant nature of the air responds to it, just as the Philosopher felt: that air is like a matter capable of receiving various qualities. Experience testifies that in some places the air seems to "blaze," in others it shudders with cold, in others it is lukewarm, and in others it becomes varied. In southern regions, as much as it boils during the day, it becomes cold again at night, whereas in other places the extremes are not so violent. 

This reasoning is sometimes aided by <term>antiperistasis<gloss>The intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite; a "crowding out" effect.</gloss></term>. For when a warm body surrounds and encloses cold spirits in the middle, yet does not transform them, the quality turns back upon itself and increases, making the air colder by degrees. From nearly all these causes, we must seek the explanation of mineral cold that exists in excess. 

*Wernherus* <note>Georg Werner (1490–1556), a writer on the geography of Hungary.</note> writes that in a mountain near the castle of **Zips** <note>original: "Zepusio". Located in modern Slovakia.</note>, there is a spring in a cave whose water flows through the winter but freezes throughout the summer. Doubtless, when the earth is closed off by external cold, internal things ferment and produce vapors, and thus the cold spirits are tempered. But in summer, when a free exit is open for the warm exhalations, the cold ones are retained and grow strong through accumulation; therefore, the water freezes—not in the channel, but in the cave where the spirits flow together in a mass. Thus, if anyone enters that cave, they would find a shivering breeze within it. 

If you ask: why is the water of the **Styx** so cold? I would point to the cold spirits from the depths. For even around the roots of **Mount Vesuvius**, there are vents of extremely cold breath; you might not absurdly place such vents around the Styx as well, even if they are not manifest. However, I do not reject the judgment concerning gypsum. For this substance, when mixed with water elsewhere, also makes it quite cold—much unlike lime <note>original: "calcis"</note>, even though gypsum itself may be burnt. 

In **Scotland**, there is a lake which freezes in its middle part during winter due to the rigor of the external air to which the water accommodates itself, with no other cause standing in the way; but in another part, it does not freeze at all, because a "vapor-room" <note>A geothermal source.</note> situated there prevents the water from obeying the external element. Or perhaps the cold is weaker there and stronger here: in one place there is "rawness," and in the other, metallic veins or other minerals supplying warm exhalations. We see this same kind of difference even in metal-bearing mountains: in places where the veins stretch out, and where there are none. The presence of stabled flocks can also be seen to contribute something, for they sometimes change the temperature of locations.

<margin>The Spring of Sarnus.</margin>
The spring of the **Sarnus** river is extremely cold, and among the **Troglodytes** <note>Cave-dwellers mentioned in classical geography.</note>, there are very cold springs; in brooks and rivers, they grow milder over a long stretch. It is consistent that vapor flying high into chambers of very cold air, because of the surroundings, freezes into water, which afterwards flows out; or at least through such "refrigerators" over a long underground stretch it becomes cold. This happens not openly, but enclosed through deep valleys, where the air warmed by the sun's rays is not so easily caught, and the cold spirits which it breathes out are exhibited by the narrowness of the place. If this is not the cause (for we do not have an exact description of the site), it must be investigated further.

<margin>The River Gela</margin>
But there is also something more hidden, which pertains more to the contemplation of minerals in this place.

<margin>A Mercury Mine.</margin>
They say that **Mercury** <note>original: "Hydrargyri". Quicksilver.</note> mines are so cold that even the miners are harmed. Indeed, mercury itself, when held in the hand, is colder than other similar things, just like the whole genus of metals; and even when it has been heated, it cools down promptly. If you pour cold water over it in a glass and test the quality with your hand, you will find the mercury colder. You might say this happens due to the density of the substance, which makes a more powerful impression because more parts are always present here than in air. But the effects of **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti viui"</note>, as well as other metals, testify that there is also an inherent frigidity. For in use, it creates tremors, makes teeth fall out, and produces diseases that are sallow and altogether "cold." For that reason, it is also believed to flee from fire so much, and to "murmur," and to draw out inflammations...

It highlights how geographical features, subterranean vapors, and inherent mineral properties (like those of gypsum) can create freezing temperatures even in summer or near volcanoes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the causes of extreme cold in mineral waters, specifically examining the properties of mercury, lead, and various salts like niter (saltpeter). It engages critically with the theories of Galen, Seneca, and Andrea Bacci regarding why certain substances and environments produce intense chill.</meta>

<page-num>169</page-num>
<header>On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 2.</header>

...to restrain it, just as cinnabar <note>A bright red mineral, mercury sulfide, used in medicine to treat "heat" in the blood.</note> seems to ward off the burning of the blood and skin eruptions by that same power. Galen used to say that cold water, when stirred with a lead pestle in a lead vessel, becomes even colder by its own action. Indeed, lead is essentially a weakly coagulated <term>mercury<gloss>The author refers to the alchemical theory that metals are composed of mercury and sulfur; lead was thought to have a high proportion of "cold" mercury.</gloss></term>. It can therefore happen that wherever there is a vein of quicksilver, both the overlying air and the waters lingering there are cooled more intensely. Such cold does not merely indicate an excess of a simple quality, but also something interior and mercurial. For a changed thing follows the nature of that which changes it, and not infrequently, not only are mercurial spirits carried along with the waters, but even the physical body of the mercury which is collected from them. The same reasoning applies to lead. The remaining metals are more "well-cooked" <note>Refers to the alchemical process of "coction" or maturation of metals in the earth.</note>, and for that reason, they have departed further from mercurial coldness. Thus, they seem to contribute not so much to the coldness of waters as to their heat.

<margin>Niter (Saltpeter)</margin>
Furthermore, it is well known how niter <note>Latin: "halinitrum." Traditionally refers to potassium nitrate or sodium carbonate; here specifically its cooling and explosive properties.</note> not only crackles in the hand because of the opposing heat and mimics ice, but also cannot endure fires as long as its cold spirits have not exhaled. Therefore, in distillations, it breaks and shatters the vessels unless it has been prepared beforehand or is subdued by a slow heat.

<margin>Hence gunpowder is cold when chewed with the teeth.</margin>
It also cools the teeth considerably, and when it is mixed with waters, it renders them as chilly as ice. For this reason, those suffering from internal heat use it to mitigate their condition, and heavy drinkers use it to cool their wines. Nevertheless, it catches fire. It has clearly coagulated from diverse spirits—namely cold and hot ones—in which the action of the cold spirits surpasses the hot ones; yet the hot ones are of such a nature that they contain themselves in their own potential like sulfur until they are activated by something external. Therefore, when niter is mixed with waters, the cold spirits released everywhere quickly cool the whole, as the nature of water also agrees with this by itself. That the most powerful spirits are those which have coagulated while cold is attested not only by their swift operation in water, the human body, and other things, but also by their "battle" with fire, which does not cease until the opposing spirits are separated. Certainly, the wiser thinkers believe that thunder is excited in the clouds by such spirits—namely nitrous and sulfurous ones, both cold and hot. For this reason, niter also "thunders" if the arrangement of its environment is suitable. From this, it also excites vaporous fumes; by the aid of which some think they can procure "playful dews" and cold sprays of air, which are welcome to those suffering from fever. Therefore, if there are either nitrous spirits in the subterranean places, or if the niter itself is dissolved in the waters, it must be judged that they become intensely cold from this. In the Nile, however, which is nitrous, and in similar places, other mixtures and external causes stand in the way of this cooling action. From this, a more ready cause is also apparent as to why subterranean cellars are cold in summer, and at that time produce niter (or rather saltpeter); for just as cold spirits are poured out from the niter, so in turn they come to its constitution, and when mixed with sulfurous juices, they grow together like frost or an icy cone. Thus, niter is mostly made from the salt and sulfur of urine or similar liquids, conspiring with the cold spirits of the earth. From this also depends the wonderful nature of the **Salt of Orion** <note>A term likely referring to a specific alchemical salt or preparation, possibly ammonium chloride or a specific grade of saltpeter.</note> in coagulating not only oils but also mercury. This is the same reason why they prepare oil of sulfur by adding niter, and why distilled sublimates and other chemical products coagulate more successfully, etc. For it possesses cold, fixing spirits. And since saltpeter or its spirits are also in *aqua fortis* <note>Nitric acid.</note>, the effect of this too is coagulating; but these matters belong to another place. When Baccius <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), a famous Italian physician and author of a major work on baths and waters.</note> explains the reason for this cooling, he says it happens by sympathy and antipathy—why niter becomes fire when with fire, and with cold water, becomes the coldest water. But in truth, the cause lies in the diverse spirits, the cold ones of which do not remain in the fire, as experience shows. And he himself acknowledges this in a way when he establishes such an axiom: *Almost all things are endowed with contrary qualities;* and: *the same thing can perform different works; likewise, it does not have the same rationale in acting and suffering toward different things, etc.* If these are to be understood not by **mere agreement** <note>original Greek: "gymnē symbasei"</note> but by **inversion** <note>original Greek: "anastrophē"</note>, they require different spirits as the managers of the actions, just as the soul in the bodies of animals effects by itself the things that are of its duty, but with the help of the vessels of different spirits.

Furthermore, the same Baccius brings forward three general causes of coldness in waters and also in the air. The first is if the region or site lacks the sight of the Sun, whether below or above the earth; this does not hold true in the middle of the air, nor in subterranean caves, especially in winter. The second: if the veins are led from a deep origin, which agrees with the former, but it is not sufficient itself, since even hot springs come out from the deep. The third: if they are led among rocks and icy places, to which belongs if they are mixed with niter, ice, and other things. This is either maimed or not sufficiently explained. Thus, he is less than universal when he says: *The less subterranean caverns are penetrated by the access of the sun's rays, the colder they are;* which is at least not true in winter, to say nothing of the deep caves of mines. Nor is this entirely sound either, where he claims that cold water becomes less cold whatever further mixture it receives, which is refuted by the mixture of niter. It may be asked whether **vitriol** <note>Latin: "atramentum," literally "ink" or "blacking," usually referring to ferrous sulfate.</note> does not contribute something to coldness, as do other marbles; especially earthy ones, since earth is also counted among the cold things? They certainly say that the Stygian water <note>The River Styx, often described in ancient geography as a real, dangerously cold spring in Arcadia.</note> is vitriolic and extremely cold. We have said that this cold seems to be from cold vents. It cannot be from the vitriol, whose breath is warm and suffocating rather than cold; and even if we could concede that some nitrous spirits were present with it, they do not predominate. Therefore, its admission does not induce so much cold in the water. If that Stygian water abounded in gypsum, as Seneca maintains, the cold would correspond more. For marbles and similar things are colder and send out cold breaths. Therefore, in stone and marble vessels, waters do not heat up as quickly. That which Baccius says is marvelous: that when earth is mixed with cold waters, they become less cold because earth is drier and not as cold as water; certainly, by this argument, the question is not obstructed or proved. It ought to have become colder from the cold earth. Dryness limits humidity; it does not hinder coldness, as in the clear northern air. But there is another rationale for mixed earth, both when digestion or mutual fermentation arises in each by the access of heat. But so much for coldness.

### CHAPTER XLVI.
#### On the alternation of heat and cold.

There are certain springs endowed with both qualities by turns, just as in Cyrenaica the **Fountain of the Sun** boils at midnight and is frigid at noon; it behaves moderately in the intervening times; which very thing they also ascribe to the fountain of Ammon. The iron-bearing waters in the Lucullan lands near Naples are cold in summer and lukewarm in winter. But even at the same time...

The author disputes previous theories by Baccius, arguing that cold is caused by specific "spirits" within minerals rather than just a lack of sunlight or the presence of earth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how mineral properties—specifically coldness and heat—manifest in natural waters. It transitions from the chemical causes of cold (mercury and niter) to the physical observation of springs that vary in temperature, the tactile qualities of minerals, and the mysterious fluctuations of water levels synchronized with the moon or tides.</meta>

<page-num>170</page-num>
<header>Commentary on Alchemy, Part II. Book VI.</header>

Indeed, in different parts [of the same source], some waters are freezing, some hot, and others lukewarm. Wernherus <note>Georg Wernher (1497–1567), an author famous for describing the remarkable waters of Hungary.</note> writes of the "Purgatory" <note>A name given to specific hot springs near Buda, likely due to their intense heat.</note> above Buda on the banks of the Danube, where the entrance from the river is initially quite cold, then lukewarm, and the deeper you penetrate into it, the hotter it becomes. In its inner recess, it is so hot that it cannot be endured. The causes of these things are manifest, and we have spoken of them before; in these cases, it is clear that a tempering occurs from the Danube near the surface, while in the depths, the source-spring is pure and hot in its own right. Regarding Lake Avernus <note>A volcanic crater lake in Italy, legendary in antiquity as an entrance to the underworld.</note>, Baccius <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), a physician and author of a famous treatise on thermal springs.</note> reports that it is sometimes lukewarm and sometimes bubbling; and if a storm is imminent, it acts as an indicator, leaping up with burning bubbles. He thinks it has hidden caverns connected to the sea, being agitated and swollen by its waves. But one ought to add the "Plutonic vents" <note>Volcanic gas vents or fumaroles, named after Pluto, god of the underworld.</note>, which, when the sea flows in, are forced more densely into the water, as if a hot spirit were being thrust in by bellows; when the sea retreats, the spirit springs back and is dissipated. Thus, the waters later return to their lukewarm state by their own nature, seeing as they were being heated by the breath of an external fire while being cold in themselves.

Regarding the bath at the castle of Vinadum <note>Likely a reference to a site in Transylvania or Upper Hungary.</note>, they record that its waters are sometimes cold and sweet, sometimes lukewarm, and sometimes intensely hot and smelling of sulfur, with a certain oily film floating on the rawer waters of the stream that flows between them. It must be thought that different veins meet here: one cold and perennial, the other hot and recurring periodically, as in the Pfäfers Baths <note>original: "Thermis fabarinis," famous Swiss hot springs.</note>. Therefore, when the cold vein is alone, the water is cold; when the thermal waters rush in, it begins to grow lukewarm, until by their delay and the constancy of their flow, they become thoroughly hot. Different springheads of this kind even break out in the same vicinity at different intervals, as in the water of Naceus at Viterbo; and at Buda, where boiling and cold waters emerge so close together that, from the same spot, one bucket can be drawn hot and the other cold. And in Carlsbad <note>original: "Carolinis."</note>, from the middle of the Teplá river <note>original: "Topela."</note>, hot veins leap out. From what has been said, it is easy to explain other questions more clearly. Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, an ancient commentator.</note> asks why

<margin>Egyptian wines are cold.</margin>
Egyptian wines are cold? He answers that they seem so in comparison with other hotter wines. But why are they cold? Because, he says, the earth, due to the heat of the sun, keeps its entire interior cold, and thus provides colder juices to the wines. This is not an absurd response. However, it could be said that the vapors—or rather the exhalations—become cold both because of *antiperistasis* <note>An ancient physical theory where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite; here, the sun's surface heat drives the cold deeper into the earth.</note> and because of nitrous spirits. For Egypt abounds in niter <note>Saltpeter or native soda.</note>, which possesses such juices, or rather frosty concretions of spirits which, when later washed by waters, constitute the body of niter. Cold spirits of this kind enter the vines and mix with the juices; when pressed, these affect the teeth with cold, just like one who chews niter or gunpowder. Nor is this opinion foreign to Aristotle, when he writes about metals and similar things born from vapors before they solidify.

### CHAPTER XLVII.
### On other tactile qualities.

**T**o the sense of touch, moreover, belongs the judgment of oiliness, smoothness, roughness, sharpness, bite, corrosion, thinness, thickness, fineness, density, tenacity, friability, hardness, softness, solidity, sandiness, and the rest. If these do not define the certainty of a thing, they certainly support and confirm the other signs. The "bite" of a substance is primarily explored with the tongue. Therefore, this matter was also discussed regarding sharp tastes. If there is a suspicion of poison or serious harm to the tongue, the fingers or other parts of the body are used—but let nothing be done rashly with things we have not previously explored. These matters will also be discussed below under "effects." Oiliness, such as is found in oil, lye, and similar things, is explored with the fingers; it immediately betrays its fatness, which, if accompanied by a cleansing sensation, will also indicate a sharp or salty juice. Soft things can be compressed, such as <term>pompholyx<gloss>A zinc oxide deposit found in smelting furnaces.</gloss></term>, the "flower of the Assian stone" <note>A type of efflorescence or mineral growth found on stones from Assos.</note>, a certain black down of silver and mercury, etc.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.
### On the abundance of water.

**C**ertain things become known through multiple senses, which are called "common sensibles," among which the multitude or abundance and deficiency of water stand out; then motion and rest, weight and lightness, etc. An abundance of water that is equally potent [in mineral content] indicates an abundance of the mineral vein; if it is less effective, it indicates much "wild" water <note>Diluted or non-mineralized groundwater.</note> and little mineral. The same applies to the contents and what is extracted or separated. The waters of certain springs are sometimes copious and sometimes meager; they increase and decrease. If this happens due to humid or rainy weather, or the opening of a floodgate—and conversely due to dry, parched weather and the removal of inflow—it has an obvious cause. In others, it is more hidden. In Syracuse, they say the Cyane spring increases and decreases with the moon. There is a similar one in Hungary, according to Wernherus, which increases with the waxing moon, diminishes with the waning moon, and fails entirely when the moon is dark. The bath of Mount Falconis in Carnia is said to follow the rise and fall of the sea, as does one in Gades <note>Cadiz, Spain.</note> and another in Bordeaux, France. Wells on the banks of the Baetis <note>The Guadalquivir river.</note> in Spain decrease as the sea approaches and abound as it recedes. It is consistent that either spirits or waters are moved by the impulse and relaxation of the sea, which then drive the springs in the same way. It is easy to say that the source of a spring that increases with the sea is dilated or extended toward the sea at the bottom, or that the sea flows in. Thus, when it is repelled and cannot retreat at the bottom, it surges back to the top. When the sea recedes, it returns to its own pools. A spring that diminishes as the sea flows in has a more abstruse cause. It must suffer a flight, whether the spirits give way or the waters do.

In Hungary, on the bank of the Vág river, certain thermal baths follow the rise and fall of the river; they break out both near the channel and further away, wherever a pit is dug when the river flows high. Where the earth is loose, the exit is easily changed, and the springhead is repelled by a stronger inflow, just as rivers are by the sea. The Inopus on the island of Delos is said to increase and be deprived of water along with the Nile. Lake Vadimo <note>A lake near Bassanello (modern Vasanello), famous for floating islands.</note>, near the town of Bassanello, is sometimes suddenly agitated by an internal cause, and sometimes overflows, yet does not flow out for a year. It is manifest that cycles of spirits occur here, whether they merely force together scattered waters at the bottom, or bring new ones from elsewhere, or even increase the springhead by coagulating together. However, it can also happen that a more abundant water...

# Part 2. On the Assessment of Mineral Waters.

...an arrival occurs. For sometimes it overflows abundantly into the Tiber, and that spring will have its own periods, just like the Fabarinus spring <note>Likely referring to a spring in the Swiss Alps near Pfäfers (Fabaria), known for its seasonal flow.</note> in the Swiss Alps, which flows in summer and ceases in winter. Some say it begins in June and ends in August, or departs in October and returns in May, because the snows there melt later and freeze again sooner; when this happens, it is inevitable that not as much water is supplied to the internal reservoir <term>aestuarium</term><note>The author uses this term to describe an underground chamber or "estuary" where water and heat interact.</note> as would be sufficient to keep the spring flowing, since the liquid does not come from the bottom but sinks down from the top. Therefore, during the time the flow ceases, the reservoir sustains itself only on its own "food" <note>Referring to the accumulated mineral matter and moisture.</note>. From this, it also follows that the water is more potent if it flows out when more juices have been dissolved in the meantime, and more fragments and dross have been collected, and the surrounding parts are imbued with a stronger tincture. Paracelsus <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541).</note> is laughable when he says that such a nature is implanted in the spring so that it appears and withdraws in turn, as if in the manner of fruits on trees, and so on.

In Dodona <note>An ancient oracle site in Greece.</note>, the Fountain of Jove increases and decreases three times a day. In Cantabria <note>A region in northern Spain.</note>, three springs dry up every twelve hours. The lake at Cerknica <note>The intermittent Lake Cerknica in modern-day Slovenia.</note> in Carniola overflows in autumn and floods the region, but at the beginning of summer, it hides itself again and leaves a place for sowing and pastures, in which fish had been stabled shortly before. Indeed, all things have their appointed times, nor can the immediate causes always be found exactly. One might say of the lake that its increases come not only from more humid air, but also from a confluence of veins that were absorbed by the Sun during summer days, so that it follows the six-month periods of the Sun, which is the most powerful governor of that whole tract, which responds with its entire disposition. Something similar seems to happen to the Cantabrian springs. For there is an analogy between night and winter, and day and summer, especially if the astronomical division is made in the middle. Regarding the fountain of Dodona <unclear>in 1/2</unclear>: unless perhaps it follows the force of the sea's reciprocating tide, or a silent influx.

## CHAPTER XLIX.

### On the Motion of Waters.

The **motion** of waters results from a downward slope, or when the narrowness of the paths forces it out as a following weight presses and urges it forward; or if they are carried through a wide space, it is nothing besides their accustomed gravity and divisibility, as is also proven in quicksilver. But if it happens beyond the usual custom of waters, a peculiar cause lies beneath. "Furious" water leaps up with force in Elbogen <note>Loket in the modern Czech Republic.</note>, as do the spring of Soracte, the Caroline Baths <note>Karlovy Vary (Carlsbad) in the Czech Republic.</note>, and others; an accompanying spirit <note>Gas or vapor.</note> drives them out through narrow passages, and this is proven both by the vapors breaking out at the same time and by the gasping crash and bubbles. In some places, a spring of this kind, when confined by upright pipes and forced upward, rises without a cover; but if a roof is placed over it, it grows calm, or is only moderately lifted, so that it is believed it will cease. To be sure, a free spirit lifts the waters with itself; but when the abundance of its way forward is taken away, it is depressed and lays the waters flat along with itself. That abundance cannot come out of straight channels as it does from open ones; therefore, being moderately raised, it also carries up a moderate amount of water. Some are not elevated high but only move in a circle where the spirits are scanter and go more gently, or emit bubbles where they are stronger. Some boil over reservoirs in which the heat itself is the cause of motion, while it produces vapors through continuous dissolution, not otherwise than if water were being cooked down in a kettle or a cauldron. Where flames and sulfurous vapors break out together, and immense crashes are joined with them, it is no wonder that such a motion occurs as happens in cannons and in the clouds when it thunders, and sometimes even cataracts of water are torn away. It was said above, however, that the principles of these things are hot and cold spirits struggling in a flame, primarily from the fuel of sulfur and saltpeter <term>sal nitri</term>, although bitumen, naphtha, and the like can also stand in for sulfur. For Baccius <note>Andrea Bacci, a 16th-century physician.</note> relates that such a thing happened in Italy: namely, that a spring of naphtha, having caught fire, leaped high with a very great sound, at the same time ejecting stones, earth, and waves in the manner of an Etnean fire <note>A volcanic eruption, like Mount Etna.</note>; I remember reading that this also happened somewhere in Germany. Likewise, in place of saltpeter, there can be ammonium salt, salt of urine, and the like. The same thing happens when spirited things are poured onto corroding and dissolving waters, such as vinegar onto a star-stone <note>Likely a fossilized coral or "astroites" used in early chemistry.</note> or chalk, etc., or nitric acid <term>aqua fortis</term> on antimony <term>stibio</term>; if this is done in a narrow vessel, the fumes break out impetuously, the glass leaps up, and finally it is broken and flies apart. When mercury <term>hydrargyrum</term> is sometimes precipitated while enclosed in hermetically sealed glass, it broke the glass into tiny parts with a vast boom over the coals, even though it was well-smeared with clay and dried. But even in earthen pots, it seeks an exit with a hissing sound. Some waters imitate the purging of the sea, which happens at every new moon, or the segregation of juices while they effervesce, as can be seen in grape-must, beer, and others. A spring of the Rhodians in the Chersonese moves itself on the New Year and rejects its purgings. Near the Rhine, not far from Andernach (says Wernherus), a health-giving spring carrying salt, sulfur, and iron tolerates nothing impure, no dust, nor any filth thrown into it, but having bubbled up, it suddenly belches it out. So some springs are also "stormy," into which if small stones are thrown, they pour out a sort of tempest of mists or vapors. But if such motion is not from the wind or the movement of external air, nor from the natural slope of the water, nor from vapors, nor from an underground reservoir of simple fire or heat, nor from the Sun’s heat, nor from a moved or shaken vessel (as in earthquakes), nor likewise from the approach or retreat of the sea or a river, nor from animals contained within, nor from winds entering caverns, but from mineral spirits—such as those that come out of metallic wells or mine shafts, and such as are poured out from the burning of minerals—the nature of that spirit must be diligently investigated. It can happen that near metal mines a small spring is agitated by fumes breaking out everywhere while the miners break and burst solid stones by lighting fires; and then the ore is immediately exposed. At other times, where the mineral juices and the beginnings of metals are still in "digestion," or where putrefaction and fermentation occur, such tempests likewise come forth. It is also the case when vitriol <term>atramenti</term> mines pour out dizzying spirits, which Galen <note>The famous Greek physician of the 2nd century AD.</note> also experienced in Cyprus; and when bitumen, sulfur, and others smoke, regarding which their own signs should be consulted. Indeed, one must not only look at the impetus of nature, but also contemplate what happens in motion during cooking in artificial pots, during distillation, and other operations. A liquid will be viscous if it rises like honey, turpentine, or the like, and if its bubbles break slowly. Oily waters are those that remain tranquil after the watery spirits have been dissipated. To common waters...

# Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book VI.
<meta>catchword: water</meta>

...those which effervesce and are boiled down in their manner will yield. Motion is also observed in hard substances that have been liquified and melted. Metals melted and heated in crucibles, as soon as a cold drop falls in at the wrong time, are thrown out with a crash <note>A warning about the dangers of steam explosions in metallurgy.</note>. At other times, when they are near purity, they tremble, as it were, with a mist riding over them. Glass and other melted substances have their own sign in this way. Dry dross <term>recrementa</term> and extracted materials can also be examined with dissolving waters, so that we may learn how they move. They are also burned in spoons or plates, and we notice whether they emit blisters or simply flow like butter; thus native soda <term>nitrum</term> <note>In this period, "nitrum" could refer to natron (sodium carbonate) or saltpeter.</note> swells up entirely when inflated. Alum placed on burning coals inflates with bubbles. Fatty vitriol <term>vitriolum</term> <note>A term for metal sulfates, like iron or copper sulfate.</note> likewise swells; lean vitriol flows and eventually dries out. The manner in which sulfur, bitumen, and similar substances flow is well known. We can also conjecture something from the manner of the pouring out. There is also something to be found in the smoke of burnt things. Smoke is heavy when it rises slowly and is reflected back when the flame is just right (for one must not exceed the measure; for excessive force corrupts nature). Mercurial spirits also settle; for instance, if you burn cinnabar <note>Mercury sulfide, a bright red ore.</note> in an iron ladle, it shows a purple flame, and white smoke is reflected back, forming a white mercurial circle. The remainder that rises, if you bring a polished plate near, adheres both below and sits on the upper part. Arsenical, sulfurous, and antimonial smoke spread out widely and follow the flow of the air. Antimonial smoke <term>stibiatus</term> adheres to iron like white down. The smoke that ascends from calamine <term>cadmia</term> <note>Zinc ore.</note>, pyrite, copper, etc., makes a kind of bubble where it congeals: hence the name *pompholyx* <note>original: "pompholygi"; from the Greek for "bubble," referring to zinc oxide residue.</note>. When salt is dried in mud exposed to the sun, it turns on its side, as it were, and stands out. Alum, saltpeter, and vitriol <term>chalcanthum</term> collect themselves into crystals. Chalk, gypsum, and similar things, sprinkled into a leek-green decoction, disturb it so much that it overflows. Daily experience will teach the rest. However, what the craftsmen advise regarding the use of the magnet is noteworthy. For if mud or gravel, or anything else, has iron filings, they follow the lead of the magnet. Thus, pure iron is collected from smoothed ore in this way. In amber, jet, and bitumen, there is no such certainty, since they pull in filth indiscriminately. Some things are sublimated all the way to the surface; others are raised even higher, which also seems to pertain to the method, just as spirits are separated by distillation, circulation, subsidence, and so on.

### CHAPTER L.
## On the unity and plurality of springs.

**One** spring is of one judgment. If there are several bubbling outlets in one stretch with a small interval, if they indeed agree in other matters, they will be from one head; if not, from different ones, where an essential disagreement is observed. For being changed by accidental circumstances does not detract from the judgment of the substance—for instance, if the channel, divided into veins, produces one higher, another lower, one in a dry place, another in the middle of a stream, and so on. It can also happen that part of the same spring comes out cold and part hot, because they were altered by being separated further apart on their path. So also in a stretch, new minerals can be acquired and new filings rolled forward; here one must observe whether the principal elements agree. That which is carried through pits <term>puttia</term> <note>Likely referring to man-made shafts or specific mineral deposits.</note> can lose its nature and spirits, while the other remains intact. Therefore, nothing absurd happens even if things flowing from one principle are clearly changed, but then the judgment is as if for different ones. If very different springs appear in the same vicinity, it is consistent that they come together from different regions. But these things are manifest.

### CHAPTER LI.
## On the distance of parts.

**An argument** is also taken from the distance and interval of parts in one water, which indeed happens from motion due to heaviness and lightness. For instance, if in one portion there is alum and vitriol <term>atramentum</term> <note>Literally "ink," but used here for black vitriol.</note>, the latter is distinguished from the former by the bottom; so in saltpeter, the saltiness in the decoction adheres to the bottom: the saltpeter stays more familiar to the waters. Salty and earthy things sink; sweet and airy things mostly float. However, the nature of some is peculiar, such as oil of sulfur, which is made by boiling in spirit of turpentine; some of its parts lie on the bottom, some float, and so it is with certain vegetable substances. As also in the smelting of metallic veins, there is at the bottom of the crucible what is called slag <term>diphriges</term> <note>A byproduct of copper smelting.</note>, upon which the metal sits, and upon this the stone, upon which again the dross. So it can also happen in mineral springs. It is a wonder that Aristotle asks why the sea is saltier at the surface, but fresher below, since it is certain that salt sinks unless it is driven out by force. And in the Northern Sea, they are forced to seek saltiness from the bottom with sampling devices <term>clepsydris</term> <note>original: "clepſydris"; likely a siphon or vessel for deep-water sampling rather than a clock.</note> to make salts, because the highest parts, being fresh, do not yield salt. One must think that the Philosopher [Aristotle] is asking about the condition of a specific place, such as where rivers enter near the bottom, which you might believe happens around the depths of the Black Sea <term>Ponti</term>.

### CHAPTER LII.
## On Weight.

**Joined** to these is the judgment of weight and lightness, if you observe parts seeking different places when at rest. If you use a scale, mineral water is usually tested against common fresh water, or even against another mineral water, or a part of it. Metallic waters, to be sure, because they are thick and earthy, are heavier; thus subtle, thin, and spirituous waters are light: those having corporeal juices are heavy. The proportion for fatty substances is not the same everywhere. So it is with the contents. Physicians also gather something about healthiness and harm from weight and lightness, which is nevertheless obscure. For it is not immediately the case that whatever is light is healthy. It is in the *Aphorisms* [of Hippocrates] that water which heats up and cools down quickly is the lightest, because it is indeed very thin and spirituous, since we see that iron and other corporeal things suffer both more slowly. Galen, however, does not understand this regarding weight, contrary to Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian (c. 2nd century AD).</note>, who says, among...

# On the judgment of mineral waters, part 2.

<margin>So Pliny, book 31, chapter 1: "Whatever the scale indicates regarding healthfulness is often a frustrated effort; for it is extremely rare for one water to be found lighter than another." Pliny says water should be as similar as possible to air.</margin>
The marks of the best water are <note>original Greek: ἂν δὴ καὶ κατὰ σταθμὸν ὅτι κοῦφον, ὃν οὕτω γαιῶδες ἔχει</note> "if it is indeed light according to the scale, because it contains little earthy material"; and so also regarding the waters of Troezen and Pangaea, <note>original Greek: τ’ ἄλλα τῶν ὑδάτων (inquit) ᾧ σωματώδη δεῖ δὲ ἔχει ὥσπερ κὶ βάψει</note> "the rest of the waters (he says) which are thick should be treated as if for dyeing." <note>This likely refers to the density or "body" of the water affecting its utility in industrial processes.</note> <note>The Greek following this in the OCR is fragmented, referring to metallic properties in winter and the capacity of vessels.</note> Agricola says: "The lighter the water, the healthier it is, provided that it is not light due to harmful spirits." <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), a foundational figure in mineralogy and metallurgy.</note> But Athenaeus notes what else is necessary here: namely, that we should bring the same water back to the scale at different times, to see if it is heavier in winter than in summer. This is reasonable because in summer it is more "cooked" <note>refined by natural heat</note>, more subtle, and better separated from its dregs. But one must take care that what happens in a decoction does not occur—namely, that due to summer squalor and drought, the thinner part is consumed, leaving only a thick residue, as when we force brine or inky lye by boiling. The same rule applies to art as to nature. Therefore, even if no such thing occurs in water left to itself, it does occur in cooked or distilled water. For when a part has exhaled or been drawn off, we examine the weight of both, so that we may know if it promises anything nutritious, and how much mineral is in how much water. The dry parts are also weighed, whether they are shavings, extracts, or otherwise joined, whenever we think the effort is worthwhile.

## CHAPTER LIII.
## On Duration and Corruption.

**After this**, one must observe the integrity of both the water and the remaining substances in terms of their total substance; namely, whether it is durable, or whether it putrefies and is easily corrupted without evident violence. Both pure coagulated spirits last a long time without decay—as we see in <term>aquas fortis</term> <note>Strong mineral acids, usually nitric acid.</note>, spirit of wine, oils, and similar essences—as do juices and bodies that are not easily overcome by the heat of the surroundings. These do not fail because they possess a firm structure and do not release their "balsam" <note>A term for the life-preserving essence or resinous quality of a substance.</note> and spiritual salt. They are more active than their surroundings, or are protected from external heat by the barrier of cold or other things immune to rot—as we see in sugar, alum, vitriol, amber, and so on. Enclosed things are more durable, just as things submerged and preserved in perpetually cold waters, brine, bitumen, or airy and fiery oils. If the water flows out pure but putrefies after a little rest, especially after exposure to the sun or light boiling, mineral spirits contained it, and they were volatile. The remaining body is of no consequence; it proves, since it putrefies so readily and acquires a stench, that it carried some contagion with it, and that the spirits were not so much a part of the mixture as they were companions. Such waters usually flow through marshes and other rotting places, joining with mineral qualities along the way. It would seem more advisable in practice to establish a separation, so that the spirits might be transferred into a more noble subject through circulations or distillations, if they cannot be used in their coagulated state alone. If the water stinks immediately upon exiting, but loses the stench through distillation, boiling, or other means, and then lasts a long time, it is a sign that more corporeal spirits or juices are present, such as salty, inky, or aluminous ones. For this reason, we also contemplate the course of the stream and the things joined to the spring, to see if any traces of rot present themselves near or far. However, not every stench proves putrefaction, as it is innate to some things, like sulfur, bitumen, <term>sory</term> <note>A mineral substance related to vitriol or copper ore.</note>, etc. We can admit this: wherever foul-smelling mud is mixed with minerals, the bitumen, sulfur, or ink-stone has not rotted, but other things mixed with them have, because fermentation was caused by the heat of these minerals acting as the environment. This is the same reason why so much rotting slime is found in salt-works. For pure juices, according to the analogy of joined things, resist putrefaction if they are perfect. If they are impure—surpassed by other rotting things—or if they are in their first stage of generation, they admit rot, just as they cannot ward it off if they are weaker in strength and smaller in quantity, or not joined perfectly at the smallest level. It is possible that both the water and its contents or surroundings receive the beginning of rot from the outside, which the diligent investigator will carefully look down upon. Those waters that do not putrefy throughout their entire course carry strong and closely mixed tinctures. Otherwise, the juice is usually stripped away in thirsty sands, and the remainder putrefies during a longer run—unless the entire region is immune to such a passion, as when the flowing waters of the Albula <note>Likely referring to the sulfurous Acque Albule near Tivoli, Italy.</note> create a marble bed for themselves, where putrefaction is prevented by the constant sliding away of new material. Likewise, when hot springs are led through channels over a great distance without putrefying, or where the force of the flow does not allow it to settle. For the act of putrefaction requires rest. If putrefaction does not occur by nature, it must be attempted by art; for instance, if the spirits are drawn off and the remaining body is placed in warm dung. This operation also aids in separation. For putrefaction returns things to their elements.

## CHAPTER LIV.
## On Violent Corruptions.

**Furthermore**, violent corruptions by fire must also be tested. It is well known that fatty and airy things are flammable. Common waters do not catch fire, nor do sandstones, flints, or pure metals. But spirits, such as those of wine or beer <term>Zythi</term>, and those similar to them—which they call "burning waters" or flammable waters—can be prepared; they can also be fashioned from flowers and other things that fill the head with their scent. Next are certain oils, either alone, like <term>naphtha</term>, or with a body. If indeed they are true oils and not just mineral liquors or "oilinesses" which are called oils by similarity. Additionally, resins and anything similar—sometimes found with wood, straw, and small stony concretions (as in <term>cadmia</term> <note>Zinc ore or cobalt.</note>, coal <term>lithanthrace</term>, slate-stone <term>lapide fissili</term>, etc.)—are known by experience to catch fire. Therefore, when they catch flame upon the application of fiery heat, it is proof that either the waters or other such things are present, or are mixed with them. A water near a village named after a valley, says Baccius <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), author of *De thermis*.</note>, between Bologna and Florence, is cold but catches fire, because it carries sulfur or a mixture of liquid bitumen. Pliny and Strabo report that the Aeolian islands burned along with the sea for several days. And the sea around Sicily has sometimes been set on fire, on account of the joined bituminous and sulfurous fatness, which is within it...

## CHAPTER LV.
### On the effect of minerals around springs.

<margin>
The foolish judgment of Paracelsus regarding the effect.
</margin>
We must often struggle with the foolishness and vanities of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), a revolutionary and controversial physician who championed the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine</note>. For his disciples cannot believe that their master went astray; even among the learned, there are those who, although they acknowledge he erred in some places, nevertheless stubbornly follow him in natural matters. They wish for that "chaos of madness"—which contains nothing good except what he took from the wise ancients, or what he instituted in imitation of them by a certain analogy and blind impulse, or perhaps stumbled upon by luck—to be handled with a soft sponge and a light touch, even though it is essentially correct but corrupted by foolish explanations. Having prioritized the truth, we cannot indulge his fury to such an extent, especially since he himself spared no other author. Therefore, it is necessary that his inept opinion not be concealed in this place. 

He commands that one should take the single and only sign of the mixture of mineral waters from their effect on diseases. Just as we judge a tree by its fruit, he believes like is cured by like, according to substance, and that diseases correspond to the variety and nature of the minerals. Thus, he claims that water has an arsenical mixture if it cures an arsenical disease, or an "atramentous" <note>inky or vitriolic</note> mixture if it cures a vitriolic disease, and so on. But he builds worse conclusions on a very poor foundation. He attributes almost every kind of disease to "tartar" <note>original: <term>Tartarum</term>. In Paracelsian medicine, "tartar" refers to stony or gravel-like deposits in the body, such as kidney stones or gouty joints, which he believed were analogous to the deposits in wine casks</note>. Yet, tartar is not found in minerals except by way of metaphor. Therefore, his reasoning falters here. 

Furthermore, even if the most simple substances were evident in that way, how could one distinguish the infinite gradations of mixtures? Many substances produce the same effect. An essence of glassy antimony <note>original: <term>stibium</term>, often referring to antimony ore</note> purges, but so do mercury <note>original: <term>hydrargyrus</term></note>, iron, copper, and the like. Imagine there is a certain generic nature in each by which this happens; but who will recognize the individual movements, since those proceed not only from the acting agent, but are made very diverse by the disposition of the patient? By what wit will he distinguish agents acting accidentally in individuals from those acting <term>by themselves</term> <note>original Greek: <term>αὐτῷ</term></note>? Let it be that gold is what comforts the heart, and silver what comforts the brain. If something comes from the "mercury of gold" that works against the "Venereal disease" <note>syphilis</note>, or if some relief is brought by the mercury of Venus <note>copper-based medicine</note>, it is not necessary that gold was in it, or that there is a gold-bearing mineral in the water. Relief could have been brought by an accident, or by the juice of a heart-comforting herb. If you say that everything that helps the heart is "golden," whether sought from heaven, earth, words, or herbs, you may indeed be allowed to rave and <term>speculate wildly</term> <note>original Greek: <term>μετεωρίζειν</term>, literally to soar into the atmosphere or talk vaguely</note>, but you will never arrive at the certainty of specific and distinct recognition. 

And why should nature be observed only in diseases? Why not also in health? Why not in the effects on other things which are not diseased, such as wood, stones, metals, and the like? And if in the destruction of diseases, why not also in their creation? Why not in death and life?

<margin>
The delirium of Graman in a famous booklet.
</margin>
A certain man <note>referring to Johannes Graman, a vocal supporter of Paracelsus</note> recently babbled that nature revealed itself only through signs of assistance. But he did not notice that thorns exist to be avoided for their sharpness and harm. Nature should not be considered such an unfair parent that she showed only the beneficial things while hiding the harmful ones; for the sake of which she granted tastes and smells even to the beasts. But setting aside these fools, let us freely admit with Jordanus <note>likely Thomas Jordan, a 16th-century physician who wrote on thermal waters</note> that there cannot be much certainty from effects, because nature is so luxurious in her causes and has <term>mixtures</term> <note>original: <term>crases</term>, from Greek <term>κράσεις</term></note> and other things so manifold that it belongs to God alone to look into them and discern them knowingly. Mercury purges, but it can be prepared so that it does not have that effect, as in cinnabar. The glass of antimony, with its "flowers," moves the whole body violently, yet whole antimony holds back, and the glass itself can be so softened by art that it does not evacuate even a little. A mercury made from copper is said to be useful for Venereal cases; yet how many people have used it rashly? If there is no indication even when it is certain what was used, what will it be when the substance itself is in doubt?

Baccius <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), author of a famous treatise on baths and mineral waters</note> advises that such experiments should be conducted in comparison to the temperament of our body: what power of acting they have, and whether they are hot or cold, moist or dry in respect to it. This is medical enough. But the physicist seeks something more—to hunt for the entire nature of the thing. Once this is known, it becomes clear how it relates to the human body. We command that experiments be made from all sides, and to judge from many if a few are not sufficient. Therefore, the consultation on effects is tied to what was said above, so that together they may achieve what they cannot separately. 

There will be two heads to this: one concerning various experiments in a natural state, the other concerning aids in those affected by disease. In the former, some things are outside the human being, and some touch the body in food, drink, baths, etc. We ask the inhabitants first whether the waters or their minerals are put to any use, or if they are neglected. If there is a use, what is it? In washing clothes, in dyeing wool and linens, in the soaking of horns, hides, and the like; in the quenching of iron tools, in making cements, in irrigating gardens, in watering livestock, in preparing human food and drink—and what each thing suffers as a result. Many such questions can be asked, but let us be content for now with what has been said.

## CHAPTER LVI.
### On the effects of waters in cleaning.

Horus asks in Macrobius <note>referring to the *Saturnalia* by Macrobius, a 5th-century Roman author</note> why the fresh water of rivers is better for cleaning clothes than sea water; and why Homer depicts Nausicaa, the daughter of Alcinous, washing linens not in the sea, but in the river. It seemed that the density or thickness of the sea stood in the way, while the thinness of fresh water was more suited for penetration and scouring, according to the opinion of Disarius, who cites Aristotle. But Eustachius corrects this opinion, blaming the oiliness of the sea and setting aside its density and saltiness. According to his judgment, if a mineral wa-

It also introduces the practical ways mineral waters are used in daily life and industry, such as dyeing and cleaning.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the physical properties of mineral waters, specifically their cleansing, corrosive, dyeing, and petrifying qualities, following the previous discussion on the presence of fire and minerals in springs.</meta>

...[if the] mineral [water] were suitable for washing clothes, it would have to be devoid of fat or grease. **Bacci** <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), an Italian physician and author of a definitive work on thermal waters</note> followed this opinion, saying that such water prevents the washing of clothes—a statement we gladly accept, provided he is speaking of pure mineral water. However, the "greasiness" of the sea is not to be so entirely slandered; rather, the opinion must be refined rather than simply opposed. Our local women first soak stained garments in a thick lye, then smear them thoroughly with fatty soap; after that, they rinse them several times in hot water, and finally in pure cold water. It is believable that **Nausicaa** <note>In Homer’s Odyssey, Princess Nausicaa goes to the shore to wash the royal laundry</note> first soaked the clothes in sea water, as it were, and dissolved the grime, scouring it away with the sea's nitrous saltiness. But afterward, she would have rinsed them in pure fresh water, because sea waters are unfit not for cleaning, but for *rinsing away* the cleaned-off grime. This is because dissolved greasy residues, unless rinsed out, will stick; and if they are allowed to settle and harden again, they increase the stains and impurity rather than removing them. If, however, the dissolved mud is washed away with pure fresh water—into which it easily recedes without leaving a spray—the linens become clean. This is because we see even salts dissolve in fresh water, though they do not dissolve in thick lyes, much like alum. Though the common experience of washerwomen proves this opinion, let us also hear the Philosophers. The author of *On Marvelous Things* writes that the water of Lake **Ascania** <note>A lake in Bithynia (modern Turkey) famed in antiquity for its naturally soapy water</note> is so nitrous that cloaks held in it seem to require no other cleaning. **Aristotle** the Philosopher testifies to the same regarding the salty marsh of Palestine. In his *Problems* (40, section 23), it is said that bitter things which become sticky are able to cleanse; they cleanse through their stickiness, not their bitterness, since mucous-like substances have a scouring power. They scour with a fatty stickiness and wash with a sweet moisture. 

Even in Holy Scripture, nitre <note>Here referring to natron, a natural soda used as soap in the ancient world</note> is famous for such uses, as is the "fuller’s earth" called Cimolian earth <note>A type of clay from the island of Kimolos used to clean and thicken cloth</note>. It is fatty and sharp, and some people add lye to it; they wash the cloths first, then treat them with sulfur vapor, and finally wash them again—or "descale" them—with that same Cimolian earth so that the tallow leaves the clothes. Indeed, pomades, soaps, and similar things are not prepared without grease. It is therefore established that even in the sea, nitrous greasiness is not useless for scouring clothes. In such cases, one should blame the earthy and muddy consistency rather than the salt if it is unfit for washing. For muddy and lime-heavy waters do not rinse; they infect and defile, just as we see when linens are bleached in the sun—if they are sprinkled with gypsum-heavy or lime-heavy well water, stains are left behind. Therefore, if mineral waters are good for washing, we suspect the presence of a diluted nitrous greasiness; if they are not, they may be gypsous, muddy, or lime-heavy, or they carry other mineral scraps that pollute rather than cleanse.

---

### CHAPTER LVII.
->*On corrosive and consuming waters.*<-

**There** are certain waters that burn, dissolve, or corrode things thrown into them, such as that water in whose depths nets and clothes are burned if they are lowered, as **Bacci** wrote following **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy"</note>. It is not difficult to judge that at its bottom there is a fiery, bituminous vent, since this does not happen in water alone, even if it is boiling. Bitumen, however, feeds a flame even under water; Bacci says the **Puteolan** <note>Waters from Pozzuoli, a volcanic area near Naples</note> waters emit a flame along with moisture. There is nothing absurd about such a thing happening here as well, for a flame can be carried that far. Hence, waters containing nitre and melanteria <note>A mineral form of iron sulfate, often called "ink-stone" because it was used to make black ink</note> consume shoes and similar items in a short time. This can also be seen in paper in which melanteria is wrapped, or a mixture of ink, saltpeter, and alum; this has the power of "coloring water" (as they call it) or "strong water" <note>Aqua fortis or nitric acid</note>, as much as its thickness does not prevent it. The water of the **Styx** <note>The legendary river of the Underworld; here the author treats it as a real, highly acidic spring in Arcadia</note> is said to have been so sharp that it destroyed all vessels except for a mule’s hoof—and perhaps things made of bone, scales, or the flesh of the fish it is said to have nourished. Certainly, art also makes such strong waters—according to **Bernhardon** <note>Likely referring to a contemporary chemist or alchemist</note>—that no glass, let alone a metal or marble vessel, is sufficient to contain them, although those from **Waldenburg** are quite firm. A sharp water near **Valencia** in **Spain** is said to consume a shoulder of mutton down to the bone within the space of one hour if it is thrown into the spring. The **Wolckenstein** waters, according to **Gäbel** <note>Andreas Gäbel, a writer on mineral springs</note>, erode wood and iron tools. This is the same effect as "spirit of salt" <note>Hydrochloric acid</note>, which is nevertheless drunk and used for washing, just as the salts that corrode the pots of potters. Inky waters in **Hungary** turn iron into a mud from which copper is made; such a lye is produced from inky pyrite. It must therefore be considered that such waters consist of melanteria, or some other sharp ink-material, as well as arsenic, mercury, cadmia <note>Zinc ore or cobalt</note>, etc., about which we will say more below when we discuss human ailments.

---

### CHAPTER LVIII.
->*Dyeing waters.*<-

**By some** waters, wood, wool, linens, and so on are dyed or otherwise colored. These waters either have thick juices mixed in them or are sharp enough to alter the surface. Oak wood, alder, and similar types are easily changed by inky juices, as are shells; they are also accustomed to turning black when soaked for a long time in rivers. Plum wood likewise turns reddish from sharp waters. Let the judgment on similar things be the same.

---

### CHAPTER LIX.
->*Waters that turn things into stone.*<-

**It is** well known that those waters in which things petrify carry marble, gypsum, alum, and similar limes. At the same time, they are sharp enough to penetrate and carry mud into the smallest parts of an object from every side. Once the mud hardens and the lime is received into the tiny pores, it appears to be stone.

### CHAPTER LX.
#### *Softening and Hardening Agents.*

**T**he substances in which horns become soft belong to the nature of lyes, vinegar, and similar things; it is easy to recognize the mineral at work here. This was discussed in the alchemical instructions <note>original: "magisteriis chymicis," referring to the master-works or practical operations of chemistry</note>. It is well known that hides do not become manageable and soft everywhere, which is attributed to the local waters. For those waters that hide marl <term>marl: a lime-rich mud or rock</term> or gypsum, or which contain aluminous and copper-rust <note>original: "aeruginosos," referring to verdigris or copper acetate/carbonate</note> juices, make the hides unmanageable. In the same way, metals are hardened in these waters—where red-hot metals are extinguished—whether they are meant to be hardened, softened, or undergo some other change. It is certain that some waters are more suitable for tempering swords than others; for instance, waters containing iron and alum, as well as vitriolated waters <term>vitriolated: containing sulfates, often of iron or copper</term>, make iron tough, while others harden it. If, after the quenching, evaporation, or soaking, "flowers" <note>mineral crusts or efflorescences</note> appear on their surface, even though iron and copper suffer the same from simple water, the craftsman can easily recognize the nature of the sharp juice—such as salt, spirit of vitriol, or sulfur—which we use in preparing *crocus martis* <term>crocus martis: iron oxide, used as a pigment or polishing powder</term>, ceruse <term>ceruse: white lead, a carbonate of lead</term>, and similar products.

### CHAPTER LXI.
#### *Tenacious Agents.*

**T**hose waters which, when added to cements, provide a gypsum-like tenacity, carry with them marl, marble, tufa, bitumen, maltha <note>a thick, tar-like natural bitumen</note>, and similar fatty and slow-flowing substances. However, even a moderate amount of salt provides some tenacity, and if niter <note>saltpeter</note> is easily produced in the cements, it is consistent that the water contains its principles. Gypsum-bearing waters produce a bounty of "fleas" <note>likely referring to small mineral inclusions or perhaps a specific type of crystalline growth</note> unless the gypsum itself has been applied. Thus, the odor or vapor of such works is suffocating. Waters that contain much salt may be tenacious at the start of the work, but later they are easily crumbled and create a defect.

### CHAPTER LXII.
#### *Affecting Plants.*

**N**itrous waters sprinkled on plants, especially cabbage, grant them a good yield and do not allow for earth-fleas or worms. However, if too much salt is allowed to reach the roots especially, it destroys them. Likewise, "inky" waters <note>original: "atramentosae," referring to vitriolic or sulfate-rich waters</note> flowing from sulfurous pyrites, cadmium <note>likely zinc or cobalt ores in this context</note>, mercury, arsenic, and similar minerals, either kill plants or make them distorted and spotted. It has been observed, however, in salty, mercurial, and copper-rust waters (if they are diluted), that plants may grow because of an abundance of "sweet juice," provided that this juice is at least available at the roots. Therefore, since the saltiness of the sea is kept away by the coastal sand while the fresh parts penetrate through, herbs can grow on shores and in marshes even in the midst of salts. The water at Valencia in Spain, which is believed to be very sharp from the spirit of mercury, produces excellent plants because the water is purified over a long distance. The Nile once provided niter, yet its water is very favorable for nurseries. The elderberry tree perishes if even just sprinkled with urine; and there are other plants affected in specific ways by specific things. If something similar happens in minerals, it will be possible to judge by analogy. The cause is manifest when nothing in the way of plants grows in boiling waters.

### CHAPTER LXIII.
#### *Those Affecting Animals.*

**W**aters by which livestock are fattened when drunk are salty or nitrous, but within moderation. Indeed, the healthy strength of the animals throughout the whole region indicates that the mineral is wholesome. In some waters, fish, frogs, and other aquatic creatures die; in others, the local ones live while the foreign ones die. As **Jordanus** <note>Thomas Jordan (1539–1585), a physician who wrote on the waters of Moravia</note> reports concerning Lake Ceicienfi: the local livestock drink from it, but foreign ones either will not touch it or they die. Similarly, in the Styx, native fish are nourished, but if transferred to other waters they cease to live, and exotic ones brought in suffer the same. It is a matter of such importance to be accustomed to and, as it were, nourished by poisons. A lake between Strapela and Seburg, says **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy"</note>, kills fish every seventh year when a pestilential breath rises. In putrid waters, there can be frogs, snakes, and other things of that kind even where fish are absent. Those waters are entirely destructive which contain minerals of poisonous cadmium, chrysocolla <term>chrysocolla: here likely referring to green copper minerals or borax</term>, arsenic, much gypsum, orpiment, sandarac <term>sandarac: red arsenic sulfide/realgar</term>, excessive amounts of sory, misy, melanteria <note>these three are various ancient terms for iron and copper sulfates/vitriols</note>, copious sulfur, alum, niter, and so on. Moderately salty and nitrous waters do not stand in the way of life, unless perhaps habit creates some effect.

### CHAPTER LXIV.
#### *Waters Used for Food and Drink.*

<margin>Bacci, Book 6, *On Thermal Baths*, Chapter 4.</margin>
**A**s for the humans themselves—for whose sake we chiefly investigate the nature of mineral waters—they either use them in foods (either in most or in specific ones) and in drink, or they abstain. There are many medicated waters with which they boil food, prepare dough, and mix wine, and which they use daily as their only source. **Bacci** <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), physician to Pope Sixtus V</note> relates that in the Anceric bath at Barbonium, food is cooked with the water and masses of bread are kneaded, even though the water is hot to the fourth degree. There is the same use for the bath of Corsena near Lucca, which is aluminous, very hot, clear, and of not unpleasant taste and smell; in its mineral content, niter, rock salt, and sulfur are detected. There is also the bath of St. John near Lucca, which they use similarly, and they even dilute wine with it. The people of Schwalbach <note>in Germany</note> and Iuncatias in Italy also drink them, as do many others, even though they manifest niter, bitumen, iron, etc. In Spain, they record that there are mercurial waters which the inhabitants flock to drink in competition. The waters at Anticolum in Campania are in familiar use for drinking, and they cook food very quickly. That a mixture of such things is not adverse to human nature is shown by the facts themselves, even though some try to defame mineral waters. From which masses of leaven—
