<header>On the Judgment of mineral waters, part 2.</header>

### On the Judgment of mineral waters, part 2.

...they ferment, which is an indication that they are "spirituous," since such a thing typically happens due to ferment, spirit of wine <note>original: "spiritu vini," referring to ethanol</note>, "burning water" <note>original: "aqua ardente," an early term for distilled alcohol or brandy</note>, and similar vaporous substances, and even from the dregs of wine and beer. If, while meat is being cooked, the pots turn white, a white foam is separated, and the meat itself turns white at the edges, it is established that the waters are gypsous <term>gypsous: containing gypsum or calcium sulfate</term>, or carry marble-lime, marl, tufa, pumice, and similar things. And certainly, sometimes when such waters are boiled alone, they even deposit much lime. From this, the wines of such places become "tartareous," which produce "tartaric diseases," as the Paracelsians <note>followers of the physician Paracelsus, who believed diseases were caused by mineral precipitates in the body</note> call them, such as colics with paresis <term>paresis: muscular weakness caused by nerve damage</term>, paralysis, etc.

In some waters, legumes are cooked and softened with difficulty. These are called *un-boilable* <note>original Greek: "ἀπέψητοι" (apepsētoi)</note> by Athenaeus, Hippocrates, and others. *Moschion* says, according to Athenaeus, "that northern winds melt <note>soften</note> the legumes; such are the nitrous and salty ones" <note>original Greek: "ὅτι τὰ βόρεια τὰ ὄσπρια τήκονσι. τοιαῦτα δὲ τὰ νιτρώδη καὶ ἁλμυρά"</note>. Agricola judges such waters to be immoderately cold and crude, and they are mostly well-waters. Some attribute this to mixed-in gypsum. And indeed, the same happens with some "marmoreal" waters <note>waters containing limestone or marble particles</note>, but which are also "crude" <note>unrefined or mineral-heavy</note>. At other times, I have been told that abundant lime is found in a certain water, but it does not hinder the softness of legumes. And Jordanus reports that there is much gypsum in the Petrovian water, yet you may cook legumes well in it.

### CHAPTER LXV.
#### On those things which afflict health

**N**onetheless, although some waters are in public use for the sustenance of life, they are so unhelpful to those using them that they seem to perpetually afflict them with adverse health, in whom a morbid constitution has become almost native. Thus, one sees many who are cacochymic <term>cacochymic: having unhealthy digestive humors</term>, cachectic <term>cachectic: suffering from physical wasting</term>, pale, bloated, suffering from hernias, distorted, hunchbacked, and in some places, a huge goiter <term>struma: a swelling of the neck or thyroid gland</term> is a familiar "ornament." Authors disagree as to what cause specifically produces this "throatiness." Some refer it to the entire nature of the place, such that it is a "populary" or endemic constitution of a certain region, with the sky, air, waters, and the whole way of life conspiring together. Nor is it nothing in the customs of a people. We see that women mostly give birth to such children as they meet in public, so that where many hunchbacks are encountered, the *imaginative power* <note>original Greek: "τὸ φαντασικὸν"</note> of a pregnant woman takes a likeness of it for herself; where many have gaping mouths, or are black, white, etc., they produce similar ones. Baccius refers this to gypsum, because the waters drunk at Callium in Italy among the Camertes are gypsous, and the people of that place are "throaty" <note>prone to goiters</note>. But in gypsum alone there is little weight for that matter, and since it hinders catarrhs and dries them up, it would rather oppose it. Nor do those who drink the Albula waters, and others containing marmoreal lime and gypsum, turn out similarly—like those who drink the Puteolan waters well-saturated with the dust of pumice. The same author also blames crudity, coldness, stagnant waters, snowy, crude, and "tenacious" ones above others, which nonetheless are not sufficient on their own, and when drunk elsewhere produce no such thing. He is therefore forced to take refuge in the nature of the entire location, especially since people become "strumous" <note>goitrous</note> even in places where they have a warm climate and well-boiled waters.

Langius thinks more correctly when he attributes this to mercurial vapors and waters affected by quicksilver <note>original: "hydrargyro," mercury</note>, but nonetheless, the "proper character" <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἴδιον ἤθος"</note> and the imagination of women must not be omitted. Otherwise, since those vapors abound in many metals, frequent goiters do not always arise from them. However, that specific condition arises from the conspiracy of mineral vapors among themselves, and with the whole nature of the place, in which the smoke of mercury prevails. For it is certain that miners are weighed down in their heads, vexed by distillations <note>fluids/mucus</note>, and from there become asthmatic, orthopneic <note>unable to breathe except when standing</note>, dyspneic <note>short of breath</note>, pleuritic, and liable to spasms, arthritis, and similar evils of the nerves and other parts because of the waste products. Those who place the cause in the crude and snowy waters of the Alps are rejected by Baccius, not without merit. Miners of mercury ore in Spain are said to be shaky and for the most part paralyzed; they do not live long, and not rarely their weakened teeth are knocked out, and they frequently emit "crudities" from the mouth and go bald. All these are effects of mercury, and they harmonize with the previous points; nor are they lacking in those who frequently deal with mercury and endure its fumes and applications.

Such was the water of Pliny, which damaged the teeth and legs with *stomacace* and *scelotyrbe* <note>terms used by Pliny for symptoms of scurvy: mouth sores and leg paralysis</note>. Such is the water of the Susians in Persia. Agricola blames metals, but more confusedly. He ought to have named the mercurial vapors in them, either not yet coagulated or else dissolved. Sometimes arsenic also effects the same, and those who strive to remove teeth by art use arsenic, orpiment <term>orpiment: a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term>, sal ammoniac, sublimated mercury, *aqua fortis* <note>nitric acid</note>, and similar things, just as they use opium, etc. From this also comes scurvy, which nonetheless a poor diet in certain maritime places also produces.

### CHAPTER LXVI.
#### On those things which change fleeces and nails.

**C**ertain waters change not only the colors of men—and first pull away the skin and nails of those using them before they grow accustomed—but also of beasts, so that they are not rarely seen with a foreign color and without hooves. Pliny wrote that the fleeces of sheep are changed from drinking from the Crathis and Sybaris rivers. Younger scholars do not believe it. However, the Sybaris is also said to blacken wool and flaxen cloths, and the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> asserted the same in his *Problems* and the 4th book of *On the Generation of Animals*. The river Clitumnus is said to whiten cattle, according to Virgil and Pliny. The Melas of Boeotia turns them black. Agricola agrees with these when he says: *If flocks of sheep drank only the black waters of rivers and those flowing with suin <note>likely "sown" or "mucky" water</note>, they could become black just like the fish that live in them. Also: Waters infected with a little "shoemaker's ink"* <term>shoemaker's ink: vitriol or iron sulfate used for dyeing</term> *and some "melanteria"* <note>a natural vitriol or mineral ink</note>, *although they do not seem very black themselves, can make the hairy bristles of animals black when drunk. But those that lick shoemaker's ink likewise, and a vein of white or black lead, acquire yellow bristles; those that lick a vein of only the other lead, white ones.* Nothing mentioned is a marvel, just as when they say hooves fall off and are changed in beasts of burden, and feathers are renewed in hens when they have eaten the flesh of vipers. There are indeed waters that corrode the nails of miners and pull away the skin of those remaining in them for a long time. There are certain medicines by whose long-term use not only the skin is changed, but also the entire temperament...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physiological effects of mineral waters, specifically how they alter the body's external features like hair and skin, and their varied effects on healthy individuals.</meta>

<header>Commentary on Alchemy. Part II. Book VI.</header>

...[the body] now lives on poisons, though it previously would have died from their careless use. Who could even imagine that such a change occurred while retaining the old waste products <note>original: "excrementis," referring to biological byproducts like hair, nails, and fluids</note> and the things born from them? How many people lose their hair from the "French Disease" <note>Syphilis</note>, the plague, and other poisonous illnesses? [ Galen notes this happened to lepers through the use of a viper-based medicine; it also happens to eagles and falcons from eating snakes. In Nova Zembla <note>an archipelago in the Arctic Ocean</note>, the Dutch ate the liver of a bear. Because of this, their skin was renewed; thus, this food is a remedy for deformed old women. The followers of Paracelsus have many such things for the renewal of a second life. ] In those with dropsy <note>edema</note>, malnutrition, or the itch, the outermost skin entirely sloughs off after healing. I knew a certain man whose black hair and beard fell out completely due to a certain disease, and it grew back white on his head alone. Nor should one think that the change happens suddenly, or that only the hair is altered, although even that would not have been absurd. The old hairs fall out gradually, and as they follow the nature of the nutrition and the powerful "tinctures" <note>medicinal extracts or internal qualities</note>, and the bodily forces recover, new hairs of a different color succeed them. Nor is that which nature does gradually in old age denied to a single violent cause—just as it is well known that hair can turn white in a single night from grief or melancholy. In cases of scabbing, leprosy, and the like, there was reason why you might judge such changes in the "excrements" <note>hair/nails</note>, and in those things sustained by waste-bearing humors, to not be absurd.

However, to define exactly what the "mixture" <term>crasis: the specific temperament or chemical balance of a substance or body</term> of these things is, from which such things happen, would perhaps be reckless. It is necessary for the acting agents to harmonize with the receiving subjects, whether vitriol, copper, or something else provides the principle of motion. Furthermore, animals that have been changed eventually return to their usual state. Thus, unless the location and the nature of the pastures are changed, such qualities remain, just as black fish remain so in their own water. As for what is said regarding hooves, one must see whether they fall off because the animals walk in sharp, acidic waters rather than from drinking them; the former is more likely. Thus, those waters which harden hooves with a stony juice do so from the animals stepping into them.

### CHAPTER LXVII.
### Other effects on healthy men.

There are also other effects that happen to healthy men from the use of mineral waters, and these are generally shared with the sick. For example, some waters stimulate the appetite, indicating the presence of salt, vitriol, iron, or alum, unless that affection comes from the coldness of the water. Some are astringent <note>tightening to the tissues</note>, such as those containing iron, alum, or gypsum. Some are purgative, such as those that are salty, nitrous <note>containing nitre/saltpeter</note>, mercurial, copper-bearing, vitriolic, or irony. Others disturb the bowels with gas, such as those that are raw, thick, and viscous, unless that is an accidental effect of the purging. There are those that produce "musty" <note>wine-like</note> belches, such as the vinous ones. Some bring on vertigo and a kind of drunkenness, especially when the vapors are inhaled along with the water; such are called bituminous <note>containing bitumen or asphalt-like minerals</note>, like the Lyncestian spring. Some make people "abstemious" <note>averse to wine</note>; namely, those that linger in the stomach and around the organs with wine-like and musty belches and are not distributed through the body. This is not such a hidden thing. If someone drinks the Schwalbach waters <note>famous mineral springs in Germany</note> and does not pass them through the bladder or bowels, they linger in his stomach and create such a nausea for wine that he cannot tolerate wine for several days, as was told to me by one to whom this happened. Conversely, it is nothing miraculous that some waters have such a "mixture" <note>crasis</note> that they beget a longing for wine, just as I remember an insatiable appetite for unfermented wine arose in a certain girl from drinking much and eating grapes. 

The vapor of some waters stings the eyes, such as those called "holy waters" near Asculum, the mineral of which is judged to be sulfurous with iron or ochre. And it is unknown to no one that the breaking down of sulfur has that power. Some waters cause choking with their copious vapor, or induce fainting; such waters are not only harmful but also health-giving, being acidic, vitriolic, sulfurous, etc., as Jordanus, Thaddeus, and others testify. Some erode the skin and the flesh of miners who linger in them, such as those tinted with *melanteria* <note>a form of iron vitriol</note>, *cadmia* <note>zinc ore</note>, the "flower of the Assian stone," *pompholyx* <note>zinc oxide</note> from metallic *cadmia* (*Realgar*), *sandaracha* <note>red arsenic</note>, arsenic, and so on. Agricola says: in Altenberg in Meissen, a black *pompholyx* is found which eats away wounds and ulcers down to the bone. It also corrodes iron. There is also a certain kind of *cadmia* that eats away the sweating hands and feet of workers and damages the lungs and eyes. They become caustic because of *mysy*, *sory* <note>various vitriolic minerals</note>, spirit of sulfur, spirit of antimony, and *spodium* found in mines, which erodes and rots things vehemently, along with orpiment, tainted mercury; some add lead, blue vitriol <note>chalcantnum</note>, alum, quicklime, poisonous sulfur, and similar things. 

Regarding mercury, however, it should be noted that elsewhere, if it is not tainted with poisonous vapors, it does not produce unhealthy mixtures, as Baccius mentions regarding four springs in Spain, although he elsewhere holds mercury in suspicion. Certainly, it is handled with the hands for a long enough time and stays in vessels without erosion. If nature produces something like "strong water" <note>aqua fortis / nitric acid</note>, or a mixture of *melanteria*, alum, and nitre, or something like sublimated mercury, poisonous Realgar, and the like, those waters are deservedly infamous. It was said above that gypsous waters cause choking. Such is said to be the Styx of Arcadia, and another in Thessaly, unless glassy vitriol or mercury, or some other poison, is the cause. To this belongs what Ovid reports of the Ciconian spring, from which the internal organs are turned to stone. In Berosus, on the hill of bulls, Vitruvius says there are three springs that kill without pain. From the Crobian water in the Alps, those who drink it collapse immediately, as did those from the spring that was once in Tarracina. The Cychros in Thrace kills even by washing in it, as does the Lycus spring in Sicily. These can be traced back to the principles mentioned above, but they are more harmful in degree, more penetrating, and infested with a peculiar "mixture" <note>crasis</note>. It is a marvel that the bath of the Ducci at Corsena plucks the feathers from chickens, yet it does not damage the hair in a poultice, nor blister the skin. Thus there are secrets in other waters as well. Red-colored <note>miniatæ</note> and bituminous waters are said to make people insane; likewise dull-witted, forgetful, blind, etc., as in Ethiopia, Boeotia, Cea, etc. For bitumen damages the senses and weighs down the head. Nitrous waters do not bite <note>sting/corrode</note> unless a biting mineral is added, as Jordanus testifies regarding the lake and mud of Ceicia.

Concerning boiling waters and those that strip or harm the skin by some other manifest quality, we shall refrain from speaking. The remaining points regarding the effect on diseases are to be sought in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER LXVIII.
### *The Folly of Paracelsus.*

**P**aracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine, often challenging traditional Greek medicine.</note> claimed a singular knowledge of minerals for himself, and as if he had explored the entirety of nature, he easily established his rules. Thus, about to comment on the effects and nature of such waters as if pointing with his finger, he brings forth his principles: salt, sulfur, and mercury. He claims their nature works in such specific ways that any effect can be traced back to a certain substance. *Those waters which heal paralytics,* he says, *are from the mercury of the Sun <note>original: "mercurio Solis," referring to the alchemical essence of Gold</note>: those for the jaundiced, from the mercury of Venus <note>original: "mercurio Veneris," referring to Copper</note>: those for ulcers, from the mercury of quicksilver: those for fevers, from the spirit of salt: those for spreading ulcers and the "French Disease" <note>Syphilis</note>, from the mercury of the body: those for leprosy, from the sulfur of antimony: those for dropsy <note>edema</note>, from rock salt <note>original: "sale gemmæ"</note> and Roche alum, and so on for others.* But as the foundation is slippery, so too is the assertion built upon it. For he has not yet proven to us that paralytics are healed by the mercury of the Sun—whether by itself, by accident, alone, or with others—and unless this is confirmed by a consistent history of examples, everything he teaches remains uncertain. He said with easy confidence that those waters which irritate and ulcerate the skin in use prove to be something corrosive, but this instruction does not answer his prior foundation, which demands those corrosives be named by their specific type. While he disapproves of such waters, he is not mindful enough of his own drinks, or of other things which irritate externally—such as mustard, salt, spirit of vitriol, vinegar, etc.—yet when diluted internally, they perform no such thing, as experience testifies in many cases. This instruction is also ridiculous when he says: *Golden waters strengthen, but only with the best diet.* But this is true not only of "golden" waters, but of any common water. He likewise falters when he writes about arsenical waters, saying they achieve their effect with abstinence. That glutton <note>The author is likely referencing the contemporary reputation of Paracelsus for heavy drinking and coarse behavior.</note> who dared to boast that he cured his patients on full stomachs now discourses here on abstinence, where the most sincere virtue of the medicine should have been displayed. Many other things help when combined with abstinence, and the effect would happen even if the waters were not added, since it is well known how much weight diet carries in diseases. You see again how frivolous and empty this author's ideas are; let no one be so mad—even among the Galenists <note>Followers of Galen, the traditional school of medicine based on the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile).</note>—as to wish to lick up the spit of this scoundrel.

Some others are able to say through experience that a sulfurous mineral dries, an aluminous one binds, an iron-based one strengthens, and a copper or nitrous one cleanses, and so on. But even these are not "catholic" <note>Universal or general rules.</note> truths, such that one may confidently declare a water is from a sulfurous mineral just because it is drying, or aluminous because it is binding, etc., since these effects do not belong to those minerals alone. Therefore, we must also warn here: we ought to hunt for certainty from a gathering of many signs. We cannot designate an indubitable mineral from a recovery achieved in only one way, unless we can occasionally confirm it by <term>direct observation</term> <note>original Greek: "αὐτοψίᾳ" (autopsia), meaning seeing it with one's own eyes.</note>.

---

## CHAPTER LXIX.
### *General Effects on Diseases.*

**R**egarding diseases, then, that water is more wonderful in words than in reality in which it is said one must "either die or recover within three days," as is reported of the water of Pesth in Hungary <note>Modern-day Budapest.</note>. For what else does this saying mean than that the water is of such remarkable power that it either accelerates death or drives out the disease? This is exactly what the Paracelsians preach about their own destructive medicines, and in this way, they strive to excuse their crimes. If a disease is incurable by nature, I would not wish to send the patient there as if "to the crows" <note>An idiom meaning to send someone to their destruction or the gallows.</note>. If it is curable, even if a delay is required, I would again earn no praise if I hurried that which cannot be rushed, and through acceleration tended toward certain ruin. If time is granted, there is nothing difficult in that pronouncement, since in every water—if you continue its use to one end or the other—you must either die or recover, unless you wish to live miserable and diseased. For the end of every disease is either the death of the sufferer or health. Therefore, setting aside these generalities, let us contemplate slightly more specific matters.

---

## CHAPTER LXX.
### *Effects in Simple "Similar" Cold Diseases.*

**W**hether these waters heal imbalances <note>original: "intemperies," referring to a lack of balance in the bodily humors or qualities.</note> that are simple or composite, and whether they are surface-level or essential, all healing proceeds from a contrary action. Although it can otherwise happen that the matter of the medicines is sometimes familiar to the suffering part and sometimes adverse—and the causes of the disease are sometimes the same and sometimes contrary—nevertheless, for the most part, we assign an adverse quality or "crasis" <note>The specific "mixture" or temperament of a person's body or an organ.</note> to the water (if it acts by itself), which is contrary to that imbalance. Thus, if any water (or a mineral from the water) heals a cold constitution, it is easy to pronounce that it is "hot," because it contains heating minerals and principles; and it suffices to have said this generically regarding its bare quality. For example: the waters of Carlsbad <note>original: "Carolinæ," the famous hot springs in the modern Czech Republic.</note> drive out cold, therefore they are hot. But in an "essential" coldness, which encompasses the temperament of certain members and constitutes their property, judgment is more difficult. If a morbid coldness of all members is helped (as if by one common suffering part, such as the heart, blood, vital spirit, liver, stomach, and others by which a common coldness can be induced), it is consistent that a healing water assists that common weakness and, by the property of its own temperament, looks after the temperament of the body. Thus, if one wishes to track down its mineral, for the heart, we shall say it is golden, or of carbuncle, or a similar gem, by whose virtue the chilled heart is assisted and receives its own proper degree of heat. Likewise, for the brain and the nervous system, we could name silver and things that have similar power. Mostly, however, in these weaknesses, the "spirits" <note>The "vital spirits" or subtle fluids thought to circulate in the nerves and blood to animate the body.</note> also have some harm, as they are either fewer than they should be, or cruder, or more sluggish. Help comes more quickly from things that are likewise "spirituous." Therefore, the "spirit" of those minerals must be brought forth. Since a deficiency of these is not repaired except by nutrition, this must also be carefully considered, as it is established that minerals nourish less because they are further removed from the familiar disposition of our bodies. And then you see—

The author specifically addresses the treatment of "cold" diseases using "hot" mineral qualities and cautions against "miracle" waters that claim to cure or kill in three days.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the systematic analysis of how mineral waters interact with the body's internal environment. While the previous page critiqued Paracelsus's specific alchemical assignments, this page applies the traditional Galenic theory of the four "distempers"—heat, cold, dryness, and moisture—to explain the healing properties of various mineral springs.</meta>

<page-num>180</page-num>
<header>Alchemical Commentaries, Part II, Book VI.</header>

We must take care not to attribute to the water what comes from elsewhere, nor to assign to one cause what is owed to many; we must not mistake an accidental property for an essential one. Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), a German scholar considered the "father of mineralogy."</note> says that sulfurous waters heal the diseases of all joints, although he is otherwise very unfavorable toward metallic substances, from which he claims the nerves are harmed. However, we can accept his statement regarding a "cold distemper" <note>An imbalance where a part of the body has become too cold, leading to sluggishness or pain.</note> for the reason that once the parts are strengthened and warmed, the sluggish spirits are revived, and a reawakened nature increases their substance. Thus, if an ailment depends on an obstruction or a cold mineral quality, once this is removed, the body rises to its work of its own accord. In a similar way, we may contemplate the remaining distempers.

### CHAPTER LXXI.
->On the Hot Distemper.<-

**F**or those things which restrain an essential hot distemper—one existing either without matter or without much of it—are judged to be cold. If the heat belongs to a specific limb or to the whole body, they will be beneficial either to that specific part or to the common principle of the body, unless something occurs by accident, of which there can be no scientific certainty. Cooling waters generally consist of "coagulated cold spirits," as we said above, as well as nitre, quicksilver, and the juices of cold gemstones, etc. This is true even though there is hardly any mineral that is not either hot by its innermost nature or at least has hot spirits and parts joined to it. Hence, although metals and earths are reckoned among the "cold" things, they also possess hot powers, whether due to sulfur, vitriolic spirits, or others. This is especially true since even quicksilver <term>hydrargyrus</term> <note>Mercury.</note> has a certain hidden heat. Baccius <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), an Italian physician and author of a famous treatise on thermal springs.</note> says that acidic waters are cold, dry, and thinned by a certain heat. If that acidity arises from putrefaction or an internal nature (as in acidic fruits), let that be agreed upon; but it is not so if it arises from alum, the spirit of vitriol, the spirit of sulfur, and similar things. These, when mixed with waters, render them acidic but not cold, unless "wild water" <note>Natural, untreated spring or forest water.</note> abounds and carries their temperament away with it. Some think that a mercurial spirit has a vitriolic nature because it is "cold with the cold and hot with the hot," etc. We understand this to mean a certain mode of tempering, so that hot things are sharpened by it, as are cold things, whereby they become more effective in their operation, given a penetrating sharpness that induces power more deeply. In their own nature, however, these juices are rather hot.

### CHAPTER LXXII.
->On Dryness.<-

**T**hose things which remove a dry distemper are more watery. Minerals have little role here, since hardly any of them are moist—even mercury, which indeed moistens the limbs, does so not by its own moisture, but by a foreign one. It liquefies the humors of the brain and nerves and either drives them out through the mouth and bowels or fixes them in the joints, while nature otherwise sends them of its own accord to those "drainage points" <term>emunctoria</term> <note>Organs or pathways for eliminating waste from the body, such as glands or the bowels.</note>, glands, joints, etc. In the meantime, it leaves them there. But the mercury itself sinks into the bones by its penetrating weight, corroding and weakening them. I am speaking here of raw quicksilver, or that which is not correctly prepared, as it is commonly used in the fumigations and ointments for the "French Disease" <note>Syphilis.</note>.

### CHAPTER LXXIII.
->On Moisture.<-

**T**here is an abundance of aids for a moist distemper in mineral waters. However, attention should be paid here to the "affinity of the whole substance" <gloss>familiaritas totius substantiæ</gloss> with certain limbs. Sulfur, bitumen, and similar things dry powerfully through their spirits communicated to the waters. But "bulky" minerals, such as sand, thick juices, mud, etc., when applied externally in poultices, are both more numerous and stronger—such as salts, gypsum, rust, etc.—especially in boiling hot baths.

### CHAPTER LXXIV.
->Distemper with Matter.<-

**W**here there is a distemper with "matter" <note>Physical excess of humors, like phlegm or bile, rather than just a quality like heat or cold.</note>, or even a mechanical ailment involving the same, and that matter is ejected from the body by the waters—whether through sweat, the bladder, the bowels, the mouth, or wherever nature has established its drainage points—we ascribe such power to those waters and the minerals within them. Hence they are called diaphoretics <note>sweat-inducing</note>, hydrotics <note>water-moving</note>, purgatives, diuretics <note>urine-inducing</note>, emetics <note>vomit-inducing</note>, discussives <note>dispersing</note>, abstergents <note>cleansing</note>, incisives <note>cutting/thinning thick humors</note>, and so on. Here, too, it is difficult to name a specific mineral for each, because not only is the same general effect noted in many different species, but it is often indistinguishable. Furthermore, one and the same substance, through varying degrees of strength and being differently affected or tempered by neighboring minerals, can perform different tasks. 

Nevertheless, use and diligent investigation of minerals have noted that those which purge through the bowels are mostly nitrous, such as the waters of Cutiliæ, Paganelli in Italy, the Botta water, Anticoli, Grotta, etc., to which nitre is attributed, but in combination with other minerals. Indeed, it is well known that nitre <term>nitrum</term> and halonitre <note>Likely a reference to saltpeter or a specific alkaline salt.</note> move the belly. However, they also move the bladder. Thus, such waters are simultaneously diuretics; others would say this happens because they are partly distributed through the body and partly remain in the bowels, and once the impurities are cleansed, the obstructions opened, and the thick matter thinned, they stimulate the excretory power and shake the waste out. 

But certain aluminous, vitriolic, and copper-bearing waters also purge through the bowels and urine, as Rhazes <note>Al-Razi (865–925), a Persian polymath and influential physician.</note> says, as do iron-rich waters with alum (like the Queen's Water in Pisa), salty waters like seawater, and those containing such mixtures. Certainly, even outside of waters, iron, copper, quicksilver, the spirit or dry smoke of antimony, vitriol, arsenic, chrysocolla <note>likely borax in this context</note>, Armenian stone, Lapis Lazuli, and the like, act as purgers. Salt is rather diuretic, and the spirit of vitriol and quicksilver prepared in a certain way also head for the bladder. The "sweetness of sulfur" moves the lungs; quicksilver moves the brain; the flower of sulfur, lime of vitriol, a small amount of chrysocolla (called borax), Armenian bole, and others move the stomach. Diaphoretics include the "calxes" <note>Oxides produced by heating.</note> of gold, antimony, quicksilver, and the like. Some strengthen the body after evacuation, such as the temperament of chalybeate <note>iron-rich</note>, aluminous, and vitriolic waters. "Saffron of Mars" <term>crocus Martis</term> <note>Iron oxide.</note>, alum, gypsum, etc., act as astringents.

# CHAPTER LXXV.
## External defects of the skin.

Nitrous, salty, bituminous, and sulfurous waters, and those of moderate strength, etc., cleanse the skin and make it soft. For ringworm, <term>honeycomb-cysts</term><note>original: "meliceridas"; skin tumors or cysts containing a honey-like substance.</note>, and the like, as well as for <term>French sores</term><note>A common historical term for syphilis.</note> and similar impurities, lead, iron, alum, and sulfur are recommended (hence the whitish <note>original: "Albulæ"</note> aluminous and sulfurous waters are suited for the French disease). However, the "mercury of bodies" is most effective, although lime water, <term>minium</term><note>Red lead or cinnabar.</note>, marble, gypsum, arsenic, and similar substances also provide benefits, especially in liquid form. Therefore, baths of these minerals are beneficial for those suffering from the French disease, leprosy, and similar affections, provided they are not hotter than is proper, the disease is not too far advanced, and the body has been properly prepared. Specifically, <term>atramentous</term><note>Inky or vitriolic waters containing iron sulfates.</note>, bituminous, and strongly ferruginous waters carrying asphalt are useful for <term>elephantiasis</term><note>In this context, a term for severe, thickening skin diseases or advanced leprosy.</note>; the "golden waters" of <term>Pfäfers</term><note>original: "Fabaris"; a famous thermal spring in Switzerland.</note> are also highly praised for this. Nevertheless, mercury and lead are not safe if they are corrupted or mixed with corrosive minerals like ammonium salt, arsenic, or <term>realgar</term><note>A toxic arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>. For milder defects of the flesh and skin, such as the itch <note>scabies</note>, etc., both those milder substances and also copper, verdigris, vitriol, gypsum, salt, marble, etc., are effective. Thus, the sharp <term>Stygian water</term><note>A highly acidic or mineralized spring near Rome, named for the underworld river due to its properties.</note> near Rome, due to its mineral content of copper and sulfur, is helpful for any skin defects, as are the marble-like "white waters," and others. In salt-works, the brine easily cures the itch; in metal workshops, the water used to quench metals and sulfur performs the same task. Agricola says that <term>vitiligo</term><note>A condition causing loss of skin pigment.</note> is healed by sulfurous substances.

Nitre, spirit of sulfur, spirit of vitriol, <term>melanteria</term><note>A black mineral juice or copperas.</note>, verdigris, burnt alum, arsenic, salt, bitumen, lead, etc., wear down calluses and absorb <term>scrofula</term><note>Swelling of the lymph nodes, usually associated with tuberculosis.</note>. Mercury, minium, lead, etc., disperse <term>edematous</term><note>Swollen with fluid.</note> tumors and inflammations. The <term>Zahárovice water</term><note>original: "Zaharouicensis"; a spring in Moravia.</note> in Moravia, consisting of vitriol, bitumen, and salt, also removes <term>struma</term><note>An older term for a goiter or scrofulous swelling.</note>, as Jordanus <note>Thomas Jordanus (1539–1585), a physician who wrote on the medicinal waters of Moravia.</note> states. Therefore, if mud, sand, or anything else from such baths has these effects, one must consider it to be due to some such mineral.

# CHAPTER LXXVI.
## On particular diseases, etc.

**F**or epileptics, it has been found that amber, spirit of vitriol, native minium, <term>ophites</term><note>Serpentine or "snake-stone" marble.</note>, and the like, are effective when used as spirits, liquids, or plasters.

For those suffering from melancholy, if a water or mineral is helpful, one should look for sulfur (just as the sulfurous Sinuessan waters <note>Springs at Sinuessa in Campania, Italy.</note> abolish insanity), vitriol, <term>chrysocolla</term><note>Historically could refer to borax or malachite (copper carbonate).</note>, Armenian stone, lapis lazuli, the magnet, iron, the black whetstone, etc., which dissolve that <term>dyscrasia</term><note>An imbalance of the bodily humors.</note> along with the humor. However, melancholy is tempered in baths that are not excessively dry and hot, but rather sweet and moderate.

Alabaster marble, ophites, the magnet, etc., are also beneficial for headaches; for "cold" ailments, amber is noble, as are balsam of sulfur, petroleum, <term>jet</term><note>original: "gagates"; a type of lignite coal used in medicine.</note>, gold, silver, etc. Just as these are applied externally to the nerves, so too are alum, salt, and antimony, which are harmed by cold—as they write regarding the <term>Cydnus</term><note>A river in Tarsus (modern Turkey).</note> of Cilicia, which brought a numbness upon Alexander the Great, Frederick Barbarossa, and others, perhaps due to a mercurial coldness.

The spirits and balsam of sulfur, and even tempered vapors, are useful for those with consumption <note>phthisis</note> and asthma. Therefore, says Bacci <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), physician to Pope Sixtus V and author of a major work on baths.</note>, Neapolitan physicians are accustomed to sending asthmatics to the Puteolan fields <note>The volcanic area of Pozzuoli near Naples.</note>, where, through the constant drying sulfurous vapor, they gradually digest such stubbornness of the disease by its specific properties against such imbalances. Galen likewise records that the air of <term>Stabiae</term><note>original: "Tabiarum"; a town near Mount Vesuvius.</note> near Vesuvius is useful for consumptives and those spitting blood. For this reason, the sick are sent there by the Neapolitans.

Salty and especially acidic waters restore the appetite to the stomach. For this reason, spirit of salt and spirit of vitriol are frequently used, and experience testifies that certain <term>acidic springs</term><note>original: "acidulæ"</note> perform the same function.

For weakness of the liver and various defects of the spleen, they recommend spirit of vitriol, <term>saffron of Mars</term><note>Iron oxide.</note>, steel, the magnet, etc. Thus, they are also used usefully for <term>dropsy</term><note>original: "hydropa"; swelling caused by excess fluid.</note>. One should check for these in waters and mud if they are beneficial for such diseases.

The ancients wrote that ferruginous <note>iron-bearing</note> waters are beneficial for diseases of the bladder. Hence a certain water is called "vesicaria" <note>The bladder-water.</note> in Tuscany. Steel has the same effect. Spirit of vitriol, essence of mercury, crystal, <term>Jew's stone</term><note>A fossilized sea-urchin spine used to treat stones.</note>, <term>lynx-stone</term><note>original: "lyncureus"; a mythical or amber-like stone believed to be formed from lynx urine.</note>, oil of amber, petroleum, native minium, etc., specifically remove stones and sand <note>kidney/bladder stones</note>. Thus, they write that acidic waters break up stones in the kidneys and bladder, such as a water in Campania which contains vitriol and a little nitre, and is said to be miraculous in that effect. The same is attributed to the iron-bearing water on the island of <term>Ischia</term><note>original: "Ænaria".</note>. A sharp mercurial water at Valencia in Spain is found to be wonderfully effective against stones. There are also some nitrous waters of the same efficacy.

Salty, nitrous, vitriolic, copper-bearing (like the copper water of Viterbo), and ferruginous waters—as well as those mixed with nitre, copper, and iron, like the <term>Grotta</term>—strengthen the uterus and, by removing bad humors, promote fertility. This is also true of the nitrous Nile and other waters in the region of Volterra. The acidic springs of Göppingen also encourage fertility. They attribute much power to gold in this regard. It is therefore surprising why the "golden" waters of Pfäfers should restrain <term>Venus</term><note>Metaphor for sexual desire or activity.</note>.

Borax, amber, nitre, and bitumen, etc., and sometimes mercury, expel uterine obstructions. One should look for these in such waters.

<margin>Hence Agricola declares that sulfurous waters are those which heal wounds and "cold, moist" defects of the joints.</margin> For those suffering from gout, hand-gout, and foot-gout <note>original: "Arthriticis, Chiragricis, Podagricis"</note>, waters and minerals of dissolved copper, iron, antimony, crystalline mercury, alum, sulfur, vitriol, etc., are beneficial. Specifically, warm washes that dissolve the matter that has flowed into the joints, soothe pain, and strengthen the limbs, and—if applied skillfully—prevent new flows of humors, such as "strong water" <note>nitric acid</note> tempered with a decoction of pain-relievers, a solution of mercury, or a decoction of glass of antimony. The vinous and sulfurous water of Mount Alceti <note>Monte Amiata/Bagni di San Filippo.</note> in the territory of Siena (says Bacci) provides a mud useful for contracted nerves. Likewise, the iron bath of mud in Italy is beneficial for the same; so too have the golden Pfäfers, the Carlsbad baths <note>original: "Thermæ Carolinæ".</note>, sulfurous and lime waters, and the vinous spring of Schwalbach <note>original: "Sbalbaci".</note> often been of service to the joints. The lead-bearing waters of Lorraine are again written to relieve contractions.

<page-num>182</page-num>
<header>Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book VI.</header>

There are also many other affections and unnatural dispositions that are driven away with the help of minerals, which have been most particularly reported by those who have written specialized commentaries on baths. For one skilled in minerals, it is not difficult to arrive at a knowledge of the ore from these effects, especially if he knows how to rightly discern accidental effects from those which are <gloss>essential</gloss> <note>original: "καθ' αυτὸ"</note>, and unique effects from common ones. There are many sleep-inducing waters because of the relaxations they produce by sending vapors to the brain, such as the <term>Schwalbach</term><note>A famous spa town in Germany known for its iron-rich "acidulous" springs.</note> waters, etc. Ophthalmic remedies are those that contain <term>stibium</term><note>Antimony, often used in eye salves since antiquity.</note>, white <term>vitriol</term><note>original: "chalcanthum album"; zinc or iron sulfate.</note>, <term>pompholyx</term><note>Zinc oxide residue from smelting furnaces, also called "philosopher's wool."</note>, verdigris, copper, nitre, <term>minium</term><note>Red lead or cinnabar.</note>, native <term>cadmia</term><note>Zinc-rich ore or furnace deposits.</note>, etc.; you should understand these to be effective whether they are found in juices, fumes, or <term>collyria</term><note>Eye salves or washes.</note>, all administered according to the medical art. Thus, the stone-waters in Pozzuoli participate in copper and nitre; likewise, Grotta contains nitre, copper, iron, and sulfur; the Ciceronian waters in Baiae contain cadmia; the Spanish waters contain minium; the copper waters of Viterbo, etc., are said to be remarkably beneficial for the eyes in cases of "little clouds" <note>Cataracts or corneal spots.</note>, dimness of vision, glaucoma, "nails" <note>original: "vnguibus"; likely pterygium, a growth on the white of the eye.</note>, and so on; to which end also <term>cadmia</term> <note>original: "canrum" (likely a typo for cadmia or calaminam)</note>, burnt alum, and other things contribute. There is a certain species of Samian earth—fatty, porous, soft, and white—called "collyrium" because of its use for the eyes. From <term>pyrite</term><note>Iron disulfide, or "fool's gold."</note> on the island of Elba (fertile in iron), they say there is a spring that is sharp and astringent, which brings a numbness to the teeth and harms the gums, but is quite profitable for discharges of the eyes; in this case, it is possible that the pyrite is copper-bearing and joined with cadmia. Those who work in nitre and copper mines say they are not easily harmed in their eyes.

Poisons are resisted and expelled by <term>diaphoretics</term><note>Substances that induce sweating.</note> which contain sapphire, crystal, gold, silver, emerald, jasper, <term>medicinal bolus</term><note>original: "bolum"; a type of therapeutic clay, often "Sealed Earth" or Terra Sigillata.</note> (of the kind stamped for use against poisons), fossil ivory, amber, petroleum; likewise sulfur and many similar things.

For <term>catarrhs</term><note>Excessive buildup of mucus or inflammation of the mucous membranes.</note>, magnetite, hematite, ophites <note>Serpentine stone.</note>, gold, silver, alabaster, etc., are recommended.

For raw <term>edemas</term><note>Swelling caused by fluid in the tissues.</note>, alum, clay, sand, mercurial mud, sulfurous mud, etc., are useful.

<term>Anodynes</term><note>Pain-relieving substances.</note> include the liquid of quicksilver, balsam of sulfur, lime water, solutions of arsenic, lead, etc.

They strengthen the gums and teeth, and are even useful in <term>scurvy</term><note>original: "scorbuto"; a disease caused by Vitamin C deficiency, leading to bleeding gums and weakness.</note>: iron, alum, copper, etc.; for which reason the chalybeate <note>Iron-rich.</note> waters in Ischia are effective.

<margin>
Azoth <note>The universal transformative agent or mercury in alchemy.</note>, red coral, and <term>Persicaria</term><note>Knotweed; Paracelsus attributed magical/sympathetic healing powers to this plant.</note> according to Paracelsus.
</margin>
They say that quicksilver, cinnabar, minium, etc., are effective against <term>spells</term><note>original: "fascina"; charms or the "evil eye."</note>, insofar as these effects are brought about through natural means.

Nitre, vitriol, etc., resist fungi.

Those who are wasted away <note>Emaciated or thin.</note> are said to be restored by a stay in aluminous and chalybeate baths, such that after fifteen days they leave fat at the Buselli baths. Nitrous waters also fatten moderately. On the other hand, vitriolic waters, if drunk for a long time, thin the body and make people lean, such as the Anticoli water mentioned by <term>Baccius</term><note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), a famous Italian physician and author of a definitive work on thermal baths.</note>, which is nonetheless simultaneously nitrous.

The "spirit of vitriol" <note>Sulfuric acid.</note>, chalybeate water, and the like remove unnatural thirst, and also help with <term>malacia</term><note>A craving for non-food items or a deranged appetite.</note>.

You may suppress burnings of the throat with chalk; consequently, chalky water, chalybeate water, aluminous water, etc., are appropriate.

<term>Sandarac</term><note>Red arsenic sulfide (realgar).</note> is believed to benefit the voice; for this reason, they say it is recommended in the water of Zame in Africa.

Depilatory waters <note>Hair-removers.</note> are attributed to <term>orpiment</term><note>Yellow arsenic sulfide.</note>; although this also applies to <term>melanteria</term><note>A mineral related to copperas or vitriol.</note>, poisonous <term>spodos</term><note>Metallic ash or furnace residue.</note>, and others.

Sea waters are prescribed for <term>hydrophobia</term><note>Rabies.</note>, although plunging into a lake of cold water also removes it; others recommend mercurials made from gold-clad silver, <term>medicinal boli</term> against poisons, and their ashes or calxes. But I shall finally cease saying more about these aids. Just as many things are harmful to the healthy, so some do not spare the sick, especially when applied perversely and without skill. Arsenical and cadmious waters, and those others we mentioned above, harm both the healthy and the sick.

One should also inquire here about the perpetuity and constancy of the effects, in which a lack of similarity is detected. For in some waters, the strength changes variously according to the weather, the Moon, inflows, transport, etc.; and the Anticoli waters in Campania, being tasteless and consisting of nitre and marble, do not spoil for many months, as is also the case with the waters of the Tiber, the Nile, etc., and the "acid" waters of St. John in Rome. Conversely, the Grotta water of Viterbo is useless if transported, and the sharp water at Valencia in Spain cannot be carried for more than three days. But let these things be judged from what was said before.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

### On the more occult properties of waters.

Thus we have embraced in our judgment of mineral waters whatever has now occurred to us, and which seemed to contribute to human health—if not to an exact knowledge, then at least to some sort of understanding. For the practitioners, however, many other things are reserved in secret, which usually occur during experimentation and in the handling of minerals: for instance, if waters corrode iron and change it into copper, they are excessively <term>vitriolic</term><note>original: "chalcanthosæ."</note>. In Bohemia, at the "New House," there is a water by which silver also takes on a copper color; and it is likewise judged to be a mixture of alum and <term>atrament</term><note>A term for vitriol or inky iron sulfates.</note>. Jordanus reports that the water and mud of Slatina in Moravia blackens a silver bowl with a tenacious clinging, which is an argument for burnt sulfur and dissolved bitumen, with atrament added; although the black ash of mercury, or a mercurial blackness mixed in such mud, could do the same; and it is known that bitumen also clings stubbornly to iron, like <term>maltha</term><note>A thick, tar-like natural bitumen or mineral wax.</note>. Baccius judges that iron is present in a spring by the Narni river, because a silver coin thrown in is drawn out a little while later tinted with a golden redness, even though otherwise it is a mineral of salt, nitre, and alum. But that tint can also come from elsewhere. [The vapors of bitumen and sulfur tint in this way. If, therefore, a liquid of bitumen is mixed with those waters, silver turns to gold therefrom.] Those waters that extract iron splinters from wounds, such as the "Imperial" and others in Baiae, likewise the Contarena baths near Pozzuoli, and the chalybeate in Ischia, are believed to be magnetic, because that is the property of the magnet. If you doubt concerning <term>amber</term><note>original: "succino."</note>, you will recognize it if, by boiling, it yields an oil of its own color, black and purple bitumen, and likewise black, pale, or white ash, and finally something thin similar to salt.

<page-num>183</page-num>
<header>On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 2.</header>

Ignited fat is not easily extinguished by water, unless the water is very abundant and muddy; it is better smothered by sand, straw, wet rags, and so on. If it catches fire quickly, it is <term>liquid bitumen</term><note>A naturally occurring petroleum or tar, often found seeping from the ground.</note>, such as that found in Italy in the territory of Modena, in Babylon, and elsewhere. Bitumen is also noted if it is soft at first but later hardens, and the waters are bitter, leaving a saltiness on those washing in them, as occurs in the <term>Asphalt Lake</term><note>The Dead Sea, known in antiquity as Lacus Asphaltites.</note>. If the mud has the power of coloring, it indicates the presence of <term>verdigris</term><note>A green pigment or crust (copper acetate/carbonate) formed on copper or brass.</note>, <term>saltpeter</term><note>Potassium nitrate, used in explosives and medicine.</note>, <term>melanteria</term><note>A vitriol or copperas-like mineral used as a black dye.</note>, and similar substances. For in this way, goldsmiths inspect gold and silver lines on a <term>touchstone</term><note>A small tablet of dark stone used for assaying precious metal alloys.</note>, after applying corrosives mixed with urine or vinegar. Sometimes we add filings or bodies extracted from the waters to metals or harder veins of ore: and if they provide an easy flow, we think of saltpeter, <term>stibium</term><note>Antimony, often used as a flux to help metals melt.</note>, <term>fluxes</term><note>original: "fluoribus"; minerals like fluorite that lower the melting point of ores.</note>, native <term>borax</term>, etc., any of which is clear to the craftsman by its own signs. Likewise, if they serve in <term>cementations</term><note>A process of refining gold by heating it with salts to remove impurities.</note> for separating metals; if, when dipped, they strip gilded items of their gold leaf; if they change colors or make metals heavier, etc., we recognize the mineral. If they fix, solidify, and harden things more, there is a suspicion of <term>magnetite</term><note>original: "magnetidis"</note>, <term>muscovite</term><note>original: "lapidis specularis"; a transparent mineral used like glass.</note>, <term>cadmia</term><note>Zinc-rich furnace deposits or ore.</note>, gypsum, alum, iron ore, and the like. They can also be distilled through retorts, in the manner of <term>strong waters</term><note>original: "fortium aquarum"; usually referring to nitric acid (aqua fortis) used to dissolve metals.</note>. If some such substance comes from it, the principles are likewise revealed, although the <term>dead heads</term><note>original: "capita mortua"; the useless solid residue left after distillation or sublimation.</note> and other signs must be observed together. If they turn to glass through <term>reverberation</term><note>Heating in a furnace where the flame is deflected onto the material.</note> and melting: one must see whether antimony, lead, salt, sandy clay, or "glass-stone," tin, and similar things lie beneath. And if that glass, by pouring or boiling, communicates a purging power to the liquid, the exploration will be more certain. If, from reverberation in a closed vessel, the vessel bursts; saltpeter, <term>sal ammoniac</term><note>Ammonium chloride, a volatile salt used in alchemy.</note>, mercury, etc., will be hidden within. If the <term>lime</term><note>original: "calx"; the powdery residue left after a substance is burned or "calcined."</note> turns out red or a shining saffron color, etc., it represents mercury. Let it then be processed by <term>descent</term><note>A method of distillation where the vapor is forced downward.</note>, or through a retort with <term>tartar</term><note>Potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking used as a chemical reagent.</note>, or let its smoke be caught on a polished plate, and living mercury will appear. If, with the addition of sal ammoniac, a coin is "cemented," and the copper is consumed without damaging the mark, sulfur or arsenic will be beneath. For inflammation does not always indicate sulfur, nor does it always stink: and it is sometimes even "fixed" and of various colors; and if it is fixed, it acquires an intense redness in the fire without loss, and it reddens white metals in the cement. But other things also provide this, which are discussed in chemical works. There is also a white "fixed salt of sulfur." The lime of <term>talc</term> or magnetite, "fixed" <term>ceruse</term><note>White lead.</note>, and similar things, whiten copper in the cement. <term>Calamine stone</term><note>A zinc ore that, when melted with copper, creates brass.</note> turns it yellow like a citron. Impure combustible sulfur furrows silver, or <term>brass</term><note>original: "orichalcum"</note>, or standard copper, and even burns it. It also <term>calcines</term><note>Reduces to powder by heat.</note> gemstones. These and infinite similar things the studious investigator of matters can note, so that he may become somewhat more certain of the minerals in waters.

## Chapter LXXVIII.
### On not despising the judgment of craftsmen.

Nor indeed should the opinion of craftsmen be cast aside, who have often judged these same waters and are practiced in many things, especially if several have reached the same conclusion, although it is rare for everyone to agree on everything. If the argument from them is not the firmest, it will nonetheless lead you by the hand to a sharper knowledge. Nor should you think that other men notice nothing and you notice everything. There is no man everywhere, nor is any one man alone wise; and it is not rare that a thought occurs to him that does not occur to me, even if by its nature it is very easy. See, therefore, whether the judgment of the experts agrees with the facts, either entirely or very nearly. If you discover something new, communicate it with wise men, so that it may be confirmed by common consensus. It is well known to what extent the persuasions of the common people should be listened to by craftsmen. The <term>Albula waters</term><note>Famous sulfurous springs at Tivoli, near Rome.</note>, as Baccius says, were commonly held to be sulfurous because of their heavy odor: but Galen, Caelius Aurelianus, Scribonius Largus, Paulus, Aëtius, and others, along with Baccius himself, found them to be <term>aluminous</term><note>Containing alum (aluminum sulfate) rather than sulfur.</note>. And although Pliny, Seneca, Silius, Martial, and Pausanias were on the side of the common folk; nevertheless, the judgment of medical physicists is stronger: although it may be that the latter recognize a stinking "spiritual sulfur" joined with other minerals, while the former do not deny the sulfurous nature, but nonetheless teach that alum is present in the waters. It is one thing for sulfur to be in the mud near the waters, and another for it to constitute the mineral itself and form an essential mixture. The <term>Paracelsians</term><note>Followers of Paracelsus, often criticized by traditionalists for their radical chemical theories and rejection of ancient authorities like Galen.</note> are men of corrupt judgment. Let them be gone. If I have not satisfied you—which must be admitted, since I myself feel the lack of many things—forgive human frailty.

> finished work I never promised.

<margin>
Read about the Nile in C. Bruerinus, book 16, on food. See also Mockius, page 236, etc.
</margin>

**W**hen I had completed the treatise on mineral waters, most excellent **Scherb**, I remembered that in previous months I had babbled something similar to you about imitating the water of the Nile, which you indicated was welcome; but until now I was ashamed of my own childishness and the audacity that compelled me to act foolishly before a man of such absolute learning and judgment. I wanted to redeem that shame with a new effort, and just as actors on the stage, once hissed at or received with laughter, usually correct their errors with more refined industry, so I was preparing to correct my former folly with more laborious diligence. Therefore, I have treated this matter again and added it to the related commentary, so that I would not seem to only teach others what to follow in the judgment of waters, but that I myself might walk the same path, and if not in substance, then by example, benefit the younger students. Out of your love for me, you will allow me to babble even this delirium, the penalties for which I know I shall pay to my adversaries. But a foreseen evil will be less troublesome. At the start, I ought to have contemplated and experienced the Nile itself and its entire region and nature in person: but it seemed more advisable to me to become wise at another’s risk. I will therefore set down what I have found here and there among authors; afterwards, I will strive to judge and imitate it.

<margin>
History of the Nile.
</margin>

Sacred history teaches that the Nile, having proceeded from the inexhaustible and eternal fountain of Paradise, encircles Ethiopia. <insert>But consider whether this might not be Eastern Ethiopia, where the Indian Mughals live. For the rivers of Genesis come from one region, and Pison is the Indus, Gihon is the Ganges, Hidekel is the Tigris, and the Euphrates. From India, the Ethiopians crossed with the Seres <note>The Seres were the people of the "Land of Silk," usually identified as the ancient Chinese or Central Asians.</note> to the marshes of the Nile.</insert> But the maps of cosmographers assert that since the Deluge, it bursts forth from other mouths, and is vomited from the Mountains of the Moon in farthest Ethiopia out of vast marshes—<gloss>consult the maps of the moderns, especially Edward Lopez, where this is denied</gloss>—and enters the sea through a vast tract from south to north through various nations and Egypt. This is the first gift that Avicenna attributes to it: namely, that it proceeds through a very wide space; and the second, that it is carried from south to north. While this happens, some say it is cast down from very high cliffs: once indeed in Ethiopia, where the greater <term>catadupe</term><note>A classical term for a waterfall or cataract, specifically those of the Nile that were said to deafen nearby inhabitants.</note> and cataracts are; then above Syene, where the minor cataracts are. Truly, this is affirmed by Cicero, Strabo, and especially Agricola, but Baccius either denies it or interprets it otherwise. For he denies it is "cast down," and seems to want to say only that it runs more excitedly through rocks and pathless stones with an immense sound, which I do not know if it is the same as what others call "being cast down," who perhaps feel it is brought down from very high places over a long tract, not suddenly dropped into a precipice. It is said likewise now to hide itself, now to come into view, now to be narrowed and squeezed by rocks, now to triumph by spreading out through open fields, and to lick vast sands, with copious waters poured out over much space. From this, Avicenna’s third and fourth gifts appear: namely, that it rolls vast waters and migrates through good lands. Some add that it also runs through an Ethiopian lake, and from there emerges so splendid with the spoils of the lands in a vast region that, left to itself, it cannot be drunk healthily, but the inhabitants—especially the Egyptians—must strain its water through a raw sleeve <note>A "sleeve" refers to a conical cloth filter or strainer.</note> or boil it and wait for the sediment to settle quietly overnight, according to Galen and Aristotle. Recently also from the narrative of Baumgartner, we have learned that the common people of Alexandria and Memphis are afflicted by many diseases from drinking its turbid water. Yet Egypt owes both its plain and its fertility in some part to that mud, as Seneca reports.

Furthermore, if its water is purified, Oribasius (citing Rufus) says it is praiseworthy for drinking, since in winter it does not putrefy nor become overly salty, and because it is moved by motion, just as others also strained by the nature of sand and stripped of all tinder of putrefaction are preserved incorrupt. Athenaeus (citing Theophrastus), Seneca, Scaliger, and others moreover think it is the sweetest. Theophrastus adds, and Seneca followed him, that it is <term>most generative</term><note>original: "πολυγενεστάτην"; implying it promotes fertility or the generation of life.</note>. For this reason, King Philadelphus is affirmed—on the authority of Polybius, whom Lang cites—to have sent it from Egypt to his daughter Berenice in Syria as a gift when she married Antiochus. Theophrastus, Rufus, and Oribasius attest that it loosens the belly, and Theophrastus adds the reason: because it is <term>nitrous</term><note>original: "νιτρώδης"; containing nitre, which in this period could mean either saltpeter or naturally occurring soda (sodium carbonate).</note>. <insert>Learn from here why the Nile becomes nitrous. It rises with other rivers from a large lake almost 14 degrees beyond the equator. From here, going back 5 degrees toward the equator under the elevation of the Antarctic pole at 8 degrees, there are mountains of salt nitre from which a great force of nitre comes. The Nile flows past that region and flows into another marsh almost under the equator. Hence its nitrosity comes, and not from the Sun as some imagine. The reason for <term>sal ammoniac</term><note>Ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy and medicine.</note> in the Nile is the same.</insert> Which, having been repeated, Agricola—with Baccius—confirmed from sources similar to the mineral of nitre. Pliny reports that King Ptolemy found mines of sal ammoniac under the sands near Pelusium, besides which there were also nitre-beds on the bank of the river, into which water was admitted and became stagnant, and was later condensed into nitre by the glowing sun.

### On the Judgment of mineral waters, part 3.

Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), a German scholar often called the "father of mineralogy."</note> provided a model for these types of soda-works. But regarding sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride, historically harvested from soot or mineral deposits)</term> there can be no doubt: for the same substance was also found later in the desolate places between Egypt and Arabia. Dioscorides, and Pliny following him, records that throughout all of Africa, and especially in Libya near Mount Cyrene, this salt was dug up from under the sands, which was thereafter called Cyrenaic and "ammoniac" <note>named after the Oracle of Ammon</note>. There is also a great quantity of fossil salt on the island of Meroë in the Nile, and Athenaeus recounts from a certain writer that sal ammoniac and Nile water were brought from Egypt to the King of the Persians.

Medicinal springs are also not lacking in Africa, especially those that are bitter and nitrous. It is consistent that their outflows are swept up by the Nile. According to Dioscorides and Pliny, the "flower of salt" <note>a fine salt crust that forms on the surface of water</note> is also carried down the Nile. Athenaeus and Seneca, citing Theophrastus, say that the Nile sometimes carried down "malignant" water, which the Greeks call **rust-colored** <note>original: "ἰώδης" (iodes), referring to a violet or rust-like tint, possibly from copper or minerals</note>, though interpreters disagree on the meaning. Seneca calls it "musty," while Agricola says it is "stained with copper-rust" when he states it occurs during times of maximum drought. Theophrastus says the water of the Nile flowed with the color of copper-rust, from which many Egyptians died; most assert this happened during **droughts** <note>original: "ἀυχοῖς" (auchois)</note> or periods of squalor. <margin>Book 31, chapter 4.</margin> Pliny also mentions rains, although others deny that it rains in Egypt—contrary to what Baumgartner asserted from actual experience. Pliny says:

> It happened three times in the Bosphorus that salty rains fell and killed the crops. Just as many times, the rains that water the Nile made the water bitter, causing a great pestilence in Egypt, a plague such as Servius describes arising from the rotting of beasts left behind by the Egyptian pools; generated within them from the water by the action of heat.

Among the other gifts of the Nile, it is counted that its water does not "breathe" <note>likely meaning it does not evaporate or release vapors easily</note>, although a pleasing breeze meets those sailing upon it, so much so that it even moves bells hung from the yardarms, as Baumgartner saw (and thus he calls that previous claim into doubt). Some say it does not breathe out mists and that it is cold: Herodotus and Athenaeus seem to testify to this regarding Egypt, where the air is **soft and mild** <note>original: "μαλακώτης καὶ ἀήρ" (malakotes kai aer)</note>; which is, moreover, very healthy. Furthermore, it is said to carry very thin and light waters, yielding to few in quality, while through the heats and summers it is long carried and "baked," acquiring healthfulness and resilience. Strabo says they "cook" <note>digest</note> more quickly than others. Your letter mentioned that the water of the Nile was dietetic, did not linger in the upper abdomen <note>original: "hypocondriis"</note>, moistened the body, and made bodies fatter—something women especially desire—and that the Egyptians count this among the gifts of the Gods, because they are persuaded it all turns into the best blood. It might seem strange to some that while it is written to be carried a long time through the heat, it is not said to be particularly hot in effect; whereas Alvise Cadamosto <note>a 15th-century Venetian explorer</note> writes that among the Black people in the interior of Africa it rains boiling water, and those rivers which are sought through a very long tract of sea through the Barbary coast into the Red Sea are wonderfully hot solely because of the Sun's heat. But lest I examine too many authors and scrape everything together from everywhere, let this be the boundary of the history.

<margin>Gifts of the Nile.</margin>
The attributes of the Nile water, as far as they pertain to the present matter, are: healthfulness when filtered, unhealthfulness when muddy or exhausted by squalor; thereafter sweetness, lightness, thinness and easy distribution, likewise "ripeness" or thorough cooking, stable duration, excellent nutrition, moistening, fattening, fertilizing, and nonetheless thinning; a lack of exhalations, loosening of the bowels, promotion of urine, aversion to rot, and although it is carried through heat, a tempering of that heat. I fear that when we ascribe such great goods to it, our **Paracelsist** <note>followers of Paracelsus who used chemical medicines, often criticized by traditional Galenic doctors</note> adversaries will draw their "Panacea-like" weapons against us, with which the throat of our Galenic medicine was recently attacked. Let us, however, follow the authors, and at the same time exercise ourselves in this question: whether there is given such a fortunate thing, be it nutriment or medicine, which can defend a person from adversity through every age and maintain them in an intact state—just as those who are poorly occupied boast about their "masteries" and "essences." Regarding its healthfulness first, I do not have much to say. <margin>Healthfulness of the Nile.</margin> It follows from its other qualities; provided it is used well, so that it not only does not offend health but is fit for preserving and defending it; nor is it of **slender** assistance in diseases that come from elsewhere. In this, perhaps nothing would be said that differs from other good waters, yet the authors want it to have some prerogative. It should be added that even in some excess, and when it is used for preparing food, for baths, for the brewing of **Egyptian beer** <term>zythos (a traditional barley beer)</term>, etc., it provides remarkable benefit, and works to successfully drive away some diseases or prevents them from arising. Thus, perhaps it is healthy in its entirety because it does not vitiate the air with bad vapors. A little further on, it will also be said to have a closer power for generating good blood, and not to contain much waste; and since simplicity stands in the way of this disposition, it must be granted some degree of proper temperament. From this, the resulting serum is not only a suitable vehicle for the humors, but also contributes to washing away, scouring, and cutting through superfluities, and driving them out through the bladder or sweat. Furthermore, the blood generated from it will not be liable to rot, it will produce the best spirits, it will maintain heat correctly, and it will not only guard the limbs in their proper mixture <note>original: "crasi"</note>, but will even make that mixture more noble. And since it is also the material for seed and milk, it follows that fertile Egypt is filled with people very well disposed toward every kind of wisdom—especially if the climate, education, discipline, and exercise agree, after the divine mercy, which willed to constitute Egypt as the mother of wisdom by these means. O happy Egyptians, then, if they lived on water alone, or had other things of that kind, which is consistent in their diet, since the cattle and plants also use the same water. But since it is said to provide so many benefits once separated from its muddy thickness, the question arises: should it be boiled first, or separated raw? It is not difficult to understand that in its season and muddiness, it is nauseating. If it is set aside at night in the open air, the mud settles to the bottom, and the water receives some cooling from the breeze, which in hot regions is colder at night. But nevertheless, it has been observed that boiled waters cool faster and more thoroughly, and likewise they deposit mixed **earthy bits** <note>original: "γεώδεις" (geodeis)</note> more quickly and purely. On the other hand, if it is thin and "baked" by the daily heats, there will be no need for boiling; indeed, it might turn out worse, because boiling breaks apart thick and impure things and thins them, but dissipates the thin parts and thickens the water with the remaining parts closer to the earth. Therefore, it ought only to be filtered, specifically through sand or gravel, so that along with the mud, the viscous juices are also retained; in place of which a raw clay pot was once sufficiently used. Let us therefore remember these things when we wish to imitate it. This also must be attended to so that it may be healthier: in what manner it ought to be drawn—from the top or from the bottom. From the top, certainly. For there the airy sweetness resides. If it is drawn from the bottom or the middle, either the preparation will be more laborious, or it will lose its reputation for healthfulness. The Egyptians obtain this more easily because the Nile flows gently in its plain, and because...
