<header>Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book VI.</header>

<margin>The harm of the Nile.</margin>
...whether they have frequent subterranean channels or water-conduits, where water sent through tunnels might stagnate and settle; otherwise, the force of the river makes the selection worse. Furthermore, since salt is so common in Egypt and the neighboring regions, and its spirit corrects the "wickedness" of the waters through its own tempering—which is proportional to the amount of nourishment—we shall also owe some of its healthfulness to this. But since other factors also concur, many of which must be mentioned in what follows, let them be recalled here. If the water is drunk not filtered, but turbid <note>muddy or clouded with sediment</note>, as the common people are accustomed to do, it is not only unhealthful but even harmful. We understand the cause to be in the disturbances or the silt itself. But if the silt is merely simple earth, I do not see why it should cause such great harm, unless one is drinking mud rather than water, which is not likely. Someone might say that obstructions arise from this, and that as the fine silt creeps into the pores of the limbs, and especially the liver, they become earthy and clearly unfit for a healthy constitution; we see this happen to those who consume "sealed earth" <note>terra sigillata: a medicinal clay used as an antitoxin</note> too copiously. And the harm seems greater when these things are ingested daily out of habit rather than as medicine. There is indeed something to this, but not so much, unless you wish to believe that beasts of burden (who mostly live on turbid waters) and fish suffer the same. And how does our beer differ from a turbid drink, even if it looks clear? How does chyle <note>the milky fluid produced during digestion</note> differ? People drink whitish waters that turn to stone almost immediately after their source without harm. We are looking for the powers of effective qualities in that mud. However, the history of the places through which the Nile runs teaches us that they do not lack sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride)</term>, nitre <term>nitre (naturally occurring soda or saltpeter)</term>, sandarac <note>original: "sandaracam," likely referring to red arsenic minerals here</note>, and other mineral juices. While these reside in the mud as if in their own mine or vein, they produce diseases through frequent and indiscriminate use. Nor can it be dismissed as a mere guess: is the muddy Nile the same for the Egyptians as it is for the crocodiles? Or like the water of the Styx is to its fish, or the Albanian water to its alum, or poison to the Indian girl, or hemlock to the Attic hag? <note>A series of classical references to organisms that thrive on substances poisonous to others.</note> The variety of "juices" <note>mineral solutions</note> stands in the way, as they are not always mixed into the Nile waters with the same temperament. However, so that these diseases are not so cruel, a copious amount of diluted moisture helps. But if the Nile suffers from filth due to a lack of thin liquid—if the rains of Ethiopia or the source itself provide water too sparingly—then the malignant quality prevails. Then, juices hostile to human nature are taken in more copiously, which certainly are not due to nitre or sal ammoniac alone, but to something more pestilential, such as the liquids or dilutions of sandarac or "white chrysocolla" <note>original: "chrysocollae albae"</note>, which they call **borax**; a small portion of this upsets the stomach and forces one to vomit, while a larger amount kills. Perhaps there are other similar things, and perchance "crocodile-stuff" <note>likely referring to crocodile dung or musk, often mentioned in ancient biology</note> is not lacking, nor the beginning of some putrefaction on the surface and at the edges; for historians attest that Egyptian mud easily rots and gives birth to frogs, mice, and other insects. However, the fact that some authors attribute this to the rains perhaps contains nothing absurd. For it is known that unusual rains, and especially spring rains, also make the mineral waters of baths unhealthful. But one might also reasonably say that at different times, many bitter and similar juices enter the river. There are certainly many bitter waters between the Nile and the Red Sea; there are nitre-works, salt-works, alum factories, etc. If such juices flow in too abundantly, they make the water disease-bearing. Next follows its sweetness.

> [**Seneca** says the Nile has the sweetest water. This sweetness seems to be mineral. Others that are bitter become sweet or drinkable by infusing barley or by adding crushed coral. Was this perhaps the nature of that sign of Moses in **Marah, Exodus 15**? <note>Referring to the biblical story where Moses sweetened bitter water with a tree.</note>]

I confess I do not quite grasp what kind of sweetness this is. We call waters "sweet" when they are not tinged with any foreign flavor beyond that which is native to water. The nature of water is truly said to be tasteless. But in the Nile, the Eulæus, the Choaspes, etc., one must suspect something peculiar, given the great eulogies of authors. Since the water is also closer to "Chyme" <note>a rich, semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</note> than to simplicity—which is why it nourishes so well, and in the past was said to change quite easily by miracle into thick blood—it produces many beasts and many plants, as if rivaling the sea in fertility; its sweetness seems to be understood as a mixture, like that of milk in water. But if this is so, the nitrous bitterness will be absent, as will the saltiness of the ammoniac and the toxicity of the chrysocolla. Such sweetness is also prone to rot. Furthermore, the mixture of mud, especially mineral mud, does not allow for it, <gloss>for many waters that are difficult to pass, both the muddy and the salty ones are troublesome, and slowly produce indigestion in the limbs</gloss> <note>original Greek: "τὰ γὰρ ὕδατα τὰ πολλὰ μηδὲ ἔχοντα δυσαπερμαζίτης, καὶ τὰ πηλώδη καὶ ἁλμυρὰ μοχθηρὰ καὶ ἀπεψίαν βραδέως τίκτοντα τὰ ὄσσεα," quoted from Athenaeus</note>. Nor do mineral waters please **Hippocrates**. Should we say that different parts are present, and these <gloss>in opposing layers</gloss>? <note>original Greek: "κατ’ ἀντίστρατας"</note> The sweet parts, being airy, float on top; the bitter and salty parts, being earthy, settle at the bottom. And indeed, the prerogative of sweetness is in the filtered and separated water; for the water that flows with filth is bitter. That this sweet water does not rot may be attributed to the spirits of nitre with which it is tempered. But we do not deny that a moderate and more "airy" juice is present. For although nitre is somewhat bitter, it is not perceived by taste except in great quantity and thickness. The Grotto in Puteoli is sweet, yet at the same time nitrous; likewise, others there are pleasant and not without nitre. Thus, nutritious sweetness and a little medicinal nitre work together for greater healthfulness. But there is a further scent of something else. They say many sugar canes, pomegranates, palms, and similar plants of sweet juice grow by the Nile. Is the water therefore altered by such juices where it touches the top of the earth? They write that a lake is bitter in some places because of the wormwood growing frequently near it. Since the Nile flows gently, why should it not acquire something similar? What if alum also contributed something? There is something of an airy sweetness in it, just as it is not entirely lacking in nitre, since it is felt on the tongue at the end. **Dioscorides** testifies that there are alum mines of every kind in Egypt. But I see that another cause pleases you, which is surely the heat cooking and digesting the water; likewise, the cataracts thinning it. It is a grave matter to oppose so great a Philosopher. I shall say with you, therefore, that the heat provides some help when it generates sweetness, but only in those things disposed and endowed with a closer "potential" <gloss>potentially</gloss> <note>original Greek: "δυνάμει"</note>, in which it, as it were, activates what was previously non-existent; and yet, the points I brought forward are not to be disparaged. Water is one thing, cabbage is another, and it is not necessary for the same effect to follow from the same cause in both; nevertheless, since the Egyptians irrigate cabbage with nitrated water and make it sweeter, and the sweetness remains in the juice, one can think that the nitre contributes something to the sweet water of the Nile, especially since this also has some nourishment of heat, from which the disposition toward better ripening can be helped. In other cases, bituminous spirits, sweetness, sulfur, copperas, lead, etc., are accustomed to produce that taste, though I do not know if they are in the Nile.

As for its "lightness," I do not know if it should be brought back to the scale <note>measured by weight</note>, or to a <gloss>natural affinity</gloss> <note>original Greek: "συμπάθειαν"</note> in the diet. I see you prefer the latter, since you say it is not heavy on the hypochondria <term>hypochondria (the upper abdomen, specifically under the ribs)</term>. But the opinion is not unfit for the scale either, if the water is thin and "airy." But then it must be set apart, and the pure liquid must be judged differently than the muddy river. Furthermore, lightness is caused both by conjoined heat and by a spirituous nature and expansiveness (or rarity); just as, conversely, the parent of heaviness is cold and earthy compaction or density.

# On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 3.

It presupposes that the same water is simultaneously thinned <note>attenuated: made less dense or more subtle</note> and that its purity has been separated out; unless you understand the spirits to be joined to the thick parts, whether dissolved or coagulated, though dry. What produces this in the Nile is not difficult to judge. One cause lies in its headlong motion and its cataracts, which even the poet Lucan recognizes. There are many arguments that motion thins a substance, and this is also established by a philosophical axiom: those things further from the center are rare <note>less dense</note> because they are agitated by motion. The second cause is heat, which thins the water by "digesting" it, separating heterogeneous parts, and resolving things that have been forced together. Since the heat burns most intensely in Egypt, and the subject or matter is airy in nature, the heat works upon it to create something like itself—just as fire, in its subject, strives toward a spiritual nature, which is rare and subtle. But I seem to recognize something else also contributing to this. Since we grant the Nile "nitrous juices" <note>nitrum: likely natron or sodium carbonate, common in the Nile region</note>, and since nitre is full of spirit, it is consistent that it deposits its own spirits into the water; even if these coagulate the water, they still retain the thinness of their own nature. Indeed, these spirits are the guardians of that thinness, preventing such vehement heat from dispersing it, which would otherwise happen. For although heat makes things rare, it does not always leave what it has thinned within the water; instead, it dissipates what has been reduced to spirit, provided there is a free path for it to breathe out. Furthermore, the external action of the sun can be aided by the internal operation of the joined juices and spirits. Something must be attributed to the "thirsty" sands, and something to the surrounding air; much is owed to its primordial nature, whether it arises from subtle vapors, falls from an eternal spring, or is the sea-water passed through the narrow pores of the earth by **distribution** <note>original Greek: ἀναδόσει (anadosei); refers to the way nutrients or fluids are distributed through a system</note>. Perhaps even the inhabitants of the Nile and the things growing in it supply something. But I leave these for you to judge more fully, as I do the opinions of the astrologers, regarding whether some fortunate celestial constitution wishes the Nile to be so adorned above all others.

<margin>Easy distribution of the Nile.</margin>
The easy **distribution** <note>original Greek: ἀναδόσει (anadosei)</note> through the veins and viscera is due to this thinness, just as we see thin wines experience the same. And although a **good temperament** <note>original Greek: εὐκρασία (eukrasia); a healthy balance of qualities</note> also plays a role, even this depends largely on that thinness. For thin things are more easily overcome and altered by heat than thick ones. Likewise, since natural distribution occurs not only by expulsion but also by "appetite" <note>the body's natural pull or attraction for nutrients</note>, it will be aided by the familiarity of the substance, which is pleasing to the attracting limbs. The Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> also **distinguishes** <note>original Greek: διορίζει (diorizei)</note> in this water a nature greater than in others, one that rivals the nature of air.

<margin>Maturity of the Nile.</margin>
Furthermore, no one will deny that the water is thoroughly "cooked" and mature, since it is carried through such great heat, does not resist the cause acting upon it, and offers itself entirely across vast plains without great depth—indeed, it even exchanges its upper and lower parts so frequently with such a great flow. Some will wish to claim that it is not only the airy and celestial heat (which, according to Seneca, is most abundant around the Nile) that achieves this, but also the heat of the sands through which it glides—though this is in vain unless a subterranean fuel is granted. For how could the sun reach covered waters? The banks can alter the nearby water, but I do not know if its progress reaches the middle of the channel. If it is increased by warm rains and headlong motion from the mountains, it becomes warm just as it becomes rare. For things that are thinned and made rare become more "skillful" <note>active or potent</note>; this is the greatest protection for "coction" <note>the process of ripening or "cooking" by heat to achieve maturity</note>. To me, however, internal heat also appeals, which you might call "congenic" <note>born together</note> by virtue of the mixture. And perhaps the crocodiles feel this when lurking in the waters at night; although the fermentation of the mud around the bottom of the river and the hiding places of animals might cherish this heat, or even **antiperistasis** <note>the compression or intensification of a quality by its opposite, such as internal heat being trapped by external cold</note> might preserve and increase it, nevertheless mineral fuels are not lacking: nitrous, salty, and perhaps even bituminous and sulfurous mud. Baccius <note>Andrea Bacci, a famous 16th-century writer on baths and waters</note> speaks to this opinion, saying that certain minerals mixed with the waters perform the same thing from within that the sun does from without. Certainly, we correct "crudities" <note>undigested or raw humors</note> in this way, and even make certain medicines boil without actual fire, such as with balls of quicklime, camphor, saltpeter, sulfur, etc., and likewise with "strong waters" <note>acids</note> and the sharpest spirits.

<margin>Durability of Nile water.</margin>
The simplest things—the airy, the fiery, and those with the most solid composition—last a long time because they do not admit the violence of the surroundings; the same is true of salty and very cold things, which are discussed elsewhere. The water of the Nile, once strained and settled, is close to a simple spirit. For its duration is not to be ascribed to the substance being impure (except for an excess of nitre, etc.), since it putrefies according to Servius and teems with beasts. Distilled things, however, testify that simple spirits are longer-lasting. This happens most especially if they are airy and fiery, like oils, or sharp and salty, like the spirit of salt, nitre, vitriol, etc.

<margin>Oribasius says it does not rot in winter.</margin>
"Burning water" <note>aqua ardens: alcohol</note> of fiery thinness, being almost entirely spirit, remains stable for a very long time. Thus, several factors contribute to the uncorrupted integrity of the Nile. Others might look at the nature of the surrounding air. Since the air is plenty cold at night but boiling and glowing during the day, it will not easily allow the beginning of putrefaction to take hold. It would have to change into something lukewarm and misty for putrefaction to occur. But you shall see about this. Baccius, following Russo and Oribasius, and others deny that it rots, because it is in motion and does not become over-heated. The Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> is the authority that something putrefies when its innate heat is overcome by the heat of the surroundings and is drawn out together with the internal moisture, and the boundary of the mixture is dissipated. Let that reasoning of Baccius prevail, then, but it must be traced deeper. Thus motion prevents corruption; but then nothing remarkable is said, since the "potentiality of the matter" is not removed if it should come to rest. Perhaps the motion of the lakes is to be understood, such as that of the sea purging itself. Among mineral waters, those do not rot which are either coagulated and sharp spirits (like the Stygian waters) or abound in such things; but once the spirituous parts are removed, they are corrupted. The same is true of sharp and fiery juices.

### How it is fit for nutrition was explained in the section on healthfulness.

<margin>Moistening by the Nile.</margin>
It is no wonder that it moistens, on account of its abundance of thin wateriness. I call it "thin" because it rivals air, whose property is to moisten if left to itself. There is another kind of moistening in nutrition, in which bodies are rendered more moist and succulent, yet with a proper "temperament." Otherwise, its healthfulness would not be established; thus it is beneficial for "dry" diseases, such as consumption, wasting, atrophy, emaciation, fevers, etc., and it resists parched air. But we must see that the "nitrousness" does not cause us a dispute; for nitre dries, digests, cuts, and thins. There will also be something in its fecundity; if this is attacked by dryness and a lack of nourishment and good blood, it will be helped by a moistening drink; but if it suffers from a superfluity of humors, the cause will labor: it will be **the medicine itself** <note>original Greek: αὐτὸ φάρμακον (auto pharmakon)</note>. In the diversity of the parts which are separated in the belly, as if in a chemist’s still, this part performs one task and that part another with moderation, so that one does not hinder the other. Thus one thing will happen **by its own nature** <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἀυτὸ (kat' auto)</note>, and another **by coincidence** <note>original Greek: κατὰ συμβεβηκός (kata symbebekos)</note>.

<margin>Fattening by the Nile.</margin>
Fattening follows moistening, and those things which are fatter in the animal kingdom are more moist, though not with a watery moisture. But whether this is the case with the Nile water, I doubt. Historians testify that in and around the Nile there is nitrous mud, which they once used for dropsy and those with spleen diseases, whom Galen says he saw cured in that manner.

### Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book VI

...seen around Alexandria; and Baccius <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), a famous Italian physician and authority on thermal waters</note> says that this quality is most suited to the land of Egypt because it is rendered entirely sandy, and therefore also salty and nitrous, by the annual floods of the Nile. This same very fine sand [see Suetonius in his life of Nero: *It happened by chance that during a public famine an Alexandrian ship was announced to have brought dust for the court wrestlers, etc.*] was brought to Rome from the Nile, according to Pliny, for the purpose of drying the skin of athletes after it had been anointed with oil. From this, a <term>cytoma</term> <note>a medicinal rubbing or application</note> was later made for <term>oedemata</term> <note>swelling caused by fluid retention</note>. The cleansing effect is due to the nitre <note>nitrum: in this context, natron (sodium carbonate), a mineral salt found in Egypt</note>. Baumgartner also says that he drank from a salty spring on the shore of the Nile between Alexandria and Rosetta. Therefore, there is no doubt that the waters of the Nile are nitrous, even if they taste sweet. Baccius reports the same thing about a certain cave in Puteoli <note>modern Pozzuoli, Italy, known for volcanic activity</note>, whose waters are sweet in flavor, clear, and odorless, but are nitrous and cold in their effects. It is certain that a moderate amount of salt and nitre makes the land fertile, and not only makes pastures lush, but also increases the fatness of beasts and men. For Baccius writes of that same spring that it fattens and fills out the body, and benefits all the internal organs. He attributes a similar power to the <term>Iuncaria</term> <note>likely a specific spring named for its reeds</note>, which is also nitrous, and to certain spring waters; the former also increases sexual desire, while the latter provides an abundance of milk and also acts as a cleanser. For nitrous substances powerfully expel phlegm, viscosity, and undigested matter from the passages everywhere. Thus, when the imbalances are corrected and impediments removed, they strengthen nature—a fact recognized by Avicenna <note>a famous Persian polymath and physician</note>, who asserted that these same waters bring strength to the stomach. Jordanus, in his book on the waters of Moravia, says that horses grow fat on nitrous waters, and that Brodensel reports that the clear and acidic springs, which cattle and men drink greedily, abound with nitre. 

It follows from this that the Nile of Egypt does not make things fat simply by moistening them, but by an accidental property: its cleansing nitrousness. By this, the natural faculties for nourishing, growing, and generating are simultaneously strengthened, so that afterwards they may better benefit both from the sweet part of the water and from other consumed foods. If we consider the generation of fat, we will understand that it requires "airy food," well-tempered and suited for producing the best blood. An abundance of this is easily set aside and remains stable where the heat of fire does not oppose it, and where the body parts are not cachectic <note>wasting away</note> or suffering from <term>cacochymia</term> <note>an imbalance of the bodily fluids or "humors"</note>. Nitre, however, aids digestion, strengthens the power of heat, and abolishes bad humors; thus, it prepares the "food" so it can be properly digested, converted, and used for nourishment. Therefore, much help is owed to it for this purpose.

<margin>Fertility of the Nile.</margin>
The same logic applies to fertility. It is well known that salt contributes to generation—not only from the abundance of mice in manure heaps, in salt mines, and on the banks of the Nile, but it is also a common belief. Thus, they provide salt to cattle, not only so that the meat becomes tastier and healthier, but also so that they grow fat and, in due time, produce numerous offspring. In Egypt, there are "twice-bearing" sheep [Trogus is the authority that in Egypt seven offspring are born from the womb at once. Elsewhere, this was once considered a portent. The three Horatii brothers testify to triplets being born.], and the earth itself also brings forth crops twice a year, which Seneca attributed to the Nile. Certainly, one seems to depend on the other: where there is a luxury of the best nourishment, there is also a copious amount of spirit and seed for generating; for this reason, the "deceptive" fat ones become fertile. Agricola wrote that the womb is made fertile by nitre, and Baccius assigns the same to the Iuncaria and the Cave in Puteoli. In the Volaterran territory, there is a nitrous spring that, by cleansing the viscosity of the womb, makes sterile women fertile. However, we experience that the fatter someone is, the less suited they are for generating; fat bodies are seen as effeminate, and either they do not produce offspring, or they produce weak, female offspring; thus, they are judged to be "cold." It is easy to respond that "cacochymic" fat (from bad humors) is an impediment to conception and the generative power, but not "pure" fat, which exists with <term>eukrasia</term> <note>a healthy, well-balanced temperament</note>. Furthermore, this fat does not sin by excess, suffocating the spirit and blocking the passages, but stays within these limits. The Egyptians live mostly on fruits. They are therefore prone to bad humors. Nitrous drink comes to the rescue, establishing a balance and a lushness of nourishment. From this comes <term>eutokia</term> <note>easy or successful childbirth</note>, and the fat does not hinder generation in those who are otherwise disposed to it. Moreover, the remarkable lake mentioned by Agricola belongs here, through which these effects of Nitre are further explained:

> *Seneca did not explain,* he says, *what the tempering of the Nile might be, because of which its water, when drunk, relaxes the womb of certain women closed by long sterility, leading to conception; nor did Pliny explain why it makes women so fertile that four, five, six, or seven offspring are born from one womb at once. But even if the Egyptians did not pour it into nitre-beds to make nitre from it, and even if Theophrastus did not write that it has a nitrous mixture, it would still be clear from this very effect that it is so. For nitrous things make the womb fit for conceiving. Since, when filtered, it provides a daily and healthy drink for the Egyptians, we understand well enough that it is moderately mixed with nitre.*

Behold how much trust he places in nitre! Furthermore, he adds the thought of whether those things written about fatness and fertility might only pertain to females and not to males. For fat males do not generate, but a fleshy woman who has found a thin man—otherwise not sluggish in the "service of Venus" nor inept—can conceive, unless some other cause of bad humors stands in the way, which nitre nevertheless grinds down. 

<margin>The Nile as an "ascender" <note>anagogos: referring to the rising of vapors</note></margin>
Ptolemy certainly sent Nile water to his daughter, not to his son-in-law.

<margin>Pliny indeed wrote this: who nevertheless in Book 21, Chapter 7, states that fragrant flowers grow in Egypt because of the misty and dewy air from the Nile river.</margin>
The claim that the Nile does not "breathe out" <note>evaporate</note> will be accepted with great faith, I believe. I think this is a fable, just as what they write about the lack of rain—either it is said because of its rarity, or just as the ancients called the air "empty" and "non-existent" because it was not subject to sight, so they deny the Nile breathes out because it lacks conspicuous clouds. In the meantime, however, because of the heat of the air and the thinness of both the water and the spirits, the behaviors and vapors are not seen—just as our breath is seen in summer hours, but in steam-rooms it is perceived as invisible until thickened by a damp cold. But if someone plainly denies it breathes out, he makes it eternal and will be ignorant of the pleasant breezes on the Nile and the winds; nor will he know that nitre is formed on the shore of the Nile by the sun absorbing the moisture and resolving it into the air. This is perhaps the situation with the rain: that it does not happen from local clouds, and the Nile does not evaporate conspicuously, but it *does* breathe out, though the spirit cannot be forced by the cold of the place to turn into clouds; yet nothing prevents dews from existing there. If it does happen, it will be due to external factors.

<margin>The Nile as a diuretic.</margin>
Furthermore, it is obvious that the water of the Nile is a diuretic and a laxative for the belly if it is nitrous—although it is not necessary that this happens "electively," as they say. Rather, if anything is stuck in the passages, it cuts into and cleanses it; thus, it does not "purge" in the strict sense, but only makes the bowels slippery, unless the bitterness and a larger substance of the nitre itself is drunk. 

<margin>A passage of Hippocrates against metallic waters.</margin>
Even for our Philosopher, bitter things act as purges. I do not need to bring forward examples of purging nitre from the histories of waters; I only ask you to explain one paradox from Hippocrates to me. He says: *Warm waters, or where iron, or copper, or silver, or gold, or sulfur, or bitumen, or alum, or nitre is born...*

### On the Evaluation of Mineral Waters, Part 3

...all [these waters] are hard and inflammatory, and are passed with difficulty as urine, and are detrimental to the evacuation of the bowels. Here, the dictates of medicine seem to be denied, yet it is a matter of common experience. I cannot resolve this myself, unless perhaps by *Alexander’s* sword <note>original: "Alexandri gladio"; a reference to "cutting the Gordian Knot"—solving a complex problem by a single bold stroke</note>. Or should a distinction be made regarding a mineral vein that is hostile to human nature, in which there is not only nitre <note>natron/sodium carbonate</note>, but other substances as well? For we know that *thermal springs* usually carry more than one mineral. If the vein is sulfurous or bituminous, and at the same time nitrous or lime-heavy, the water will turn out hard, inflammatory, and difficult.

The reason is now clear why it does not allow for putrefaction in the body: namely, because it contains the spirits of salt and nitre, or a refined juice—specifically that part which is drinkable, that is, the filtered portion. But more on these matters in the section on healthfulness.

<margin>The Nile does not boil.</margin>
Why it does not boil even though it flows through intense heat, although it possesses a certain lukewarmness, is easily understood from the Nitre, which, when mixed into the waters, deposits cold spirits into them. This was debated in the section on the coldness of mineral waters.

<margin>The Palm of the Nile.</margin>
Thus far concerning the nature of the *Nile*. However, as for the fact that the "palm" <note>the prize or preeminence</note> is awarded to it for such gifts, we must see whether this is not too unusual, and a matter of affection rather than true judgment. The entire healthfulness of *Egypt* is not owed to it, even though *Timaeus* calls it <term>εὐτυχῆ</term> <note>original: "eutychē"; fortunate or prosperous</note> on that account. *Herodotus* assigned this to the air; yet air is not lacking in other places, just as *Horace* wrote of *Baiae* <note>a Roman resort town</note> that no place in the world outshines it. In *Thessaly*, *Ethiopia*, among the *Macrobians* <note>a legendary people of long life</note>, and elsewhere, the sky is narrated to be equally or even more mild. *Virgil* glories in *Italy*, and *Pliny* prefers it to all lands. In second place is *India*, unless that be a fable; then maritime *Spain*. In the former, the *Tiber* is turbid in appearance, but it clears through rest without leaving silt behind, and lasts for a long time without putrefying because it receives medicinal springs: it does not seem to yield to the *Nile*, though it does not overflow, *Italy* being fertile enough on its own. Likewise, *Pliny* grants the "palm of healthfulness" to the water of *Mattia*, or *Aufesa*, brought to *Rome* from the *Peligni*. He also praises the *Virgo* <note>Aqua Virgo, a Roman aqueduct</note>, etc. In the thinness of its waters, the Nile yields to the *Borysthenes* <note>the Dnieper River</note>, which *Pliny* says is the thinnest of all rivers, so much so that it even floats upon the *Hypanis*. The water of the *Pyrene* spring of *Corinth* is said to be the lightest of all waters in *Greece*, and they attribute this also to the *Eulaeus*. In the pleasure of drinking, it is surpassed by a water in *Spain* at *Accis*, near the town of *Almagia*, which is so sweet that people compete to drink it day and night, according to *Baccius*. The Persian *Choaspes*, on the authority of *Pliny* and *Herodotus*, was sought after by kings. Concerning it, *Athenaeus* says: <margin>Pliny book 31 ch. 3</margin> <term>The King of the Persians, as Idon says in the first book of the *Agesilaus*, drinks from the Choaspes which flows all around Susa. Only of this does the King drink; and when he goes away, many four-wheeled wagons follow him with this water in silver vessels. Ctesias the Cnidian relates how this royal water is boiled, and how it is carried for the King in silver vessels, saying it is the lightest and sweetest.</term> <note>Translated from the Greek passage provided in the text</note>

These are the words of *Athenaeus*, where either its sweetness and lightness are praised above all, or it is said to be not inferior to the *Nile*. It should be noted, however, that this water is boiled because it is carried through more cultivated and less hot places than the *Nile*. The *Eulaeus* of Media also holds such praise. Among the *Macrobians*, they report there was a spring of oil with a violet scent, almost the sole cause of their longevity and good health, which was so divisible and weak that nothing could float in it, as if it were the "water of eternity." That the Nile increases the land by silting is a trait common to many. For so too the *Niger* of Mauritania, and the *Ganges* of India, and others enrich their own regions. What they report concerning fertility, *Seneca* almost mocks, holding it among the rashly publicized myths. That a water is sweet and nitrous at the same time is true of Lake *Ascanius*, certain springs around *Chalcis*, and some at *Puteoli*, in which the surface is sweet and the bottom is nitrous; *Athenaeus*, quoting *Aristobulus*, assigns this also to the *Achillean* spring in *Miletus*, as <term>the stream is very sweet at the top, but the lower part is salty</term>. *Baccius* relates that on the road to *Toledo* in *Spain* there is a spring in white earth, whose upper water is sweet to the taste, but if one lowers a pipe to the bottom of the well, the water drawn out is of the sharpest acidity—due to the meeting, as he thinks, of sweet and sharp channels from different directions. As for the claim that it does not "breathe" <note>emit vapors</note> or emit mists, *Agricola* <note>Georgius Agricola, 1494–1555, a pioneer of mineralogy</note> does not entirely agree when he says: *If that is true, it does not seem to come from the temperament of the waters, but from another cause. For those parts of rivers where there are no veins or fibers in the beds cannot breathe out any air. Therefore Egypt, which consisted of the silt brought in by the Nile, formerly did not feel earthquakes, but later it did. And from that time it is likely that the Nile, like other rivers, breathes out air.* And *Pliny* overturns this [claim of no vapors]. Therefore, this glory [of the Nile] falls away, although it was determined otherwise above, as *Agricola* wished. But even if that is granted, nevertheless the *Borysthenes*, according to *Pliny*, snatches that praise away from it, <margin>Pliny book 31 ch. 2</margin> as does the *Anaurus* of Thessaly, which earned its name from this very argument <note>Anaurus means "without breeze" or "without air" in Greek</note>. Whether it is incorruptible <note>does not spoil</note>, I do not know if I believe, although if it were so, there is a cause for it. But nevertheless, it is far surpassed by the water at the town of *Aquarium* between *Modena* and *Reggio Emilia*, which *Fallopius* <note>Gabriele Falloppio (1523–1562), famous anatomist</note> drank after it had been kept entirely pure for two hundred and twenty years. But perhaps there are not as many good qualities in other waters combined as there are in the *Nile*, though for the health of their inhabitants, nothing is lacking. Truly, these things might suffice for a Philosopher, who mostly conducts his contemplations for the pleasure of it, but not so for a physician, who additionally hunts for utility in practice. If we had the *Nile* at hand, we would delight our sick with its use, and we could even cast certain sterile women into the hope of offspring. However, we should not expect "water-drinkers" <note>original: "hydropotas"</note>. Our people love good wine more than a thousand *Niles*, and if you wished to persuade them to mix it with their cups, you would not succeed: they delight in neat wine. Yet those who lack such help are not to be abandoned. Therefore, if I chat with you about imitating the *Nilotic* water, though others may call it a vain question, nevertheless by your fairness you will bear with me.

<margin>Healthy water in the style of the Nile</margin>
It is agreed that water is required at the beginning. For it is the matter and subject of mineral virtue for drinking in this category. It is either thick and mixed with filings, mud, viscous juices, etc., or it is thin and pure of itself, yet "raw" <note>unrefined</note>, or otherwise different in virtue from the *Nilotic* water, even though it may be mature and elaborated enough in terms of thinness and lightness: or it comes closest to it, even with medicinal power from the minerals by which it has been affected. Most command that water which is thick and raw, or which is infused with foreign juices, or mixed with lime and similar things, be boiled. For as *Avicenna* says, *If salts are heated to the point of boiling and afterwards cooled, they acquire thinness*; which *Alexander* confirms when he says: *Water once heated does not return to its previous state when cooled, but remains thinner.* [Rural writers test mixtures by sprinkling water on a wiped bronze basin. If it is stained, it is infected; if not, it is approved. They also boil it in a bronze pot. Silt at the bottom proves its badness. *Diophanes* throws laurel leaves into healthy cistern waters: he lets silty water settle in earthenware vessels. The use of bitter almonds is well known. Concerning starch, dill flour, and distillation by which turbid waters are corrected, see *Bolcasis* <note>Albucasis/al-Zahrawi, the surgeon</note> in treatise 11. Others boil unhealthy waters down to a tenth and let them cool again. But you should trust your own experiments. The water of the *Nile* is boiled more easily than others. *Strabo* book 15.] If there are dissimilar parts mixed with it, these [settle] during cooling in rest...

It concludes with practical medical advice on how to "imitate" the Nile's purity through methods like boiling, filtering, and additives.</summary>

# Commentaries on Alchemy, Part II, Book VI

<margin>Pliny, Book 24, Chapter 1 & Book 31, Chapter 3.</margin>
...they are separated, and that which is heavy and earthy is deposited, while that which is light remains on the surface. In this way, they boil even those waters called "hard" by *Hippocrates* <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note>: thus they treat putrid and dreg-filled waters. Some, however, add **polenta** <note>A thick barley meal or groats.</note>. *Nitrous and bitter things*, says Pliny, *are mitigated by the addition of polenta, so that they may be drunk within two hours*. Diocles boiled water down to one-third, throwing in egg whites and half a *sextarius* <note>A Roman measure, roughly a pint.</note> of clay mixed in jars; once this was done, he immediately poured it off. Others simply pour muddy waters from one vessel to another. Aristotle boils seawater, or even draws out its sweetness by transferring it through the sides of a wax vessel; Solinus filters it. Others dig pits near lakes, although in these, sometimes the water comes out sweet at first, then metallic or salty. Some strain it through double or triple vessels full of sand; there are those content with letting a sediment form, sometimes adding bitter almonds. But if we wish to imitate the condition of the Nile, we must find a certain tempering of **nitrous mud** <note>original: "luti nitrosi"; likely referring to natron, a natural sodium carbonate found in Egypt.</note> with water that has been boiled and passed through sand. Therefore, I would place clay or gravel, or hot or boiling sand, or bricks, or broken flints into perforated vessels, and arrange them so that the water flows from one to another in the proper sequence. I would initially pour in pure water to wash away any foreign qualities. Afterward, I would prepare it according to the mind's command in the likeness of the Nile, until I achieved the desired result or came close to it.

<margin>Nitre is made in Egypt by letting the Nile into the nitre-beds, which, as it recedes, dry out, soaked in the juice of nitre for 40 days, etc., says Pliny. The same is reported by Pliny in Book 37, Chapter 10.</margin>
But if thin, boiled, and pure water were at hand, I would not heat the sand or stones; instead, I would at least filter water tinged with nitre, or with nitrous juice or spirit. For water that is naturally thin and boiled loses its airy portions and retains its earthy ones if boiled further. If it contained anything metallic, which would be heavy, I would filter it more often, even changing the gravel. Lest anyone say we lack nitre, I would point out that the Nile has not ceased to be the Nile. From there, it can be obtained and transported more easily than water. If it is a burden to seek it from there, there is the lake of *Cejcensis* in Moravia, which *Iordanus* writes is so fertile with nitre that two ounces come out of every six pounds. If even this is not pleasing, common **halinitre** <note>Rock-salt or a crude form of saltpeter.</note> may be separated from its dregs through solution and coagulation. For when salt is poured in and settles in the vessel, the nitre alone is drawn off. There were also many nitre-beds scattered throughout Italy, but *Baccius* reports they are now lacking "body." If we also think that **sal ammoniac** <note>Ammonium chloride.</note> contributes anything to the Nile mixture, let us substitute **rock salt** <note>original: "salem gemmeum"</note> or native salt sought from Cyrenaica. Indeed, industry even surpasses nature. Since natural waters can be compensated for by minerals prepared through the **Chymical art** <note>The early science of chemistry and alchemy.</note>, we shall be even more fortunate than those living by the Nile in treating every ailment. There is also another way, more ingenious indeed, but more laborious and requiring greater expense. For whatever waters are muddy and carry thick dregs are sufficiently thinned by appropriate distillation, provided that the thick parts are not raised by a fire greater than necessary. It will perhaps be enough to draw off a third or half, depending on the nature of the water; but if mineral spirits are present and they are harmful, I would think they should be omitted; if they are harmless and suited to the present use, they should not be rejected.

To water purified in this way, one must mix salts of nitre, or acidic or sweet **vitriols** <note>Sulfate minerals; "acidic" refers to sulfuric acid, "sweet" to more neutralized forms.</note>, just as sulfurous and other salts can be used for convenience, but in a specific quantity that corresponds to the goal. Above all, I would praise the **spirit of vitriol** <note>Sulfuric acid.</note> infused with what they call **Rock Candy** <note>original: "saccharo quod Candi vocant"</note>. For its skillful tempering has been found to be healthier than others in certain diseases. It has the power to cut through viscous humors, to open obstructions, to cleanse and dissolve, and to purge both the bowels and the bladder; for which reason it is beneficial for those suffering from epilepsy, arthritis, colic, stones, and so on.

<margin>Pliny says the ash of **tartar** <note>The potassium bitartrate crust from wine barrels.</note> has the nature and powers of nitre. It will therefore imitate the Nile in this regard.</margin>
Thus, such a mixture will more closely approach the gifts of the Nile; and with moderate use or the proper proportion, it could even fatten the body and make fertile those wombs made sterile by **bad humors** <note>term: "cacochymia" - an imbalance of the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile).</note>, just as the acidic waters of **Göppingen** <note>Mineral springs in Germany.</note> and many other vitriolated waters likewise promise. But if these actions become potions, or are used too frequently, they even thin the body through excessive dispersion and prevent the increase of fat, which is also known regarding salt. Such a mixture thins the waters more and "cooks" them. Some soak **tartar**, and for those who are melancholic or suffering from quartan fevers (for whom the spirit of vitriol is also a help), and likewise for those with fevers, they prepare a pleasant drink: as if washed tartar were infused into water filtered through hot bricks—or in which these bricks had been extinguished—and then passed through sand and strained again. But in these matters, there is immense variation that cannot be described in writing. Some prefer water treated with steel, or with gold, and so on.

However, I do not deny that this imitation can be challenged: for what is so solid that it cannot be undermined by clever arguments, at least for some? They will deny that the sweetness of the Nile can be found in the imitation. We are not yet certain what that "sweetness" designates: if it refers to the usual taste of simple water, which might be called sweet compared to mineral water, it is easy to obtain this from an abundance of boiled and processed water. If "sweet" means pleasant and fit for nourishment—just as bitter willows are pleasant to goats—and perhaps for that reason the Nile is sweet due to a fitting mixture of saltiness: here too we shall not be slow. If we require a milky and honeyed sweetness, there is the spirit of sugar, there is its extract, there is honey; and among minerals, there is the "sweetness of **Saturn**" <note>Lead acetate, which has a sweet taste but is highly toxic.</note>, the "sweetness of vitriol," and so on; let us add these. But we look rather toward healing, where not infrequently acidity and tempered saltiness are more pleasing than sweetness. Regarding the matter of fattening, a dispute can also be raised, but one that is solved both by ingenious mixing and skillful use. Neither saltiness nor acidity stands in the way of fatness. Those participating in something metallic dry out the body rather than moisten and fatten it. Indeed, I say they dry it if the metallic nature dominates and is not suppressed. If it is moderate and tempered by the goodness of the water, the opposite happens: very fat beasts live in the sea, and the sea is very salty. We also eat almost nothing without salt, yet we do not all grow thin. Those from the **Schwalbach** <note>A German spa town famous for its iron-rich springs.</note> wine-fountain, as well as their cattle, become robust. The same was said above regarding nitrous waters. From walls grow **Aizoum** and **Telephium**, which are fat herbs, like **alkali** <note>Saltwort or glasswort.</note> on the shores. *Mesue* <note>An influential medieval Arabic physician.</note> relates that **Sarcocolla** <note>A medicinal tree resin.</note> is hot and dry, and purges phlegmatic superfluities; he states nonetheless that by its use it fattens the body and increases seed.

<margin>A passage from Hippocrates on preparing water. 6. Epidemics 4.9.</margin>
To finally conclude this exercise, I will add what I think about the passage from Hippocrates, which you proposed to be explained in your letter. It concerns the preparation of water for proper use, and has these words:
> "*Water* (says that old man) *is best when it is least affected by the sun, is not flatulent, and has a cover.* <note>original Greek: "Ὕδωρ ἄριστον τὸ μὲν ὡς ἥχιστα τὸν ἥλιον, τὸ δὲ μὴ εἶναι φυσητὸν, καὶ ἐπίθεμα ἔχειν."</note>
Drawn water is at its best only if it receives or admits air, provided it is not in a vessel filled to the very top, and it should be in a covered earthenware jar. You write that an explanation of this is given by **Caesalpinus** <note>Andrea Cesalpino, a 16th-century Italian physician and botanist.</note> as follows, when he says: *Although Galen explains this passage in various ways...*

<summary>This page discusses various alchemical and traditional methods for purifying hard water to imitate the medicinal and nourishing qualities of the Nile. It explores the use of nitre, vitriol, and tartar to treat ailments like gout and stones, while debating whether mineral waters lead to bodily thinning or fattening.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on water purification, specifically examining how ancient medical theories from Hippocrates and Galen align with contemporary alchemical practices like "circulation" and "distillation" to improve water quality.</meta>

<page-num>191</page-num>

-># On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 2<-

I think this should be understood in the following way: that while the water is boiled, it should admit air not in an open vessel, but one that is closed and half-full. For the trapped air causes the vapors raised during boiling to be taken up. Furthermore, a lid is added so that the vapors are not given an exit, but rather descend down the sides of the vessel once cooled. In this way, a "circle" is formed by the material continuously ascending as vapor and descending as water. If the vapors were able to fly out, two disadvantages would follow: first, the material being boiled would largely vanish; second, only that which is thicker and heavier would remain, as **Aristotle** notes in the second book of his *Meteorology* regarding the saltiness of the sea. For that which is drawn upward by heat is the most subtle and sweet, while what remains is thicker and salty. You have these points under the name of **Caesalpino** <note>Andrea Cesalpino (1524–1603), an Italian physician and botanist who blended Aristotelian philosophy with early chemistry.</note>, for I do not have his commentary at hand.

If I follow him correctly, he believes **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine," whose works often discussed the health impacts of different types of water.</note> speaks universally about how any water should be prepared in one specific way according to the rules of the chemical art, which they call **circulation**. In this process, a vessel filled to a third or a half, covered and sealed so it cannot breathe, is moved toward heat. Then, the material is thinned and reduced into a spirit; by a reciprocal motion, it is carried back and forth, thinned a thousand times, and again coagulated into water, until it is brought to the "nobility" we seek. If an escape were granted, the most noble spirits would withdraw, leaving behind a thick phlegm <note>In early chemistry, "phlegm" referred to the tasteless, watery, or watery-residue part of a substance after distillation.</note>. However, when Hippocrates says that air must be received, he means the empty space between the water and the lid. This opinion would not be absurd if the nature of all waters were equal, and if it were a single rule that the thicker part subsisting at the bottom of the vessel should be discarded after the thinner part is poured off. But if that thicker part remains, since its nature is unfit to receive spiritual excellence, the spirits would be polluted again, and the labor would be instituted in vain. It is well known, however, that authors in such a setup—even when boiling in the common way—do not omit separation, whether by settling and pouring off, or by straining through a cloth <note>original: "colaturam fabularem"</note>, unless the water is at least so thick that it requires "discussion" <note>A medical/chemical term for breaking down or dispersing thick humors or fluids.</note>, like a "hanging" wine; though I do not know if the goal of the art is sufficiently met in that way.

**Galen** more correctly writes that a <term>division</term> <note>original Greek: "diairesis," meaning a logical distinction or classification.</note> was made in that sentence; and indeed, the passage can be understood as Hippocrates proposing two kinds of waters: one carrying harmful spirits and fumes opposed to a healthy constitution, and another that is merely "crude" <note>In this context, "crude" water refers to water that is "unripe" or full of raw minerals that need "cooking" or digestion to be safe.</note>. Or, he may be speaking of cooling boiled water for the benefit of the sick—sometimes in an open vessel, sometimes in a closed one. This is how **Nero** used to boil his waters, burying the covered vessel in snow; or the way the Egyptians exposed heated waters to the night air and stored them in leaves before sunrise, as **Langius** says, citing **Galen** and **Athenaeus**.

<margin>Book 1, Letter 31.</margin>
If the first method is considered—for waters where, along with crudity, there is a certain malignancy residing in the more "spirited" part—they must be boiled in an open vessel and then left until they cool. Once a sediment has formed, the drinkable part should be poured off and used; this is established for the health of both the healthy and the sick. Such waters are frequent in many places, especially in metallic regions, and unless they are prepared this way, they are better not drunk. However, for those waters that have no harmful ferocity but are merely crude, muddy, or "marbly" <note>Likely referring to hard water that leaves mineral deposits.</note> mixed with thick juices, etc.—or others that are thin and airy so that the best part would easily vanish—these should be boiled under a lid in a **double-boiler** <note>original: "diplomate," a vessel within a vessel, like a bain-marie.</note> or exposed to the burning sun. For when they have been "worked" by the heat, a separation of the thin parts from the thick ones occurs through rest; they are easily separated after cooling, which is also expected in a closed vessel. For if you open it immediately after boiling, the thin part would nonetheless evaporate. The second method, which Galen rather embraces, follows the first. For this reason, some waters are to be cooled in a covered vessel lest the subtle parts perish; but others in an open one, lest the noxious and poisonous breaths remain together. 

**Caesalpino** rightly proposes "circulation" for the time when the thin parts have been segregated from the thick, and the harmful spirits have departed. For in this way, any essence is made more excellent, and circulation was invented to "exalt" <note>To refine or increase the potency of a substance.</note> it. It would not be difficult to draw Hippocrates to this view, since he says <term>to spout up</term> <note>original Greek: "anablyzein," describing the bubbling or rising of the water.</note>, but the text would have to be corrected and written as "the part of the..." etc. Some condemn boiling using Caesalpino’s second argument, approving only the "Virgilian washing" through gravel. But **Avicenna** <note>The Persian polymath and physician (980–1037).</note> resists them in Book 1. So does **Alexander**, and many others, along with the example of the kings of Persia and the Egyptians, who ordered even thin waters to be boiled and worked under the burning sun.

If I may joke with you: behold Hippocrates transformed into one whom some moderns call a **Spagyrist** <note>A term coined by Paracelsus for a chemist who uses the techniques of separation and recombination.</note>, and the ancients an **Alchemist**. If water is to be boiled, use **distillation** instead of simple boiling, either with separate vessels or joined ones. Distillation with separate vessels is done in a pot, a kettle, or a **cucurbit** <note>A gourd-shaped chemical flask.</note>, over which an **alembic** <note>The "cap" or head of a distilling apparatus.</note> hangs with air admitted at intervals; or wool, or bread, or fleece, which may coagulate the captured vapors while the bad spirits depart into the open air—this they call distillation by the "bell" or "dish." Or, if the water has nothing malignant and is thin but mixed with thick or crude parts, etc., join the alembic to the cucurbit and distill it "closed," or **sublime** <note>To convert a substance into vapor and back into solid/liquid to purify it.</note> it. Then the vessel should be filled only to the middle and placed in the slow digestion of a "bath" <note>A water bath or bain-marie.</note>, so that the crudity may be corrected and the thickness cut away, while the light and thin portions are gradually transferred, leaving the stubborn parts at the bottom. This interpretation through sublimation or distillation is not absurd, nor was it perhaps unknown to Hippocrates, since Avicenna orders waters to be distilled or sublimed, and **Dioscorides** mentions vapors captured by fleece. But enough on this for now. If you think I have erred in anything, friend, advise your friend of it; you will find him compliant. Farewell.

### THE QUESTION OF THE NILE

**Pliny** writes that the river **Nigrin** <note>Possibly the Niger River or a legendary African river mentioned in classical geography.</note> increases and decreases in the same manner and at the same time as the **Nile**. [Consult **Scaliger** on *Subtlety*, Exercise 181; also Exercise 37; Pliny Book 5, Chapter 9; **Seneca**, *Natural Questions*, Book 4, Chapter 16, etc., where he says it is not increased by waters from above, but returned from the depths. And indeed, on the authority of **Theophrastus**, it once brought down seawater. However, **Lopesius** and American history confirm the cause to be perennial rains throughout the winter of those places.] The same applies to the **Inopus** spring at Delos, which changes along with the Nile. It is also clear from **Wernher's** history that Lake **Zircknitium** <note>Lake Cerknica in modern Slovenia, famous for being an intermittent lake that disappears and reappears.</note> in Carniola overflows in autumn and hides itself again in summer. Pliny reports that the mathematician **Timaeus** wrote that the Nile sinks into tunnels and is recalled at the solstice. The question is: is the cause not the same in both cases, such that it is not necessary to resort to the rains of Ethiopia for an explanation?

<summary>This page explores the alchemical purification of water through "circulation" and distillation, applying these concepts to the medical theories of Hippocrates and Galen, before questioning the hydrological causes of the Nile's seasonal flooding.</summary>
<keywords>water purification, alchemy, circulation, distillation, Hippocrates, Galen, Caesalpino, Nile river, Lake Cerknica, Spagyrist, Avicenna, hydrogeology</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes Part II of the alchemical commentaries, moving from the general discussion of mineral waters and distillation (on page 191) to a specific critique and methodology for the chemical analysis of human urine. The author bridges the gap between traditional Galenic medicine and the newer chemical (alchemical) practices of the late 16th century.</meta>

### CONCERNING CERTAIN MATTERS OF URINE.

**F**rivolous and empty is that distillation and judgment of urine which some hold in high admiration, following the judgment of a certain inept Paracelsist <note>A follower of Paracelsus (1493–1541), a physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine but was often criticized by traditionalists for his mystical theories.</note>. For although every single limb in the human body has its own excrement and can mix it into the urine, there is no reason why it should "return" to where it came from, let alone obey descriptions within a glass vessel and remain in the exact spot you have designated, and so forth. If urine maintains such a "familiarity" with its own limb, why was it expelled as if it were a foreign substance? Why did nature establish for itself <term>emunctories</term> <note>Organs or canals in the body that carry off waste, such as the kidneys or pores.</note> by which to separate what is troublesome? Nor can one argue for "urinal essences" that preserve an old relationship. Nature deposits nothing from its entire treasure house in such a way, nor will anyone find one so keen-eyed <note>original: "lynccum," a reference to the lynx, legendary for its piercing sight.</note> as to recognize that what came from the heart is the "essence of the heart." But let such foolish things be gone. It was a matter of chance if anything was divined from it—or rather, it was fraudulent—since whatever you might indicate, ignorant patients recognize it in themselves, and sometimes the truth was already evident through other signs.

True practitioners acknowledge no other resolution of urine, nor any other judgment, than that which has been set forth above, while preserving its unique properties. Therefore, if such a task is to be undertaken, and the entire disposition of the patient’s urine (or even that of a healthy person) is known as far as is currently possible, they first judge it whole as it flowed out, and afterwards as it has become cooled and settled. From urine alone, little is revealed about diseases of the brain, the lungs, "spiritual" poisons, and the like; and often, while other limbs are suffering—such as the eye, the ears, etc.—the instruments of digestion and the blood are doing well. Likewise, in fevers, the urine is sometimes healthy; and sometimes nature expels the causes of disease without a disease ever having formed; and sometimes, due to differences in digestion or various exercises, very different types of urine are produced. Thus, reddish, bilious urine is sometimes passed by a healthy person, while raw and white urine may be passed by a healthy person after a somewhat over-indulgent drink of unmixed wine. If it is judged alone, it is uncertain. If you ask for it frequently and emitted at different times, there is a fear that, in the meantime, a good opportunity for action may pass by.

Therefore, one must absolutely know the constitution of the person to whom it belongs if you wish to learn anything from it for the purpose of healing, and not merely to know the custom of nature. If what is necessary for acting well is already apparent, there is no urgent need for a chemical judgment. Sometimes, however, the mixtures and the nature of the juices existing in the body, as well as <term>dyscrasias</term> <note>An imbalance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed in ancient medicine to cause disease.</note>, are so hidden that it can scarcely be discerned what kind they are: what is in excess, what is causing the most affliction, whether the humor alone is at fault, or if there is also an "intemperance" of heat or cold, or if this alone is the cause of the suffering; what produces obstructions, and so on.

Therefore, we can also establish this operation: take the urine at its proper time, and first reduce it to its quantity and weight immediately while it is still naturally warm. Afterwards, allow for sediment and cooling through rest, at which time the signs that occur should be noted, and the whole body <gloss>of the liquid</gloss> weighed again, so that it may be clear what quantity of "spirits" was present—although this is usually detected by the space in the vessel rather than by a scale. For if the space occupied by the urine is no longer as great as before, a large departure of spirits has occurred (or a small one, depending on the difference in the interval). To also know what kind of spirit that is, immediately place an <term>alembic</term> <note>The cap or head of a distilling apparatus.</note> upon the urinal flask, and thus you will settle both matters in one operation. 

Afterwards, filter the thick parts through clean paper, and note again the nature of what remains. You will easily recognize fats, blood, sands, phlegm, pus, "bran-like" <note>original: "furfures," referring to scaly or dandruff-like particles in the urine.</note> or floury secretions, hair-like pieces, and the rest. If, however, you also strive to know the interior, depending on the quantity available, you shall examine it by fire or by the sun—by roasting, distilling, sublimating, burning, etc. You will discern what appears to the circumspect judgment of the senses, just as in minerals.

Let what passed through the paper settle again, and judge it by itself according to sensible differences. Then pour it into a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped chemical vessel used in distillation.</note> and distill it halfway or more. Evaluate the distillate by itself. Consider also what remains in the vessel—first while warm, then after letting it cool—and see whether any sediment, fat, cloud, or a hardened "crown" like a <term>tophus</term> <note>A "tophaceous" deposit refers to a stone-like or calcified crust, similar to what forms in the joints during gout.</note> forms in the vessel. Such a thing usually happens if corporeal juices are present. Pay attention to its nature and so forth. Then insert stalks or small sticks and keep them in a warm place so that salt may grow upon them. Once this is done, strain the remaining liquid again and see what adheres to the glass. Usually, either small sands or little crystals settle; sometimes also a certain stickiness. Once strained, boil the liquid in a new glass until it thickens, which you will see gradually coagulate, and afterwards you will explore its nature in various ways as described above.

From this, it is hardly possible that you will not grasp far more accurately than if you were merely to look at it. You will see here that we are not rarely deceived by "spiritual" tints, judging a urine to be bilious when it is not. You will notice an abundance of "false phlegm" or false urinals which you had not seen before, yet those are what produce diseases. There will also present itself more clearly a <term>tartareous</term> <note>Derived from "tartar," the hard crust in wine casks; in medicine, it refers to stony obstructions like kidney stones.</note> or stony secretion that produces stones, which had previously escaped the sight. Thus, sometimes a bitter salt will be found, which you might call nitrous or bilious; sometimes a diluted salt, which matches common and weak <term>vitriol</term> <note>A historical name for various sulfate minerals (e.g., iron or copper sulfate).</note>; sometimes a sub-acid salt from acidic phlegm or black bile, which you might call aluminous or vitriolated—the latter of which mostly corresponds to sharp black bile, the former to phlegm. A sharp, biting, burning salt is indicated as "arsenical" and is bilious.

In this way, you will easily reconcile the humors named by the Galenics <note>Followers of Galen (c. 129–216 AD), whose system of the four humors dominated medicine for over a millennium.</note> with mineral juices; nor will you err whether you judge it in this way or that. However, it is more correct to call those things which have their own names in minerals outside of man by their accustomed names, even though they are not of exactly the same species as those within man, so that the arts may be distinct in their method of discipline. If, however, you wish to compare one to the other, you will commit no absurdity if you say that the "aluminous" juice—which they call "glassy and acidic phlegm"—is of the nature of alum; or if you call that which sets the teeth on edge (being both acidic and sharp) "vitriolated"; and so on. For since the human body can suffer the same things, or the same things can happen in the human body as occur elsewhere outside—just as stones are produced in both, and in both there are flammable juices and sulfur that is foul and putrid, very much like dung—one should not be so angry if one is compared to the other.

->So much for urine.<-

->The End of Part II of the Alchemical Commentaries.<-
